title: A.2 Why Least Squares Is Maximum Likelihood
text: A.1 derived \(\hat\beta = (X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top y\) as the minimizer of RSS. This page derives the same formula as the maximum-likelihood estimate under Gaussian noise — the reason least squares is not just a geometric convenience but a statistical model, and the reason its failures (outliers, heteroscedasticity) are exactly the failures of the Gaussian assumption.
crumbs: A.2 Why Least Squares Is Maximum Likelihood

title: A.2 Why Least Squares Is Maximum Likelihood
text:
1. Basic Concept
The model. Assume the data-generating process is
\[y = X\beta + \varepsilon, \qquad \varepsilon \sim N(0, \sigma^2 I)\]
— the mean is linear in the features, and the noise is Gaussian, independent, and identically distributed. Then \(y \sim N(X\beta, \sigma^2 I)\), and the likelihood of the parameters given the data is the product of \(n\) Gaussian densities. The log-likelihood:
\[\ell(\beta, \sigma^2) = -\frac{n}{2}\log(2\pi) - \frac{n}{2}\log\sigma^2 - \frac{1}{2\sigma^2}(y - X\beta)^\top(y - X\beta)\]
The key observation: the only term involving \(\beta\) is the last one, and it is negative RSS. So maximizing the likelihood over \(\beta\) is exactly minimizing RSS — for any \(\sigma^2\):






The full MLE, including \(\sigma^2\):






The MLE of the noise variance is \(\hat\sigma^2 = \text{RSS}/n\) — the average squared residual. Note the divisor: \(n\), not \(n - p\). The MLE is biased (it ignores the \(p\) degrees of freedom spent fitting \(\beta\)); the unbiased estimator divides by \(n - p\) — the 2.4 correction, now derived rather than asserted.
The numerical check:

title: A.2 Why Least Squares Is Maximum Likelihood
text:
2. Concept Questions

The log-likelihood’s \(\beta\)-dependent term is \(-\text{RSS}/(2\sigma^2)\). Why does this mean the MLE of \(\beta\) doesn’t depend on \(\sigma^2\) — and what breaks if the noise is not i.i.d. (heteroscedastic)?
The MLE of \(\sigma^2\) divides by \(n\); the unbiased estimator divides by \(n-p\). Derive the bias: show \(\mathbb{E}[\text{RSS}] = (n-p)\sigma^2\) (hint: the residual is the projection of the noise onto the orthogonal complement of the column space, which has dimension \(n-p\)).
Least squares is the MLE under Gaussian noise. What is the MLE under Laplace (double-exponential) noise, and what does that imply about which estimator is robust to outliers?
The Gaussian assumption gives least squares; the sampling distribution of \(\hat\beta\) (its standard errors, 2.3) also comes from it. What exactly does the Gaussian assumption buy beyond the point estimate?
Why is “least squares = MLE” not a justification of least squares for causal questions — what does the likelihood say about the data-generating process, and what doesn’t it say?



Answers


Because \(\sigma^2\) enters only as a positive constant multiplier of RSS in the \(\beta\)-dependent term — the argmax over \(\beta\) is unchanged by any fixed \(\sigma^2\). With heteroscedastic noise (\(\text{Var}(\varepsilon_i) = \sigma_i^2\)), the likelihood weights each observation by \(1/\sigma_i^2\) — the MLE becomes weighted least squares (A.1 Q1), and unweighted OLS is no longer the MLE (still unbiased, but inefficient — not minimum-variance).
The residual \(r = (I - H)\varepsilon\) where \(H\) is the hat matrix; \((I-H)\) is a projection onto an \((n-p)\)-dimensional space, so \(\|r\|^2 = \varepsilon^\top(I-H)\varepsilon\) has expectation \(\sigma^2 \text{tr}(I-H) = \sigma^2(n-p)\). The fit “absorbs” \(p\) dimensions of the noise — the residuals are smaller than the noise by exactly the degrees of freedom spent.
Under Laplace noise the log-likelihood is \(-\sum |y_i - x_i^\top\beta|/\text{scale}\) — the MLE is least absolute deviations (LAD), which is robust to outliers (the absolute loss doesn’t square the big residuals). The correspondence is exact: Gaussian noise → squared loss → OLS; Laplace noise → absolute loss → LAD. The loss function is the noise model, read backwards.
The sampling distribution: under the Gaussian model, \(\hat\beta \sim N(\beta, \sigma^2(X^\top X)^{-1})\) — which is where the standard errors, \(t\)-tests, and confidence intervals of 2.3 come from. The point estimate needs only the mean structure; every uncertainty statement needs the distributional assumption. (And by the CLT, \(\hat\beta\) is approximately normal even under non-Gaussian noise — the intervals are more robust than the exact theory.)
The likelihood describes \(p(y \mid x, \beta)\) — the distribution of the data given the parameters. It says nothing about whether \(\beta\) represents a causal effect: that requires the exogeneity assumption \(\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon \mid x] = 0\) (2.10), which is a property of the data-generating process, not of the likelihood. The MLE is the best fit to the conditional distribution; “best fit” and “true effect” coincide only under assumptions the likelihood can’t verify.

title: A.2 Why Least Squares Is Maximum Likelihood
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Derive the MLE of \(\sigma^2\) jointly with \(\beta\): show that plugging \(\hat\beta\) into the likelihood and maximizing over \(\sigma^2\) gives \(\hat\sigma^2 = \text{RSS}(\hat\beta)/n\), and verify the second derivative is negative (a maximum, not a minimum). Then compute the bias factor \((n-p)/n\) for the course’s typical regimes and state when the bias matters.


Solution







The first derivative is \(-\frac{n}{2\sigma^2} + \frac{\text{RSS}}{2\sigma^4}\); setting it to zero gives \(\hat\sigma^2 = \text{RSS}/n\), and the second derivative at that point is \(-\frac{n^3}{2\text{RSS}^2} < 0\) — a maximum. The bias factor: \(\mathbb{E}[\hat\sigma^2_{\text{MLE}}] = \frac{n-p}{n}\sigma^2\). For \(n\) = 10,000 and \(p\) = 10 the bias is 0.1% — irrelevant; for \(n\) = 50 and \(p\) = 10 it’s 20% — the difference between a calibrated and a badly miscalibrated uncertainty estimate. The rule: the MLE’s bias matters exactly when \(p/n\) is non-negligible — the small-sample, many-feature regime (5.6), which is also where the unbiased correction is most needed for honest standard errors.

Exercise 2. The loss-is-the-noise-model dictionary: for each noise distribution below, write the log-likelihood and name the resulting estimator — (a) Gaussian, (b) Laplace, (c) the contaminated Gaussian \(\varepsilon \sim 0.95 N(0,1) + 0.05 N(0, 100)\) (a few large outliers). Then simulate: fit OLS and LAD (via iteratively reweighted least squares or a simple subgradient descent) on data with 5% outliers, and compare the slope estimates.


Solution













OLS’s slope is dragged toward the outliers (the squared loss makes a 15-unit residual cost 225 units of gradient); LAD’s is nearly unaffected (the absolute loss gives the same gradient magnitude to a 15-unit residual as to a 1-unit one). The dictionary in action: choose the loss by choosing the noise model you believe — and when you don’t believe any of them, Huber (quadratic near zero, linear in the tails) is the standard compromise that keeps the best of both.

Exercise 3. The Gauss–Markov theorem, verified by simulation: under the assumptions of 2.10 (linearity, exogeneity, homoscedasticity, no collinearity), OLS is the best linear unbiased estimator (BLUE) — minimum variance among all linear unbiased estimators, not just among OLS-type ones. Simulate: compare the variance of \(\hat\beta_{\text{OLS}}\) against an alternative linear unbiased estimator (e.g., a weighted average of the per-observation slopes with non-optimal weights) over 10,000 datasets, and verify OLS has the smaller variance.


Solution







The alternative estimator is linear and unbiased (its expectation is the true slope) but has several times the variance — Gauss–Markov verified empirically. The theorem’s content: among linear unbiased estimators, OLS’s variance \(\sigma^2(X^\top X)^{-1}\) is the minimum — no reweighting, no clever alternative beats it. The caveat the theorem doesn’t tell you: “best” is within the linear-unbiased class — a biased estimator (ridge, A.4) can have lower mean squared error by trading variance for bias, which is the entire bias–variance trade-off of 4.4 in one sentence.

title: A.2 Why Least Squares Is Maximum Likelihood
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

The Gaussian assumption buys the intervals, not the point estimate. \(\hat\beta\) is unbiased under mere exogeneity (\(\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon|x]=0\)); the standard errors and \(t\)-tests need the distribution — but the CLT makes them approximately valid under much weaker conditions. The exact finite-sample theory needs Gaussianity; the asymptotic theory needs far less.
MLEs are not automatically unbiased — \(\hat\sigma^2\) divides by \(n\) and is biased low; the MLE of a nonlinear function is generally biased (Jensen’s inequality). “Maximum likelihood” is a consistency and efficiency claim, not an unbiasedness claim.
The loss function is a modeling assumption, not a default. Squared loss = Gaussian noise = outlier-sensitive. Before reaching for OLS, ask what the noise is: heavy tails (financial returns, biological measurements) argue for Huber or LAD; count data for Poisson GLMs (3.6); binary outcomes for logistic (A.3).
Least absolute deviations has no closed form — the absolute value isn’t differentiable at zero, so LAD needs iterative methods (IRLS, linear programming). The same non-differentiability that makes lasso sparse (A.5) makes LAD robust — the kink is doing statistical work in both.
The likelihood is a function of the model, not the truth. Maximizing it finds the parameters that make the data most probable under the model — if the model is wrong (wrong noise, wrong mean structure), the MLE is the best answer to the wrong question. Model checking (2.10’s residual diagnostics) is how you find out.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated likelihood function has three bugs. Diagnose before running the fixed version.
# AI-generated: Gaussian log-likelihood for regression (will not run here — spot the bugs)
def log_likelihood(X, y, beta, sigma):
    resid = y - X @ beta
    n = len(y)
    ll = -n/2 * np.log(2 * np.pi) - n/2 * np.log(sigma) - np.sum(resid**2) / (2 * sigma)  # BUG 1
    return ll

def fit(X, y):
    beta = np.linalg.lstsq(X, y)[0]
    sigma = np.sqrt(np.mean((y - X @ beta)**2))
    return beta, sigma, log_likelihood(X, y, beta, sigma)   # BUG 2

def aic(X, y, beta, sigma):
    ll = log_likelihood(X, y, beta, sigma)
    return 2 * len(beta) - 2 * ll                            # BUG 3


What’s wrong, and the fix


\(\sigma\) vs \(\sigma^2\): the Gaussian density has \(\log\sigma^2\) and divides by \(\sigma^2\) — the code uses \(\sigma\) in both places (missing the square). The likelihood is wrong by a factor that depends on \(\sigma\), so any comparison across models is corrupted.
The MLE of \(\sigma^2\) is RSS/\(n\), not the mean of the squared residuals with the wrong divisor — actually np.mean(resid**2) is RSS/\(n\), so this line is right; the bug is that fit returns the likelihood computed with the unsquared \(\sigma\) from bug 1 — the two functions are inconsistent. (The deeper issue: the code never checks that the returned likelihood is the maximum — it just evaluates at the OLS \(\beta\), which is correct for \(\beta\) but the \(\sigma\) handling is broken.)
AIC’s parameter count: AIC counts all estimated parameters — \(\beta\) and \(\sigma^2\) — so the penalty is \(2(p+1)\), not \(2p\). The missing \(+2\) is small but it’s the difference between the correct criterion and a slightly-too-generous one.

# fixed
def log_likelihood(X, y, beta, sigma2):
    resid = y - X @ beta
    n = len(y)
    return -n/2 * np.log(2 * np.pi) - n/2 * np.log(sigma2) - np.sum(resid**2) / (2 * sigma2)

def fit(X, y):
    beta = np.linalg.lstsq(X, y, rcond=None)[0]
    sigma2 = np.sum((y - X @ beta)**2) / len(y)      # MLE: RSS/n
    return beta, sigma2, log_likelihood(X, y, beta, sigma2)

def aic(X, y, beta, sigma2):
    return 2 * (len(beta) + 1) - 2 * log_likelihood(X, y, beta, sigma2)

title: A.2 Why Least Squares Is Maximum Likelihood
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. The MLE under a misspecified noise model: suppose the truth is Laplace noise but you fit OLS (the Gaussian MLE). Show that OLS is still consistent for the conditional mean (if the mean structure is right) but is no longer the minimum-variance estimator — and compute the asymptotic relative efficiency of OLS vs LAD under Laplace noise (the answer is a famous number). Then state the general principle.


Hint

Under Laplace noise, the asymptotic variance of the LAD estimator is \(b^2 / n\) (scale squared), while OLS’s is \(\sigma^2 (X^\top X)^{-1}\) with \(\sigma^2 = 2b^2\) — compare.



Solution

Under Laplace noise with scale \(b\): \(\sigma^2 = \text{Var} = 2b^2\), so OLS’s asymptotic variance is \(2b^2(X^\top X)^{-1}\) per unit; the LAD (MLE) asymptotic variance is \(b^2(X^\top X)^{-1}\) — the ratio is 2, so OLS uses half the data efficiency (asymptotic relative efficiency \(1/2\); the famous result is that under Laplace noise, LAD is twice as efficient as OLS — and under Gaussian noise, OLS is infinitely more efficient than LAD in the tail sense). The general principle: the MLE is efficient under the true model; under misspecification, the pseudo-MLE (OLS here) remains consistent for the mean but loses efficiency — the loss is bounded and computable, and the robust choice depends on how wrong you think the model is. This is the 2.10 diagnostic program turned into a theorem: check the residuals, and if they’re heavy-tailed, the Gaussian MLE is leaving efficiency on the table.

Q2. From likelihood to Bayes: place a prior \(\beta \sim N(0, \tau^2 I)\) on the coefficients and derive the posterior mode. Show it equals the ridge solution \((X^\top X + \lambda I)^{-1}X^\top y\) with \(\lambda = \sigma^2/\tau^2\) — the Bayesian reading of A.4. Then state what the prior means (in words a reviewer would accept) and why this makes ridge’s \(\lambda\) interpretable rather than arbitrary.


Hint

The posterior is proportional to likelihood × prior; the log-prior is \(-\|\beta\|^2/(2\tau^2)\) — a quadratic penalty.



Solution

\(\log p(\beta \mid y) \propto \ell(\beta) - \frac{1}{2\tau^2}\|\beta\|^2 = -\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\text{RSS} - \frac{1}{2\tau^2}\|\beta\|^2 + \text{const}\). Maximizing over \(\beta\) is minimizing \(\text{RSS} + \frac{\sigma^2}{\tau^2}\|\beta\|^2\) — ridge with \(\lambda = \sigma^2/\tau^2\). The prior means: “before seeing the data, I believe the coefficients are centered at zero with spread \(\tau\)” — a statement about effect sizes, not a fudge factor. The interpretability: \(\lambda\) is the ratio of noise to signal — large \(\lambda\) means the data is noisy relative to your prior belief in the coefficients, so shrink hard; small \(\lambda\) means trust the data. This is why ridge’s \(\lambda\) isn’t arbitrary to choose: it’s the noise-to-prior ratio, and cross-validation (4.6) is just estimating that ratio from the data. The Bayesian view also explains ridge’s one weakness: the prior is centered at zero, which is right for “no effect” but wrong when effects are known to be large — the empirical-Bayes fix (estimate \(\tau\) from the data) is the next step.

title: A.2 Why Least Squares Is Maximum Likelihood
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (MLE × A.3 logistic × 3.3). Logistic regression is the MLE under a Bernoulli model — derive its log-likelihood and gradient the same way this page derives OLS’s, and note the structural parallel: both are GLMs with a canonical link, both have gradients of the form (prediction − target) × features, and both need iterative solvers because the mean is a nonlinear function of the parameters. The Gaussian case is the special one where the linearity makes the MLE closed-form.
C2 (MLE × 12.5 resampling × 2.3). The bootstrap is a likelihood-free way to get the sampling distribution of \(\hat\beta\) — resample the rows, refit, repeat. Contrast with the Gaussian theory: the bootstrap needs no distributional assumption but costs \(B\) refits; the theory is exact under Gaussianity but approximate otherwise. Run both on the same dataset (the drill-3 simulation) and state when each is preferable — the 12.5 answer, now with the Gaussian benchmark to compare against.

title: A.2 Why Least Squares Is Maximum Likelihood
text:
7. Summary

Under Gaussian noise, the log-likelihood’s \(\beta\)-term is \(-\text{RSS}/2\sigma^2\) — so the MLE of \(\beta\) is the least-squares solution, for any \(\sigma^2\).
The MLE of \(\sigma^2\) is RSS/\(n\) — biased low by \((n-p)/n\); the unbiased estimator divides by \(n-p\) (the degrees of freedom the fit spends).
The loss function is the noise model read backwards: Gaussian → squared, Laplace → absolute (robust), contaminated → Huber.
Gauss–Markov: OLS is minimum-variance among linear unbiased estimators — but biased estimators (ridge) can win on MSE (4.4).
The Gaussian assumption buys the intervals; the point estimate needs only exogeneity, and the CLT covers the rest approximately.
Ridge is the posterior mode under a Gaussian prior — \(\lambda = \sigma^2/\tau^2\), the noise-to-prior ratio (A.4).
Next: A.3 Logistic regression: deriving the gradient — the same MLE logic for a nonlinear mean.

title: A.7 AUPRC Trapezoidal Estimator, Worked Example
text: 3.1.5 introduced the area under the precision–recall curve as the right metric for skewed data. This appendix page derives the estimator itself: the trapezoidal rule that turns a ranked list of predictions into a number, the subtle choices that make two libraries disagree, and a fully worked example you can check by hand.
crumbs: A.7 AUPRC Trapezoidal Estimator, Worked Example

title: A.7 AUPRC Trapezoidal Estimator, Worked Example
text:
1. Basic Concept
The curve. Sort the test instances by predicted score (descending). Walk down the list, computing at each threshold \(t\):
\[\text{precision}(t) = \frac{\text{TP}(t)}{\text{TP}(t) + \text{FP}(t)}, \qquad \text{recall}(t) = \frac{\text{TP}(t)}{P}\]
where \(P\) is the total number of positives. The precision–recall (PR) curve plots precision against recall as the threshold sweeps from \(+\infty\) to \(-\infty\). The area under it (AUPRC) summarizes the whole curve in one number.
The trapezoidal estimator. The curve is a step function of the ranked list, but the standard estimator connects the observed (recall, precision) points with straight lines — the trapezoidal rule:
\[\text{AUPRC}_{\text{trap}} = \sum_{i=1}^{m} (r_i - r_{i-1}) \cdot \frac{p_i + p_{i-1}}{2}\]

title: A.7 AUPRC Trapezoidal Estimator, Worked Example
text:
2. Concept Questions

The trapezoid connects (recall, precision) points with straight lines, but the empirical PR curve is a step function. When does the trapezoid overestimate the step area, and when does it underestimate? (Think about the shape of the precision function between thresholds.)
The baseline of the PR curve is the prevalence \(\pi = P/n\) (a random ranker’s expected AUPRC), while the baseline of the ROC curve is always 0.5. Why does the PR baseline move with the class balance, and why does that make AUPRC — not AUC-ROC — the honest metric for rare positives?
The step function’s area (the “empirical” AUPRC) and the trapezoid’s area differ. Which one does sklearn.metrics.average_precision_score compute, and why is it not the trapezoid?
The trapezoid assigns zero area to the horizontal segments (where recall is flat but precision drops). What does an AUPRC of 1.0 require, and what does the gap from 1.0 measure?
Why is AUPRC not comparable across datasets with different prevalences — and what is comparable (the normalized version)?



Answers


Between two consecutive thresholds, recall changes only at positive instances. The step function holds precision constant between them (a horizontal step); the trapezoid draws a diagonal. When precision drops between the points (a negative instance was ranked between two positives), the diagonal lies below the step — the trapezoid underestimates. When precision rises (impossible in the standard construction — precision can only drop or stay as you go down the list), the diagonal would overestimate. In practice the trapezoid is a slight underestimate of the step area for the usual decreasing-precision curve — the price of connecting points instead of integrating the step.
A random ranker’s precision at any threshold is the prevalence \(\pi\) (the expected fraction of positives in a random subset) — so its PR curve is the horizontal line at \(\pi\), and its area is \(\pi\). The ROC baseline is 0.5 because a random ranker’s TPR = FPR by symmetry. The PR baseline moves because precision is a preconditioned quantity (it conditions on the prediction being positive), and the precondition’s base rate is \(\pi\). For a 1% prevalence, a random AUPRC is 0.01 — and a model at 0.05 is 5× better than random but looks “terrible” next to an ROC AUC of 0.85. The PR view exposes what the ROC view hides.
average_precision_score computes the step-function area: \(\sum_i (r_i - r_{i-1}) \cdot p_i\) — precision times the recall gain at each positive, with no averaging of adjacent precisions. It’s the exact area under the step curve, not the trapezoidal approximation. (auc(recall, precision) is the trapezoid — the two functions differ, and the difference grows with the number of positives.)
AUPRC = 1.0 requires every positive ranked above every negative (perfect ranking). The gap from 1.0 measures the “ranking damage” — how many negatives sit above positives, weighted by how far down the list they are. It’s the metric’s sensitivity to the top of the ranking that makes it the right choice for retrieval and screening (3.1.5): the errors that matter are the ones at the top.
AUPRC’s value depends on the prevalence (the baseline is \(\pi\)), so 0.4 on a 50%-prevalence dataset and 0.4 on a 1%-prevalence dataset are not the same achievement. The comparable quantities: the normalized AUPRC (AUPRC − baseline)/(1 − baseline), or the lift over random (AUPRC/π), or — best — the AUPRC on a fixed, shared benchmark prevalence. This is the 13.7 benchmarking trap again: metrics with data-dependent baselines need the baseline reported alongside.

title: A.7 AUPRC Trapezoidal Estimator, Worked Example
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Derive the trapezoidal AUPRC formula from the step function: show that \(\text{AUPRC}_{\text{step}} = \sum_{i=1}^{m} (r_i - r_{i-1})\, p_i\) (the precision at each positive times the recall gain), and that the trapezoid replaces \(p_i\) with \((p_i + p_{i-1})/2\). Then compute both on a random dataset with 50 positives and quantify the gap as a function of the number of positives.


Solution







The gap shrinks as the number of positives grows: with few positives, the precisions at adjacent thresholds differ a lot (each positive moves precision by a big step), so the trapezoid’s averaging is a coarse approximation; with many positives, adjacent precisions are nearly equal and the two estimators coincide. The practical rule: for rare-positive settings (few positives), use the step estimator (average_precision_score) — it’s the exact area under the empirical curve — and report which estimator you used, because the two are not interchangeable.

Exercise 2. The prevalence dependence, quantified: generate datasets with prevalence \(\pi \in \{0.5, 0.1, 0.01\}\) and a ranker of fixed quality (AUC 0.85), and compute the AUPRC in each. Show that the same model gets wildly different AUPRC, then compute the normalized AUPRC (AUPRC − π)/(1 − π) and show it’s stable. State the reporting rule.


Solution







The same-quality ranker scores 0.83 at 50% prevalence, 0.47 at 10%, and 0.083 at 1% — a 10× spread that says nothing about the model and everything about the baseline. The normalized AUPRC (the lift over the random baseline, scaled to [0,1]) is stable at ~0.66. The reporting rule: always report the prevalence alongside the AUPRC, and for cross-dataset comparisons use the normalized version or a fixed-prevalence benchmark. This is the 13.7 benchmarking principle (report the baseline) applied to the metric itself.

Exercise 3. The connection to the F1 score: show that the F1 at a threshold is the harmonic mean of precision and recall at that point, and that the maximum F1 over the curve is a single-point summary (the “F1-max” operating point). Compute both the AUPRC and the F1-max on a random dataset, and state when each is the right summary — the AUPRC (whole curve, threshold-free) vs the F1-max (one operating point, deployment-shaped).


Solution







AUPRC summarizes the whole ranking (threshold-free — the right summary for “how good is the ranker”); F1-max finds the best single operating point (the right summary for “where do we set the threshold in deployment”). They answer different questions: AUPRC for model comparison and development, F1-max for the deployed decision rule. The general principle: threshold-free metrics for development, threshold-specific metrics for deployment — and the deployment metric must be computed on data that didn’t choose the threshold (the 12.3 discipline: pick the threshold on the dev set, evaluate it once on the test set).

title: A.7 AUPRC Trapezoidal Estimator, Worked Example
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Two functions, two estimators: average_precision_score (step area) vs auc(recall, precision) (trapezoid) give different numbers on the same data. Always check which one a paper or library reports — and prefer the step version for rare positives (Exercise 1).
The left endpoint is a convention: the curve starts at (recall=0, precision=1) — the “perfect precision at zero recall” anchor. Different libraries handle the anchor differently; the sklearn convention prepends (0, 1), which is why the first trapezoid can differ from a hand computation.
Precision is non-monotone down the list (drill 4): it rises whenever a positive passes accumulated negatives. The PR curve is therefore not a decreasing function — another reason the trapezoid (which assumes smoothness) is an approximation, and another reason the step function is the honest empirical object.
The baseline is the prevalence — a random ranking scores \(\pi\), not 0.5. Reporting an AUPRC without the prevalence is reporting a number without its reference point; the 3.1.5 argument for choosing AUPRC over AUC-ROC is exactly that the PR baseline moves with the class balance and the ROC’s doesn’t.
Interpolation choices are not neutral. The trapezoid, the step, and the “interpolated precision at each recall level” (the Pascal VOC convention) give three different numbers. The field has settled on the step estimator for average precision; the trapezoid survives in auc(). Know which you’re reading.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated AUPRC function has three bugs. Diagnose before running the fixed version.
# AI-generated: AUPRC via the trapezoidal rule (will not run here — spot the bugs)
def auprc(y_true, scores):
    order = np.argsort(scores)                   # BUG 1
    y = y_true[order]
    tp = np.cumsum(y)
    fp = np.cumsum(1 - y)
    recall = tp / y.sum()
    precision = tp / (tp + fp)
    return np.sum(np.diff(recall) * precision)  # BUG 2

y = np.array([1, 0, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0])
s = np.array([0.9, 0.8, 0.7, 0.6, 0.5, 0.4, 0.3, 0.2])
print(auprc(y, s))


What’s wrong, and the fix


Ascending sort: np.argsort(scores) sorts worst-first — the curve is built from the bottom of the ranking, and the recall gains are attached to the wrong precisions. Sort descending: np.argsort(-scores).
Missing the left endpoint and the precision averaging: the formula np.diff(recall) * precision drops the origin (recall=0, precision=1) — the first positive’s contribution is lost — and uses the raw precisions instead of the trapezoid’s average (or the step’s right-end precision). The trapezoid needs the prepended (0, 1) point and the averaged precisions; the step estimator needs the prepended point and the right-end precisions.

# fixed (step estimator == sklearn's average_precision_score)
def auprc(y_true, scores):
    order = np.argsort(-scores)                          # descending
    y = y_true[order]
    tp = np.cumsum(y)
    r = np.concatenate([[0.0], tp / y.sum()])
    p = np.concatenate([[1.0], tp / np.maximum(tp + np.cumsum(1 - y), 1)])
    return np.sum(np.diff(r) * p[1:])                    # step: precision × recall gain

title: A.7 AUPRC Trapezoidal Estimator, Worked Example
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. The PR curve’s shape under a perfect and a random ranker: show that a perfect ranker’s PR curve is the horizontal line at precision 1 (AUPRC = 1), and a random ranker’s is the horizontal line at precision \(\pi\) (AUPRC = \(\pi\)). Then derive the AUPRC of a ranker with a given AUC under a parametric model (e.g., binormal scores) — the famous result is that AUPRC is a function of AUC and prevalence, and the function is nonlinear. State the practical consequence.


Hint

Under the binormal model, both TPR and FPR are normal CDFs of linear functions of the threshold; precision is TPR/(TPR + (1−π)/π · FPR) — integrate over the threshold.



Solution

Perfect: every positive outranks every negative, so at every threshold above the lowest positive, precision = 1 — the curve is the horizontal line at 1, area 1. Random: at any threshold, the expected precision is the prevalence (a random subset’s positive fraction), so the curve is the horizontal line at \(\pi\), area \(\pi\). The binormal derivation: with scores \(s^+ \sim N(\mu, 1)\) for positives and \(s^- \sim N(0, 1)\) for negatives, \(\text{TPR}(t) = \Phi(\Phi^{-1}(1 - \text{FPR}(t)) + \mu)\) and \(\text{precision}(t) = \frac{\pi \cdot \text{TPR}}{\pi \cdot \text{TPR} + (1-\pi)\cdot\text{FPR}}\) — a one-parameter family indexed by \(\mu\) (equivalently, by AUC = \(\Phi(\mu/\sqrt{2})\)). The practical consequence: AUPRC is not an independent quality axis from AUC — it’s a reparametrization that mixes in the prevalence. Two rankers with the same AUC have AUPRCs that diverge as \(\pi\) shrinks (the better ranker’s advantage concentrates at the top, which the PR view rewards); two rankers with the same AUPRC can have different AUCs at different prevalences. The rule: report AUC and prevalence and AUPRC together — any two of the three (plus the model) determine the third, and reporting one without the others is underspecified.

Q2. The AUPRC as an expectation: show that \(\text{AUPRC} = \mathbb{E}[\text{precision at the rank of a random positive}]\) — the step estimator is the average precision at which a randomly chosen positive is retrieved. Then use this to derive the AUPRC’s sampling variance (the variance of a mean of per-positive precisions) and state why this makes AUPRC unstable with few positives — the rare-positive regime’s central problem.


Hint

The step estimator sums \(p_i/P\) over the \(P\) positives — each term is the precision at positive \(i\)’s rank. It’s a sample mean over positives; its variance is the per-positive variance over \(P\).



Solution

\(\text{AUPRC} = \sum_{i=1}^{P} \frac{1}{P} p_{(i)}\) where \(p_{(i)}\) is the precision at the \(i\)-th positive’s rank — exactly the mean of the per-positive precisions. So AUPRC’s sampling variance is \(\text{Var}(p_{(i)})/P\) — the per-positive precision variance divided by the number of positives. With few positives, the variance explodes: a dataset with 5 positives has an AUPRC whose standard error can be 0.1+ regardless of the model’s quality. This is the rare-positive regime’s central problem — the metric is unstable exactly when the class is rare — and the mitigations: (i) report the AUPRC with a confidence interval (bootstrap the positives); (ii) use more positives (the 3.1.5 advice: AUPRC needs enough positives to be meaningful); (iii) for very rare positives, the normalized AUPRC or the lift over random is more stable (the baseline subtraction removes the prevalence-driven component). The deep point: every metric’s reliability is a sample-size statement, and the PR metrics are the most sample-hungry in the toolbox.
crumbs: A.7 AUPRC Trapezoidal Estimator, Worked Example

title: A.7 AUPRC Trapezoidal Estimator, Worked Example
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (AUPRC × 3.1.5 × 12.4 FDR). The FDR and the PR curve are two views of the same quantity: precision at a threshold is 1 − FDR (the false-discovery rate among the called positives), so the PR curve is the FDR-vs-recall curve, and AUPRC is the recall-weighted average of (1 − FDR). Derive this identity, then state the consequence: the BH procedure of 12.4 controls the FDR at a fixed threshold, while AUPRC averages over all thresholds — the FDR is the threshold-local version, AUPRC the threshold-global one. Genomics screens (fixed threshold, FDR-controlled) and retrieval evaluations (threshold-free, AUPRC) are the same statistics at different zoom levels.
C2 (AUPRC × 13.7 × 13.6). RAG evaluation as a PR problem: the retrieved chunks are the “predicted positives,” the relevant chunks are the true positives, and the retrieval AUPRC (average precision at k) is the standard metric. Trace the identity: retrieval precision at k = (relevant in top-k)/k, recall at k = (relevant in top-k)/total relevant — the same construction as this page, with “retrieved” replacing “predicted positive.” Then state the two places the RAG evaluation diverges from the classification version (the ranking is over chunks, not instances; the “prevalence” is the number of relevant chunks per query, which varies) — and why that makes per-query average precision the right aggregation.
crumbs: A.7 AUPRC Trapezoidal Estimator, Worked Example

title: A.7 AUPRC Trapezoidal Estimator, Worked Example
text:
7. Summary

The PR curve: sort by score, walk down, plot precision vs recall; the trapezoid connects the points, the step function is the empirical curve.
Trapezoidal AUPRC = \(\sum (r_i - r_{i-1})(p_i + p_{i-1})/2\); the step estimator (sklearn’s average_precision_score) = \(\sum (r_i - r_{i-1}) p_i\) — the two differ, most when positives are few.
The baseline is the prevalence \(\pi\), not 0.5 — a random ranker scores \(\pi\). Report prevalence with AUPRC; use the normalized (AUPRC − π)/(1 − π) for cross-dataset comparison.
AUPRC = 1 requires a perfect ranking; the gap from 1 measures top-of-ranking damage — the right metric for retrieval and screening.
AUPRC is a reparametrization of AUC + prevalence — report all three; F1-max is the deployment-point companion to the threshold-free AUPRC.
With few positives, AUPRC’s variance explodes (it’s a mean over positives) — bootstrap the positives or use more of them.
This completes the appendix — and the course. The derivations are the floor; the judgment is the craft.

title: A.6 PCA: Deriving the First Principal Component
text: A.1 solved a linear system; A.5 optimized under a constraint. PCA is the constrained-optimization member of the family: find the direction of maximum variance, subject to being a unit vector. The Lagrange multiplier turns out to be an eigenvalue — and that single fact is the whole of principal component analysis.
crumbs: A.6 PCA: Deriving the First Principal Component

title: A.6 PCA: Deriving the First Principal Component
text:
1. Basic Concept
The problem. Given centered data \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times p}\) (each feature has mean zero), find the unit vector \(w \in \mathbb{R}^p\) maximizing the variance of the projected data \(Xw\):
\[\max_w \; w^\top X^\top X w \quad \text{subject to} \quad w^\top w = 1\]
The projected variance is \(w^\top X^\top X w\) (the scatter matrix, \(n\) times the covariance); the constraint keeps the scale from running away.
The derivation — Lagrange multipliers:






Setting the gradient to zero: \(2Sw - 2\lambda w = 0\), i.e.
\[S w = \lambda w\]
The first principal component is an eigenvector of the scatter matrix \(X^\top X\) — and the Lagrange multiplier is the corresponding eigenvalue. Which eigenvector? The objective’s value at the solution is \(w^\top S w = \lambda w^\top w = \lambda\) — so maximizing the variance means taking the largest eigenvalue’s eigenvector.
The numerical check:
crumbs: A.6 PCA: Deriving the First Principal Component

title: A.6 PCA: Deriving the First Principal Component
text:
2. Concept Questions

The Lagrange multiplier \(\lambda\) turned out to be an eigenvalue — and the objective’s value at the solution is exactly \(\lambda\). Why does this make “maximize variance” and “find the top eigenvector” the same problem?
Why must the data be centered before PCA? What does the first component become if you skip centering (two cases: the mean is small vs large)?
The second principal component is the top eigenvector orthogonal to the first. Derive this: maximize \(w^\top S w\) subject to \(w^\top w = 1\) and \(w^\top w_1 = 0\) — what does the second constraint’s multiplier do?
PCA is not scale-invariant: the first component of unstandardized data points along the largest-variance feature, regardless of the underlying structure. Why is this a units problem, and what is the fix?
The eigenvalues \(\lambda_1 \ge \lambda_2 \ge \dots\) are the variances along the components. What does \(\sum_j \lambda_j / \lambda_1\) tell you, and why is it the natural “how many components do I need” diagnostic?



Answers


At a constrained optimum, the gradient of the objective is parallel to the gradient of the constraint — that’s the Lagrange condition \(\nabla f = \lambda \nabla g\), which here is the eigenvalue equation \(Sw = \lambda w\). And since the objective’s value at the solution is \(w^\top S w = \lambda\), the constrained maximum is the largest eigenvalue. “Maximize the quadratic form over the sphere” and “find the spectral decomposition” are the same theorem — the Rayleigh quotient’s maximum is the top eigenvalue, attained at its eigenvector.
PCA finds directions of maximum variance around the mean. Without centering, the scatter matrix \(X^\top X\) includes the mean’s contribution — the first component points toward the mean vector itself (the data’s “location”), not its spread. If the mean is small relative to the spread, the distortion is minor; if the mean is large (the common case — e.g., gene expression with a big baseline), the first component is dominated by the mean and the structure is lost. Centering makes the components describe variation, which is what PCA is for.
With the extra constraint \(w^\top w_1 = 0\), the Lagrangian gains a second multiplier: \(L = w^\top S w - \lambda(w^\top w - 1) - \mu(w^\top w_1)\). The stationarity condition becomes \(Sw - \lambda w - \mu w_1 = 0\); left-multiplying by \(w_1^\top\) and using \(w_1^\top S = \lambda_1 w_1^\top\) gives \(\mu = 0\) — so the condition reduces to \(Sw = \lambda w\) again, but now \(w\) must be orthogonal to \(w_1\). The largest eigenvalue whose eigenvector satisfies that is \(\lambda_2\) — the second component. The constraints peel off the eigenpairs in order: each new orthogonality constraint removes the previous components from consideration, and the maximum is always the next eigenvalue.
Variance is in units of the feature squared — a feature measured in millimeters has variance \(10^6\) times the same feature in meters. Unstandardized PCA’s first component is just “the feature with the biggest units,” which is arbitrary. Standardizing (dividing by each feature’s standard deviation) puts every feature in units of its own spread, so the components describe correlation structure, not unit choices. The fix: standardize when features are in incommensurate units; the cost: the components then describe the correlation matrix, not the covariance.
\(\sum_j \lambda_j = \text{tr}(X^\top X)\) = total variance, so \(\lambda_j / \sum_k \lambda_k\) is the fraction of variance explained by component \(j\), and the cumulative sum is the scree plot of 9.2. The diagnostic: how many components are needed to explain, say, 95% of the total variance — the “elbow” of the scree plot is where the remaining components are noise-level. It’s the natural diagnostic because the eigenvalues are the variances — the question “how many dimensions matter” is literally “how many eigenvalues are big.”
crumbs: A.6 PCA: Deriving the First Principal Component

title: A.6 PCA: Deriving the First Principal Component
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Derive the second principal component with the two-constraint Lagrangian (Q3 above): show the second multiplier \(\mu = 0\), so the condition reduces to \(Sw = \lambda w\) with \(w \perp w_1\), and the solution is the second-largest eigenvector. Then verify numerically that the components are orthogonal and the variances are the eigenvalues in order.


Solution







With \(w \perp w_1\) (the second constraint), \(\mu = 0\) and the condition is \(Sw = \lambda w\) again — but \(w_1\) is already taken (it’s the \(\lambda_1\) eigenvector), so the largest remaining eigenvalue is \(\lambda_2\). The components are orthogonal because eigenvectors of a symmetric matrix with distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal — and the variances along them are the eigenvalues in decreasing order. Numerical check: the SVD drill already showed the right singular vectors are the PCs; the orthogonality is \(V^\top V = I\) by construction, and the variance along PC \(j\) is \(d_j^2/n = \lambda_j\).

Exercise 2. PCA as reconstruction error minimization: show that the top-\(k\) principal components also solve \(\min_{\text{rank-}k\, B} \|X - XB\|_F^2\) — the best rank-\(k\) approximation of the centered data (in the Frobenius norm). This is the Eckart–Young theorem. Verify numerically: project a dataset onto its top-\(k\) PCs and show the reconstruction error equals the sum of the discarded eigenvalues.


Solution







The reconstruction error of the rank-\(k\) projection is exactly \(\sum_{j > k} \lambda_j\) — the variance the discarded components carried. This is the Eckart–Young theorem in the PCA special case: the variance-maximizing projection (Section 1) and the error-minimizing approximation are the same projection. The two views are complementary: variance maximization says “keep the directions that matter”; error minimization says “the directions you drop cost you their variance.” Both are why the scree plot’s cumulative variance is the right diagnostic — it’s literally the fraction of the data you keep.

Exercise 3. The scale sensitivity, measured: take a dataset with two features — one with variance 100, one with variance 1 — and a true underlying structure at 45°. Show that unstandardized PCA’s first component points at the high-variance feature (not the structure), while standardized PCA recovers the 45° direction. Then state the rule for when to standardize.


Solution







Unstandardized, PC1 is within a few degrees of the high-variance feature’s axis — the structure (the 45° direction) is invisible because feature 1’s variance dominates the scatter matrix. Standardized, PC1 recovers the 45° structure — the correlation, not the units. The rule: standardize when the features are in incommensurate units (the common case: gene expression + age + blood pressure); skip it only when the units are comparable and the variance differences are meaningful (e.g., all features are the same measurement in the same units). The general principle: PCA answers “where is the variance?” — and if the variance is an artifact of units, so is the answer.
crumbs: A.6 PCA: Deriving the First Principal Component

title: A.6 PCA: Deriving the First Principal Component
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Centering is not optional — the scatter matrix \(X^\top X\) (vs the covariance \(\frac{1}{n}X^\top X\) after centering) includes the mean’s outer product, and the first component degenerates toward the mean direction (drill 2). Every PCA implementation centers internally; the pitfall is feeding it data you think is centered but isn’t.
Standardization is a modeling choice, not a default. Standardizing makes PCA describe the correlation matrix (unit-free); not standardizing makes it describe the covariance (units matter). Neither is “correct” — they answer different questions. The pitfall is running the default without asking which question you have.
The components are not interpretable by construction. PC1 is a weighted sum of all features — the weights (loadings) can be inspected, but “what PC1 means” is a judgment, not a derivation. The 9.2 interpretation step is where PCA projects meet domain knowledge.
PCA is a linear method — it finds directions, not manifolds. Curved structure (the Swiss roll, 9.7) is invisible to it; the eigenvalues will look fine while the structure is missed. Always plot the projection, not just the scree.
The SVD is the stable algorithm — never form \(X^\top X\) explicitly (it squares the condition number, A.1’s warning); compute the SVD of the centered \(X\) and read off the components. sklearn’s PCA does this; the eigen-decomposition of \(X^\top X\) is the teaching version.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated PCA has three bugs. Diagnose before running the fixed version.
# AI-generated: PCA via the eigen-decomposition (will not run here — spot the bugs)
def pca(X, k):
    S = X.T @ X                              # BUG 1
    eigvals, eigvecs = np.linalg.eigh(S)
    W = eigvecs[:, :k]                       # BUG 2
    return (X @ W) @ W.T

X = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4], [5, 6]])      # BUG 3


What’s wrong, and the fix


No centering: X.T @ X is the scatter matrix of uncentered data — the first component points at the mean (drill 2). Center first: X = X - X.mean(0).
Wrong eigenvector order: np.linalg.eigh returns eigenvalues in ascending order — eigvecs[:, :k] takes the smallest eigenvalues (the least variance). The top components are eigvecs[:, -k:] (or reverse the order).
Integer-typed input: np.array([[1, 2], ...]) is int64 — the mean subtraction and the matmul silently truncate. Cast to float.

# fixed
def pca(X, k):
    X = np.asarray(X, dtype=float)
    X = X - X.mean(axis=0)                   # center
    _, _, Vt = np.linalg.svd(X, full_matrices=False)   # the stable algorithm
    W = Vt[:k].T                             # top-k right singular vectors
    return (X @ W) @ W.T
crumbs: A.6 PCA: Deriving the First Principal Component

title: A.6 PCA: Deriving the First Principal Component
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. The variance-maximization and error-minimization views are one theorem (Eckart–Young, Exercise 2). Derive the general form: for any matrix \(X\), the best rank-\(k\) approximation in any unitarily invariant norm is the truncated SVD. Then state the two consequences: (a) PCA is optimal not just for the Frobenius norm but for the spectral norm and every Schatten norm; (b) the same theorem is why low-rank matrix completion (9.3) works — the observed entries are approximated by a low-rank matrix, and the theorem guarantees the approximation is the best possible.


Hint

The Eckart–Young–Mirsky theorem: the truncated SVD minimizes \(\|X - A\|\) over rank-\(k\) \(A\) for every unitarily invariant norm. The proof sketch: the singular values of the error are bounded below by the discarded singular values of \(X\).



Solution

The theorem: for \(X = UDV^\top\) and any rank-\(k\) matrix \(A\), \(\|X - A\| \ge \|X - X_k\|\) where \(X_k = \sum_{j \le k} d_j u_j v_j^\top\) — the truncated SVD — for every unitarily invariant norm (Frobenius, spectral, Schatten/nuclear). The proof’s core: the singular values of \(X - A\) majorize the discarded singular values \(d_{k+1}, \dots\) of \(X\) (a Weyl-type inequality), and the truncated SVD achieves equality. Consequence (a): PCA’s rank-\(k\) projection is the best rank-\(k\) approximation under any of these norms — the choice of Frobenius norm in Exercise 2 is not a limitation. Consequence (b): matrix completion (9.3) — filling in missing entries with a low-rank matrix — is the same theorem with a twist: the norm is only observed on the known entries, and the theorem’s optimality becomes the objective that alternating minimization or nuclear-norm minimization pursues. The deep point: the SVD is the unique right answer to “best low-rank approximation” — every method in this space is an approximation to it, exact or computational.

Q2. PCA as a probabilistic model — PPCA: suppose the data is generated by \(x = Wz + \mu + \varepsilon\) with \(z \sim N(0, I)\) (latent) and \(\varepsilon \sim N(0, \sigma^2 I)\) (isotropic noise). Show that the MLE of \(W\) is the top-\(k\) principal components (up to rotation), with the noise variance \(\sigma^2\) equal to the mean of the discarded eigenvalues. Then state what the probabilistic view buys: a likelihood (model comparison, A.2), a generative model (sampling, imputation), and a principled missing-data handling.


Hint

The marginal distribution of \(x\) is \(N(\mu, WW^\top + \sigma^2 I)\) — maximize its likelihood over \(W\) and \(\sigma^2\); the solution’s \(W\) spans the principal subspace.



Solution

The marginal covariance is \(C = WW^\top + \sigma^2 I\); the MLE of \(C\) is the sample covariance, and the MLE of \(W\) is \(W = V_k (D_k - \sigma^2 I)^{1/2} R\) for an arbitrary rotation \(R\) — the columns span the top-\(k\) principal subspace, with the noise variance \(\sigma^2 = \frac{1}{p-k}\sum_{j>k}\lambda_j\) (the mean of the discarded eigenvalues). What the probabilistic view buys: (i) a likelihood — so \(k\) (the number of components) can be chosen by BIC or a held-out likelihood, not just the scree elbow; (ii) a generative model — sample new data, and impute missing values by their posterior given the observed ones (the 9.3 connection); (iii) a noise model — the discarded eigenvalues are explicitly “noise variance,” which is the right frame for the scree plot’s tail. The classical PCA of Section 1 is the \(\sigma^2 \to 0\) limit of PPCA — the same components, but without the likelihood that makes them comparable.

title: A.6 PCA: Deriving the First Principal Component
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (PCA × A.1 normal equations × A.4 ridge). The normal equations solve \(X^\top X \beta = X^\top y\); PCA diagonalizes \(X^\top X\). Show that in the PCA basis, the OLS solution is \(\beta = \sum_j \frac{1}{d_j}(u_j^\top y) v_j\) — each principal direction contributes independently, scaled by \(1/d_j\) — and ridge’s solution is the same sum with \(1/d_j\) replaced by \(d_j/(d_j^2 + \lambda)\). The three methods are one spectral computation: OLS inverts the eigenvalues, ridge shrinks them, PCA selects them. This is the unifying view of the appendix’s linear algebra.
C2 (PCA × 9.4 k-means × A.5 lasso). PCA and k-means are both “find structure in \(X\)” — PCA finds a linear subspace, k-means finds a partition. Show that k-means’ objective (within-cluster sum of squares) is minimized by an alternating algorithm whose assignment step is a nearest-centroid rule and whose update step is a per-cluster mean — and that the cluster means span a subspace that PCA would find if the clusters were the only structure. Then state the general principle: every unsupervised method is a constrained approximation of the data — PCA constrains the rank, k-means constrains the representation to \(k\) points, lasso constrains the support — and the constraint is the model.
crumbs: A.6 PCA: Deriving the First Principal Component

title: A.6 PCA: Deriving the First Principal Component
text:
7. Summary

PCA: maximize \(w^\top X^\top X w\) subject to \(w^\top w = 1\) — the Lagrange condition is the eigenvalue equation \(Sw = \lambda w\); the solution is the top eigenvector, the multiplier the variance.
Center first (or the first component points at the mean); standardize when units are incommensurate (or the first component points at the units).
The components peel off in eigenvalue order: each orthogonality constraint removes the previous one, and the next component is the next eigenvector.
Variance-maximization = error-minimization (Eckart–Young): the rank-\(k\) projection’s error is the sum of the discarded eigenvalues — the scree plot is the diagnostic.
The SVD is the stable algorithm (never form \(X^\top X\)); eigh returns ascending order — take the last columns.
PPCA: the probabilistic version — the MLE of the loading matrix spans the principal subspace, and the noise variance is the mean of the discarded eigenvalues.
Next: A.7 AUPRC trapezoidal estimator, worked example — the appendix’s final derivation, for the metric that matters on skewed data.

title: A.4 Ridge Regression: Deriving the Closed Form
text: A.1’s normal equations break when \(X^\top X\) is singular; A.3’s likelihood breaks under separation. Ridge regression is the one-line fix for both: add \(\lambda\|\beta\|^2\) to the objective. This page derives the closed form, shows why \(\lambda I\) is exactly the right repair, and reads the solution through the SVD — where ridge’s behavior becomes visible.

title: A.4 Ridge Regression: Deriving the Closed Form
text:
1. Basic Concept
The objective. Ridge minimizes the residual sum of squares plus a penalty proportional to the squared coefficient magnitude:
\[\hat\beta_\lambda = \arg\min_\beta \; \underbrace{(y - X\beta)^\top(y - X\beta)}_{\text{RSS}} + \lambda \underbrace{\beta^\top\beta}_{\|\beta\|^2}\]
The derivation — A.1’s calculus with one extra term:






Setting the gradient to zero: \(-2X^\top(X\beta - y) + 2\lambda\beta = 0\), i.e.
\[(X^\top X + \lambda I)\,\beta = X^\top y \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \hat\beta_\lambda = (X^\top X + \lambda I)^{-1}X^\top y\]
Why \(\lambda I\) is exactly the right repair: \(X^\top X\) is positive semidefinite — its eigenvalues are \(\ge 0\), and singularity means some are exactly zero (the collinear directions of A.1). Adding \(\lambda I\) shifts every eigenvalue up by \(\lambda\) — the zero eigenvalues become \(\lambda > 0\), the matrix becomes positive definite, and the inverse exists for any \(\lambda > 0\). The penalty doesn’t just regularize — it repairs the algebra.
The numerical check:

title: A.4 Ridge Regression: Deriving the Closed Form
text:
2. Concept Questions

The ridge solution is \((X^\top X + \lambda I)^{-1}X^\top y\). What happens as \(\lambda \to 0\) and as \(\lambda \to \infty\), and why are both limits the “right” answers?
The SVD view: with \(X = UDV^\top\), show \(\hat\beta_\lambda = \sum_j \frac{d_j}{d_j^2 + \lambda} (u_j^\top y) v_j\). Which singular directions does ridge shrink most, and why is that the right thing to shrink?
Why is the intercept (and generally, any unpenalized coefficient) excluded from the penalty? What breaks if you penalize it?
Ridge requires standardized features — why does the penalty’s scale-dependence make standardization a mathematical requirement, not a convenience?
The Bayesian reading (A.2 Q2): ridge is the posterior mode under \(\beta \sim N(0, \tau^2 I)\). What does \(\lambda = \sigma^2/\tau^2\) mean in words, and how does it tell you when to use a large \(\lambda\)?



Answers


\(\lambda \to 0\): \(\hat\beta_\lambda \to (X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top y\) — the OLS solution (recovered when \(X^\top X\) is invertible). \(\lambda \to \infty\): every coefficient \(\to 0\) — the penalty dominates and the model predicts the mean. Both limits are the correct extremes: no regularization and total shrinkage.
The shrinkage factor is \(\frac{d_j^2}{d_j^2 + \lambda}\) (multiplying the OLS coefficient’s component along \(v_j\)). Directions with large singular values \(d_j\) (strong, well-identified signal) are barely shrunk; directions with small \(d_j\) (weak, noisy — the collinear ones) are shrunk toward zero. Ridge spends its bias budget exactly where the data is weakest — the 4.4 trade-off made visible in the spectrum.
The intercept represents the mean of \(y\) — penalizing it shrinks the predictions toward zero, which is wrong whenever the outcome’s mean isn’t zero (it forces the other coefficients to compensate, biasing them). The calibration guarantee (\(\sum r_i = 0\), A.2) also breaks. Standard practice: center \(y\) and \(X\), fit without an intercept, add the mean back.
The penalty \(\lambda\|\beta\|^2\) is in units of the coefficients — and the units depend on the feature’s scale. A feature measured in millimeters has coefficients 1000× smaller than the same feature in meters, so the penalty treats them 1000× differently. Standardizing (mean 0, variance 1) puts every feature in the same units, making \(\lambda\) comparable across coefficients — without it, \(\lambda\) is not one knob but a different knob per feature.
\(\lambda = \sigma^2/\tau^2\) is the noise-to-prior ratio: \(\sigma^2\) is how noisy the data is, \(\tau^2\) is how large you believe the coefficients are a priori. Large \(\lambda\) = noisy data or small believed effects = shrink hard. This makes \(\lambda\) interpretable: it’s not a magic number but a statement about signal-to-noise, and cross-validation (4.6) is just estimating that ratio from the data.

title: A.4 Ridge Regression: Deriving the Closed Form
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Derive the SVD form of the ridge solution: with \(X = UDV^\top\) ( \(D\) diagonal with \(d_j\) ), show \(\hat\beta_\lambda = V \,\text{diag}\!\left(\frac{d_j}{d_j^2 + \lambda}\right) U^\top y\), and verify it against the direct solve on a random matrix. Then state what happens to the coefficients along each singular direction as \(\lambda\) grows.


Solution







The SVD form: \(X^\top X = VD^2V^\top\), so \((X^\top X + \lambda I)^{-1} = V\,\text{diag}\!\left(\frac{1}{d_j^2 + \lambda}\right)V^\top\), and \(\hat\beta_\lambda = V\,\text{diag}\!\left(\frac{d_j}{d_j^2 + \lambda}\right)U^\top y\). The OLS solution has factor \(1/d_j\) along direction \(j\) — which explodes for small \(d_j\) (the collinear directions). Ridge’s factor \(\frac{d_j}{d_j^2 + \lambda}\) is bounded by \(\frac{1}{2\sqrt{\lambda}}\) — no explosion, ever. As \(\lambda\) grows, every direction shrinks toward zero, but the small-\(d_j\) directions shrink first (their factor hits half-max at \(d_j = \sqrt{\lambda}\)). Ridge is a spectral filter: it keeps the well-identified directions and damps the noisy ones.

Exercise 2. The Bayesian derivation: place the prior \(\beta \sim N(0, \tau^2 I)\) on the coefficients of the A.2 Gaussian model and derive the posterior mode. Show it equals the ridge solution with \(\lambda = \sigma^2/\tau^2\), and verify numerically that the posterior mean (which equals the mode here) shrinks toward zero as the prior tightens.


Solution







The posterior is Gaussian (likelihood Gaussian × prior Gaussian = Gaussian), so the mode equals the mean, and it is exactly the ridge solution with \(\lambda = \sigma^2/\tau^2\). The prior’s meaning: “before the data, I believe the coefficients are zero-centered with spread \(\tau\).” The posterior is a precision-weighted compromise: data precision \(1/\sigma^2\) pulls toward the OLS solution, prior precision \(1/\tau^2\) pulls toward zero, and \(\lambda\) is the exchange rate between them. Numerical check: as \(\tau^2\) decreases (tighter prior), the posterior mean shrinks toward zero — the prior’s pull strengthens.

Exercise 3. The \(\lambda\) path: compute ridge solutions for \(\lambda\) on a log grid from \(10^{-4}\) to \(10^4\) on a collinear dataset, and plot each coefficient against \(\lambda\) (a regularization path). Verify three behaviors: (a) as \(\lambda \to 0\), the coefficients approach the OLS solution (which may be wild under collinearity); (b) as \(\lambda\) grows, all coefficients shrink smoothly to zero; (c) the collinear pair’s coefficients share the signal as \(\lambda\) grows (they move together) — ridge’s “fairness” toward correlated features.


Solution







The path is the bias–variance trade-off (4.4) made visible: at the left edge, OLS’s variance is on full display (the collinear coefficients swing wildly); as \(\lambda\) grows, the variance collapses and the bias grows smoothly. The collinear pair’s “sharing” is ridge’s answer to 5.1’s selection problem: where lasso picks one of the correlated features, ridge keeps both and splits the effect — the coefficients move together, and the sum is stable even as the individual split wobbles.

title: A.4 Ridge Regression: Deriving the Closed Form
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

\(\lambda\) is in units of the data. The objective is \(\text{RSS} + \lambda\|\beta\|^2\) — RSS is in units of \(y^2\), so \(\lambda\)’s meaning depends on \(n\) and the feature scales. This is why every implementation standardizes first and why \(\lambda\) values aren’t comparable across datasets. The path (Exercise 3) is the scale-free way to see it.
Don’t penalize the intercept — and more generally, don’t penalize coefficients you want at their natural value (e.g., a known confounder). Partial penalization (penalty factors) is the generalization.
Ridge never zeroes a coefficient — the L2 ball is round, so the solution is always interior (all coefficients nonzero). If you need selection (exact zeros), that’s lasso’s L1 diamond — A.5 derives why the shapes differ. Elastic net (5.4) mixes the two.
The SVD view is the right mental model: ridge = spectral filter. Small singular values = directions the data doesn’t identify = noise amplification; ridge damps them. When you understand the solution as “OLS with the noisy directions filtered,” the hyperparameter choice becomes intuitive.
Generalized ridge: any positive definite matrix \(P\) can replace \(I\) — \(\text{RSS} + \lambda\beta^\top P\beta\) encodes structured priors (e.g., \(P\) = a graph Laplacian for spatial smoothness). The derivation is identical; only the meaning of the penalty changes.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated ridge solver has three bugs. Diagnose before running the fixed version.
# AI-generated: ridge regression (will not run here — spot the bugs)
def ridge(X, y, lam):
    n, p = X.shape
    beta = np.linalg.solve(X.T @ X + lam * np.eye(p), X.T @ y)   # BUG 1 (below)
    return beta

def standardize(X):
    return X / X.std(axis=0)                    # BUG 2

X = np.array([[1, 2], [1, 4], [1, 6]], dtype=float)   # BUG 3
y = np.array([1, 2, 3], dtype=float)


What’s wrong, and the fix


The intercept is penalized: the np.eye(p) adds \(\lambda\) to the intercept’s diagonal too — shrinking the mean of \(y\) toward zero and biasing every slope. Fix: penalize only the non-intercept coefficients — add \(\lambda\) to the submatrix, or center \(y\) and \(X\) and fit without an intercept.
Standardization without centering: X / X.std() scales but doesn’t center — the features keep their means, so the intercept column (if present) isn’t orthogonal to them, and the penalty still distorts the fit. Standardization is both: (X - X.mean(0)) / X.std(0).
The design matrix is integer-typed: np.array([[1, 2], ...]) without dtype=float creates int64 — X.T @ X is integer arithmetic and the solve can silently truncate. Always cast.

# fixed
def standardize(X):
    X = np.asarray(X, dtype=float)
    return (X - X.mean(axis=0)) / X.std(axis=0)

def ridge(X, y, lam):
    X = np.asarray(X, dtype=float); y = np.asarray(y, dtype=float)
    yc = y - y.mean()
    Xc = standardize(X[:, 1:])                     # center + scale the features
    beta = np.linalg.solve(Xc.T @ Xc + lam * np.eye(Xc.shape[1]), Xc.T @ yc)
    return np.concatenate([[y.mean()], beta])     # intercept = mean (unpenalized)

title: A.4 Ridge Regression: Deriving the Closed Form
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Ridge as a spectral filter, quantified: using the SVD form, compute the effective degrees of freedom of a ridge fit: \(\text{df}(\lambda) = \sum_j \frac{d_j^2}{d_j^2 + \lambda}\). Show it decreases from \(p\) (at \(\lambda = 0\)) to \(0\) (as \(\lambda \to \infty\)), and verify it against the hat matrix trace \(\text{tr}(H_\lambda)\) where \(H_\lambda = X(X^\top X + \lambda I)^{-1}X^\top\). Then state why this is the right complexity measure for the bias–variance trade-off.


Hint

The hat matrix’s trace counts the “number of parameters the fit effectively uses” — for OLS it’s exactly \(p\); for ridge it’s the sum of the shrinkage factors.



Solution

\(H_\lambda = X(X^\top X + \lambda I)^{-1}X^\top = U\,\text{diag}\!\left(\frac{d_j^2}{d_j^2 + \lambda}\right)U^\top\), so \(\text{tr}(H_\lambda) = \sum_j \frac{d_j^2}{d_j^2 + \lambda}\). At \(\lambda = 0\) the sum is \(p\) (OLS uses all \(p\) directions); as \(\lambda \to \infty\) it decays to 0 (the fit uses nothing). Each direction contributes its shrinkage factor — the well-identified directions count almost fully, the noisy ones count not at all. This is the right complexity measure because the variance of the fit is \(\sigma^2 \text{tr}(H_\lambda^2)\) and the effective number of parameters controls the variance–bias balance: \(\text{df}(\lambda)\) is the dial of 4.4, set by \(\lambda\). It’s also what makes generalized cross-validation (5.2) cheap: GCV’s formula only needs \(\text{tr}(H_\lambda)\), not the full hat matrix.

Q2. The limit connection — ridge as OLS on augmented data: show that the ridge solution is the OLS solution on the augmented system \(\tilde X = [X; \sqrt{\lambda}\,I]\), \(\tilde y = [y; 0]\) — stack \(\sqrt{\lambda}\) rows of “the coefficients should be zero” onto the data. Then state the two readings this gives: (a) the penalty as data (pseudo-observations pulling \(\beta\) to zero), and (b) why this makes ridge’s solution always exist even when \(X^\top X\) is singular.


Hint

The augmented RSS is \(\|y - X\beta\|^2 + \lambda\|\beta\|^2\) — exactly the ridge objective. The normal equations of the augmented system are the ridge normal equations.



Solution

The augmented OLS problem \(\min_\beta \|\tilde y - \tilde X\beta\|^2\) has objective \(\|y - X\beta\|^2 + \|\sqrt{\lambda}I\beta - 0\|^2 = \text{RSS} + \lambda\|\beta\|^2\) — the ridge objective, so the solutions coincide. Reading (a): the penalty is \(p\) extra observations saying “the coefficient vector is zero,” each with weight \(\sqrt{\lambda}\) — the prior made literal. Reading (b): the augmented design \(\tilde X = [X; \sqrt{\lambda}I]\) has full column rank for any \(\lambda > 0\) (the appended \(\sqrt{\lambda}I\) supplies the missing directions), so \(\tilde X^\top \tilde X = X^\top X + \lambda I\) is always invertible — ridge is OLS on a system the data alone couldn’t identify. This is the cleanest statement of what regularization is: adding just enough information to make the problem well-posed, whether that information is a prior, a penalty, or pseudo-data.

title: A.4 Ridge Regression: Deriving the Closed Form
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (ridge × A.5 lasso × 5.3). Ridge’s L2 ball gives smooth shrinkage; lasso’s L1 diamond gives exact zeros. Derive both from the same constrained form — \(\min \text{RSS}\) s.t. \(\|\beta\|_q \le t\) — and show the constraint’s shape (round vs pointy) is the whole difference: the round ball’s smooth boundary is never axis-aligned, so the constrained solution never lands exactly on an axis; the diamond’s corners are on the axes, so the solution lands there and zeroes coefficients. The geometry of the constraint is the geometry of the solution.
C2 (ridge × A.6 PCA × 5.5). Ridge and PCR both damp the small singular directions of \(X\) — ridge smoothly, PCR by truncation. Show that PCR (regress \(y\) on the top-\(k\) principal components) is the \(\lambda \to \infty\) limit of ridge per direction: ridge with \(\lambda\) between \(d_{k+1}^2\) and \(d_k^2\) keeps directions \(1..k\) almost fully and damps the rest — a soft truncation. Then state when you’d prefer each (interpretability vs smoothness), and why partial least squares (5.5) — which finds directions that matter for \(y\), not just \(X\) — is the \(y\)-aware version of the same idea.

title: A.4 Ridge Regression: Deriving the Closed Form
text:
7. Summary

Ridge: \(\hat\beta_\lambda = (X^\top X + \lambda I)^{-1}X^\top y\) — A.1’s normal equations with \(\lambda I\) added.
\(\lambda I\) shifts every eigenvalue up by \(\lambda\): the singular directions become invertible — the penalty repairs the algebra.
The SVD view: ridge shrinks each singular direction by \(\frac{d_j^2}{d_j^2 + \lambda}\) — strong directions kept, weak directions damped. OLS’s \(1/d_j\) explosion is bounded by \(1/(2\sqrt{\lambda})\).
Standardize first (the penalty is scale-dependent); never penalize the intercept.
Ridge is the posterior mode under \(\beta \sim N(0, \tau^2 I)\) — \(\lambda = \sigma^2/\tau^2\), the noise-to-prior ratio.
Ridge = OLS on augmented data \([X; \sqrt{\lambda}I]\), \([y; 0]\) — regularization as information, not magic.
Next: A.5 Why lasso has no closed form — the L1 penalty’s kink, and why it buys sparsity at the price of closedness.

title: 13.7 Evaluation and Limitations
text: Every previous page built capability; this page builds honesty about capability. LLM evaluation is where the course’s statistical habits — calibration, multiple testing, contamination, the winner’s curse — meet a field that moves faster than its benchmarks. The limitations are not footnotes: knowledge cutoff, hallucination, bias, and the gap between “passes the benchmark” and “works in your workflow” are the difference between a demo and a deployment.

title: 13.7 Evaluation and Limitations
text:
1. Basic Concept
The evaluation stack, from weak to strong:



Level
What it measures
Failure mode




Perplexity (13.1)
fit to a text distribution
corpus-dependent; gameable by memorization


Benchmarks (MMLU, GSM8K, HumanEval)
task accuracy vs a reference
contamination, saturation, narrow tasks


Chatbot Arena (human preference)
real-user satisfaction
prompt-selection bias, non-representative voters


Your own eval set
your task, your data
the only one that predicts your deployment



The four limitations that no benchmark captures:

Knowledge cutoff — the model knows only its training corpus. Post-cutoff events, private data, and anything unwritten are invisible. RAG (13.6) is the standard fix.
Hallucination — the model generates fluent, confident, false text. It is not a bug in the sense of a broken component; it is the direct consequence of the objective (13.1): the model is a next-token predictor, and a plausible continuation is not a verified fact. Hallucination rate is task-dependent and risks being highest exactly where the model sounds most confident.
Bias and sycophancy — the model reproduces the corpus’s biases (13.3) and, after RLHF, tends to agree with the user. Both are training-data facts, not alignment failures that more alignment fully fixes.
The reliability gap — a model that is right 90% of the time on a benchmark is right 90% of the time on the benchmark’s distribution. Real workflows have long tails (rare inputs, adversarial inputs, distribution shift) where the rate is lower — and the tail is where the cost lives.

Worked example — the winner’s curse, measured: a lab evaluates on 40 benchmarks and reports the best:






With a true accuracy of 0.50 and benchmark noise of ±0.05, the mean of 40 benchmarks is an unbiased estimate — but the best of 40 reports 0.55–0.60. That gap is pure selection, and it is exactly 12.2’s family-wise problem: 40 chances to beat the truth by noise. The fix is the same: pre-register the benchmark, or correct for selection (12.4’s FDR logic).

title: 13.7 Evaluation and Limitations
text:
2. Concept Questions

Why is perplexity a necessary but not sufficient evaluation? What can a model optimize to lower perplexity without becoming more useful?
Benchmark contamination: a model scores 90% on a benchmark whose questions appear in its training data. Why is this not “the model knows the material,” and what does the 13.3 contamination exercise imply about the size of the effect?
The reliability gap: a model is 95% accurate on your eval set of 200 examples. Why is that number still not the number you should quote for deployment? What would you compute instead?
Hallucination vs lying: why is “the model lied” the wrong frame, and what does the correct frame imply about mitigation?
Chatbot Arena ranks by human preference. What are the two selection biases in who votes and what prompts get voted on, and how do they distort the ranking?



Answers


Perplexity measures fit to a text distribution — a model can lower it by memorizing the test corpus (contribution: zero generalization), by learning surface statistics (no understanding), or by genuinely improving prediction. It’s necessary because a model that can’t model text can’t do anything else, but insufficient because the objective is a surrogate: the things that make a model useful (honesty, reasoning, instruction-following) are only correlated with next-token fit. The 13.3 Q1 argument, as an evaluation criterion.
Scoring 90% on seen questions measures retrieval, not capability — the model is recognizing training text, not answering questions. The 13.3 Exercise 3 simulation showed the effect size: contamination can inflate scores by points with zero capability change, and at trillion-token scale the boundary between “seen” and “near-seen” (paraphrases, translations) is fuzzy — so the honest move is to treat any benchmark score as an upper bound and evaluate on held-out, post-cutoff, or adversarially-constructed data.
200 examples at 95% has a 95% CI of roughly ±3% — and that’s the statistical uncertainty on the eval distribution. The deployment number must also cover the tail: rare input types, adversarial inputs, and distribution shift between the eval set and production. Quote instead: the accuracy on a stratified eval (by input type), the worst-slice accuracy, and a monitoring plan — the 4.1 generalization problem, where the deployment distribution is the test set you can’t see.
Lying requires intent to deceive; the model has no intent — it generates the most probable continuation, and falsehoods are probable continuations whenever the model’s knowledge is incomplete or the training data was wrong. The correct frame is “the model is a calibrated-ish probability machine that can’t tell you when it’s guessing” — which implies mitigation by design: RAG (ground it in sources), tool use (verify with computation), confidence elicitation (ask it to flag uncertainty), and human review for high-stakes outputs. You can’t prompt away a structural property; you can only route around it.
Who votes: Arena voters are self-selected — technically inclined, English-speaking, heavy users — so the ranking optimizes for that population’s preferences. What prompts: the prompts that get voted are the ones users thought to try — which over-represents the model’s marketing strengths and under-represents the long tail of real use. The ranking is a real signal about preferred behavior on tried prompts by willing voters — a biased sample of “is this model good for your work.”

title: 13.7 Evaluation and Limitations
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. The multiple-testing correction for leaderboards: a lab reports its model’s score on 40 benchmarks, best = 0.72. Using the drill-1 simulation framework, estimate the selection bias (best − mean) as a function of the number of benchmarks and the per-benchmark noise. Then state the two honest reporting practices that remove the bias, and connect to 12.3/12.4.


Solution







The bias grows with the number of benchmarks (more chances for a lucky draw) and with the per-benchmark noise (noisier benchmarks give more room for luck). At 40 benchmarks the bias is ~0.05–0.08 — enough to flip a leaderboard ranking. Honest practices: (i) pre-register the primary benchmark before seeing results (the 12.3 fix — one test, no selection); (ii) if multiple benchmarks must be reported, report the mean (or a pre-specified aggregate) alongside the best, and treat the best as exploratory — the 12.4 distinction between confirmatory and exploratory findings. The deep point: a leaderboard position is a selected statistic, and selected statistics need selection-aware inference — the entire lesson of Part 12, applied to ML’s own evaluation.

Exercise 2. Hallucination rate on a toy task: generate 100 answers from a “model” (a stochastic resampler with a known truth distribution), and measure (a) the hallucination rate (fraction of answers that are confident and wrong), (b) the calibration (does “I’m 90% sure” match 90% accuracy?), (c) the effect of RAG (grounding reduces hallucination to the retrieval error rate). State the general principle each measurement illustrates.


Solution








The hallucination rate is the confident-and-wrong rate — the dangerous kind, because the confidence is what makes users trust it. (b) The calibration buckets show whether confidence tracks accuracy — a well-calibrated model’s 90%-confident answers are right 90% of the time; LLM confidence is typically miscalibrated (overconfident), which is why “the model said so” is weaker evidence than it sounds. (c) RAG converts hallucination into retrieval error — a different, more tractable failure mode (you can measure and fix the retriever). The general principle: decompose the error into its sources (knowledge gap, reasoning gap, retrieval gap, expression gap) and measure each — the 4.1 habit of evaluating the system, not the vibes.


Exercise 3. The knowledge-cutoff experiment: simulate a model whose knowledge is a training corpus with a cutoff date. Questions about pre-cutoff facts: 95% accuracy. Post-cutoff: the model confabulates — 10% accuracy but 90% confidence. Compute the expected accuracy on a mixed benchmark (50% pre, 50% post) and show why the benchmark score (52.5%) is meaningless without the cutoff breakdown. Then state the two deployment mitigations.


Solution







The mixed score (52.5%) is a number that describes neither slice — it’s the 1.1 fallacy of the unstratified mean: an average over a bimodal distribution. The deployment mitigations: (i) know the cutoff — treat any question about post-cutoff events as out-of-scope and route it to RAG or a search tool (13.6); (ii) stratify your eval — report per-slice accuracy (pre/post cutoff, per domain, per input type) so the average can never hide a failing slice. The general principle: a single accuracy number is a summary, and summaries fail exactly when the distribution is multimodal — the same reason 1.1 insists on distributions, not just means.

title: 13.7 Evaluation and Limitations
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Benchmarks saturate, and saturation is not capability. When a benchmark’s top score approaches 100%, it stops measuring anything — the remaining errors are annotation noise and edge cases. A new benchmark is then invented, and the cycle repeats. The honest response: treat benchmark scores as historical measurements, not current capability.
Goodhart’s law is the field’s shadow: “when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.” Training on benchmark questions (directly or via contamination) optimizes the measure, not the capability. The 13.3 contamination exercise is Goodhart’s law with a p-value.
Prompt sensitivity is an evaluation confound: the same model can score 10 points apart depending on the prompt template. Any single-prompt benchmark score is a draw from a prompt-distribution — report the variance, or average over a prompt set.
