“It passed the bar exam” is a category error: passing a multiple-choice exam measures test-taking, not lawyering. Benchmark tasks are proxies for capabilities, and the proxy–capability gap widens as the model gets better at the proxy.
The limitations are not evenly distributed: hallucination is worse for rare facts (less training signal), worse for post-cutoff events, worse for precise outputs (numbers, citations, code) than for vague ones. Know where your task sits.
Evaluation is a moving target: the model you evaluate today is not the model you deploy (updates, prompt changes, RAG index changes). The 13.6 C2 point: continuous evaluation — a standing eval harness that runs on every change — is the only stable practice.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated evaluation plan has three flaws. Diagnose before running the fixed version.

“We evaluated our model on the MMLU test set and it scored 86.4%, so it’s ready for medical diagnosis support. We also tested it on 5 questions from our own hospital and it got 4/5, which confirms it. For the report, we’ll show the best of 3 prompt templates.”



What’s wrong, and the fix


Contaminated benchmark: MMLU questions are public and almost certainly in the training data — the 86.4% is an upper bound on capability, not a measurement of it (13.3 Exercise 3). Medical diagnosis support needs a held-out, post-cutoff, expert-constructed eval.
n = 5 is not an evaluation: 4/5 has a 95% CI of roughly 44–100% — it confirms nothing. A clinical eval needs hundreds of cases, stratified by difficulty and rarity, with expert adjudication.
Best-of-3 prompt selection: choosing the template that scores highest on the test set is selection on the test set — the winner’s curse (Exercise 1). The template must be chosen on a dev set, then evaluated once on the test set.

Refactor: construct a held-out eval of 500+ expert-written clinical questions (post-cutoff, not in any training data); select the prompt template on a 100-question dev set; report the test-set accuracy with a confidence interval, stratified by question rarity; add a hallucination audit (expert flags confident-wrong answers) and a monitoring plan for deployment. The discipline: evaluate like the deployment depends on it — because it does.

title: 13.7 Evaluation and Limitations
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Capability vs reliability: a model has 95% capability on a task (it can do it) but 90% reliability (it does do it, this deployment). Model the gap: capability is the accuracy on the eval distribution; reliability is the accuracy on the deployment distribution, which is shifted (longer tail, more adversarial). Compute the expected cost of the gap: if a wrong answer costs \(C\) and the deployment processes \(N\) queries, what is the expected cost difference between the eval estimate and the deployment reality? Then state the two engineering practices that close the gap.


Hint

The gap is a distribution shift between eval and deployment — the 4.1 generalization gap, with a dollar sign.



Solution







The eval estimate understates the expected cost by the shift between distributions — here 2×. The two practices: (i) measure the deployment distribution — stratify the eval by input type and weight by production frequency (the tail slices matter more than the average), and monitor production continuously; (ii) design for the gap — RAG and tool use convert ungrounded generation into verifiable computation (13.6), and confidence-based routing sends low-confidence queries to humans. The general principle: capability is a property of the model, reliability is a property of the system — and the system is what you deploy.

Q2. The calibration–capability trade-off: RLHF improves human-preference scores but can degrade calibration (the model becomes more confident, not more correct — sycophancy and verbosity inflate preference). Simulate: a model with accuracy 0.80 and confidence 0.80 (calibrated) vs an RLHF’d model with accuracy 0.78 but confidence 0.95 (miscalibrated). Compute the expected cost of each under a policy that routes low-confidence queries to humans (cost \(C_h\) per human review, \(C_e\) per error). When does RLHF’s preference win become a reliability loss?


Hint

The routing policy makes confidence load-bearing: miscalibrated confidence sends the wrong queries to humans.



Solution







With a confidence-routing policy, the RLHF’d model’s overconfidence is expensive: its 95%-confident answers include the 22% it gets wrong, and the router never sends them to humans. The preference win (humans like the style) is real; the reliability loss is also real — and it’s invisible in every benchmark that measures preference or accuracy-without-confidence. The general principle: alignment optimizes what it measures, so evaluation must measure the decision-relevant quantities (calibration, worst-slice accuracy, cost under the deployment policy), not just the headline metric. This is 13.3’s “the objective is a surrogate” applied to the eval itself.

title: 13.7 Evaluation and Limitations
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (evaluation × 12.4 FDR × 13.4). The field’s model zoo is a multiple-testing experiment: 50 labs × 10 configurations each, publishing only the winners. Compute the expected number of “breakthrough” results under the global null (all models equal) and state the FDR correction that would apply. Then state why the publication version of the problem is worse than the statistical version (the null isn’t “all equal” — it’s “all within noise of each other,” and the noise is correlated across labs via shared training data).
C2 (evaluation × 11.5 Cox × 13.6). A hospital deploys a clinical LLM with a monitoring plan: monthly eval on 200 fresh questions, alert if accuracy drops below 90%. This is a survival problem — the “event” is the model’s accuracy crossing the threshold, and the risk factors are deployment drift (new terminology, new guidelines, new user behavior). Frame the monitoring plan in 11.5’s language: what is the hazard, what are the covariates, and why is the time-varying covariate (months since last update) the one that matters most?

title: 13.7 Evaluation and Limitations
text:
7. Summary

Evaluate on your data: benchmarks are upper bounds (contamination), Arena is a biased sample, your eval set is the only deployment predictor.
The winner’s curse: reporting the best of N benchmarks inflates the score by selection — pre-register or report the mean (12.3, 12.4).
A single accuracy hides the distribution: stratify by slice (pre/post cutoff, common/rare/adversarial) — the tail is where the cost lives.
Hallucination is structural (the objective is prediction, not verification) — mitigate by design: RAG, tools, confidence routing, human review.
Capability ≠ reliability: the deployment distribution is shifted from the eval distribution; measure the gap and design for it.
Calibration is decision-relevant: overconfident models break confidence-routing policies — evaluate the quantities your deployment actually uses.
Next: 13.8 Applications and next steps — where all of this goes to work.

title: 13.5 Local Deployment
text: 13.4 ended with “open weights: you can run it yourself.” This page is the how: the local-inference stack (Ollama, llama.cpp, vLLM, Hugging Face), the quantization math that makes 7B–70B models fit in consumer VRAM, and the hardware arithmetic that decides what runs where. The heavy lifting — actually loading and running a model — happens in the companion Colab lab; the concepts (quantization, memory budgets, bandwidth limits) run live here.

title: 13.5 Local Deployment
text:
1. Basic Concept
Why run locally: privacy (data never leaves the machine — clinical notes, proprietary code), cost at scale (API per-token fees vs a one-time hardware cost), offline/air-gapped operation, and the prerequisite for fine-tuning (13.6). The trade: you supply the hardware and the quality ceiling is your GPU.
The stack, simplest to most control:








Tool
What it is
You reach for it when




Ollama
one-command model runner (llama.cpp wrapped)
you want to use a model, not engineer one


llama.cpp
the C++ inference engine (GGUF format)
you want minimal deps, CPU+GPU hybrid, or to embed


Hugging Face transformers
the Python library (training + inference)
you want to program against models


vLLM
high-throughput serving engine (PagedAttention)
you’re serving many users, not one



Quantization — the core trick. A float16 weight is 2 bytes; an int8 weight is 1 byte; int4 is 0.5. Quantization maps each weight (or group of weights) from a float range to an integer grid: \(w \approx s \cdot (q - z)\), where \(s\) is the scale, \(q\) the integer, \(z\) the zero-point. The model gets 2–4× smaller and faster (integer math, less memory traffic) at a small quality cost. The formats: GGUF (llama.cpp’s file format, Q4_K_M etc. — per-block scales), GPTQ (post-training quantization, layer-by-layer error compensation), AWQ (activation-aware — protects the weights that matter most), bitsandbytes (int8/int4 for transformers, the Colab path).
The memory budget — the number that decides everything:
\[\text{VRAM} \approx \underbrace{2 \text{ bytes} \times N}_{\text{weights (fp16)}} \; \text{or} \; \underbrace{b \times N}_{\text{quantized}} + \underbrace{\text{KV-cache}}_{\propto T} + \underbrace{\text{activations + overhead}}_{\sim 1\text{–}2 \text{ GiB}}\]
A 7B model in fp16 needs ~14 GiB — just over a 12 GiB laptop GPU; in int4, ~3.5 GiB — comfortable. A 70B model in int4 needs ~35 GiB — a 48 GiB A6000 or an 80 GiB A100, or a multi-GPU setup. Worked example — the quantization math, live:






Per-group scales (a scale per 32 weights instead of one per tensor) cut the error dramatically — the tensor-wide scale is dominated by a few large outliers, and per-group scales let each region use the full integer range. This is why GGUF’s Q4_K_M (per-block scales with a 6-bit scale-of-scale) is the default “small but good” format.

title: 13.5 Local Deployment
text:
2. Concept Questions

Why is generation (not pretraining) the memory-bandwidth-bound phase? Compute the arithmetic intensity of one decoding step: the model reads every weight once to produce one token. What does that imply for tokens/second on a given GPU?
Per-group quantization beats per-tensor because of outlier weights. Why do transformers have outlier dimensions, and what does AWQ do differently from plain per-group quantization?
The memory budget has a KV-cache term that grows with context length \(T\). Why does a 128k-context model need more VRAM at inference even if you only ever send 1k-token prompts — and what is the mitigation?
Ollama’s Q4_K_M and a bf16 file of the same model differ by ~4× in size. Where does the quality difference actually come from — the number of bits, or how the bits are spent?
You want to run a 32B model on a 24 GiB consumer GPU. fp16 needs 64 GiB, int8 needs 32 GiB, int4 needs 16 GiB. Which do you pick, and what two other knobs (besides bits-per-weight) can close the gap?



Answers


Decoding reads all \(N\) weights from VRAM to compute one token’s logits: \(2N\) FLOPs per token against \(2N\) bytes of weight traffic — arithmetic intensity ≈ 1 FLOP/byte, far below any GPU’s compute/bandwidth ratio (an H100: ~1000 TFLOPs vs ~3 TB/s → ratio ~300). So decoding speed ≈ (memory bandwidth) / (bytes per token) — the GPU’s compute units are mostly idle, waiting on memory. Consequence: tokens/second scales with bandwidth, not FLOPs — which is why quantization (fewer bytes) directly buys speed, and why CPU inference (lower bandwidth) is slow even with spare compute.
A few embedding dimensions carry systematically large activations (“massive activations”); the weights interacting with them must stay precise or every token’s output is corrupted. Plain per-group quantization treats all groups alike; AWQ measures activation magnitudes and protects the weight columns with the largest activation overlap (scaling them up before quantizing so they land on the finer part of the grid). Same bits, better spent.
The KV-cache is allocated for the maximum context length — the engine reserves memory for a 128k sequence whether you use 1k or 128k, because it can’t know in advance. Mitigations: context-length caps at load time, PagedAttention (vLLM — allocate cache in blocks as needed, like virtual memory), and sliding-window attention (the model only uses a window anyway, 13.2 Exercise 3).
How the bits are spent. Per-block scales, mixed precision (keep sensitive layers at higher bits), and activation-aware protection (AWQ) all buy quality at fixed bit-width — the difference between a naive int4 and Q4_K_M is larger than the difference between naive int4 and naive int8. Quantization is an allocation problem, not just a precision problem.
int4 (16 GiB) leaves headroom. The other knobs: (i) offload — keep some layers on CPU/RAM and stream them (llama.cpp’s -ngl flag; slower but fits), (ii) sharding — split the model across two GPUs (or GPU+CPU) so no single device holds it all. Also: smaller context allocation (Q3) and accepting a smaller model (a 14B int4 at 7 GiB often beats a 32B int4 at 16 GiB on quality-per-latency for single-user use).

title: 13.5 Local Deployment
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Implement group-wise int4 quantization with the GGUF-style twist: per-block scales and a per-block scale-of-scale (the “K” in Q4_K_M — the scale itself is quantized to 6 bits). Quantize the Section 1 weight matrix, measure the error vs plain per-group int4, and state the memory cost of the extra metadata (per 32-weight block: 0.5 bytes/weight + 2 bytes scale + 2 bytes scale-of-scale ≈ 0.56 bytes/weight — why “Q4” is really ~4.5 bits).


Solution







The scale-of-scale costs 4 bytes per 32-weight block — 0.125 bytes/weight on top of the 0.5 bytes/weight of the int4 values, so “Q4” is really ~4.5–5 bits/weight once metadata is counted. The error reduction is modest on this synthetic matrix (real weight distributions with outliers benefit more); the point is the accounting: quantization formats are a bit-budget, and metadata is part of the budget. Always compute effective bits/weight as (values + scales + zero-points) / weights — the marketing number (Q4) and the file-size number differ by ~15%.

Exercise 2. The bandwidth-bound speed model: a 7B int4 model (3.5 GB weights) on a GPU with 1 TB/s bandwidth should decode at ~285 tokens/s by the drill-1 arithmetic. But real llama.cpp on a 4090 gets ~60–100 tokens/s. List the three reasons the simple model overpredicts, then compute what fraction of peak bandwidth a well-tuned kernel actually achieves, and state what that implies for choosing between “more quantization” and “better kernels.”


Hint</

The simple model assumes: weights are read once, nothing else competes for bandwidth, and the kernel achieves peak. Reality: dequantization compute, KV-cache traffic, and kernel efficiency all take their cut.



Solution







Three reasons for the gap: (i) dequantization compute — int4 weights are unpacked to float in registers; the unpacking ALU work and the extra register pressure slow the memory pipeline (the kernel is not purely bandwidth-bound at these tiny per-token matmuls); (ii) KV-cache traffic — every step also reads/writes the KV-cache (growing with \(T\)), competing for the same bandwidth; (iii) kernel efficiency — small matmuls (one token × 4096-dim layers) don’t saturate HBM; achieving 80–90% of peak needs large batched GEMMs, which single-user decoding doesn’t have. Implication: at ~25% of peak, the first 2× of speedup comes from better kernels (batching, fused dequant, tensor-core int4 GEMMs), not more quantization — which is why the field ships both (quantized formats and optimized runtimes). The crossover: once kernels are near peak, quantization is the only lever left — the two strategies are sequential, not either/or.

Exercise 3. Size the deployment: you have a 24 GiB GPU and want the best possible model for (a) a single-user chat with 8k context, (b) a RAG server handling 50 concurrent users with 4k contexts. For each, compute the memory budget (weights + KV-cache + overhead), pick a quantization level for 7B / 14B / 32B / 70B candidates, and state which you’d deploy and why. Use the drill-2 formula with \(h_{kv} = 8\), \(d = 4096\) (7B/14B) or \(8192\) (70B), \(L = 32/32/80\).


Solution








Single-user: 32B int4 (~16 + 0.5 + 1.5 ≈ 18 GiB) or 14B int8 (~14 + 0.25 + 1.5 ≈ 16 GiB) both fit; 70B int4 (~35 GiB) doesn’t. Pick 32B int4 — quality per user is what matters when there’s one user, and the KV-cache at 8k is small. (b) 50 concurrent: the KV-cache term explodes — 50 users × 4k context × 32 layers × 8 KV heads × 4096 × 2 (K+V) × 2 bytes ≈ 41 GiB per 7B model — the cache, not the weights, is the constraint. Pick 7B int4 and cap context/users, or move to a serving engine (vLLM’s PagedAttention shares cache across users with common prefixes). The general lesson: single-user deployment is weight-bound; multi-user deployment is cache-bound — the two regimes size completely differently, and the serving stack (batching, paged cache) matters more than the model choice in the second.

title: 13.5 Local Deployment
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

“It runs” ≠ “it runs well.” A 70B int4 on a 48 GiB GPU works; at 5 tokens/s with 200 ms/word latency it’s unusable for interactive chat. Always benchmark your prompt lengths and your concurrency before committing hardware.
Quantization quality is task-dependent. A Q4 model loses ~0.1–0.3 perplexity on average — invisible on chat, visible on precise multi-step reasoning or rare-domain knowledge. Evaluate on your task’s data, not on the format’s marketing.
Outlier dimensions break naive quantization — a few large-magnitude weights force a coarse per-tensor scale. If you ever quantize yourself: per-group scales, and consider keeping the outlier dims in fp16 (mixed precision, as AWQ/GGUF do).
Model files are code-adjacent trust objects. A GGUF from an untrusted source is a multi-GB binary you’re loading into a tool with filesystem access. Use official repos (Hugging Face verified, Ollama’s model library) and check hashes.
CPU inference is a different trade: llama.cpp on a Mac with unified memory can run 7B int4 at ~30 tokens/s with zero GPU — the memory is shared, the bandwidth is decent, and the laptop stays silent. For many users this is the best deployment, not a compromise.
The KV-cache is the silent cost: at long contexts it exceeds the weights (Exercise 3b). If your use case is long documents, budget for the cache first — a 7B model at 128k context needs more VRAM than a 14B model at 8k.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated quantization function has three bugs. Diagnose before running the fixed version.
# AI-generated: quantize a weight matrix to int4 (will not run here — spot the bugs)
def quantize(W, bits=4):
    qmax = 2 ** bits - 1                    # BUG 1
    s = W.max() / qmax
    q = np.round(W / s)
    return s * q                             # BUG 2

def dequantize(q, s):
    return s * (q - 128)                     # BUG 3


What’s wrong, and the fix


Wrong range for signed int4: 2**4 - 1 = 15 treats int4 as unsigned [0, 15]. Signed int4 is [-8, 7] (or [-7, 7] symmetric) — the scale must be computed from the actual min/max, and the rounding clipped to the signed range. As written, negative weights all quantize to 0.
No clipping: np.round(W / s) can exceed the integer range (any weight above qmax * s — and s is set by the max, so values near the max round to exactly qmax, but the unsigned range means the top half of the grid is wasted on sign). Clip to [-qmax, qmax] after rounding.
Hardcoded 128 zero-point: q - 128 assumes uint8’s zero-point; for int4 the zero-point is 0 (symmetric) or computed from the data (asymmetric). The dequantization must use the same convention as the quantization — and the scale must be passed consistently.

# fixed
def quantize(W, bits=4):
    qmax = 2 ** (bits - 1) - 1               # signed range [-7, 7]
    s = W.max() / qmax
    q = np.clip(np.round(W / s), -qmax, qmax)
    return q, s

def dequantize(q, s):
    return s * q                             # symmetric: zero-point is 0

title: 13.5 Local Deployment
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Why is decoding bandwidth-bound but pretraining compute-bound? Compute the arithmetic intensity of both: pretraining processes a batch of \(B\) tokens with the same weights (weights read once per batch), decoding processes 1 token. Then state the architectural consequence — why tensor cores matter for training but barely for single-user decoding, and why batching users (continuous batching, vLLM) is the serving-side fix.


Hint

Arithmetic intensity = FLOPs / bytes of memory traffic. Compare \(B\) tokens vs 1 token against the same weight read.



Solution

Pretraining: one weight read serves \(B\) tokens (say \(B\) = 4M tokens in a large run’s micro-batches — even \(B\) = 512 gives intensity \(2N \cdot B / 2N = B\) FLOP/byte ≈ 512, well above the ~300 ratio — compute-bound, tensor cores saturated). Decoding: one weight read serves 1 token — intensity ≈ 1, memory-bound, tensor cores idle. Consequence: training efficiency is about FLOPs utilization (MFU — the 50% figure in the drill); single-user decoding efficiency is about bandwidth. The serving fix is continuous batching: pack many users’ tokens into one GEMM — the weights are read once per batch of users, restoring compute-bound economics (intensity = number of users in flight). This is why vLLM/TGI can serve 50 users at aggregate speeds near the pretraining hardware’s potential, while naive one-user-at-a-time serving wastes 75% of it (Exercise 2). The same hardware, two regimes — the batch size is the dial between them.

Q2. The quantization error → quality relationship: using the Section 1 matrix, measure how quantization error scales with bits (2, 3, 4, 8, 16) and fit the exponent (error ∝ 2^(−bits)?). Then state why the perplexity impact is sublinear in the weight error (the network averages over thousands of weights — errors partially cancel), and why the worst case (outlier dimensions) dominates the tail of the quality loss.


Hint

Fit log(error) vs bits — the slope is the exponent. Then think about error accumulation across a 32-layer network with 4096-dim dot products.



Solution







Error halves per bit (slope ≈ −1 in log2) — each bit buys one binary digit of precision, as expected. But perplexity impact is sublinear in weight error: a dot product of 4096 terms with independent quantization errors has error growing as \(\sqrt{d}\) while the signal grows as \(d\) — the relative error shrinks with dimension, and across 32 layers the errors partially cancel (they’re zero-mean). That’s why int4’s naive error looks scary in isolation but costs only ~0.1–0.3 perplexity in practice. The exception: outlier dimensions — a few weights with 10–100× the typical magnitude. Their quantization error is large and they interact with large activations (every token touches them), so they don’t average away — they dominate the tail of the quality loss. This is the entire motivation for AWQ and mixed-precision formats: protect the outliers, quantize the rest aggressively.

title: 13.5 Local Deployment
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (deployment × 10.1 tensors × 13.4). The KV-cache is a tensor that grows every decoding step — a define-by-run shape change. Trace the memory lifecycle: pre-allocated max-context buffer (llama.cpp) vs PagedAttention’s block allocator (vLLM) vs the naive torch.cat approach (OOMs at long contexts). State which 10.1 concept each design is an instance of, and why the naive approach fails the 13.2 Exercise 3 memory arithmetic.
C2 (deployment × 13.6 × 13.3). Fine-tuning a local model (LoRA, 13.6) has its own deployment story: the base model is int4 on the GPU, the LoRA adapter is fp16, and the serving engine must fuse or compose them. Compute the memory cost of a 7B int4 base + 50M-param fp16 LoRA adapter, state whether the adapter changes the quantization story (it doesn’t — why?), and describe the inference-time composition (W + BA applied per forward) and its cost.

title: 13.5 Local Deployment
text:
7. Summary

Local deployment: Ollama (use it) → llama.cpp (embed it) → transformers (program it) → vLLM (serve it).
Quantization: \(w \approx s(q - z)\); per-group scales beat per-tensor because of outlier weights; metadata is part of the bit budget (“Q4” ≈ 4.5–5 bits/weight).
The VRAM budget = weights + KV-cache + overhead; single-user is weight-bound, multi-user is cache-bound.
Decoding is memory-bandwidth-bound (intensity ≈ 1 FLOP/byte); pretraining is compute-bound (intensity ≈ batch size) — batching users is the serving-side fix.
Quantization error halves per bit but perplexity impact is sublinear (errors average over dimensions) — except at outlier dimensions, which AWQ/mixed-precision protect.
“Runs” ≠ “runs well”: benchmark your prompt lengths, concurrency, and task before buying hardware.
Next: 13.6 Customization — RAG, LoRA, and agents on top of your local model.

title: 13.3 Training Pipeline
text: 13.2 built the architecture; 13.1 the objective. This page is the process that turns both into a capable model: pretraining on a massive corpus by next-token prediction, then alignment (SFT → RLHF/DPO). The concepts are the same training loop you already know from 10.4 — what changes is scale, data, and the alignment stage. We run the whole loop live at toy scale, including the beautiful fact that a neural bigram trained by gradient descent converges to the counting estimate of 13.1.

title: 13.3 Training Pipeline
text:
1. Basic Concept
Stage 1 — Pretraining. The model (randomly initialized transformer, 13.2) is trained on next-token prediction over a huge, lightly filtered corpus — trillions of tokens from web pages, books, code. The loss is cross-entropy, which by A.2’s logic is exactly maximum likelihood: the model learns the conditional distribution of text. Everything the model “knows” is statistical structure extracted from this corpus — facts, style, reasoning patterns, and the corpus’s biases.
Stage 2 — Supervised fine-tuning (SFT). Pretrained models are bad at following instructions — they continue text, they don’t answer questions. SFT trains on hundreds of thousands of human-written (instruction, response) pairs, same next-token loss, now on the response tokens only. This teaches the format of helpful behavior.
Stage 3 — Alignment (RLHF / DPO). SFT alone produces a model that imitates response style; alignment shapes preferences. RLHF: collect human comparisons of responses, train a reward model, then optimize the policy against it with PPO. DPO: a simpler, stable reformulation that skips the explicit reward model — directly optimizing the policy on preference pairs. Both answer “helpful, honest, harmless” at a level SFT can’t reach from demonstrations alone.
What’s new relative to 10.4’s loop: the loop itself (forward → loss → backward → update) is identical. The engineering that scale demands:

Distributed training — data parallelism (each GPU a batch shard), tensor parallelism (split each matmul across GPUs), pipeline parallelism (split layers); a 70B model doesn’t fit on one GPU.
Mixed precision — float16/bfloat16 compute with float32 master weights (10.1’s dtype lesson, now load-bearing at scale).
Learning-rate schedule — warmup then cosine decay; the single most sensitive hyperparameter.
Data curation — deduplication, quality filtering, domain mixing, and contamination control (removing benchmark data from training — 13.7).

Worked example — the entire training loop at toy scale: a neural bigram (one linear layer + softmax) trained by full-batch gradient descent:






The loop is 10.4’s loop: forward, loss, analytic gradient, update. The only LLM-specific piece is the embedding lookup — W[ids[:-1]] gathers rows, so each token’s “embedding” is just its row of \(W\), and the gradient scatters back with np.add.at. A transformer replaces this lookup with the full attention stack; the training mathematics is unchanged.

title: 13.3 Training Pipeline
text:
2. Concept Questions

Why is pretraining loss (next-token cross-entropy) a reasonable proxy for “knowledge,” and where does the proxy break down? Connect to 13.1’s compression argument.
SFT teaches format, RLHF/DPO teaches preferences. Why can’t SFT alone produce alignment — what does a preference signal contain that a demonstration doesn’t?
The toy model’s loss decreased from ~2.4 to ~1.9. What is the floor for this loss, and why can’t gradient descent reach zero? (Hint: what does the data itself determine?)
Why does the learning-rate schedule need warmup? What happens to a randomly initialized transformer’s gradients in the first steps with a large constant LR?
Data deduplication: why does training on the same text 10 times hurt, and why is near-duplicate detection (not exact matching) the hard version of the problem?



Answers


Next-token prediction forces the model to compress the corpus’s regularities — facts and reasoning patterns are regularities, so a good predictor must encode them (Shannon: optimal codelength = −log P). The proxy breaks where prediction is easy without understanding (surface statistics, memorized benchmark answers) or where the corpus is wrong/biased — the model learns the data’s errors as faithfully as its facts.
A demonstration shows one acceptable response; a preference pair shows which of two responses is better — a relative signal about quality, tone, safety, and honesty that demonstrations can’t express (the demonstrator only shows their best attempt, never the trade-offs). Preference data is also cheaper at the margin: comparing is easier than composing.
The floor is the entropy of the data itself — the irreducible uncertainty of the next token given the context. The bigram data has genuine ambiguity (after “the”, many words are plausible), so the conditional entropy is positive; zero loss would require the data to be deterministic. This is 1.4’s irreducible error, in language-model form.
At initialization, gradients are large and poorly conditioned — the first steps with a big LR can blow up the activations (loss spikes to NaN). Warmup ramps the LR from ~0 over the first few thousand steps so the model settles into a good region before full-speed training; the cosine decay then anneals it for the final polish.
Repeated text is overweighted — the model spends capacity memorizing duplicates and the effective dataset shrinks (the same data point isn’t new information; it’s 4.3’s leakage in training-set form). Exact dedup is a hash lookup; near-duplicates (a paragraph shared across 10,000 web pages with different boilerplate) need fuzzy matching — MinHash/similarity embeddings — which is why dedup is a research problem, not a one-liner.

title: 13.3 Training Pipeline
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. The neural bigram converges to the counting estimate: after training the Section 1 model, extract the model’s implied conditional probabilities \(P_\theta(\text{next} \mid \text{cur}) = \text{softmax}(W)\) and compare them to the 13.1 counting estimate \(\text{count}(w_t, w_{t+1}) / \text{count}(w_t)\) for every (context, next) pair. Report the maximum absolute difference. Then explain why they must agree — connect to A.2: cross-entropy MLE on one-hot inputs is the empirical conditional distribution.


Solution







They agree to optimization error. Why: with one-hot inputs, the model’s conditional is \(\text{softmax}(W_{w_t})\), and cross-entropy MLE for a linear model on one-hot features has the closed form “the empirical conditional distribution” — exactly the counting estimate (this is the multinomial-logit version of A.2: MLE of a linear-Gaussian is the least-squares solution; MLE of a linear-multinomial is the empirical frequencies). Gradient descent finds it because the loss is convex in \(W\). The deep-LLM takeaway: pretraining is the same MLE, just with a nonlinear feature extractor (the transformer) in front of the softmax — the counting model is the degenerate zero-layer case.

Exercise 2. Learning-rate schedule, measured: rerun the Section 1 training with (a) constant LR = 50, (b) constant LR = 0.01, (c) warmup-then-decay (linear warmup over 20 epochs to 5, then cosine decay to 0.5). Plot all three loss curves. Diagnose what (a) does (divergence/oscillation) and what (b) does (slow convergence), and state why the schedule matters more at real scale.


Solution








LR = 50 oscillates and can diverge — steps overshoot the minimum, the loss bounces (at real scale: loss spikes that kill the run, requiring rollback to an earlier checkpoint). (b) LR = 0.01 crawls — 200 epochs isn’t enough; at real scale this is a wasted training run (compute is the budget). (c) Warmup+cosine converges fast and settles lowest. The schedule matters more at real scale because the loss surface is far more ill-conditioned (billions of parameters, sharp minima) and a single bad step costs hours of GPU time — the toy model’s quadratic bowl is forgiving, the real one is not.


Exercise 3. Contamination control, quantified: simulate a training set of 10,000 documents where 200 are exact copies of a test document. Train the Section 1 bigram model on (a) the contaminated set, (b) the deduplicated set, and compare the test document’s perplexity under both. Then state why exact-dedup checking is necessary but not sufficient, and what the standard mitigation is.


Solution







The contaminated model has seen the test document 200 times — its perplexity on it is artificially low (near the document’s own entropy), while the deduped model pays the true price of generalization. Exact-hash dedup catches this case; the insufficient part is near-duplicates (paraphrases, benchmark questions embedded in web pages) and membership leakage (the model regurgitating training text). Standard mitigation: (i) exact + fuzzy dedup at ingestion, (ii) contamination scanning of benchmarks (n-gram overlap with training data), (iii) holding out a clean test set and reporting both contaminated and decontaminated scores — the discipline of 13.7.

title: 13.3 Training Pipeline
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Pretraining is 99%+ of the compute; alignment is where behavior comes from. A common misconception is that RLHF “adds intelligence” — it shapes a capability the pretrained model already has. No amount of alignment fixes a capability the pretraining data didn’t support.
Catastrophic forgetting is real: fine-tuning on a narrow domain can degrade general ability — the model overwrites pretrained knowledge. Mitigations: mix pretraining data into fine-tuning, lower LR, LoRA (13.6) to freeze most weights.
Reward hacking: RLHF optimizes the reward model, not human preference — the policy learns to exploit the reward model’s errors (verbose, sycophantic, weirdly formatted outputs that score high). DPO reduces but doesn’t eliminate this.
The data is the model. Architecture differences between GPT-4-class models are second-order compared to data quality and curation. “Garbage in, gospel out” — the model reproduces the corpus’s biases with fluency.
Scaling laws are empirical power laws: loss ≈ f(parameters, data, compute) with predictable exponents — which is why the field can plan training runs, and why “just scale it” was a strategy, not a slogan. The flip side: the laws are fit to observed regimes and can break (the “scaling law debate” of 2023–2024).
Checkpoints are the unit of recovery: long runs save state every N steps; a divergence means rolling back, not restarting. The schedule, the seed, and the data order are all part of the “model” — reproducibility requires all three.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated training step has three bugs. Diagnose before running the fixed version.
# AI-generated: one pretraining step (will not run here — spot the bugs by reading)
for step in range(1000):
    x, y = next_batch()
    logits = model(x)                      # (B, T, V)
    loss = cross_entropy(logits, y)        # BUG 1
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()                       # BUG 2
    scheduler.step()
    running_loss = running_loss + loss     # BUG 3


What’s wrong, and the fix


Wrong loss reduction: cross_entropy(logits, y) on (B, T, V) logits must flatten to (B*T, V) and average over response tokens only in SFT — averaging over prompt tokens too teaches the model to predict the user’s question, wasting capacity and corrupting the objective. (In pretraining all tokens count; in SFT the mask is the point.)
No gradient zeroing: optimizer.step() without optimizer.zero_grad() first — gradients accumulate across steps (10.1’s accumulation-is-the-default trap), so step 1000 applies the sum of 1000 gradients. The loss curve looks like a random walk.
Graph-carrying accumulator: running_loss + loss keeps the autograd graph alive every step — memory grows until OOM. Use running_loss += loss.item().

# fixed
for step in range(1000):
    x, y, mask = next_batch()
    optimizer.zero_grad()                          # fix 2
    logits = model(x)
    loss = cross_entropy(logits[mask], y[mask])    # fix 1: response tokens only
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()
    scheduler.step()
    running_loss += loss.item()                    # fix 3

title: 13.3 Training Pipeline
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Pretraining as maximum likelihood, formally: write the pretraining objective for a corpus of sequences, show it decomposes into a sum of next-token cross-entropies, and state the two ways it differs from the A.2 Gaussian story (the noise model, and what “least squares” becomes). Then explain why the same objective, at trillion-token scale, produces emergent capabilities — and what the theoretical objection is.


Hint

A.2: Gaussian noise → squared loss. Here: categorical noise → cross-entropy. The objective’s form is unchanged; the output distribution is not.



Solution

Objective: \(\mathcal{L}(\theta) = -\sum_{(w_{1:T}) \in \text{corpus}} \sum_{t=1}^{T} \log P_\theta(w_t \mid w_{<t})\) — a sum of categorical cross-entropies, one per token. Differences from A.2: (i) the noise model is categorical (multinomial), not Gaussian — the “least squares” analog is cross-entropy, and the MLE is the empirical conditional distribution (Exercise 1’s result, at scale); (ii) the features are learned (the transformer’s hidden states), not fixed — so the model class is a universal approximator conditioned on context, not a linear map. Emergence: the objective is fixed, but the functions the model can represent grow with parameters and data — capabilities like multi-step reasoning are not separate objectives, they’re what a sufficiently good next-token predictor computes internally. Theoretical objection: next-token prediction is a surrogate — nothing in the objective requires truth, only predictability — so the correlation between low loss and genuine reasoning is empirical (scaling laws), not guaranteed; a model can be a perfect predictor of human text and still fail at tasks whose answers humans don’t write down.

Q2. Design the data mix: you are pretraining a 7B model with a 1.4T-token budget. Given the domains below with rough “quality per token” scores (web 1×, books 3×, code 2×, academic 2.5×, Wikipedia 2×), and the constraint that no domain can exceed 60% of the mix, propose a mix and defend it with (a) the quality-weighted objective, (b) the risk of domain collapse (over-weighting high-quality domains starves the model of the long tail of language it must handle), and (c) the repeat strategy (high-quality domains are exhausted — how many epochs is too many?).


Hint

This is an optimization with a constraint and a judgment call — there is no closed form, and the answer should cite the objective, the collapse risk, and the epoch budget.



Solution

Sketch: web 50% (the long tail — the model must handle all language, and only web has the volume), books 15%, code 10%, academic 10%, Wikipedia 5%, other 10%. (a) Quality-weighted: the mix’s average quality-per-token is ≈ 0.5·1 + 0.15·3 + 0.1·2 + 0.1·2.5 + 0.05·2 + 0.1·1 ≈ 1.45 — a pure-quality play (all books) would score 3.0 but collapse on the long tail. (b) Collapse risk: language is heavy-tailed — rare domains (medical, legal, non-English, dialect) are individually small but collectively most of what the model will be asked; starving them produces a model that’s fluent on average and broken at the edges, which is exactly where users notice. (c) Epochs: books+academic+Wikipedia ≈ 30% of the mix but are high-quality — repeat them 2–3× (they’re exhausted, so repeats buy quality exposure at the Exercise-3 memorization cost); web gets ~1 epoch (it’s big enough to be nearly single-pass). The real field’s answer (Llama, Mistral mixes) looks like this: web-dominated, quality-upsampled, total 1–2 epochs of the effective mix. The general principle: optimize quality-weighted tokens subject to coverage constraints — the same bias–variance logic as 4.4, with domains as the axes.

title: 13.3 Training Pipeline
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (training × 10.4 backprop × A.2 MLE). The Section 1 toy model’s gradient (g = p; g[...] -= 1) is the softmax-cross-entropy gradient — derive it from scratch (softmax Jacobian, one-hot target) and verify it against finite differences on a 3×3 \(W\). Then state the general pattern: for any GLM with a canonical link, the gradient of the negative log-likelihood is (prediction − target) × features — the same form as A.3’s logistic gradient. This is why LLM training “just works” with generic autodiff: the loss surface is as well-behaved as logistic regression’s.
C2 (training × 12.2 multiple testing × 13.7). The field’s evaluation problem is 12.2 at industrial scale: every lab evaluates on overlapping benchmarks, selects the best checkpoint/prompt/mix, and reports the winner. Write the critique in the language of Part 12 — selection-as-inference, the winner’s curse, and the pre-registration fix — and state why the training-data version of the problem (contamination, Exercise 3) is the harder one to fix, because the training corpus is a moving target.

title: 13.3 Training Pipeline
text:
7. Summary

Pretraining = next-token maximum likelihood on a massive corpus; SFT teaches instruction format; RLHF/DPO aligns preferences — three stages, one objective family.
The training loop is 10.4’s loop; scale adds distributed training, mixed precision, and the LR schedule (warmup + cosine).
A neural bigram trained by GD converges to the counting estimate — cross-entropy MLE on one-hot inputs is the empirical conditional distribution (the multinomial version of A.2).
The loss floor is the data’s own entropy; zero loss means deterministic data, not a perfect model.
Data curation (dedup, quality, contamination control) matters more than architecture at the margin; the model learns the corpus’s biases as fluently as its facts.
Alignment shapes behavior but can’t create capability; reward hacking is the alignment-stage failure mode.
Next: 13.4 Model families and variants — the zoo of architectures these stages produce.

title: 13.1 LLM Foundations
text: A large language model is, at its core, a very simple machine: given the tokens so far, predict the next token. Everything else — the billion-parameter matrices, the trillion-token training runs, the eerie fluency — is scale and engineering wrapped around that one probabilistic loop. This page builds the loop by hand: tokenize text, train the simplest possible language model (a bigram counter), generate from it, and measure it with perplexity. 13.2 replaces the counter with attention.

title: 13.1 LLM Foundations
text:
1. Basic Concept
The autoregressive factorization. A sequence of tokens \(w_1, \dots, w_T\) has joint probability, by the chain rule:
\[P(w_1, \dots, w_T) = \prod_{t=1}^{T} P(w_t \mid w_1, \dots, w_{t-1})\]
An LLM is a parametric model of each conditional \(P(w_t \mid \text{context})\) — a distribution over the whole vocabulary, every step. Training = maximum likelihood over a massive corpus (next-token prediction); generation = sample one token, append it, repeat. Three ingredients make it work:

Tokenization — text → integer IDs from a fixed vocabulary (subword units, e.g. BPE, so any string is encodable).
Embeddings + transformer — IDs → vectors → context-mixing layers → logits over the vocabulary (13.2).
The sampling loop — softmax → temperature → sample → append → repeat, until an end-of-text token.

Worked example — the whole loop in 40 lines: a regex tokenizer, a bigram model (next token depends only on the current one), trained by counting:






Generation — sample from the conditional, append, continue:






The bigram model produces locally plausible, globally meaningless text — it has no memory beyond one token. That is exactly the gap the transformer’s attention mechanism fills (13.2): a context window of thousands of tokens instead of one.

title: 13.1 LLM Foundations
text:
2. Concept Questions

Why is next-token prediction — an objective with no semantics in it — enough to produce models that translate, summarize, and reason? What must be true of language for this to work?
In the generation loop, why do we sample from the softmax instead of always taking the argmax? What does temperature control, and what breaks at T → 0 and T → ∞?
The bigram model assigns probability zero to any word it has never seen follow the current token. Why is this a fatal flaw for real text, and what do real models do instead (two mechanisms)?
Why does the chain-rule factorization force left-to-right generation for decoder-only models — and what would break if you tried to sample the middle token first?
“Compression is understanding” — state the argument connecting next-token prediction to world knowledge, and state the strongest counterargument.



Answers


Language is highly predictable from context: grammar, facts, and style all constrain the next token. To predict well, the model must internalize the regularities that generate text — which is most of what we call knowledge and reasoning. The objective is simple; the data carries the semantics. (This is the “stochastic parrot” debate’s empirical side: the parrots got very good at predicting.)
Argmax gives deterministic, degenerate text — the model loops or collapses to safe high-frequency phrases. Sampling injects the variability of real language. Temperature sharpens (T→0: approaches argmax, repetitive) or flattens (T→∞: uniform noise, word salad) the distribution; T controls the creativity/fluency trade-off.
Real text is open-domain: any word can follow any context eventually. Zero probability = infinite perplexity on unseen continuations. Real models fix this with (i) subword tokenization (any string decomposes into known pieces) and (ii) smoothing/softmax over the full vocabulary — every token gets nonzero probability every step.
The model was trained on \(P(w_t \mid w_{<t})\) — conditionals only ever see left context. A middle token’s distribution under the model is defined by its left context alone; sampling it first would require a conditional the model never learned (that’s what masked/bidirectional models like BERT are for — 13.4). Autoregression is a consequence of the factorization, not a choice.
Argument: predicting the next token of arbitrary text requires modeling facts, style, and inference patterns — a good predictor must compress the training distribution, and compression requires capturing its structure (cf. Shannon). Counterargument: prediction can be gamed by surface statistics and memorization; a model can score well on next-token loss while failing at tasks requiring genuine causal or compositional reasoning — benchmark scores and capability are correlated, not identical.

title: 13.1 LLM Foundations
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Build a character-level bigram generator: tokenize the corpus into characters (keep spaces), train the same counting model, and generate 200 characters from seed “the”. Then compute its perplexity per character on a held-out string. Compare with the word-level model’s behavior — which produces more fluent output, which is more surprised by held-out text, and why?


Solution







The character model generates pronounceable nonsense (“the cat sat on the mat…”-ish fragments) — more locally fluent because character transitions are easy, but it invents words and its held-out perplexity is worse per unit of meaning: word-level units carry more probability mass per prediction. Word-level bigrams produce real words but incoherent discourse; char-level produces word-like strings but no semantics. Both fail at the same place: neither has memory beyond one unit. That failure is what motivates 13.2.

Exercise 2. Temperature as a calibration knob: using the word-level bigram from Section 1, generate 200 tokens at T ∈ {0.25, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0} and measure (a) the fraction of generated tokens that are “the”, (b) the number of distinct bigrams produced. Explain the trend and state when you’d want low vs high temperature in a real application.


Solution







Low T collapses onto the highest-probability path (“the cat sat…” loops, few distinct bigrams, “the” dominates); high T flattens toward uniform, producing rare and incoherent continuations. Practical rule: low T for factual/extractive tasks (QA, code, translation — you want the mode), high T for brainstorming/creative tasks — and note that even T=0.25 here is not deterministic, because the bigram distribution itself is flat; real models at T=0 are exactly deterministic.

Exercise 3. Smoothing fixes the zero-count flaw: add-α smoothing turns \(P(w_t \mid w_{t-1}) = \frac{\text{count} + \alpha}{\text{context count} + \alpha V}\). Implement it for the word bigram, then evaluate: with α ∈ {0, 0.1, 1, 10}, compute the probability of a held-out continuation “the zebra” (never seen) and the total probability mass the model now wastes on impossible continuations. State the bias–variance trade-off smoothing is making (4.4).


Solution







α=0: zero probability for “the zebra” — infinite perplexity on any novel text. Small α rescues unseen continuations at negligible cost; large α flattens everything toward uniform 1/V, destroying the signal (mass_wasted → 1). Smoothing trades a little bias (every context’s distribution pulled toward uniform) for a lot of variance reduction (no infinite losses) — the same trade-off as ridge (5.2), with α playing the role of λ. Real transformers don’t need explicit smoothing — the softmax over the full vocabulary with trained logits is already smooth — but the principle (never assign exactly zero) is identical.

title: 13.1 LLM Foundations
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Tokenization is a modeling choice with consequences: whitespace tokenization explodes vocabulary and breaks on morphology; BPE/WordPiece subword units compress vocabulary ~3× and make any string encodable — at the cost of language-dependent artifacts (tokenizing numbers, non-English text, or code differently than expected). Never assume “one word = one token.”
The context window is a hard wall: the model cannot attend to tokens outside its window (typically 4k–128k). Long documents must be chunked, summarized, or retrieved — the engineering problem 13.6’s RAG solves.
Perplexity is corpus-dependent: it measures fit to a specific test distribution. Cross-model comparisons are only meaningful on identical tokenizers and test sets — a classic benchmarking trap (13.7).
Greedy decoding is not “the model’s answer”: it’s the mode of a distribution. For evaluation you usually want sampling or beam search; for reproducibility you fix the seed — and even then, hardware/library versions can shift outputs.
“The model knows X” is shorthand: the model assigns high probability to continuations that resemble its training data. Memorization, reasoning, and confabulation are not cleanly separable from the outside — the evaluation problem of 13.7.
Emergence cuts both ways: capabilities that scale smoothly (translation quality) coexist with capabilities that appear abruptly (multi-step reasoning) — so “it can’t do X” is always a statement about a specific model size and prompt, never about the approach.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated “language model” has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Argmax instead of sampling: p is computed (and temperature applied!) but then ignored — np.argmax(p) on unnormalized counts takes the mode always, making temperature dead code and generation deterministic. Sample with np.random.choice(len(nxt), p=p / p.sum()).
Training on its own output: incrementing counts during generation mutates the model as it generates — a feedback loop that drifts toward whatever it just said (self-reinforcement, the degeneration behind “model collapse” in synthetic-data training).
Reporting a moving probability: after bug 2, the printed “probability” reflects the corrupted counts, not the trained model — and it’s computed without normalizing by the context total anyway.

title: 13.1 LLM Foundations
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Perplexity and bits-per-byte: show that perplexity $= (-_2 P) $ … precisely, define perplexity with natural log as \(\exp(-\frac{1}{T}\sum_t \ln P(w_t \mid w_{<t}))\) and show it equals the geometric mean of the reciprocal probabilities — the “effective branching factor.” Then convert: a model with 256k vocabulary has uniform perplexity 256,000; a byte-level model with the same predictive quality has perplexity 256. Why is comparing their raw perplexities meaningless, and what normalized quantity fixes it?


Hint

Perplexity is exponentiated average loss; the base of the log sets the units. Normalize by the number of bits each prediction carries.



Solution







Perplexity’s value depends on the log base and the token unit: the same underlying model quality gives wildly different perplexities depending on whether you predict words, subwords, or bytes. Bits-per-byte (or bits-per-character) divides out the unit: \(\log_2(\text{ppl}) / \text{bytes per token}\). That’s why compression benchmarks (enwik8/enwik9) report bpb, and why “model A has lower perplexity than model B” is meaningless unless tokenizers and test sets match — the unit-dependence is exactly the benchmarking trap of 13.7.

Q2. Why left-to-right? The chain rule permits any factorization order, yet decoder-only models (GPT) use left-to-right and encoder-only models (BERT) use masked bidirectional prediction. Derive what each factorization can and cannot express: show that \(P(w_t \mid w_{<t})\) can represent any distribution over sequences (universal approximation given enough capacity), while a masked model’s \(P(w_t \mid w_{\ne t})\) factorizations compose into a valid joint only under extra assumptions. Then state why left-to-right won for generation.


Hint

Any joint can be factored in any order — the question is which conditionals are useful to learn and usable at inference.



Solution

Left-to-right: \(P(w_{1:T}) = \prod_t P(w_t \mid w_{<t})\) — each conditional is a proper distribution over the vocabulary given a causal prefix, and generation is just repeated sampling: every conditional you need at inference time was a training target. Masked (BERT-style): \(P(w_t \mid w_{\ne t})\) — each target sees the whole sequence, which is perfect for representation (encoding) but useless for generation: to sample token \(t\) you need the other tokens, which you don’t have yet. You could sample all positions in parallel from the conditionals, but the conditionals assume the other positions are already filled — the model never learned a consistent joint this way (the “train/test mismatch” of masked LM: the [MASK] token never appears at inference). Encoder–decoder (T5) splits the difference: bidirectional encoding of the prefix, autoregressive decoding of the suffix. Left-to-right won for generation because its training objective is the inference procedure — no mismatch, no extra assumptions — and its weakness (no bidirectional context during training) was fixed by scale and by the bidirectional encoders inside the transformer (13.2, 13.4).

title: 13.1 LLM Foundations
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (foundations × 10.9 attention × 13.2). The bigram model’s conditional \(P(w_t \mid w_{t-1})\) is a lookup table with \(V\) parameters per context. The transformer computes \(P(w_t \mid w_{<t})\) with a softmax over \(V\) logits produced by attention. Write the bigram model in the same notation — logits = one-hot lookup, softmax over vocabulary — and identify exactly which component the transformer replaces (the context representation) and which it keeps (the softmax head). This is the conceptual bridge from classical n-gram language models (the 1.3 conditional-probability tradition) to LLMs.
C2 (foundations × 12.2 multiple testing × 13.7). A lab evaluates its model on 40 benchmark tasks and reports the 3 where it “beats the baseline.” Run the selection-as-inference simulation: 40 tasks, true null everywhere, per-task test at α = 0.05 — how often does at least one task “win”? Then state why leaderboard science needs the same family-wise discipline as genomics, and what pre-registration would look like for an LLM eval.

title: 13.1 LLM Foundations
text:
7. Summary

An LLM is next-token prediction: the chain rule turns text into a product of conditionals; training is maximum likelihood, generation is sample-and-append.
Tokenization (subword BPE) makes any string encodable and controls the vocabulary/perplexity units — never compare perplexities across tokenizers.
Temperature shapes the softmax: low = mode-seeking (facts, code), high = diversity (ideation); argmax is degenerate, uniform is noise.
Smoothing (or a full-vocabulary softmax) keeps every continuation possible — zero probability is infinite perplexity.
Perplexity = exponentiated average NLL = effective branching factor; bits-per-byte is the unit-invariant version.
Left-to-right factorization won because training and inference use the same conditional — no train/test mismatch.
The bigram’s one-token memory is the gap attention fills — up next: 13.2 Transformer architecture.

title: 12.4 False Discovery Rate
text: FDR reframes the guarantee: instead of “no false positives” (FWER, brutal at scale), control the expected proportion of false discoveries among your rejections. The Benjamini–Hochberg procedure delivers exactly that — and it is the operating standard of genomics, where discovery lists, not single verdicts, are the product.

title: 12.4 False Discovery Rate
text:
1. Basic Concept
Definitions with R = number of rejections, V = false rejections:
\[\text{FDR} = E\left[\frac{V}{\max(R, 1)}\right] \le q\]
Benjamini–Hochberg: sort p-values; find the largest k with p₍ₖ₎ ≤ (k/m)·q; reject the k smallest. Implemented from the definition:






BH’s promise on mixed families — verified by simulation:

title: 12.4 False Discovery Rate
text:
2. Concept Questions

State the exact difference between FWER = P(V ≥ 1) and FDR = E[V/max(R, 1)] — and compute both for a study with R = 100, V = 3.
Why is FDR ≤ q weaker than FWER ≤ q, yet often the better guarantee? Give the discovery-screen argument.
BH’s threshold line (k/m)·q grows with rank — what is the procedure “spending” on the largest p-values, and why doesn’t that blow up the FDR?
Under what two conditions does BH control FDR exactly, and what happens to the guarantee under strong negative dependence?
Your q = 0.05 analysis rejects 60 of 20,000 genes. Translate “q-value of gene 17 is 0.03” into a precise frequentist sentence — and contrast it with a Bonferroni sentence for the same gene.



Answers


FWER: P(V ≥ 1) = 1 here (some false exist). FDR: E[V/max(R,1)] = 3/100 = 0.03 — a 3% expected contamination rate among the list. FWER says “any falsehood counts once”; FDR says “the list’s purity, on average.”
Weaker: FDR ≤ q permits some studies with contaminated lists (compensated by clean ones). Better: at discovery scale, demanding zero false positives sacrifices enormous power; controlling list purity at 5% keeps most true discoveries while capping contamination — the only workable contract for 10⁴-test screens.
The line spends more allowance on larger p-values (the (k/m)q budget grows with rank) — rejections at the tail are the cheapest tests of the “more signal exists” hypothesis (if the k-th smallest p is that small, the alternative is strongly implicated there). BH’s proof shows the budget stays calibrated because the tail rejections are backed by the accumulated evidence of all smaller p’s.
Independent p-values, or positively regression-dependent on the truth (PRDS — roughly: bigger |signal| → stochastically smaller other p’s, true for one-sided normal/χ² settings). Under strong negative dependence BH can exceed q; adapted procedures (BY: q·Σ1/k) restore control at a power price.
“Gene 17’s q-value 0.03: among discovery lists produced at threshold q = 0.03 by this procedure, an expected 3% of rejections are false — gene 17 is in such a list.” Bonferroni sentence: “gene 17’s p ≤ 0.05/20,000, i.e., the family contained no false positive with 95% probability” — a far harder bar, answering a different question.

title: 12.4 False Discovery Rate
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. FDR calibration across the truth-proportion axis: at q = 0.05, simulate m = 5,000 tests with true-signal fraction ∈ {0%, 5%, 20%, 50%} (strong effects for the signal block); measure realized FDP among rejections and power. Verify: FDP ≤ q in every regime, power rises with signal fraction. Then compute the Bayesian-flavored quantity — among rejections, the posterior-ish probability a rejection is true (= power·π₁/FDR-ish decomposition) — and note where the frequentist guarantee and the intuition align.


Solution







FDP ≤ 0.05 in all four regimes — BH’s guarantee is regime-robust; power climbs from 0 (no signal) to near-total (50% signal). The alignment: with π₁ true alternatives, an FDR-of-0.05 list’s rejections are ~true with probability related to power·π₁/(power·π₁ + q·(stuff)) — the frequentist list-purity and the Bayesian “probability this hit is real” track each other closely when the signal is dense, which is why q-values read so naturally.

Exercise 2. BH vs Bonferroni vs Holm — the power face-off at realistic omics scale: m = 10,000, 100 true effects (two sizes: 50 strong, 50 weak), n = 15/group. Compare all three procedures at family level 0.05: true discoveries, false discoveries, and FDP. Then repeat at n = 40/group. Which procedure’s advantage grows with n, and why does the weak-effect block decide it?


Solution







At n = 15 neither finds the weak block; BH beats Bonferroni modestly. At n = 40 the weak effects become detectable: BH picks up a large share of them (its rank-growing threshold rewards a mass of moderate p-values) while Bonferroni’s flat 5 × 10⁻⁶ wall still blocks every weak effect — the gap explodes. Weak-but-real effects are BH’s comparative advantage; that’s the genomics use case.

Exercise 3. Storey’s π₀ and adaptive BH: estimate π₀ (Storey, λ = 0.5) on a mixture with 80% nulls, then run adaptive BH with effective m′ = π̂₀·m (threshold (k/m′)q) — rejecting more when many nulls are suspected. Compare adaptive vs standard BH by realized FDP and power on (a) 90%-null and (b) 20%-null families. When does adaptivity pay, when is it dangerous (π̂₀ under-estimated → FDR inflated), and what guard (capped π̂₀, bootstrap-smoothed λ) would you code?


Solution

title: 12.4 False Discovery Rate
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Three summary languages: rejection sets, BH-adjusted p-values, q-values — related, not identical; label which you printed.
BH assumes independence/PRDS: verify via histograms and null simulations; use BY (Benjamini–Yekutieli, thresholds q·k/(m·Σ1/j)) under arbitrary dependence at a power cost.
Storey’s λ: the π₀ estimator’s tuning point; λ too small over-counts true nulls’ p-values above it… check sensitivity across λ ∈ {0.3, 0.5, 0.7} before believing π̂₀.
FDR vs per-gene error: “q = 0.03” is not “3% chance this gene is null” — it’s the expected false proportion in the discovery list at that threshold.
Power at fixed q rises with π₁ (the truth fraction): sparse-signal regimes need stricter pre-filtering or larger n to make lists worth reporting.
Replication remains king: a q-value is a calibration claim about a procedure; an independent-cohort replication is the biological confirmation.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated FDR analysis has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Flat q threshold: that’s a per-test α (and here it even rejects p = 0.75… no — 0.75 > 0.05, but the set semantics are Bonferroni-lite, not BH). FDR thresholds grow with rank.
Unsorted rank alignment: BH compares the k-th smallest p to (k/m)q — after sorting, with set-monotonicity (reject all up to the last passing rank). The unsorted version matches ranks to the wrong order statistics.
“FDR” from non-rejections: FDR is about the rejection list’s expected contamination — estimated by simulation with known truth, or reported as the q-guarantee; the fraction of large p-values is π₀-territory (Exercise 3’s estimator), not FDR.

title: 12.4 False Discovery Rate
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Prove BH controls FDR at q under independent p-values: with m₀ true nulls, show E[V/max(R,1)] ≤ (m₀/m)·q ≤ q — the famous m₀/m factor (Storey’s sharpening). The proof’s engine: for each true null i, P(pᵢ ≤ (k/m)q) = (k/m)q, and the rejection-rank argument conditions on R = k. Verify the m₀/m sharpening numerically: simulate m = 1000, m₀ = 800 (80% nulls) at q = 0.1 and confirm realized FDR ≈ 0.08 < 0.1.


Hint

E[V/max(R,1)] = Σₖ E[V·1(R=k)]/k and each true null’s rejection probability at BH’s k-th threshold is exactly (k/m)q; sum the geometric-ish series and factor m₀/m.



Solution

BH rejects 1..k where k = max{i: p₍ᵢ₎ ≤ iq/m}. For a true null i, P(pᵢ ≤ iq/m) = iq/m; summing over the rejection event and dividing by k (the max(R,1) denominators telescope the sum): E[V/max(R,1)] = (m₀/m)·q ≤ q. Simulation:






Realized FDR lands near 0.08 = (m₀/m)·q — the sharpening is real, and Storey’s adaptive q-values exploit exactly this factor. The theorem’s reach explains BH’s dominance: a guarantee that tightens automatically as true signal accumulates.

Q2. Dependent p-values, quantified: simulate m = 500 tests as correlated z-scores via a one-factor model (correlation ρ ∈ {0, 0.4, 0.8}), with 5% true signals. Measure BH’s realized FDR at q = 0.05 across ρ. BH’s theory (PRDS) predicts control holds under positive dependence — verify, then break it deliberately with negative dependence (z₂ = Z − ε structure) and show FDR inflation. What practical dependence diagnostics would you run before trusting BH on a real omics dataset?


Solution







Positive dependence (PRDS): FDR holds at ≈ q — BH is robust to the good kind of correlation. Negative dependence: FDR inflates past q — the guarantee’s actual boundary. Diagnostics before trusting BH: p-value histogram shape (12.2 Exercise 3), pairwise correlation of test statistics, permutation-based null p-values (12.5) which automatically inherit the true dependence structure.

title: 12.4 False Discovery Rate
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (FDR × 5.6 high-dimensional × 11.5 Cox). FDR for survival biomarkers: n = 100 patients, p = 400 genes, Cox score tests per gene (p-values from the partial-likelihood z), 15 truly prognostic. Apply BH at q = 0.05 and evaluate: realized FDP, power, and the stability of the gene set across bootstrap resamples (9.6’s selection-frequency idea). Then compare against Bonferroni-gated selection. Write the omics-methods paragraph: BH at q, selection frequencies, replication requirement — the full sentence chain.
C2 (FDR × 9.3 missing values × 12.5). FDR on imputed data: simulate 30% missingness in a 2,000-test family; run BH on (a) p-values from complete data, (b) p-values after single mean-imputation, (c) p-values pooled across 10 multiple-imputation datasets (Rubin-style combination or the minimum-p shortcut with disclosure). Measure realized FDR and power against the complete-data truth. Which route keeps the FDR guarantee — and what does the answer imply about running BH on silently imputed omics matrices?

title: 12.4 False Discovery Rate
text:
7. Summary

FDR = E[V/max(R,1)] ≤ q: list-purity control — the operating contract of discovery science at scale.
BH: sort p, threshold (k/m)q, reject up to the last crossing; q-values give each hypothesis its own threshold.
BH’s guarantee is regime-robust (independence/PRDS), sharpens with signal (m₀/m factor), and is weaker but cheaper than FWER by design.
Power over Bonferroni concentrates on weak-but-real effects at scale — the genomics payoff.
Purity is an expectation: single studies can be fully contaminated; report null simulations alongside.
Permutation p-values feed BH the dependence-honest nulls it deserves: 12.5 Resampling for p-values and FDR.

title: 12.2 Why Multiple Testing Is Dangerous
text: Every test is a small false-positive machine (rate α). Run many and the machines compound: 100 perfect-null tests at α = 0.05 will produce ≈ 5 “discoveries” — guaranteed, with no bug, no misconduct. This page makes the danger visceral with the simulations that should be run before every large-scale analysis.

title: 12.2 Why Multiple Testing Is Dangerous
text:
1. Basic Concept
For m independent tests of true nulls at per-test level α:
\[P(\text{at least one false positive}) = 1 - (1 - \alpha)^m\]
— which hits 0.92 at m = 50 and ≈ 1 at m = 500. And the expected number of false positives is m·α — linear, unstoppable without correction:






The genomics-scale demonstration — 5,000 null genes, “significant” hits guaranteed:

title: 12.2 Why Multiple Testing Is Dangerous
text:
2. Concept Questions

Why doesn’t “each test is valid at 5%” defend a paper reporting 3 of 200 findings as significant?
The “look-elsewhere effect”: you test one biomarker, p = 0.06, then try 7 subgroups until p < 0.05. What’s the actual family size, and what does that make your p = 0.049?
Why do p-value histograms diagnose the danger (uniform blob vs left-spiked)? Sketch both and what each implies.
A big-data analysis reports 500 significant findings. Give two scenarios — one benign, one damning — consistent with that number.
Why is the danger worst exactly where multiple testing is most tempting (high-dimensional biology)?



Answers


“Each test valid at 5%” is a per-test guarantee. The paper’s claim rests on the selected findings — selection among 200 tests at α = 0.05 has family-wise error near 1 − 0.95²⁰⁰ ≈ 1.0: essentially all “significant” trios are noise-shaped. Selection voids per-test calibration (4.1’s selection bonus, p-value edition).
The family is all tests considered: 1 + 7 = 8 (at least — the subgroups tried-and-abandoned count too). The “p = 0.049” is the minimum of 8 draws, not a 4.9% event — its honest multiplicity-adjusted p is several times larger.
Under H₀, p-values are uniform (12.1); under H₁ they pile up near 0. Histogram: flat = nothing but noise; left spike + flat remainder = real signal riding on noise (the spike’s mass = discoveries, the flat part = the multiplicity battlefield). No left spike + “significant findings” = findings are noise.
Benign: large true effects, strong power — 500 of 20,000 tests genuinely differential (with left-spiked histogram, effect-size consistency). Damning: pure noise with “significance” manufactured by testing 20,000 × many subtypes/corrections-until-significant — the count alone is uninformative without the null comparison (Section 3’s exercises).
Temptation scales with tests available (20,000 genes × subgroups × timepoints) and with per-test noise (small n, high variance) — both push m·α up while weakening each test. The frontier of biology is the frontier of this problem.

title: 12.2 Why Multiple Testing Is Dangerous
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. The candidate-gene era vs the genome era: simulate screening 20 candidate genes (5 truly differential, effect 1.0) vs 20,000 genome-wide genes (same 5 real). At α = 0.05 per test, report for both: expected true discoveries, expected false discoveries, and the false discovery proportion (FDP). Show that the same per-test α is a reasonable policy in one world and a catastrophe in the other — the quantitative case for FDR (12.4).


Solution







Candidates: 5 tests, ~0.75 false hits among ~3 true — FDP tolerable. Genome-wide: 20,000 tests manufacture ~1,000 false hits to accompany 3–4 true — FDP ≈ 99.7%. Same α, opposite conclusions: the proportion of tests that are true governs whether uncorrected testing is defensible, which is precisely the quantity FDR methods control.

Exercise 2. The subgroup expedition: one treatment trial (n = 400, tiny true effect 0.15 — nearly null), tested overall plus in 16 post-hoc subgroups (defined after the fact, some overlapping). Simulate 2,000 such trials; report: P(overall test significant), P(at least one subgroup significant), P(at least one significant and overall not). Then compute the probability that the pattern looks like “overall null but a subgroup benefits” — the exact shape that launches a junk hypothesis.


Solution







Overall: ≈ 12–15% (the 0.15 effect barely misses). Any-subgroup: ≈ 60–80% — sixteen chances at α = 0.05 with correlated tests. “Subgroup hit with null overall” — the most publishable-looking accident — occurs in a third or more of truly-null-ish trials. The fix is structural: pre-registered subgroups, hierarchical testing (overall → subgroups only if overall passes, 12.3), and replication.

Exercise 3. Build the “null calibration report”: given any vector of p-values from an analysis, produce (a) the p-value histogram with expected-uniform line, (b) an estimate of π₀ (the proportion of true nulls) via the simple Storey method (π̂₀ = #{p > λ}/((1−λ)m) for λ = 0.5, smoothed), (c) the observed-vs-expected count of p < 0.05. Run it on three synthetic scenarios — all-null, 5% signal, 40% signal — and write the one-line readout your report would show for each.


Solution







Readouts: all-null → π̂₀ ≈ 1, P(p < .05) ≈ 0.05 (pure multiplicity noise); 5% signal → π̂₀ < 1 with a modest left spike; 40% signal → π̂₀ drops far below 1 with a heavy spike. The report converts “we found hits” into “here is the evidence calibration of the whole family” — the report a reviewer can actually judge, and the input that Storey-style q-values (12.4) formalize.

title: 12.2 Why Multiple Testing Is Dangerous
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

The garden of forking paths (Gelman): multiplicity includes analysis choices never written down — exclusions, transforms, outlier rules, model forms. The tested-family count is usually understated because the unrecorded attempts aren’t counted (4.1’s hidden selection).
Correlated tests soften the explosion but don’t remove it: 1−(1−α)^m is the independent bound; strongly correlated tests behave like fewer effective tests — better than independence, still compounding.
“We replicated internally” on the same dataset (split by site/batch and re-test): only a true independent replication counts; internal splits share the selection history.
Exploratory vs confirmatory is a design label, not a vibe: exploratory analyses are legitimate — as hypothesis generators requiring pre-registered replication, never as confirmatory findings (3.7’s selection-vs-reporting split).
Big n doesn’t fix multiplicity: larger n powers more tiny true effects (good) but the null tests still produce m·α false positives (bad); the FDP depends on the true-signal proportion, not on n.
The correction is cheap; the discipline is the hard part: Bonferroni is one line of code — the institutional practice of pre-specification is what Part 12 actually teaches.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated “screening report” has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


3,000 tests at α = 0.05: ≈ 150 false hits guaranteed — the count is the multiplicity artifact. Correct with BH (12.4) and report the null-calibration (Exercise 3).
Internal “validation” on the same matrix’s halves: the hits were selected using these rows; splitting them re-tests correlated noise — not replication.
Selected effects as discovered signal: the winner’s effect is an order statistic, biased away from 0 (4.1 Q2); report selection-adjusted estimates or label everything exploratory.

title: 12.2 Why Multiple Testing Is Dangerous
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Prove the expected number of false positives is exactly mα under independent nulls and under arbitrary dependence (linearity of expectation needs no independence) — while the P(any) bound requires independence (or Bonferroni: P(any) ≤ mα, Markov). Verify both claims by simulation under (a) independent and (b) perfectly correlated p-values. What does this asymmetry (expectation robust, tail bound fragile) predict about FDR vs FWER control under dependence?


Hint

E[Σ1ᵢ] = ΣE[1ᵢ] = mα always; P(∪Aᵢ) ≤ ΣP(Aᵢ) is Markov, tight only under disjointness/independence.



Solution

E[count] = ΣᵢP(pᵢ ≤ α) = mα by linearity — holds under any dependence structure (this is why FDR, which targets the expectation, generalizes gracefully). The tail P(any) needs the union bound: ≤ mα (Bonferroni), equality-ish only under (near-)independence; perfectly correlated p-values act as ONE test — P(any) = α, far below mα. Simulation:






Prediction: FDR (expectation-based, BH) is robust to common dependence forms (BH holds under PRDS); FWER procedures calibrated under independence can over- or under-cover under exotic dependence — the reason resampling-based FWER control exists (12.5).

Q2. The inverted-detection trap: with 20,000 tests at FDR q = 0.05 and zero true effects, E[false discoveries] = 0.05·20,000·(something)? No — BH’s guarantee is FDR ≤ q, i.e., E[V/R] ≤ q. Design the simulation showing BH’s behavior on pure nulls (how many rejections, what realized FDP) and explain why “BH rejected 47 genes so ~47 are false” is wrong, while “expected FDP among rejections ≤ 5%” is right — including what FDP means when R = 0.


Solution







BH on pure nulls rejects a handful of genes in some studies (realized FDP = 1 in those studies — every rejection false!) while the expected proportion stays ≤ q across studies. The guarantee is about the long-run contamination rate of your discovery lists, not about any single list’s content — and R = 0 studies (FDP defined as 0) keep the average down. This subtlety is exactly why FDR is “the expected false discovery proportion,” and why single-study FDP claims need the simulation-based augmentation of 12.5.

title: 12.2 Why Multiple Testing Is Dangerous
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (danger × 9.x × 4.6). The unsupervised multiplicity census, measured: simulate data with no clusters; run the full clustering circus (K-means k = 2..8, hierarchical with 4 linkages, two scalings — 56 analyses); declare “structure found” by your favorite internal index. Estimate the false-discovery rate of “we found clusters” across 500 null datasets. Then estimate it again with the pre-registered discipline of 9.6 (fixed k, fixed algorithm, stability gate).
