Quantify the discipline’s FDR reduction — the experiment that justifies pre-registration in unsupervised biology.
C2 (danger × 7.4 forest importances × 12.4). Importance lists are multiple testing too: on null data (no signal), fit a random forest 100 times (resamples, seeds) and record which features enter the top-5 importances at least once. What fraction of features earn “top-5 at least once” status across 40 pure-noise features? Then run the same with a real signal. Design the permutation-test-based importance gate that separates the two worlds — implementing the null first, as 12.5 teaches.

title: 12.2 Why Multiple Testing Is Dangerous
text:
7. Summary

m tests at α ⇒ ≈ mα false positives (always) and P(any) → 1 (fast): multiplicity is arithmetic, not misconduct.
Selection (min-p, subgroup hunting, best-of-many) converts calibration into optimism — before any model is fit.
p-value histograms and π₀ estimates diagnose how much of your family is noise vs signal.
Per-test validity survives; family-level claims die without correction — the corrections are Part 12’s next three pages.
Exploratory ≠ confirmatory: the label must match the design, and replication must be independent.
The corrections and their power trade-offs: 12.3 Family-wise error rate.

title: 11.5 Cox Proportional Hazards Regression
text:
The Cox proportional hazards model regresses survival on covariates without assuming any baseline hazard shape:
\[h(t \mid x) = h_0(t)\, e^{\beta^\top x}\]
h₀(t) stays unspecified (a nonparametric nuisance); β’s exponentials are hazard ratios. The partial likelihood — which conditions on the risk sets, discarding h₀ — is what makes this possible, and the binary-covariate Cox is literally the log-rank test (11.3).

title: 11.5 Cox Proportional Hazards Regression
text:
1. Basic Concept
The partial log-likelihood (Breslow ties):
\[\ell(\beta) = \sum_{i: \delta_i = 1} \Big[ \beta^\top x_i - \log \sum_{j \in R_i} e^{\beta^\top x_j} \Big]\]
— each event compares its covariates against everyone still at risk. Fitted with statsmodels, interpreted as hazard ratios:






The sanity anchor — binary covariate Cox ≈ log-rank (11.3):

title: 11.5 Cox Proportional Hazards Regression
text:
2. Concept Questions

What does “partial” likelihood partially out, and why doesn’t the unspecified h₀(t) bias β?
State the proportional-hazards assumption in terms of two patients’ hazards — and what it implies about their hazard ratio over time.
HR = 1.4 per SD of a biomarker. Write the full clinical sentence — including the word “instantaneous” and where it sits.
Why does Cox regression use only event-ordering information (the partial likelihood throws away actual time values), and what stays valid — estimation of β or prediction of S(t)?
A covariate violates PH (effect fades after year 2). Name three legitimate responses, in escalating modeling effort.



Answers


It partials out the baseline hazard h₀(t): each event’s likelihood compares the covariate pattern of the failer against the risk set at that moment — h₀(t) multiplies everyone in both numerator and denominator and cancels. β estimation needs only the ordering structure of events and risk sets.
h(t | x₁) / h(t | x₂) = e^{βᵀ(x₁−x₂)} — constant over time. Their hazard ratio never changes; their absolute hazards both follow the same unspecified h₀ shape.
“Each additional SD of the biomarker multiplies the instantaneous event rate by 1.4 at every time point, holding other covariates fixed” — a relative-rate statement whose absolute benefit depends on the (unmodeled) baseline hazard (11.4 Q3).
The partial likelihood discards information about how long follow-up intervals were and where events sit on the time axis (only their order vs risk sets matters). β estimation: fully valid — it’s the MLE of the Cox model. Absolute survival prediction S(t|x): NOT available without estimating h₀ (Breslow baseline) — a real limitation for risk-prediction uses.

Split follow-up at the divergence time (time-dependent effect via epoch dummies); (2) add time-varying/interaction terms (x × log t); (3) switch to models with non-PH machinery — AFT, RMST-based comparisons, or stratified Cox (baseline per group).

title: 11.5 Cox Proportional Hazards Regression
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. The partial likelihood, by hand: for 4 subjects with covariates x = (0, 1, 2, 1), events at times 1, 2, 3 (subject 4 censored at 4), write the partial log-likelihood as a function of β: at each event, numerator e^{βxᵢ} and denominator the risk-set sum. Then maximize it numerically (scipy.optimize) and verify against PHReg on the same data. Which risk sets appear in each term — and which subject appears in no denominator?


Solution







Risk sets: event at t = 1 → everyone (all ≥ 1); t = 2 → subjects 2, 3, 4; t = 3 → subjects 3, 4. Subject 4 appears in all three denominators (censored after everything) — a censored last subject contributes plenty of partial-likelihood mass despite never eventing. The correction to the printout’s tease: censoring removes subjects from later risk sets, never from earlier ones.

Exercise 2. PH diagnostics with Schoenfeld residuals: simulate Cox data (β = 0.8, PH holds) and non-PH data (β decays: 0.8·exp(−t/2) effect via two hazard regimes). Fit PHReg to each and compute the trend of Schoenfeld residuals against event time (correlation of residual × event-time). Verify: near-zero trend under PH, clear trend under violation. Then state the decision this diagnostic drives (time-varying term vs stratification vs RMST).


Solution







Under PH the Schoenfeld residuals scatter unsystematically around 0 (trend ≈ 0); under violation they drift with time — the residual is the time-varying beta signal. Decision: a flagged trend → add x × log(t) interaction, or stratify, or present RMST — but always with the diagnostic plot attached, not just the test p-value.

Exercise 3. Risk prediction from Cox: Breslow baseline + linear predictor. Fit Cox on training data; extract fit.baseline_cumulative_hazard_ (statsmodels provides the baseline estimate); build S(t|x) = exp(−H₀(t)·e^{βᵀx}) for two new patients; validate calibration on test data (predicted vs KM-observed survival in risk-score terciles). This closes the “Cox can’t predict absolutely” gap from Concept Question 4 — with the baseline hazard doing the absolute work.


Solution







The Breslow baseline converts relative risks into absolute survival — the bridge from “HR = 2.46 per SD” to “this patient has 63% predicted survival at 2 years.” Tercile calibration (predicted vs observed within risk groups) is the minimum reporting for any clinical risk model: without it, HRs and AUCs say nothing about whether the level of predicted risk is right.

title: 11.5 Cox Proportional Hazards Regression
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Ties: Efron’s method handles tied events more accurately than Breslow and is the recommended default (statsmodels accepts ties=; survival software defaults vary — check yours).
PH violation handling ladder: (1) verify (log-minus-log plots, Schoenfeld tests — 11.4 Exercise 2); (2) split follow-up or add interactions; (3) stratified Cox (separate h₀ per stratum — loses that stratum’s HR but keeps others); (4) time-varying coefficients or alternative models (AFT, RMST).
Stratified Cox: baseline hazards per stratum, shared β — adjust for strong confounders without requiring their PH; can’t give HRs for the stratification variable itself.
Time-varying covariates: values that change during follow-up need the counting-process (start–stop) data format (PHReg supports exit/entry); naive “baseline value carried forward” biases toward baseline-era effects.
Cox doesn’t extrapolate h₀: predictions beyond observed follow-up inherit the baseline’s endpoint — the same range-policing as every model (2.1), plus a baseline-estimation caveat.
Report alongside HRs: absolute survival curves by covariate pattern (Exercise 3), event counts, median follow-up — HR-only reporting is a review flag.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated Cox pipeline has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Dropping censored rows: deletes at-risk information and biases β (the informative-censoring sin of 11.1); censored rows carry partial-likelihood denominators. Fit on all rows.
No PH check in the workflow: even when this simulation is PH, production code must run the Schoenfeld/log-minus-log diagnostics — the model’s central assumption deserves a test, not hope.
HR as risk reduction: HR is an instantaneous rate ratio — “risk reduced by 27%” conflates rate with cumulative risk (11.4 Q3); report “hazard ratio” with survival curves for absolute statements.

title: 11.5 Cox Proportional Hazards Regression
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Show that the binary-covariate Cox score test equals the log-rank test: with a single 0/1 covariate, write the partial-likelihood score U(β) = Σᵢ∈events [xᵢ − weighted mean of x over Rᵢ] at β = 0 and verify it equals Σⱼ(O₁ⱼ − E₁ⱼ) from 11.3’s table. Verify numerically that the Cox score statistic and log-rank χ² agree to machine precision without ties. What does the derivation explain about the Cox model’s relationship to every stratified/weighted log-rank variant?


Hint

At β = 0 all weights in the risk-set averages are equal (1/nᵢ), so x’s weighted risk-set mean is the risk-set’s group-1 fraction — exactly E₁ⱼ’s building block.



Solution

At β = 0, the risk-set mean of x in Rᵢ is n₁ᵢ/nᵢ (fraction of at-risk in group 1), so U(0) = Σ_{events i}(xᵢ − n₁ᵢ/nᵢ) = Σⱼ[(# events in group 1 at j) − dⱼn₁ⱼ/nⱼ] = Σⱼ(O₁ⱼ − E₁ⱼ) — the log-rank numerator, term by term; the variances match likewise (both hypergeometric per risk set).






The identity explains the whole family: stratified log-rank = Cox with strata; weighted log-ranks = Cox variants with time-weighted score contributions; and “Cox with covariates” is simply the log-rank generalized to continuous adjustment. Learning Cox is learning the generalization of the test you already built.

Q2. Partial likelihood vs full likelihood — what’s lost: write the full likelihood for censored exponential data and the Cox partial likelihood; identify the h₀-dependent factor the partial version drops. Then demonstrate the practical consequence: fit Cox and exponential-AML (accelerated) on Weibull-generated data; compare β estimates (should be similar-ish) and absolute survival predictions (where they diverge). State the rule: β questions vs S(t) questions route to different models.


Solution

Full likelihood: ∏ᵢ [h₀(tᵢ)e^{βxᵢ}]^{δᵢ} · exp(−H₀(tᵢ)e^{βxᵢ}) — the second factor (cumulative-hazard term) involves h₀ and is what the partial likelihood discards by conditioning on risk sets. Consequence demo:






β estimates agree in direction and roughly in magnitude under this exponential truth (Cox’s β = −AFT’s b), but absolute S(t|x) predictions require the baseline: Cox needs the Breslow estimate (previous page’s exercise), AFT carries its scale parameter natively. Rule: questions about relative hazards (does the biomarker matter?) → Cox partial likelihood; questions about predicted survival times → parametric/AFT or baseline-augmented Cox. Choosing the wrong one means answering a different question with high confidence.

title: 11.5 Cox Proportional Hazards Regression
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (Cox × 5.3 lasso × 12.4). Penalized Cox for wide survival data: n = 150 patients, p = 80 genes, 6 truly prognostic. Implement L2-penalized Cox by hand (partial-likelihood gradient + ridge — extend your 11.6 gradient code) with penalty tuned by CV on the partial-likelihood deviance. Compare against unpenalized Cox (fails or unstable at p ≈ n/2) by test-set concordance. Write the survival-analyst’s regularization paragraph — the workflow for omics-Cox.
C2 (Cox × 9.4 clustering × 6.7 GAM preview). From clusters to survival signatures: cluster patients on baseline features (K-means k = 3), fit Cox with cluster dummies + clinical covariates, and plot KM per cluster adjusted (Cox-based predicted survival per cluster). Simulate data where cluster membership truly modifies survival vs where the apparent cluster effect is confounded by age. Quantify both fits’ age-adjusted HRs and write the paragraph that separates “risk signature” from “confounded grouping” — the applied microbiology of cluster-then-survive.

title: 11.5 Cox Proportional Hazards Regression
text:
7. Summary

Cox: h(t|x) = h₀(t)e^{βᵀx}; h₀ unspecified; partial likelihood conditions on risk sets — β without distributional assumptions.
HRs: e^β multiplicative, time-constant under PH; absolute predictions need the Breslow baseline.
PH is testable and central: log-minus-log plots, Schoenfeld residuals; violations have a response ladder.
Ties: Efron preferred; the binary-covariate Cox is the log-rank (score-test identity).
Time-varying covariates need start–stop formatting; stratified Cox trades a stratum’s HR for assumption safety.
Wide-data Cox needs penalization (11.6 builds it); HR-only reporting is incomplete — absolute curves required.
With classical survival in hand, the ML frontier: penalized/predictive survival models — 11.6 Survival ML.

title: 11.3 The Log-Rank Test
text: Two KM curves look different — is the difference real? The log-rank test compares observed vs expected events at every event time and combines them: the standard nonparametric two-group survival comparison, null-calibrated by construction, and here built from its risk-table atoms.

title: 11.3 The Log-Rank Test
text:
1. Basic Concept
At each event time tⱼ: observed events in group 1 (O₁ⱼ) vs expected under the null of equal hazards (E₁ⱼ = dⱼ·n₁ⱼ/nⱼ). Sum over times:
\[\chi^2 = \frac{(O_1 - E_1)^2}{V}, \qquad V = \sum_j \frac{d_j (n_j - d_j)\, n_{1j}\, n_{2j}}{n_j^2 (n_j - 1)} \sim \chi^2_1 \text{ under } H_0\]
Hand-rolled, then verified against statsmodels’ survdiff:






Same machinery inside a full report — the number clinicians expect:

title: 11.3 The Log-Rank Test
text:
2. Concept Questions

“Expected events” E₁ⱼ assumes what null hypothesis exactly — and why does the at-risk ratio n₁ⱼ/nⱼ make the test robust to censoring-pattern differences between groups?
Why combine (O − E) over all event times instead of running one χ² per time — what does the summation buy statistically?
The log-rank weights all event times equally. Name a weighting alternative and the alternative-hypothesis shape it targets.
Your log-rank is “significant” with p = 0.04 — the KM curves cross at year 3. What’s the caveat, and which plot accompanies the p-value?
The test is unadjusted. What does that mean in a randomized trial vs an observational cohort — and which page’s machinery adjusts (11.5)?



Answers


H₀: both groups share the same underlying hazard function at every time (S₁(t) = S₂(t) identically). Under it, each event time’s dⱼ events distribute across groups in proportion to at-risk counts — hypergeometric expectation with the n₁ⱼ/nⱼ ratio — so censoring that differs by group is absorbed through each time’s risk sets.
Per-time counts are ~1 event — no power. Summing accumulates signal across all times into one statistic with a known χ²₁ null (hypergeometric variances add independently across times): the Mantel–Cox construction.
Weighted log-rank variants: Gehan–Breslow (weight nⱼ — early times), Tarone–Ware (√nⱼ), Fleming–Harrington (s-specific: late-heavy with (p, q) versions). Targets: early vs late hazard differences — the choice is a hypothesis about when curves diverge.
Log-rank has best power for proportional hazards (constant separation); crossing curves can cancel (excess early events in one group, late in the other → O ≈ E overall). Always present the KM plot — and consider crossing-specific tests or restricted mean survival time (RMST) comparisons.
In a randomized trial, unadjusted is valid (randomization balances covariates in expectation). In observational data, confounding contaminates the comparison — Cox regression with covariates (11.5) is the adjusted analog.

title: 11.3 The Log-Rank Test
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Build logrank_table(t, e, group) returning the per-event-time risk table with O₁ⱼ, E₁ⱼ, Vⱼ columns, plus the totals — the transparent version of the test. Verify against statsmodels.survdiff on real-ish data. Then answer: which single event time contributes the most to (O₁ − E₁), and what does that time represent in the KM plot (11.2)?


Solution







The largest contributor is typically where the KM curves gape widest — mid-follow-up where at-risk sets are still large but separation has developed. The table turns the test into readable evidence: each row is a moment of comparison.

Exercise 2. Crossing curves defeat log-rank — demonstrated: arm A has high early hazard then low; arm B constant. Simulate via piecewise exponentials (A: rate 1.5 for t < 1, then 0.2; B: rate 0.6 throughout). Run log-rank (expect weak/insignificant despite a real, clinically huge difference) and then compare restricted mean survival time (RMST) up to τ = 3 by integrating each KM curve (trapezoid on your 11.2 step curves). Report log-rank p vs RMST difference. Write the rule about crossing hazards.


Solution







Crossing curves: early excess deaths in A cancel late ones, so the log-rank statistic — which weights all times equally — washes the difference out. RMST (expected event-free time within τ) summarizes the whole curve and answers “how much survival time does the treatment buy within 3 years” — a clinically direct quantity immune to the crossing pathology. Rule: check curves for crossing before trusting log-rank; crossing → RMST or time-specific comparisons.

Exercise 3. Log-rank as a score test — the Cox connection: the log-rank test is the score test of β = 0 in a Cox model with a single binary group covariate (11.5). Verify numerically: fit PHReg on the binary covariate and compare its score test (or the Wald z² of β̂) to your hand log-rank χ². Report both p-values on several datasets and note when they diverge slightly (ties!). What does this equivalence tell you about what Cox regression is to the log-rank test?


Solution







With no ties they coincide exactly (score test identity); ties introduce small divergences because the Cox default handles them differently than the log-rank’s hypergeometric variance. The equivalence’s meaning: Cox regression generalizes the log-rank test — the binary-covariate Cox is log-rank, and adding covariates turns it into the adjusted comparison (11.5); the test you built by hand is the score test of the model you’re about to fit.

title: 11.3 The Log-Rank Test
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Significant ≠ clinically big: with n = 5,000, a trivial hazard separation achieves p < 0.001 — report the KM curves, median difference, or RMST alongside (1.4’s effect-size law, survival edition).
Log-rank assumes PH under H₁ — it’s most powerful there; crossing/tapering effects need RMST or weighted variants (Gehan/Tarone–Ware/Fleming–Harrington), chosen before looking (4.6 discipline).
Stratified log-rank: for a known confounder (stage, site), strata-specific (O−E)/V sums preserve within-stratum comparisons — the log-rank’s adjustment-before-Cox option.
Ties: log-rank’s hypergeometric variance handles ties natively (it was born on discrete event tables); Cox needs Efron/Breslow corrections — one place the “simple” test is more exact than the model.
Competing risks: log-rank on the cause-specific event censors competing deaths — the comparison is about cause-specific hazard, not the patient’s observed experience; say which you’re testing (11.1’s competing-risks note).
Multiple arms/pairs: k > 2 groups need an overall k−1 df test first, then pairwise tests with multiplicity correction — the Part 12 machinery (12.3) arriving on schedule.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated comparison has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


t-test on times with censoring: censored observations aren’t observed event times — a t-test on mixed (event, censor) times answers nothing (and ignores the censoring mechanism entirely — 11.1). Log-rank consumes (t, status) pairs.
A 2×2 cut at an arbitrary time: this is a Fisher-style “survived past 3?” table — a different, cruder question that discards timing within bins and the censored rows’ partial information. Use the risk-table log-rank.
Smallest per-timepoint p: pure optional stopping/looking (1.4 Q2, 12.2) — the minimum of many correlated tests is not a p-value at any valid level.

title: 11.3 The Log-Rank Test
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Derive the log-rank’s expectation and variance: under H₀, conditional on the risk set at time j, the dⱼ events are a random sample of the nⱼ at-risk — so E[O₁ⱼ] = dⱼn₁ⱼ/nⱼ (hypergeometric mean) and Var(O₁ⱼ) = dⱼ(nⱼ−dⱼ)n₁ⱼn₂ⱼ/(nⱼ²(nⱼ−1)) (hypergeometric variance, finite-population corrected). Then verify by simulation: at a fixed risk configuration, the empirical variance of O₁ⱼ over repeated hypergeometric draws matches the formula.


Hint

Drawing dⱼ events without replacement from nⱼ subjects of which n₁ⱼ are group-1: mean and variance of the hypergeometric.



Solution

The null randomizes which at-risk subjects event: O₁ⱼ ~ Hypergeometric(N = nⱼ, K = n₁ⱼ, draws = dⱼ), with E = dⱼK/N and Var = dⱼ·(N−dⱼ)·K·(N−K)/(N²(N−1)) — the formula. Simulation:






Var → σ²; summed over times (conditionally independent given risk sets) the χ²₁ calibration follows. The log-rank is hypergeometric arithmetic stacked over a risk table — no likelihood, no parametrics, exactly calibrated.

Q2. Power and sample-size intuition via simulation: for a log-rank comparing Exp(2) vs Exp(3) groups, estimate power at n per arm ∈ {50, 100, 200, 400}. Verify Schoenfeld’s approximation — events needed ≈ 4(z_{α/2} + z_β)²/(log HR)² — against your simulated requirement (interpolate n to the 80% power point, convert to events ≈ n). What does the log(HR)² denominator say about detecting small effects — and why do survival trials chase events rather than patients?


Solution







Power climbs with n and with (log HR)² — halving the hazard ratio quadruples the required events. Survival trials size on events, not enrollment: 1,000 patients with 50 events is underpowered; 200 patients with 150 events is not. That inversion — vs every Part 2 sample-size intuition — is the survival-specific fact this derivation fixes.

title: 11.3 The Log-Rank Test
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (log-rank × 12.3–12.4). Biomarker-defined subgroups: run log-rank within each of 20 biomarker-defined subgroups (one truly benefits, 19 null); report how many “significant” subgroup findings appear at α = 0.05 raw, with Bonferroni, and with the hierarchical “overall test first, subgroup only if overall significant” design. Simulate 1,000 trials to estimate each strategy’s false-positive rate — the regulatory standard (overall-then-subgroup) implemented and defended (12.3 machinery, applied).
C2 (log-rank × 9.4 clusters × 4.6 tuning). Clustering-then-testing, honestly: cluster patients on baseline features at k ∈ {2, 3, 4}, run log-rank per k, select the best — the naive pipeline. Then the honest version: select k by clustering-internal criteria only (silhouette/stability, blind to survival), then test. Simulate 500 datasets (some with survival-relevant clusters, some without) and compare both pipelines’ false-positive rates and power. The result is the unsupervised→survival multiplicity lesson (12.2) with a survival face.

title: 11.3 The Log-Rank Test
text:
7. Summary

Log-rank = Σ(O − E) over event times with hypergeometric variance: χ²₁ under “equal hazards at all times.”
Risk-set arithmetic makes it robust to (non-informative, group-specific) censoring patterns.
Best power under proportional hazards; crossing curves cancel — check the KM plot, consider RMST.
Weighted variants (Gehan/Tarone–Ware/Fleming–Harrington) target early/late differences — pre-specify.
It’s the score test of the binary-covariate Cox model — the on-ramp to adjusted survival analysis.
Unadjusted means “valid under randomization”; observational data needs Cox’s covariate machinery.
The Cox model itself — partial likelihood, hazard ratios, PH diagnostics: 11.5 Cox proportional hazards regression, after hazards in 11.4.

title: 11.1 Why Survival Data Is Special
text: Clinical and biological data rarely records whether something happened — it records when, or that it hadn’t yet (right-censoring). Naive tools break on this: deleting censored cases biases every estimate, and “average time” is undefined while events are still accruing. Survival analysis is the machinery for time-to-event data, and this page installs its vocabulary and the first simulation engine you’ll reuse all part.

title: 11.1 Why Survival Data Is Special
text:
1. Basic Concept
Each subject contributes a pair: observed time \(T_i = \min(T_i^{\text{event}}, C_i)\) (event or censoring time, whichever comes first) and status δᵢ = 1 if the event was observed, 0 if censored. The key assumption that makes everything work: non-informative censoring — censored subjects’ future risk resembles those who remain under observation.
Why naive tools fail — demonstrated:

title: 11.1 Why Survival Data Is Special
text:
2. Concept Questions

A subject exits the study at year 3 alive, when the median survival is year 6. What do the naive strategies (“drop them”, “count 3 as their time”) each assert about that subject — and why is both wrong?
Why is the complete-case mean of observed times biased downward here, while the naive mean was biased too — what did each include that it shouldn’t?
State non-informative censoring in one sentence, and give one censoring mechanism that violates it.
Which quantity does survival analysis target instead of the mean when censoring dominates, and why is it estimable under censoring?
Your dataset has status ∈ {0, 1} and time ≥ 0 with 40% censored. What three checks would you run before any survival model?



Answers


Dropping asserts “their risk profile is uninformative and can leave” — deleting the longest survivors biases the survival curve downward at later times. Counting 3 as the event time asserts “they had the event at 3” — fabricating an outcome. Survival analysis treats them as known to be alive at 3, event status afterwards unknown — exactly what censored likelihood encodes.
Naive mean included censored times as if events occurred at censoring (they didn’t) — diluting/pulling the mean depending on censoring time. Complete-case mean kept only those who had events before censoring — a systematically shorter-tailed (sicker) subgroup. Both misuse the censoring information; the KM estimator uses it correctly (11.2).
“Censoring time is independent of event time given covariates” — censored subjects carry the same future risk as those still followed. Violation: censoring because the patient worsened (transferred to hospice) — censoring then tracks the event, and all standard estimators bias downward.
The survival function S(t) = P(T > t) (and its derived median): S(t) is estimable under right-censoring because each event time contributes (1 − d/n) using everyone still at risk — censoring only reduces the risk set, correctly.

status ∈ {0, 1} with 0 = censored (not “no event happened” — semantics!); (b) time > 0 everywhere and censoring isn’t informative (why do people leave?); (c) enough events (censoring fraction vs event count drives power — 1.4).

title: 11.1 Why Survival Data Is Special
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Build the survival dataset constructor make_survival(n, scale, censor_cap, seed) returning (obs_time, status) from exponential events with uniform censoring. Then plot the censoring fraction as a function of censor_cap ∈ {1, 2, 4, 8, 16} and overlay the theoretical value 1 − E[min(T,C)]-implied curve shape. At what cap does censoring fall below 10% for scale = 2? Compute analytically: P(T > C) with T ~ Exp(2), C ~ U(0, cap).


Solution







Censoring falls below 10% when cap ≈ 5.2 (solve (2/cap)(1 − e^{−cap/2}) = 0.1). The analytic formula — integrate the exponential survival function against the uniform censoring density — is exactly the calculus every censoring-fraction question reduces to; simulation verifies the algebra.

Exercise 2. Informative censoring damage, quantified: simulate frailty-driven data (as in drill 3) where both event and censoring hazards depend on frailty, and estimate “median survival” by the complete-case median vs the true population median (computable: T ~ mixture of exponentials by frailty… use a large no-censoring run as ground truth). Show the complete-case median is biased even though the censoring is independent given frailty — i.e., conditionally non-informative but marginally informative. What does this say about the word “independent” in the assumption?


Solution







Censoring independent of T given frailty is still dependent on T marginally (both track frailty), and complete-case analysis conditions on nothing — it inherits the selection. The vocabulary precision matters: “non-informative” must be judged against the analysis population, and covariate-adjusted methods (Cox, 11.5) are how conditional independence gets used rather than assumed away.

Exercise 3. The counting-process view: build the at-risk/event table by hand for a small dataset (10 subjects with times and statuses): at each distinct event time, compute n at risk, d events, c censored. Then verify two identities: (a) Σd = number of events; (b) events + censored + still-at-risk-at-end = n. This table is the data structure beneath KM, log-rank, and Cox — implement it as risk_table(t, e) returning a DataFrame.


Solution







The risk table is the counting-process backbone: KM multiplies (1 − d/n) over its rows, log-rank compares (O − E) across groups on its rows, and Cox’s partial likelihood conditions on its risk sets. Every survival method in this part is arithmetic over this table.

title: 11.1 Why Survival Data Is Special
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Status semantics flip across software: 1 = event in most Python/R tools, but some datasets code “1 = alive” — relabel and re-check frequencies before anything else; a flipped status silently inverts every survival curve.
Administrative vs loss-to-follow-up censoring: administrative censoring (study ends) is typically non-informative by design; loss-to-follow-up often isn’t. Report which kind your censoring is.
Interval censoring (event known only between visits) needs different likelihoods (interval-censored methods); treating interval-censored as right-censored biases toward visit times.
Left truncation (subject enters study at risk only from a later age): handled via entry times (entry= in statsmodels) — ignoring truncation biases toward including time-at-risk that was never observed.
Competing risks: death precludes relapse — naive KM treats competing events as censored and overestimates the relapse curve; cumulative-incidence estimation (CumIncidenceRight in statsmodels) is the correct object when competing risks exist.
Censoring fraction ≠ information: a dataset can be 90% censored yet well-powered (long follow-up, few but late events) or 30% censored and hopeless (no events yet). Report event count, not just censoring fraction.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated “survival prep” has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Status flipped: here 1 marks censored (true_t > censor) — every downstream tool assuming 1 = event will invert survival curves and HR directions. Fix the semantics at ingestion: status = (true_t <= censor).astype(int).
Complete-case median: it’s the median of the shortest follow-ups, not survival. Use the Kaplan–Meier median (11.2).
Dropping censored rows: discards legitimate at-risk information and biases toward fast events. Keep (time, status) pairs — regression on times isn’t even the right frame; Cox regression (11.5) consumes the pairs.

title: 11.1 Why Survival Data Is Special
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Prove that the complete-case mean of observed times is not consistent for E[T] under independent censoring: with T ⊥ C, E[T | T ≤ C] = E[T·1(T ≤ C)]/P(T ≤ C) ≠ E[T] — show the bias direction depends on the censoring distribution’s support. Then verify: for T ~ Exp(2), C ~ U(0, c), compute the exact complete-case mean E[T · 1(T ≤ C)]/P(T ≤ C) analytically and match it by simulation for c ∈ {2, 4}.


Hint

Condition on C: E[T·1(T ≤ C) | C = c] = ∫₀^c t·f_T(t)dt; integrate over c, and P(T ≤ C) = E[1 − e^{−C/scale}].



Solution

With T ~ Exp(λ) (λ = 1/2), C ~ U(0, c): ∫₀^c t·λe^{−λt}dt = (1/λ)(1 − e^{−λc}(1 + λc)). Averaging over C: numerator = (1/λ)[1 − (1 − e^{−λc}(1+λc))/(λc)·… ] — the closed form is messy; the point is it’s strictly less than E[T] = 1/λ whenever censoring bites, because events beyond the censoring window are systematically excluded:






The complete-case mean converges to ≈ 1.24 vs true 2.0 at c = 4 — a 38% underestimate with independent censoring, purely from conditioning on T ≤ C. Consistency fails because each sample answers a different question (“mean of the uncensored”). Survival analysis exists because these conditioning events are the data.

Q2. Design the censoring-diagnostic report: your dataset has 35% censoring. Build (code skeleton + reasoning) the diagnostic panel: (a) censoring-time distribution (histogram of censoring times among censored), (b) censoring vs covariates (logistic of censored-on-covariates), (c) KM of censoring (treat censoring as the event!) per subgroup, (d) reverse KM for median follow-up (Snaith’s method: flip status). For each, state the decision it informs (e.g., “censoring times bunched at study end → administrative, benign”). Implement the panel on simulated data with a known informative-censoring contamination and show it flags the contamination.


Solution







Panel logic: (a) a spike at the study end declares administrative censoring (benign); (b/c) censoring related to patient state flags informativeness (adjust or restrict); (d) median follow-up contextualizes the S(t) curve’s trustworthy range. This panel runs before any model — it’s the survival-data analog of 0.4’s EDA protocol.

title: 11.1 Why Survival Data Is Special
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (survival × 4.4 bias–variance). The censoring-information trade: with fixed n = 100 events budget, compare designs — (a) 100 subjects, 0% censored; (b) 300 subjects, 67% censored (same event count) — by the variance of the KM estimator at t = median (simulate 500 datasets each). Which design wins, and what does the answer say about why clinical trials maximize follow-up time before sample size?
C2 (survival × 9.3 missing data). Censoring as missingness: map the survival problem onto the missing-data taxonomy — status = 0 is “event time missing, censoring time observed.” Which mechanism (MCAR/MAR/MNAR) does non-informative right-censoring correspond to? Then show that KM is a special-purpose analogue of the MAR machinery: construct a tiny dataset where complete-case deletion vs KM differ, and explain the mapping in the 9.3 vocabulary.

title: 11.1 Why Survival Data Is Special
text:
7. Summary

Survival data = (observed time, status) pairs; censoring means “alive at exit,” not “no event.”
Naive means and complete-case analyses are biased under censoring — in opposite directions.
Non-informative censoring is the load-bearing assumption; conditionally-independent censoring can still be marginally informative — adjust for covariates.
S(t) is the estimand of choice under censoring; the risk table (n at risk, d events) is the data structure beneath every estimator.
Diagnose censoring (panel: distribution, covariates, reverse KM) before modeling; report event counts, not censoring fractions.
Competing risks and interval censoring need their own machinery — naive KM misstates both.
The first estimator that gets all this right: 11.2 Kaplan–Meier survival curves.

title: 10.8 LSTM and GRU
text: 10.7 ended on a diagnosis: the recurrent update multiplies the gradient by \(D\,W_h\) every step, so long-range credit assignment decays or explodes. LSTM (and its leaner cousin GRU) re-engineer that update: multiplicative gates decide what to forget, write, and expose, and an additive cell state gives gradients a near-constant path through time. This page builds the gates by hand and watches memory survive 100 steps — live in NumPy.

title: 10.8 LSTM and GRU
text:
1. Basic Concept
The LSTM cell keeps two vectors: hidden state \(h_t\) (what it exposes) and cell state \(c_t\) (what it remembers):
\[
\begin{aligned}
f_t &= \sigma(W_f[h_{t-1}; x_t] + b_f) &&\text{forget gate} \\
i_t &= \sigma(W_i[h_{t-1}; x_t] + b_i) &&\text{input gate} \\
\tilde c_t &= \tanh(W_c[h_{t-1}; x_t] + b_c) &&\text{candidate} \\
c_t &= f_t \odot c_{t-1} + i_t \odot \tilde c_t &&\text{additive update} \\
o_t &= \sigma(W_o[h_{t-1}; x_t] + b_o) &&\text{output gate} \\
h_t &= o_t \odot \tanh(c_t)
\end{aligned}
\]
The gradient through the cell state is \(\partial c_t / \partial c_{t-1} = \mathrm{diag}(f_t) + (\text{gate terms})\) — when \(f_t \approx 1\) and writes are gated off, the derivative passes at ≈ 1 per step: the constant error carousel. Memory decays (or persists) by learned decision, not by forced multiplication.
GRU merges the two states and three gates into two (\(z\) = update, \(r\) = reset):
\[
\begin{aligned}
z_t &= \sigma(W_z[h_{t-1}; x_t]), \qquad
h_t = (1 - z_t) \odot h_{t-1} + z_t \odot \tilde h_t
\end{aligned}
\]
Same idea — convex blend between old state and candidate — with ~25% fewer parameters.
Worked example — gates as arithmetic, memory by construction:






The vanilla state is gone (multiplied by ≈0.9 one hundred times); the gated cell survives by choosing not to forget. Training sets those choices.

title: 10.8 LSTM and GRU
text:
2. Concept Questions

\(\partial c_t/\partial c_{t-1} = \mathrm{diag}(f_t)\) when the candidate term is ignored. Why is additive + diagonal the crucial pair — what breaks if the update were \(c_t = \tanh(W_c c_{t-1} + \ldots)\) (i.e., a vanilla cell with forget-gating painted on)?
All gates are sigmoids initialized near 0.5, but practitioners initialize the forget-gate bias to +1 or +2. What failure does this default prevent, and why doesn’t the same trick help the vanilla RNN?
Count LSTM parameters for input dim \(d\), hidden size \(h\); same for GRU. At \(d = h = 128\), what is the ratio — and what does each parameter buy in the gate story?
GRU has no separate output gate. What replaces \(o_t\)’s job, and when does that matter (which tasks miss the output gate least)?
The cell state is exposed to the output through \(\tanh(c_t)\) but the recurrent path carries \(c_t\) raw. What breaks if you feed \(\tanh(c_t)\) forward as the next cell state instead?



Answers


Product of Jacobians again: \(D_c W_c\) multiplies per step — same vanishing disease with extra steps. The fix works because (a) addition doesn’t shrink (gradient +1 path), (b) diagonal means each memory channel decays independently at its own learned rate — no cross-channel mixing to compound. Gating a multiplicative cell only slows the disease.
With random init, forget gates start ≈ 0.5 → memory half-life of ~1 step → early training sees only local gradients and never discovers long memory (a chicken-and-egg: long-range credit is needed to learn long-range memory). Bias +1/2 starts gates ≈ 0.73–0.88 → multi-step memory from step one, so the gradient that would reward remembering exists. The vanilla RNN has no gate to bias — its per-step factor is structural (\(D W_h\)), not a parameter.
LSTM: \(4(dh + h^2 + h)\) (4 gates × weights, recurrent block, biases); GRU: \(3(dh + h^2 + h)\). At 128/128: LSTM 131,584 vs GRU 98,688 — ratio 4:3. Each gate buys one decision channel over the same memory: LSTM spends the extra on separating “what to erase” from “what to write” and “what to show”.
The GRU’s exposure is fixed: \(h_t\) is always the (blended) full state. Tasks that read every step (sequence labelling, language modeling) barely miss \(o_t\) — the update gate \(z_t\) already modulates exposure indirectly. Tasks that must store something while emitting something unrelated (rare, e.g., certain pointer/memory tasks) lose the cheapest mechanism for it.
Then the gradient path picks up the tanh slope again (\(\tanh' \le 1\), ≈ 0 near saturation) — you’ve rebuilt a (softer) multiplicative bottleneck and reintroduced vanishing. The cell’s raw linear highway is the point; \(\tanh(c)\) is only the readout squashing.

title: 10.8 LSTM and GRU
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Minimal LSTM cell in NumPy: implement the six equations vectorized for one sequence, with weights you set by hand (not trained): (a) a “rememberer” (\(f{=}1, i{=}0\)) that stores the first input and ignores the rest; (b) an “accumulator” (\(f{=}1, i{=}1, \tilde c{=}x\)) that sums inputs into the cell; (c) a random-weight cell for contrast. Feed each a 50-step sequence and plot \(c_t\), \(h_t\). Which hand-set cell solves “output the first token” — the task where 10.7’s vanilla RNN demonstrably fails?


Solution







The rememberer’s input gate is h-gated: the first pulse writes itself into \(c\) and the resulting \(h\) slams the gate shut against later ones — memory doing its own access control, which is exactly why the input gate reads \(h_{t-1}\). Nothing here was trained: the gate parameterization makes “store one thing, ignore the rest” a representable, easy-to-reach configuration — which is why optimization finds it where the vanilla RNN’s multiplicative dynamics can’t even express it.

Exercise 2. Gradient autopsy, gated vs vanilla: for the Exercise-1 rememberer and for a random vanilla cell (\(h_t = \tanh(W h_{t-1})\), \(\rho(W) = 0.9\)), compute \(\partial c_T/\partial c_0\) (or \(\partial h_T / \partial h_0\)) numerically — perturb \(c_0\) (or \(h_0\)) and measure output change — for T ∈ {10, 30, 100}. Report the three magnitudes. Then set \(f = 0.9\) in the LSTM and redo: what half-life do you measure, and does it match \(\ln 0.5 / \ln f\)?


Solution







With \(f = 0.999\) the 100-step gradient survives at 0.90; the vanilla cell is at \(0.9^{100} \approx 3{\times}10^{-5}\) — four orders of magnitude, from one parameter’s difference. Setting \(f = 0.9\) moves the LSTM’s gradient to exactly \(f^T\): measured half-life 6.6 steps, matching \(\ln 0.5/\ln f\). The cell’s memory is a dial the optimizer turns; the vanilla RNN’s is baked into the spectrum of \(W_h\).

Exercise 3. LSTM vs GRU vs vanilla, trained small: in scikit-learn terms this needs the Colab lab, but the decision table can be built live: for tasks (a) next-step sine (local, T=20), (b) first-token recall (T=100), (c) counting pulses over 200 steps — predict the ranking of vanilla/GRU/LSTM by parameter efficiency and by achievable accuracy, then verify against the qualitative results table below (fill it in the Colab lab with nn.RNN/nn.GRU/nn.LSTM at matched hidden sizes). Which task punishes the parameter-hungry LSTM most, and why is “GRU first” the sane default?


Solution







Expected pattern: on local tasks all three tie and the LSTM’s 4/3 parameter surplus is pure overfit risk (the punishing case) — GRU or even vanilla wins the efficiency argument. On long-range recall/counting, gates are decisive and GRU ≈ LSTM (GRU’s merged state suffices in most benchmarks; LSTM pulls ahead mainly on very long sequences or when separate output/read memory matters). Default: GRU first (fewer params, fewer states to carry, ≈ tied accuracy); upgrade to LSTM only when the task demonstrably needs independent write/erase/read. Vanilla RNN is for teaching pages like this one.

title: 10.8 LSTM and GRU
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

The 4× parameter wall: LSTM layer params are \(4(dh + h^2 + h)\) — doubling hidden size quadruples the recurrent block. On small corpora this is the difference between fitting and memorizing (10.5’s whole toolkit applies).
Carry both states: nn.LSTM returns (h, c); saving only h between chunks of a long document silently flushes the cell — the model “forgets the beginning of the paper” mid-stream.
Forget-gate bias init (nn.LSTM(..., bias) custom init at +1): the default random init makes early training local-memory-only; the +1 bias is a two-line change with outsized effect on long-sequence tasks.
Bidirectional ≠ causal: a BiLSTM reading the whole sequence before emitting \(h_t\) uses future information — fine for tagging a fixed transcript, catastrophic for online forecasting; keep directions straight per task.
Output-per-step vs final output: nn.LSTM returns outputs for all t plus the final state; sequence classification wants the final (or a pooled) readout, labelling wants the full series — mixing these silently changes the task.
Gradient clipping still applies: gates tame vanishing; exploding survives (long chains × unlucky batches) — clip the global norm (10.7).


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated stateful inference loop for a trained nn.LSTM has three bugs. Diagnose before opening the fix.
model.eval()
h = torch.zeros(1, 1, H)            # hidden
c = torch.zeros(1, 1, H)            # cell
for chunk in document_chunks:
    out, (h, c) = model(chunk, (h, c))
    probs = torch.softmax(model.head(out), dim=-1)     # BUG 1
    pred = probs.argmax(-1)
    h = h.detach()                                      # BUG 2
    # BUG 3: c is never detached/re-used correctly — see below
    print(pred.item(), probs.max().item())


What’s wrong, and the fix


Softmax then argmax: argmax is softmax-invariant — the softmax wastes compute and, worse, invites using probs as calibrated probabilities (they’re not, absent calibration work — 10.2). Take logits straight to argmax; keep softmax only if you actually need a distribution.
h detached, c carried with graph: c still references the autograd graph, so the “inference” loop grows memory every chunk until it OOMs — the LSTM’s long-term memory is exactly the tensor someone forgot to cut loose.
Inconsistency (the real killer): detaching one state and not the other means the graph alive through c pins every intermediate chunk’s forward activations. Detach both (or run the whole loop under torch.no_grad() — simpler and impossible to get half-wrong).

model.eval()
h = torch.zeros(1, 1, H); c = torch.zeros(1, 1, H)
with torch.no_grad():
    for chunk in document_chunks:
        out, (h, c) = model(chunk, (h, c))
        pred = model.head(out).argmax(-1)
        print(pred.item())

title: 10.8 LSTM and GRU
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Prove the “constant error carousel” claim precisely: for the LSTM with output gate bypassed (gradients w.r.t. \(c_t\) only), show \(\partial c_t / \partial c_{t-1} = \mathrm{diag}(f_t)\) plus a term through the candidate, and derive the condition under which the through-\(\tilde c\) term vanishes. Then show the total per-step Jacobian is lower-bounded by \(\min_s f_s\) over the path — the property no multiplicative cell of the vanilla form enjoys — and explain what the optimizer must do to earn it.


Hint

Differentiate \(c_t = f_t \odot c_{t-1} + i_t \odot \tanh(W_c[h;x])\) w.r.t. \(c_{t-1}\): direct path through \(f_t\); indirect paths through \(h_{t-1}\) (which feeds all gates). When do the indirect paths carry zero?



Solution

\(\partial c_t/\partial c_{t-1} = \mathrm{diag}(f_t) + \sum_{g \in \{f,i,\tilde c, o\text{-via-}h\}} \frac{\partial c_t}{\partial g_t}\frac{\partial g_t}{\partial h_{t-1}}\frac{\partial h_{t-1}}{\partial c_{t-1}}\). The indirect terms pass through \(h_{t-1} = o_{t-1} \odot \tanh(c_{t-1})\) and every gate’s Jacobian — products of σ′ and tanh′ factors. They vanish when output gate \(o_{t-1} \approx 0\) (cell decoupled from the exposed state — nothing written lately) or when gate gradients saturate. Then the direct path alone gives per-step factor \(f_t \in (0,1)\): the gradient decays at the learned, per-channel rate, and can be held ≈ 1 by \(f \to 1\) — but the optimizer must first receive long-range gradient to want that (hence forget-bias init: seed the property, let gradient refinement keep it). The vanilla cell has no such decoupling: every step’s factor is \(D_h W_h\) regardless of what the task needs.

Q2. Gating vs attention on the copy task: sequence-to-sequence copy (“echo input token 0 after T distractors”) is solvable by an LSTM cell and trivially by attention over inputs. Sketch both mechanisms’ parameter and path-length cost as T grows: LSTM (fixed params, O(T) path, gate-dependent survival) vs attention (O(T) memory for the KV cache at inference, O(1) path). For T = 10³ and T = 10⁶, state which mechanism is viable and why — this is the load-bearing argument for 10.9’s replacement of recurrence.


Hint

Count what must persist: LSTM compresses history into h, c (fixed size); attention keeps all tokens (linear memory). Path length: how many multiplicative steps separate token 0 from the output?



Solution

LSTM: fixed-size state regardless of T; token 0 must survive T gate steps — survival probability is the product of per-step keep factors; trainable, but at T = 10³ even f = 0.999 leaves \(0.999^{1000} \approx 0.37\) and practical training rarely holds f that close to 1 across all channels. Attention: token 0’s key/value sit in a table; the query reads them in one hop — path length O(1), gradient O(1), no decay; cost is O(T) memory (KV cache) and O(T²) compute per layer. At T = 10³: attention wins outright (10³ scalars is nothing; the LSTM needs learned perfection for 10³ steps). At T = 10⁶: attention’s O(T²) attention matrix and O(T) cache dominate (the reason Part 13’s long-context LLM work exists), while an LSTM’s fixed state is free — but 10⁶-step credit assignment through gates is beyond practical training. Field summary: recurrence scales state, attention scales access; modern sequence models pay memory for access because compute got cheap and data got long.

title: 10.8 LSTM and GRU
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (× 10.5 × 10.7 clipping). Regularization a gated cell differently: dropout on recurrent connections breaks the memory (the cell reads a zeroed \(h_{t-1}\)) — hence variational/stateful dropout schemes (same mask all steps) vs input/output-only dropout. Design the experiment on the first-token recall task: vanilla dropout vs same-mask-every-step dropout vs no dropout, at two corpus sizes. Which scheme preserves recall while regularizing, and what does the answer generalize to (10.9’ attention dropout — applied where, exactly?)
C2 (× Part 13 LLM concepts × 10.9). Write the two-paragraph design memo: your team must choose between “stacked BiLSTM encoder” and “pretrained transformer encoder (frozen + linear head)” for tagging 10k clinical notes on a single GPU. Cover: parameter/data budget, transfer availability (what exists on the hub for each), path-length vs domain-jargon trade-off, and the decision rule that follows from 10.10. (The honest answer leans on transfer, not architecture — make that conclusion earned by the memo’s numbers.)

title: 10.8 LSTM and GRU
text:
7. Summary

LSTM: gates (forget/input/output) + additive cell state ⇒ per-step gradient factor is a learned diagonal — memory by decision, not by multiplication.
The constant error carousel needs additive updates and a raw linear carry path; tanh-ing the cell state re-breaks it.
GRU merges states and gates: 3/4 the parameters, ≈ LSTM accuracy in most benchmarks — the sane default.
Forget-gate bias ≈ +1: seed long memory before the gradient can ask for it.
Carry both (h, c) across chunks; detach both at inference; bidirectionality is a causality decision, not a free lunch.
Gates fix vanishing; attention removes the need for the relay entirely — 10.9 attention and transformers.

title: 10.6 Convolutional Neural Networks
text: A dense layer on images wastes its parameters re-learning the same edge at every position, and throws away the fact that nearby pixels belong together. Convolutions fix both: small kernels, shared across space, composed into features (edges → textures → parts). This page builds the operation by hand in NumPy on scikit-learn’s digits — every concept cell runs live — and the PyTorch training lab runs in Colab.

title: 10.6 Convolutional Neural Networks
text:
1. Basic Concept
Discrete 2-D convolution (DL’s version is technically cross-correlation — see pitfalls): slide a small kernel \(K\) (\(k \times k\)) over the image, computing each output pixel as a weighted local sum:
\[\text{out}[i, j] = \sum_{u,v} \, \text{in}[i+u, j+v] \cdot K[u, v] + b\]
Two properties make this the right inductive bias for images:

Locality: each output sees only a \(k \times k\) neighborhood — nearby pixels first (vs a dense layer’s global dot product).
Weight sharing: the same \(K\) at every position — translation equivariance (shift input → features shift) with vastly fewer parameters.

Output size: \(\lfloor (n + 2p - k)/s \rfloor + 1\) for input size \(n\), padding \(p\), stride \(s\). Pooling (\(2\times2\) max) halves resolution, buying a little translation invariance on top of equivariance.
Worked example — kernels as edge detectors, live on a real digit:






Each map is one “channel” a CNN layer would compute — a trained CNN just learns the kernels instead of hand-picking Sobel filters, and stacks layers so layer-2 sees layer-1’s edges.
Parameter arithmetic — the payoff of sharing: mapping 32×32×3 → 32 filters of 3×3:

title: 10.6 Convolutional Neural Networks
text:
2. Concept Questions

The dense layer mapping 8×8 digits to 8×8 outputs has how many weights? The 3×3-kernel conv (1 channel in, 1 out) has how many? Which one can transfer from a digit photographed slightly off-center?
Padding “same” vs “valid”: an 8×8 input with 3×3 kernel gives which output sizes? Why do deep stacks need padding (what happens to edge information without it)?
Pooling gives invariance; convolution gives equivariance. State both relations as “if input shifts by δ, then output …”. Where does each property help recognition?
A conv net with all kernels 1×1 is exactly what model? And a conv with kernel size = input size?
Stride-2 convolution vs conv-then-pool: both downsample 2×. What does each do to the information thrown away?



Answers


Dense: 64×64 = 4,096 (+64 bias). Conv: 9 (+1). The conv transfers: its “vertical edge” detector works at any position — the dense layer has no such sharing, so off-center digits are effectively new inputs.
Same: 8×8 (p=1); valid: 6×6. Without padding, each layer shaves k−1 pixels: edge pixels get seen by fewer layers’ outputs (their receptive-field contribution dies) and feature maps shrink until pooling has nothing to pool.
Convolution: input shifts δ ⇒ feature maps shift δ (with interior effects at borders). Pooling: input shifts by less than the pooling window ⇒ pooled output often unchanged. Equivariance lets layer 2 find “edge wherever it is” from layer 1; invariance at the end lets the classifier not care where the digit sits in the frame.
1×1 kernels = a dense layer applied per-pixel across channels only — a channel mixer / bottleneck (used everywhere in modern architectures). Kernel = input size = a fully-connected layer (weight sharing degenerates — there’s only one position).
Stride-2 conv: a learned linear projection evaluated on a sparse grid — trainable downsampling. Max-pool: fixed nonlinear selection of the local max — no parameters, hard “winner-takes-all” discarding; average-pool softens. Learned stride convs are standard in modern nets; pooling survives mostly as final global-average-pool.

title: 10.6 Convolutional Neural Networks
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Implement conv2d (single channel, valid mode) with loops; verify it against scipy.signal.correlate2d; then state why DL libraries call this “convolution” without flipping the kernel. Time the loop version against the FFT-free vectorized alternative (correlate2d) on a 64×64 input with 3×3 kernel — how many conv layers can your CPU do per second, and what does that imply about training real CNNs in a browser?


Solution







DL “convolution” is cross-correlation: it never flips the kernel. Mathematically the flip matters only for convolution’s algebraic properties (commutativity with the Fourier theorem); for learning, the kernel is free parameters — flipping a learned kernel is absorbed by re-learning, so libraries skip it. Timing: even the C scipy path does only hundreds of single-channel layers/sec; a real net (32 channels × 2 layers × forward+backward × thousands of images) is why CNN training lives on GPUs/Colab, not in Pyodide.

Exercise 2. Hand-conv feature extractor: build a tiny pipeline on a 8×8 digit — conv (vertical edge) → ReLU → 2×2 max-pool → conv (horizontal edge) → ReLU → pool — implemented with your conv2d/correlate2d and NumPy only. Visualize every intermediate map. Then compute the receptive field of one final pixel (how many input pixels influence it) and its stride relative to the input.


Solution







One final pixel’s receptive field, computed stepwise: conv1 → 3, pool1 → \((3-1){\cdot}2+2 = 6\), conv2 (3×3, stride 1) → \((6-1)+3 = 8\), global pool → the whole 8×8 image. Deep stacks grow receptive fields multiplicatively with depth — the geometry that lets layer-5 units see whole objects while stride keeps intermediate grids coarse.

Exercise 3. Shared vs unshared, measured: scikit-learn’s digits (1,797 samples of 8×8), flattened: fit LogisticRegression (dense, unshared, linear) vs a hand-rolled conv-feature pipeline — convolve each image with the 4 kernels from Section 1, pool to 3×3 each, flatten (4×9 = 36 features), then logistic regression on top. Compare 5-fold CV accuracy. The conv features are hand-picked and untrained — what does the gap (or its absence) tell you about what learned kernels add, and where the real win of CNNs lies?


Solution







Hand-picked edge/blur features are competitive with raw pixels on easy digits — because logistic regression on 64 pixels is already a linear-shape-matcher. The CNN’s real win is compositionality at scale: learned kernels arranged in a hierarchy (edges → corners → strokes → digit parts) with weight sharing, trained end-to-end on data where 64 pixels aren’t enough (MNIST/CIFAR — the Colab lab shows the gap properly). Fixed features top out; learned hierarchical features scale with data — the exact argument of 10.10’s “structure + data” quadrant.

title: 10.6 Convolutional Neural Networks
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

It’s cross-correlation: DL convolutions don’t flip kernels. Consequence-free for training, but confusing when porting signal-processing filters or implementing deconvolution.
Layout chaos: PyTorch is NCHW (batch, channel, height, width); TensorFlow defaults NHWC. A (8, 8) single image needs shape (1, 1, 8, 8) in torch — “missing channel dimension” is the day-one error.
Border effects: without padding, valid convolutions shrink maps and underweight border pixels (they appear in fewer receptive fields); same padding mitigates but pads with zeros — reflect/replicate padding is kinder for images with meaningful borders.
Flatten loses spatial layout: flatten → dense after convs works but discards the 2-D arrangement; global average pooling is the modern replacement (fewer params, translation-tolerant).
Small data + big CNN = instant overfit (10.5): augmentation (shifts/rotations) is not optional on datasets of hundreds; weight sharing is a prior, not a guarantee.
Receptive field ≠ resolution: stride/pooling grow receptive fields but sample them coarsely — dilated convolutions grow the field without losing grid density (segmentation’s standard trick).


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated conv layer (NumPy) has three bugs. Find them before running the fixed version.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Wrong output shape: valid mode must produce (H−k+1, W−k+1) = (6, 6); claiming (8, 8) fills only the interior and leaves a silently-zero border — fake “features” that the next layer will happily consume.
Copy-paste batch bug: imgs[0] inside the loop gives every image the first image’s feature maps — the classic AI copy-paste error, invisible because shapes are all correct.
Off-by-one write: storing at i + 1, j + 1 shifts every feature map down-right by a pixel; after flattening, the model sees displaced edges as real spatial structure.







The general lesson: hand-rolled array code must assert shapes — NumPy slicing truncates silently, and a wrong-but-shaped output is worse than an exception.

title: 10.6 Convolutional Neural Networks
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Equivariance, precisely: prove that convolution with kernel \(K\) commutes with integer translations — \(T_\delta(C(x)) = C(T_\delta(x))\) for the interior of the output — and identify exactly where the proof breaks (borders; stride; pooling). Then show max-pooling is not equivariant but is approximately invariant for shifts smaller than the pool window. Why do CNN stacks pair the two in this order?


Hint

Write both compositions as index sums; the kernel slides with the image. For pooling, compare argmax sets under small shifts.



Solution

Translation by δ: \(C(T_\delta x)[p] = \sum_u K[u]\,x[p + u - \delta] = (C x)[p - \delta] = T_\delta(Cx)[p]\) — kernel and image translate together, so outputs translate (valid-mode interior). Breaks: (i) borders — the sum clips differently at edges, so equivariance is approximate there; (ii) stride s — outputs exist only on a subgrid, translation by non-multiples of s has no corresponding output shift; (iii) pooling — max over a window: shifting input moves the max but if it crosses a window boundary the output changes non-uniformly (not a shift), yet for sub-window shifts the same max usually survives — approximate invariance. The stack order exploits both: convolutions carry position information equivariantly upward (layer 2 can reason about arrangement), while pooling locally forgets small displacements so downstream layers see stabler features; only at the top does full invariance (global average pool) feed the classifier.

Q2. The 1×1 bottleneck: a residual block conv3×3(C→C) → conv3×3(C→C) costs \(2C^2 \cdot 9\) params; the bottlenecked version 1×1(C→C/4) → 3×3(C/4→C/4) → 1×1(C/4→C) costs… compute both for C = 256, verify numerically with a parameter-count function, and explain what the 1×1 convs are doing semantically (channel mixing/pca-style projection — connect to 9.2 PCA). When is the bottleneck not a good trade?


Hint

Bottleneck ≈ 2·C²/4·… just compute. The 1×1 layers are linear maps across channels at each pixel — exactly PCA-whitening’s job if the data cooperated.



Solution







Standard: 2·256²·9 ≈ 1.18M; bottleneck: 2·(256·64) + 64²·9 ≈ 69K — 17× cheaper, which is why ResNet-50’s deeper bottlenecked blocks cost less than ResNet-34’s plain ones. Semantically, the 1×1s are per-pixel linear maps across channels — compressing to a 64-dim subspace where the 3×3 spatial mixing happens, then re-expanding: PCA-flavored dimensionality (9.2) with learned components. Bad trade when channels are already few (C = 32: bottleneck of 8 strips capacity), or when the task needs full-width interactions in every 3×3 (fine-grained textures) — compression is a prior that locality-of-information lives in a subspace.

title: 10.6 Convolutional Neural Networks
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (× 10.5 augmentation × 9.2 PCA). Weight sharing bakes in translation equivariance; augmentation bakes in more invariances (rotation, shear). On the digits data, quantify the overlap: augment training images with small rotations, re-run Exercise 3’s two pipelines, and measure how much of the augmentation gain the conv-feature pipeline already captures (hand kernels are themselves edge-detectors). Hypothesize before measuring: does augmentation help the raw-pixel pipeline more than the conv pipeline? Why does that ordering reveal what each representation already “knows”?
C2 (× 10.9 attention × 10.7). Convolutions hard-code locality; attention is global from layer 1. Sketch (no training) the compute cost of one layer over a 224×224 image for (a) a stack of 3×3 convs reaching a global receptive field, (b) single-head self-attention over all pixels. Compute parameter counts and FLOPs-as-matrix-sizes for C = 64. Then state the modern synthesis (local conv stem + attention blocks) as a cost/benefit argument rather than a fashion choice — and why image transformers still keep patch embeddings (10.9’ quadratic term, tamed).

title: 10.6 Convolutional Neural Networks
text:
7. Summary

Convolution = locality + weight sharing: translation-equivariant features with orders-of-magnitude fewer parameters.
Output shape \(\lfloor(n+2p-k)/s\rfloor+1\); padding preserves borders; pooling adds local invariance on top of equivariance.
1×1 convs are per-pixel channel mixers — bottleneck blocks trade width for depth cheaply.
NumPy slicing truncates silently: hand-rolled convolutions must assert patch shapes.
Hand-picked kernels get you surprisingly far on easy images; learned hierarchical kernels are what scale — that’s the data+structure argument of 10.10.
Images stack spatially; sequences need memory — next: 10.7 recurrent neural networks.

title: 10.4 Gradient Descent and Backpropagation
text: Training a network = descending a loss surface by repeated chain rule. This page builds the whole machinery by hand in NumPy — gradient descent, then backpropagation as dynamic programming on the computation graph — and gradient-checks it. Everything runs live; the companion Colab re-runs the same network in PyTorch so you can see autograd reproduce your manual derivatives line for line.

title: 10.4 Gradient Descent and Backpropagation
text:
1. Basic Concept
Gradient descent: to minimize a differentiable loss \(L(\theta)\), iterate
\[\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - \eta \, \nabla L(\theta_t)\]

\(\eta\) (learning rate) trades stability against speed: too small crawls, too large overshoots and diverges.
Stochastic GD approximates \(\nabla L\) from a mini-batch — cheap steps with noisy gradients; the noise itself regularizes (10.5).
Backpropagation computes \(\nabla L\) efficiently: the chain rule applied in reverse topological order over the computation graph, reusing each node’s stored forward value once. It is dynamic programming: each node’s gradient is computed exactly once from its children’s gradients.

Worked example — GD on a 1-D quadratic, where every step can be checked in closed form (\(x_{t+1} = (1-2\eta)x_t\)):






For a network, \(L\) has millions of coordinates and \(\nabla L\) must be assembled by the chain rule across layers — that assembly is backprop, built next.

title: 10.4 Gradient Descent and Backpropagation
text:
2. Concept Questions

In the quadratic demo, why does the closed form \(x_t = (1-2\eta)^t x_0\) predict divergence exactly at \(\eta > 1\)? What is the analogous closed-form condition for general quadratic losses in terms of the Hessian’s eigenvalues?
Backprop visits each edge once. What two quantities must each node store from the forward pass, and what single operation combines them with downstream gradients?
Mini-batch SGD’s gradient is unbiased but noisy. Name one good and one bad consequence of the noise.
Why is backprop (reverse mode) the right choice for training — what would forward mode’s cost be for a net with \(P\) parameters? (If unsure, 10.1 Q1.)
Momentum adds \(v_{t+1} = \beta v_t + \nabla L\), \(\theta \mathrel{-}= \eta v_{t+1}\). What does \(\beta = 0.9\) average over, and which two pathologies does this smooth away?



Answers


\(|1-2\eta| < 1\) ⇔ \(0 < \eta < 1\); the update is a geometric shrink factor. General diagonalizable quadratic: convergence iff \(\eta < 2/\lambda_{\max}\) (per-mode shrink \(|1-\eta\lambda_i|\)) — hence the practical rule “η near \(1/\lambda_{\max}\), i.e., near the reciprocal of the largest curvature”.
Its forward output (activation) and its local Jacobian (∂output/∂input). Combine: multiply the incoming upstream gradient by the local Jacobian, then route pieces to parents (vector–Jacobian products).
Good: escapes saddle regions/sharp minima, acts as implicit regularization, lets you afford n-sized epochs. Bad: gradient estimates jitter — needs lr decay or averaging for fine convergence; noisy estimates of gradient norms complicate clipping (10.7).
Reverse mode: all \(P\) parameter gradients in ~2 forward-pass costs. Forward mode: \(P\) passes (one tangent each) — impossible at \(P\) = millions.
An exponentially-weighted average of recent gradients (effective window ≈ \(1/(1-\beta) = 10\) steps). Smooths oscillation across ravines (high-curvature direction keeps cancelling) and accelerates consistent directions; doesn’t fix per-step noise entirely, but decorrelates the steps’ zig-zag.

title: 10.4 Gradient Descent and Backpropagation
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1 — the centerpiece. Implement a 1-16-1 MLP with tanh hidden activation and MSE loss with manual backpropagation; fit \(\sin\) on \([0, 2\pi)\) from 64 noisy points; plot the loss curve and the fit. Structure the code as forward (storing activations), backward (chain rule, layer by layer), update. Verify gradients by finite differences once, then trust the loop.


Solution







Every line of backward is 10.1 Exercise 1’s chain rule in matrix clothes: dz2 (residual) → dW2/db2 (outer products) → dh (transpose matmul) → dz1 (times local slope 1-h²) → dW1/db1. The gradient check is the habit that catches sign errors, missing 1-h², and transposed matmuls before they cost an afternoon.

Exercise 2. Gradient descent vs momentum vs “too-large lr” on the Exercise-1 problem: rerun the fit with (a) plain GD, lr = 0.1; (b) momentum β = 0.9, lr = 0.02; (c) plain GD, lr = 1.0. Plot the three loss curves on one log-scale axis. Which converges furthest in 2000 steps, and what does (c)’s curve teach about diagnosing divergence?


Solution







Momentum wins on this ravine-shaped loss (the oscillating tanh curvatures average out); lr = 1.0 diverges — the signature is a loss curve that steps upward or NaNs within a few steps, not a plateau. Diagnosis order: (1) diverges? cut lr by 10; (2) plateaus high? raise lr or add momentum; (3) noisy but descending? it’s just SGD.

Exercise 3. Batch-size anatomy: using the Exercise-1 network, train with batch sizes {8, 16, 32, 64} (lr 0.05, 3000 epochs-worth of updates normalized so each setting sees the data equally). Compare final loss and compute cost. Then state the linear-scaling heuristic and when it breaks.


Solution







Smaller batches descend further here (more updates, noise helps escape tanh plateaus) at the same sample-passes; the classic linear-scaling rule (“scale lr ∝ batch size”) holds near small batches for large-scale vision workloads but breaks when lr approaches the stability edge (\(2/\lambda_{\max}\) of the batch Hessian) or with normalization layers whose statistics depend on batch size. Rule of thumb: tune lr per batch size, or keep batch small enough that noise remains useful.

title: 10.4 Gradient Descent and Backpropagation
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Sum vs mean reduction changes the effective learning rate by the batch size: gradients from a summed loss are n× larger. Mixing reductions between train/eval or across batches silently rescales your lr.
Accumulation across steps (torch’s default): forgetting to zero gradients between steps adds stale gradients — equivalent to an unintended momentum of 1.0 with garbage memory (10.1).
Vanishing/exploding products: backprop through L layers multiplies L Jacobians; with tanh slopes < 1 the product collapses exponentially (10.7 lives in this regime), with large init weights it explodes — gradient clipping (rescale when the norm exceeds a threshold) is the practical tourniquet.
Learning-rate schedules are optimization, not decoration: step decay, cosine, warmup — all acknowledge that the useful η shrinks as you approach the minimum (the quadratic analysis: optimal fixed η is only optimal at the minimum’s curvature).
Numerical gradient checks: use central differences (O(ε²) error), ε ≈ 1e-6 for float64 (1e-2 relative for float32), compare relative error |a−n| / max(|a|+|n|, tiny) < 1e-7 — and disable any stochastic parts (dropout) first.
GD ≠ Newton: first-order methods ignore curvature; on badly scaled problems (features with wildly different scales) GD’s isotropic step is the bottleneck — standardization is cheap second-order medicine.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated backprop for the Exercise-1 network has three bugs. Find them before running the fixed cell.








What’s wrong, and the fix


No mean reduction: dz2 keeps the factor 2 but drops /n — the effective learning rate is silently 64× larger than intended; the run destabilizes (the printed final MSE is nan — the divergence is the symptom, not the bug itself).
Wrong activation in the output gradient: ∂z2/∂W2 passes through h, not the pre-activation z1 — a plausible-looking hallucination that corrupts dW2’s direction every step.
Wrong local slope: tanh’s derivative is 1 − tanh²(z) = 1 − h², not 1 − z1². The AI confused pre- with post-activation — exactly the error a one-line gradient check catches.

title: 10.4 Gradient Descent and Backpropagation
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Prove backprop’s cost claim on the matrix-chain problem: computing \(\nabla_{W_1,\dots,W_L} \|(\cdots((XW_1)W_2)\cdots W_L)\|^2\) — show that right-to-left (reverse mode) costs one extra pass equivalent to the forward pass, while left-to-right (forward mode) costs one pass per parameter entry. Where in your Exercise-1 code is the “reverse” visible as an index pattern?


Hint

Reverse mode carries one matrix (the adjoint) backward; forward mode carries one tangent direction per parameter entry forward. Count matrix multiplications of both plans.



Solution

Forward pass: L matrix products, storing each \(A_\ell\). Reverse: \(\delta_L = 2A_L\), then \(\delta_{\ell-1} = \delta_\ell W_\ell^\top\) (one product per layer), gradients \(A_{\ell-1}^\top \delta_\ell\) (one product per layer) — total ≈ 2L products, i.e., ~2× forward. Forward mode with tangent direction \(E_{ij}\) for parameter entry \((i,j)\): one full L-layer pass per entry → \(P\) passes (\(P\) = total entries). In Exercise 1, reverse mode is visible as the pattern gradients use stored activations from the same step (dW2 = h.T @ dz2 reuses h; dW1 = X.T @ dz1 reuses X) and the adjoint dz flows input-ward (dz2 → dz1), never recomputing a forward quantity. That reuse — each edge’s contribution computed once — is the dynamic-programming content of backprop.

Q2. Learning-rate theory, made empirical: for the Exercise-1 network at initialization, estimate the largest Hessian eigenvalue \(\lambda_{\max}\) of the loss by power iteration on finite-difference Hessian–vector products, and check that GD diverges precisely when \(\eta > 2/\lambda_{\max}\). Then explain why practitioners still tune η by grid/search rather than computing \(2/\lambda_{\max}\) — and why the optimal η changes during training.


Hint

Hessian–vector products need only gradients: \(v^\top H v \approx \frac{\|\nabla L(\theta + \epsilon v)\| \text{ directional}}{\epsilon}\) via central differences of the directional derivative. Power-iterate a random vector.



Solution







Power iteration on Hessian–vector products (gradient differences — no n² Hessian ever formed) recovers \(\lambda_{\max}\); GD with η just over \(2/\lambda_{\max}\) explodes, just below it converges slowly — matching the quadratic theory. Practitioners still search η because (i) the Hessian changes as the network trains (loss surfaces are only locally quadratic; \(2/\lambda_{\max}\) at init doesn’t bound later curvature), (ii) mini-batch noise regularizes in ways the exact Hessian ignores, and (iii) schedules (decay/warmup) deliberately traverse regimes. The theory gives the scale of η; search finds the constant.

title: 10.4 Gradient Descent and Backpropagation
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (× 4.6 hyperparameter tuning × 5.2 ridge). The learning rate is a hyperparameter like any other — but unlike ridge’s λ it interacts with time. Design and run an honest tuning protocol for (η, β) on the Exercise-1 problem: a coarse random search over 20 (η, β) pairs on a validation split, then report the test loss of the winner. How different is the winner from the best test pair (the one you must never select)? Quantify the tuning optimism, and connect to 4.3’s discussion.
C2 (× 9.2 PCA). Gradient descent on whitened inputs: whiten the Exercise-1 X (PCA-whitening, 9.2) and retrain at the same η. Measure speed-to-loss-threshold vs raw inputs, and explain via the Hessian’s condition number — then state why modern architectures instead normalize internally (batch/layer norm, 10.5 and 10.9) rather than preprocessing once.

title: 10.4 Gradient Descent and Backpropagation
text:
7. Summary

GD iterates \(\theta \mathrel{-}= \eta\nabla L\); stability requires \(\eta < 2/\lambda_{\max}\) — divergence within a few steps is the diagnostic.
Backprop = reverse-mode chain rule over the recorded graph: each node multiplies the upstream gradient by its local Jacobian; each edge computed once (dynamic programming).
Momentum averages recent gradients: tames ravines, accelerates consistent directions.
Mini-batching trades gradient quality for update frequency; the noise is regularization, not just cost.
Gradient-check every hand-written backward pass once — central differences, relative error < 1e-7.
Sum-vs-mean reductions, stale gradients, and lr schedules are where training loops actually break.
A net that trains is not a net that generalizes — the machinery for not overfitting is next: 10.5 regularization for neural networks.

title: 10.2 Single-Layer Neural Networks
text: One neuron — an affine map followed by a nonlinearity — is the atom every later page composes. Choose the pieces carefully and the single neuron is your old friends: sigmoid + log-loss is logistic regression (3.3); identity + squared error is linear regression (2.2). Deep learning begins when you stop hand-picking features and start stacking these atoms.

title: 10.2 Single-Layer Neural Networks
text:
1. Basic Concept
A single neuron computes, for input \(x \in \mathbb{R}^d\):
\[z = w^\top x + b, \qquad a = g(z)\]
with \(g\) the activation. The pairing of \(g\) with a loss is not arbitrary:









task

sigmoid

regression

BCE each
