Training by gradient descent (10.4 develops the machinery): for BCE with sigmoid, the derivatives collapse beautifully to \(\nabla_w = X^\top(\hat y - y)/n\) — the same residual form as linear regression (2.2).
Worked example — train one sigmoid neuron on two-moons with plain gradient descent, and watch it fail exactly as logistic regression would:






The boundary is a single line — one neuron cannot bend. Stacking neurons is 10.3’s whole point.

title: 10.2 Single-Layer Neural Networks
text:
2. Concept Questions

In what precise sense is a sigmoid neuron with BCE loss the same model as logistic regression from 3.3? What differs (if anything) in how each course page fits it?
Why does the gradient \(\nabla_w = \tfrac{1}{n}X^\top(\hat y - y)\) have no factor that looks like the sigmoid derivative \(p(1-p)\) — where did it go?
The worked example standardizes \(X\) first. Which two pathologies does unscaled input cause for (a) gradient descent, (b) the sigmoid itself?
A neuron’s output is 0.9999 on a negative example. What is its BCE contribution and its gradient component — and what is this regime called?
K sigmoid neurons on the same input with independent targets: how many models is that, and what would you change to make them share what they learn?



Answers


Same parameterization (\(w^\top x + b\) through a sigmoid), same likelihood, same MLE problem. Only the fitter differs: 3.3 used Newton/IRLS (statsmodels); here, plain first-order gradient descent. Same optimum for convex loss; different path to it.
The sigmoid derivative cancelled: BCE’s ∂/∂z contributes \(p - y\) and sigmoid’s ∂a/∂z contributes \(p(1-p)\); the chain rule cancels the \(p(1-p)\) exactly (do it once by hand — it’s the reason sigmoid+BCE is the “matched pair”). Unmatched pairs (sigmoid + MSE) don’t cancel → slow, plateau-prone learning.

GD is isotropic: features on scales 1 and 1000 force a tiny learning rate that crawls along the flat direction (the ridge pathology of 5.2 in dynamics form). (b) \(z = w^\top x\) large in magnitude saturates the sigmoid → gradients ≈ 0 at initialization.

Loss \(-\log(1 - 0.9999) \approx 9.2\) (vs 0.69 at chance) and gradient ≈ (0.9999 − 0)·x: a strong, correctly-signed push — saturation is only a problem when the model is confidently wrong in a way it can’t escape (here it can). The dangerous saturation is confidently wrong with tiny gradients — MSE + sigmoid.
K independent logistic regressions (one-vs-rest). Sharing starts when neurons feed common downstream structure — hidden layers (10.3) — or when outputs share a body via multitask heads.

title: 10.2 Single-Layer Neural Networks
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Train the single sigmoid neuron on two-moons as in Section 1, then fit sklearn’s LogisticRegression on the same standardized data. Compare accuracy and the coefficient vectors. How close is 300 steps of plain GD to the Newton-solver optimum — and what would shrink the gap (without changing models)?


Solution







Identical model, near-identical coefficients — the loss is convex, so any sane optimizer lands in the same basin; only convergence speed differs. Shrinking the gap: more steps, feature scaling (done), or a smarter first-order method (momentum/Adam, 10.4); or the second-order route statsmodels took. For a convex problem the “optimizer wars” are about iteration cost only.

Exercise 2. A neuron can only cut with a hyperplane — prove it to yourself constructively: for the four XOR points, show that no choice of \((w, b)\) achieves 4/4 accuracy by (a) arguing geometrically in two sentences, and (b) brute-force checking a grid of \((w_1, w_2, b)\). Then show one hidden layer of two sigmoid neurons fixes it (forward pass only — hand-pick the weights).


Solution


XOR’s positive points are diagonal corners: any half-plane containing both also contains a negative corner, because the positive set is not linearly separable (its convex hull intersects the negatives’).







The grid confirms 3/4 is the ceiling; the hand-set hidden layer computes AND and an OR-like unit, and the output neuron implements “OR but not AND” — a composition of two cuts. Two neurons bought non-convexity: this is the entire plot of 10.3.

title: 10.2 Single-Layer Neural Networks
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

The activation–loss pairing is load-bearing: sigmoid+BCE (and softmax+CE) cancel their Jacobians into the clean residual form; sigmoid+MSE multiplies every gradient by \(p(1-p)\) — vanishing exactly when the neuron is confident. If you write a custom head, keep the matched pairs.
Class imbalance moves the threshold, not the model: a 1:100 problem still trains fine; accuracy and the 0.5 cutoff become meaningless (see 3.1.5 AUPRC). The neuron doesn’t know it should prefer precision or recall — you choose the operating point.
Initialization matters even here: \(w = 0\) is a valid start for a convex single neuron (symmetry can’t trap you with no hidden layers), but with hidden layers zero init is fatal — all neurons receive identical gradients (10.3).
Full-batch GD on 200 points is fine; streaming is not free: mini-batching adds gradient noise whose scale interacts with the learning rate — the first place to look when a torch run “explodes” (10.4).
predict_proba is a calibration claim: a sigmoid outputs a probability only under correct specification; miscalibration is the norm under imbalance or regularization (check reliability before quoting probabilities clinically).


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated single-neuron trainer has three bugs. Diagnose, then compare with the fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Huge random init + raw scales: \(z\) lands at \(\pm\) hundreds → saturated sigmoid → gradients of either sign barely move the loss; and unstandardized features give an ill-conditioned problem. Fix: small (or zero) init, standardize inputs.
Wrong sigmoid sign: 1/(1+exp(z)) computes σ(−z) — the model’s outputs (and hence the loss surface) are mirrored; combined with bug 3 the dynamics are nonsense. Fix: 1/(1+exp(-z)).
Wrong residual: the BCE gradient is \(X^\top(p - y)/n\), not \(X^\top(p + y)/n\). The AI “hallucinated” a plus — the kind of error gradient-checking catches in one line (10.4 Exercise 2).

title: 10.2 Single-Layer Neural Networks
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. The single-neuron BCE loss is convex in \((w, b)\) — prove it by composing known facts (affine ∘ log-concave sigmoid ∘ convex log-loss), then answer: since a convex function has no bad local minima, why do people still observe “stuck” runs with a single neuron? Construct the stuck case numerically with a poorly scaled feature and a large learning rate (divergence and plateau both count).


Hint

Convexity rules out local traps, not divergence, plateaus of ill-conditioning, or numerical saturation. Plot the loss for lr ∈ {0.01, 1, 100} on raw (unscaled) moons.



Solution

\(z = w^\top x + b\) is affine in \((w,b)\); \(L(z) = -[y\log\sigma(z) + (1-y)\log(1-\sigma(z))]\) is convex in \(z\) (each term: −log of a log-concave function composed affinely); affine ∘ convex is convex; sums of convex are convex. QED — no local minima, but: divergence (lr too large overshoots along the steep direction; loss oscillates upward), plateaus (ill-conditioned curvature: progress along the flat direction is glacial even though the direction is “correct”), saturation (logits far from 0 make float arithmetic lose the gradient before the math does). Live:






Convexity is about the destination, not the speed — optimization difficulty survived into deep learning as conditioning, not as local minima.

Q2. Sigmoid outputs claim probabilities. On the imbalanced two-moons variant (flip 90% of class-1 labels to 0, so prevalence ≈ 5%), train the single neuron, draw its reliability table (predicted-probability quintiles vs observed frequency), then fit Platt scaling — one more sigmoid mapping logit → label, by MLE — and report \((a, b)\). Interpret the fitted values: what would \(a < 1\) have fixed, and what does \(a \approx 1, b \approx 0\) (near-calibration) tell you about when post-hoc calibration is needed at all?


Hint

Under heavy imbalance the raw sigmoid still ranks well but pushes probabilities toward the majority; a second sigmoid fit on held-out logits is the classical fix.



Solution







The deciles show modest overconfidence in the low bins (p̂ = 0.012–0.054 vs observed 0–0.1) — yet the global Platt fit returns \(a \approx 1, b \approx 0\): with a two-parameter monotone remap there is little to fix at this noise level. The lesson cuts both ways: local bin plots reveal miscalibration structure that a global two-parameter fix may not address, and a near-identity Platt fit certifies calibration rather than assuming it. The layered structure (representations → head → calibrator) is standard for deep nets: modern nets are excellent rankers whose probability outputs must be checked (and often Platt/temperature-scaled on held-out logits) before clinical use.

title: 10.2 Single-Layer Neural Networks
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (× 3.3 × 4.4 bias–variance). You have two fits on the same data: statsmodels’ IRLS logistic regression and your 300-step GD neuron, both unregularized. For n ∈ {30, 60, 120, 240, 480}, compare test accuracy in a small simulation. Where do they differ and why — connect optimizer convergence speed to sample size (hint: at small n the variance dominates and both converge to similar fits; at large n, an under-converged GD run is the biased one).
C2 (× 5.2 ridge × 8.3 soft-margin SVM). Three linear classifiers, three penalties, one geometry: logistic+BCE (log-loss), linear SVM (hinge), ridge regression sign (squared). For the moons data with a fixed labeled outlier flipped far away, fit all three (sklearn) and overlay the boundaries. Which loss’s gradient saturates at the outlier and which grows linearly/unboundedly — and how does that explain the robustness ordering you observe? (This is hinge’s margin story from the neuron’s-eye view.)

title: 10.2 Single-Layer Neural Networks
text:
7. Summary

One neuron = affine + activation; paired with the right loss it is logistic or linear regression.
sigmoid+BCE (softmax+CE) are matched pairs: the Jacobian cancels, leaving gradient = residual form.
One neuron cuts with a hyperplane — XOR-style structure needs composition (next page).
Saturation, scaling, and imbalance are the single-neuron’s three horsemen; standardize, match pairs, and choose thresholds deliberately.
Convexity guarantees no local minima — not speed, not stability, not calibration.
Outputs are rankers’ probabilities; calibrate on held-out data before clinical use.
Two neurons already beat XOR: time to stack — 10.3 multilayer networks.

title: 10.1 PyTorch Foundations
text: A torch.Tensor is a NumPy array that knows three extra things: where it lives (device: CPU/GPU), how precisely (dtype: usually float32), and how it was made (the autograd graph). Everything else — broadcasting, reshaping, @, reductions — transfers from NumPy almost word-for-word. This page builds that mental model with live NumPy cells; the PyTorch itself runs in the companion lab.

title: 10.1 PyTorch Foundations
text:
1. Basic Concept








NumPy
PyTorch

—
loss.backward()
reverse-mode differentiation (new concept)



The three additions, in one breath:

Autograd — every op on a tensor with requires_grad=True records a node in a computation graph; loss.backward() walks it in reverse and accumulates ∂loss/∂parameter into each .grad.
Devices — the same tensor code runs on CPU or GPU; tensors on different devices cannot be mixed.
torch.nn + torch.optim — layers, losses, and optimizers as composable objects (10.2 onward).

Worked example — the graph autograd automates, computed by hand (live NumPy): one gradient-descent step of linear regression on a single point:






In PyTorch (run the Colab lab), the identical step is written without any derivatives:
import torch
x = torch.tensor([2.0]); y = torch.tensor([7.0])
w = torch.tensor(1.0, requires_grad=True)
b = torch.tensor(0.0, requires_grad=True)

loss = ((w * x + b) - y) ** 2
loss.backward()                        # fills w.grad, b.grad
with torch.no_grad():
    w -= 0.1 * w.grad
    b -= 0.1 * b.grad
    w.grad.zero_(); b.grad.zero_()     # grads ACCUMULATE between backward calls
Every hand-derived factor above becomes a graph edge; backward() multiplies them for you. 10.4 builds the manual version end-to-end so the automation is never magic.

title: 10.1 PyTorch Foundations
text:
2. Concept Questions

Why must the PyTorch snippet call w.grad.zero_() after stepping, when the NumPy version has no analogous line?
requires_grad=True is set on w and b but not on x and y. What question is each flag answering?
PyTorch defaults to float32 while NumPy defaults to float64. Give one reason for the choice and one consequence you must respect when comparing against NumPy results.
You get RuntimeError: Expected all tensors to be on the same device. What two lines of your script disagree, and what is the fix?
What does with torch.no_grad(): prevent, and why do both inference and the parameter update itself need it?



Answers


Autograd accumulates into .grad across calls (so gradients can be summed over multiple passes); NumPy locals are recomputed fresh each iteration. Forgetting zero_() is the classic “loss went down but model went crazy” bug — you are summing stale gradients from every previous step.
“Do I need the derivative with respect to this tensor?” We need ∂loss/∂w and ∂loss/∂b (things we update), never ∂loss/∂x (data). Fewer graph nodes = less memory and compute.
Reason: float32 halves memory and doubles GPU throughput, and DL tolerates the precision. Consequence: bitwise agreement with float64 NumPy is impossible — compare with tolerances (rtol=1e-5-ish), and watch accumulated sums (Exercise 2).
The model’s parameters were moved with model.to("cuda") but the input batch stayed on the CPU (or vice versa). Fix: move everything — X = X.to(device) next to model.to(device).
no_grad() stops graph construction. Inference: you don’t need gradients, and building the graph wastes memory (it also lets you feed huge batches). The update: w -= lr * w.grad is itself an op — under grad-tracking it would be recorded into the graph and pollute the next backward pass.

title: 10.1 PyTorch Foundations
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run — every reflex here transfers word-for-word to torch.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Hand-computed gradients for a two-layer graph: with h = tanh(W1 @ x), y = W2 @ h, L = sum(y**2), derive ∂L/∂W2 and ∂L/∂W1 in matrix form, implement them in NumPy, and verify every entry against central finite differences. Where does the chain rule force you through tanh'?


Solution

∂L/∂W2 = 2y hᵀ; ∂L/∂W1 = (W2ᵀ · 2y) ⊙ tanh′(W1x) xᵀ, with tanh′(u) = 1 − tanh²(u).






The tanh′ factor is the local slope of the nonlinearity — the term that vanishing/exploding gradients (10.4, 10.7) are made of. In torch, loss.backward() produces exactly dL_dW1, dL_dW2 in W1.grad, W2.grad.

Exercise 2. dtype discipline: PyTorch’s float32 default is a real precision trade. Sum the sequence 1, 0.1, 0.1, … (10⁶ terms, plus the leading 1) in float32 and float64, and compare each to the float64 truth computed pairwise. Then do the same for np.sum on float32 without changing dtype but using math.fsum-style pairwise summation (np.sum already pairs) vs a Python loop. What does this teach you about trusting 7 significant digits?


Solution







Pairwise summation keeps the float32 error near √n · eps (~1e-3 relative at best for eps ≈ 1.2e-7); the sequential loop drifts linearly worse. Torch accumulations on GPU are float32 by default: gradient checks against NumPy float64 must use tolerances ~1e-3–1e-5, never ==, and loss curves plotted from float32 can wobble at the 4th digit — that is the hardware’s arithmetic, not your learning rate.

title: 10.1 PyTorch Foundations
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Grad accumulation is the default, not a bug fix you do once: any training loop needs optimizer.zero_grad() (or zero_grad(set_to_none=True)) before each backward() — unless you deliberately want gradient accumulation over micro-batches.
Leaf vs non-leaf: .grad is only populated for leaf tensors created with requires_grad=True. Gradients w.r.t. intermediates need tensor.retain_grad() — rarely what you want; restructure instead.
In-place ops on graph tensors (x += ..., x.relu_()) can silently invalidate saved activations and raise “a variable needed for gradient computation has been modified”. Prefer out-of-place ops in layers you write.
.item() / .cpu() are device synchronizations: calling them every step to log the loss stalls GPU pipelines — log every k steps, or use loss.detach().
Module vs functional: model.train() / model.eval() switch behavior of dropout/batchnorm (10.5) — forgetting eval() corrupts every validation metric.
Reproducibility: torch.manual_seed seeds CPU + CUDA, but torch.backends.cudnn.deterministic and dataloader worker seeding are separate switches — a “random” rerun may differ for reasons that are all documented, not mysterious.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated training step has three bugs. Diagnose before running the fixed version.
# AI-generated: one training step (will not run here — spot the bugs by reading)
for X_batch, y_batch in loader:
    X_batch, y_batch = X_batch.to("cpu"), y_batch.to("cuda")   # BUG 1
    logits = model(X_batch)
    loss = criterion(logits, y_batch)
    optimizer.step()                                            # BUG 2
    loss.backward()
    running_loss += loss                                        # BUG 3


What’s wrong, and the fix


Device split: data on CPU, model (implicitly) moved to CUDA — or the reverse; every batch raises the device-mismatch error. Move both with the same device variable.
Step before backward: optimizer.step() applies gradients that are zero/stale; the order is zero_grad() → backward() → step().
Graph-carrying accumulator: running_loss += loss keeps the whole graph alive via the loss tensor — memory grows every iteration. Use running_loss += loss.item() (or loss.detach()).

# fixed
for X_batch, y_batch in loader:
    X_batch, y_batch = X_batch.to(device), y_batch.to(device)
    optimizer.zero_grad()
    loss = criterion(model(X_batch), y_batch)
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()
    running_loss += loss.item()

title: 10.1 PyTorch Foundations
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Reverse-mode autodiff computes all parameter gradients in one backward pass costing ~2× the forward pass, regardless of whether there are 10 parameters or 10 billion. Explain why forward-mode (one directional derivative per pass) is hopeless for training but superior for functions with 1 input and many outputs — and connect this to why JAX/PyTorch offer both modes.


Hint

Count passes needed: gradients w.r.t. every parameter (many inputs → one loss) vs a Jacobian with one input row and many output columns.



Solution

Reverse mode propagates one adjoint vector backward through the graph: cost O(graph size) total, delivering ∂L/∂θ for all θ at once — exactly DL’s shape of question (scalar loss, millions of parameters). Forward mode carries one tangent direction forward: it yields one column of the Jacobian per pass, so getting all parameter gradients needs P passes — 175 billion passes for a 175B-parameter model. Conversely, for f: ℝ → ℝⁿ (one input, n outputs), forward mode gets the whole Jacobian in one pass while reverse needs n. Tooling follows the question: training = reverse mode; sensitivity analysis of a scalar parameter or implicit-function derivatives (e.g., hyperparameter gradients through a converged solver) often favor forward mode. The deep-learning stack standardized on reverse mode because of this cost argument, not taste.

Q2. Design (in NumPy, live) the semantics of an optimizer step with gradient accumulation over k micro-batches: implement accumulate-then-step for the linear model of Section 1 and show the accumulated update equals the full-batch gradient step exactly when the micro-batch losses are means of equal-sized batches. Where does exactness break (unequal batch sizes, dropout, batchnorm)?


Hint

Mean-of-means equals the global mean only when the denominators match; write the two formulas and subtract.



Solution







Exact because every chunk contributes meanᶜ/n·k with equal sizes: (1/k)Σ meanᶜ = global mean. Breaks: (i) unequal chunks — (1/k)Σ meanᶜ ≠ global mean (weight by chunk size); (ii) dropout — each micro-batch samples different masks, so accumulated ≠ single-pass dropout; (iii) batchnorm — batch statistics differ per micro-batch. This is why gradient accumulation for memory-constrained training changes the function being optimized slightly under normalization/dropout, not just its schedule.

title: 10.1 PyTorch Foundations
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (foundations × 10.4 manual backprop). Implement the Section 1 single-point example for a batch of 50 points, both by hand-derived formulas and by an automatic table-driven graph (each op appends (parent_refs, local_derivative_fn) to a list; backward walks it in reverse). Verify both against each other. What structure of your table mirrors torch’s dynamically-recorded graph — and why does that design (define-by-run) make control flow like variable-length sequences natural?
C2 (foundations × 5.2 ridge × 4.6 tuning). The torch update w -= lr * (grad + wd * w) is ridge regression by SGD. For the linear model, derive the fixed point and show it matches the ridge closed form scaled by nothing (identical solution) — then explain why, for deep nets, weight decay strength and learning rate interact (decoupled AdamW) and what that does to any learning-rate sweep that was tuned without decay.

title: 10.1 PyTorch Foundations
text:
7. Summary

A tensor = NumPy array + device + dtype + autograd graph; ops and broadcasting transfer 1:1.
backward() = your hand chain-rule, automated over a recorded graph; .grad accumulates — zero it before each step.
requires_grad marks what you differentiate with respect to; no_grad() stops graph building for inference and updates.
float32 is the default: compare against float64 references with tolerances, not equality.
Device mismatches and stale graphs (.item(), detach(), eval()) are the day-one operational bugs.
Reverse-mode’s one-pass-for-all-parameters cost is the economic reason deep learning is trainable at all.
The atom of everything ahead is one linear map + one nonlinearity — up next: 10.2 single-layer networks.

title: 9.6 Practical Clustering Issues
text: Every previous clustering page deferred the same questions: how do I choose k defensibly, which validation do I report, what do I do about mixed data types, outliers, and the fact that clustering is an optimization game with many legitimate answers? This page assembles the practical machinery — stability, internal indices, external validation — into one honest workflow.

title: 9.6 Practical Clustering Issues
text:
1. Basic Concept
The validation triad, defined precisely:

Internal — silhouette, inertia-based indices: does the partition fit the chosen metric? (necessary, never sufficient)
Stability — do partitions reproduce under resampling/perturbation/seed changes? (reproducibility evidence)
External — do clusters align with domain-known variables (outcomes, batches, replicated cohorts)? (the only truth-adjacent evidence)







Stability as the workhorse — the full implementation (revisited from 9.1 Exercise 2, now with per-k curves):

title: 9.6 Practical Clustering Issues
text:
2. Concept Questions

Silhouette’s formula rewards which geometry, and what truth-shape makes it systematically misleading?
Stability selects reproducible partitions. Construct (in one sentence) the case where a partition is perfectly stable and scientifically wrong.
External validation correlates clusters with outcomes. What does a strong cluster–outcome association not prove (two answers: one statistical, one causal)?
Mixed data types (continuous + categorical): why does one-hot + Euclidean quietly distort, and what does the distortion favor?
You report “we found 4 clusters (silhouette-selected among k = 2..9).” Name the two selection games you just played and the evidence a reviewer should demand.



Answers


Silhouette = (b − a)/max(a, b): cohesion-to-nearest-other-neighbor ratio. It rewards convex, well-separated, similarly-sized clusters and penalizes elongated/ring/uneven truths even when perfectly recovered (9.4’s rings; spectral methods score “poorly” on silhouettes they solve perfectly).
Stable-but-wrong: K-means with k = 4 on two true blobs at a strong scale artifact — resamples reproduce the same 4-way artifact every time (stability measures the procedure, the truth lives outside it — 9.1 Q2).
Statistical: no multiple-testing control (you tested many clusterings/covariates until one “worked” — 12.x stub). Causal: cluster membership is a derived feature; association with outcome may ride on the same confounders that shaped the clustering — clusters are not interventions.
One-hot categorical columns contribute 0/1 coordinates whose scale (k levels → unit spacing) silently weights them against standardized continuous features (or for them, with many levels); distances become an accidental blend. Favor: whichever block the encoding happened to amplify — dominant-axis behavior (9.1’s sensitivity, encoded).

The k-selection game (9 values tried, best reported — the 4.6 selection bonus); (2) the index-selection game (silhouette chosen from the index zoo). Demanded: stability at reported k, index-agreement, external validation, and all tried values disclosed.

title: 9.6 Practical Clustering Issues
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. The full k-selection tribunal: implement select_k(X, k_range, B=40) producing a DataFrame with, per k: inertia, silhouette, bootstrap stability (mean ARI), and the gap-style null comparison (mini). Run it on (a) 4 planted blobs, (b) null uniform data. Report both tables. Define the selection policy you’d pre-register (e.g., “k must maximize ≥2 indices, achieve stability > 0.8, and beat the null silhouette by ≥ 0.1”) and check what each dataset yields.


Solution







Pre-registered policy example: “k must have stability ≥ 0.75, silhouette within 0.05 of the max, and gap > 0.1; ties resolved toward smaller k.” The two gap columns are the whole point. On planted data the policy selects k = 4 — stability 0.994, silhouette 0.605 (the max), gap 0.876 — the reassuring case. On structureless Gaussian data the uniform-reference gap never drops below 0.87 and the policy happily passes k = 6 (stability 0.780, silhouette 0.365 = max, gap 0.896): the pipeline “discovers” six clusters in noise and reports it as confidently as the real answer. Nothing is wrong with the code; the mistake is the reference distribution. The gap statistic asks “is this fit much better than a structureless fit?”, and a uniform bounding box is a terrible structureless fit for Gaussian data — far too diffuse, so k-means beats it regardless of the data. Swap in a null matched to the data’s own per-coordinate mean and SD and the gate starts working: the same null data now yields gaps of −0.014 to +0.072, all below 0.1, so nothing passes and the pipeline refuses, while planted k = 4 keeps a gap of 0.946. The general rule — it extends well past the gap statistic — is that any “is this better than chance?” threshold needs its chance distribution matched to the data’s shape, and a pre-registered policy that has never been run against a negative control will confirm whatever it is pointed at. Run the null case; make refusing a pre-registered outcome, not a failure.

Exercise 2. External validation done right: on a dataset with a known binary covariate (treatment arm) and a known continuous outcome, cluster into k = 3 and test cluster–treatment (chi-square) and cluster–outcome (ANOVA/Kruskal) associations with multiplicity control over k ∈ 2..6 (report best p-value vs Bonferroni threshold). Then invert the causal framing: the clusters were built from features including the outcome-correlated ones — what does that contaminate? Rebuild excluding those features and re-test. Write the association-claim sentence that survives.


Solution







The leaky features manufacture cluster–outcome association by construction (the outcome shaped the clustering) — no causal or even associational claim survives; the multiplicity correction alone doesn’t save it. Rebuilt without outcome-correlated features, any surviving association is at least arguable. Surviving sentence: “Clusters derived from baseline features (excluding outcome-correlated measurements) were associated with the outcome at Bonferroni-corrected p = …, requiring replication in an independent cohort” — associations, replicated, with the construction disclosed.

Exercise 3. Mixed-type and outlier-safe workflow: on a cohort with 3 numeric + 2 categorical features (some rows also outliers), implement (a) one-hot + standardized-numerics K-means with categorical weight as a tuned parameter (compare weight 1 vs √(levels)), (b) outlier screen (IsolationForest or IQR) before clustering with the removed rows reported separately, (c) full validation battery on the final k. Report the pipeline’s choices as a reproducible spec — the “methods paragraph” for mixed-data clustering.


Solution







Methods paragraph: “Numeric features were standardized; categorical features were one-hot encoded and weighted at w = √(levels) (comparable total mass to the numeric block; w tuned by silhouette sensitivity). Isolation-forest outliers (n = …) were flagged and analyzed separately. K was selected by combined silhouette/stability criteria over k = 2–4, and the resulting partition was tested against treatment and outcome associations with multiplicity correction.” Every number in that paragraph came from a check you’ve now implemented — that’s what makes it reproducible rather than narrative.

title: 9.6 Practical Clustering Issues
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

The index zoo is not the law: dozens of internal indices (Davies–Bouldin, Calinski–Harabasz, …) exist; they disagree systematically by geometry — pre-commit to your index set and policy, or report the zoo (12.x stub’s multiplicity, again).
Subsampling changes k: stability curves can cross — k stable at bootstrap B₁ unstable at B₂ means your “clusters” live at one sampling density; report the stability curve, not one point.
Outliers both create and destroy clusters: one outlier = one hijacked centroid; a dense outlier pocket = a “real” cluster of artifacts. Detect, report, and decide by mechanism (7.2’s ledger for trees; here for points).
Batch effects outrun biology (5.6): audit clusters against batch/site first — a cluster that’s 95% one batch is a process finding, not a discovery.
Clustering ≠ classification of a latent truth unless you validate externally: the “confusion matrix” against a known labeling is a bonus analysis (ARI), not the definition of success (9.1 Q1’s impossibility).
Reproducibility spec: algorithm, version, distance, scaling, k (and how chosen), initialization/restarts, seed, outlier policy — a clustering without this spec is a rumor.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated “validated clustering” has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Argmax over the k × metric zoo: the selection bonus (4.1 Q2) plus index-shopping — report all tried values and pre-commit the policy.
Validation by the selection metric: circular by construction; validation must be a different evidence family (stability, external).
Cluster–batch agreement rebranded as subtypes: high agreement means the clustering reproduced the artifact. Audit, disclose, batch-correct, and re-cluster — then look for structure that isn’t the batch.

title: 9.6 Practical Clustering Issues
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Prove the silhouette–stability independence: construct two datasets with identical mean silhouette for k = 3 but different bootstrap stability (one with a genuinely separated 3-group geometry, one with three coin-flip partitions of uniform data). Implement both and verify. What does this construction prove about composing internal and stability evidence — and why is the composition necessary rather than redundant?


Hint</summary»
Silhouette is a fixed-dataset geometric average; stability is a resampling property. Uniform data can be carved into 3 well-separated-by-chance regions in one draw.



Solution</summary»
Uniform data’s one draw can show decent silhouette by luck (three separated-looking patches from the triangulation of randomness), while resampling reshuffles the patches — stability collapses. Conversely a stable partition can have modest silhouette (elongated truth). Construction:






The composition is necessary because the two evidences measure orthogonal failure modes: internal indices can’t detect sampling fragility; stability can’t detect geometry mismatch with the truth. Any single-number validation claim (“silhouette 0.6, good clustering”) commits at least one of the two errors this construction isolates.

Q2. Consensus clustering, built and judged: implement the consensus matrix for K-means across 200 subsampled runs at a given k — C_ij = fraction of runs where i and j co-occur. Visualize C (sorted by consensus ordering) for the planted-blob dataset at k ∈ {2, 3, 4, 5}: the true k shows a clean block-diagonal C, others show ragged off-blocks. Define the summary statistic (mean within-block vs between-block consensus gap) and verify it peaks at the true k. Then state the one caution: consensus measures clustering-algorithm agreement, not truth — connect to 9.1 Q1.


Solution







The gap peaks at the planted k: within-consensus near 1, between near 0 only when k matches the true block structure. Caution: consensus quantifies how self-consistently the algorithm partitions this dataset — a memorizable-but-wrong structure is equally capable of high consensus (stable-artifact case, 9.1 Q2). Consensus is the strongest internal reproducibility evidence available; external validation still outranks it.

title: 9.6 Practical Clustering Issues
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (practical × 7.x ensembles × 9.2). Ensemble-clustering pipeline: build a co-association matrix from 100 K-means runs (varying seeds, subsamples, feature subsets) instead of one run; cluster the co-association matrix (hierarchical, ward) for the final partition. On planted data with an ambiguous k, compare consensus-ensemble partition vs single-run K-means by ARI and stability. Quantify the ensemble dividend, name its cost (compute + lost per-run interpretability), and connect to why bagging works for trees (7.3) — variance reduction by averaging unstable structures.
C2 (practical × 2.5 confounding × 9.1). Clusters as covariates, honestly: derive cluster dummies from an unsupervised run, then use them as covariates in a regression predicting an outcome. Simulate data where (a) clusters genuinely moderate the outcome-gradient and (b) clusters are pure noise. Compare: treating cluster dummies as fixed known covariates (ignoring the estimation of clusters) vs the uncertainty-aware view (clusters are estimated — the classic classification-measurement-error issue). Quantify the SE overconfidence of the naive route across 300 simulations, and write the reporting sentence that acknowledges the two-stage estimation.

title: 9.6 Practical Clustering Issues
text:
7. Summary

Validation is a triad: internal (metric fit), stability (resampling reproducibility), external (domain evidence) — claims need the members their language implies.
Silhouette rewards convex geometry; stability rewards procedure reproducibility; neither certifies truth — compose them and add external evidence.
Choose k by pre-registered multi-evidence policy; refusal (“no defensible clusters”) is a publishable outcome.
Mixed data: encoding weight is a hyperparameter; outliers are audited before k; batch is audited before biology.
Consensus/co-association matrices are the strongest internal reproducibility evidence — algorithm agreement, not truth.
Clusters as downstream covariates are estimated quantities: their uncertainty propagates; disclose the two-stage design.
The unsupervised toolkit is complete. From here the course’s remaining parts (survival analysis, multiple testing, LLMs) lean on it — and on everything Parts 0–8 drilled: this was the checklist chapter. The one tool the checklist did not cover is manifold embedding — t-SNE, UMAP, and autoencoders, which find curved structure that 9.2’s linear projections cannot: 9.7.

title: 9.4 K-means Clustering
text: K-means partitions data into k groups by minimizing within-cluster distance to centroids: pick k centers, assign points to the nearest, move each center to its cluster’s mean, repeat. It is fast, scalable, universally available — and explicitly assumes spherical, equal-sized groups. Knowing exactly what it optimizes tells you exactly when it lies.

title: 9.4 K-means Clustering
text:
1. Basic Concept
The objective (inertia):
\[\min_{C_1, \ldots, C_k} \sum_{j=1}^k \sum_{i \in C_j} \|x_i - \mu_j\|^2, \qquad \mu_j = \text{mean of cluster } j\]
Lloyd’s algorithm alternates assign↔︎update until convergence — each step never increases inertia, so it converges (to a local optimum; hence n_init restarts):






Lloyd’s algorithm, by hand:

title: 9.4 K-means Clustering
text:
2. Concept Questions

Why does K-means implicitly assume spherical, equal-variance, equal-size clusters — derive each from the Euclidean-distance-to-centroid criterion?
Why must centroids be initialized well (n_init, k-means++), and what does Lloyd’s convergence guarantee not include?
Elbow vs silhouette vs gap statistic for choosing k: state what each measures and their shared blind spot.
Your feature is “income” in dollars and another is “age” in years. What happens to the clustering, and why is this the same disease as 9.1 Exercise 1?
K-means on data with one categorical feature encoded as integers (0, 1, 2)? What breaks, and what are the two standard repairs?



Answers


The criterion cares only about distance to the centroid (a single point): (a) elongated clusters get split (a long ellipse has far corners even with one true group — variance in every direction costs); (b) unequal variances misassign (the wide cluster’s points sit “closer” to the tight neighbor’s centroid); (c) unequal sizes bias boundary placement toward the big cluster (6.2-style bias, Voronoi edition).
Lloyd’s converges to a local optimum — bad inits (two centers in one true cluster) converge to poor partitions that still satisfy the fixed point. n_init restarts take the best; k-means++ seeds centers far apart probabilistically — better optima, fewer restarts.
Elbow: inertia vs k, look for the bend (subjective; inertia always falls). Silhouette: mean (b−a)/max(a,b) per point — cohesion vs separation (−1..1, computable, biased toward convex shapes). Gap statistic: inertia vs its null-expectation under uniform sampling (principled, costlier). Shared blind spot: all measure spherical-metric fit — none can tell you the true k for structured/non-spherical data.
Dollars dominate Euclidean distance by units — income decides everything, age is invisible. Same disease: unscaled features weight the metric; standardize (or weight features deliberately).
Integer-coded categories fabricate arithmetic: category 2 is “twice” category 1 and between 0 and 3 — the centroid becomes a meaningless average label. Repairs: one-hot the categorical (then distances are Hamming-ish on that block) or use k-modes/mixed-type distances (9.6).

title: 9.4 K-means Clustering
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Init sensitivity, quantified: for the 3-blob data, run K-means with n_init=1 over 200 different random seeds; record the final inertia and cluster quality (ARI). Plot the histogram of inertias — how many distinct optima exist, and what fraction of seeds found the global one? Then rerun with k-means++ (init="k-means++") and report the same. What does n_init=10 default buy you?


Solution







Random init finds the global optimum only some fraction of the time — the rest converge to split-cluster/merge-cluster locals with visibly worse inertia. k-means++ seeding (far-apart probabilistic starts) hits the global basin nearly always, which is why it’s the modern default and why n_init remains as insurance.

Exercise 2. Choosing k with three judges: for data with a planted k* = 4 (unequal weights), compute for k ∈ 2..9: (a) inertia (elbow by eye + second-difference knee detection), (b) mean silhouette, (c) a mini gap statistic (compare inertia to the mean inertia of uniform data in the same bounding box, B = 20 draws). Report the table and each judge’s verdict. Where do they disagree, and which do you trust for the final claim — with what supporting evidence?


Solution







The three judges typically agree on the planted k here, but through different evidence: silhouette peaks (separation quality), gap spikes (vs null), inertia elbows (rate change). When they disagree: silhouette/gap answer “is this partition defensible”, the elbow answers “where do returns vanish” — for a claim (“there are 4 groups”), demand the stability evidence of 9.1 Exercise 2 on top: no single index crowns k.

Exercise 3. Break it three ways, then fix what’s fixable: (a) two moons (hand-rolled crescents), (b) three clusters with wildly different variances, (c) one big uniform blob with 5% far outliers. For each: K-means k = true-k ARI, then the best repair among {more clusters + merge, K-means on PCA-2 (9.2), scaling tweaks, or “wrong tool — use a different family”}. Write the diagnosis-to-algorithm mapping sentence for each.


Solution








Non-convex truth: K-means’ Voronoi cells cannot represent crescents — change algorithm family (spectral, DBSCAN), not hyperparameters. (b) Shape/size assumption: Gaussian mixtures relax K-means’s hard spherical prior while staying in the centroid family. (c) Outliers hijack centroids (a single far point is its own “cluster’s” gravity) — outlier removal/detection is a preprocessing obligation. The mapping sentence: diagnose which assumption fails — convexity, variance-equality, or outlier-freedom — and switch algorithms at that assumption, not at the accuracy number.

title: 9.4 K-means Clustering
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

K-means is a special case of a Gaussian mixture (equal spherical covariances, hard assignment) — GMMs (Exercise 3b) are the generalization when clusters differ in shape/size/weight.
n_init and random_state belong in every report: K-means’ local optima make runs incomparable otherwise; report the initialization scheme, restarts, and convergence criterion.
The k-choice is a claim: “k = 4 subtypes” enters papers; support it with stability + external validation (9.1 Q2, 9.6), not the elbow alone.
Feature weighting is hidden tuning: scaling up a feature weights it in every distance — deliberate weighting (domain-informed) is legitimate; accidental weighting (units) is the 9.1 disease.
Empty clusters: a centroid can lose all its points; sklearn relocates it — but your hand-rolled version (Exercise 0’s update) needs the guard (we kept the old center).
K-means on PCA scores (9.2) is standard for wide data (denoised, decorrelated distances) — but it clusters the projection: structure in discarded components is invisible (C2 of 9.2’s batch caution).


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated clustering has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


n_init = 1 with no initialization report: the run is a lottery ticket on local optima. Use k-means++ with n_init ≥ 10 and report stability (9.1 Exercise 2).
Integer-coded category in Euclidean space — the Concept Question 5 breakage: one-hot (or k-modes); the category now dominates distance by its arbitrary spacing.
Inertia as quality: it only ever decreases with k and says nothing about validity — report silhouette/stability alongside, and interpret inertia only comparatively at fixed k and features.

title: 9.4 K-means Clustering
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Prove Lloyd’s algorithm never increases inertia, and that it converges in finitely many steps: (a) the assignment step (each point to nearest centroid) cannot increase inertia for fixed centers; (b) the update step (centroid = cluster mean) minimizes within-cluster squared distance for fixed assignments; (c) finitely many partitions ⇒ termination. What does this proof not promise — and which quantity’s monotonicity would an observer track to detect a buggy implementation?


Hint

Each step is an exact coordinate-wise minimization of the same objective; monotone decrease + finite states ⇒ convergence.



Solution


For fixed centers, nearest-centroid assignment minimizes each point’s contribution — inertia weakly decreases. (b) For fixed assignments, each Σ‖xᵢ − c‖² over a cluster is minimized at c = mean — weakly decreases again. (c) Inertia strictly decreases unless the partition repeats; partitions are finite ⇒ termination at a local optimum. Not promised: global optimality, a bound on iterations, or correctness of k. The tracked quantity is inertia per iteration — it must be monotone non-increasing; any increase means an implementation bug (misaligned assignment/update, or empty-cluster handling).


Q2. K-means vs GMM on unequal variances, theory and measurement: a GMM with full per-cluster covariances reduces to K-means when all covariances = σ²I and responsibilities are hard. Construct data where K-means and a fitted 2-component GMM disagree (variance ratio 4:1), fit both (GaussianMixture if available, else compare K-means on raw vs per-cluster-standardized features as the poor-man’s GMM), and report ARI vs truth for each. What does the GMM’s soft responsibility fix that hard assignment cannot?


Hint

Hard assignment sends wide-cluster points at the boundary to the tight cluster; soft responsibilities weigh by each cluster’s density — variance-aware.



Solution

K-means’ Voronoi boundary equidistant in raw space ignores that one cluster is supposed to be wider; a GMM’s responsibility compares densities — a point moderately far from the wide cluster’s mean is still probably wide-cluster. With equal-variance assumption dropped, the boundary curves around the tight cluster.






GMM’s soft responsibilities also give graded membership — points near boundaries are honestly uncertain instead of hard-assigned, which downstream pipelines can propagate. The general lesson: K-means is the spherical hard special case; each relaxation (covariance, softness) buys validity on a wider cluster family at the cost of parameters and compute.

title: 9.4 K-means Clustering
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (K-means × 5.6 × 9.2). Wide-data clustering protocol: n = 200, p = 500 (5 planted clusters, strong batch direction). Compare pipelines: (a) raw → K-means; (b) scale → K-means; (c) scale → PCA-5 → K-means; (d) scale → batch-corrected → PCA-5 → K-means. Evaluate ARI vs biological truth AND vs batch. Write the pipeline decision and the audit that justified it — the realistic omics workflow in miniature.
C2 (K-means × 9.6 × 12.x stub). The k-selection multiplicity experiment: run the full k-selection circus (elbow, silhouette, gap, stability) on null data (no clusters) for k ∈ 2..9, 100 datasets. How often does each judge declare some k “clearly best”? Implement the correction (require judge agreement + stability + effect-size floor) and measure the false-discovery rate of “we found k clusters” claims. This is Part 12’s logic wearing unsupervised clothes.

title: 9.4 K-means Clustering
text:
7. Summary

K-means minimizes within-cluster squared distance to centroids: Lloyd assign/update, monotone, local-optimum.
Assumptions: spherical, equal-variance, equal-size clusters in Euclidean space — each breakage has a named failure mode.
k-means++ + n_init manage initialization; report the setup or the run isn’t reproducible.
k is chosen by converging evidence — elbow + silhouette + gap + stability — and it’s a claim, not a setting.
Categorical codes, unscaled units, outliers, non-convex shapes: each is a diagnosed assumption violation with a mapped repair.
GMMs generalize; spectral/density methods change families; the diagnosis-first rule routes you.
Clusters need validation, comparison, and honesty about selection — the practical centerpiece: 9.6 Practical clustering issues, after hierarchical trees of clusters in 9.5.

title: 9.2 Principal Component Analysis
text: PCA finds the orthogonal directions along which the data varies most, and re-expresses it in those directions. It is simultaneously a dimension-reduction tool, a decorrelation machine, a visualization device, and the algebraic backbone of ridge (5.2) and PCR (5.5) — the most reused object in applied statistics.

title: 9.2 Principal Component Analysis
text:
1. Basic Concept
PC1 = the unit vector w maximizing Var(Xw) = wᵀΣw subject to ‖w‖ = 1 — the solution is the top eigenvector of the covariance matrix; subsequent PCs are the next eigenvectors, orthogonal to the rest. Equivalent view: PCA is the SVD of the (centered) data matrix.






Scores, loadings, and the reconstruction — the three objects to keep straight:

title: 9.2 Principal Component Analysis
text:
2. Concept Questions

PCA is unsupervised — state precisely what it does not look at, and recall the page where that blindness cost it (5.5).
Why must features be centered before PCA? Scaled? When is scaling the wrong choice?
Your PC1 has loadings (−0.7, +0.7, 0.05, 0.1). Interpret it — and state the two sign/scale caveats.
What does “PCA loses information” mean numerically, and which quantity measures exactly what’s lost per component?
PCA on raw counts (skewed, huge-variance features) found “PC1 = one gene.” Diagnose, and name the two standard fixes.



Answers


It never sees y. Consequence: PCs rank by X-variance, which may be irrelevant to the response — the low-variance-signal pathology (5.5 Exercise 2), and the supervised alternative (PLS) exists for exactly this.
Center: PCA finds directions through the origin of the data cloud — uncentered, PC1 points at the mean (garbage directions). Scale: PCA’s criterion is variance — without scaling, big-unit features own the components; scale whenever features have arbitrary units. Wrong to scale: when features share a natural unit and their variances ARE the signal (e.g., same-assay measurements) — then raw-covariance PCA respects the physics.
“A contrast: feature 1 loads negative, feature 2 positive, equally; features 3–4 uninvolved” — PC1 is roughly feature2 − feature1. Caveats: (a) sign is arbitrary (−w is the same component — sklearn flips signs by its own convention); (b) loadings are unit-scaled — interpret the pattern (ratios, signs), not absolute numbers.
Reconstruction error: ‖X − X_M‖² = Σ_{j>M} λⱼ (sum of discarded eigenvalues) — PCA drops exactly the orthogonal variance along dropped directions, and explained_variance_ratio_ is the kept fraction. Loss is orthogonal-projection loss: the best rank-M summary possible (Eckart–Young: PCA is optimal in Frobenius norm).
Diagnosis: unscaled, skewed data — the huge-variance gene dominates PC1 by units, not biology. Fixes: log-transform skewed features (0.4), then standardize. Then PC1 becomes a pattern, not a unit artifact.

title: 9.2 Principal Component Analysis
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. PCA by hand, via covariance eigendecomposition and via SVD: center a dataset, compute Σ = XᶜᵀXᶜ/(n−1), take np.linalg.eigh, and compare its eigenpairs to sklearn’s PCA output (match signs, compare explained ratios). Then do it via np.linalg.svd and verify the identity λⱼ = sⱼ²/(n−1). Owning this equivalence demystifies every PCA discussion in the course.


Solution







Three roads, one decomposition. Eigen-route exposes “eigenvectors of covariance”; SVD-route exposes “best rank-M projection” (Eckart–Young); sklearn emits the latter. Any PCA claim you’ll ever read reduces to objects you just computed.

Exercise 2. The scree decision, done with eyes: on a dataset with a planted structure (3 latent factors + noise, p = 12), plot (a) explained-variance ratios, (b) cumulative variance, (c) the reconstruction error as M grows. Mark where the scree “elbows” and where reconstruction error flattens. Then verify against the truth: M = 3 captures the planted structure. Finally, state when the elbow is ambiguous and which tool arbitrates (6.5’s dial logic, transplanted).


Solution







Planted rank shows as the scree’s cliff (huge λ₁₋₃, noise-floor λ₄₊). Ambiguous elbows (gradual decay) happen when signal and noise variances blend — then the choice is a bias–variance trade like any M-selection (5.5 CV-tunes M; 9.6 stability-checks it), and visualization is a legitimate “M = 2 by fiat” use.

Exercise 3. Biplot discipline: on the 4-feature cohort-style data below, produce (a) PC1/PC2 score scatter, (b) loading vectors overlaid, (c) each feature’s correlation with PC1/PC2 as a table. Interpret PC1 in a sentence a domain reader could accept, and identify which feature the biplot says is redundant (nearly collinear with another) — verify by direct correlation. Note explicitly what a biplot cannot tell you (name the supervised question it ignores).


Solution







The biplot’s geometry: features pointing the same direction are correlated (expr1/expr2 nearly overlap — redundancy visible before any correlation call); features opposing are anti-correlated; scores near a loading tip have high values of that feature. What it can’t say: anything about y — PCA is blind to outcomes by construction (5.5), and “PC1 = severity” needs external validation (9.1’s reification trap).

title: 9.2 Principal Component Analysis
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

PCA on the covariance vs correlation matrix: scaling = correlation-PCA; raw = covariance-PCA — a modeling choice with the 9.1 assumption weight (Exercise units; Q2b).
PCA is not feature selection: components are combinations of all features — sparse variants (sparse PCA) exist if you need actual feature drops (5.1’s selection, rotated).
Outliers own variance: one extreme point can be PC1; robust PCA (or inspection before fitting) for dirty data (2.10 leverage, unsupervised edition).
PCA inside pipelines: fit on training folds only — the leakage law (0.5); Pipeline(StandardScaler(), PCA(), model) is the mechanical guarantee (5.5 Exercise 3).
Interpretation limits: loadings are basis vectors of a rotated coordinate system — components can mix causally unrelated features; correlations between scores and external variables are the validation, not the discovery (9.1 Q3).
Sign and rotation freedom: eigenvectors are sign-arbitrary; with near-equal eigenvalues, subspaces rotate freely — small data perturbations can “swap” PCs (stability diagnostics again, 9.6).


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated PCA pipeline has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Unscaled PCA: the 1000-mean feature’s variance dominates — PC1 is a units artifact. Standardize (or justify raw-covariance PCA by shared units).
Choosing the component by correlation with y: (a) that’s supervised selection wearing PCA clothes — the honest tool is PLS/PCR-with-CV (5.5); (b) with 2 components the “choice” is trivial anyway. Keep PCA unsupervised and use all M components downstream, or justify M by variance/CV.
Two different PCAs for train/test: bases must match — fit the transformer on training data, transform test (the Pipeline law, 0.5).

title: 9.2 Principal Component Analysis
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Prove PCA’s optimality (Eckart–Young): among all rank-M approximations C of centered X, PCA’s reconstruction X·V_M·V_Mᵀ (V_M = top-M right singular vectors) minimizes ‖X − C‖_F. Verify numerically that no other rank-2 orthogonal projection of a fixed dataset achieves lower reconstruction error, and connect the result to the SVD identity λⱼ = sⱼ²/(n−1) from Exercise 1.


Hint

Eckart–Young: truncating the SVD at rank M minimizes Frobenius error; PCA’s subspace IS the top-M right singular subspace.



Solution</summary»
By the SVD X = USVᵀ, the best rank-M approximation in Frobenius norm is U_M S_M V_Mᵀ (Eckart–Young theorem) — keeping the M largest singular values. PCA’s projection X V_M V_Mᵀ is exactly this object; the discarded error is Σ_{j>M} sⱼ² = (n−1)Σ_{j>M} λⱼ.






PCA and truncated SVD coincide to float precision; any other rank-2 projection loses strictly more — PCA is the unique best low-rank linear summary (up to rotation within the subspace). This optimality is in X’s own geometry — nothing about y (5.5’s recurring caveat).

Q2. PCA stability under correlated noise: generate data with a planted PC1 and increasing noise correlation among the noise features; measure (a) the angle between refit PC1 across bootstrap resamples and (b) the explained-variance-ratio stability, as noise correlation grows. Show PC subspace stability degrading before the variance ratio does — then write the reporting rule: which PCA claims need stability analysis (subspace interpretation) and which are robust (aggregate variance summaries)?


Solution







As noise features correlate, the noise block gains a single dominant direction (eigenvalues 0.2×6 and 5.8 at ρ = 0.8, versus seven ties at ρ = 0), and that — not the planted signal — is what stabilizes PC1. The angles fall (72.6° → 7.0° → 2.2°) as ρ rises, and the explained-variance summary moves only slightly (PC1’s SD across resamples 0.009 → 0.025 → 0.015). So the intuition to discard is “correlated noise destabilizes the top eigenvector.” The truth is the reverse, and the reason is instructive: after StandardScaler every column has variance 1, so the planted column (raw variance 9) has been demoted to a peer of the seven noise columns. With ρ = 0 those seven are exchangeable, PC1 is free to be any mixture of them, and its identity is essentially arbitrary — which is why it wobbles by 72°. At ρ = 0.8 they share one common direction worth ~74% of the block’s variance, so PC1 locks onto it. Identifiability here comes from the noise block’s structure, not from the signal’s. Two reporting rules follow. Subspace stability, not variance explained, is what licenses the phrase “PC1 captures X% of the variance” — quote the EVR only alongside a bootstrap angle, because an EVR of 0.74 here describes a direction that has nothing to do with the planted latent factor. And note the failure mode this experiment nearly walked into: the original covariance was written 1 + rho * (ones − eye), which adds rho to the off-diagonals too, implying correlation 1+rho > 1. That matrix is indefinite (eigenvalues −0.4×6), and multivariate_normal does not raise — it projects onto the nearest PSD matrix, so the “noise” quietly became seven near-identical columns and the experiment ran to completion producing a clean, confident, meaningless answer.

title: 9.2 Principal Component Analysis
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (PCA × 7.4 forests × 3.6 GLM). Representation learning bake-off: on wide data (n = 150, p = 100, mixed linear/nonlinear signals), compare downstream classifiers trained on (a) raw features, (b) PCA-20 scores, (c) PCA-5 scores — nested CV. When does compression help (noise dilution) and when hurt (nonlinear signal spread across PCs)? Connect to 5.5’s PCR findings and write the dimension-reduction routing rule: raw vs compressed, by signal type and n/p ratio.
C2 (PCA × 9.4 K-means × 12.x batch stub). The cluster-on-PCs pipeline: cluster (K-means, k = 3) on (a) raw scaled features and (b) the top-3 PC scores of wide data with planted clusters and a planted batch direction. Measure agreement with true biological clusters vs with batches, both pipelines. Does PCA-to-3 dims remove the batch artifact or preserve it (hint: batch is a variance direction)? Write the caution about “we clustered in PC space, so it’s denoised” — and the correct order of operations (batch audit before, not after, compression).

title: 9.2 Principal Component Analysis
text:
7. Summary

PCA = eigendecomposition of covariance = SVD of centered data: directions of maximal variance, orthogonally.
Three objects: scores (data in PC space), loadings (the rotation), explained-variance ratios (the budget).
Center always; scale unless units are meaningful; fit inside pipelines; the outcome-blindness is structural.
Reconstruction loss = dropped eigenvalues; PCA is the optimal rank-M summary (Eckart–Young) in X’s geometry.
Scree picks M when the cliff is real; CV picks it when it’s a bias–variance trade.
Interpretation claims need subspace stability; variance claims are sturdier.
PCA compresses; the next problem is what to do when the data is incomplete — 9.3 Missing values and matrix completion.

title: 8.6 Multiclass SVM
text: Binary SVMs answer “this class or that one?” — real problems ask “which of k?” Two standard extensions compose binary machines into multiclass classifiers: one-vs-rest (OvR: k machines, each against everyone) and one-vs-one (OvO: k(k−1)/2 machines, each on a pair). SVC runs OvO internally; knowing what that means for scores, calibration, and imbalance is this page’s job.

title: 8.6 Multiclass SVM
text:
1. Basic Concept
OvR: train fₖ(x) = “class k vs not-k” for each k; predict argmaxₖ fₖ(x). OvO: train f_{kl} on classes k and l only; predict by pairwise-vote majority (decision_function returns the k(k−1)/2 vote margins).






SVC’s built-in OvO and its decision-function shape:

title: 8.6 Multiclass SVM
text:
2. Concept Questions

OvR with 1% positive class: what happens to each rest-vs-one machine’s training balance, and which page’s remedy applies to each binary subproblem?
OvO trains on only 2/nᵏ-ish of the data per machine. Why is that fine for SVC specifically (name the scaling behavior it dodges)?
decision_function for SVC multiclass returns 3 scores for 3 classes. Are these probabilities? Are they comparable across rows?
When do OvR and OvO disagree most, and give one dataset property favoring each.
Your 10-class problem needs calibrated probabilities for downstream cost decisions. What is the two-step pipeline, and which model class makes it trivial?



Answers


Each OvR machine sees ~1% positives vs 99% rest — the imbalanced binary problem k times over. Apply class weights / stratified folds / PR-metric evaluation per machine (3.1); the argmax across machines then compares scores trained on different balances — a known OvR wart.
SVC’s dual training scales roughly between n² and n³; restricting each machine to 2·(2n/k) rows slashes total cost for large k — OvO is the scaling-friendly choice for kernel-SVC multiclass (sklearn’s default for exactly this reason).
No and no. They’re pairwise vote margins in arbitrary per-machine scales (each pair’s SVM has its own w‖); comparable within a row for voting, not calibrated probabilities across rows or samples (8.5’s probability caveat, k-fold worse).
Disagreement peaks near class boundaries and under imbalance (OvR’s rest-class dominates its machine; OvO’s votes fragment). Favor OvO: large k with kernel-SVC (compute); favor OvR: few classes, per-class interpretability (“class k’s own machine”), or sparse outputs.
Model that emits real per-class probabilities (multinomial logistic — softmax, 3.3 extension) then calibrate + apply costs (3.7); SVM route: OvR/OvO scores → probability calibration (extra layer, extra caution).

title: 8.6 Multiclass SVM
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. OvR vs OvO vs multinomial, three ways: fit LinearSVC(OvR), SVC(OvO), and LogisticRegression(multinomial softmax) on a 5-class Gaussian problem; compare CV accuracy, fit time, and prediction agreement rates. Then answer: where do OvR and softmax disagree most — and which disagreement is “probability-shaped” vs “margin-shaped”?


Solution







Softmax differs from the SVMs on confidence geometry: it’s the one producing comparable per-class probabilities, so its “disagreements” with margin models concentrate where probabilities (not margins) would rank classes differently — near boundaries between close pairs. Margins answer “which side,” softmax answers “how much of each” — related questions, different answers, choose per downstream need.

Exercise 2. Imbalance across 4 classes (1%, 4%, 15%, 80%): compare SVC-OvO with and without per-pair class_weight="balanced" by macro-F1 and per-class recall (3.1). Which classes get sacrificed by default, and does balancing fix every class or shift the sacrifice? Write the deployment rule for imbalanced multiclass problems.


Solution







Unweighted OvO sacrifices the 1% class almost entirely (recall ≈ 0) and leans on the 80% class; class_weight="balanced" rescales each pair’s penalties, rescuing rare-class recall at the cost of the majority’s precision — recall mass moves, it doesn’t appear. Deployment rule: imbalanced multiclass needs per-class recall targets set by the costs of missing each class, encoded via class weights (or resampling), and evaluated by macro-averaged metrics — never by accuracy or micro-F1 alone.

Exercise 3. Codebook features vs native multiclass: build a 6-class problem where classes sit on a hierarchy (2 supergroups × 3 subclasses). Compare (a) flat 6-class SVC, (b) a two-level strategy: supergroup SVM → subclass SVC within predicted supergroup. Report flat vs hierarchical accuracy (overall and per-subclass). When does the hierarchy help (signal lives at the top level), when does it double-punish (early error propagates), and what does this preview about structured prediction?


Solution







The hierarchy helps when the top split is real and clean (supergroups well separated) — each subproblem becomes easier; it hurts when supergroups overlap, because one wrong top-level call guarantees a wrong subclass — error compounding. Same trade as any structured/sequential prediction: decompose only along genuinely strong boundaries, and measure the top level’s accuracy before trusting the cascade.

title: 8.6 Multiclass SVM
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

decision_function shape is the tell: (n, k) → OvR scores (LinearSVC, LogisticRegression); (n, k(k−1)/2) → OvO votes (SVC). Code that assumes k columns breaks silently when swapping SVC/LinearSVC.
OvR’s scale non-comparability: each rest-machine has its own w scale; argmax compares apples to slightly different apples — probability calibration or shared-margin formulations fix it if scores must travel.
OvO’s vote ties: with even class counts, votes can tie; sklearn breaks them by a deterministic rule — for audit-sensitive applications, inspect decision_function rather than trusting the tiebreak.
Compute crossover: LinearSVC OvR ≈ k fast primal fits (scales to big n); SVC OvO = k(k−1)/2 dual fits on small pairs (scales to big k with kernels) — the reason SVC defaults to OvO.
class_weight semantics per strategy: OvR applies it per binary machine; OvO per pair — the effective weighting of rare classes differs; verify with per-class recalls, not the API name.
Calibration multiclass: calibrating k OvR machines independently doesn’t calibrate the argmax distribution — use proper multiclass calibration if probabilities matter (3.7).


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated multiclass pipeline has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Vote margins ≠ probabilities: SVC’s decision_function returns k(k−1)/2 pairwise scores; calling them class probabilities misstates both count and meaning. Use probability=True (Platt) — or a softmax model.
Flat accuracy on 25:5:1 imbalance hides total sacrifice of class 2 — macro-F1 + per-class recall (Exercise 2).
Vote margins aren’t cross-row comparable confidence: each pair-machine normalizes differently. Calibrated probabilities (or per-row softmax-style rescaling with validation) are the comparable currency.

title: 8.6 Multiclass SVM
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Count and compare the training cost of OvR vs OvO for k classes, n rows, kernel-SVC at ~n²-per-fit: derive O(k·n²) vs O(k²·(2n/k)²) = O(4n²) — OvO is constant in k while OvR grows linearly! Verify empirically for k ∈ {3, 6, 12} on fixed-size data, then explain why OvO’s advantage strengthens exactly when n per class also grows (and when OvR’s simplicity wins anyway).


Hint

OvO: k(k−1)/2 machines, each on 2n/k rows → cost per machine ∝ (2n/k)²; multiply out.



Solution

OvR: k machines on n rows → k·n²-scale. OvO: k(k−1)/2 ≈ k²/2 machines on 2n/k rows each → (k²/2)·(2n/k)² = 2n²·(k²/k²)·… = O(4n²) — independent of k.






Fit time grows mildly with k (more machines, smaller each) — the flat-in-k prediction holding. OvO’s advantage strengthens when n is large (n² dominates everything) and kernels make dual training unavoidable; OvR wins when interpretability of per-class machines matters, when using linear primal solvers (already linear in n), or when k is small enough that the difference is noise.

Q2. Design multiclass calibration properly: you have OvR scores from a 4-class SVM and need probabilities for a cost matrix (misclassification costs differ per class pair). (a) Show why independently calibrating each OvR machine breaks (probabilities needn’t sum to 1). (b) Implement a fix: normalize (softmax over calibrated scores) or use a validation-set multiclass calibration, and evaluate proper multiclass calibration via log-loss before/after. (c) State which confusion-matrix entries the cost matrix should reweight, and where the thresholds live now (not in the model — in the decision layer).


Solution








Independent per-class calibrators produce k numbers with arbitrary sums — “probabilities” that violate the probability simplex. (b) A downstream softmax (or a validation-fitted multiclass calibrator) restores the simplex and measurably improves log-loss. (c) The cost matrix lives in the decision layer: given calibrated p, choose the class minimizing Σⱼ C(predicted j, true k)·pⱼ — thresholds become cost-weighted argmax rules, tunable without refitting the SVM. This separation — calibrated model + explicit decision layer — is the clean architecture for any cost-sensitive deployment.

title: 8.6 Multiclass SVM
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (multiclass × 3.7 comparison × 7.4 forest). The k-way bake-off: 6-class problem with per-class different geometries (one linear, one radial, one XOR-ish, three Gaussian). Compete SVC-OvO (tuned), LinearSVC-OvR, multinomial logistic, and random forest by macro-F1 (nested CV) plus per-class recall. Which classes does each method sacrifice, and what does the per-class pattern tell you about matching model geometry to class geometry rather than picking one global winner?
C2 (multiclass × 9.4 K-means preview). Clusters as pseudo-labels: run K-means with k = 6 on unlabeled data, then treat cluster IDs as classes for an SVC-OvR. Compare (a) supervised accuracy against true labels, (b) the stability of cluster-to-class mappings across seeds. What breaks when clusters ≠ classes (split/merged clusters), and what does this thought experiment teach about the unsupervised→supervised handoff coming in Part 9?

title: 8.6 Multiclass SVM
text:
7. Summary

Two compositions: OvR (k machines vs the rest; argmax scores) and OvO (k(k−1)/2 pairwise machines; vote majority — SVC’s default).
decision_function shapes differ ((n,k) vs (n,k(k−1)/2)); neither is probability — calibrate for that.
Compute: OvO is flat-in-k for kernel-SVC; OvR is simple and interpretable; LinearSVC makes OvR scale.
Imbalance: per-machine/per-pair class weights, macro metrics, per-class recall — accuracy lies at k > 2 too.
Hierarchical/structured decompositions help only when the top boundary is real; early errors compound.
Probabilities and cost-sensitive decisions live in the calibration + decision layer, not the SVM.
Part 8’s geometry chapter is done. Everything so far had labels — Part 9 removes them: 9.1 The unsupervised mindset.

title: 8.4 Kernel SVM
text: The kernel trick is the SVM’s superpower: replace every inner product xᵢᵀxⱼ with a kernel function k(xᵢ, xⱼ) that implicitly computes inner products in a vast expanded space — nonlinearity without ever building the features. Circles in, circles classified; dimensions infinite, cost unchanged.

title: 8.4 Kernel SVM
text:
1. Basic Concept
The dual’s predictions depend only on inner products (8.2): f(x) = Σαᵢyᵢ⟨xᵢ, x⟩ + b. Substitute any valid kernel k:
\[f(x) = \sum_i \alpha_i y_i k(x_i, x) + b\]
The RBF (Gaussian) kernel — the default workhorse:
\[k(x_i, x) = \exp(-\gamma \|x_i - x\|^2)\]
— implicitly an infinite-dimensional basis. The classic circle problem, solved:






The explicit feature map, once — to demystify the trick, do it manually for the quadratic kernel:






The check line is the part that matters. The obvious quadratic map \(\Phi(x) = (x_1^2, x_2^2, \sqrt2 x_1x_2)\) realises \(k = (x^\top z)^2\) — a different kernel from sklearn’s poly(degree=2, coef0=1), which computes \((x^\top z + 1)^2\). Because both happen to classify this easy circular dataset perfectly, the bug hides: the two accuracies match at 1.0 and the cell looks like it passed. Expanding \((x^\top z + 1)^2\) shows the missing pieces are the linear terms, so the map needs six coordinates — \((x_1^2, x_2^2, \sqrt2 x_1x_2, \sqrt2 x_1, \sqrt2 x_2, 1)\) — after which the inner products agree to machine precision (both 0.521637). The general lesson: whenever you verify the kernel trick by building the feature map, verify it with a numerical inner-product check, not by comparing accuracies. Accuracy is a single number with enormous tolerance; \(\Phi(a)\cdot\Phi(b)\) versus \(k(a,b)\) is exact and catches the mistake immediately.

title: 8.4 Kernel SVM
text:
2. Concept Questions

State the kernel trick’s two-part bargain: what must the algorithm never do, and what may it only use?
Why does the RBF kernel create closed, local boundaries while polynomial kernels create open, global ones?
γ in the RBF kernel: what does large γ do to each training point’s influence, and which failure does extreme γ reproduce (7.1)?
What makes a function a valid kernel (the Mercer condition, in one sentence), and name two practical consequences of validity.
SVC.support_vectors_ after an RBF fit: are these points in the original space or the expanded one — and how many coordinates does the expanded space have?



Answers


Never: materialize φ(x) or use any property of features beyond inner products. Only: inner products ⟨xᵢ, xⱼ⟩ (and ⟨xᵢ, x⟩ at prediction) — replace with k(xᵢ, xⱼ) and everything stays valid if k is a real inner product in some space.
RBF similarity decays with distance (Gaussian bump around every SV): boundaries are unions of local closed contours — a point’s class is decided by nearby support vectors. Polynomials are global monomials: boundaries extend to infinity as open curves — decided by global orientation (6.3’s local-vs-global bases, kernel edition).
Large γ → narrow bumps → each training point influences only its own micro-neighborhood → the fit approaches “memorize every point” — a 1-NN with kernels, the same overfitting endpoint (7.1’s k = 1).
Valid = positive semi-definite: Σcᵢcⱼk(xᵢ, xⱼ) ≥ 0 for all coefficients — i.e., it IS an inner product in some Hilbert space. Consequences: the optimization stays convex (a QP), and predictions are consistent geometry (no paradoxical “similar to both classes” pathologies).
Original space — support vectors are training points (stored as-is); the expanded space has infinitely many coordinates for RBF (the map is infinite-dimensional), which is exactly why you never build it.

title: 8.4 Kernel SVM
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Implement the RBF-kernel SVM’s prediction function by hand from a fitted SVC: extract dual_coef_, support_vectors_, intercept_; compute f(x) = Σ αᵢ k(xᵢ, x) + b yourself on a query grid; verify exact agreement with decision_function. Then confirm the kernel matrix your function implies (SVs × queries) matches rbf_gram — the whole model is these numbers.


Solution







A fitted kernel SVM is its support vectors, their dual coefficients, and an intercept — everything else (γ, C) shaped those numbers. This representation is also the deployment format: store ~n_support vectors, evaluate kernels on demand.

Exercise 2. The γ × C landscape: for the circle dataset, grid-search (γ, C) over log grids with 5-fold CV; display the CV-accuracy heat map. Identify the three regimes visible in the map (underfit smooth / well-fit / memorize), and mark the CV optimum. Then state the two-dial tuning recipe — which knob acts like model complexity, which like the fit-price — and their interaction.


Solution







Reading: low γ or low C → underfit (smooth blob, ~50–70%); high γ AND high C → memorize (train-perfect, CV-crippled); the diagonal ridge between them is the operating zone — γ sets per-point locality (complexity), C sets how hard violations are chased (fit price), and jointly they trace the 4.4 U-curve in 2-D.

Exercise 3. Kernel zoo, honestly compared: on three truths (linear, circle, XOR-corner), compare linear / poly(degree 2) / RBF kernels by CV accuracy — plus the “kernel + linear truth” sanity row. Report the 3(kernel) × 3(truth) table. Write the kernel-selection heuristic the table supports, including the role of the linear baseline as a lower-bound guard against needless kernels.


Solution







Reads: linear kernel wins its own truth and never embarrasses elsewhere (the guard); poly2 takes XOR (its basis contains x₁x₂); RBF wins circles and corners (local freedom) but gains nothing on linear truths. Heuristic: always run the linear baseline; reach for RBF when validation says the boundary curves; try poly when domain theory names the interaction order. Kernels are hypotheses about geometry — test them like hypotheses.

title: 8.4 Kernel SVM
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

γ and C multiply each other’s effect — the same fit can be reached by (γ↓, C↑) or (γ↑, C↓) along the flat valley; tune jointly on log grids, never independently (4.6).
Scaling is non-negotiable: RBF distance is Euclidean in raw units; unscaled features decide the geometry (8.1’s law, now with teeth — γ’s meaning changes with scale too).
SV count explodes with overlap: RBF SVMs on noisy data can retain most of the training set as SVs — prediction cost and memory scale with it; LinearSVC or trees for huge n.
gamma="scale" (default) is 1/(n·Var(X)) — data-dependent, sensible, but changes between datasets: never port γ across problems.
Probabilities: SVC(probability=True) fits Platt scaling post-hoc (internal CV) — calibrated-ish but slower and slightly different model; quote decision_function for ranking, probabilities only after this step (3.7).
Precomputed kernels: you can pass your own Gram matrix (kernel="precomputed") — the door to custom/domain-specific similarity functions (strings, graphs, alignments) — validity (PSD) is on you.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated kernel pipeline has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix
