γ = 50 on unscaled data: distance² of typical points is tens-to-hundreds → kernel values ≈ e^{-thousands} ≈ 0 — every point isolated, training memorizes (train ≫ test). Scale features; tune γ on a log grid.
One loss → verdict: the linear baseline is a guard, not a rival; on a circle truth it should lose, and kernels don’t “always win” — linear truths punish them (drill 3).
Scores ≠ probabilities: decision_function is the unbounded margin; calibrate (Platt) if probabilities are needed downstream.

title: 8.4 Kernel SVM
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Verify the polynomial-kernel identity on a small case: for x, z ∈ R², k(x, z) = (xᵀz + 1)² equals ⟨φ(x), φ(z)⟩ for φ = (x₁², x₂², √2x₁x₂, √2x₁, √2x₂, 1). Check numerically across random pairs. Then explain why this equivalence means the explicit-map SVM and the kernel SVM are the same model — and construct (conceptually) the case where the explicit map is still preferable (name the resource that becomes the bottleneck).


Hint

Expand (xᵀz + 1)² = (x₁z₁ + x₂z₂ + 1)² term by term; match coefficients to inner products of the φ coordinates.



Solution

(xᵀz + 1)² = (x₁z₁)² + (x₂z₂)² + 2x₁z₁x₂z₂ + 2x₁z₁ + 2x₂z₂ + 1 = x₁²z₁² + x₂²z₂² + (√2x₁x₂)(√2z₁z₂) + (√2x₁)(√2z₁) + (√2x₂)(√2z₂) + 1·1 — exactly ⟨φ(x), φ(z)⟩ for the stated φ. Numerics:






Same model: SVM-in-φ-space with a linear kernel ≡ SVM with (xᵀz+1)² — identical optimum, identical predictions. Explicit map preferred when φ is low-dimensional and you predict millions of times (basis evaluation beats SV-kernel sums) or need φ’s coefficients for interpretation; the kernel wins when dim(φ) is huge (degree 10 → ~66+ dims; RBF → infinite).

Q2. The γ–distance reading: show that for the RBF kernel, the decision function is a signed weighted sum of bumps centered at support vectors, and that γ determines each bump’s radius (∝ 1/√γ). Design and run the diagnostic: for a fitted RBF SVM, plot the decision function along a 1-D slice, mark SV locations, and show how the boundary interpolates between SV classes as γ varies over {0.2, 2, 20}. Write the “γ-as-resolution” sentence a practitioner should carry.


Solution







γ is the resolution dial of a bump-sum representation: 1/√γ is bump width. Low γ: one wide bump family — smooth, nearly-linear boundaries. High γ: a bump per point — the decision function reproduces training labels individually (memorization). Carry the sentence: “γ sets how far one training point’s vote reaches; C sets how expensive it is to disagree — tune them together.”

title: 8.4 Kernel SVM
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (kernels × 5.x high dimensions × 7.4 forests). The nonlinear tabular rematch: n = 200, p = 50, truth = 4 linear signals + 2 interaction signals + 1 radial signal. Compete RBF-SVM (tuned), random forest, and lasso (5.3) by nested CV. Report test error and each method’s capture of the three signal types (importances/coefficient paths). Which inductive bias wins when signals are heterogeneous — and what ensemble-of-diverse-models conclusion does the table support?
C2 (kernels × 8.2 support vectors × 12.x stability stub). SV stability under resampling: fit RBF SVMs (CV-tuned γ, C) on 100 bootstrap resamples; measure (a) the Jaccard overlap of SV sets, (b) prediction agreement, (c) the overlap of top-importance features if any. Compare against a logistic model’s selected-feature stability. Which model’s “explanation artifact” (SV set vs coefficient signs) is more reproducible — and what does that imply about publishing SVM-derived SV analyses?

title: 8.4 Kernel SVM
text:
7. Summary

Kernel trick: predictions need only inner products — swap in k(xᵢ, xⱼ), get the expanded space for free.
RBF = local bumps (closed boundaries, γ = resolution); poly = global monomials (open boundaries); linear = the guard.
Scale features; tune (γ, C) jointly on log grids; the flat valley between underfit and memorize is the target.
Fitted model = support vectors + dual coefficients + intercept — deployable, inspectable, kernel-generic.
Valid kernels are PSD: convexity preserved, geometry consistent, custom similarities welcome.
Nonlinearity now costs a kernel choice, not a basis build — but probabilities, scaling, and SV-cost caveats ride along.
Linear SVM vs logistic, margins vs likelihoods, side by side: 8.5 SVM vs logistic regression.

title: 8.2 The Maximal-Margin Classifier
text: Given linearly separable data, infinitely many hyperplanes classify it perfectly. The hard-margin SVM picks the one with the fattest cushion — the maximal margin between the classes — and identifies a handful of support vectors as the only points that matter.

title: 8.2 The Maximal-Margin Classifier
text:
1. Basic Concept
The optimization, in the canonical form:
\[\max_{w, b} \; M = \frac{2}{\|w\|} \quad \text{subject to} \quad y_i (w^\top x_i + b) \ge 1 \;\; \forall i\]
— every point correctly outside its margin line; equivalently minimize ‖w‖²/2. The points with yᵢ(wᵀxᵢ + b) = 1 are the support vectors: removing any non-support point changes nothing.






Only the support vectors matter — the experiment:

title: 8.2 The Maximal-Margin Classifier
text:
2. Concept Questions

Why does the hard-margin SVM require separability — what happens to the constraint set when one point crosses the margin?
If a new data point lands far from the boundary on the correct side, how does the classifier change? What if it lands inside the margin?
Explain “the maximal-margin hyperplane depends only on the support vectors” both computationally and geometrically.
Two candidate hyperplanes both separate the data: one with margin 0.4, one with margin 1.2. Which does the SVM choose, and what implicit belief about future data justifies it?
A support vector sits exactly on the margin line. What is its value of yᵢ(wᵀxᵢ + b), and what does the constraint say about points beyond it?



Answers


The constraints yᵢ(wᵀxᵢ + b) ≥ 1 must be simultaneously satisfiable; one mispositioned point makes the feasible set empty — no solution exists, full stop. (The soft margin of 8.3 relaxes exactly this.)
Far-and-correct: nothing — it’s not a support vector, the classifier is unchanged (this is the SVM’s famous stability-to-far-points, the mirror image of 2.3’s leverage worries). Inside the margin: it becomes a support vector with a constraint violation — in the hard-margin world it would make the problem infeasible.
Computationally: the solution’s KKT conditions force non-support points’ multipliers to 0 — they appear nowhere in w = Σαᵢyᵢxᵢ. Geometrically: the fattest cushion is pressed against the closest points on each side — the boundary of the convex hulls; interior points don’t touch it.
Margin 1.2 — with the justification that future draws from the same distribution will, with high probability, fall in the cushion you measured on this sample (1.3’s logic applied to geometry): maximal margin is maximum-confidence classification under a stability assumption.
Exactly 1 — the constraint is tight (KKT: non-zero multiplier ⟺ tight constraint). Points beyond have yᵢ(wᵀxᵢ + b) > 1 — slack constraints, zero multipliers, no influence.

title: 8.2 The Maximal-Margin Classifier
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Maximal margin by brute force: for a tiny 2-D separable dataset (6 points), enumerate a fine grid of candidate (w-angle, b) hyperplanes, keep the separating ones, and maximize the margin. Compare your brute-force winner to sklearn’s SVC(C=1e6) solution (normalize both to the ±1 convention first). This exercise is the SVM, before the optimization theory.


Solution







Scanning directions and centering the slab finds the same solution the QP does — the optimization theory is a fast, principled shortcut through exactly this search. Two conventions have to line up or the numbers disagree by a factor of two or three, which is worth internalizing: (i) the margin is the full width between the two margin lines, i.e. the 2/‖w‖ convention sklearn uses, not the half-width some texts quote; and (ii) project with X @ w and take min over positives / max over negatives. Writing it as y * (X @ w) and then mixing min and max across the two classes silently mixes a projection with a signed score and reports a margin several times too large — the failure is silent because the code still returns a plausible-looking number.

Exercise 2. The fragility experiment: take a separable dataset and its hard-margin SVM. Add one new point far away but on the correct side — measure the change in w, b, and predictions. Then add one point inside the margin (violating) — the hard-margin problem becomes infeasible; observe sklearn’s behavior with C = 1e6 (and connect to 8.3’s fix). Quantify both perturbations: which data points does the SVM care about?


Solution







Far-correct points: zero influence (the support-vector claim, demonstrated). Violating points: infeasibility for the true hard margin — C = 1e6 silently approximates it by allowing tiny slacks at enormous cost, which is exactly the tension the soft margin (8.3) makes explicit and tunable.

Exercise 3. Margin as confidence: for the hard-margin fit, plot decision_function magnitude against distance-to-boundary for 2000 fresh points from the same distribution, and estimate: P(correct classification | |score| > 1) vs P(correct | |score| < 0.2). Then explain in margin language why large-margin points are “safe” — and one way this intuition fails (distribution shift, e.g., the covariate-shift experiment of 4.2 Q2).


Solution







(|score|) is distance-to-boundary in canonical units: points with cushion almost never flip, borderline points flip often — the margin literalizes “confidence.” The failure: under covariate shift the boundary itself may be misplaced relative to the new distribution, and every confidence statement inherits that error — margins quantify position-in-sample geometry, not distributional safety.

title: 8.2 The Maximal-Margin Classifier
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Hard margin is a classroom object: real data has overlap; C = 1e6 is a soft margin pretending (8.3) — with numerical instability as a bonus. Use honest C tuning in practice.
C=1e6 ≠ hard margin: it’s soft with astronomically expensive slacks — sklearn may warn about convergence; the fix is the soft-margin formulation, not more iterations.
Support vector count and dimension: in p ≥ n separable data every point can be a support vector (5.6’s interpolation world) — the “only a few matter” intuition is a low-dimension luxury.
SVC’s decision_function is (wᵀx + b) in the canonical scale — margin units, thanks to the ±1 normalization; interpret |score| as cushion honestly only for linear kernels (kernels change the space, 8.4).
LinearSVC vs SVC(kernel="linear"): different solvers (liblinear vs libsvm), slightly different numerical answers, same geometry; LinearSVC scales to big n, SVC exposes support vectors directly.
Class imbalance: hard margins tilt toward the majority class’s geometry; class_weight rescales the constraints per class (3.1).


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated SVM has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Overlapping classes + C = 1e6: the hard-margin assumption is false; the solver strains to satisfy near-impossible constraints (warnings, poor margin, borderline numerical behavior). Use tuned soft C.
“Margin” from slacked solutions: with slacks, 2/‖w‖ overstates the effective separation — violated support vectors sit inside the reported cushion. Report margins only with the slack picture (fraction violated, C).
Support-vector fraction misread: with heavy overlap, half the points become support vectors — the “efficient summary” story collapses; also SV-based prediction shortcuts are an implementation detail, not a data-efficiency claim.

title: 8.2 The Maximal-Margin Classifier
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Derive the support-vector-only representation: the SVM dual has w = Σᵢαᵢyᵢxᵢ with αᵢ > 0 only for support vectors (KKT complementary slackness). Verify numerically that predictions via Σαᵢyᵢ(xᵢᵀx) + b (using only SVs) reproduce decision_function exactly, and explain why this representation is (a) the gateway to kernels (8.4) and (b) a statement about which data the model compresses.


Hint

KKT: constraints with slack have αᵢ = 0; tight constraints may have αᵢ > 0. w is a sum over αᵢyᵢxᵢ — zero terms vanish.



Solution

Complementary slackness ties each αᵢ to its constraint’s tightness: yᵢ(wᵀxᵢ + b) > 1 ⇒ αᵢ = 0. So w = Σαᵢyᵢxᵢ sums over SVs only, and predictions need only inner products xᵢᵀx against SVs:







Replacing xᵢᵀx by a kernel k(xᵢ, x) gives nonlinear SVMs without ever materializing coordinates — the dual only ever sees inner products. (b) The model compresses the dataset to its boundary-adjacent skeleton: a data-efficiency statement in separable low-noise regimes, and a warning when everything is a support vector.


Q2. Maximal margin vs logistic boundary, geometrically: on separable data, fit both (SVC C=1e6; LogisticRegression) and compare boundary angles and margin widths across 100 resamples. Which boundary is stable, which drifts, and why does the logistic boundary depend on all points while the SVM’s doesn’t (7.2’s stability lens applied to geometry)? State the resulting division of labor.


Solution







Both boundaries wander (resampled data, overlapping tails), but the SVM’s direction is pinned by a handful of extreme points while logistic’s is pulled by the whole sample — different sensitivity profiles. Division of labor: SVM geometry when the boundary is what matters and data is separable-ish; logistic when probabilities, calibrated rankings (3.7), or full-data robustness are the product. Full comparison: 8.5.

title: 8.2 The Maximal-Margin Classifier
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (max margin × 1.3 probability). Margin as a probability guarantee, stress-tested: for separable data with margin M, a classical result bounds future misclassification by (roughly) R²/M²-type ratios (R = data radius). Simulate: vary the noise level to produce margins M ∈ {0.2, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0}, measure test error over fresh draws, and plot error vs M. Does fatter margin → lower error hold empirically? Where does the monotonicity break (name the two competing effects: margin vs fit-to-distribution)?
C2 (max margin × 2.6 Simpson). The pooled-margin trap: two clusters with different internal geometries where the pooled maximal-margin boundary bisects neither. Construct the data, fit pooled vs per-cluster hard margins, and quantify boundary disagreement. When is a “single global margin” the wrong object — and does the kernel trick (8.4) or explicit group features (2.6) resolve it more honestly?

title: 8.2 The Maximal-Margin Classifier
text:
7. Summary

Hard-margin SVM: maximize 2/‖w‖ s.t. every point sits outside its margin line — solvable only when separable.
Support vectors (yᵢ(wᵀxᵢ + b) = 1) fully determine the classifier; all other points are deletable.
Far-correct points cost nothing; margin-violating points break feasibility — the soft margin’s reason to exist.
Margin = measured cushion = confidence geometry — valid in-sample, conditional on the distribution.
The dual representation (predict via inner products with SVs) is the on-ramp to kernels.
Overlap and p ≥ n dissolve the clean story — tune softness, expect many SVs.
Real data overlaps: pay for slack, tune the price — 8.3 The soft-margin classifier.

title: 7.7 Bayesian Additive Regression Trees (BART)
text: BART keeps boosting’s “sum of small trees” architecture but replaces sequential greedy fitting with a Bayesian posterior: a prior over tree shapes and leaf values, MCMC sampling over the space of tree ensembles, and — the payoff — honest uncertainty intervals on predictions from a nonlinear, interaction-friendly model. No BART library runs in Pyodide, so this page builds the Bayesian machinery the model rests on, hands you the concepts, and flags where the production implementations live.

title: 7.7 Bayesian Additive Regression Trees (BART)
text:
1. Basic Concept
The BART model:
\[y = \sum_{m=1}^M g(x; T_m, M_m) + \varepsilon, \qquad \varepsilon \sim N(0, \sigma^2)\]
— M small trees (T = shape, M = leaf values) with a regularizing prior: shallow trees favored (deep splits penalized), leaf values shrunk toward 0, σ² given its own prior. Fitting = MCMC over (T₁…T_M, M₁…M_M, σ²), sampling tree grows/prunes/swaps and leaf draws.
The Bayesian core you can run here: a conjugate Bayesian linear model — prior + likelihood → posterior → credible intervals. This is the identical inference object BART produces, just with a linear basis instead of trees:






Posterior sampling — the MCMC connection — via direct draws from that conjugate posterior:

title: 7.7 Bayesian Additive Regression Trees (BART)
text:
2. Concept Questions

What does BART’s tree-shape prior (prefer shallow, shrink leaves) accomplish, in regularization language (5.2)?
Contrast fitting: boosting finds one greedy sequential ensemble; BART samples many ensembles from a posterior. What does the second buy at prediction time?
Why is BART’s uncertainty interval meaningfully different from a bootstrap band (4.5) — even though both are intervals around predictions?
The sum-of-trees form with M small trees resembles boosting’s Σνhₘ. What replaces boosting’s learning rate and residual chasing?
Name two practical reasons BART remains niche despite its uncertainty output — and the niches where it wins anyway.



Answers


A prior favoring shallow trees and shrunken leaves is L0-on-structure + shrinkage-on-values simultaneously: the model starts regularized, and the data moves it only as far as evidence pushes — the Bayesian rendering of “keep trees weak” (boosting enforces it by construction via depth limits and ν).
A posterior predictive distribution: every future prediction can carry its own interval, and new-observation uncertainty is separate from fit uncertainty (the σ² layer). Boosting gives a point prediction; intervals must be bolted on (4.5-style), with weaker guarantees.
Bootstrap bands reflect resampling variability of a procedure, assuming the model; posterior credible bands reflect conditional uncertainty given the prior and likelihood — they can differ when the prior matters, and they natively separate parameter-uncertainty from observation-noise layers.
The prior plays ν’s role (shallow+shrunk = small steps are likely a priori), and MCMC’s grow/prune moves play residual-chasing: the chain revises trees wherever the current ensemble’s residuals are largest, stochastically rather than greedily.

MCMC compute: thousands of tree-ensemble draws vs one greedy pass — slow on big n/p; (b) implementation maturity/deployment tooling (boosting libraries are industrial; BART’s are research-grade, R-centric). It wins where uncertainty-qualified predictions are the product — clinical dosing, causal-effect estimation with interactions, small-n scientific inference.

title: 7.7 Bayesian Additive Regression Trees (BART)
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.
























The first block is the bug worth internalizing: a deterministic learner has no posterior. Setting random_state=0..19 on a depth-2 tree fitted to the same rows produces twenty bit-identical fits, so “averaging over the posterior” silently degenerates to “fitting once” — the printed SDs are equal to three decimals, and any claim about posterior spread built on that is fiction. Posterior variation must come from somewhere real. BART’s source is honest: it grows each tree on a noisy copy of (X, y), perturbing both the split rule and the leaf values, so successive draws genuinely differ. The bootstrap+jitter surrogate above does the same thing cheaply, and the ρ ≈ 0.9 it reports is itself the useful number — posterior draws agree a lot (they all chase the same sine) but not perfectly, and the disagreement is exactly the width of the credible band. The mean over draws is a smoother function than any single draw, which is the mechanism BART relies on.


Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Full conjugate workflow: given X (n = 50, 3 features incl. intercept), y, prior N(0, τ²I) with τ = 2, σ² = 1: compute (a) posterior mean and covariance, (b) 95% credible intervals for each β, (c) the posterior probability that β₂ > 0 (via draws). Compare the interval for β₂ against the frequentist OLS CI (statsmodels). Where do they differ, and which prior choice drove the difference?


Solution







With τ = 2 the prior is weak — Bayesian and OLS intervals nearly coincide (the data dominates). Shrink τ and the Bayesian intervals contract toward 0 by assumption, while OLS stays data-only; the difference between the two outputs is exactly the prior’s influence — know what you chose. The P(β₂ > 0) statement is the Bayesian bonus: direct probability claims about parameters, no null-hypothesis machinery.

Exercise 2. The sum-of-trees prior, simulated: implement a toy “BART-lite”: fit B = 200 tiny ensembles where each ensemble is 5 depth-2 trees fit on bootstrap data with leaf values shrunk by a factor κ ∈ {0.2, 1.0}; predict as the average. Measure test MSE and the SD of predictions across ensembles at fixed points, for both κ. Shrinkage (small κ) is the prior doing regularization — verify its variance/accuracy signature and connect it to boosting’s learning rate ν (7.5).


Solution







κ = 0.2 (strong prior shrinkage) tames each tree’s contribution — lower variance across ensembles, often better test MSE on noisy truths; κ = 1 lets each tree speak at full volume (variance up). This is ν-as-prior: BART’s leaf-shrinkage prior plays precisely boosting’s learning-rate role, but inside a sampling framework where the “right” amount is informed by the data through σ² and the marginal likelihood.

Exercise 3. Uncertainty layers, separated: using the conjugate model, produce three intervals for a new observation at a test point x₀: (a) the posterior interval of the mean f(x₀), (b) the predictive interval of a new y, (c) the OLS-style interval ignoring parameter uncertainty (just ±1.96σ̂). Plot all three and compute coverage of each over 500 simulated datasets. Which layer does each interval answer — and which would you show a patient (a new individual) vs a review board (the model’s claim)?


Solution







Read these in the order a decision-maker would, because the ordering is the lesson. (b) is the only interval that answers the question you usually have. A predictive interval for a new patient must contain both parameter uncertainty and the new observation’s own noise, so it is the widest of the three and it overcovers here (1.00) because σ = 0.5 is large relative to the parameter spread at n = 40 — harmless conservatism. (a) is narrower and calibrated for a different question, “where is the mean function here” (0.95, as intended). (c) is the trap: it ignores parameter uncertainty entirely and, because σ happens to dwarf that uncertainty at this n, it overcovers (1.00) rather than undercovering. The direction of (c)’s failure is set by the ratio of σ to the posterior SD — with small n, or a noisier signal, that ratio inverts and (c) becomes undercovering. So “it undercovers whenever parameter uncertainty is real” is the wrong claim: the safe statement is that (c) is un-calibrated in an n-dependent direction, which is a stronger reason to avoid it than pessimism would be. BART’s headline feature is delivering (a) and (b) for nonlinear tree ensembles — the same layering, no conjugate shortcut required.

title: 7.7 Bayesian Additive Regression Trees (BART)
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Priors are design decisions: BART’s defaults (depth-limiting probabilities, β-shrinkage quantiles, σ prior) encode “sparse, weak interactions” — check them against your problem instead of outsourcing the choice to the library default.
MCMC diagnostics are mandatory: run multiple chains, check mixing of σ² and tree counts; BART’s credible intervals are only as trustworthy as the chain’s convergence — the Bayesian tax for the uncertainty feature.
BART is not fast: minutes on n = 1,000 where boosting takes milliseconds; parallel chains help but the algorithm is inherently sequential. For speed-uncertainty trade-offs, quantile-regression forests are the cheaper cousin.
Variable selection leanings: BART underuses weak features under strong priors (like all shrinkage) — presence in the model ≠ importance; use inclusion frequencies across MCMC draws as the diagnostic.
Causal inference is BART’s flagship niche (treatment-effect estimation with exchangeability assumptions): the posterior over heterogeneous effects is exactly what applied micro is after — but the causal validity lives in the design, as always (2.2 Q2).
Binary/count responses: BART extends via probit/logit link versions (MCMC gets latent-variable steps) — the additive-GAM-to-GLM move (6.7) replayed in Bayesian key.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated “Bayesian model” has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Precision/convention flip: the conjugate posterior is (XᵀX/σ² + I/τ²)⁻¹ — multiplying by τ² (instead of dividing) strengthens the prior as τ² grows, backwards. Get the precision algebra right; it’s the entire estimator.
Posterior SD ≠ rescaled mean: it’s √diag(posterior covariance). Hand-waving SDs make every downstream interval fiction.
Predictive intervals need σ²: new observations add the noise layer — parameter uncertainty alone undercovers new points (Exercise 3’s layer separation).

title: 7.7 Bayesian Additive Regression Trees (BART)
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Derive the conjugate update: prior β ~ N(0, τ²I), likelihood y ~ N(Xβ, σ²I) ⇒ posterior N(μₙ, Σₙ) with Σₙ = (XᵀX/σ² + I/τ²)⁻¹, μₙ = ΣₙXᵀy/σ². Verify that as τ² → ∞ you recover OLS and as τ² → 0 you recover β = 0 — the two endpoints matching ridge’s λ → 0/∞ (5.2 Q2). Then compute the posterior probability P(β_j > 0) via draws and show it equals Φ(μⱼ/√Σⱼⱼ) — no simulation needed.


Hint

Complete the square on β in the joint density; Gaussian arithmetic; the marginal of a Gaussian is Gaussian.



Solution

Joint ∝ exp(−‖y − Xβ‖²/2σ² − ‖β‖²/2τ²); expanding in β and completing the square gives precision Λ = XᵀX/σ² + I/τ² and mean μₙ = Λ⁻¹Xᵀy/σ². Limits: τ² → ∞ removes the prior term → Λ = XᵀX/σ², μₙ = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy = OLS; τ² → 0 forces μₙ → 0. Since marginals of Gaussians are Gaussian, β_j | y ~ N(μⱼ, Σⱼⱼ), so P(β_j > 0) = Φ(μⱼ/√Σⱼⱼ):






The closed form is the sampling-based one at infinite draws — Bayesian inference for conjugate models is exactly computed, and BART’s MCMC exists because tree ensembles forfeit conjugacy, not because sampling is inherently superior.

Q2. BART vs boosting uncertainty, head-to-head design: on 200 simulated datasets (n = 60, smooth truth), compare three interval producers — (a) boosted trees + residual ± band, (b) bootstrap-banded forest (4.5), (c) the conjugate Bayesian interval on the correct basis — by nominal-95% coverage of the truth and of new points. Which achieves nominal coverage for the function, which for observations, and what structural feature does (c) have that (a)/(b) must borrow? Write the practical guidance you’d give before someone reaches for bands.


Solution







The correctly-specified Bayesian interval hits nominal coverage for both layers because it carries the two uncertainty sources separately. Boosted trees ± residual band covers observations roughly but has no parameter-uncertainty layer (function claims undercoverage); bootstrap bands estimate procedure variability (often near-nominal for the function on stable learners) but can’t separate the layers without adding σ̂. Guidance: decide which claim you’re making first — function vs new point — then pick the machinery that natively states it; and remember (c)’s advantage came from knowing the basis, i.e., from model correctness, which no interval machinery can grant.

title: 7.7 Bayesian Additive Regression Trees (BART)
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (BART × 7.5 boosting × 4.5 bootstrap). The uncertainty triathlon on one dataset: point predictions from boosting, bootstrap bands from a forest, and (on the correct linear basis, as BART-stand-in) posterior bands. Compare widths and calibration of the three intervals for both functions and new points over 200 simulations. Write the decision tree a practitioner should follow: “if you need ___ and can assume , use ” — three branches, honestly conditioned.
C2 (BART × 2.5 confounding × 12.x stub). Treatment effects, BART’s home turf: simulate an observational study with a binary treatment, confounders, and heterogeneous effects (effect varies with x₁). Using the conjugate Bayesian machinery on a basis that includes treatment × covariate terms, compute the posterior distribution of the effect at several x₁ values. Report the effect curve with credible bands, and state precisely what design assumption (unconfoundedness) the bands still require — the Bayesian machinery quantifies uncertainty, not identification.

title: 7.7 Bayesian Additive Regression Trees (BART)
text:
7. Summary

BART = boosting’s sum-of-small-trees, fitted by MCMC under a regularizing prior — the Bayesian answer to nonlinear tabular regression.
The prize: posterior predictive distributions — function-uncertainty and new-observation uncertainty as separate, honest layers.
The conjugate Bayesian model is the runnable core: same updates, same credible intervals, closed-form (drills).
Priors replace boosting’s ν; MCMC replaces greedy residual-chasing; tree-depth preferences replace depth caps.
Costs: MCMC compute, implementation maturity, and mandatory chain diagnostics.
Niche of strength: small-to-mid n, uncertainty-qualified predictions, causal effect estimation — not the 100M-row leaderboard.
Part 7 closes with the full arc: one greedy algorithm → ensembles → sequential → Bayesian. Next, geometry takes the stage: 8.1 Geometry essentials.

title: 7.5 Gradient Boosting
text: Boosting flips bagging’s logic: instead of fitting independent trees to resampled data in parallel, fit trees sequentially, each to the residuals the previous ones left behind. Each weak tree contributes a small correction; the sum climbs toward the truth. Gradient boosting generalizes the idea to any differentiable loss — and introduces the first ensemble in this course that can overfit with more trees.

title: 7.5 Gradient Boosting
text:
1. Basic Concept
For squared-error loss, gradient boosting is plain residual fitting:
\[f_m(x) = f_{m-1}(x) + \nu \cdot h_m(x), \qquad h_m = \text{tree fitted to } (y_i - f_{m-1}(x_i))\]
ν (the learning rate) shrinks each step; the general “gradient” version fits \(h_m\) to the negative gradient of any loss — which for squared loss is exactly the residual, and for other losses (deviance, absolute error) is the loss-specific pseudo-residual.
Hand-rolled on 1-D data — watch the staircase grow:






sklearn’s version, with the staged test-error curve — the overfitting watch:

title: 7.5 Gradient Boosting
text:
2. Concept Questions

Contrast the roles of B: why is “more trees” safe for forests but a tuning parameter for boosting?
What exactly does the learning rate ν trade — and what is the classic ν × M coupling rule of thumb?
For absolute-error loss, what is the “gradient” that each tree fits? What does this buy over the squared version?
Why are boosting’s base trees kept shallow (depth 3–5) while forest trees grow deep?
Two features are perfectly correlated. How do forest importances and boosting importances behave differently — and why does sequential fitting encourage early features to monopolize credit?



Answers


Forest trees are i.i.d.-ish draws: averaging more draws monotonically reduces variance toward the ρσ² floor — no overfitting mechanism. Boosting trees are sequentially adapted to the current error: later trees encode increasingly specific structure of this dataset (including noise), so past the optimum test error turns up — B must be tuned (or early-stopped).
ν scales each correction; small ν (0.01–0.1) with large M gives gentle, stagewise refinement — better test error, more compute. Coupling: smaller ν wants proportionally larger M (M ≈ a few/ν as folklore) — tune ν·M as a pair.
The negative gradient of absolute loss is +sign(residual): for \(L = |y - f|\), \(\partial L/\partial f = -\text{sign}(y-f)\), so the negative gradient the tree actually fits is \(+\text{sign}(y-f)\) — always pointing downhill on the error, which is the sign that matters. Trees fit the sign pattern of errors — robust to outliers (magnitude-blind), the boosting version of 1.1’s median-vs-mean. sklearn exposes it as loss=“absolute_error” (Huber for in-between).
Each boosting tree corrects what’s left — a small, structured residual. Deep trees would refit noise wholesale in one step (large ν-equivalent) and erase the stagewise refinement; shallow trees force the ensemble to spread learning over many steps, which is what makes the shrinkage work.
Forest trees are independent draws — twins split importance stochastically (7.4). Boosting is greedy-sequential: the first tree to grab a correlated pair’s signal takes it, the second finds little residual to justify itself — credit concentrates in the earlier feature, an order-dependence forests don’t have. Importances remain advisory.

title: 7.5 Gradient Boosting
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. The ν × M coupling, mapped: fit boosters on the sinusoid over the grid ν ∈ {0.5, 0.1, 0.02} × M ∈ {50, 200, 800}. Report a 3×3 table of test MSEs. Verify the folklore “small ν + big M beats big ν + small M at equal compute” — and locate the one cell that is dangerous (high ν, high M) and explain its failure in stagewise terms.


Solution







The table’s sweet corner is small ν + large M (each small step averages over many refinements — variance tamed by shrinkage); the dangerous cell is ν = 0.5, M = 800: each tree makes aggressive corrections to already-aggressive fits, and the ensemble chases noise late into training. ν·M coupling: (0.5, 50) ≈ (0.1, 200) in fit quality — pick small ν for accuracy, scale M, and early-stop on validation.

Exercise 2. Boosting vs bagging head-to-head, with the 7.3 contrast you now own: on (a) the noisy sinusoid and (b) pure-noise data (null), compare single tree, bagged trees (B = 200), and boosted trees (tuned shallow) by test MSE (with early stopping via staged predictions for boosting). Report the 3×2 table. Which method degrades more gracefully on the null — and what does that say about their variance budgets?


Solution







On signal, boosting usually edges bagging (its sequential bias-reduction suits the smooth truth). On the null, boosting’s early stopping limits damage but its tuned optimum still fits noise structure the bag never looks for — bagging’s variance-only budget degrades most gracefully. Boosting’s power is bias-attacking; on nulls that power is aimed at nothing.

Exercise 3. Early stopping, industrialized: use validation_fraction, n_iter_no_change, and tol (sklearn’s built-in early stopping) vs your manual staged-prediction stop, on the same data. Compare (a) chosen M, (b) test MSE, (c) compute (fit time). Then explain what the validation split costs relative to staged stopping on ALL training data — and when each is the right tool.


Solution







The built-in early stop holds out a validation slice inside training, watches it, halts — deployable and automatic. Staged prediction over the test set diagnoses the curve but is not a legitimate stopping rule for reporting (it’s tuned-on-test). Cost: the validation split trains on 80% of data — the same pessimism trade as 4.2; CV-wrapped early stopping is the fully honest version.

title: 7.5 Gradient Boosting
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

The dials and their defaults: learning_rate (ν, 0.01–0.1), n_estimators (tune with early stopping), max_depth (2–5: interaction depth), subsample (0.5–0.8 stochastic boosting — bagging-flavored variance reduction inside boosting).
Boosting ≠ parallelizable like forests: trees depend on predecessors; the sequential dependence is the algorithm (distributed variants exist but lose the simple story).
Loss choice matters: squared (default), absolute_error (robust), Huber (robust + smooth), deviance for classification — the pseudo-residual changes, everything else identical (2.1’s loss-matching principle, automated).
Overfitting signature: staged test error U-curve — always plot it before trusting a fit; the trained n_estimators is part of the model spec.
Feature importances inherit the sequential-greedy bias (7.1‘s note): early features absorb correlated partners’ credit; permutation importance on held-out data for claims.
Interactions via depth: max_depth = 2 allows pairwise interactions per tree; the ensemble composes higher orders through accumulation — check whether your truth needs depth or just more trees.
Scale-invariant like all trees, but subsample and early stopping make forests-of-seeds matter: pin random_state for reproducibility.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated boosting pipeline has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Aggressive everything: ν = 0.5 with depth 8 over 1000 steps is a noise-chaser — train R² ≈ 1, test collapses. Small ν, shallow trees, early stopping.
M tuned on test: the staged/test-peeking selection is diagnosis, not protocol; choose M via validation split or CV.
Depth ≠ interactions here: with one feature, “interactions” don’t exist; depth 8 just overfits wiggles. Depth is the interaction-order dial (2.7 vocabulary), meaningful in multivariate problems.

title: 7.5 Gradient Boosting
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Derive why fitting trees to residuals equals gradient descent in function space: parameterize the model as f(x) = Σₘ ν·hₘ(x); the squared-loss gradient w.r.t. f(xᵢ) is −2(yᵢ − f(xᵢ)); hence “fit the negative gradient” = “fit the residual.” Then verify numerically that one gradient-boosting step with squared loss reproduces the residual fit exactly, and state what changes for Huber loss (which points’ pseudo-residuals shrink?).


Hint

Gradient descent in “function space”: the “parameter” at each training point is the function’s value there; the tree approximates the descent direction.



Solution

With loss L = Σᵢ L(yᵢ, f(xᵢ)), gradient descent updates f(xᵢ) ← f(xᵢ) − ν·∂L/∂f(xᵢ). For squared loss ∂L/∂f(xᵢ) = −2(yᵢ − f(xᵢ)) — the negative gradient IS the residual vector, so “fit a tree to residuals” is exactly “take a tree-approximated gradient step.” Verification:






For Huber loss, pseudo-residuals equal plain residuals for small |r| but are clipped at δ·sign(r) beyond it — large errors contribute bounded direction, not magnitude: boosting with Huber loss is robust regression built from trees.

Q2. Stochastic boosting’s variance attack, and why it needs shrinkage. Using sklearn’s own regularization setup (Hastie-10-2, max_leaf_nodes=4, small training set), run the five configurations — no shrinkage, shrinkage only, subsample only, shrinkage + subsample, and shrinkage + max_features=2 — reporting best and final test deviance. Then answer the design question: subsample alone is the worst cell, yet adding subsample to shrinkage gives the best. Explain that interaction via the bias-variance decomposition of 4.4, and say what the final column tells you that the best column hides.


Solution







The result is an interaction, not a main effect, and that is the whole lesson:

Subsampling on its own is the worst configuration here (0.5732), exactly as sklearn’s own documentation states: “Subsampling without shrinkage usually does poorly.” Yet adding it to shrinkage produces the best model (0.4579), beating shrinkage alone by 0.11 nats. The decomposition explains the sign flip. Each large step (ν = 1) on a resampled tree produces a high-variance update, and with a small training set those updates chase noise — subsampling reduces the variance of each step but does nothing about the fact that the step is simply too large, so the sequence overshoots and never settles. Shrinkage is what makes the sum well-behaved; subsampling then reduces the residual variance of the increments it has made safe. Variance reduction is only useful once the bias is already controlled — the dials are sequential, not interchangeable.
Two further things the final column shows that best hides. The unregularized model reaches a respectable 0.5194 at iteration 103 and then degrades to 0.6957 — a 34% swing. Reporting only the best-iteration number makes overfitting look like a tuning success; the gap between best and final is the overfitting, and you only see it by looking at the end. And note that the two best cells are still descending at iteration 300, so “best” here is censored by the budget: the honest statement is that shrinkage + subsample was still improving when the loop ran out, which is a tuning-budget question, not a convergence one.

title: 7.5 Gradient Boosting
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (boosting × 7.3–7.4 × 4.4). The ensemble family portrait: single tree, bagged trees, random forest, boosted trees on the same truth (sinusoid + interaction feature) — all honestly evaluated (nested CV for tuned members). Produce the accuracy table and a bias/variance annotation for each member (from the 4.4 protocol where feasible). Write the “family reasoning”: given a new tabular problem, what diagnostics would tell you which member to try first?
C2 (boosting × 3.1 metrics × 7.6 preview). Boosted classification with deviance loss: fit GradientBoostingClassifier to an imbalanced problem (5% positives); evaluate staged AUC and staged log-loss on validation. Do their optima coincide? Connect the divergence to what each metric rewards (ranking vs probability sharpness), and predict what calibration step (3.7) the deployed model needs at the AUC-optimal M.

title: 7.5 Gradient Boosting
text:
7. Summary

Boosting = sequential trees on negative gradients (residuals, for squared loss): bias attacks with shrunken steps.
ν small + M large + shallow trees: the canonical configuration; ν·M couple; early stopping or CV sets M.
Unlike forests, boosting can overfit with more trees — the staged curve is the instrument panel.
Loss choice is a dial (squared/absolute/Huber/deviance): the same machinery, different pseudo-residuals.
Subsample injects bagging into the sequence: variance reduction inside bias correction.
Sequential greediness concentrates importances in early features — advisory only.
The ideas graduate to industrial libraries with histogram speeds and native NaN handling: 7.6 Modern boosting libraries.

title: 7.3 Bagging
text: Bagging (bootstrap aggregation) fits many models on bootstrap resamples and averages them. Its entire logic is the variance decomposition of 4.4: averaging B unstable fits divides variance by ~B — and trees are the perfect fuel, unstable enough to benefit, cheap enough to grow hundreds.

title: 7.3 Bagging
text:
1. Basic Concept
Given B bootstrap samples, fit \(\hat f^{(b)}\) on each and predict by the average (regression) or majority vote (classification):
\[\hat f_{\text{bag}}(x) = \frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^B \hat f^{(b)}(x)\]
Why it works — for (approximately) uncorrelated, identically-distributed estimators:
\[\text{Var}(\hat f_{\text{bag}}) = \rho\sigma^2 + \frac{1 - \rho}{B}\sigma^2\]
where ρ is the pairwise correlation between trees. Averaging kills the second term; ρ (shared signal structure) sets the floor.






The B-curve: test error falling with ensemble size, then plateauing:

title: 7.3 Bagging
text:
2. Concept Questions

Why must bagging use bootstrap resamples rather than k fresh splits of the data — what does each replicate lose, and what does it gain?
In Var = ρσ² + (1−ρ)σ²/B, what sets ρ, and which later method attacks ρ directly?
Bagging is said to “reduce variance while leaving bias roughly unchanged.” Why roughly — when does bagging actually change bias?
What is the out-of-bag (OOB) estimate, and which CV concept is it a bootstrap-flavored cousin of (4.3)?
Your bagged tree ensemble extrapolates flat outside training x — same as one tree. Which property survived averaging (per 7.2)?



Answers


Bootstrap resamples share rows (≈ 63% distinct) — each replicate is worse (trained on a sample of a sample) but available in quantity from one dataset. Fresh splits would give better individual models but you’d need a k× bigger dataset. Bagging trades per-model quality for ensemble quantity — a bargain only because averaging punishes independent noise, not individual skill.
ρ = pairwise correlation between trees’ predictions — set by how strongly the same signal structure dominates every bootstrap fit. Random forests (7.4) attack ρ by forcing trees to consider random feature subsets, decorrelating them at the cost of slightly worse individual trees.
The bagged average lives in the convex hull of the base fits — for squared loss, averaging can’t add bias outside the single-model bias pattern, but it can smooth the staircase into something closer to the truth (jaggedness was partly bias-like misfit of the piecewise-constant approximator), so effective bias often drops slightly — most visibly for unstable approximators of smooth truths.
Each bootstrap fit never saw ≈ 36.8% of rows; predicting those OOB rows and aggregating gives a test-error estimate without a separate holdout — the bootstrap cousin of CV, free with the fit (4.5).
Averaging preserves each base model’s support — predictions remain convex combinations of leaf means, so outside training x the ensemble is as flat as its members. Ensembles fix variance, not bias; the axis-parallel and no-extrapolation biases are inherited (7.2’s ledger).

title: 7.3 Bagging
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Implement bagging from scratch (no sklearn ensemble classes) and verify it matches BaggingRegressor behavior: same B, same bootstrap draws (same rng pipeline), compare test MSEs within tolerance. Then decompose: report the average single-tree test MSE, the bagged test MSE, and the mean pairwise tree correlation ρ — check the variance formula ρσ² + (1−ρ)σ²/B approximately holds using σ² = mean single-tree squared-deviation.


Solution







The scratch version lands beside sklearn’s (differences: rng streams and sklearn’s internal bootstrap details). The variance story checks out to first order: bagged variance ≈ ρσ² + (1−ρ)σ²/B — and since ρ ≈ 0.6–0.9 for full trees, the floor ρσ² dominates — the number random forests exist to crush.

Exercise 2. Instability → benefit mapping: for stability-ranked learners (linear regression, depth-3 tree, full tree), bag each with B = 100 and measure the relative test-MSE improvement (single vs bagged). Report the 3-row table. Then state the bagging selection rule: which base learners deserve bagging, and what does the linear row predict about “bagging everything” as a workflow?


Solution







Improvement ordering is exactly the instability ordering: full tree gains hugely, depth-3 moderately, linear ~zero (sometimes slightly negative — averaging stable learners adds nothing and the bootstrap samples’ mild quality loss can dominate). Rule: bag unstable, low-bias learners; don’t bag a stable model for accuracy (do it only for uncertainty quantification via OOB, or to parallelize).

Exercise 3. OOB as an honest validator: for one dataset, compare (a) the ensemble’s OOB score, (b) 5-fold CV of the same bagging procedure, and (c) true test error on fresh data. Repeat over 100 dataset draws; report mean and SD of each estimator’s error-in-estimating-the-truth. How does OOB’s accuracy as an estimator compare with 5-fold CV, and at what compute price?


Solution







OOB tracks the truth nearly as well as 5-fold CV while costing zero extra fits — the bootstrap samples are already there. (Details differ: OOB is R²-based by default and uses ≈63%-sized training sets like 4.5’s .632 discussion.) For ensembles specifically, OOB is the default internal referee — with nested CV still required when the procedure itself is tuned (4.6).

title: 7.3 Bagging
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

More trees never hurt (accuracy-wise): bagged test error decreases monotonically in B and plateaus — B is a compute dial, not a tuning dial (7.5 breaks this rule: boosting can overfit with B).
ρ is the enemy: bagging full-grown trees on wide data yields highly correlated trees (the strong feature wins every bootstrap) — the variance floor stays high. max_features < 1 decorrelates and becomes… a random forest (7.4).
OOB subtleties: OOB estimates each row’s prediction from ≈ B·0.368 trees (not all B) — slightly noisier and more pessimistic than the full ensemble; fine for monitoring, tuned-claim rules still apply.
Averaging kills calibrated-by-construction class fractions: bagged classification votes are fractions of trees, not of data — probability calibration still needs checking (3.7).
Bagging linear models ≈ feature subspace ensembling — occasionally useful for stability selection vibes, useless for accuracy (drill 4/Exercise 2’s law).
Bias interactions: because bootstrap trees are trained on ≈63% distinct rows, each is weaker; for stable-but-high-bias learners, bagging can even hurt — measure, don’t assume.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated bagging pipeline has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Bagging stable learners: the improvement is ~0 (Exercise 2’s law) — the base learner must be unstable (trees) for averaging to pay.
B = 2 is not bagging: two trees average to two trees; the comparison “bagging hurts” is an artifact of B too small to average anything. Use B ≥ 50–100 and watch the B-curve (Section 1).
Stumps bagged silently: depth-1 trees have high bias; bagging can’t fix bias — the mush is bias, measured by nothing in the snippet. Report single vs bagged with the same base learner, across B, with an honest test set.

title: 7.3 Bagging
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Derive the bagged-variance formula: for B i.i.d. estimators with variance σ² and pairwise correlation ρ, show Var(mean) = ρσ² + (1−ρ)σ²/B, and hence the plateau as B → ∞ is ρσ². Then verify by simulation for bagged trees: estimate ρ and σ² from an ensemble’s prediction matrix, predict the B → ∞ plateau, and compare against the empirical B = 500 error. What does this decomposition predict about the relative value of adding trees to a forest with B = 10 vs B = 1000?


Hint

Var(mean) = (1/B²)[Bσ² + B(B−1)ρσ²]; divide and split into diagonal + off-diagonal terms.



Solution

Var(mean) = (1/B²)(Bσ² + B(B−1)ρσ²) = σ²/B + ρσ²(1 − 1/B) = ρσ² + (1−ρ)σ²/B — diagonal variance dies as 1/B; the correlated floor ρσ² never does. Simulation:






The marginal value of a tree decays like (1−ρ)σ²/B: at B = 10 each addition still matters; past a few hundred, more trees buy smoothness of the OOB aggregate, not accuracy — spend compute on ρ (random forests) or on sequential bias-fitting (boosting, 7.5) instead.

Q2. Bagging and bias for smooth functions: theory says averaging convex combinations can’t increase squared bias, but for trees it often decreases it. Verify: measure bias² of a single depth-unlimited tree vs a B = 200 bag of them (multi-training-set protocol of 4.4) on the sinusoid, and explain the mechanism — averaging piecewise constants with different cutpoint locations approximates a smoother function whose expected value lands nearer f. Then state when bagging would leave bias untouched.


Solution







Different bootstrap trees cut at slightly different x’s; their average has cutpoints spread — an effective finer partition whose mean function tracks the smooth truth better. Note the sign of the measured effect: bagging’s bias² goes up slightly (0.00116 → 0.00177), not down and not flat. That is the expected direction, and it is exactly what sklearn’s own reference example reports for this estimator on a comparable 1-D problem:
Tree:          0.0255 (error) = 0.0003 (bias^2) + 0.0152 (var) + 0.0098 (noise)
Bagging(Tree): 0.0196 (error) = 0.0004 (bias^2) + 0.0092 (var) + 0.0098 (noise)
Bias² up (0.0003 → 0.0004), variance down by 40% (0.0152 → 0.0092), noise untouched, total error down. Averaging step functions rounds off the step edges, which costs a little bias on a smooth truth while buying a large variance reduction. Bagging leaves bias essentially unchanged when the base model is stable (linear models: the bootstrap fits barely differ, so the average equals one fit) or when the truth is itself piecewise-constant aligned with typical cuts. The headline: bagging changes the bias/variance mix in practice — “variance-only” is the textbook simplification, not the measurement, and the bias cost is real but small. Getting any of these numbers at all requires that the bootstrap index be shared between x and y; drawing two independent indices pairs each x with a random stranger’s y, and the “bagged” model then looks catastrophically biased (a 400× error) for reasons that have nothing to do with bagging.

title: 7.3 Bagging
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (bagging × 4.4 bias–variance). Decompose bagging across B: with the multi-training-set protocol, estimate bias²/variance for B ∈ {1, 5, 25, 200} bagged full trees. Confirm variance falls ~ (ρ + (1−ρ)/B) while bias² drifts slightly down; overlay the total. Then answer: at which B does adding trees stop mattering for your data, and how does that B scale with the base tree’s instability?
C2 (bagging × 3.7 comparison × 9.x). Bagged classifiers and calibration: fit a bagged tree classifier (B = 200 vote fractions) on an imbalanced problem; evaluate AUC, Brier, and a reliability diagram against a single tree and a logistic model. Explain mechanistically why vote-averaging improves the Brier score (votes average out leaf-fraction noise) yet still trails logistic calibration — and design the calibration step you’d add before deployment.

title: 7.3 Bagging
text:
7. Summary

Bagging = bootstrap + average: variance ÷ B for the independent part, ρσ² floor for the correlated part.
Works exactly as well as the base learner is unstable — trees are the canonical fuel; linear models don’t benefit.
B is compute, not tuning; the plateau is set by ρ, which random forests (7.4) attack directly.
OOB gives a free internal validation estimate — the bootstrap’s gift to ensembles (4.5).
Bias is roughly preserved — and measurably slightly improved for unstable approximators of smooth truths.
Inherited unchanged: axis-parallel bias, flat extrapolation, vote-fraction calibration caveats.
The floor ρσ² is the target now: force trees to disagree — 7.4 Random forests.

title: 7.1 Decision Trees
text: A decision tree predicts by asking a sequence of yes/no questions about the features, splitting the data into ever-purer regions. It is the first model in this course that learns its own basis functions — the adaptive step functions of 6.2, with cutpoints chosen by greedy RSS/impurity reduction — and the atom from which the most successful tabular learners (Parts 7.3–7.6) are built.

title: 7.1 Decision Trees
text:
1. Basic Concept
Growing a tree = recursive binary splitting: at each node, search every feature × every cutpoint for the split that most reduces impurity — RSS for regression, Gini or cross-entropy for classification:
\[\text{Gini}: \; G = \sum_k \hat p_k (1 - \hat p_k), \qquad \text{RSS} = \sum_{i \in R} (y_i - \hat y_R)^2\]
Grow deep, then prune back (cost-complexity: minimize RSS + α·|leaves|) — because a fully grown tree interpolates its training data (4.1).






Classification trees and their region structure:

title: 7.1 Decision Trees
text:
2. Concept Questions

Why grow deep and then prune, rather than stopping early at “no split looks useful”?
The greedy split at the root maximizes immediate impurity reduction. Construct (in words) a truth where this misses the optimal first split.
What exactly does min_samples_leaf trade, and how does it differ in spirit from max_depth?
A tree needs no feature scaling — why, and which earlier models contradicted that requirement?
Your tree’s regression fit is piecewise-constant, so predictions within a leaf don’t move. Name two modeling consequences.



Answers


Early stopping is myopic: a split that looks useless now enables a powerful split one level down (the XOR/interaction structure of 2.7). Grow-full-then-prune evaluates subtrees globally against data via cross-validated α — a better search over tree sizes than greedy stopping.
Two features where the best pair of splits is diagonal but each single split is weak: e.g. class = “x1 XOR x2 > 0”. Any first axis-parallel split leaves both children 50/50 (zero impurity gain), so greedy stops — while a diagonal cut at 45° separates perfectly. Trees can still represent XOR with two levels, but greedy search needs luck (or the data volume) to find it.
Both limit complexity, but min_samples_leaf enforces a data-density guarantee (every prediction rests on ≥ m observations — stable leaf means, honest confidence), while max_depth caps interaction depth regardless of density. Deep-but-wide and shallow-but-narrow are different failure shapes.
Splits compare features via ordered thresholds — invariant to any monotone rescaling. Ridge/lasso/PCA/KNN all depended on magnitudes/distances (5.2, 0.5); trees don’t, which is also why they’re forgiving with mixed units.

The response is discontinuous at every split — an artifact unless the world truly steps (6.2); (b) smooth trends are approximated as staircases — many leaves needed for accuracy, and derivatives are zero inside leaves. Model averaging (7.3) smooths both problems.

title: 7.1 Decision Trees
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Pruning, done properly: grow a full tree on noisy regression data (n = 150), extract the cost-complexity path, and select α by 5-fold CV over the path. Report (a) leaves and test MSE for the unpruned tree, (b) for the CV-pruned tree, (c) for the true-model oracle (degree-known step fit). Then state what pruning bought and what it cost.


Solution







Pruning removes the interpolation tail (hundreds of leaves → a handful), recovering most of the achievable accuracy; the cost is a few hundredths of MSE vs the theoretical best plus one CV loop. This grow-then-prune is the template every ensemble in this part inherits.

Exercise 2. The greedy trap, demonstrated: build the diagonal-separability truth — classes split by the line x₁ + x₂ = 0 with noise — and fit trees of depth 1, 2, 4. Plot boundaries and report test accuracy. Then fit a rotated model: tree on features (x₁+x₂)/√2, x₁ (a basis trick from 6.3). Write the lesson about axis-parallel bias and what fixes it (rotation, ensembles, or kernels — 8.4).


Solution







A single depth-1 stump on raw features is near a coin flip (the diagonal truth gives no axis-parallel purchase); depth 4 stitches four axis-parallel cells into a staircase approximating the line. One rotated feature makes a stump near-perfect. Axis-parallel greediness is the tree’s bias; basis rotation, oblique trees, ensembles of perturbed trees, or kernel methods are the standard remedies — each paying a different price.

Exercise 3. Impurity zoo: fit classification trees with criterion="gini" vs "entropy" on the same 6 datasets (varying class overlap and balance), comparing test accuracy and tree size (leaves). Then implement Gini by hand for a node with class proportions p and verify against tree.compute_feature_importances-style arithmetic on one split: predict the impurity drop of a candidate split manually and confirm it matches the reduction the fitted tree realized at that node (via tree_.impurity).


Solution







Gini vs entropy: cosmetic — the criteria are nearly proportional for two classes; neither fixes greediness or axis-alignment (the real tree biases). The hand computation is the whole learning algorithm in four lines: weighted impurity drop, maximized over splits.

title: 7.1 Decision Trees
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Instability is the defining flaw: resample the data and the root split can move to a different feature entirely — small structural changes, big prediction changes. This is precisely what bagging (7.3) exploits and cures.
Impurity-based feature importances are biased toward high-cardinality/continuous features and unreliable under correlated features (7.4 covers the fix: permutation importance).
No extrapolation: regression trees predict leaf means — flat outside and between (2.1’s warning at its extreme); time-trended data needs care (or linex tricks).
Unbalanced classes: deep trees isolate rare-class pockets happily; use class_weight="balanced" or stratified evaluation (3.1).
random_state matters more than it should: tie-breaking among equally-good splits is random — pin seeds for reproducibility, but note ties indicate the data doesn’t care which split it got.
Interpretation caveat: a single small tree is genuinely interpretable (export_text); a deep tree is a maze — “interpretable model class” ≠ “this particular 500-leaf object is readable.”


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated tree has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Unpruned default tree: train R² = 1.0, test R² collapses — the interpolation pathology; prune (ccp_alpha via CV) or cap depth/leaves.
Pointless scaler: trees are scale-invariant; the transform is dead weight that will silently bite later (transforming serving data with a scaler the model never needed). Drop it — knowing why is the point.
Extrapolated “trend”: the tree returns a leaf mean for x = 5 — the last leaf’s constant, dressed as a forecast. Refuse out-of-range queries or switch to a basis that extrapolates deliberately (6.4).

title: 7.1 Decision Trees
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Regression trees are adaptive step functions — show it: prove that a depth-d tree partitions the feature space into ≤ 2^d rectangles and predicts the mean of each. Then verify numerically that for a single feature, the depth-1 stump’s chosen threshold equals the RSS-minimizing split over all candidate cutpoints (compute both by brute force). What does the greedy-vs-exhaustive distinction cost when splits interact (2.7)?


Hint

Induction on depth for the partition; for the stump, each candidate cut creates two means — compute RSS directly.



Solution

Each internal node splits a rectangle into two rectangles by one threshold, so depth-d yields ≤ 2^d disjoint rectangles, and each leaf’s prediction is its training mean — a piecewise-constant function (6.2 with data-chosen boundaries). For the stump:






They match to the candidate grid. Greediness costs nothing at the stump (exhaustive over one variable’s cutpoints is cheap); the bill arrives with interactions: the best pair of splits may look worthless individually (2.7’s XOR), and greedy trees find such structures only when data volume makes intermediate gains real — the honest argument for deeper search or ensembles.

Q2. Cost-complexity pruning as a regularization path: relate the ccp objective RSS(T) + α|T| to ridge’s penalty (5.2) — what is the “norm” being constrained (|T| = leaf count = L0-style), and why does the α-path exist as a finite sequence of distinct trees (verify: len(path.ccp_alphas) ≪ 2^leaves)? Then plot test MSE vs α on one dataset and mark the CV choice — identifying the U-curve of 4.1 in tree space.


Solution

ccp penalizes the L0 “norm” of the tree (number of leaves) — combinatorial regularization, vs ridge’s smooth L2. The key fact: as α increases, the optimal subtree changes only at O(#internal nodes) critical values — the whole pruning path is computable in one pass (that’s what cost_complexity_pruning_path returns), not a search over 2^leaves subsets.






Same U-curve, same CV discipline — pruning is regularization where the penalty counts leaves instead of coefficient mass, and the path algorithm is what makes it tractable.

title: 7.1 Decision Trees
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (trees × 6.2 step functions). Face-off in their home game: truth = a true threshold (y = 1 + 2·1(x > t) + noise, t unknown). Compare (a) hand grid-searched 2-bin step (6.2 Exercise 3), (b) depth-1 stump, (c) depth-3 tree, by threshold-recovery error and test MSE over 200 simulations. Connect the stump’s threshold variance to 6.2 Q2 and state why ensembles of trees (7.3) both stabilize predictions and blur individual thresholds — is that blur a scientific loss?
C2 (trees × 5.x no other fixes). Trees in p ≫ n: n = 80, p = 500, 8 true signals. Fit a pruned tree, lasso-linear, and a random forest (7.4, teaser) with nested CV. Compare test MSE and which true features land in the top-10 importances. Which method’s feature ranking would you trust for follow-up, and does the tree’s axis-parallel greediness help or hurt under sparse signal?

title: 7.1 Decision Trees
text:
7. Summary

Trees = greedy recursive partitioning: impurity-drop splits, grow deep, prune by cost-complexity.
Adaptive axis-parallel step functions: no scaling needed, interactions reachable in depth, boundaries always rectangular.
Default = interpolation: pruning (ccp_alpha via CV) is not optional.
Greedy search misses XOR-style structures at shallow depth; basis rotation or ensembles compensate.
Single trees are unstable — a flaw so central that the next three pages turn it into a superpower.
Piecewise-constant predictions: no extrapolation, no smoothness — fine for regimes, wrong for trends.
The fix for instability without losing adaptivity: average many trees — 7.2 Advantages & limitations first catalogues what we’re averaging.

title: 6.6 Local Regression (LOESS)
text: Local regression fits the curve one query point at a time: at each x₀, fit a low-degree polynomial to the nearby points, weighted by distance, and read off the value. No global basis, no knots — just “fit locally, slide along.” It is smoothing at its most intuitive and the bridge between weighting (KNN) and global fitting.

title: 6.6 Local Regression (LOESS)
text:
1. Basic Concept
At query point x₀:

Take the s nearest points (span s — the dial), or all points within a bandwidth.
Weight them by a tricube kernel of their distance: \(w_i = \left(1 - \left(\frac{|x_i - x_0|}{d_{\max}}\right)^3\right)_+^3\). (Note the inner cube: this is not the biweight \((1-|\cdot|)^2_+\). At 10% of the bandwidth the tricube is still 0.997 — it is deliberately flat near the centre, which is what lets a local line fit the local level accurately.)
Fit weighted least squares (usually a line; LOESS = locally estimated scatterplot smoothing).
\(\hat f(x_0) = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 x_0\) from that local fit. Slide x₀ across the domain.

Hand-rolled, once:






The battle-tested version — statsmodels.lowess:

title: 6.6 Local Regression (LOESS)
text:
2. Concept Questions

Span vs bandwidth: what does each control, and what happens at span → 0 and span → 1?
Why weight by the tricube kernel rather than uniformly over the neighborhood — what changes visually?
Local linear vs local constant fitting: where does the difference show up, and why does LOESS prefer degree 1?
LOESS has no closed-form coefficients to report. What ARE its reportable quantities, and how do you get uncertainty?
Cost: LOESS prediction at one new point requires refitting. Quantify the compute difference vs a spline’s predict, and name when that matters.



Answers


Span = fraction of data in each local fit (bandwidth = absolute radius). Span → 0: k = degree+2 points — interpolation-grade wiggle; span → 1: everything weighted (far points at weight ≈ 0) — nearly the global fit. Same U-curve, familiar dial.
Uniform weights fit a line through the whole window — a constant slope across it — while tricube downweights the window’s edges, so the local line tracks the center of the window; the result is visibly smoother and less biased at windows’ shoulders.
The difference explodes where f curves: local constants are biased on any slope (each window’s fit lags the function), local lines absorb linear trend exactly. LOESS uses degree 1 because bias is then O(h²)-small while variance stays manageable; degree 2 buys a little more for jaggedness.
The smooth itself (plotted/tabulated), its effective df (tr of the smoother — computable but pricey), and bootstrap/CV-derived bands. Report the curve with a band, not coefficients.
Spline predict = basis evaluation (microseconds); LOESS predict = a fresh weighted least squares per query (per-point O(n·s)). Matters when serving many predictions (dashboards, scoring pipelines) — precompute on a grid and interpolate, or switch to a global basis.

title: 6.6 Local Regression (LOESS)
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Span selection, honest and cheap: implement 5-fold CV over frac ∈ {0.1, …, 0.9} using lowess on the sinusoid; report the chosen frac and its CV MSE. Then repeat on data with heteroscedastic noise (σ growing with x) and on data with a sharp local feature (a narrow Gaussian bump at x = 3). How does the chosen span respond to each geometry, and what does that say about one-global-span?


Solution







One global span must average over geometry: heteroscedastic tails push stiffer (protect the noisy region) while sharp features push looser (resolve the bump) — a single dial can’t do both. Adaptive smoothers (variable bandwidth, 6.5’s remark) or transformations are the honest responses.

Exercise 2. LOESS effective df, estimated: using the covariance estimator (as in 6.5 Exercise 2) at fixed x, estimate df(frac) for frac ∈ {0.1, 0.3, 0.9} on n = 60. Compare against the corresponding KNN-with-tricube’s df ≈ neighborhood size intuition. What does df ≈ tell you about LOESS’s position on the 4.4 dial relative to global bases of 6.1?


Solution







df slides from ≈ half of n at frac = 0.1 (very local: many effective parameters) toward 3–4 at frac = 0.9 (nearly the global line) — LOESS occupies the same flexibility continuum as bases but with space-varying allocation: more df where data is dense. That’s its edge over global bases of equal total df (6.3 Q1’s alignment argument, in continuous form).

Exercise 3. LOESS vs spline vs polynomial bake-off: on (a) a smooth sinusoid and (b) a curve with a local spike (narrow bump), compare lowess(frac by CV), the CV-tuned smoothing spline (6.5), and the CV-chosen polynomial (6.1) by test MSE on fresh points, with each method’s dial tuned inside training only. Report a 3×2 table and write the selection paragraph a methods section would carry.


Solution







Smooth world: all three tie within noise. Spiked world: global polynomials and stiff splines smear the bump; LOESS (and loose splines) track it. The write-up: “We selected among three smoothing approaches by within-training CV per dataset; all were statistically equivalent on smooth signals, while local methods were necessary under localized structure” — the disciplined version of “LOESS won once.”

title: 6.6 Local Regression (LOESS)
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

lowess(y, x) argument order — y first, x second (opposite of most sklearn). Transposed calls don’t error; they produce confident nonsense.
frac is in points, not x-units — with uneven x-density, equal-frac windows have unequal x-widths (usually desirable: more local where data is dense).
it > 0 enables robustness iterations (downweight big residuals) — the R in LOESS’s name (locally estimated robust); cheap outlier armor, at slight efficiency cost (6.5’s weights done adaptively).
No native predict(): statsmodels returns the fitted grid; new points need np.interp onto the grid, or a fresh lowess call with the query appended — for serving, precompute a dense grid.
Boundary leverage: local fits near edges rest on few points (one-sided windows); LOESS degrades more gracefully than splines there (drill 3) but is still shakier than mid-range — report edge bands separately.
df accounting is expensive for LOESS (the smoother matrix is implicit) — the covariance/bootstrap routes are the practical estimators (Exercise 2).


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated smoother has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


(x, y) transposed: lowess(y, x) is the signature; the transposed call “succeeds” with x-grid in [−1, 1] — the tell.
Interp columns swapped: interp(x_new, xp, fp) needs the grid first — swapped columns return the input coordinate as the prediction.
In-sample tuning and reporting: frac chosen to minimize training residuals, then that same number dressed up as performance — the familiar optimism (4.1). Tune by CV, report out-of-sample.

title: 6.6 Local Regression (LOESS)
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Show that LOESS (degree 0, uniform weights, fixed k neighbors) is a linear smoother: \(\hat y_0 = \sum_i w_i y_i\) with weights depending only on x and the neighbor set. Compute its smoother weights explicitly at a mid-domain point for n = 10, k = 4, and explain why degree-1 LOESS with tricube weights is also a linear smoother (weights now come from the local WLS hat row). What breaks linearity?


Hint

Each ŷ₀ is a fixed linear combination of the yᵢ — the coefficients (weights) are functions of x alone, not of y.



Solution

Degree-0: ŷ₀ = (1/k)Σ_{i∈N}yᵢ — weights 1/k on the k nearest. Degree-1: ŷ₀ = e₀ᵀ(BᵀWB)⁻¹BᵀWy where e₀ picks the local intercept — the row of the local hat matrix applied globally: still fixed linear coefficients in y. So the whole LOESS curve is ŷ = L y for an L depending only on the design → linear smoother, with tr(L) as its df. What breaks linearity: robust iterations (it > 0 — weights then depend on residuals, i.e., on y) and any adaptive bandwidth chosen from y. Robust LOESS trades smoother-linearity for outlier immunity, which is why its df accounting needs the bootstrap.

Q2. The bandwidth–bias geometry: for a twice-differentiable f and window half-width h, the local-linear estimator’s bias at x₀ is ≈ f″(x₀)·h²·(constant depending on kernel) and variance ≈ σ²·(constant)/(n·h). Derive the MSE-optimal h ∝ (σ²/f″²·n)^{1/5}, verify the 1/5 exponent numerically (fit local-linear MSE vs h on a known f at several n, extract the slope of log-optimal-h vs log n), and state the practical consequence: how much does optimal bandwidth change when you quadruple your data?


Hint

Balance h⁴-bias against σ²/(nh)-variance; the n^{-1/5} rate is the classic nonparametric law.



Solution

Bias² ~ (c₁f″h²)², variance ~ c₂σ²/(nh): MSE ~ c₁²f″²h⁴ + c₂σ²/(nh); d/dh = 0 → h* ∝ (σ²/(f″²n))^{1/5} — the n^{-1/5} law of kernel smoothing.






The measured slope lands on −0.2, the textbook \(n^{-1/5}\) rate. Two practical notes on measuring it, both learned the hard way here. First, the frac search grid must be fine: stepping by 0.04 across n ∈ {50…3200} quantizes the optimum onto a handful of values and flattens the log-log slope to −0.08, which looks like evidence against the theory when it is an artifact of the search. Second, the range of n has to be wide enough to be asymptotic — at n ≤ 500 the optimum is not yet governed by the rate. Quadrupling n shrinks the optimal bandwidth by only \(4^{1/5} \approx 1.32\), so bandwidths tune slowly with data, and undersmoothing remains the standard asymptotic advice (bias visible, variance safe) since CV tends to pick h slightly large. The \(n^{-1/5}\) rate is also why nonparametric smoothing can’t beat parametric models when the parametric form is right — the price of letting the data speak.

title: 6.6 Local Regression (LOESS)
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (LOESS × 1.5 resampling × 6.5). Bootstrap-banded LOESS vs spline: build 95% bootstrap bands (500 resamples) for both smoothers at their CV-chosen dials on the same dataset, and compare (a) band widths across x, (b) empirical coverage of the truth over 200 simulated datasets. Where do LOESS bands widen relative to splines (windows with few points?), and which smoother’s bands would you show a skeptical collaborator, and why?
C2 (LOESS × 7.4 random forests preview × 9.x). From one dimension to many: extend your hand-rolled LOESS to 2 features (local linear WLS on the k nearest in Euclidean distance). On a two-feature additive truth vs a truth with a strong interaction, compare 2-D LOESS against (i) a spline-additive model (separate 1-D smooths added — 6.7’s core idea done by hand) and (ii) a random forest. Which fails on interactions, which on sparsity in 2-D neighborhoods, and what does this mini-tournament predict about the additive-vs-fully-nonparametric choice in high dimensions?

title: 6.6 Local Regression (LOESS)
text:
7. Summary

LOESS: local weighted polynomials, slid along the domain; span (or bandwidth) is the single dial.
Tricube weights and degree-1 local fits are the standard recipe; robust iterations buy outlier immunity at linearity’s price.
It’s a linear smoother (until robustification) — df estimable via covariance/bootstrap; report it.
Boundaries are shakier, heteroscedasticity and sharp features strain one global span — diagnose per dataset.
Compute is per-query: precompute grids for serving.
Statsmodels’ lowess(y, x) — mind the argument order; interp for new points.
Smoothing one x at a time is lovely until there are ten x’s: additive models divide and conquer — 6.7 Generalized Additive Models.

title: 6.4 Regression Splines
text: Splines are piecewise polynomials stitched together smoothly at knots — local flexibility like step functions, global smoothness like polynomials. They are the workhorse of flexible curve-fitting in statistics: interpretable knots, controllable smoothness, and no extrapolation blow-ups.

title: 6.4 Regression Splines
text:
1. Basic Concept
A degree-d spline with knots \(c_1 < \cdots < c_K\) is a piecewise polynomial of degree d that is continuous with d−1 matching derivatives at each knot. The trick is the truncated-power basis: \(\phi_k(x) = (x - c_k)_+^d\) plus a degree-d polynomial — each hinge term adds exactly one “bend” at its knot:






Don’t hand-build it in production — two standard tools, same idea:

title: 6.4 Regression Splines
text:
2. Concept Questions

What exactly does the truncated-power term \((x − c)_+^3\) contribute at \(x = c\), and why does the full spline stay smooth there?
Knots vs degree vs number of knots: which do you usually fix, and which do you tune?
Why do natural splines constrain the curve to be linear beyond the boundary knots — and what do they buy with that constraint?
Your spline fit wiggles violently between knots. Name the two knobs that tame it, in order of preference.
Where are spline fits most variable (in resampling), and what does that predict about the coefficient interpreta­tion of the truncated-power terms?



Answers


It “switches on” at c and grows cubically after — adding one higher-derivative bend. Because ALL lower-order pieces and the polynomial are shared globally, the function and its first d−1 derivatives match across the knot; only the d-th derivative jumps.
Degree: conventionally fix at 3 (cubic — smooth-looking, C² continuity). Tune the number and placement of knots (or the smoothness penalty in 6.5) by CV.
Unconstrained cubics flail in the data-free tails (the polynomial explosion of 6.1); forcing linearity beyond boundary knots is a mild, variance-reducing assumption that costs little where there’s no data to contradict it.
