Fewer knots (or coarser placement); (2) a smoothness penalty — ridge on the basis, which is precisely 6.5’s smoothing splines.

Variance concentrates at the knots (the basis’s bending degrees of freedom live there) and in the boundary regions. Truncated-power coefficients are stable-mixture-unstable — like all correlated bases, interpret differences/derivatives, not individual terms.

title: 6.4 Regression Splines
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Build compare_spline_models: for the sinusoid data, evaluate (a) natural spline via patsy cr(x, df) for df ∈ {3, 5, 8, 12}, (b) SplineTransformer with n_knots ∈ {3, 6, 10, 20}, (c) global cubic. Report a CV table. Which flexible option fails (and how — check its boundary behavior on a plot), and why does the natural spline’s boundary constraint rescue it?


Solution







The unconstrained SplineTransformer at many knots starts flexing in the data-free tails (its basis isn’t boundary-linear), inflating CV error versus the natural spline at matched df. The natural spline’s linearity beyond boundary knots is free variance insurance — the same physics as 6.1’s extrapolation, cured by construction.

Exercise 2. Knot placement matters: put 5 knots (a) uniformly on [0, 10], (b) at quantiles of x, (c) all bunched in [4, 6] — on data whose curvature is concentrated in [4, 6] (y = a steep transition there, flat elsewhere: y = 2·sigmoid(4(x−5)) + noise). Compare CV MSE and plot fits. Where should knots go, in general, and how would you automate that decision honestly?


Solution







Bunched knots win — curvature lives in [4, 6], and knots are the basis’s bending budget. General rule: place knots where the function bends (steepness/curvature heuristics, or quantiles of the residual-driving region), not merely where data sits. Automation: adaptive knot selection is a hyperparameter search — CV over candidate placements (4.6), or skip the problem entirely with 6.5’s penalty, which spends flexibility continuously instead of at fixed sites.

Exercise 3. Spline diagnosis under the microscope: fit a cubic spline with 8 knots to data whose true f is smooth, then examine (a) the fit’s second derivative (numerically) across the domain — where do the “kinks” land? (b) the fit’s SD across 300 bootstrap resamples as a function of x. Verify variance concentrates near knots and boundaries; then compare against the same diagnostics for the smoothing spline of 6.5 (teaser).


Solution







The bend degrees of freedom are the knot terms, so resampling wiggles the fit at the knots — visible as SD spikes there and elevated SD at the boundaries (least data, most leverage). This is the spline’s version of 2.3’s coefficient-variance geography: uncertainty lives where the basis can bend.

title: 6.4 Regression Splines
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Knot count is the dial, degree is the convention: cubic (d = 3) is near-universal — smooth to the eye, C² continuous; degree 1 is piecewise-linear (6.2 Exercise 1); degree 0 is steps.
Two parameterizations, one space: truncated powers (human-readable) vs B-splines (numerically superb, what SplineTransformer emits). Never interpret B-spline coefficients directly — use the truncated-power view or rotate back.
df accounting: a cubic spline with K interior knots has K + 4 parameters; natural splines drop 4 (2 per boundary) — budget accordingly when comparing with Cp/AIC (5.1).
Spline terms in formulas: cr(x, df) (patsy) is natural cubic; bs(x, df, degree) is the B-spline flavor. Mixing them across models without noting df semantics produces apples-to-oranges Cp comparisons.
Multidimensional splines: tensor products of univariate splines explode combinatorially — the additive alternative is 6.7’s whole point.
Boundary extrapolation: splines extend as their boundary polynomial (or linearly, if natural) — vastly saner than polynomials, still not data. Police the range (2.1).


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated spline pipeline has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


100 knots on 150 training points: ≈102 columns for 150 rows — near-interpolation; any noise gets three knots of its own. Knot counts must be modest/CV-chosen.
Refitting the transformer on test: st_te.fit_transform builds a different basis (different knot positions) — predictions are from a different model. Transform once, transform everywhere: one fitted transformer (or a Pipeline).
B-spline coefficients ≠ effects: B-splines are a numerically-chosen basis; their coefficients are basis-local mixing weights. Interpret via predictions/plots, or the truncated-power view, or rotated-back coefficients (5.5’s loading caution, again).

title: 6.4 Regression Splines
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Show that the truncated-power basis and any B-spline basis for the same knots/degree span the same space: argue by counting (both have K + d + 1 dimensions for K knots) and by the derivative-matching characterization of splines. Then verify numerically that the OLS fits on both bases agree to machine precision on a small dataset — and explain why their coefficients differ wildly (relate to 6.3 Q2’s conditioning discussion).


Hint

A piecewise polynomial with d−1 matching derivatives at K knots is determined by (K + d + 1) free numbers — a dimension count both bases meet; same space follows.



Solution

Dimension: on each of K + 1 intervals a cubic has 4 coefficients (4(K+1)); each knot imposes 3 matching conditions (−3K) → 4K + 4 − 3K = K + 4 free parameters — matched by both bases (truncated power: d + 1 polynomial terms + K hinges; B-splines: K + d + 1 columns). Same dimension + both ⊆ spline space (each satisfies the smoothness conditions by construction) ⇒ same space. Numerically:






Identical predictions; condition numbers differ by orders of magnitude — B-splines are the numerically civilized coordinate system for the same function space (6.3’s Chebyshev moral, reprised). Interpret in one, compute in the other.

Q2. Knot selection as sparse-basis selection: given 20 candidate knots, choosing which 5 to include is a best-subset problem (5.1). Verify that Lasso on the full 20-hinge basis (tuned by CV) recovers a competitive fit to the best 5-knot subset search (greedy forward selection on knots), on data with a sharp transition at x = 5. Report both CV MSEs and the selected knots from each. What does the lasso’s answer (a spread of small hinge coefficients vs the subset’s one big one) say about correlated bases and selection stability?


Solution







The lasso spreads weight across correlated neighboring hinges (stable fit, mushy selection), while greedy subset picks (nearly) the single right knot with a hair better CV MSE but far higher selection variance across resamples. Correlated bases defeat exact recovery — the honest outputs are predictions and stability diagnostics, whichever selector you use.

title: 6.4 Regression Splines
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (splines × 5.2 ridge × 6.5 preview). Fix a fine knot grid (50 knots) and tune ridge α on the spline basis by CV — you have (nearly) built a smoothing spline. Compare against scipy’s UnivariateSpline smoothing-spline fit (s tuned by CV) on the sinusoid: CV MSE, effective df (trace of the smoother’s hat matrix), and visual wiggle. Show the two converge as the ridge α maps to the smoothing parameter — the theoretical identity (6.5) made practical.
C2 (splines × 2.7 interaction × 6.7 preview). Two-feature smooth surface, two ways: (a) tensor-product spline basis (SplineTransformer on x₁ ⊗ x₂ — count the columns), (b) additive model (spline in x₁ + spline in x₂, no interaction). Generate data that is (i) additive, (ii) with an interaction. Compare CV MSE of (a) vs (b) under each truth, and note the column counts. Write the modeler’s decision rule: when is the additive bet worth it?

title: 6.4 Regression Splines
text:
7. Summary

Splines = piecewise polynomials with enforced smoothness at knots: local bends, global elegance.
Truncated powers for understanding, B-splines for computing, natural splines for safe boundaries.
Tune knot count/placement (or switch to penalized smoothness) by CV; knots go where curvature lives.
Variance concentrates at knots and boundaries — diagnostics and interpretation follow the geometry.
B-spline coefficients are not effects; the basis spans the same space with better conditioning.
Lasso-on-hinges ≈ adaptive knot selection — with all of 5.1’s stability caveats.
Why choose knots at all when a penalty can spend flexibility continuously everywhere: 6.5 Smoothing splines.

title: 6.2 Step Functions
text: The most local basis possible: cut the range of x into intervals and fit a separate constant to each. Step functions trade smoothness for robustness and interpretability — and make the knots (cutpoints) an explicit, debatable modeling decision instead of a hidden one.

title: 6.2 Step Functions
text:
1. Basic Concept
Choose cutpoints \(c_1 < c_2 < \cdots < c_K\); build dummy columns \(C_k(x) = \mathbb{1}(c_{k-1} < x \le c_k)\) (plus the intercept as the first cell’s level, or all K cells with no intercept — the cell-means trick from 2.6). OLS on these columns fits the mean of y within each bin:






Bins as features in a predictive pipeline (with CV choosing the resolution):

title: 6.2 Step Functions
text:
2. Concept Questions

More bins = more flexibility. What are the two failure modes at K → ∞ and K = 1?
Uniform-width vs quantile bins: when does each starve?
Where do discontinuities come from, and when is a discontinuous model the right answer (name two real settings)?
Your step fit jumps at x = 5 but the scatter looks smooth there. What made the jump, and which alternative basis would remove it?
How does the step function’s bias behave within a bin, and why is it worst exactly where the true curve is steepest?



Answers


K → ∞: one observation per bin — the fit interpolates noise (zero bias, maximal variance; the k = 1 KNN of regression). K = 1: the global mean — maximal bias. Between them, the same U-curve as always.
Uniform bins starve where data is sparse (tails: bins with 2 points produce wild constants) and waste bins where data is dense; quantile bins equalize counts (stable constants) but let bin widths vary wildly, so the x-resolution is uneven. Match the strategy to the design: uniform for even designs, quantile for skewed designs.
From the basis’s own discontinuity at each cutpoint — the model cannot be smooth there. Right answer when the world genuinely steps: drug dosing tiers, tax brackets, age-risk categories, tissue types along an anatomical boundary.
The jump is bin-boundary arithmetic (adjacent constants straddling a steep true slope differ by slope × width) — not found structure. Continuous bases (6.4) trade away the discontinuity.
The constant equals the bin’s mean of f — bias at x is f(x) minus that mean: zero at the bin’s “center of mass,” growing toward the edges, maximal where |f′| is large (steep regions sweep across more f-values per bin).

title: 6.2 Step Functions
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Piecewise-constant vs piecewise-linear: fit (a) 5-bin step function, (b) 5-bin piecewise-linear (bins + bin×x interaction within each bin — implement via KBinsDiscretizer + manual within-bin centering), on the sinusoid. Compare CV MSE and plot both. Which basis removes the edge bias without adding discontinuities within bins, and what’s the cost?


Solution







Adding (x − bin mean) within each bin upgrades constants to local lines: bias drops where the truth slopes, discontinuities at boundaries shrink (adjacent lines nearly meet), and the price is 2K parameters instead of K. This is, in fact, a crude linear spline — 6.4 does it with proper continuity.

Exercise 2. Quantile vs uniform under skewed x: x ~ lognormal, y = √x + noise. Compare 6-bin uniform vs quantile step fits by CV, and by worst-bin error (max |bias| over bins estimated on a dense grid). Explain the winner’s mechanism, and state when the loser’s strategy would flip to winning.


Solution







Quantile wins: lognormal x piles mass near 0, so uniform bins leave the extreme right tail with a handful of points (variance explosion) and the dense left region over-binned (wasted flexibility). Quantile bins equalize evidence per bin. The flip: if the true function bends most in the sparse tail, uniform bins’ finer resolution out there can win — bin strategy should follow where the curve is interesting, not just where the data is dense.

Exercise 3. The threshold hunt: simulate a true jump at unknown t* (y = 1 + 2·1(x > t) + noise, t = 6.3). Estimate t* by fitting step functions on a fine grid of candidate cutpoints and choosing the cut whose two-cell fit minimizes RSS. Report the estimate over 200 simulations (bias, SD). Then explain why this is change-point detection, how it relates to the basis view, and what the inference caveat is for the chosen t̂*.


Solution







The grid-of-cells fit is a two-bin step model — change-point detection is basis selection with the cutpoint as hyperparameter. Caveat: t̂’s sampling distribution is nonstandard (the cutpoint is a discrete argmin over candidate fits), so naive “±SE” statements about t̂ are unreliable; proper inference uses specialized change-point machinery, and reporting the estimate with a bootstrap distribution is the honest middle ground.

title: 6.2 Step Functions
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Cutpoint choice is a hyperparameter — chosen on validation data, never by staring at the scatter (4.6); bins chosen from the full data then CV’d leak (the 0.5 law, again).
pd.cut on test data with bins from training — freeze the edges: use KBinsDiscretizer fitted in-pipeline, or carry pd.cut(..., bins=frozen_edges); re-deriving quantiles on new data silently changes the basis.
Edge handling: include_lowest=True for the left edge; decide explicitly whether bins are (lo, hi]; off-by-one rows at boundaries are classic.
Empty or tiny bins produce unstable constants; enforce a minimum bin count (quantile strategy + n_bins sanity) or merge cells.
Trees are adaptive step functions (Part 7): they choose cutpoints from the data by RSS reduction — the machinery this page builds by hand, automated and greedy.
Dose responses and policy bands are genuinely discontinuous; forcing a smooth basis there underfits the phenomenon — mismatched smoothness is a modeling error in both directions.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated binner has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Edges re-derived per split: train and test are binned by different boundaries — the feature spaces differ; quantile edges must be frozen from training (that’s what KBinsDiscretizer.fit stores).
The last “bin” is empty, and that is the rank deficiency. With an intercept, \(K-1\) nested indicators of the form \((x > e)\) are not collinear — the design \(\{1, (x>e_1), (x>e_2), (x>e_3)\}\) has full rank. The actual problem is the fourth column: edges_tr[1:] includes \(e_4 = \max(\text{training } x)\), so (x > e_4) is all zeros for every training row, and no training point can ever land in that bin. The design is 150×4 with rank 3, and LinearRegression’s pseudo-inverse silently splits the signal across arbitrary directions (the printed coefficients will not even be non-negative). The fix is to drop the degenerate final indicator — use the first \(K-1\) thresholds, or use interval dummies / cell means.
New data outside the training range: pd.cut returns NaN for x = 11 — a silent production crash. Clip, extend the edge bin, or refuse explicitly.

title: 6.2 Step Functions
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Derive the step-function fit explicitly: with K cells and cell-means parameterization, show the OLS solution assigns each cell its sample mean, that the hat matrix is block-constant, and that tr(H) = K. Then prove the within-bin bias identity: E[μ̂_k] − f(x) = f̄_k − f(x) for x in cell k, and show the integrated bias² over a bin equals the variance of f within the bin (exactly the quantity minimized by optimal binning around steep regions).


Hint

Cell dummies are disjoint indicators; each cell’s normal equation decouples (the 2.6 Q1 argument, geometrically). For the bias: integrate (f̄_k − f(x))² over the bin.



Solution

Each row of the design has exactly one 1, so the normal equations decouple per cell: μ̂_k = mean of y in cell k, H is block-diagonal with (1/nₖ) blocks — tr(H) = K effective parameters. Bias at x ∈ cell k: E[μ̂_k] = f̄_k (mean of f over the cell under uniform-x), so bias = f̄_k − f(x); integrating its square over the bin gives ∫(f − f̄_k)²dx = nₖ·Var_bin(f) — the bin’s internal variance of the true function. Hence optimal bins concentrate boundaries where f′ is large: equalize f-variance, not point counts (the refined version of Exercise 2’s moral).

Q2. Step functions as the t = 0 limit of trees, and the CV consistency question: implement a one-split “stump” fit (threshold chosen to minimize RSS) on the sinusoid; compare its CV MSE against the best 5-bin step model. Then simulate 200 datasets: how often does the stump’s chosen threshold fall within ±0.2 of the bin boundary with the smallest within-bin bias? What does the answer say about data-driven cutpoints as estimators — consistent, noisy, or both?


Solution







The stump’s threshold has SD ≈ 3.35 at n = 120, and lands within ±0.2 of the lowest-bias bin boundary essentially never. That is not “noisy” in the ordinary sense — it means the parameter is not identified. The truth is \(\sin(1.5x)\) on \([0,10]\): a smooth curve with no kink anywhere, so every cutpoint splits it into two roughly-equal-RSS halves and the RSS surface is nearly flat around its minimum. You are sampling the minimum of a flat function, so the spread of the estimator reflects the flatness, not the noise. The general lesson is stronger than “cutpoints are unstable estimators”: a data-driven cutpoint is a consistent estimator only if the truth genuinely has a jump there, and a story built on an estimated threshold needs the target to exist before the estimate means anything. (The train-MSE comparison shows the familiar second lesson: the stump’s 0.6423 edges the fixed 5-bin fit’s 0.6431 purely because it was chosen for this dataset — in-sample selection flattery again.)

title: 6.2 Step Functions
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (steps × 2.6 categorical × 2.7 interaction). Two-group step surfaces: y depends on x through different step patterns per group. Fit (a) pooled bins, (b) bins + group, (c) bins + group + bin×group, comparing CV MSE. When does (c) beat (b), and what does the bin×group interaction matrix look like (the subgroup version of cell means)? Connect to how decision trees grow group-specific splits (7.1).
C2 (steps × 4.4 bias–variance). Decompose the K-bin step estimator’s error across K (protocol of 4.4, 300 training sets, n = 40): bias², variance, and total. Verify: variance ≈ K·σ²/n-scaled, bias² tracking the integrated f-variance within bins (Q1’s identity). Then overlay the same three curves for piecewise-linear bins (Exercise 1) and state the K-vs-basis trade in one sentence.

title: 6.2 Step Functions
text:
7. Summary

Step functions = dummies over intervals: maximal locality, minimal smoothness, K effective parameters.
Cutpoints are hyperparameters (frozen from training, chosen by CV); quantile vs uniform is an evidence-distribution decision.
Bias concentrates within bins in steep regions — the f-variance identity tells you where the basis hurts.
Discontinuities are basis artifacts unless the world truly steps (doses, brackets, boundaries).
One-split stumps are adaptive step functions — unstable cutpoints, the seed of Part 7’s trees.
Adding within-bin slopes fixes edge bias cheaply — the segue to proper splines.
Continuous local bases with enforced smoothness: 6.3 Basis functions generalizes, 6.4 Regression splines perfects it.

title: 5.6 High-Dimensional Data
text: Genomics asked statistics a question it wasn’t built for: 20,000 features, 40 samples. In the p ≫ n regime every rule from Part 2 inverts — OLS fits perfectly and means nothing, R² = 1 is the default state of noise, and the disciplines of Parts 4–5 stop being best practice and become survival equipment.

title: 5.6 High-Dimensional Data
text:
1. Basic Concept
Three structural facts define the regime:

Interpolation is guaranteed: p ≥ n means a hyperplane through every training point exists — training error = 0 always (4.1).
Classical inference collapses: OLS SEs need df = n − p − 1 > 0; with p ≥ n there are no residual degrees of freedom, so no σ̂², no t-tests, no F-tests.
Selection is unavoidable: you cannot “use all features” — some reduction (penalty, components, filters) is mathematically mandatory.

The R² = 1 noise miracle, witnessed:






The regime’s survival kit, applied to a realistic simulation (n = 60 patients, p = 400 genes, 6 truly active):

title: 5.6 High-Dimensional Data
text:
2. Concept Questions

Why exactly are there no residual degrees of freedom when p ≥ n, and which downstream quantities die first as p approaches n?
Your colleague reports an OLS on 200 samples with 500 covariates and “significant” adjusted R² of 0.95. Name the three disqualifications.
Why does CV become more important in p ≫ n — and what special care does stratification/selection need here?
Lasso can select at most n features when p ≫ n. You need “the” biomarker panel of 12. Is lasso’s 12-feature selection from 5,000 candidates trustworthy as a discovery list?
Distance-based methods (KNN, 2.9) fail hardest in high dimensions. Why, and which Part 5 tools repair them?



Answers


df = n − (p + 1); it hits 0 at p = n − 1. σ̂² = RSS/(n − p − 1) becomes 0/0 or negative → every t-test, F-test, CI, RSE, and Cp/AIC penalty built on σ̂² dies in sequence.

p > n: the fit interpolates — R² is 1 by construction, not by skill; (2) adjusted R²’s formula assumes p ≪ n and is garbage in this regime; (3) “significant” claims require SEs, which don’t exist (Concept 1). The 0.95 is the interpolation identity wearing a suit.

Because model selection (which penalty, which features, which M) now carries the whole burden — with no unpenalized fallback, tuning choices dominate the outcome, so the selection must be honest and repeated (4.3). Selection stability across folds/resamples must be reported because single supports are noise.
No. It’s one arbitrary draw from a near-tie set of correlated candidates (5.1 instability, 5.3 twins); the defensible products are (a) its predictive performance (nested CV), (b) selection frequencies across resamples — never a fixed “panel of 12” narrative.
High-dimensional distances concentrate: nearest and farthest neighbors converge (2.9’s curse), so neighborhoods stop being local. Repair: reduce dimension first (PCR directions, 5.5), or select features so distances are computed in the signal subspace — both are Part 5 tools.

title: 5.6 High-Dimensional Data
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. The p/n frontier, mapped: fix n = 100 and sweep p ∈ {10, 50, 100, 200, 500} with a fixed 5-signal truth (signals in the first 5 features when p allows; extra features pure noise). For each p, report OLS train R², OLS test R², and RidgeCV’s test R². Where does OLS’s train R² hit 1.0, and how does each method’s test performance degrade with p? State the “usable dimensionality” rule of thumb this table supports.


Solution







Train R² pins to 1.0 exactly at p = n; OLS’s test R² turns negative beyond and stays dead. Ridge degrades gracefully, retaining real predictive value even at p = 5n. Rule of thumb: unpenalized regression is defensible while p stays a small fraction of n (and effects are strong); the moment p/n ≳ 0.5, penalized methods are the toolset, full stop.

Exercise 2. Selection stability at genomic scale: n = 50, p = 300, 8 true genes. Run LassoCV selection on 100 bootstrap resamples; report (a) how often each true gene is selected, (b) how often each of the top-5 most frequently selected noise genes is selected, (c) the median support size. Then compute the overlap of consecutive supports (Jaccard). Write the two-sentence methods paragraph reporting this honestly — the paragraph your genomics paper needs.


Solution







True genes are selected often (but not always — power at n = 50); several noise genes cross 20–40% selection by chance, and consecutive supports overlap only partially. Honest paragraph: “Lasso selection at CV-chosen penalization was repeated across 100 bootstrap resamples. Features are ranked by selection frequency; we report the full frequency table rather than a fixed panel, noting that individual supports are unstable under resampling (median support size X, mean pairwise Jaccard Y). Predictive performance was assessed by nested cross-validation.”

Exercise 3. The full high-dimensional workflow, end to end: n = 80 patients, p = 600 genes, outcome binary (case/control, 40/40), driven by 5 genes with moderate effect. Build and honestly evaluate: standardize → lasso-logistic (C tuned by inner CV) → outer 5-fold stratified CV → report AUC, plus selection frequencies per gene across outer folds. Then answer: which single number in your report is the performance claim, and which artifact is the exploratory output?


Solution







The performance claim is the outer-CV AUC with its SD — that number prices the whole procedure including feature selection. The gene list (and its frequencies) is exploratory: it generates hypotheses for validation in fresh cohorts, and its instability across folds is exactly why frequencies, not a fixed list, get reported. Conflating the two — quoting the AUC and presenting the support as discovered truth — is the p ≫ n era’s signature overreach.

title: 5.6 High-Dimensional Data
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

No unpenalized fallback exists: in p ≥ n, “just fit OLS” is not an option, so the entire modeling decision space is Part 5’s — penalty family, strength, and preprocessing are the model.
Batch effects and unwanted variation are high-dimensional biology’s confounders: they correlate with thousands of features at once and dominate PCA/lasso if uncorrected — normalization/combat-style adjustment precedes everything (and must itself live inside CV for honest evaluation).
Multiplicity is ambient: 20,000 genes ⇒ 20,000 implicit tests even before you “test” anything; every marginal screen needs FDR machinery (12.4 stub), and lasso-style joint selection needs stability reporting (5.1).
Prediction ≠ discovery, twice over: the selected genes are not validated by the model’s AUC (they rode along with it); conversely, a well-validated model can consist mostly of non-causal tags. State which claim each result supports.
Effective sample size may be smaller than n: correlated samples (related patients, batches, repeated measures) shrink n below its nominal value exactly when you need every row — the grouped-splitting discipline of 4.3 applies to the units, not rows.
Double descent’s home turf: at p ≈ n test error peaks, and overparameterized interpolators can descend again (4.4 Q2) — a real phenomenon, but not a license: the descent region’s gains are model-specific and modest relative to just collecting more samples.
Reporting standards: n, p, prevalence, penalty family, tuning grid, inner/outer CV protocol, selection frequencies, and a null-simulation calibration check. If any is missing, the result isn’t reproducible.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated “biomarker study” has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


OLS at p ≫ n: the 1.0000 train R² is the interpolation identity; no SEs exist; the fit is meaningless.
Screen-then-fit on the same rows: with a null outcome, this manufactures “hits” with inflated in-sample R² — the entire result is the selection’s shadow (5.1 Exercise 2).
Discovery claim from marginal p < 0.05 over 800 tests: expect ~40 false positives at this rate; no FDR control, no validation, no stability — nothing supports the word “identified.”

title: 5.6 High-Dimensional Data
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Derive the expected training R² under the null for OLS with n rows and p ≤ n−1: using E[RSS] = (n − p − 1)σ² (errors dominate), show E[R²] ≈ p/(n − 1). Verify by simulation across a p-sweep, and connect the formula to (a) the adjusted-R² penalty, (b) why train R² = p/n-lookalikes certify nothing in high dimensions.


Hint

TSS ≈ (n−1)σ² under the null; RSS ≈ (n−p−1)σ²; R² = 1 − RSS/TSS → p/(n−1).



Solution

Under the null (y independent of X), OLS consumes p + 1 df on noise: E[RSS] = (n − p − 1)σ², and TSS ≈ (n − 1)σ², so E[R²] = 1 − (n − p − 1)/(n − 1) = p/(n − 1).







Adjusted R² subtracts exactly this noise inflation (that’s its whole job — and why its derivation assumes p ≪ n). (b) In the p ≈ n regime the “explained variance” of a null fit approaches 1 — every in-sample goodness number is the complexity charge in disguise, and only out-of-sample estimates retain meaning.


Q2. You must choose between two p ≫ n studies to trust: Study A reports a 15-gene panel selected by lasso with CV AUC 0.84; Study B reports the same genes independently validated (AUC 0.71) in an external cohort of 200 samples. Construct the argument (with a mini-simulation if useful) for why B’s lower AUC is the stronger scientific claim, and design the combined analysis you’d actually run given both datasets (selection in A, frozen evaluation in B, then pooled refit with stability reporting).


Solution

A’s 0.84 prices selection adaptivity but lives on n = 40-ish effective samples and resampling within one dataset — its CI covers optimistic territory (selection bonus + small-n noise + any batch structure). B’s 0.71 is a pre-registered (frozen-panel) evaluation on fresh rows: no selection degrees of freedom, so 0.71 is a claim about the world, not the procedure. Simulation sketch:






The transfer number typically sits below the internal number (selection + small-n optimism) yet carries more evidential weight. Combined analysis: tune/choose on A (or pooled inner folds), freeze, evaluate on B untouched; finally refit on all data and report per-gene selection frequencies across resamples — with the two datasets’ batch structures declared. The hierarchy of evidence: frozen external validation > internal nested CV > internal CV of the selected model > anything with “significant” and p ≫ n in the same sentence.

title: 5.6 High-Dimensional Data
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (p ≫ n × 5.2–5.5 family reunion). At n = 60, p = 800 (latent-factor truth, 8 active features, duplicate-block structure): run the complete Part 5 tournament — ridge, lasso, net, PCR, PLS — each tuned inside an outer CV. Deliver (a) the accuracy table, (b) each winner’s complexity measure (effective df / support size / M), (c) selection stability for the sparse methods. Write the discussion paragraph: which method would you pre-register for the next cohort, and what information would justify changing?
C2 (p ≫ n × 12.4 FDR stub × 3.1.5 AUPRC). Connect the two selection languages: run a marginal screen (p-values for 1,000 features under a sparse truth), apply BH-FDR at q = 0.05 to get a “significant” set, then run LassoCV selection on the same data. Compare the two feature sets (size, truth overlap) and their precision (fraction true). Show that lasso’s support behaves like a data-adaptive FDR-thresholded set — and identify the condition (strong signal, weak correlation) under which the vocabularies coincide, previewing Part 12’s formal treatment.

title: 5.6 High-Dimensional Data
text:
7. Summary

p ≥ n: interpolation guaranteed, R² = 1 meaningless, residual df gone — inference and unpenalized fitting are off the table.
E[train R²] ≈ p/(n−1) under the null: in-sample numbers measure complexity, not discovery.
Survival kit: penalized regression (ridge/lasso/net), direction methods (PCR/PLS), filters — all inside honest nested CV.
Selection in this regime is unstable by nature; report frequencies and validation, never fixed panels as discoveries.
Frozen external validation outranks every internal number; batch/unwanted variation and unit-level splitting are design-level duties.
The p ≫ n workflow’s product is a calibrated claim: performance for prediction, hypotheses for discovery, never both from one number.
Part 5 closes the classical toolkit. Next the models bend shape — polynomials, splines and smoothing in Part 6 — then trees, SVMs, and unsupervised structure beginning with the PCA depths at 9.2 PCA.

title: 5.4 Elastic Net
text: Ridge groups correlated features but never zeroes them; lasso zeroes features but coin-flips among correlated twins (5.2, 5.3). The elastic net mixes both penalties, getting sparsity and grouping — and introduces a second hyperparameter that captures a real modeling question: how much do you believe features are interchangeable?

title: 5.4 Elastic Net
text:
1. Basic Concept
\[\hat\beta = \arg\min_\beta \Big\{ \sum_i (y_i - \beta_0 - x_i^\top\beta)^2 + \lambda \big( \tfrac{1-\alpha}{2}\|\beta\|_2^2 + \alpha\|\beta\|_1 \big) \Big\}\]
Two dials: λ (overall penalty — sklearn’s alpha) and α (the L1 share — sklearn’s l1_ratio). Endpoints recover the classics: α = 1 → lasso, α = 0 → ridge.






The grouping experiment — correlated twins: lasso splits them, the net keeps them together:






Tuning both dials with ElasticNetCV over a grid:

title: 5.4 Elastic Net
text:
2. Concept Questions

In sklearn’s parameterization, what do alpha = 0.1, l1_ratio = 0.7 mean — and what does alpha = 0 give you exactly, regardless of l1_ratio?
Why does the ridge component stabilize selection among correlated twins? Explain via the penalty’s geometry (edges vs corners).
The elastic net has two tuning parameters. What does the CV surface over (λ, α) typically look like, and what does a flat ridge along α tell you?
Your lasso selects 3 of 30 features; the net selects 8 (including near-duplicates). Which model would you deploy for (a) a $1-per-feature measurement budget, (b) pure prediction with no measurement cost?
Why does elastic net sometimes select more features than n (unlike lasso’s ≤ n cap)? When does that matter?



Answers


The objective penalizes 0.15·‖β‖² + 0.7·‖β‖₁ (times λ = 0.1): mostly-L1 with a ridge floor. alpha = 0 zeroes the whole penalty → plain OLS at any l1_ratio — the ratio only matters when a penalty exists.
The L1 diamond has sharp corners/edges where optima sit — among equal twins the fit picks one edge/vertex (a winner). The L2 ball’s boundary is round: moving along the twin-subspace costs (nearly) nothing, so both twins can share the coefficient smoothly. Ridge’s grouping + L1’s sparsity = twins selected jointly with shrunken, stable values.
Typically a long, flat valley along λ at moderate-to-high α: many (λ, α) pairs score within noise (4.6’s landscape flatness). A flat ridge along α says the data doesn’t care about the mixing share — pick by parsimony of the selected set, not the argmax.

The 3-feature lasso — measurement cost is real money and the twins carry no extra signal. (b) Either on prediction grounds (indistinguishable by CV); the net is safer under future drift/collinearity because it doesn’t bet everything on one twin.

The ridge component lets correlated groups enter jointly; a group of size g can share one “selection ticket” per member, so p_selected can exceed n. It matters when you’re interpreting support size as complexity, or in extreme p ≫ n where the net’s support can balloon — cap with stronger λ.

title: 5.4 Elastic Net
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Map the two-dial landscape by hand: on a fixed dataset (n = 120, p = 25, 4 true signals, one duplicated pair), fit ElasticNet over α ∈ logspace(−3, 0, 10) × l1_ratio ∈ {0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9, 1.0}, recording 5-fold CV MSE and support size per cell. Display the two heatmaps side by side. Locate: (a) the MSE argmin, (b) the smallest support within 1 SE of the best MSE. How different are their supports?


Solution







The landscape is the familiar flat valley (4.6): many cells tie within noise; the parsimony pick usually has a third of the support at statistically identical MSE — the one-SE rule, two parameters deep.

Exercise 2. The grouping staircase: build 8 features in 4 correlated pairs (within-pair ρ = 0.95, between pairs independent), with one pair truly active. Trace each method’s selected set across α (lasso: l1_ratio = 1) vs net (l1_ratio = 0.3) at matched CV-chosen λ. Report the “family selection rate”: how often does each method select both or neither member of the active pair, over 100 bootstrap resamples? This number is the operational definition of grouping.


Solution







The lasso’s rate hovers near coin-flip territory (it takes one twin and ignores the other), while the net’s rate approaches 1 — it treats the pair as the atom. When features come in natural groups (gene pathways, duplicate sensors), that rate is the property you’re buying.

Exercise 3. Method bake-off with honest evaluation (4.6): on one dataset (p = 40, sparse truth with a duplicated pair), compare OLS-with-top-k-filter (5.1), ridge, lasso, and elastic net — each tuned by inner 5-fold CV — evaluated by outer 5-fold nested CV. Report nested test MSE per procedure and the paired fold differences between the winner and runner-up. Write the two-sentence conclusion for a methods section.


Solution







Typical outcome: all four land in the same band and the pairing cannot separate the top two — lasso is nominally best (751) with filter+OLS close behind (781), and ridge/net a little behind both (853/849); the lasso-vs-filter paired p is 0.55, so the ordering is not real. Two conclusions, both worth writing down. First, the slogan “hard selection pays a variance tax” is not visible here: with 5 informative features out of 40 and k=10 selected, the filter has little room to make a damaging mistake. Second — and this is the part that actually transfers — a bake-off that cannot reject the null cannot license a choice on predictive grounds. The write-up therefore says “all procedures performed equivalently (paired CV p > 0.05); we selected lasso for its sparsity property, not because it predicted better.” Choosing the winner of a tie is fine as long as you are honest that the ranking was a coin flip.

title: 5.4 Elastic Net
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Two dials, twice the selection tax: tuning (λ, α) jointly searches a bigger space than either parent — expect a slightly larger selection bonus and use nested CV accordingly (4.6).
sklearn’s alpha rescales with l1_ratio (the mixing formula divides by 1 − α/2-terms): comparing alphas across l1_ratio values is meaningless — compare CV scores, not parameter values.
l1_ratio = 1 is lasso, 0 is ridge — but tiny nonzero ratios aren’t pure anything: a 0.95 net is “lasso with insurance”; a 0.05 net is “ridge with occasional zeros.” Name the operating point, don’t just cite the class.
Standardization remains mandatory — the mixed penalty still counts coefficient magnitudes.
Groups need not be prescribed: the net groups correlated features automatically; for known groups (pathways), the group lasso exists beyond sklearn’s core — same spirit, structured penalty.
Support size ≠ degrees of freedom for the net: with twins jointly selected, df grows less than support (shared signal) — don’t reuse the lasso’s df = |support| identity here (5.3 Q2).
Convergence warnings matter: the mixed penalty is harder to optimize; watch max_iter, and prefer the CV wrappers that warm-start across the path.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated net workflow has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Unscaled net: feature 3’s tiny coefficient dodges both penalties — selection by units again. Standardize inside a pipeline.
The dials swapped: l1_ratio = 0.1 is mostly ridge (few zeros expected); the sparsity knob is l1_ratio near 1. Reading support size off the wrong dial produces confident nonsense.
Test-set tuning: the reported score is an order statistic over 4 tries. Tune with ElasticNetCV on training; spend the test set once.

title: 5.4 Elastic Net
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Geometric derivation: draw (for p = 2) the lasso diamond, ridge disk, and the elastic net’s rounded diamond. Show that the net’s boundary has (a) corners on the axes (producing exact zeros like lasso) and (b) straight edges between corners that are flattened arcs (allowing twins to ride together like ridge). Explain why a fit at an edge gives equal coefficients to twins while a fit at a diamond’s edge forces |β₁| + |β₂| = c — one winner.


Hint

The penalty region {(β₁,β₂): λ[(1−r)/2·‖β‖² + r‖β‖₁] ≤ c} mixes the diamond’s linear edges with quadratic arcs; the L1 part dominates near axes, the L2 part dominates near the diagonal.



Solution

The net’s constraint region is a superellipse between diamond and disk. Near an axis (one coefficient large), the L1 term’s linear boundary dominates → sharp corner → solutions sit at β₂ = 0 exactly (sparsity). Along the diagonal (equal coefficients), for twins the L1 term still contributes 2r·λ|β| but the L2 arc’s curvature — driven by (1−r)/2·(β₁²+β₂²) — rounds the boundary; a tangency with correlated data’s elliptical RSS contours can occur mid-edge with β₁ = β₂ ≠ 0 (grouping). The pure diamond’s edge is dead straight: its tangency logic forces the fit to a vertex (one twin zero). Geometry is the whole story: corners select, curves share, and l1_ratio interpolates the boundary.

Q2. Design and run the stability-driven α choice: for the twins dataset, choose α_mix not by CV-MSE argmin but by maximizing selection stability (Jaccard overlap of supports across 50 bootstrap resamples) among candidates whose CV MSE is within 1 SE of the best. Report the chosen α_mix, its CV MSE vs the argmin’s, and the stability scores of both. When does this procedure change the answer, and what principle is it an instance of?


Solution







High-α (lasso-like) values show lower overlap — the twin coin-flip decorrelates supports; mid ratios stabilize. The procedure only changes the answer when the CV valley is flat (elsewhere it wastes stability on worse fits); it is the one-standard-error rule (4.6) with a second-order criterion swapped in: among statistically tied models, pick by a property you actually care about — here, reproducibility of the selected set.

title: 5.4 Elastic Net
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (net × 2.5 collinearity × 5.2–5.3). Build a truth with 5 blocks of 4 highly-correlated features each (2 blocks active). Compare ridge, lasso, and net (α tuned) on: prediction MSE (outer CV), true-block recovery rate, and within-block coefficient equality (max/min ratio). Produce the 3×3 summary table and write the guidance sentence for a biologist whose features are pathway members — which method answers which scientific question.
C2 (net × 0.5 splitting × 4.3). The full pipeline audit: implement the net workflow (standardize → tune (λ, α) by inner CV → refit → predict) and wrap the entire thing in an outer CV, tracking per-fold selected supports. Report (a) outer MSE, (b) how many folds agree on the support, (c) the Jaccard distance between per-fold supports. What does the support disagreement across folds predict about the stability of your final published feature list — and what are your two honest options (report frequencies; fix α by domain reasoning and disclose)?

title: 5.4 Elastic Net
text:
7. Summary

Elastic net = λ[(1−r)/2·‖β‖² + r‖β‖₁]: sparsity from L1, grouping from L2; r = l1_ratio interpolates the parents.
Two dials mean two-dial selection tax and flatter CV valleys — one-SE/parsimony reasoning applies twice over.
Twins: lasso splits, net shares — the family-selection rate is the operational difference.
Endpoint sanity: l1_ratio 1/0 recover lasso/ridge exactly; alpha = 0 is OLS at any ratio.
Compare CV scores across (λ, α), never parameter values; standardization is still law.
Stability-driven choice of α (within 1 SE) buys reproducible supports when prediction can’t decide.
What if you never regress on features at all — regress on their principal directions instead? 5.5 PCR and PLS.

title: 5.2 Ridge Regression
text: Ridge regression keeps every feature but shrinks its coefficient toward zero, buying variance down with bias up. It is the canonical answer to collinearity (2.5) and the first stopping point on the regularization dial that Part 5 spends three pages exploring.

title: 5.2 Ridge Regression
text:
1. Basic Concept
Ridge replaces least squares with penalized least squares:
\[\hat{\beta}^{\text{ridge}} = \arg\min_\beta \Big\{ \sum_i (y_i - \beta_0 - x_i^\top\beta)^2 + \lambda \sum_j \beta_j^2 \Big\}\]
Excluding the intercept from the penalty (as above — always, in practice): the center of the data shouldn’t be regularized. The solution has a closed form:
\[\hat{\beta} = (X^\top X + \lambda I)^{-1} X^\top y\]
λ > 0 makes the matrix invertible even when \(X^\top X\) is not — ridge exists precisely where OLS breaks (2.5’s singular design). The closed form, verified against sklearn (on centered data, so no intercept needed):






Bias–variance in action (4.4): λ buys variance down:






The coefficient path — every coefficient shrinking smoothly as λ grows (the visual signature of ridge, vs lasso’s sharp zeros in 5.3):

title: 5.2 Ridge Regression
text:
2. Concept Questions

Why is ridge not scale-equivariant, and what preprocessing does that force on you?
λ = 0 recovers which estimator? λ → ∞ recovers which prediction rule?
Show from \((X^\top X + \lambda I)^{-1}\) why ridge is computable when p > n while OLS is not.
Your colleague ridge-fits and then reports “effect of xⱼ = β̂ⱼ, p < 0.05.” Two problems with that sentence?
In the bias–variance decomposition at fixed x₀, what does increasing λ do to each term — and why does total error eventually rise?



Answers


The penalty Σβⱼ² depends on coefficient magnitudes, so multiplying xⱼ by 10 (dividing βⱼ by 10) changes the penalty for the same fit. Standardize features first — the penalty then says “each SD of signal costs equally.”
λ = 0 → OLS (exact). λ → ∞ → coefficients → 0 → predictions collapse to ȳ (the mean-model of 2.1) — ridge interpolates between OLS and the null model.
\((X^\top X + \lambda I)\) adds λ to every eigenvalue; even if \(X^\top X\) has zero eigenvalues (p ≥ n or perfect collinearity), all become ≥ λ > 0 — invertible. OLS needs \(X^\top X\) itself invertible.

β̂ⱼ is shrunk — it underestimates the effect by design; quoting it as an effect size biases every claim toward zero. (2) The usual SEs/p-values don’t apply to penalized fits (4.6’s warning) — ridge is for prediction; for inference use OLS on selected/refit models or Bayesian machinery.

Variance falls (shrunk coefficients wobble less across training sets), bias² rises (systematically short of the truth), σ² untouched. Total = U-shaped in λ: the sweet spot is where marginal variance savings stop exceeding marginal bias cost.

title: 5.2 Ridge Regression
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Prove the closed form: expand \(\sum(y - X\beta)^2 + \lambda\beta^\top\beta\), differentiate in β, set to zero, solve. Then verify numerically that the ridge solution equals OLS on the augmented dataset obtained by appending rows of zeros y=0 (a trick: penalized = unpenalized with pseudo-data). What does each pseudo-row “say” to the fit?


Solution

Objective: \((y - X\beta)^\top(y - X\beta) + \lambda\beta^\top\beta\). Gradient: \(-2X^\top(y - X\beta) + 2\lambda\beta = 0 \Rightarrow (X^\top X + \lambda I)\beta = X^\top y \Rightarrow \hat\beta = (X^\top X + \lambda I)^{-1}X^\top y\). The augmentation: appending √λ·I as rows with targets 0 makes the unpenalized RSS on the augmented data exactly RSS + λ‖β‖² — so OLS-on-augmented = ridge.






Each pseudo-row whispers: “imagine an observation where all features are √λ and the outcome is 0 — a fit with large coefficients would miss it.” That’s the prior in data clothing (and the Bayesian MAP connection of Complex C2).

Exercise 2. The collinearity payoff, priced: build y = 2x₁ + ε with x₂ = x₁ + noise (heavy collinearity, n = 60). For λ ∈ {0, 0.1, 1, 10, 100}: (a) record the variance of β̂₁ across 500 training sets (fix the scale by standardizing), (b) record test MSE on fresh data. Produce the two-row table. Which λ minimizes variance, which minimizes test MSE, and how does the OLS row (λ = 0) illustrate 2.5’s “coefficients see-saw”?


Solution







SD of β̂₁ collapses monotonically as λ grows (variance cure), while test MSE bottoms around λ ≈ 1–10 and rises at λ = 100 (bias takes over) — the U-curve in one table. At λ = 0, note how unstable the standardized coefficient is despite the model predicting fine: collinearity wrecks interpretation, not prediction — and ridge is the interpretation-preserving compromise.

Exercise 3. Tune λ honestly (4.6): with RidgeCV and with GridSearchCV-in-pipeline, select α on training data over a log grid; report the chosen α, its CV score, and a nested outer estimate of the whole procedure. Then compare the nested estimate against the naive best_score_ — quantify the selection optimism you now expect.


Solution







best_score_ sits above the nested estimate by the usual order-statistic margin — now predictable, because you’ve measured this gap three ways (4.1 Q2, 4.3 Exercise 2, here).

title: 5.2 Ridge Regression
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Standardize first — no exceptions. Unscaled ridge penalizes measurement units, not information; the pipeline is the enforcement mechanism (0.5).
Ridge coefficients are biased by construction — never quote them as effect sizes or feed them to inference machinery. If you need effects after shrinkage: post-ridge OLS refit on the (all) features with honest caveats, or Bayesian ridge with credible intervals.
The intercept is unpenalized (sklearn’s fit_intercept=True default) — centering by the intercept handles the mean; penalizing it would fight the data’s level for no reason.
λ’s meaning is n-dependent — but check the normalization before you quote it: Ridge minimizes \(\|y-X\beta\|^2 + \alpha\|\beta\|^2\) (the unnormalized RSS form — verified: Ridge(alpha=3) equals \((X^\top X + 3I)^{-1}X^\top y\) exactly, not \((X^\top X + 3nI)^{-1}X^\top y\)), so “α = 1” means different shrinkage at n = 100 vs n = 100,000. Lasso and ElasticNet, by contrast, use the \(1/(2n)\) form. The two estimators’ α are therefore not on the same scale even for the same data — never copy an α from one to the other, and never copy alphas between studies. Tune per dataset.
Ridge keeps all p features — if p ≫ n and most features are dead, ridge’s predictions can still be good but its weight spread is ugly; that’s lasso territory (5.3).
The SVD view: ridge divides each principal-component direction’s contribution by (1 + λ/sᵢ²) — low-variance directions (9.2 preview) are shrunk hardest. Ridge is soft PCR, which is exactly 5.5’s comparison.
Correlated groups share credit smoothly — two near-duplicates get similar shrunken coefficients (no coin-flip), which is often the scientifically honest answer, and exactly where lasso behaves worse (5.4).


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated ridge pipeline has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Unscaled ridge penalizes columns by their units — the big-variance feature is shrunk least regardless of signal. StandardScaler inside a pipeline.
Test-set alpha shopping — the test set spent on tuning (4.6). Tune with RidgeCV/GridSearchCV on training folds.
Shrunken coefficient as “effect” — it’s biased toward zero by construction; and no p-value can accompany it. Report it as a model parameter of a predictive model, or do inference separately.

title: 5.2 Ridge Regression
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Using the SVD \(X = U S V^\top\), derive the ridge fit as \(\hat y = U\, \text{diag}\!\left(\frac{s_i^2}{s_i^2 + \lambda}\right) U^\top y\) and conclude: (a) ridge shrinks each principal direction by the factor \(s_i^2/(s_i^2 + \lambda)\); (b) directions with tiny \(s_i\) (near-collinearity) are crushed first. Verify numerically on a rank-deficient design that ridge’s fitted values are finite and stable while OLS’s minimum-norm solution swings wildly across resamples.


Hint

OLS fitted values are \(U U^\top y\) (projection); ridge replaces the indicator \(1\{s_i > 0\}\)-style weights with smooth shrink factors.



Solution

\(\hat\beta = V\,\text{diag}\!\left(\frac{s_i}{s_i^2+\lambda}\right)U^\top y\), so \(\hat y = X\hat\beta = U\,\text{diag}\!\left(\frac{s_i^2}{s_i^2+\lambda}\right)U^\top y\): each SVD direction passes through with a shrink factor — small-\(s_i\) directions (where OLS divides by \(s_i\), amplifying noise) are suppressed. Verification:






The SVD story lands exactly where the algebra says it should, and it is worth reading the four numbers as pairs. OLS’s individual coefficients swing by SD ≈ 26 — the fit is free to put all the signal on x₁ in one replicate and all of it on x₂ in the next, because the tiny \(s\) direction along \((1,-1)/\sqrt2\) makes that trade nearly free. Ridge pins them (SD ≈ 0.11, a 230× reduction) via exactly the \(s_i^2/(s_i^2+\lambda)\) damping. But the sum \(\hat\beta_1+\hat\beta_2\) — the one combination the data can actually identify — has the same SD under both (0.219 vs 0.212), and so do the fitted values (0.237 vs 0.234). So the honest conclusion is narrower than “ridge fixes collinearity”: ridge does not improve predictions here, because the unstable direction is orthogonal to the test design. What it fixes is interpretation — you get numbers you can put in a paper. This is the precise link to PCR (5.5): PCR truncates small directions (hard), ridge damps them (soft).

Q2. Bayesian ridge: with a Gaussian prior \(\beta \sim N(0, \tau^2 I)\) and Gaussian likelihood, show the MAP estimate equals ridge with \(\lambda = \sigma^2/\tau^2\). Verify numerically that Ridge(alpha)’s solution matches the posterior mode from a simple Gaussian-prior least-squares objective. What does this buy you (credible intervals, prior knowledge encoding) and what does it cost (name the assumption)?


Hint

Maximize the log posterior: log-likelihood − ‖β‖²/(2τ²); match coefficients with the ridge objective.



Solution

Log posterior ∝ \(-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\|y - X\beta\|^2 - \frac{1}{2\tau^2}\|\beta\|^2\). Multiplying by \(2\sigma^2\): \(\|y-X\beta\|^2 + \frac{\sigma^2}{\tau^2}\|\beta\|^2\) — ridge with \(\lambda = \sigma^2/\tau^2\). The MAP of “Gaussian likelihood + zero-mean Gaussian prior” IS ridge.






Buy: a principled reading of λ (prior variance ratio), credible intervals from the posterior (Gaussian: covariance \((X^\top X/\sigma^2 + I/\tau^2)^{-1}\)), and a place to encode genuine prior knowledge (e.g., effects near zero and bounded). Cost: the prior assumption itself — credible intervals are statements conditional on Gaussianity of effects, and treating the prior as “just regularization” while quoting Bayesian intervals is having it both ways.

title: 5.2 Ridge Regression
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (ridge × 4.4 bias–variance). Measure the full decomposition across λ: 300 training sets (n = 40, p = 20, 5 real features), record bias²/variance of predictions on a fixed grid for λ ∈ {0.01, 1, 100}. Show the variance curve falling monotonically, bias² rising, and the sum bottoming between — then locate the λ that CV chose on one representative dataset and mark it on the decomposition. How close is CV’s choice to the decomposition optimum?
C2 (ridge × 9.2 PCA stub × 5.5 preview). Construct the classic pathological direction: y driven by a component whose variance is smallest (signal in the noise directions of X). Show ridge (which damps low-variance directions) underperforms OLS-with-selectkbest or PLS here, and quantify the gap by CV. This is the “ridge fails when variance ≠ relevance” experiment — the exact motivation for supervised direction methods, and the reason 5.5 exists.

title: 5.2 Ridge Regression
text:
7. Summary

Ridge = least squares + λ‖β‖²; closed form \((X^\top X + \lambda I)^{-1}X^\top y\); λ > 0 rescues singular problems.
Bias for variance: paths shrink smoothly, never to zero; λ interpolates OLS → mean-model.
Standardize first; leave the intercept unpenalized; tune α by CV inside a pipeline; nested CV for claims.
Shrunken coefficients are parameters, not effect sizes — no naive p-values.
SVD view: each direction damped by \(s_i^2/(s_i^2+\lambda)\) — soft, stable, blind to direction relevance.
Collinear groups share credit smoothly — honest under duplication, unlike coin-flip subset selection.
Shrink-to-zero is often what you actually want — sparsity next: 5.3 Lasso regression.

title: 4.6 Hyperparameter Tuning
text: Every model from Part 2–3 has dials you don’t fit from data: polynomial degree, KNN’s k, regularization strength, tree depth. Hyperparameter tuning chooses them by validation — and inherits every trap of 4.1–4.5 in concentrated form, because tuning is selection, and selection is optimism. This page builds the honest tuning machine: grids, pipelines, nested CV, and the reporting discipline that keeps the numbers true.

title: 4.6 Hyperparameter Tuning
text:
1. Basic Concept
The separation of hats: hyperparameters are chosen on validation data (inner loop); performance of the whole choose-and-fit procedure is estimated on untouched data (outer loop). Conflating the hats — tuning and reporting on the same data — is the single most common inflated number in applied ML.






The tuning landscape itself — mean CV score per k with its fold spread:






Note the landscape’s flat top: neighboring k values are statistically indistinguishable — the one-standard-error rule (below) exists for exactly this reason.

title: 4.6 Hyperparameter Tuning
text:
2. Concept Questions

Why is search.best_score_ NOT an unbiased estimate of the tuned model’s performance — describe the mechanism in one sentence.
State the one-standard-error rule and the philosophy behind preferring the simpler model within 1 SE of the best.
Grid vs random search: when does random win, and what property of real hyperparameter landscapes makes it so?
Your pipeline = scaler + feature-selector + model, all tuned. Why must the selector’s parameters also live inside the CV loop?
After nested CV selects and scores the procedure, what model do you deploy, and what number do you quote for its expected performance?



Answers


best_score_ is the maximum over candidates of noisy CV estimates — an order statistic. Even on pure noise it beats the true optimum; its expected value = true performance + selection bonus (measured in 4.1 Q2). Only an outer loop (or fresh test set) prices the selection itself.
Among models whose CV scores lie within 1 SE of the best, choose the most parsimonious (largest k, strongest penalty, fewest features). Rationale: those scores are indistinguishable from the best; the simpler model has less variance, better interpretability, and typically better deployment behavior — you give up nothing measurable and buy robustness.
When the grid is larger than a handful of dimensions or several parameters are irrelevant (low effective dimensionality of the response surface). Landscapes are usually dominated by a few parameters (e.g., k, learning rate) while others barely matter — random points find the important dimensions faster than a lattice that spends equal effort on all.
Because feature selection fits parameters to data (which features look informative): leaving it outside the loop means validation folds were pre-filtered using their own labels — leakage by another name (0.5, 4.3). The fold must contain the entire data-dependent chain.
Deploy the chosen configuration refit on all available data; quote the outer (nested) estimate as the expected performance of the procedure — not the inner best score, not the refit model’s training score.

title: 4.6 Hyperparameter Tuning
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Two grids, honestly compared: candidate A tunes KNN over k ∈ {1..30}; candidate B tunes k ∈ {1..30} and weights ∈ {uniform, distance} and p ∈ {1, 2} — 30 × 2 × 2 = 120 combos. On the same outer 5-fold nested evaluation, compare the two procedures’ nested scores. Does the bigger grid win? By how much — and is the gain inside noise? Then relate the answer to the selection-inflation drill: which procedure pays more selection tax?


Solution







Typical result: grid B edges out A by a fraction of a percent — often within the outer-fold SD. The 4× larger search pays roughly 4× the selection tax on its inner best score; the outer estimate, which prices that tax, shows the true (small) gain. Lesson: bigger grids mostly buy bigger reported inner numbers, not performance — tune what theory says matters, not what the grid can enumerate. (Count the combos before you quote a multiplier: 30 × 2 × 2 = 120, a factor of 4, not the 6 an off-the-cuff “three times bigger on each axis” would suggest.)

Exercise 2. The one-standard-error rule in action: from Section 1’s GridSearchCV, compute the SE of the best score’s folds, mark the 1-SE band, and list all k whose mean score falls within it. Choose the largest such k and compare its held-out test accuracy to the argmax k’s. Repeat over 30 different random states — how often does the 1-SE model match or beat the argmax on test?


Solution







The 1-SE model matches or beats the argmax most of the time despite (usually) being smoother — its test luck is comparable and it’s the model you’d rather deploy (larger k = stabler). The rule isn’t magic; it’s a tie-breaker that spends a tie on robustness.

Exercise 3. Build nested_compare(procedures, X, y, outer_k=5) where each procedure is an unfitted GridSearchCV — returning each procedure’s outer mean/SD plus a paired comparison of the top two (fold-wise differences, t-test). Demonstrate on (a) KNN with tuned k, (b) logistic with tuned C, (c) LDA (no tuning) on one dataset. Report the ranking, the paired p-value for the leaders, and the honest sentence you’d write about “the best model.”


Solution







Nested comparison answers “which procedure generalizes better,” with pairing across outer folds and a real test — and the usual outcome on modest data is “statistically indistinguishable,” which is a finding, not a failure: it licenses choosing by interpretability, cost, or simplicity (3.7’s ethic, formalized).

title: 4.6 Hyperparameter Tuning
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

The tuning metric must be the deployment metric — tuning accuracy to deploy a precision@k system optimizes the wrong thing; set scoring deliberately (roc_auc, average_precision, f1, custom).
Grid resolution is a bias-variance choice: coarse grids miss optima (bias), fine grids inflate selection tax and compute. Log-spaced grids for scale parameters (C, α, learning rate) are the efficient default.
Search over preprocessing counts too — imputation strategy, scaling flavor, selector’s k are hyperparameters and belong in the grid (inside the pipeline); anything data-dependent outside the loop is leakage.
Refit-on-all-data after selection (GridSearchCV does it by default: refit=True) — but the number you report is the outer/nested one, never best_score_.
Flat landscapes are informative: if a wide band of hyperparameters scores identically, the data cannot distinguish them — pick by parsimony/interpretability and say so, rather than reporting the argmax as if it were discovered.
Compute budgeting: nested CV multiplies fits (outer × inner × grid); for heavy models use coarse inner grids, random search, or successive halving — but never drop the outer layer: that’s the whole page.
Tuning on the test set via iteration (“we only looked at the test score a few times”) is optional stopping (1.4) — the test set’s budget is spent by attention, not by fit calls.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated “tuning pipeline” has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Scaling before split + tuning — leakage (scaler saw test rows) and the inner CV scores are computed on pre-scaled data. Pipeline + refit-per-fold.
Argmax on the test set across 7 Cs — the test set just became a training set; final_C is selection-on-test (4.1). The test set gets ONE evaluation of the frozen winner.
The reported number is the max of 7 noisy test numbers — pure order-statistic optimism. Report the frozen model’s single test score (or better, a nested CV estimate).

title: 4.6 Hyperparameter Tuning
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Derive (or verify by simulation) the expected selection bonus for M candidates whose scores are i.i.d. N(μ, s²): it is μ + s·E[max of M standard normals] ≈ μ + s·√(2 ln M). Then measure the bonus empirically for M = 10, 100, 1000 with s = 0.02 and compare against the formula. What does the logarithmic growth imply about adding candidates to a search — and about the honesty of “we searched 10,000 configurations and found X”?


Hint

E[max] of M standard normals grows like √(2 ln M); the bonus scales with the noise s, not the effect sizes.



Solution







Agreement is close (√(2 ln M) is an asymptotic approximation, slightly high at small M). Implications: the bonus grows only logarithmically — 10× more candidates buys little extra inflation — but it grows without bound, and it scales with score noise s: noisy small-validation searches suffer most. A “10,000-configuration search” must therefore report performance from an outer/nested estimate; the search’s own best score is guaranteed flattery worth ≈ s√(2 ln M).

Q2. Successive halving / Hyperband-style tuning spends more budget on promising candidates. Design a miniature version for 60 KNN configurations (k ∈ 1..60) on a fixed dataset: start all on 2-fold CV over 200 rows, keep the top 20, then 4-fold over 400 rows, keep top 7, then full 5-fold on all rows. Compare the winner and total fit-count against exhaustive GridSearchCV (60 configs × 5 folds). Does the cheap scheme pick the same k? Implement and report — and state the failure mode it imports (which honest-estimator principle does the multi-stage scoring bend?).


Solution







The cheap scheme usually lands on the same k or a neighbor (flat landscape) at a fraction of the fits. The bent principle: candidates are compared on different amounts of data at different stages — early elimination can kill a config whose advantage only shows at full data (variance-vs-budget trade). Remedies: generous early stages, random restarts, or accepting a small probability of eliminating the true optimum — the same order-statistic humility as everything else on this page.

title: 4.6 Hyperparameter Tuning
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (tuning × 4.3 CV × 3.7 comparison). Design and run the full “honest bake-off”: 4 model families (logistic+C, KNN+k, random-forest-ish depth dial — use a shallow DecisionTreeClassifier with tuned max_depth, LDA fixed), each tuned by inner 5-fold over sensible grids, compared by outer 5-fold nested CV with paired fold-differences and a multiplicity-aware verdict (Bonferroni across the 6 pairs). Deliver the table, the pairwise p-value matrix, and the deployment sentence — this is the capstone artifact of Parts 2–4.
C2 (tuning × 12.x multiplicity preview). Show that hyperparameter search over M configurations is structurally identical to testing M hypotheses: simulate null data; for each of M = 100 random configurations compute a CV score and its (approximate) p-value vs a fixed baseline; count “significant improvements” at α = 0.05 raw and after Bonferroni. Write the paragraph connecting the family-wise-error view to the selection-bonus view of 4.1 Q2 — two languages, one phenomenon — and state which controls what in practice.

title: 4.6 Hyperparameter Tuning
text:
7. Summary

Tuning is selection; selection is optimism; the outer loop (nested CV or a virgin test set) is the only honest scoreboard.
best_score_ is a marketing number; the nested estimate is the performance claim; deploy the refit-on-all-data winner.
Grid/random: log-spaced scales, few meaningful dimensions, random search for big spaces; the one-SE rule buys robustness for free.
Every data-dependent step — scaling, selection, imputation — lives inside the fold pipeline.
Selection bonus ≈ s·√(2 ln M): grows with score noise and candidate count; budget score noise (bigger validation folds) and candidate count deliberately.
Comparison of tuned procedures needs identical budgets, pairing, and multiplicity awareness — the 3.7 rules at full depth.
Parts 2–4 are complete: you can build models, price their uncertainty, and choose among them honestly. Next, Part 5 turns regularization into a first-class citizen — the shrinkage dials this page kept referencing.

title: 4.4 The Bias–Variance Trade-off
text: Every model’s expected error on a new point decomposes into three parts: bias² (systematic wrongness), variance (sensitivity to the training sample), and irreducible noise. The U-curve of 4.1 is this decomposition plotted against flexibility. Here you derive it, then watch it move under your own simulations.

title: 4.4 The Bias–Variance Trade-off
text:
1. Basic Concept
At a fixed query point \(x_0\), with training set \(T\) treated as random:
\[\mathbb{E}_{T}\big[(y_0 - \hat{f}_T(x_0))^2\big] = \underbrace{\big(f(x_0) - \mathbb{E}_T[\hat{f}_T(x_0)]\big)^2}_{\text{bias}^2} + \underbrace{\mathbb{V}\text{ar}_T\big(\hat{f}_T(x_0)\big)}_{\text{variance}} + \underbrace{\mathbb{V}\text{ar}(\varepsilon)}_{\sigma^2}\]
Derivation (one completing-the-square trick): write \(\hat f_T(x_0) - y_0 = (\hat f_T - \mathbb{E}\hat f) + (\mathbb{E}\hat f - f) - \varepsilon\). The cross-terms vanish because ε is independent of T and mean-zero, and \(\mathbb{E}_T[\hat f - \mathbb{E}\hat f] = 0\). Averaged over \(x_0\): total test MSE = bias² + variance + σ².
Empirical decomposition — bias and variance are measurable with many training sets:






Averaged over the grid, the three curves and their sum:

title: 4.4 The Bias–Variance Trade-off
text:
2. Concept Questions

Where does the irreducible σ² term come from in the formula, and why can no model remove it?
KNN: as k → 1 and as k → n, state the bias/variance limits at a fixed x₀.
Your colleague says “the bias–variance trade-off means you should always pick the middle.” Give a dataset property that pushes the optimum to the flexible end, and one that pushes it rigid.
Why does more training data decrease variance but (mostly) leave bias unchanged — and which classical model is the exception where data shrinks bias too?
Bootstrapped bagged trees average many trees trained on resamples. In decomposition language, what does the averaging buy, and what doesn’t it fix? (Preview of Part 7.)



Answers


ε enters the prediction target \(y_0 = f(x_0) + \varepsilon\); since ε is independent of the training set, its variance adds in full. No function of the training data can predict ε — it’s the noise floor of 2.1.
k = 1: \(\hat f(x_0) = y_{\text{nearest}} = f(x_{\text{near}}) + \varepsilon_{\text{near}}\) — bias ≈ f(x_near) − f(x₀) ≈ 0 for dense data (low bias), variance = Var(ε) plus neighbor-identity jitter (high). k → n: prediction → global mean \(\bar y\) — maximal bias (|f(x₀) − f̄|) and variance → Var(ȳ) ≈ σ²/n → 0.
Flexible-friendly: large n, low noise, complex wiggly f (bias dominates rigid models). Rigid-friendly: small n, high noise, simple f — or high dimension d ≫ n, where variance of flexible models explodes (2.9/3.5 curse).
Variance is estimation noise: more points pin each parameter/local average tighter (∝ 1/n effects). Bias is structural — wrong model class — so extra data from the same process doesn’t help. The exception: KNN and other local methods — more data shrinks neighborhoods, reducing approximation (bias) too; that’s why nonparametric methods converge to truth.
Averaging i.i.d.-ish model fits cuts variance (∝ 1/B for uncorrelated members; less for correlated trees) while leaving each member’s bias intact. Bagging fixes instability, not mis-specification — and boosting (Part 7) attacks bias by sequential fitting instead.

title: 4.4 The Bias–Variance Trade-off
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Build bias_variance(model_factory, make_data, x0, reps=1000) returning bias, variance, and total MSE at point x0 for any sklearn-style model. Apply it to KNN with k ∈ {1, 5, 25, 100} on the sinusoid (n = 100, σ = 0.3); produce the k-vs-(bias², variance) table. Verify: total − σ² = bias² + variance within Monte Carlo error, and identify the MSE-minimizing k.


Solution







The table shows the trade exactly: k = 1 has tiny bias, large variance; k = 100 (≈ mean model at n = 100) has huge bias, vanishing variance; the MSE-optimal k sits between. Note bias isn’t monotone in a trivial way at one point — averaging over x (as in Section 1) smooths the picture.

Exercise 2. Noise and flexibility interact: rerun the degree-sweep decomposition (Section 1’s second figure) at σ = 0.05 and σ = 0.6. For each noise level, report the MSE-optimal degree. Write the one-line design rule linking noise to the flexibility you can afford, then connect it to why 2.10’s equal-variance violations matter for model choice and not just inference.


Solution







Low noise → optimal degree near the true complexity (variance is cheap); high noise → optimal degree drops hard (each estimated parameter imports σ² worth of variance). Rule: affordable flexibility scales inversely with noise. Heteroscedasticity (2.10) makes noise region-dependent — so flexible features are locally affordable, one motivation for adaptive smoothers (Part 6) and variance-aware likelihoods (GLMs, 3.6).

Exercise 3. The data-rescue curve, decomposed: fix degree 9 (overparameterized for n = 30) and rerun the decomposition at n ∈ {30, 100, 300, 1000}. Report bias², variance, and total at each n. Which component dies with data, which refuses, and what does the surviving component’s floor equal (compute it analytically for reference)?


Solution







Variance collapses roughly like (number of effective parameters)/n as n grows; bias² barely moves (degree 9 can represent the sinusoid, so its residual bias is small from the start — try degree 2 to see bias refuse to die). The floor is σ² = 0.09, exactly the irreducible term. Data cures variance; only a richer model class cures bias — the two diseases, two medicines.

title: 4.4 The Bias–Variance Trade-off
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

The decomposition is for squared loss — classification’s 0-1 loss has bias/variance notions but they’re subtler (multiple decompositions exist; correlations between bias and variance signs). Don’t force the additive story onto accuracy or AUC.
Bias and variance need not trade monotonically at every point — the trade is an average statement; at particular x₀, or with correlated estimators, both can move together (and modern double-descent breaks the U entirely beyond interpolation — hold the classical picture for classical models).
Ensembles exploit the decomposition, not vibes: bagging attacks variance (averaging correlated fits helps less — trees’ correlation is why random feature subsampling (Part 7) works), boosting attacks bias (sequentially fitting residuals).
Regularization (Part 5) is variance purchase with bias currency: ridge shrinks coefficients (bias ↑, variance ↓); the penalty is the exchange rate. Every Part 5 method is a point on this dial.
Estimating the decomposition from ONE training set is impossible — bias and variance are properties of the estimator across training sets (4.1 Exercise 1); single-fit diagnostics speak to residuals, not to the decomposition.
σ² estimation matters for everything downstream: RSE (2.4), Cp/AIC penalties, and “are we at the floor” verdicts all consume σ̂²; a biased σ̂ (from a mis-specified model) corrupts the whole accounting.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated “bias-variance analysis” has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Bootstrap resamples of ONE training set measure stability-to-resampling of that fit — not the estimator’s sampling variance across training sets (it underestimates it and confounds data noise with fit jitter).
Training MSE ≠ test MSE (4.1) — on 30 points degree 9 interpolates: ≈ 0. Fix with fresh evaluation data.
Bias is defined against f, not against a noisy realization — regressing toward interpolated noise corrupts the target. Bias needs the true f (known in simulation) or a principled proxy.

title: 4.4 The Bias–Variance Trade-off
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Prove the decomposition rigorously: define \(\bar{\hat f}(x_0) = \mathbb{E}_T[\hat f_T(x_0)]\), expand \(\mathbb{E}_T[(y_0 - \hat f_T(x_0))^2]\) by adding and subtracting \(\bar{\hat f}(x_0)\), and show both cross-terms vanish — one by independence of ε from T, one by the definition of expectation. Then explain where the proof fails for 0-1 loss (why no clean additive decomposition exists there).


Hint

E[(A + B + C)²] with A = ȳ-type zero-mean term, B = bias, C = −ε; check E[A] = 0, E[AC] = E[A]E[C] = 0 by independence.



Solution

Let \(A = \bar{\hat f} - \hat f_T\), \(B = \bar{\hat f} - f(x_0)\), \(C = -\varepsilon\). Then \(y_0 - \hat f_T = A + B + C\). Squaring and taking \(\mathbb{E}_T\): E[A²] = Var, B² = bias², E[C²] = σ². Cross-terms: E[AB] = B·E[A] = 0; E[BC] = B·E[C] = 0 (ε mean-zero, independent of everything T-derived); E[AC] = E[A]E[C] = 0 by independence. Sum = bias² + var + σ². For 0-1 loss the indicator \((y_0 \ne \hat f_T)\) doesn’t expand into squares — bias and variance interact (high variance can correct systematic boundary bias — “variance cancels bias” — which squared loss forbids). That’s why classification intuition sometimes rewards instability, and why the clean U-curve is a squared-loss picture.

Q2. Double descent, demonstrated small: with n = 40 points and a linear model in k random Fourier features (X → sin/cos features), sweep k from 5 to 300 and plot train and test MSE. Identify the interpolation threshold (train MSE ≈ 0) and describe test error’s behavior around and beyond it. Then explain in bias/variance language why the classical U-curve story needs extending — and why you should still not casually interpolate your next dataset.


Solution







Around p ≈ n the minimum-norm interpolating fit is unstable — test error peaks (the classical story ends at this wall). Beyond it, the minimum-norm solution among infinitely many interpolants becomes smoother/more benign as p grows, and test error descends again. Bias/variance language extends via “effective capacity” and norm-based complexity rather than parameter count. Practical stance: the descent region requires specific (min-norm/implicit-regularized) solvers and lots of features — for classical tabular work, the U-curve and its remedies (Part 5) remain the operating manual.

title: 4.4 The Bias–Variance Trade-off
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (bias–variance × 2.6–2.7 model classes). Three nested model classes for one truth with group-specific slopes: additive (shared slope), interaction (two slopes), saturated (per-group curvature). For each class and n ∈ {40, 200, 1000}, measure test MSE by multi-training-set simulation.
