Produce the 3×3 table and read it in decomposition language: which cell’s error is bias-dominated at n = 40 but variance-dominated at n = 40 for the saturated class, and how does the ranking of classes change with n?
C2 (bias–variance × 4.6 tuning preview). The decomposition explains what CV’s minimum finds: rerun Exercise 1’s KNN sweep while recording the decomposition; overlay the empirical test-MSE minimum k with the k minimizing (bias² + variance) from the ground-truth simulation. How often (across 100 dataset draws) does CV pick within ±1 neighbor of the decomposition-optimal k? The frequency you observe is the empirical content of “CV approximates the bias-variance optimum” — and its failure cases are your introduction to why tuning needs care.

title: 4.4 The Bias–Variance Trade-off
text:
7. Summary

Test MSE = bias² + variance + σ²; the proof is one completing-the-square; σ² never leaves.
Flexibility buys bias down at variance’s price; the U-curve is that exchange plotted.
More data kills variance, not bias; local (nonparametric) methods are the exception — neighborhoods shrink.
Noise sets the flexibility budget: high σ ⇒ rigid optima (Exercise 2).
Bagging/boosting/regularization are the decomposition’s applied children: variance-, bias-, and exchange-machines.
The decomposition is a squared-loss, classical-model story — 0-1 loss and interpolation-threshold regimes need amended maps.
With error anatomy understood, the bootstrap gives it standard errors without new theory: 4.5 The Bootstrap.

title: 4.2 The Validation Set Approach
text: The simplest honest estimator: hold out a chunk of data, fit on the rest, evaluate once on the holdout. It is the prototype of every validation scheme — and its weaknesses (variance, wasted data, single-number confidence) are exactly the weaknesses the rest of Part 4 exists to fix.

title: 4.2 The Validation Set Approach
text:
1. Basic Concept
Protocol: split rows into training and validation sets (say 70/30). Fit the model on training. Compute the metric once on validation. That number estimates out-of-sample error.






The weaknesses, demonstrated rather than described. First, variance: the estimate depends heavily on which rows land in validation:






Second, bias from smaller training: validation-error estimates are pessimistic because the model is trained on only 70% of the data — deployment would use 100%:

title: 4.2 The Validation Set Approach
text:
2. Concept Questions

Your validation MSE is 0.31 on one 70/30 split. What is the (approximate) standard error of that single number if σ² ≈ 0.09 and n_validation = 60 — and what does it say about reporting “0.31” to three decimals?
Why is validation error said to overestimate the error of the final model refit on all data?
Which two competing pressures determine the validation fraction, and what happens at the extremes (10% vs 50% holdout)?
You use the validation set to pick among 15 models, then report the winner’s validation MSE. Which error from 4.1 have you committed, and what’s the minimal fix?
For a time-ordered dataset, what must change in the protocol, and why is a random split actively wrong?



Answers


SE(MSE) ≈ σ²·√(2/n_val) ≈ 0.09 × √(2/60) ≈ 0.0164. So 0.31 ± 0.033 (95%): the third decimal is noise; report 0.31 ± 0.02 or the CI — or average over splits (4.3).
The validation model trained on 70% of data; with less data its error is higher than the refit-on-100% model’s (4.1’s data-rescue law). The estimator is pessimistically biased for the deployment model.
Big validation → precise estimate but badly undertrained model (pessimistic, wasteful); small validation → near-deployment training but noisy estimate. 20–30% is the customary compromise; CV removes the trade-off.
Selection on the validation set converts it into a second training set — the winner’s number is an order statistic, inflated. Minimal fix: a third, untouched test split; the full fix is nested CV (4.6).
Time-ordered data needs forward chaining: train on the past, validate on the future (random splits let the model train on the future — temporal leakage). Metrics then answer “how well do we predict tomorrow,” the only deployment-honest question.

title: 4.2 The Validation Set Approach
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Validation-vs-truth calibration: for a fixed data-generating process, compute (a) the true test MSE of a model trained on 70% of n = 150 (evaluated on 100k fresh points), and (b) the distribution of single-split validation estimates over 300 seeds. Report the mean of (b) vs (a), the SD of (b), and the fraction of 95% intervals (estimate ± 1.96·SE, SE from validation residuals) that contain (a). Is the validation estimator centered where it claims?


Solution







The per-split mean matches the truth (the estimator is centered for the 70%-trained model); within-split SEs describe split-to-split scatter well (coverage ≈ 0.93–0.95). The two failure modes to remember: it’s centered for the smaller training set (pessimism for deployment), and single-split numbers carry ±SE-sized error bars people rarely print.

Exercise 2. The learning-curve use case: for n_train ∈ {15, 30, 60, 120} (from a pool of 600), estimate test MSE by validation on a fixed 200-row holdout, replicating each size 100 times. Plot mean ± SD vs n_train. Identify where the curve flattens (“more data stops helping”) and connect to 4.1 Exercise 2’s law — what does the flatten point say about how much more data to collect?


Solution







The curve falls steeply then flattens: past the elbow, additional samples buy little — the residual error is dominated by noise floor + bias, not estimation variance. The flatten point is the empirical answer to “how much data is enough,” and it shifts left or right with model flexibility (simpler models flatten earlier).

Exercise 3. Validation-set selection inflation, in miniature: 20 candidate polynomial degrees (1–20) evaluated on ONE validation split; record the winner’s validation MSE. Repeat over 300 datasets; report the mean winner-vs-fixed-degree-3 validation ratio under a sinusoidal truth where degree 3 is genuinely near-optimal. Compare with selecting by 5-fold CV instead (averaged within each dataset). How much does honest selection reduce the inflation?


Solution







CV-based selection picks degrees closer to optimal and its winners’ true errors are lower — the single validation split’s noisier estimates select flashy degrees (selected-on-noise). The deeper lesson though: in both cases the winner’s own selection score must not be reported as performance; the numbers here are TRUE errors of refit winners, which is why they’re comparable at all.

title: 4.2 The Validation Set Approach
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

One number, no error bar — the validation estimate’s SE is computable from the validation residuals (drill 4) and should be printed; most published single-split numbers would fail that audit.
The holdout is a budget too: every model evaluated on it spends it (0.5); “validation” that saw 15 models is a training set wearing a costume.
Pessimism by undertraining — correction strategies exist (e.g., learning-curve extrapolation), but the clean fix is CV, which refits on (K−1)/K of data per fold.
Stratification for classification, grouping for clustered data, temporal order for time series — the split’s design is part of the estimator (0.5).
Post-selection refit: after choosing on validation, refit on ALL data before deployment — but then the validation number describes the pre-refit model, not the deployed one; only CV/nested schemes price the full pipeline.
Validation on a different distribution than deployment (site shift, prevalence shift) measures the wrong thing — the split cannot fix a sampling problem (3.7 C2).


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated pipeline has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Pre-split scaling leaks validation statistics into training inputs (0.5). Scale inside the training fold only.
Selection and report on the same holdout: winner’s score is an order statistic (4.1 Q2). Reserve a third split, or select by CV.
Score transplant: the validation number belongs to the 70%-trained model; the deployed all-data model’s performance was never estimated. Estimate the full pipeline honestly (CV over the entire choose-and-fit procedure).

title: 4.2 The Validation Set Approach
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Derive the SE of a validation MSE estimate: given validation residuals e_i with mean-zero assumption violations aside, SE = sd(e²)/√(n_val). Compare, by simulation, this plug-in SE to the observed SD of validation MSEs across 500 splits. When do they disagree (name the distributional cause), and what does the disagreement do to naive “± SE” error bars?


Hint

e² has a skewed distribution (χ²-like when errors are Gaussian); its mean’s SE uses e²’s own variance — but heavy tails or heteroscedasticity make the plug-in unstable.



Solution







Under Gaussian errors the plug-in SE is unbiased for the across-split SD (they estimate the same sampling variability); they diverge when errors are heavy-tailed (e² ’s variance is dominated by rare huge residuals, so the plug-in is itself noisy — sometimes 2× off) or heteroscedastic (validation mix shifts). Consequence: treat “± SE” bars on single-split estimates as approximate, and prefer averaging across splits, which makes the across-split SD directly measurable.

Q2. Your deployment population drifts: the validation set was drawn from distribution P, deployment sees Q (same relationship, different x-mix). Design a simulation where the validation estimate is unbiased for P and biased for Q, quantify the bias as a function of the drift’s magnitude, and derive the reporting rule for validation estimates under anticipated drift (report per-stratum estimates or reweight to Q’s mix — never the pooled number alone).


Solution







The validation number is a perfectly good estimate of error-on-P and a biased estimate of error-on-Q; the bias grows with how much Q’s x-mass sits outside (or disproportionately inside) regions where the model misfits (here: extrapolation region x > 1). Rule: validation estimates are distribution-conditional; under anticipated drift, report stratified/reweighted errors — the pooled MSE is a weighted average with weights (P’s) that deployment doesn’t have. This is covariate shift, and it converts “validation” from a statistic into a design decision.

title: 4.2 The Validation Set Approach
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (validation × 0.5 stratification × 3.1.5 AUPRC). On a 1%-positive dataset with n = 1000, compare unstratified vs stratified 70/30 validation for estimating AUPRC: 200 splits each, report the spread (SD and IQR) of the estimates. Which procedure’s estimate would you publish, and what sample size of positives would make the unstratified version tolerable (verify empirically)?
C2 (validation × 4.3 CV preview). Using the same dataset and model, run the head-to-head: 200 independent single 70/30 splits vs 5-fold CV (repeated 40 times) as estimators of the same quantity. Compare (a) bias (vs a huge fresh test truth), (b) variance across repetitions, (c) total compute (fits per estimate). You should find CV’s variance advantage at 5× the compute — the explicit price list that makes 4.3’s conventions legible.

title: 4.2 The Validation Set Approach
text:
7. Summary

Validation = fit on one part, evaluate once on an untouched part — the prototype of honest estimation.
Its estimate is noisy (single split) and pessimistic (smaller training); both defects are measurable and both are CV’s motivation.
The validation set is a budget: selection on it converts it to training; keep a third split or use nested CV.
Print uncertainty: plug-in SEs from validation residuals, or split-to-split SDs — never a bare 3-decimal number.
Split design (stratify, group, temporal order) is part of the estimator, not an implementation detail.
Estimates are distribution-conditional: drift between validation and deployment breaks the number, not the math.
The fix for both defects — reuse every row for validation while keeping folds clean — is cross-validation: 4.3 Cross-validation.

title: 3.7 Classification Model Comparison
text: You now own five classifiers (logistic, LDA, QDA, Naive Bayes, KNN). Choosing between them is where careless pipelines go to lie to themselves: comparing on one split, one metric, or — worst — the metric that was also used to tune. This page builds the honest comparison protocol: same folds, paired tests, calibration checks, and decision-aware selection.

title: 3.7 Classification Model Comparison
text:
1. Basic Concept
Three principles of fair comparison:

Same folds, paired evaluation — models see identical train/test partitions; differences are then within-fold, far less noisy than independent estimates.
Metrics match the decision — AUC/AP for ranking, calibration for probabilities, operating-point metrics for budgets (3.1, 3.1.5).
Uncertainty on differences, not just points — a 0.01 AUC gap between two models on one split is noise until tested.

The canonical setup, all five models on identical CV folds:






Paired comparison — the same fold’s differences, tested. For two models’ predictions on the same test rows, McNemar’s test asks whether the disagreement pattern is asymmetric:






Calibration — do predicted probabilities mean what they say? The reliability diagram:

title: 3.7 Classification Model Comparison
text:
2. Concept Questions

Why is a paired comparison (same folds) so much more powerful than comparing two independent 5-fold means?
Two models have AUC 0.81 and 0.83. List, in order, the three facts you need before believing the second is better.
What does a model above the diagonal in a reliability diagram (observed > predicted) indicate, and name one common pipeline step that causes systematic miscalibration.
Why can Naive Bayes have a worse Brier score but nearly identical AUC to logistic — and when would you still ship NB?
You tuned model A’s hyperparameters by CV and want to compare against untuned model B. What does honest comparison require?



Answers


Fold-to-fold difficulty dominates variance (easy folds flatter everyone). Pairing differences out that shared noise: Var(diff) = Var(A) + Var(B) − 2Cov(A,B), and the fold-correlation makes the covariance term large — paired tests see the signal that independent-mean comparisons drown in. The same logic as paired t-tests (1.4).

Uncertainty: is 0.02 within fold/seed noise (paired fold-wise test)? (2) Same preprocessing/tuning budget for both? (3) Does the metric match the deployment question — and does the gap replicate on a held-out set or fresh data?

Observed frequency exceeds predicted probability → the model is systematically underconfident in that region. Causes: training on resampled/oversampled data (case–control sampling shifts the intercept — 3.3 C2); regularization that shrinks logits toward the base rate in the wrong direction; score warping in NB under feature correlation.
Brier scores squared-error penalties punish NB’s overconfident probabilities (3.4); AUC, being rank-based, is blind to that inflation. Ship NB when you consume rankings (top-k retrieval) and cost nothing by probability errors — its speed and small-sample stability then win.
Either tune B with the identical CV protocol (same folds/grid budget) or evaluate both with an outer CV layer untouched by tuning — nested evaluation (4.6). Comparing a tuned model’s selection-optimized number against an untuned model’s plain number conflates selection luck with model quality.

title: 3.7 Classification Model Comparison
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Build compare_models(models, X, y, k=5, seed=0) returning a DataFrame of mean±SD accuracy, AUC, AP plus pairwise McNemar p-values on pooled out-of-fold predictions. Run it on the five classifiers of Section 1; identify (a) the statistical leader, (b) the pair whose difference is not significant, (c) which metric(s) disagree with accuracy’s ranking.


Solution







Caveat carried forward: pooled out-of-fold predictions are not fully independent across folds for the McNemar counts (models refit per fold), but the paired structure is preserved — for publication-grade claims, repeat across outer resamples (4.3). The table + test pattern is the deliverable regardless.

Exercise 2. Calibration repair: the NB probabilities from Section 1’s reliability data are inflated. Implement a simple Platt-style fix: fit a 1-D logistic regression mapping NB’s logit-scored output to the true labels on a validation split, apply to test. Show Brier before/after and the reliability diagrams side by side. Confirm AUC is unchanged (rank-preserving map) — then state when this fix is not legitimate (which data it must not touch).


Solution







The calibration map is fit on a dedicated split that played no role in training the NB — touching the test set (or the original training set) for calibration would re-introduce optimism (0.5). AUC is invariant (monotone map); Brier collapses toward the logistic’s. This split discipline — fit, calibrate, test on three disjoint samples — is the production-grade pattern.

Exercise 3. Decision-theoretic selection: two models, fixed budget of 100 follow-ups per 5,000 screened (1% prevalence). Compute for each model the expected number of true hits in its top-100 (per 10 bootstrap resamples of the screening population), with a CI on the difference. Also compute each model’s precision@100. Which model wins the deployment question, and does it match the AUC winner?


Solution







The bootstrap CI on hits-in-top-100 is the deployment metric with uncertainty attached. If it excludes 0, the decision is made regardless of what AUC says — models with similar AUC can differ sharply in the head of the ranking, and budgets only ever buy the head.

title: 3.7 Classification Model Comparison
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

The comparison protocol IS the result: same folds, same preprocessing (pipelines), same tuning budget, paired tests, uncertainty on differences. Deviating from any of these resets the table to anecdote.
Pooled out-of-fold predictions (Exercise 1) preserve pairing but fold-refitting leaks mild dependence across folds — fine for exploration; use repeated outer resampling for claims.
McNemar’s exact test is binomial on discordant pairs — b and c only; concordant pairs carry no comparison information. Low discordance = low power, whatever the accuracies say.
Brier vs AUC rank: fixing calibration never changes AUC (monotone maps) — which is why “we recalibrated and AUC didn’t move” is expected, not suspicious.
Multiple models ⇒ multiple comparisons: 5 models = 10 pairwise tests; control family-wise error (Bonferroni ×10) or pre-specify the primary comparison (12.3–12.4 preview).
Selection on the comparison metric: if the winner’s metric then becomes the reported performance, the number is selection-inflated — the nested-CV discipline of 4.6 applies with full force.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated “model selection” has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Model selection on the full dataset including the evaluation rows — the test set is spent tuning (0.5). Select by CV inside training only.
Training accuracy as final performance: KNN(k=1) scores 1.0 — pure memorization crowned winner. Report held-out/CV.
A single split’s gap declared decisive: the fixed seed does make the comparison paired — both models see identical rows — which is right, and worth keeping. But one split is still one draw: its accuracy gap carries the variance of the split itself, so a difference of a few points is noise (4.1). Keep the shared seed, then replace the single split with repeated/paired CV and a McNemar-style test before naming a winner.

title: 3.7 Classification Model Comparison
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. The “no free lunch” caveat says no classifier dominates universally. Construct two 2-D problems — one where logistic beats KNN decisively, one where KNN beats logistic — with identical n and noise. Report both test-accuracy tables and explain each winner’s edge in terms of assumption alignment (linear boundary vs local structure). What legitimate conclusion is possible about “the best classifier” for a new problem before looking at its data?


Solution







Linear truth: logistic wins (0.880 vs 0.770) — and note how it wins. Its inductive bias matches the boundary, and the four irrelevant features cost it nothing: a linear model simply assigns them a near-zero weight. KNN has no such luxury, because every feature enters every distance, so irrelevant ones dilute the neighbourhood and corrupt the local votes. Spiral: the boundary is wildly nonlinear; KNN’s local votes trace it (0.985) while logistic caps out at a straight line (0.880). Both results are statements about the problem, known only after seeing the data — which is exactly why Part 4’s machinery exists. Model choice is an empirical property, not a prior belief.

Q2. You must compare k=7-KNN and logistic and report a p-value for “A is better.” Walk through the construction of a paired, replicated comparison: (a) why fold-wise paired t on 5 folds is weak (df = 4, dependence), (b) how repeated 5×2-fold CV (or 20 random 80/20 replications) restores power, (c) what exactly the unit of analysis is (a replication’s difference), and (d) the multiplicity caveat if 8 models enter the same protocol. Implement (b) for two models and report the CI for the accuracy difference.


Solution








5-fold paired t has df = 4 and folds share training rows — dependence inflates the nominal Type I error (the famous Dietterich point). (b) Each replication is a fresh split: differences are far less correlated across replications; 40 replications give a stable CI. (c) The unit is the replication-level difference — treat replications as the sample. (d) Eight models ⇒ 28 pairwise CIs; multiplicity control (Bonferroni/Holm) or a pre-registered primary comparison keeps the family-wise error honest (12.3 preview).

title: 3.7 Classification Model Comparison
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (comparison × 0.5 splitting × 4.3 CV). Build the full “league table” experiment: 6 classifiers × 20 repeated stratified 5-fold CVs, recording accuracy, AUC, and Brier per repeat. Produce (a) a ranked mean table with per-model CIs, (b) a paired heatmap of p-values (all pairs), (c) a stability statement — which model’s variance across repeats is worst and what does that imply for reproducibility of a published winner? This deliverable is the reusable template for every future model-selection question in the course.
C2 (comparison × 3.1.5 AUPRC × 1.3 Bayes). Two hospitals each evaluate your two models; hospital A has 2% disease prevalence, hospital B has 25%. Show empirically that model rankings can flip by metric family (AUC stable, AP and precision@budget flip or compress) across the two prevalences, then write the reporting paragraph that tells both hospitals which model to deploy and why — in language that survives their different baselines.

title: 3.7 Classification Model Comparison
text:
7. Summary

Compare models on identical folds, paired; differences need uncertainty, points don’t settle arguments.
McNemar for hard labels; paired fold differences for scores; replicate for power.
Rank metrics (AUC/AP), probability metrics (Brier, calibration), and operating-point metrics answer different questions — pick per decision, report several.
Calibration is a separate axis: Platt/isotonic fixes on dedicated data; AUC is blind to it, Brier isn’t.
Same tuning budget for every candidate; selection metrics must never double as reported performance.
With several candidates, multiple-comparisons discipline applies — previewing Part 12.
Comparison done honestly is model selection’s foundation: Part 4 formalizes the machinery — starting from why held-out error is the only currency: 4.1 The generalization problem.

title: 3.5 KNN Classification
text: K-nearest-neighbors classification votes: a query’s class is the majority class among its k nearest training points. No assumptions about distributions or boundaries — the data is the model. Combined with 2.9’s regression twin, this page completes the neighborhood-methods toolkit and its biases.

title: 3.5 KNN Classification
text:
1. Basic Concept
The algorithm at query \(x_0\):

Find the k nearest training points (any distance metric — Euclidean by default).
Output the majority class (or, usefully, the vote fraction as a probability estimate).

k is the flexibility dial: k = 1 draws maximal boundaries around every point (train accuracy 100%); k = n predicts the majority class everywhere.






The vote fraction doubles as a (crude) probability estimate — coarser as k grows:






Vote by hand once:

title: 3.5 KNN Classification
text:
2. Concept Questions

Why is k = 1’s training accuracy always 100%, and what is the only thing its test performance demonstrates?
KNN “probabilities” from vote fractions take k+1 distinct values. What are the consequences for (a) calibration curves, (b) threshold tuning granularity?
Which KNN failure mode is shared with every distance-based method (2.9) and fixed identically?
In a 3-class problem with k = 4, what happens on ties, and name two resolutions.
Odd k is folk-wisdom for binary problems. Why does it not fully protect against ties in practice?



Answers


Each point is its own nearest neighbor, so training predictions are the training labels verbatim. Zero training error demonstrates memorization capacity — nothing about generalization; only held-out performance means anything (0.5).

Calibration plots show ≤ k+1 distinct predicted values — a step function, no fine calibration possible; (b) thresholds between adjacent vote levels do nothing — decision granularity is coarse (with k = 5, you cannot build a 60%-threshold classifier). Use larger k for finer probability resolution, or distance weighting.

Feature scaling — distance domination by large-range features. Fix identically: StandardScaler inside a pipeline, fitted per-fold (2.9, 0.5).
With k = 4, a 2–2 vote tie is possible (and 1–1–2 in 3 classes). Resolutions: use odd k; break ties by distance-weighted votes, by the closer class-sum, or by sklearn’s default (order/prior-based choice — check the docs, don’t assume).
Distances can tie exactly (identical/duplicated points, integer coordinates), and multiclass problems create majority-less splits at any k. Odd k reduces, not eliminates, ambiguity — know your library’s tie rule.

title: 3.5 KNN Classification
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Implement multiclass KNN by hand with (a) majority vote, (b) distance-weighted vote (weights 1/d, aggregate per class, argmax), and verify both against sklearn on 25 random queries. Report one query where the two methods disagree and explain the neighborhood geometry that caused it.


Solution







Disagreements happen when the majority class sits marginally farther on average: uniform vote follows the count, weighted vote follows the close points. Both are defensible; the choice is part of the model.

Exercise 2. Boundary-artifact tour: for two Gaussian classes, plot k = 1, 3, 15 decision boundaries; then report test accuracy for each on a large fresh sample, together with train accuracy. Produce the k-vs-error table (train, test) and identify the overfitting/underfitting regions — then argue from the table which k you’d ship, and what extra experiment would firm that up.


Solution







k = 1: perfect train, visibly worse test (islands around single points). Test error bottoms in the mid-k range then climbs as neighborhoods straddle the true boundary. To ship a k: repeat across splits/CV and pick by mean test (or CV) error — the table from one split is indicative, not decisive (4.3).

Exercise 3. Curse-of-dimensionality face-off: signal in 3 of d dimensions (d = 3, 30, 300), n = 400 training points, KNN (CV-tuned k) vs penalized logistic regression; report CV-chosen k and test accuracies. Explain the k-trend with d and the reason logistic degrades gracefully — then state the dimension threshold past which you’d stop considering plain KNN for this data shape.


Solution







CV-chosen k grows with d (the only useful neighborhoods are huge), and KNN’s accuracy sags as neighborhoods stop being local; logistic’s linear score ignores the junk dimensions’ distances entirely and loses only mild precision from estimating extra coefficients. Threshold judgment call: for this linear-signal shape, KNN stops competing around d ≈ tens-to-hundreds — the exact number depends on signal strength and n, which is why the honest answer is “measure it by CV,” not folklore.

title: 3.5 KNN Classification
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Evaluate with predict_proba, decide with costs: vote fractions are the model’s probability surrogate; their coarseness (Concept Question 2) makes fine thresholding impossible — a reason to prefer logistic when calibrated probabilities matter.
Scaling, always, inside the pipeline — the single most common KNN bug in the wild, shared with 2.9.
Multiclass ties: sklearn breaks count ties deterministically (order-dependent); make k odd per problem, prefer distance weighting, or aggregate with weights="distance" for smoother ties.
Duplicated points make distance ties and destabilize neighbor identity — deduplicate or add tiny jitter; also watch duplicated rows leaking across train/test (0.5 bug #3).
Prediction cost scales with training size (no model compression); KD-tree/ball-tree speedups decay in high d — for deployment-sized training sets, KNN is a service, not a function.
KNN’s boundary is not learnable features — nothing interpretable comes out; if a stakeholder asks “why classified so?”, the answer is a list of neighbor cases (which is sometimes exactly the right answer — case-based reasoning).


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated classifier has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Train = test evaluation: k = 3 on its own training data reports memorization-flattered accuracy. Split first (0.5).
k tuned on training accuracy: k = 1 (or small) always wins that sweep — tune by CV within training.
Unscaled features, and raw scores quoted as risks. Two problems in this block. First, distances are dominated by read count (0–50,000), so the biomarker carrying all the signal (range 0–1) is invisible; StandardScaler belongs inside a pipeline. Second, predict_proba returns the fraction of the k neighbours voting positive — a vote share, not a calibrated probability. A neighbour that is itself a 51% case counts as a full vote, so 3/3 gives 1.00 no matter how marginal each neighbour was.

title: 3.5 KNN Classification
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Show that KNN’s training-set leave-one-out (LOO) error can be computed without refitting for every k simultaneously: sort each point’s distances once, then for each k count label agreement with the k-th neighbor set. Implement it and verify against cross_val_score(KNeighborsClassifier(k), cv=KFold(n_splits=n))-style LOO for k = 1..15 on a small dataset. Why does the naive LOO shortcut not apply to logistic regression?


Hint

Removing a training point changes the neighbor sets only for queries near it; for the left-out point itself, its k neighbors are found among the remaining n−1 regardless of k.



Solution

For point i left out: its neighbors are drawn from the other n−1 points, and the k-NN prediction for i is determined by i’s distance ranks among those n−1 — computable from one sort of row i. Sweep k along the sorted row and tally agreement; one O(n²) pass yields LOO errors for every k. Verification:






Logistic refits coefficients on every LOO fold — leave-one-out changes the global fit, so no per-row shortcut exists. KNN’s locality (each prediction touches k points) is exactly what makes its LOO cheap; parametric fits are global and must be redone.

Q2. KNN’s vote fraction estimates P(y=1|x) with variance ≈ p(1−p)/k and bias whenever the class probability varies within the neighborhood. For 1-D data with a sharp probability transition at x = 5, quantify both effects empirically: for k ∈ {5, 25, 125}, estimate the bias of the vote-fraction estimate at x = 4.9 (true p ≈ 0.72) and its Monte-Carlo variance across 2,000 training sets. State the k that minimizes MSE at that point and how it shifts with the transition’s sharpness.


Solution







Small k: near-zero bias (neighborhood stays on one side of the transition), high variance. Large k: variance shrinks but bias grows as the neighborhood averages across the transition. The MSE-optimal k sits where the two curves cross — and as the transition sharpens (larger slope in the sigmoid), the bias term grows for every k, pushing the optimal k smaller. This local bias–variance diagram is the pointwise version of the global picture in 4.4.

title: 3.5 KNN Classification
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (KNN × 3.1 metrics × 3.7 preview). On a moderately imbalanced two-Gaussian problem, compare KNN (CV-tuned k), logistic, and LDA on both ROC-AUC and PR-AP, and plot both curve families on one figure per model. Which model’s advantage shrinks the most under the PR lens, and how does the coarse vote-fraction ladder of KNN explain its curve’s shape?
C2 (KNN × 4.6 tuning × 2.9). Jointly tune k and the distance-weighting scheme (uniform/distance) with GridSearchCV over a pipeline, then compare against tuning k alone at fixed uniform weights — honest nested estimates both times. Quantify the extra optimism the wider grid buys and state when the extra hyperparameter is worth its selection cost (connect to the selection-inflation experiments of 4.6).

title: 3.5 KNN Classification
text:
7. Summary

KNN classifies by neighborhood vote; k sets the smoothness, vote fractions are coarse probability estimates.
k = 1 memorizes (train acc 1.0); k = n = majority class; test error is U-shaped in k.
Scaling inside a pipeline is non-negotiable; ties, duplicates, and even-k quirks need explicit policy.
The curse of dimensionality caps KNN’s reach; linear/penalized models degrade more gracefully in high d.
LOO errors for all k come free from one distance sort — locality has computational perks.
Pointwise, vote-fraction MSE balances bias (wide neighborhoods across transitions) against variance (few voters).
Several classifiers now produce scores; the question becomes comparing and calibrating them: 3.7 Classification model comparison.

title: 3.3 Logistic Regression
text: Logistic regression models P(y = 1) as a sigmoid of a linear score — bounded, Bernoulli-likelihood-honest, and the workhorse classifier of applied statistics. Its coefficients speak in log-odds, which is either its greatest interpretive feature or its greatest PR problem, depending on how well you’ve drilled this page.

title: 3.3 Logistic Regression
text:
1. Basic Concept
The model:
\[p(x) = \frac{e^{\beta_0 + \beta_1 x}}{1 + e^{\beta_0 + \beta_1 x}} \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad \log\frac{p(x)}{1 - p(x)} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x\]
The logit (log-odds) is linear in x; the sigmoid maps it back to [0, 1]. Coefficients are log-odds ratios: \(e^{\beta}\) multiplies the odds of the outcome per unit of x. Fitting maximizes the Bernoulli log-likelihood — no closed form, solved by iteration (Newton/IRLS):
\[\ell(\beta) = \sum_i \big[ y_i \log p_i + (1 - y_i)\log(1 - p_i) \big]\]






Note penalty=None: sklearn’s default penalizes the fit (C = 1.0) — worth knowing before comparing coefficients against statsmodels’ unpenalized MLE:






The decision boundary and probability surface, drawn:

title: 3.3 Logistic Regression
text:
2. Concept Questions

β = 0.693 for a binary treatment. Translate twice: once into odds, once into a sentence a patient understands.
Where is the decision boundary in terms of the linear score, and why does moving β₀ shift it but moving β₁ rotate it?
sklearn’s default C = 1.0 penalizes coefficients. What happens to the fitted coefficients as C → ∞ and as C → 0, and what real-world failure does the C → 0 extreme prevent?
Logistic regression has no closed-form solution. Why (in one sentence), and what does the algorithm actually optimize?
Your model’s predicted probabilities are well-ranked but poorly calibrated (everything too extreme). Which metric family is blind to this, and what might have caused it?



Answers


Odds multiply by e^0.693 = 2.0 — treatment doubles the odds. For a patient: “if your baseline chance were 1-in-10 (odds 1:9), treatment moves you to about 2-in-9 ≈ 18% chance.” (Odds doubling ≠ probability doubling — the translation must go through the patient’s baseline.)
Boundary = where p = 0.5 = where linear score = 0 (a line, β₀ + β₁x = 0). β₀ shifts the line (offset); β₁ changes its direction/steepness (in 2-D: the normal vector). β₁’s magnitude sets how quickly probability transitions across the boundary.
C → ∞ = no penalty = unpenalized MLE (coefficients as large as likelihood demands); C → 0 = coefficients crushed toward 0 (predicting base rate everywhere). Small C prevents coefficient blow-up under separation or p ≫ n — a ridge penalty in disguise (Part 5).
The log-likelihood is nonlinear in β (β sits inside a sigmoid), so no algebraic zero exists; software maximizes ℓ(β) iteratively — Newton–Raphson/IRLS — the same machinery statsmodels’ summary then reuses for SEs (inverse Hessian).
AUC/AP (3.1, 3.1.5) — rank-based, calibration-blind. Causes: training/serving prevalence mismatch, regularization, resampled training data (oversampling positives), or a drifted population — the fixes live in 3.7’s calibration section.

title: 3.3 Logistic Regression
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Hand-compute a prediction: given fitted β₀ = −4.0, β₁ = 0.08 (age, in years) for disease status — compute P(disease) at ages 40, 50, 60 by hand (sigmoid), the odds at each age, and verify the odds ratio between consecutive ages equals e^(0.08×5) ≈ 1.49. Then compute the risk ratio between ages 50 and 60 and explain why it differs from the odds ratio. (Keep β₁ small on purpose: a steep slope plus a large negative intercept would push every age to P ≈ 1 and flatten the whole demonstration.)


Solution







The odds ratio is constant (1.49 per 5 years — the model’s defining constraint: the log-odds is linear, so equal log-score steps mean equal multiplicative odds steps). The risk ratio depends on where you are on the curve: 1.38 for 50→60 but 1.61 for 40→50, even though the underlying odds ratio is identical in both intervals. Odds ratios are portable and log-symmetric; risk ratios are what many audiences think they’re hearing, and they shrink toward 1 as risk approaches 0 or 1 — always know which one you quoted.

Exercise 2. The separation problem: construct x where all y = 1 for x > 0 and y = 0 for x < 0 (perfect separation). Fit unpenalized (penalty=None) and watch the coefficients; then fit with C = 0.1 and C = 100. Report coefficient magnitudes, and explain why the MLE “does not exist” here and what the small-C fit is implicitly doing about it.


Solution







Under perfect separation, likelihood increases forever as the slope grows (the model can approach zero training error by steepening the sigmoid) — the MLE diverges to ±∞. The penalty (small C) caps the climb, acting as the prior/regularization that makes the problem well-posed: a finite, conservative boundary. Symptoms in the wild: “convergence warnings” + absurdly large coefficients + predicted probabilities at exactly 0/1 — fix with regularization or better data, not more iterations.

Exercise 3. Logistic regression in a pipeline with honest tuning: build make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=5000)), tune C over a log grid with 5-fold CV (GridSearchCV), and report (a) the chosen C, (b) CV AUC, (c) test AUC on a held-out set, and (d) the odds ratios from the refit model. Then re-run everything with random_state changed — how stable are (a)–(d)?


Solution







Everything is stable to ~a decimal place except C’s exact position on the grid (neighboring Cs perform nearly identically — see the one-standard-error discussion in 4.6). The pipeline guarantees scaling is fit per-fold; the test set answers once, at the end.

title: 3.3 Logistic Regression
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Odds ratios vs risk ratios vs percentage points — three languages for one coefficient. e^β multiplies odds; converting to risk changes requires knowing the baseline (Exercise 1); quoting “30% increase” for e^β = 1.3 is wrong unless p is small.
sklearn penalizes by default — penalty=None (or huge C) for MLE-comparable inference; statsmodels Logit for SEs/p-values. Mixing the two without checking is a silent-model-swap bug.
Regularized coefficients are biased — their SEs are not the inverse-Hessian values; statsmodels-style inference on a penalized fit is invalid (bootstrap if you must).
Separation/quasi-separation → diverging coefficients and zero-width CIs; recognize the convergence warnings, regularize or collect data (Exercise 2).
Complete-data quirks: sklearn’s classes are order-sensitive in coef_ sign conventions; predict_proba[:, 1] is P(class 1) — with string labels, “class 1” is classes_[1], alphabetically determined. Check model.classes_.
Logistic is additive in log-odds — interactions and nonlinearities enter exactly as in Part 2 (2.7, 2.8) but their interpretation happens on the odds scale, which multiplies rather than adds.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated classifier has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Penalized coefficients read as MLE odds ratios: default C = 1 shrinks the coefficient, so the “odds ratio” understates the association. Use penalty=None for interpretable coefficients (or disclose the penalty).
Saturated probabilities described with certainty language: predicted probabilities are never “100% risk” — 0.9997 ≠ certainty; and the 0.5 threshold has no clinical meaning by default. Report ranges and set thresholds from costs (3.1).
Unit-dependent coefficient comparison: multiplying x by 1000 divides the coefficient by 1000 — neither magnitude means anything without units. Standardize (per-SD odds ratios) to compare.

title: 3.3 Logistic Regression
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Derive the gradient of the Bernoulli log-likelihood for logistic regression and show it equals \(X^\top (y - p)\) — the same form as linear regression’s normal equations. Two consequences to explain: (a) why Newton–Raphson for logistic = iteratively reweighted least squares, (b) why a perfect-separation dataset makes both the gradient and the Hessian misbehave (relate to Exercise 2).


Hint

ℓ = Σ[y log p + (1−y) log(1−p)]; dp/dz = p(1−p) with z = x^Tβ; then differentiate ℓ in β via the chain rule.



Solution

With z_i = x_i^Tβ and p_i = σ(z_i): ∂ℓ/∂β = Σ (y_i − p_i) x_i = X^T(y − p). Setting it to zero mirrors OLS’s X^T(y − Xβ) = 0, but p depends on β through sigmoids, so the equation is transcendental — no closed form. Newton–Raphson needs the Hessian H = −X^T W X with W = diag(p(1−p)); the update solves the weighted least-squares problem X^TWX β_new = X^TW z_working — IRLS: iteratively reweighted least squares with working response z = x^Tβ + (y−p)/(p(1−p)). Under separation, as ‖β‖→∞, p_i → 0/1 matching y_i, the gradient X^T(y−p) → 0 along the diverging direction while the log-likelihood itself → its supremum: the iteration drifts to ‖β‖ = ∞ and W’s entries vanish (Hessian degenerates) — numerically rendered as “failure to converge,” statistically as a non-existent MLE.

Q2. LDA vs logistic — the famous equivalence: for two Gaussian classes with shared covariance, both models yield parallel linear boundaries, and their coefficients are proportional. Verify numerically (fit both, compare coefficient directions), then break the equivalence twice — (a) unequal covariances, (b) heavy-tailed features (t-distributed) — and report which model degrades more in each case and why (generative assumption vs discriminative flexibility).


Solution







Equal covariances: directions align (cos ≈ 1) — the two are near-proportional estimates of the same boundary. Unequal covariances: LDA’s shared-covariance assumption is false → its single pooled boundary is mis-specified (QDA is the fix), while logistic, modeling only P(y|x), flexibly fits some linear boundary (though now the Bayes boundary itself is quadratic — both are limited). Heavy tails: LDA’s means/covariances are moment-based and outlier-driven; the logistic likelihood, depending only on y given the score, is typically more robust. Moral (Efron/Friedman): generative models win when their density assumptions hold (faster convergence, fewer parameters); discriminative models are safer when assumptions are questionable.

title: 3.3 Logistic Regression
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (logistic × 2.6–2.7). Build a treatment × biomarker model: logit(P(response)) ~ treatment * biomarker_high. (a) Fit and interpret each coefficient in odds-ratio language, including the interaction. (b) Convert the interaction into a difference of log-odds — then show numerically that a positive interaction in log-odds can correspond to a negative difference in absolute risk change at high baselines. What does this imply for presenting “effect modification” to non-statistical audiences?
C2 (logistic × 4.6 Tuning × 1.3 Bayes). Train on a case–control dataset with 50% positives (sampled prevalence ≠ population prevalence of 5%). Show that (unpenalized) logistic regression estimates coefficients consistently but its intercept — hence all predicted probabilities — is miscalibrated by the sampling ratio; correct it with the logit-offset correction (subtract log(sampling odds)) and verify calibration before/after on a population-prevalence test set. This intercept-transport trick is standard in epidemiology and worth owning.

title: 3.3 Logistic Regression
text:
7. Summary

p = σ(linear score): bounded probabilities, Bernoulli likelihood, MLE by IRLS.
Coefficients are log-odds ratios — translate consciously (odds ≠ risk), and standardize before comparing.
sklearn penalizes by default; statsmodels gives unpenalized MLE inference — know which model you fitted.
Separation breaks the MLE; regularization is the practical answer, warnings the tell.
Boundary: score = 0; intercept shifts it, slopes rotate it; probabilities are smooth across it.
Additivity holds in log-odds: interactions multiply odds, not risks — mind the audience.
Discriminating classes without a parametric story is next: 3.4 Generative classifiers (LDA, QDA, Naive Bayes).

title: 3.1 Classification Fundamentals
text: Classification predicts a categorical response. The output of a classifier is really two things: a score (a probability-like number per case) and a decision rule (a threshold converting scores to labels). Confusing the two is the root of most classification-metric confusion — this page separates them and builds the metric toolkit: confusion matrix, sensitivity/specificity, precision/recall, F1, and ROC.

title: 3.1 Classification Fundamentals
text:
1. Basic Concept
Every classifier worth using exposes scores. The confusion matrix tabulates decisions vs truth:




Predicted +
Predicted −




Actually +
TP (hit)
FN (miss)


Actually −
FP (false alarm)
TN (correct rejection)



From it, the quartet that all others are ratios of:
\[\text{Sensitivity/Recall/TPR} = \frac{TP}{TP + FN} \quad \text{Specificity/TNR} = \frac{TN}{TN + FP}\] \[\text{Precision/PPV} = \frac{TP}{TP + FP} \quad \text{FPR} = \frac{FP}{FP + TN}\]
Accuracy folds everything into one number — and hides everything, too (3.1.5 is dedicated to that trap).






Scores + threshold. Moving the threshold slides cases across the decision boundary — trading recall for precision/specificity along a fixed frontier:






ROC sweeps the threshold and plots TPR against FPR; the area under it (AUC) has a beautiful interpretation — the probability a random positive is scored above a random negative:

title: 3.1 Classification Fundamentals
text:
2. Concept Questions

A screening test has sensitivity 0.99 and specificity 0.90. In plain words, what do those two numbers promise — and what do they not tell you about a positive result?
Why can accuracy be uninformative while sensitivity/specificity stay excellent? Construct the extreme case.
Your classifier’s scores get monotonically squashed (e.g. all scores squared, order preserved). Which metrics change: accuracy at t = 0.5? AUC? AP?
Precision and recall pull in opposite directions as the threshold moves. State what each one’s denominators “cost” and why no single number captures both.
Two models have identical AUC. Are they interchangeable? Name one axis on which they can differ.



Answers


Promise: 99% of diseased people test positive (few misses); 90% of healthy people test negative. Not promised: that a positive result means disease — that’s PPV, which depends on prevalence (the Bayes result of 1.3: at 0.1% prevalence it’s ~1%… here: 0.99·0.001/(0.99·0.001+0.10·0.999) ≈ 0.98%).
Extreme case: 1% prevalence, “always predict healthy” — accuracy 99%, sensitivity 0. The two class-conditional rates (sensitivity/specificity) are computed within true classes, so they’re immune to prevalence; accuracy isn’t. Report both families or use prevalence-aware metrics.
Squashing destroys the absolute score scale but not the ranking. Accuracy at a fixed threshold can change arbitrarily (t = 0.5 lands somewhere new); AUC is invariant (it uses ranks only); AP likewise (rank-based). Threshold-dependent metrics care about calibration; ranking metrics don’t.
Precision’s denominator (TP+FP) pays for every false alarm the threshold admits; recall’s (TP+FN) pays for every miss. Loosening the threshold admits both more TPs and more FPs — recall ↑, precision typically ↓. Their trade-off is the operating curve; F1 summarizes it at one point, losing the shape.
No — AUC measures ranking quality only. They can differ wildly in calibration (does 0.8 mean 80%?), which matters for cost decisions and downstream probability uses; also in score distribution (threshold placement) and per-region behavior (one may win high-specificity operating points, the other high-sensitivity).

title: 3.1 Classification Fundamentals
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. From the ranked list below, compute by hand (paper or code, no sklearn) the confusion matrix at threshold 0.5, then TPR/FPR at every possible threshold, the full ROC, and AUC via concordant pairs. Verify every number against sklearn.


Solution







The sweep logic — walk down the ranked list, accumulating hits and false alarms — is the same walk every ROC/PR implementation takes. Owning it once demystifies the curves forever.

Exercise 2. Show the threshold-cost trade in dollars: a screening context has FN cost = $2000 (missed disease), FP cost = $100 (needless follow-up), TN/FN-free = $0. Using the scores from Section 1, compute expected cost at thresholds 0.1–0.9 (step 0.1) and find the cost-optimal threshold. Compare it to the Youden-optimal threshold (max TPR − FPR) and explain when/why the two disagree.


Solution







Youden treats error types symmetrically; real costs almost never are. With FN 20× costlier than FP, the optimal threshold drops (screen loose, confirm hard). Metric choice is a decision-theory choice — there is no threshold-free “best.”

Exercise 3. Cross-validated metric honesty: generate a moderate-signal classification dataset (n = 300, 20% positives), and compare in-sample vs 5-fold-CV values of accuracy, balanced accuracy, F1, and AUC for a logistic classifier. Which metric’s in-sample–CV gap is largest, and why does AUC’s gap behave differently from accuracy’s?


Solution







All in-sample numbers are optimistic; the ranking of metrics is preserved but the gaps differ with each metric’s sensitivity to the specific borderline cases the model tuned on. AUC’s gap tracks the same overfitting — the lesson is not “trust one metric” but “compute every metric out-of-sample,” the discipline Part 4 industrializes.

title: 3.1 Classification Fundamentals
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

confusion_matrix row/column convention: sklearn rows = true, columns = predicted. Transposed matrices are a classic silent error — print it once, label it forever.
AUC pairs with ties count 0.5 (the hand formula above); scores from a coarse model (few distinct values, e.g. a 5-bin risk score) lose AUC resolution through ties.
predict vs predict_proba: predict uses the (possibly inappropriate) 0.5 threshold; decision problems usually want predict_proba + your own threshold from costs (Exercise 2).
Macro vs micro vs weighted averaging of F1 across classes: macro treats a 2% class equally with the 98% class (each class one vote); micro ≈ accuracy. Know which your library reports by default.
AUC ignores calibration — great for ranking, dangerous if someone downstream multiplies your scores into decisions as if they were probabilities; calibration gets its own treatment in 3.7.
Class imbalance doesn’t bias AUC as an estimate of ranking skill, but its sampling noise grows as the positive count shrinks — with 10 positives, one swap changes AUC by 0.02+ (1.4 logic applies to metrics too).


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated evaluation has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fixed version


Accuracy is the wrong headline on 2%-positive data. It reports 0.503 here, but note why it is not ~0.98: a random score vector thresholded at 0.5 flags ~half the sample positive, and half of those are wrong. Any classifier that predicts almost everything negative would post 0.98 and look better still. Accuracy near the majority rate certifies nothing — pair it with prevalence-aware metrics (recall/precision/F1/AP — see 3.1.5).
Recall without precision is a trap. Recall is 0.400, which reads as “the model finds 40% of positives, acceptable.” But 493 of 1000 samples are flagged positive and only 8 of them are true — precision is 0.016. A rule that flags everything has recall 1.0 and precision 0.02; quoting recall alone is how that gets shipped. Report precision (or F1) next to recall, never alone.
AUC on hard 0/1 predictions throws away the ranking within thresholds — with 0/1 scores, AUC degenerates to a tie-contaminated balanced-accuracy proxy (0.453 here, barely distinguishable from the 0.463 you get from the raw scores). Feed continuous scores to ranking metrics; the tiny gap is itself the lesson — these scores are pure noise.

title: 3.1 Classification Fundamentals
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Derive AUC as the Mann–Whitney U statistic: show that AUC = U/(n₊n₋) where U counts concordant positive-negative pairs (ties as ½), and use this to (a) prove AUC = 0.5 under exchangeable scores, (b) construct the null SD of AUC (≈ √((n₊+n₋+1)/(12·n₊·n₋))) and compute how many positives you need for AUC ± 0.05 at n₋ = 500.


Hint

Each positive-negative pair contributes 1, ½, or 0 to the numerator; under the null each pair is a fair coin.



Solution

By definition of the empirical ROC, each threshold pair (TPR, FPR) increment is (1/n₊, 1/n₋); the area integrates the fraction of pairs with score₊ > score₋ — exactly U/(n₊n₋). (a) Under H₀ (scores exchangeable across labels) each pair is concordant/discordant with probability ½ ⇒ E[AUC] = ½. (b) Var per pair ≈ 1/12 (variance of a fair three-way ±1/½/0 trial scaled); SD(AUC) ≈ √((n₊+n₋+1)/(12n₊n₋)). Setting 1.96·SD ≤ 0.05 with n₋ = 500: n₊ ≈ 1.96²·501/(12·500·0.05²) ≈ 128 positives. Moral: the 10-positive biomarker studies quoted with 3-decimal AUCs are noise — cite the interval, not the point.

Q2. A colleague argues: “We shouldn’t fix the threshold at 0.5; we should report sensitivity and specificity at their best threshold on the test set.” Give the two failures of this plan (optimism and interpretation), then implement the honest version: choose the threshold on a validation split, freeze it, report test-set sensitivity/specificity at the frozen threshold, and compare the two procedures’ reported numbers over 200 resamples.


Solution

Failures: (1) Selection optimism — picking the threshold that maximizes test performance then reporting that same performance is tuning on the test set (0.5); the reported best point is an extreme order statistic, biased upward. (2) Interpretation — the “best” point is noise-selected per dataset; across studies the reported sensitivity/specificity are not the same operating point, so they’re not comparable or replicable. Honest version:






The frozen threshold generalizes; the per-dataset-max procedure would report visibly rosier pairs on average (run both to see the gap). One threshold, chosen where tuning is allowed, applied where it isn’t — the Part 4 ethic in miniature.

title: 3.1 Classification Fundamentals
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (metrics × 1.3 Bayes). A classifier has sensitivity 0.9 and specificity 0.95. Plot PPV as a function of prevalence from 0.1% to 50% (log x-axis). Mark the prevalence at which PPV crosses 50%, and connect the curve to the F1-vs-AP discussion in 3.1.5: which metric family bakes prevalence in, and which keeps it out — and which does your reporting audience actually need?
C2 (metrics × 0.5 Splitting × 4.3 preview). Generate a dataset with 2% positives and fit logistic regression; compute recall at the 0.5 threshold on (a) the full training set, (b) each of 10 stratified CV folds, (c) 10 folds without stratification. Report the spread of recall across folds in (b) vs (c) and tie it to the stratification lessons of 0.5 — then predict what happens to the unstratified recall when prevalence drops to 0.5%.

title: 3.1 Classification Fundamentals
text:
7. Summary

A classifier = scores + threshold; the confusion matrix is where decisions meet truth.
Sensitivity/specificity are prevalence-immune; precision and accuracy are not — know which question each answers.
AUC = probability a random positive outranks a random negative; rank-based, threshold-free, calibration-blind.
Thresholds are decision-theory: costs set them, validation selects them, test sets only measure them.
On imbalanced data, accuracy flatters; balanced accuracy/F1/AP keep you honest.
All metrics inherit sampling noise — small positive counts make small AUC differences meaningless.
When positives get truly rare, even ROC starts flattering: the precision–recall view is next — 3.1.5 AUPRC for skewed datasets.

title: 2.9 KNN Regression
text: K-nearest-neighbors regression abandons functional form entirely: to predict a point, average the responses of its k closest training points. It is the prototype nonparametric method — flexible, assumption-light, and the cleanest lens on the flexibility–data trade before Part 4 formalizes it.

title: 2.9 KNN Regression
text:
1. Basic Concept
The algorithm for predicting at query point \(x_0\):

Compute the distance from \(x_0\) to every training point.
Take the \(k\) nearest.
Predict \(\hat{y} = \frac{1}{k} \sum_{i \in N_k(x_0)} y_i\) — their average (optionally distance-weighted).

One hyperparameter, \(k\), controls everything: \(k = 1\) reproduces the training data exactly (maximally flexible); \(k = n\) predicts the global mean everywhere (maximally rigid).






Distance weighting softens the steps without a new hyperparameter family:






Implement it by hand once — the whole method is a NumPy one-liner away:

title: 2.9 KNN Regression
text:
2. Concept Questions

What does KNN with k = n predict everywhere, and which model from Part 2 is it identical to?
Why does KNN require feature scaling, while OLS arguably doesn’t?
Your KNN has excellent training predictions and poor test predictions. Which end of the k dial are you on, and what single change is the first thing to try?
In 1-D with n = 100 and k = 10, roughly what fraction of the x-range does each neighborhood cover? What happens to that fraction as dimensions grow at fixed n and k?
KNN’s fitted curve is wiggly at k = 5 but smooth at k = 50 — restate that sentence in bias–variance language.



Answers


The global average \(\bar y\) at every query — identical to the intercept-only regression of 2.1/2.2 (whose training RSS = TSS). The two “models” at the extremes of flexibility are the same object.
KNN’s only notion of “near” is a distance metric in raw coordinates; a feature measured in thousands (gene counts) swamps one measured in fractions (GC content), so the neighborhood becomes 1-D along the biggest-scaled axis. OLS multiplies each feature by its own learned coefficient — scale is absorbed by β̂ (up to conditioning) — so it is scale-equivariant, not scale-blind.
Small k (overfitting: variance dominant). First change: increase k — then validate properly (4.6); scaling too if features aren’t comparable.
With uniformly spread points, k = 10 of 100 points spans ~10% of the range. In d dimensions with fixed n and k, the same 10 points live in a shell whose radius explodes (concentration of distances) — neighborhoods become huge relative to any one axis: the curse of dimensionality. KNN degrades toward the global mean unless n grows exponentially in d.
k = 5: low bias (local averages track the true curve) but high variance (each neighborhood’s few points swing the estimate) — wiggly. k = 50: high bias (averages over genuine structure) but low variance (many points stabilize it) — smooth. The dial trades one against the other, exactly the 4.4 decomposition.

title: 2.9 KNN Regression
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Implement full 2-D KNN regression by hand (vectorized distances, argsort, averaging) and verify exact agreement with KNeighborsRegressor on 20 random queries with k = 7. Then switch to distance weighting in both and re-verify (weights ∝ 1/d, handling d = 0 by falling back to that point alone).


Solution







Agreement to float precision (sklearn’s weighting is the same 1/d scheme). Writing KNN once makes its failure modes concrete: ties, zero distances, and the cost — every query scans all n training points (no “fit” to speak of; the data is the model).

Exercise 2 — KNN vs OLS under two truths. Generate 100 training points under (a) a linear truth and (b) a wiggly sinusoidal truth (same noise). Fit OLS and KNN (k chosen by 5-fold CV over k = 1..30) to each; evaluate both on large fresh test sets. Report a 2×2 table of test MSEs. Which method wins under which truth, and what does that table say about “model choice” as a statement about the world?


Solution







Linear truth: OLS wins (KNN wastes effort estimating zero curvature). Wiggly truth: KNN wins (OLS’s bias dominates). Neither method is “better” — methods are hypotheses about structure; CV chooses the hypothesis the data supports. This 2×2 is the whole model-selection story in miniature (Part 4).

Exercise 3 — the curse, quantified. Generate data with signal only in the first 2 of d features (\(y = x_1 x_2 + \varepsilon\), remaining features pure noise, all scaled comparably). For d = 2, 5, 20, fit CV-tuned KNN and OLS on n = 300 and report test MSE on fresh data. Watch KNN degrade with d while OLS merely gets noisier — then explain in neighborhood-radius language.


Solution







In d = 20, “5 nearest neighbors” are no longer local — they’re scattered across a huge radius, so the average mixes unrelated points (bias explodes), while the useful signal lives in a 2-D slice KNN can’t isolate. OLS degrades gracefully: extra noise features only add mild variance to the coefficient estimates. Nonparametric flexibility is bought with locality, and locality is the first casualty of dimension — the reason Part 5’s regularization exists for wide data.

title: 2.9 KNN Regression
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

No training phase, all query cost: prediction is O(n·d) per point (brute force); KD-trees/ball trees help in low d and stop helping in high d. “The model” is a lookup table — deploy size = training size.
Scaling is part of the model: put the scaler inside the pipeline so CV/tuning refit it per fold (0.5 leakage rule).
k = 1 on training data scores perfectly — reporting it is the canonical overfitting self-own; evaluate on held-out data only.
Ties and even k: with classification (Part 3) even k can produce vote ties; with regression ties are harmless (averages), but distance ties in argsort are resolved arbitrarily — reproducibility note for numeric features with many duplicates.
Weighted KNN interpolates between k-sensitivity and locality: weights="distance" reduces the discontinuity at neighborhood boundaries but doesn’t fix dimensionality.
KNN has no coefficients, no p-values, no global story — it predicts, it doesn’t explain. Using it where inference is the goal is a category error.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated KNN pipeline has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fixed version


Tuning on training error selects k = 1 always (perfect memorization) — hyperparameters must be chosen by CV within the training set.
Unscaled features: distances are dominated by the 10,000-range column; the sin structure in feature 1 is invisible. Fix: StandardScaler in a pipeline.
k=1 training error as quality: by construction zero — it measures memory, not skill. Fix: report CV (tuning) and held-out test error.

title: 2.9 KNN Regression
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Show that uniform KNN regression is a linear smoother: \(\hat{y} = S y\) where \(S = D^{-1} W\) with \(W_{ij} = 1\{x_j \in N_k(x_i)\}\). What are the diagonal entries of \(S\) at k = 1, and how does that make the “training error = 0” fact inevitable? Relate the trace of S to an “effective degrees of freedom” and compute it for k = 1 and k = n.


Hint

Each fitted value is an average of a subset of the y’s — write the averaging weights as a matrix.



Solution

\(\hat y_i = \frac{1}{k}\sum_{j \in N_k(i)} y_j\) ⇒ \(\hat{\mathbf y} = S\mathbf y\) with row i of S equal to 1/k on the k neighbor columns. At k = 1, each row has a single 1 (the point itself is its own neighbor), so S = I: \(\hat y_i = y_i\) exactly — zero training error by identity, and tr(S) = n = “n effective parameters” (maximal flexibility). At k = n, S has every entry 1/n: \(\hat y_i = \bar y\), tr(S) = 1 (one effective parameter, the mean). The smoother matrix’s trace interpolates between — the KNN analog of polynomial degree. (For OLS, S is the hat matrix H with tr(H) = p + 1 — same bookkeeping, which is how KNN and regression become comparable on a flexibility axis.)

Q2. KNN predictions are discontinuous at neighborhood boundaries; kernel smoothing (Part 6) fixes this by distance-decaying weights. Demonstrate the discontinuity: construct a 1-D dataset where shifting a query point by ε changes its prediction by a jump, measure the jump, and then show the same dataset under weights="distance" yields a continuous prediction path. Why might you nevertheless prefer uniform KNN?


Solution







Crossing the boundary where a far point swaps into the neighborhood changes the average by (y_in − y_out)/k — up to 2σ/k. Distance weighting fades the swap continuously. Uniform KNN is still preferred when: interpretability of “local average of the 5 most similar cases” matters, computation must be cheapest, or the distance scale itself is questionable (weights amplify metric artifacts). Smoothness is a virtue for curve display (Part 6’s smoothing splines are the refined endpoint of this line of thought).

title: 2.9 KNN Regression
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (KNN × 4.4 Bias–variance preview). Simulate 300 training sets (n = 60) from a known f; for each k in 1..40, fit KNN on every training set and evaluate on a fixed dense grid. Estimate bias² (mean prediction vs f)², variance (SD of predictions)², and total MSE per k; plot all three. Identify the k minimizing total MSE and verify the bias/variance crossover story — you will reuse this exact experimental design on the theory page.
C2 (KNN × 0.5 Splitting × 4.3 CV). Compare two k-selection strategies on 200 fresh simulations: (a) pick k by CV, report that CV value as the error estimate; (b) pick k by CV, then report a nested outer-CV estimate. How big is the optimism of (a), and does it grow with the number of candidate k values? (This prefigures the tuning trap of 4.6.)

title: 2.9 KNN Regression
text:
7. Summary

KNN predicts by local averaging; k is the single flexibility dial from memorization (k=1) to the mean-model (k=n).
Distances make scaling part of the model — scale inside a pipeline, never outside.
It is a linear smoother: tr(S) = effective df; k=1 is the identity map (zero training error, zero information).
The curse of dimensionality inflates neighborhood radius; nonparametric methods need exponentially more data in high d.
KNN vs OLS is bias-vs-flexibility: each wins under the truth it assumes; CV adjudicates.
No coefficients, no inference: KNN predicts, it doesn’t explain.
Before returning to model form, audit the regression machinery’s fine print: 2.10 Regression assumptions.

title: 2.7 Interaction Terms
text: So far every model assumed additive effects: each predictor shifts y by a fixed amount regardless of the others. An interaction lets the effect of one predictor depend on another — the model’s most commonly forgotten question, and the difference between “drug works” and “drug works in women under 60.”

title: 2.7 Interaction Terms
text:
1. Basic Concept
Add a product column:
\[y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \beta_3\, x_1 x_2 + \varepsilon\]
Now the effect of \(x_1\) is \(\beta_1 + \beta_3 x_2\) — a function of \(x_2\), not a number. If \(\beta_3 \ne 0\), the lines/planes tilt against each other; there is no single “effect of \(x_1\)” to report.






Read the coefficients directly: male slope = dose = 0.80; female slope = dose + dose:female = 0.80 − 0.12 = 0.68; the female level offset at dose 0 = female = −1.0.
Continuous × continuous — the effect of one variable changes linearly with the other:

title: 2.7 Interaction Terms
text:
2. Concept Questions

In yield ~ temp * conc, what exactly does the conc coefficient mean now? Why is it “the effect of conc at temp = 0”?
Your interaction p-value is 0.4 but a main effect’s p-value is 0.001. May you drop the interaction and keep the main effect? May you drop the non-significant main effect and keep a significant interaction?
Interaction vs correlation between predictors (2.5 collinearity) — what’s the difference in what each breaks?
The model says the drug×sex interaction is 0.5 (p = 0.01). A headline says “drug works better in women.” What extra number does the headline need?
Why do people center variables before forming interactions, and what changes vs stays the same?



Answers


With the product term present, the conc effect is \(\beta_{conc} + \beta_{temp:conc}\,\text{temp}\) — it has no single value; by the algebra of “hold everything else fixed,” the printed \(\beta_{conc}\) is the conc effect evaluated at temp = 0. Since temp = 0 may be outside the data, that number can be meaningless — center temp and it becomes “at average temp.”
Drop the interaction: yes (back to the additive model — standard hierarchy downward is fine after a null result). Drop a main effect while keeping its interaction: no — the hierarchy principle: an interaction contains the main effects, and removing them forces the model through artificial constraints (e.g., zero effect at the other variable’s zero) that bias everything.
Collinearity is about redundant information (identifying coefficients; inflates SEs); interaction is about structure (whether effects multiply/moderate each other). Two collinear predictors can have zero interaction; two interacting predictors can be perfectly independent. Fixing one never fixes the other.
The two slopes (or the two marginal effects at meaningful values) with CIs: “slope in women = a (b to c), in men = d (e to f)” — the interaction coefficient alone doesn’t say which group is bigger, and “better” needs the scale (also: a significant interaction can mean “less bad in men”!).
Centering (subtracting means) makes main-effect coefficients interpretable at typical values of the moderator and reduces the correlation between the product column and its ingredients (numerical conditioning). It does not change fitted values, R², the interaction coefficient, or its test (with raw quadratic terms, tiny rounding aside).

title: 2.7 Interaction Terms
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Simulate a cross-over interaction: treatment helps at low severity, harms at high severity (y = 10 + 1.0·sev − 0.8·trt + 0.2·sev·trt + noise). Fit the interaction model; compute the treatment effect at severity 2, 5, 8 with CIs (delta-method-free: refit with re-centered severity); find the severity where the effect crosses zero and verify by plotting both lines.


Solution







Re-centering the moderator converts “effect at severity s” into a main effect with proper SE and CI — no delta method needed. The cross-over point (≈ 4 here) is where the treatment recommendation flips; interactions are how subgroup medicine becomes honest instead of a fishing expedition.

Exercise 2. Test the parallel-slopes assumption from 2.6 Exercise 3 properly: fit the age × tissue model on that cohort, use anova_lm to compare against the additive model, and draw the fitted age-lines per tissue on one plot. Then write the sentence the additive model would have printed if the interaction were real but ignored — what goes wrong in it?


Solution







The pooled slope is a precision-weighted average of different per-group slopes; an “age effect” headline from the additive model would be an artifact of group composition — Simpson-adjacent, and invisible without the interaction test.

Exercise 3. Continuous × continuous as a surface: fit yield ~ temp * conc (data regenerated below), then plot the marginal effect of conc (with 95% CI) as a function of temp using the re-centering trick at a grid of temperatures. At which temperatures is conc’s effect significantly positive? This “moderated effect plot” is the professional alternative to staring at coefficient tables.


Solution







The effect grows linearly with temp (that IS the interaction) and its CI clears zero everywhere here — but the plot is what a collaborator can read: “the concentration benefit ranges from ~1.5 at 10° to ~3 at 40°.” Tables report; plots convince.

title: 2.7 Interaction Terms
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Hierarchy principle: keep main effects whenever their interaction is present (dropping them constrains effects at the origin and biases estimates). Adding a non-significant interaction downward (simplifying) is fine; building interaction-only models is not.
“No significant interaction” ≠ “no interaction” — power for interactions is famously low (you’re estimating a difference of slopes); absence of evidence again (1.4). Check what effect size the CI rules out.
Interpretability of main effects dies with the interaction — the printed β̂_x is the effect at moderator = 0, often outside data. Center, or report effects at grid values (Exercise 1/3 pattern).
Polynomial terms are self-interactions: x² is “x interacting with x” (curvature), x³ more so — everything on this page (centering, hierarchy, interpretation at values) applies to 2.8.
Multiplicative hypotheses hide in logs: log(y) ~ x * g interactions are ratios of ratios — a significant interaction can mean “proportional effect differs,” which looks different back on the raw scale.
Multiple interactions multiply the search space — each added product is another test (Part 12’s problem in miniature); pre-specify the interactions theory predicts rather than sweeping all pairs.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated subgroup analysis has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fixed version


Two subgroup fits test slopes informally and underpowered: comparing two p-values (“significant here, not there”) is not an interaction test — differences of significant/non-significant are themselves noisy. Fix: one model with dose * sex, interaction tested once with full power.
dose + dose:sex violates hierarchy: no sex main effect forces both groups’ lines through the same intercept — a strong, unjustified constraint that biases the interaction estimate itself.
“+1.0 for everyone” contradicts the model being fit: with an interaction, the dose effect is slope + interaction×sex — the sentence is only true for sex = 0 (and the printed main effect is at sex = 0 by construction).

title: 2.7 Interaction Terms
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Show algebraically that centering both predictors before forming the product leaves the fitted values, R², and the interaction coefficient unchanged, and derive exactly what happens to the main-effect coefficients. Then state the one situation in which centering changes conclusions.


Hint

Write \(x_1 = \tilde x_1 + m_1\) (m = mean), expand the product term, and match coefficients between parameterizations.



Solution

With \(x_1 = \tilde x_1 + m_1\), \(x_2 = \tilde x_2 + m_2\): \(x_1x_2 = \tilde x_1\tilde x_2 + m_2\tilde x_1 + m_1\tilde x_2 + m_1m_2\). Substituting and regrouping shows the new model is a reparameterization of the same column space (each new column is a combination of old columns), so fitted values and R² are identical; the interaction coefficient is unchanged (\(\tilde\beta_{12} = \beta_{12}\)) while new mains absorb shifts: \(\tilde\beta_1 = \beta_1 + m_2\beta_{12}\) — precisely “the x₁ effect at \(x_2 = m_2\).” The SEs of the mains change (they estimate different quantities at different points). Conclusions change only when you interpret the main effects: at moderator = 0 (raw, possibly absurd) vs moderator = mean (centered, meaningful). Same model, different sentences — which is why centering is an interpretation tool, not a statistics fix.

Q2. An interaction is significant in a discovery cohort (n = 400) and you plan a confirmatory cohort (n = 400). Given that interaction power is low, design the confirmation: what is tested, what alpha, what counts as replication (same sign? CI overlap? pre-registered effect size?), and what does the “winner’s curse” of the discovery estimate imply for the expected confirmatory effect size? Demonstrate the winner’s curse by simulation.


Solution







Design: (1) test the same, pre-registered interaction in the confirmation cohort at one-sided α = 0.05 in the pre-stated direction; (2) replication = significant and same sign, ideally with effect size inside the discovery CI’s plausible range; CI overlap alone is far too weak (overlapping CIs are consistent with significant differences); (3) the winner’s curse: conditional on being selected for p < 0.05 under the null, the discovery estimate averages ~1 SE in magnitude (simulation above: false hits with mean |β̂| ≈ 0.1 SD against truth 0) — so shrink expectations: the confirmatory estimate will typically be smaller than the discovery headline even when real. Report both cohorts’ estimates side by side, never the discovery estimate alone as “the effect.”

title: 2.7 Interaction Terms
text:
6. Complex Questions
