C1 (interaction × 2.6 Categorical × 1.2 Simpson). Construct data where: pooled slope is positive, every group’s slope is negative, and the group×x interaction is significant. This is Simpson’s paradox with heterogeneous slopes — show the three nested models (pooled, dummies, dummies×x) and write which model each of three stakeholders (hospital administrator, per-site clinician, meta-analyst) should read.
C2 (interaction × 4.6 Tuning preview). Generate data with a true interaction and compare the out-of-sample performance of (a) the additive model, (b) the correctly specified interaction model, (c) the all-pairs-interactions model (x1:x2, x1:x3, x2:x3, x1:x2:x3 with 4 predictors), across n = 40, 100, 400. Which model wins at each n, and what does this tell you about interaction hunting as a function of sample size — before you ever look at a p-value?

title: 2.7 Interaction Terms
text:
7. Summary

An interaction makes an effect a function: β₃ ≠ 0 means “the effect of x₁ depends on x₂.”
Report effects at meaningful moderator values (re-center and read main effects) — never the raw table alone.
Hierarchy principle: keep main effects with their interaction; simplify downward only.
Subgroup p-value comparisons are not interaction tests; one product term, tested once, has the power.
Centering changes interpretation, never fit; polynomial curvature is interaction with itself.
Interaction power is low; absence of evidence needs the CI’s effect-size statement.
Linearity itself is now the last standing structural assumption — 2.8 Nonlinear feature transformations bends the line without leaving the linear-model world.

title: 2.5 Multiple Linear Regression
text: Multiple regression models \(Y\) as a linear function of several predictors at once — which is where regression earns its keep: adjusting for confounders, isolating each variable’s contribution, and predicting from combined structure. It also introduces the two new failure modes that dominate applied work: collinearity and confounding.

title: 2.5 Multiple Linear Regression
text:
1. Basic Concept
The model becomes a vector equation:
\[Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + \cdots + \beta_p X_p + \varepsilon\]
Fitted by the same least-squares principle, now in \((p+1)\)-dimensional coefficient space: \(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = (X^\top X)^{-1} X^\top \mathbf y\) (requires the columns of the design matrix \(X\) to be linearly independent). The key interpretive discipline: \(\hat\beta_j\) is the expected change in \(Y\) per unit of \(X_j\) holding the other predictors fixed — an adjusted association, not a raw one.






Compare each coefficient’s simple (one-at-a-time) estimate with its multiple (adjusted) estimate — the discrepancy is confounding in action:






The F-statistic asks whether any predictor helps: \(H_0: \beta_1 = \cdots = \beta_p = 0\) against the mean-model:

title: 2.5 Multiple Linear Regression
text:
2. Concept Questions

In y ~ hours + practice, β̂_hours = 1.8. State the exact operational meaning of that number.
Why can R² rise while every individual p-value falls above 0.05? (Two predictors, strongly collinear, jointly informative.)
What breaks mathematically when two predictors are perfectly collinear (x2 = 2·x1)?
The F-test p = 0.2 but one predictor’s t-test p = 0.03. Possible? What’s going on?
You add a confounder and your key coefficient collapses toward zero. Two explanations — which is the happy one?



Answers


“Increasing study hours by 1 predicts +1.8 in y, for fixed practice problems” — the comparison is between two otherwise-identical subjects. It is not the raw effect of forcing extra hours on a real person (that would include the practice-hours they’d lose — an interaction/mediation issue).
Strongly collinear predictors share their explanatory work: together they lift R², individually neither looks “significant” because each coefficient’s SE is inflated by the redundancy (the model can’t decide which one gets the credit). The F-test (joint) is significant while the t-tests (each alone) are not — the classic collinearity signature.
\(X^\top X\) becomes singular — non-invertible, so \((X^\top X)^{-1}\) doesn’t exist and β̂ is not unique (infinitely many coefficient pairs give identical predictions). Computationally you get huge, unstable estimates; conceptually, the data cannot distinguish the two channels even in principle.
Yes — it’s exactly answer 2’s situation: joint F rejects (the pair helps) while each individual t fails (credit-splitting inflates both SEs). The F-test and the collection of t-tests answer different questions.

Happy: the confounder was inflating the coefficient; your predictor’s adjusted effect is genuinely smaller — this is learning. (b) Sad: the “confounder” is a mediator or a collider, or you adjusted away real signal (overadjustment). Which one depends on the causal structure, not on the regression output.

title: 2.5 Multiple Linear Regression
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1 — the confounder lab. Simulate a classic confounded observational study: hidden z drives both x and y (x = 0.8z + noise, y = 2x + 1.5z + noise). Estimate the effect of x three ways: (a) simple regression, (b) multiple regression adjusting for z, (c) multiple regression adjusting for an irrelevant variable w. Which estimate recovers the truth, and what does (c) demonstrate?


Solution








inherits z’s influence through corr(x, z) and overshoots; (b) recovers 2.0 — adjustment works when the confounder is measured; (c) ≈ (a): adjusting for an unrelated variable changes nothing except a hair of precision. The entire value of multiple regression for inference is (b) — and its limit is that z must have been measured.


Exercise 2 — VIF by hand. Compute the variance inflation factor of each predictor in a 3-predictor model without variance_inflation_factor: regress each predictor on the others, take \(1/(1-R^2_j)\); verify against the library. Then state, numerically, what VIF = 10 does to SE(β̂_j) relative to an uncorrelated design.


Solution







VIF \(j\) = how many times larger \(\text{Var}(\hat\beta_j)\) is than it would be if predictor \(j\) were uncorrelated with the rest; SE inflates by √VIF. VIF = 10 is the common “serious” threshold, but the number to internalize is the mechanism: redundant predictors make individual coefficients unidentifiable in practice even while the model as a whole predicts fine (drill 2).

Exercise 3 — model building discipline. Using the statsmodels formula API on the built-in-style data below, run the classic workflow: (a) fit the full model y ~ x1 + x2 + x3; (b) use a partial F-test (anova_lm) to decide whether x3 earns its place; (c) refit without it if not. Report final coefficients with CIs, and give the one-sentence interpretation of each that a subject-matter reader could use.


Solution







Interpretation template: “holding x2 fixed, each additional unit of x1 predicts +1.2 (95% CI a to b) units of y; similarly for x2 with sign −0.7.” Note what the model doesn’t claim: causality (that needs design) and constancy of the x1 effect across x2 (that’s 2.7 Interaction’s question).

title: 2.5 Multiple Linear Regression
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Adjusted ≠ causal, still. Multiple regression blocks the measured confounders’ backdoors; unmeasured ones survive. The regression is honest; the causal claim needs the design.
Collinearity doesn’t hurt predictions, only interpretations: the fitted surface is stable even when individual coefficients seesaw (drill 2). Report predictions confidently, coefficients humbly.
The F-test tests the joint null — a significant F with null t-tests means collinearity; a null F with a “significant” t is a red flag (multiple testing or a fluke).
Adding predictors always weakly improves in-sample fit (the noise-collector theorem of 2.4); selection — which variables to keep — is a Part 5 topic, and must be judged out-of-sample.
Categorical predictors and interactions slot into this machinery as extra columns — dummy variables (2.6) and products (2.7) — so everything on this page applies to them unchanged.
Too many predictors relative to n (n ≲ 2p) makes OLS unstable or singular: the high-dimensional regime is a different sport (Part 5).
statsmodels vs sklearn: statsmodels gives inference (SEs, tests) and no penalty; sklearn gives prediction machinery and (in LinearRegression) no SEs. Choose by goal — the models are the same math.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated analysis has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fixed version


Raw coefficients aren’t comparable — dosage spans 0–100 (per-mg effect) while age spans ~40 (per-year effect); the magnitude ranking mixes units with importance. Standardize (z-score) predictors if you need a “which moves y more per SD” statement.
age_celsius_like = 2×age is perfect collinearity — design matrix singular; statsmodels (via pinv) silently returns an arbitrary split, values differ run to run conceptually and SEs explode. Drop the duplicate column; check condition numbers/VIFs when columns might be linear combinations.
“CAUSES” from an observational fit — adjustment does not manufacture randomization. Report the adjusted association; causal language needs the design to back it.

title: 2.5 Multiple Linear Regression
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Show from \(\hat\beta = (X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top y\) that if a predictor column is an exact linear combination of others, β̂ is not unique. Then explain why near-collinearity manifests as large coefficient variance: relate \(\text{Var}(\hat\beta) = \sigma^2 (X^\top X)^{-1}\) to a small eigenvalue of \(X^\top X\) and to the VIF.


Hint

Rotating to the eigenbasis of \(X^\top X\): coefficients along near-null directions are determined by dividing by a tiny eigenvalue.



Solution

Exact collinearity: \(X = X_{-j} c\) for some \(c\) makes \(X\beta = X_{-j}(c\beta_j + \beta_{-j})\); infinitely many β produce identical fitted values, so \((X^\top X)\) is singular and the inverse mapping doesn’t exist. Near-collinearity: diagonalize \(X^\top X = Q\Lambda Q^\top\); the coefficient component along an eigenvector with tiny λ has variance \(\sigma^2/\lambda\) — enormous. The data constrain only the combination of predictors well, not each separately. The VIF is the pairwise-oriented version of the same geometry: \(\text{VIF}_j = 1/(1 - R_j^2)\) where \(R_j^2\) is how well x_j is explained by the rest; the two views coincide through \(\sigma^2(X^\top X)^{-1}\)’s diagonal. Predictions are unaffected because prediction happens in row space, where near-dependence costs little — only coefficient identification is damaged.

Q2. Construct a suppressor variable: a predictor with zero correlation with y that improves the multiple-regression fit and flips another coefficient’s sign. Explain the mechanism in terms of partialled variables: \(\hat\beta_1\) is the slope of y on x₁ after both are cleaned of x₂ — and cleaning can reveal structure that raw correlation hid.


Solution







Mechanism: x2 is a proxy for part of x1’s noise. Controlling for x2 subtracts that noise from x1 (partialling), unmasking x1’s true coefficient; x2 itself picks up −1 from the shared-noise path. The lesson generalizes: raw correlations are projections onto single axes, multiple-regression coefficients are projections after residualization — different objects that can differ in sign or magnitude. (This is also why “delete predictors with insignificant t-stats” is a bad automatic rule.)

title: 2.5 Multiple Linear Regression
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (multiple regression × 1.2 Relationships). Build the full Simpson’s paradox dataset (three groups, positive within-group slopes, negative pooled slope). Show (a) the pooled simple regression, (b) the multiple regression with group dummies (preview of 2.6 — you may hardcode the dummy columns), (c) slope-per-group via interaction (preview of 2.7). Verify (b) recovers the common within-group slope and explain why the dummy adjustment is the paradox’s resolution.
C2 (multiple regression × 0.5 Data splitting × 2.4). On n = 100, compare: in-sample R² of the 10-predictor model vs its 5-fold R², when only 3 predictors are real. Then repeat at n = 1000. Write the “sample size needed per predictor” folklore you observe, and connect it to why Part 5’s penalized methods exist.

title: 2.5 Multiple Linear Regression
text:
7. Summary

Multiple regression estimates each predictor’s association holding the others fixed — an adjusted, not raw, statement.
Adjustment fixes measured confounding; unmeasured confounding survives, and causality still needs design.
Collinearity damages coefficient identification (VIF, inflated SEs, F-vs-t splits) but not prediction quality.
The F-test judges the joint model; t-tests judge individual channels — collinearity decouples them.
In-sample fit creeps up with any added column; adjustment, penalties, and CV are the honest referees.
Design matters: spread predictors, measure the confounders, and mind n vs p.
All predictors so far are numeric; real data has groups and labels — next page: 2.6 Categorical predictors.

title: 2.3 Accuracy of the Coefficients
text: A slope estimate is a random variable — a different sample gives a different line. This page quantifies how much it moves: standard errors, t-tests on coefficients, and confidence intervals. This is the inference layer that separates “there’s a slope” from “we know the slope to ±0.2.”

title: 2.3 Accuracy of the Coefficients
text:
1. Basic Concept
Under the model \(y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \varepsilon\) with homoscedastic, independent errors, the slope estimator has standard error
\[\text{SE}(\hat{\beta}_1) = \frac{\hat{\sigma}}{\sqrt{\sum_i (x_i - \bar x)^2}} = \frac{\hat\sigma}{s_x\sqrt{n-1}} \qquad\text{where } \hat{\sigma}^2 = \frac{\text{RSS}}{n - 2}\]
(The \(n-1\) is not a rounding convention: with \(s_x\) the ddof=1 sample SD, \(\sqrt{\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2} = s_x\sqrt{n-1}\) exactly. Using \(s_x\sqrt n\) understates the SE by \(\sqrt{(n-1)/n}\).)
Three levers, all visible in the formula: more noise (σ) widens; more spread in x (\(s_x\)) narrows; more points (\(\sqrt{n-1}\)) narrows. The coefficient’s t-statistic and CI follow the universal pattern from 1.4:
\[t = \frac{\hat\beta_1}{\text{SE}(\hat\beta_1)}, \qquad \hat\beta_1 \pm t_{0.975,\,n-2}\,\text{SE}(\hat\beta_1)\]






Same information, human-readable — and the residual-based estimate of σ:






Verify the formula by brute force — the SE is just the SD of the estimator across hypothetical samples:

title: 2.3 Accuracy of the Coefficients
text:
2. Concept Questions

Two datasets have identical σ and n, but dataset A’s x spans 0–100 and B’s spans 0–1. Which has the more precise slope, and which term of the SE formula says so?
What exactly is \(H_0\) when P>|t| for a slope is 0.03? And what is not being tested?
Why do we divide RSS by \(n-2\) (not \(n\)) to estimate σ²?
Your 95% CI for a slope is (0.02, 0.11). A reviewer says “the effect is tiny.” What’s the correct reply?
If you double all y values, what happens to \(\hat\beta_1\), its SE, its t-statistic, and its p-value?



Answers


A — via \(s_x\) (x-spread) in the denominator: the same noise, stretched over a wider x-range, is harder to confuse with a slope. Note it is the spread, not the range per se — a single far point adds range without usable spread (and adds leverage instead).
\(H_0: \beta_1 = 0\) — “no linear relationship with this predictor, in this model,” tested with data this size. Not tested: the effect’s practical importance (0.03 doesn’t mean “large”), causality, or the effect conditional on predictors not in the model.
Two parameters (\(\beta_0, \beta_1\)) were fitted from the same residuals, consuming 2 degrees of freedom; residuals from a fitted line are systematically smaller than true ε. Dividing by \(n - p - 1\) (here p = 1) corrects the optimism — the same logic as \(n-1\) for a variance (1.1).
“Statistically significant but small, and the estimate is 0.02–0.11 y-units per unit x.” Significance ≠ importance; the CI is the effect-size statement — argue importance against the interval’s values, not its exclusion of zero.
\(\hat\beta_1\) and SE double (both scale with y’s units) → t and p unchanged. Slope SEs live in y-units: 2× the outcome units, 2× the uncertainty — but the same evidence. (This scale-invariance of t is why p-values don’t answer “is the effect big.”)

title: 2.3 Accuracy of the Coefficients
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. For the data below, compute SE(β̂₁) by hand from the formula \(\hat\sigma / s_x\sqrt n\) (using residuals for σ̂), then match it against model.bse[1]. Construct the 95% CI manually and compare with conf_int().


Solution







Identical to 3 decimals. The formula’s three levers are now concrete: σ̂ from residuals, spread from \(s_x\), and \(\sqrt n\). (Column name “x1” is statsmodels’ generic name when X is a bare array.)

Exercise 2. Show empirically that a wider x-range buys precision for free: fix σ = 3, n = 30, true slope 0.5; compare the empirical SD of β̂₁ over 3,000 simulations when x ~ U(0, 1) vs x ~ U(0, 10). Verify the ratio matches the theory ratio \(s_{x,B}/s_{x,A}\).


Solution







A 10× wider design makes the slope estimate ~10× more precise at the same cost per observation. This is the experimental-design lever: spread your inputs (or your doses, or your temperatures) before you buy more replicates.

Exercise 3. An experimenter runs the regression below and reports: “slope p = 0.31, so x has no effect; but the R² is 0.4, so the model is strong.” Reconcile the two statements. Then demonstrate the resolution: simulate data where x has zero linear effect but determines the variance of y, and show what p-value and R² each report.


Solution

The two statements can coexist: R² measures explained variance (any source — including x’s effect on spread), while the slope p-value tests a mean-shift of y per unit x. x can move the distribution strongly (its spread) with zero mean shift:






Both statements are “right” and answer different questions — the experimenter’s sentence glued them together. The fix is reporting what was tested: for variance effects, model the spread explicitly (heteroscedastic models, GLMs 3.6), not the mean.

title: 2.3 Accuracy of the Coefficients
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Formula SEs rest on all four classical assumptions (linearity, independence, homoscedasticity, rough normality for the t reference). Heteroscedasticity or correlated errors invalidate the SEs even when the slope estimate stays unbiased — the point estimate and its uncertainty fail independently (2.10).
Heteroscedasticity-robust (HC) SEs are one line in statsmodels — fit(cov_type="HC3") — and are a sensible default for observational cross-sectional data.
Multiple predictors change the SE story: \(\text{SE}(\hat\beta_j)\) now depends on collinearity — the variance inflation factor (2.5); a coefficient can be noisy because its partners are redundant, not because n is small.
The intercept’s SE is usually the largest (it lives at the edge, \(x = 0\)): don’t be alarmed, and don’t interpret its p-value as a test of “does the model work.”
p = 0.049 vs 0.051 — no meaningful boundary; report effects with CIs and treat thresholds as conventions (1.4).
statsmodels column names: bare arrays give generic x1, x2...; use DataFrames or formulas (smf.ols) for self-documenting output.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated inference report has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fixed version


Intercept p-value misread: it tests whether the line’s value at x = 0 differs from 0 — usually meaningless (x = 0 outside data) and never a verdict on the model.
p ≠ effect size: with n = 25 and σ = 3 this p-value coexists with a CI like (0.1, 1.5) — potentially important or trivial. Report β̂ ± CI.
z instead of t: at n − 2 = 23 df the t-critical value is 2.069, not 1.96 — small samples widen; use conf_int() (or t-quantile) so the interval is honest.

title: 2.3 Accuracy of the Coefficients
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Derive \(\text{SE}(\hat\beta_1) = \hat\sigma / \sqrt{\sum (x_i - \bar x)^2}\) in two steps: (a) write \(\hat\beta_1\) as a weighted sum of the \(y_i\) with weights \(w_i = (x_i - \bar x)/S_{xx}\), and (b) apply the independent-errors variance rule from 1.3. Which property of the weights (\(\sum w_i = 0\)) makes β̂₀ drop out?


Hint

\(\hat\beta_1 = \sum w_i y_i\) exactly; variances add for independent errors and intercept enters only through the centered cross-product.



Solution


\(\hat\beta_1 = \frac{\sum (x_i - \bar x) y_i}{S_{xx}}\) (the \(-\bar y\) term vanishes since \(\sum (x_i - \bar x) = 0\)) — a linear combination \(\sum w_i y_i\) with \(w_i = (x_i - \bar x)/S_{xx}\). (b) With independent homoscedastic errors: \(\text{Var}(\hat\beta_1) = \sum w_i^2 \sigma^2 = \sigma^2 \frac{\sum (x_i - \bar x)^2}{S_{xx}^2} = \sigma^2 / S_{xx}\). The same centering (\(\sum w_i = 0\)) makes \(\hat\beta_1\)’s sampling distribution independent of where β₀ sits — the two estimates’ covariance is zero under normality (basis of independent slope/intercept CIs). This is the seed of the full covariance matrix \(\sigma^2 (X^\top X)^{-1}\) for multiple regression (2.5).


Q2. Estimate the sampling distribution of β̂₁ by bootstrap for the Exercise 1 data and compare: (a) bootstrap SD vs formula SE, (b) bootstrap percentile CI vs t-CI. Now regenerate the data with heteroscedastic noise (\(\sigma \propto x\)) and repeat. Which comparison breaks, and what is the bootstrap version measuring that the formula no longer estimates?


Solution







Homoscedastic: the two agree (formula valid). Heteroscedastic: they diverge — the formula assumes one σ, the bootstrap re-encounters the actual error structure in the resamples, so it estimates the real sampling variability. The bootstrap is the general-purpose audit of any formula SE; when they disagree, trust the bootstrap and fix the assumptions (robust SEs or a GLM).

title: 2.3 Accuracy of the Coefficients
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (coefficient accuracy × 0.5 Data splitting). Fit the same SLR on 200 different 80/20 splits; collect slope estimates and their formula SEs each time. Plot SE(slope) against the x-spread of the training split. What relationship emerges, how does it connect to the SE formula, and why does stratifying or blocking matter more for slope stability than for intercept stability?
C2 (coefficient accuracy × 2.5 Multiple regression preview). Generate \(y = 2x_1 + 0 \cdot x_2 + \varepsilon\) with \(x_2 = 0.95 x_1 + \text{noise}\) (collinear partners). Compare the SE of the \(x_1\) coefficient in (a) the single-predictor model and (b) the two-predictor model. Quantify the inflation and explain it as redundancy: the data cannot tell the two “explanations” apart, so uncertainty per coefficient explodes — the multicollinearity story of 2.5.

title: 2.3 Accuracy of the Coefficients
text:
7. Summary

\(\text{SE}(\hat\beta_1) = \hat\sigma/(s_x\sqrt{n-1})\): less noise, wider x-spread, more n — tighter slopes.
t = β̂/SE against \(H_0{:}\,\beta = 0\); the CI, not the p-value, is the effect-size statement.
σ̂ uses \(n - p - 1\) df: fitted parameters consumed the residual information.
t-tests are scale-invariant (double y → double β̂, SE; same t) — they measure evidence, not size.
Formula SEs assume linearity, independence, homoscedasticity; robust SEs and the bootstrap are the practical audits.
Wide x-design is the cheapest precision you will ever buy.
One coefficient is one part of the model; next page scores the whole fit: 2.4 Accuracy of the full model.

title: 2.10 Regression Assumptions & Diagnostics
text: Every SE, t-test, CI, and F-test in Part 2 rests on assumptions: Linearity, Independence, Normality, Equal variance (of errors). Violations don’t just “break the model” abstractly — each one breaks a specific thing (usually inference, sometimes prediction), and each has a signature plot. This page makes the diagnostics reflexive.

title: 2.10 Regression Assumptions & Diagnostics
text:
1. Basic Concept
The assumptions, what each buys, and what its violation costs:









Assumption
Formal statement
Needed for
Violation’s cost




Linearity
\(\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon \mid X] = 0\)
unbiased β̂, meaningful coefficients
biased estimates; everything downstream is about the wrong model


Independence
errors uncorrelated across rows
valid SEs, tests, CIs
SEs wildly wrong (often underestimated); p-values meaningless


Normality
\(\varepsilon \sim N(0, \sigma^2)\)
exact t/F reference distributions
only mild at large n (CLT); matters at small n and for prediction intervals


Equal variance
\(\text{Var}(\varepsilon \mid X) = \sigma^2\)
SEs, exact tests
wrong SEs; OLS no longer most efficient



Key triage: prediction needs linearity (systematic structure captured); inference needs all four.
The diagnostic quartet, on one simulated misspecification each:






Reading guide: residuals-vs-fitted should show a structureless horizontal band (curvature ⇒ nonlinearity; funnel ⇒ heteroscedasticity); QQ should hug the diagonal (S-curves ⇒ heavy tails/skew); scale-location should be flat (trend ⇒ variance grows with the mean).

title: 2.10 Regression Assumptions & Diagnostics
text:
2. Concept Questions

Which assumption does a U-shaped residuals-vs-fitted plot violate, and what’s the two-column fix?
Your errors are independent but heteroscedastic. Are your β̂ biased? Your SEs? Name the one-line remedy that fixes the SEs.
Why is normality of errors the least worrying of the four at n = 500, but a genuine worry at n = 8?
Residuals are correlated in time order (a drifting instrument). Which printed numbers become lies, and does the slope estimate itself have to be wrong?
Why must diagnostics use residuals, never the raw y?



Answers


Linearity (systematic curvature left unmodeled). Fix: add \(x^2\) (or a spline basis) — two columns in, assumption restored; refit and re-diagnose (2.8).
β̂: unbiased (linearity intact — OLS is still the right center). SEs: wrong (they assume one σ). Remedy: heteroscedasticity-robust SEs — fit(cov_type="HC3") — or model the variance (GLM, 3.6).
At large n, the CLT makes t/F statistics approximately valid regardless of error shape (influence of each single point vanishes). At n = 8, one outlier is the distribution — the t-reference is fiction, CIs undercover, and no CLT rescue exists.
Every SE, t, p, CI — they all assume independent errors; positive serial correlation makes the effective sample size much smaller than n (n = 200 correlated readings ≈ far fewer independent ones). The slope estimate can remain unbiased but its precision claim is fantasy.
Raw y mixes signal f(x) with error: a “non-normal y” can come entirely from a skewed x-distribution with perfectly normal errors. Residuals isolate ε̂ — the only thing the assumptions speak about.

title: 2.10 Regression Assumptions & Diagnostics
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.
























The regressor being serially correlated as well is the whole story, and it is easy to miss. If x is iid, the score \(u_i = x_i\varepsilon_i\) has \(\text{Cov}(u_i, u_{i+k}) = E[x_i x_{i+k}]E[\varepsilon_i\varepsilon_{i+k}] = 0\) for \(k \neq 0\) — the regressors decorrelate for you, and the naive SE is already right no matter how badly \(\varepsilon\) is correlated. Make x a time series and the \(x_i x_{i+k}\) cross-terms no longer vanish: the effective sample size collapses, and HAC inflates the SE by roughly 2× here (and 1.5–2× across seeds). This is exactly why the “effective n shrinks” claim applies to panel and time-series designs and quietly does not apply to designed experiments (randomized treatment, iid subjects) — the design, not the noise, does the work.


Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Build diagnose(fit) — a function taking a statsmodels fit and returning a dict of verdicts: residual–fitted curvature score (correlation of residuals with fitted²), funnel score (Spearman |ρ| of |residuals| vs fitted), and normality p-value (Jarque–Bera). Run it on the four synthetic datasets from Section 1 and confirm it flags the right problem in each. What can a verdict dictionary not tell you that the plot can?


Solution







The scores separate the cases (curvature high only for “nonlinear”, funnel only for “hetero”, JB only for “heavy-tail”). What the dict can’t show: patterns a scalar compresses away — e.g. one wild leverage point inside a clean cloud scores fine numerically but is obvious in the plot, and residual-vs-fitted plots reveal which region of x misbehaves. Numbers triage; eyes diagnose.

Exercise 2. The repair menu, demonstrated: for each mis-specified fit below, apply the indicated fix and re-run the diagnostic that failed. (a) quadratic truth + linear model → add x²; (b) heteroscedastic → log-transform y (verify the funnel flattens) and compare HC3 SEs; (c) heavy-tailed → report the HC3 SE alongside classical and note which coefficients lose significance.


Solution







Each repair targets the assumption its diagnostic flagged — and the diagnostics after repair verify the fix rather than trusting it.

Exercise 3. Leverage vs outlier. Construct a 30-point dataset where one point has extreme x (high leverage, y consistent with the line) and another has extreme y at typical x (outlier, low leverage). Fit with and without each point; report slope changes. Which point is more dangerous to the slope? Then connect to Cook’s distance (get_influence().cooks_distance[0]) — which point does it flag?


Solution







Deletion only makes sense against the design the point was actually in: np.delete(x, 0) on the base 30 removes an ordinary random point and tells you nothing about the special point. Note the asymmetry — removing the leverage point barely moves the slope (it agreed with the line, so it was not doing any work), while removing the outlier restores the baseline almost exactly. Leverage alone is not influence; a high-leverage point only hurts when its y is also discrepant, which is precisely the combination Cook’s distance encodes.

title: 2.10 Regression Assumptions & Diagnostics
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Diagnostics are for the training residuals, decisions are for the study — after repair (transform, robust SEs), refit and re-diagnose; one pass is not a workflow.
Testing normality with p-values on residuals (Shapiro/JB) is a weak tool: at small n it lacks power, at large n it flags trivial departures. The QQ plot, read as a shape, is more informative than any single p-value.
Independence is the assumption you cannot plot away — it comes from the design (time order, clustering, relatedness). Residual-vs-order plots and HAC/mixed models (the drill) manage known structure; unknown structure needs better data.
Heteroscedasticity has two fixes with different goals: robust SEs fix your uncertainty about β̂ (inference), WLS/GLM/log-transform fix efficiency and prediction intervals (the model). Pick by goal.
Leverage ≠ outlier ≠ influential (Exercise 3): check Cook’s distance (or DFFITS) rather than residual magnitude, especially before deleting anything — deletion is a modeling decision to report, not hygiene.
Don’t diagnose the test set: split integrity (0.5) applies — diagnostics belong to the modeling loop on training data; the test set is spent once.
Multicollinearity (2.5) is sometimes listed as a fifth assumption — it is not an assumption violation (the model can be true!) but a data condition that inflates SEs; diagnose with VIFs, not residual plots.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated validation script has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fixed version


Normality of y ≠ normality of ε — y’s distribution is dominated by f(x)’s shape; the assumption concerns residuals only. (Here x is uniform, y is U-shaped — the test “fails” for a reason irrelevant to the model.)
Funnel signature is |residuals| vs fitted — correlation of signed residuals with y mostly re-detects the slope, not variance structure. Fix: Spearman(|resid|, fitted), or compare residual SD across fitted-value halves.
Inference on a visibly mis-specified model: the quadratic truth leaves systematic curvature; the classical p-value’s null distribution is wrong. Fix the specification first, then read tests.

title: 2.10 Regression Assumptions & Diagnostics
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Derive the exact variance function of OLS residuals for a binary-style Bernoulli-mean response and show it is inherently heteroscedastic (\(\text{Var}(\varepsilon \mid x) = p(x)(1-p(x))\)), peaking at p = 0.5. Use this to explain why linear-probability models always show funnel diagnostics and why the logistic/GLM view (3.2, 3.6) resolves rather than repairs the problem.


Hint

If y ∈ {0,1} with mean p(x), write y = p(x) + ε and compute Var(ε|x).



Solution

y ∈ {0,1}, E[y|x] = p(x) ⇒ ε = y − p(x) takes values −p(x) and 1−p(x), so Var(ε|x) = p(x)(1−p(x)) — maximal (0.25) at p = 0.5, shrinking to 0 at the extremes. The linear-probability model therefore cannot satisfy equal-variance for any σ: the funnel is structural, baked into binary outcomes. No transform or robust SE “fixes” the model; the likelihood that matches the data-generating mechanism (Bernoulli with logit link — logistic regression) makes the variance function part of the model. This is the template for GLMs generally: choose the variance function from the response’s nature, then the mean model — the organizing idea of 3.6.

Q2. A dataset has grouped structure: 30 patients × 5 repeated measurements (150 rows), with patient-level random drift. (a) Demonstrate empirically that OLS SEs are too small (simulate 500 such datasets; compare the empirical SD of β̂ across simulations to the average classical SE). (b) Show that simply averaging each patient’s rows (n = 30) restores honest SEs at the cost of power, and (c) name the two standard remedies that keep all 150 rows (cluster-robust SEs; mixed models) — verify (a)’s lie and one remedy numerically.


Solution







The classical SE assumes 150 independent errors; with 30 patients’ shared drift, effective information ≈ 30-ish units, so the true SD of β̂ is several× the naive SE. Remedies keeping all rows: fit(cov_type="cluster") with patient IDs (fixes inference) and linear mixed models (random patient intercepts — models the structure, often more efficient). Averaging (b) is the transparent sanity check that exposes the lie.

title: 2.10 Regression Assumptions & Diagnostics
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (assumptions × 2.8 Transforms × 3.6 GLMs preview). For count data generated as Poisson(\(e^{1+0.3x}\)): fit (a) OLS y ~ x, (b) OLS log y ~ x (adding 0.5 to dodge zeros), (c) a Poisson GLM with log link. Compare the coefficient estimates to the truth and run residual diagnostics on (a) and (b). Which problems are repairable by transforms and which are baked into the response’s nature? Write the sentence that motivates GLMs in one breath.
C2 (assumptions × 4.1 Generalization preview). Generate 300 datasets where the true model is quadratic but analysts fit lines. Split each dataset, record (a) the linear model’s test MSE and (b) its slope p-value. What fraction of datasets show a “highly significant” slope alongside clearly worse-than-quadratic test performance? What does this experiment say about the independence of inference validity from predictive adequacy — and why does Part 4’s out-of-sample discipline catch what diagnostics+tests can miss?

title: 2.10 Regression Assumptions & Diagnostics
text:
7. Summary

L-I-N-E: linearity (unbiasedness), independence (valid SEs), normality (small-n exactness), equal variance (efficient, valid SEs).
Residuals — never raw y — are the diagnostic subject: residuals-vs-fitted, QQ, scale-location.
Each violation has a repair menu: +x²/splines, transforms, robust/HAC/cluster SEs, GLMs.
Influence ≠ leverage ≠ outlier; Cook’s distance is the deletion diagnostic.
Serial/grouped correlation silently multiplies your p-values’ confidence — design awareness, not plots, is the defense.
Diagnose → repair → re-diagnose; and never diagnose on the test set.
Part 2’s regression toolkit is complete. Part 3 turns to categorical responses, where the equal-variance assumption dies by definition — beginning with what classification is and how it’s scored: 3.1 Classification fundamentals.

title: 1.5 Resampling Intuition
text: When the formula for an uncertainty is messy or unknown — a median, a difference of AUCs, a ratio — resampling replaces the mathematics with computation: shuffle or resample the data you have, recompute the statistic many times, and look at the spread. It is the bridge between classical inference and the cross-validation you will use for every model.

title: 1.5 Resampling Intuition
text:
1. Basic Concept
The bootstrap treats your sample as a stand-in for the population: draw new samples with replacement, same size as the original, recompute the statistic, repeat. The variability across bootstrap replicates mimics the sampling variability of the statistic.






Let’s do that cleanly for the median — the statistic where formulas hurt:






The permutation test answers a different question — “is this association real?” — by shuffling labels to simulate a world where the null is exactly true, and asking how extreme the real statistic is among the shuffled ones:






The jackknife — leave one out, recompute, look at the spread — estimates bias and SE from n recomputations (cheap, deterministic, less flexible):

title: 1.5 Resampling Intuition
text:
2. Concept Questions

Why must bootstrap resampling be with replacement, and what would happen without it?
What null does a permutation test simulate, and why don’t we need to know any distribution’s shape?
When does the bootstrap fail even with lots of data? Give one statistic and one data structure.
How does a bootstrap CI for a mean compare to the t-formula CI for near-normal data — and for skewed data?
Conceptually, how is K-fold cross-validation (0.5) a resampling method, and what statistic does it resample for?



Answers


With replacement generates variability — each replicate is a new pseudo-sample whose composition differs (some points twice, some never). Without replacement every replicate is the original sample in a different order — zero variability, zero information.
The null of exchangeability: group labels carry no information, so any shuffling of labels is as probable as the observed one. The p-value counts how often shuffled data produces a statistic at least as extreme as observed — no distributional formula required, only the labels being exchangeable under H₀.

Extreme order statistics — the min/max (bootstrap resamples contain ≤ n distinct values; the max can never exceed the observed max, so its distribution is degenerate). (b) Dependent data — time series or spatial data: i.i.d. resampling destroys the dependence structure that the statistic is about (fixes exist: block bootstrap).

Near-normal: nearly identical (bootstrap ≈ t-interval, slightly wider with percentile method). Skewed: the bootstrap CI inherits the skew of the statistic’s sampling distribution — often more honest than the symmetric t-CI (1.4 Exercise 3).
CV repeatedly partitions the sample, recomputes model performance on held-out parts, and reads stability from the spread — resampling the rows rather than resampling within a statistic’s input. Bootstrap estimates the variability of a statistic; CV estimates the variability of an estimation procedure’s performance.

title: 1.5 Resampling Intuition
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Bootstrap the difference in medians between two skewed groups (5000 replicates), report the 95% percentile CI, and compare with the CI you’d get from a difference-in-means t-interval. Which pair of estimates is the better summary for skewed data and why?


Solution







For skewed data the medians + bootstrap CI pair is the defensible summary: medians resist the tail, and the bootstrap CI carries the actual (asymmetric) uncertainty. The t-CI on means is dominated by a handful of large values and its symmetric shape misrepresents the uncertainty.

Exercise 2. Implement the permutation test for a difference in means as a reusable function perm_test(a, b, n_perm=10_000, seed=0), then apply it to (a) clearly separated groups, (b) identical distributions. Verify in case (b) that p-values are approximately uniform on (0,1) over 500 repeats — the defining calibration property of a valid test.


Solution







The uniformity check in (b) is the gold-standard self-test of any test implementation: under a true null, p-values must be ~Uniform(0,1), so P(p < α) = α. If your p-values pile up near 0 under the null, your permutation scheme is broken (usually: statistic computed on non-pooled data, or shuffling within groups).

Exercise 3. Bootstrap vs formula SE shootout. For n = 8, 30, 200 samples from a lognormal, compute (a) the t-formula SE of the mean, (b) the bootstrap SE of the mean, (c) the bootstrap SE of the median. Plot/inspect how the three quantities and their stability change with n. Write the two-sentence takeaway.


Solution







Takeaways: (1) formula and bootstrap SE of the mean agree closely — the bootstrap recovers textbook results, validating the machinery; (2) for skewed data the median’s bootstrap SE is smaller and its own sampling distribution is more stable — another argument for robust summaries on skewed biological measurements.

title: 1.5 Resampling Intuition
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

The bootstrap resamples observations, not noise: each replicate should reproduce the original sample size and structure (paired rows stay paired; per-group sizes preserved by stratified bootstrapping).
Percentile CIs under-cover for small n and skewed statistics — improvements (BCa) exist; know that “bootstrap CI” is a family, not one object. Report the method.
Permutation tests require exchangeability under H₀ — with confounded group assignments (e.g. all treated samples run on batch 2), shuffling labels tests the wrong null. Design before inference.
Number of replicates: 1,000–10,000 for CIs; more for tail quantiles. Monte Carlo error of a percentile ≈ \(\sqrt{p(1-p)/B}\) — at B = 1,000 the 2.5% quantile itself wobbles.
Bootstrap cannot see beyond the sample: it inherits your outliers and your range (the max degeneracy drill). If the sample missed the tails, the bootstrap is confidently wrong about them.
rng.choice vs rng.integers indexing: rng.choice(x, size=(B, n), replace=True) in one call is far faster than a Python loop of resamples — vectorize your resampling like everything else.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated bootstrap has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fixed version


replace=False — every “replicate” is just the original data minus one point (a jackknife in disguise); no bootstrap variability.
size=len(data)-1 — replicates must match the original n; smaller samples underestimate the statistic’s variance.
[5, 95] percentiles — that’s a 90% interval labeled as a CI; 95% needs the 2.5/97.5 percentiles. (Minor: a Python loop of 1,000 resamples is fine here but the vectorized form is idiomatic and 100× faster.)







Note the outlier: watch how the bootstrap CI for the mean is stretched rightward while stat=np.median would give a tight, stable interval — run both and compare.

title: 1.5 Resampling Intuition
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Explain precisely why the bootstrap estimate of a statistic’s SE converges to the true SE as n → ∞, and why the approximation is double (empirical distribution → population, plug-in resampling → true sampling distribution). Where does small n hurt first?


Hint

The bootstrap replaces F (unknown population CDF) with F̂ (empirical CDF). Two questions: how well does F̂ approximate F, and how well does the bootstrap world mimic the real one for your statistic?



Solution

The bootstrap is a plug-in: it pretends F̂ (the empirical distribution — the sample itself) is the truth, then simulates sampling from F̂. By the Glivenko–Cantelli theorem, F̂ → F uniformly as n grows, so for statistics that depend smoothly on the distribution (means, moments, regression coefficients), the bootstrap SE → true SE. The error is two-layered: (1) F̂ ≠ F (sampling error of the original study — unavoidable, shrinks as n grows), and (2) the statistic’s behavior in the bootstrap world ≠ its behavior in the real world (mild for smooth statistics, severe for extremes/discontinuous ones like the max). Small n hurts first through layer (2) for non-smooth statistics and through percentile-CI undercoverage — with n = 10, the empirical distribution has only 10 distinct values and every resample is a sparse remix of them.

Q2. Your permutation test compares a treated group (n = 6) to controls (n = 40). (a) How many distinct label assignments exist, and what is the smallest nonzero p-value the test can ever return? (b) What practical consequences does this have for small-n study design and for reporting “p < 0.001” from a permutation test with 6+40 samples?


Solution


\(\binom{46}{6} = 9{,}366{,}819\) distinct assignments (treated labels are indistinguishable among themselves). The smallest nonzero p is \(1/\binom{46}{6} \approx 1.07 \times 10^{-7}\) — so in principle tiny p-values are attainable. (b) The real constraint is resolution vs replicates: with B = 10,000 random permutations, the add-one p-value has resolution ≈ 10⁻⁴ and Monte Carlo error ~\(\sqrt{p(1-p)/B}\); reporting “p < 0.001” from 10⁴ permutations is not supportable — report “p < 10⁻⁴” or increase B. Design lesson: permutation tests inherit the exact-conditional guarantee but their resolution is bounded by combinatorics and B — small treated groups are fine for moderate p-values, hopeless for “highly significant” claims without huge B (or full enumeration).

title: 1.5 Resampling Intuition
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (resampling × 0.5 Data splitting). Implement a bootstrap comparison of two models’ test accuracies: fit both models on each of 200 bootstrap resamples of the training set, evaluate both on the same fixed test set, and build the CI of the accuracy difference. Then explain why this underestimates the uncertainty from training-set variation compared to refitting on fresh splits, and how the “.632 bootstrap” style corrections (4.5) address the overlap problem.
C2 (resampling × 4.6 Hyperparameter tuning preview). You tune a hyperparameter by picking the K-fold CV optimum, then report that optimum’s CV score as the performance estimate. Simulate this procedure under a null (no signal: y random) with 20 candidate values and show the optimistic bias (selected score vs true score on fresh data). Which resampling discipline (nested CV) fixes it, and what does this have in common with the optional-stopping bug of 1.4?

title: 1.5 Resampling Intuition
text:
7. Summary

Bootstrap: resample rows with replacement, same n, recompute — the spread across replicates estimates uncertainty for almost any statistic.
Permutation test: shuffle labels under exchangeability; the p-value is the rank of the observed statistic among shuffled ones; distribution-free by construction.
Jackknife: leave-one-out; cheap deterministic bias/SE estimates.
Percentile bootstrap CIs match t-CIs for tame data and outperform them for skewed statistics.
Failure modes: order statistics (max), dependent data, non-exchangeable labels, tiny n, and reading more precision out of B replicates than B provides.
Vectorize resampling: one rng.integers/choice call for all replicates.
Uncertainty about a statistic is solved; uncertainty about a model’s predictions is the subject of Part 4 — starting from why held-out data is the only honest judge: Part 2 builds the first models, and Part 4 formalizes their evaluation.

title: 1.3 Probability Essentials
text: Probability is the language in which every model speaks: a predicted probability, a p-value, a 95% interval, a likelihood. This page drills the rules, the three distributions that do most of the work in ML (binomial, Poisson, normal), and the one formula — Bayes’ rule — that most people’s intuition gets wrong.

title: 1.3 Probability Essentials
text:
1. Basic Concept
The rules. For events A and B:

Complement: \(P(A^c) = 1 - P(A)\) — “at least one” questions become “1 minus none.”
Addition: \(P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)\) — the intersection is counted twice, subtract once.
Multiplication / conditioning: \(P(A \cap B) = P(A \mid B)\,P(B)\); independence means \(P(A \cap B) = P(A)P(B)\), so for independent events conditioning changes nothing.
Bayes: \(P(A \mid B) = \dfrac{P(B \mid A)\,P(A)}{P(B)}\) — the flip between “evidence given cause” and “cause given evidence.”







Random variables and their machines. A distribution assigns probability to outcomes. The three workhorses:









Distribution
Models
Parameters
scipy




Binomial
# successes in n independent yes/no trials
n, p
stats.binom


Poisson
# events in fixed time/space (counts, reads)
λ (rate)
stats.poisson


Normal
sums/averages of many small effects (CLT)
μ, σ
stats.norm









Expectation and variance are the distribution’s center and spread: \(E[X] = \sum x\,p(x)\); for the sum of independent variables, means add and variances add (this additive rule powers everything from portfolio risk to the SE of a mean).

title: 1.3 Probability Essentials
text:
2. Concept Questions

A test is 99% sensitive and 99% specific; prevalence is 1/1000. Roughly what fraction of positive results are true positives, and which two quantities fought each other in the Bayes computation?
When does Poisson model counts well, and what does it assume that binomial does not?
What is P(X = 4.0) for a continuous random variable, and what do we evaluate instead?
Why do variances add but standard deviations don’t?
If A and B are independent with P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.8, what is P(A ∪ B)?



Answers


About 9%. The fight: the evidence actually observed (true positives, \(0.99 \times 0.001\)) versus the much larger pool of false positives generated by the huge healthy majority (\(0.01 \times 0.999\)). Base rate dominates when prevalence is low.
Poisson fits counts of events in a fixed window when events are rare and independent (reads overlapping a gene, mutations per kb). It assumes events occur with a constant rate and no upper bound; binomial counts successes in a fixed number of trials n.
Zero — a point has no width, so its probability mass is 0. We evaluate \(P(X \le x)\) (CDF) or \(P(a < X < b)\) (density integrated over the interval).
Variance adds because the cross-terms of independent variables average to zero: \(\text{Var}(X+Y) = \text{Var}(X)+\text{Var}(Y)\). SD is the square root of that sum, and square roots don’t add: \(\sqrt{a+b} \ne \sqrt a + \sqrt b\).
\(P(A\cup B) = 0.5 + 0.8 - 0.5\times0.8 = 0.9\).

title: 1.3 Probability Essentials
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1 — the full Bayes computation. Disease prevalence 0.1%, test sensitivity 99%, specificity 99%. Compute (a) P(disease | positive), (b) the same for prevalence 10%, (c) how high specificity must be at 0.1% prevalence for PPV ≥ 50%. State each result as one sentence.


Solution








9% — a positive result is usually false at 0.1% prevalence. (b) 92% — the same test is excellent in a high-risk population. (c) specificity ≈ 99.90% — the false-positive rate per healthy person must be driven below the true prevalence. Same machine, three different decisions — this is why screening policies depend on prevalence, not just on test quality.


Exercise 2 — Monte Carlo verification. Verify analytically-computed probabilities by simulation: (a) at least one six in 4 rolls; (b) P(Binomial(20, 0.3) ≥ 10); (c) P(Normal(0,1) within ±1.5). Report simulated vs exact to 3 decimals.


Solution







Note the pattern — sf(9, ...) for “≥ 10” (sf is P(X > k), so use k−1). Monte Carlo with N = 10⁶ carries ~0.05% MC error; agreement to 3 decimals is expected, and this verify-by-simulation habit will debug countless probability computations later.

Exercise 3 — the law of total probability in a lab setting. 1% of samples are contaminated. Contaminated samples fail QC 80% of the time; clean samples fail 2% of the time. What fraction of samples fail QC? Given a sample failed QC, what’s the probability it was contaminated?


Solution







Two-step structure: total probability pools the failure rate across the two sample types; Bayes re-weights to ask about the cause. Even a 40× higher failure rate for contaminated samples only gets you to 28.8% — because clean samples are 99× more numerous. Always ask what population produced this positive.

title: 1.3 Probability Essentials
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

P(A|B) vs P(B|A) — transposing the conditional is the prosecutor’s fallacy; DNA-match statistics are its most famous victim. Every Bayes computation should start by naming which conditional you have and which you want.
Independence is not “small correlation” and not “no obvious relationship” — it is \(P(A \cap B) = P(A)P(B)\) exactly. Rarely true for biological measurements (batch, relatedness, shared environment).
pdf values are not probabilities — stats.norm.pdf(0) ≈ 0.4 yet P(X=0) = 0; the density integrates to probability. Only CDFs and intervals carry probability meaning.
sf(k) = P(X > k) (strictly greater) — the classic off-by-one: P(X ≥ 10) = sf(9), not sf(10). Write the inequality before writing the function call.
Poisson has variance = mean; real count data routinely violates this (overdispersion) — the reason negative-binomial models exist in RNA-seq DE analysis (12.6).
CLT applies to standardized sums of many independent contributions — not to heavy-tailed data at small n, and not to highly skewed counts at n = 5.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated “screening calculator” has three bugs. Run it, then fix.








What’s wrong, and the fixed version


Complement misuse: the stray “× 3” multiplies the none-detect probability by 3, producing a negative “probability”. The complement of “at least one” is “none”, full stop: \(1 - 0.9^3\).
sf off-by-one: sf(8) = P(X > 8) = P(X ≥ 9); for P(X ≥ 8) use sf(7).
pdf differences are not probabilities — subtracting densities is meaningless. Integrate: cdf(1.96) - cdf(-1.96).

title: 1.3 Probability Essentials
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Derive the 9% PPV result symbolically and explain in terms of the Bayes numerator and denominator why increasing sensitivity barely helps at low prevalence, while increasing specificity helps enormously.


Hint

Write PPV \(= \frac{sp\,\pi}{sp\,\pi + (1-sc)(1-\pi)}\) and ask: which term shrinks when sens ↑ vs spec ↑, at \(\pi = 0.001\)?



Solution

PPV \(= \dfrac{\text{sens}\cdot\pi}{\text{sens}\cdot\pi + (1-\text{spec})(1-\pi)}\). At \(\pi = 0.001\): the numerator term is ≈ sens × 0.001 — small no matter how good sens is (bounded by prevalence itself). The denominator’s second term is \((1-\text{spec}) \times 0.999\) — nearly the whole healthy population times the false-positive rate. Raising sens 0.99 → 0.999 multiplies the numerator by ~1.009; raising spec 0.99 → 0.999 divides the false-positive term by 10. At low prevalence, PPV is governed by specificity — which is why screening programs chase specificity and why confirmatory (more specific) tests follow any positive screen.

Q2. Two independent watchtowers detect fires with probabilities 0.8 and 0.7 respectively. Given exactly one detection occurred, what is the probability it was tower 1? Compute symbolically and verify by Monte Carlo.


Hint

Enumerate the four detection outcomes with their probabilities; condition on the two “exactly one” outcomes.



Solution

Outcomes: both \(= 0.8 \times 0.7 = 0.56\); neither \(= 0.2 \times 0.3 = 0.06\); only-1 \(= 0.8 \times 0.3 = 0.24\); only-2 \(= 0.2 \times 0.7 = 0.14\). Given “exactly one”, it was tower 1 with probability \(0.24/(0.24 + 0.14) = 0.632\).






Note the method: enumerate + condition, or simulate — both beat formula-hunting when the event structure gets any more complicated.

title: 1.3 Probability Essentials
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (probability × 0.5 Data splitting). A test set has n = 50 samples with true accuracy p = 0.8. Compute the exact probability (binomial) that the measured accuracy is ≥ 0.9 (i.e., ≥ 45 correct). Now compute the same for n = 500. What does each number say about the credibility of “90% accuracy!” claims at the two sample sizes — and connect this to the binomial SE formula used in 0.5 Q2.
C2 (probability × 12.4 FDR preview). You test 10,000 genes for differential expression at α = 0.05; none are truly differential. (a) How many false positives do you expect? (b) What’s the probability of at least one? (c) If 100 are truly differential with 80% power, what is the positive predictive value of your “significant” list? This single calculation is the entire motivation for FDR correction — predict what q-values do before learning them.

title: 1.3 Probability Essentials
text:
7. Summary

Complement turns “at least one” into “1 − none”; addition subtracts the double-counted intersection.
Conditional probability is the primary object; independence is \(P(A \cap B) = P(A)P(B)\), not an adjective.
Bayes’ rule converts P(evidence|cause) to P(cause|evidence); at low prevalence, specificity dominates PPV.
Binomial = n trials; Poisson = counts in a window (variance = mean); Normal = the CLT’s destination.
pdf values are densities, not probabilities; CDF/sf carry probability, and sf is P(X > k) — mind the off-by-one.
Variances add for independent sums; SDs don’t.
Verify any analytic probability with a Monte Carlo one-liner — cheap, and it catches unit/interval bugs.
With probability as the language, the next step is the sentence structure of statistics: estimation and testing — 1.4 Statistical inference.

title: 1.1 Descriptive Statistics
text: Descriptive statistics compress a sample into a few honest numbers: where is the center, how wide is the spread, what shape is the distribution. Every model diagnostic, every “significant difference,” every anomaly alert you will ever compute rests on these primitives — so the definitions (including the ones with silent variants, like population vs sample SD) must be reflexes.

title: 1.1 Descriptive Statistics
text:
1. Basic Concept
Center. The mean \(\bar{x} = \frac{1}{n}\sum x_i\) is the balance point; the median is the middle value by rank. They coincide for symmetric data; for right-skewed data, mean > median (a few large values drag the mean).
Spread. The variance is the average squared deviation from the mean. Two flavors:
\[s^2_{\text{pop}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2 \qquad s^2_{\text{sample}} = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2\]
The \(n-1\) (Bessel’s correction) in the sample version compensates for the fact that \(\bar{x}\) was estimated from the same data — deviations from an estimated center are systematically too small. Standard deviation is the square root, back in data units.






Position and shape. Quartiles split the sorted data into quarters; the IQR (Q3 − Q1) is the spread of the middle half — robust to outliers. Skewness measures asymmetry (positive = right tail).






Robustness ranking (how much a single extreme value can move the statistic):

mean, SD — sensitive (breakdown point 0%)
median — robust (breakdown point 50%)
IQR — robust, but less so than the median (breakdown point 25%: a quarter of the sample sent to infinity replaces \(Q_1\) or \(Q_3\) and the IQR follows)
trimmed mean — tunable middle ground

title: 1.1 Descriptive Statistics
text:
2. Concept Questions

Why does the sample variance divide by \(n-1\) instead of \(n\)?
Your gene-expression distribution has mean 210 and median 85. What shape do you suspect, and which two numbers would you report?
Is the IQR affected by multiplying all values by 10? By adding one extreme value?
When is the mode the most informative measure of center?
What does ddof=0 vs ddof=1 change in np.std, and which does pandas use by default?



Answers


Deviations are taken from the sample mean, which is itself fitted to the data; the fitted center absorbs part of the variability, shrinking deviations. Dividing by the degrees of freedom \(n-1\) unbias the estimate of the population variance (for normal data, exactly).
Strong right skew (a minority of very high values). Report median and IQR (robust pair); if you must report the mean, report it with the median so the skew is visible.
Multiplying by 10: IQR scales by 10 (it’s in data units). One extreme value beyond the fences: IQR is unaffected as long as it doesn’t cross the 25th/75th percentiles — that’s the point of quartile-based spread.
For categorical or discrete data (“most common category”), and for multimodal continuous data where mean and median both describe nothing real (“typical patient: bimodal, modes at X and Y”).
ddof = delta degrees of freedom subtracted from n. ddof=0 → population formula; ddof=1 → sample formula. NumPy defaults to 0, pandas to 1 — mixing pandas and NumPy without noticing this is a classic silent bug.

title: 1.1 Descriptive Statistics
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.




















Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Write summarize(x) returning {"n", "mean", "sd", "median", "iqr", "min", "max"} using sample SD. Test it on normal data and on lognormal data; state which summary number changes most between the two and why.


Solution







The mean and SD blow up under lognormal data (they inherit the heavy tail), while median and IQR stay near their symmetric-data values — the empirical demonstration of robustness. Report median/IQR for skewed data.

Exercise 2. IQR outlier rule: flag values outside \([Q_1 - 1.5\,\text{IQR},\ Q_3 + 1.5\,\text{IQR}]\) in the dataset below. Then compute z-scores and flag \(|z| > 3\). Compare the flagged sets and explain the disagreement.


Solution







The z-score rule uses the mean and SD — which the outlier itself inflates. One extreme value widened the SD so much that even the outlier isn’t 3 SDs out (masking). Quartile-based rules don’t have this self-blinding property: for small samples, prefer the IQR fence.

Exercise 3. Empirically verify Bessel’s correction: sample n = 5 points from a known distribution many times; for each sample compute variance with ddof=0 and ddof=1; average each. Which average converges to the true variance?


Solution







ddof=0 averages to \(0.8\sigma^2\) here (\((n-1)/n = 4/5\)) — a 20% underestimate, every time, silently. This is why the divisor choice is not a technicality.

title: 1.1 Descriptive Statistics
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

pandas vs NumPy ddof defaults disagree (pandas std/var use ddof=1; NumPy uses ddof=0). Numbers in mixed reports can differ by ~√(n/(n−1)) for no reason.
NaN handling differs: np.mean poisons, np.nanmean skips, pandas .mean() skips and warns differently — know which behavior produced a reported number.
Percentile interpolation: np.percentile linearly interpolates by default; small-n quartiles depend on this convention (9 conventions exist; R’s type=7 matches NumPy’s linear).
SD is not the “typical deviation” for skewed data: with a heavy right tail, most deviations are below the SD. IQR communicates spread more honestly there.
The mean minimizes squared error, the median absolute error — which is why least squares regression (Part 2) is mean-focused and least-absolutes-deviations is median-focused.
stats.mode behavior changed across SciPy versions (now returns a ModeResult object); pd.Series.mode is the stable, readable choice.
Descriptives ≠ inference: a summary is a claim about this sample; Part 1.4 is about claims regarding the population.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated summary function has three bugs. Run it on the test data and find them.








What’s wrong, and the fixed version


Population SD (ddof=0) — for a sample summary this underestimates spread; specify and use ddof=1.
range on data containing NaN returns nan, not a number — one missing value destroys the statistic with no warning. range is also a fragile descriptives choice (a single typo’d value sets it); report min/max separately at most, or use a robust span.
No NaN policy — the function does not die on the NaN, which is worse: mean, sd and range all come back nan and the caller gets a dict of silent garbage. Make the policy explicit (dropna=True, or raise on missing data).

title: 1.1 Descriptive Statistics
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Prove (or verify by simulation) that the sample mean is the value \(c\) minimizing \(\sum_i (x_i - c)^2\), and the sample median minimizes \(\sum_i |x_i - c|\). What does each say about which errors the mean vs median take most seriously?


Hint

Differentiate \(\sum (x_i-c)^2\) in \(c\); for the absolute value, argue by moving \(c\) across data points and counting how many terms’ slope changes.



Solution

Mean: \(f(c)=\sum(x_i-c)^2\) has \(f'(c) = -2\sum(x_i-c)\), zero exactly at \(c=\bar{x}\) (second derivative \(2n>0\)). Median: \(g(c)=\sum|x_i-c|\) has slope \(= (\#\,\text{points} < c) - (\#\,\text{points} > c)\), which changes sign where the counts balance — the median. So the mean’s optimality is defined in squared error: a single far point contributes quadratically, dominating the objective — hence the mean chases outliers. The median’s objective is linear in each error: one far point costs the same as one near point — hence its robustness. This one paragraph explains robust statistics, why least-squares regression is outlier-sensitive, and why quantile regression exists.

Q2. Two labs each report SD ≈ 2.0 for the same assay. Lab A ran n = 5, Lab B ran n = 5,000. Construct a scenario where both reports are true, and explain which additional number distinguishes them (preview: it is not the SD).


Solution

Both labs can honestly report \(s \approx 2.0\) — SD describes individual measurement spread and barely depends on n. What distinguishes them is the precision of their estimated means: the standard error \(s/\sqrt{n}\) ≈ 0.89 for Lab A vs 0.028 for Lab B — a 30-fold difference. SD answers “how noisy is one measurement,” SE answers “how well do I know the center.” Confusing the two (reporting SD where SE is meant, or vice versa) is a notorious publication bug; the inference machinery that formalizes it arrives in 1.4 Statistical inference.

title: 1.1 Descriptive Statistics
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (descriptives × 0.4 EDA). For the lognormal samples from Section 1, produce side-by-side: (a) histogram of x, (b) histogram of log x with a normal-density overlay scaled to the log data. Which single transformation converts all the robust-vs-sensitive summary disagreements (mean/median, SD/IQR) into non-issues, and what does that imply about when those disagreements matter?
C2 (descriptives × 3.1.5 AUPRC preview). A screening cohort has 1% disease prevalence. Compute the mean/median of the binary label vector and explain, in descriptive-statistics language, why accuracy is a nearly useless summary for a classifier on this data (predicting all-healthy scores 99%). Which descriptive statistic of the confusion matrix would you report instead, and why is it robust to the prevalence imbalance?

title: 1.1 Descriptive Statistics
text:
7. Summary

Center: mean (balance, sensitive) vs median (rank, robust); skew shows as mean − median.
Spread: SD for symmetric data, IQR for skewed; ddof=0 vs 1 is a real bias, and pandas/NumPy disagree by default.
Quartiles + IQR fences detect outliers without being blinded by them; z-scores can be.
NaN policy is part of the statistic: nan-skipping is a decision, not a default to trust blindly.
Mean ↔︎ squared error, median ↔︎ absolute error: robustness follows from the loss function.
SD describes single measurements; SE describes the precision of a mean — next pages formalize this.
Summaries describe samples; to argue about populations you need probability and inference: 1.2 Relationships first asks how two variables move together.

title: 0.4 Visualisation & Exploratory Analysis
text: Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) is the discipline of interrogating data before modeling: distributions first, relationships second, anomalies always. matplotlib is the plotting engine under nearly every Python plotting library (pandas plotting calls it, seaborn wraps it), so we drill it directly.

title: 0.4 Visualisation & Exploratory Analysis
text:
1. Basic Concept
matplotlib has two layers: the pyplot state machine (plt.plot(...)) for quick plots, and the object-oriented interface (fig, ax = plt.subplots(); then ax.plot(...)) which is the right habit for anything non-trivial. Anatomy you should be able to name: Figure (the canvas), Axes (one plot panel), axis (with limits, ticks, labels), title, legend.






The three plots that carry 90% of EDA:






EDA is a loop, not a plot. The minimal protocol you should run on any new table:

.head(), .shape, .dtypes — what is this, actually?
.describe() and .isna().sum() — ranges, centers, holes.
Histogram of every numeric column — skew, multimodality, impossible values (negative ages).
Scatter/correlation for relationships you care about.
Boxplots by group — does grouping explain spread?

title: 0.4 Visualisation & Exploratory Analysis
text:
2. Concept Questions

In fig, ax = plt.subplots(), what is the type and role of ax?
Your histogram has one tall bar at 0 and a flat sea of bars to the right. What transform should you almost certainly try?
Why is alpha=0.3 or smaller essential when scatter-plotting thousands of points?
What does a boxplot’s whisker-cap convention actually mark, and what is plotted as individual points?
Name two questions a groupby + boxplot answers that describe() alone cannot.



Answers


ax is an Axes object — one panel. All plotting methods hang off it (ax.hist, ax.set_xlabel); the OO interface avoids pyplot’s hidden global state and is required for multi-panel figures.
A log transform (np.log10 / np.log1p). Mean ≫ median in .describe() is the numeric tell; a spike at zero with a long right tail is the visual tell.
Overplotting: with thousands of points, opaque markers hide density — the plot then shows only where points exist, not where they concentrate. Alpha (transparency) makes density visible as darkness.
Whiskers mark the most extreme data points within 1.5×IQR of the quartiles; points beyond are drawn individually as (candidate) outliers. The fence is a convention, not a definition of “outlier.”
Whether distributions differ in shape (not just center) between groups, and whether sample sizes are comparable (a tiny group’s mean is noise). describe() pools everything.

title: 0.4 Visualisation & Exploratory Analysis
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Small plotting reflexes. For each: predict the shape of the output, run, compare.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Full EDA pass on the simulated cohort in one figure: (a) 2×2 grid with histograms of age, log10(marker), a scatter of age vs log-marker, and a boxplot of log-marker by group. Every panel titled and every axis labeled.


Solution







Note the log transform before plotting the skewed marker — the histogram becomes readable and the boxplot comparison becomes fair.

Exercise 2. Demonstrate bin-width sensitivity: plot the same 200-point sample as 5, 20, and 100-bin histograms side by side. Write one sentence on what the “right” number of bins depends on.


Solution







There is no “right” bin count — it depends on sample size and the question (rough guides: Sturges 1+log2(n), Freedman–Diaconis based on IQR). With n=200, 100 bins mostly display sampling noise; 5 bins can hide bimodality. Look at several.

Exercise 3. Build a scatter matrix (pairplot by hand): for the 3 numeric columns of the cohort, produce a 3×3 grid, diagonal = histograms, off-diagonal = scatter. No seaborn.


Solution







This double loop is the whole idea of a pairs plot (R: GGally::ggpairs). You will later recognize PCA and clustering as ways to make such grids interpretable in high dimensions.

title: 0.4 Visualisation & Exploratory Analysis
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Y-axis truncation exaggerates differences. Bar charts starting at non-zero are a classic misleading visual (and a classic reviewer complaint). For line charts truncation is fine; for bars, don’t.
Dual axes are a lie amplifier. Two independent y-scales let you manufacture any “correlation.” Prefer two stacked panels sharing an x-axis.
Log scales with zeros/negatives break (log(0) = -inf): use symlog or transform with np.log1p after checking for non-positives.
Histograms are model statements: bins impose structure that may not exist (bimodality can appear/vanish with bin width — Exercise 2).
Correlation plots lie under nonlinearity: r ≈ 0 says “no linear relation,” nothing more (see 1.2 Relationships).
Colorblind-safe palettes (tab10, viridis) and direct labeling beat red-green pairs and remote legends.
matplotlib in Pyodide: always end with plt.show(); set fig-width/fig-height cell options (inches) rather than figsize when you want consistent embedding.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated figure has four problems (three visual, one data). Run it, list them before opening the solution.








What’s wrong, and the fixed version


Truncated bar axis (y from 9.0): turns a modest mean difference into a towering bar. Bars must start at 0 — or better, show the distribution instead of two means.
Unlabeled, indistinguishable scatter series: same color/marker for both groups, no legend, x-axis meaningless. Need labels + legend + real x (e.g. strip/jitter plot).
Wrong Axes: the histogram is drawn on the bar chart’s panel (axes[0]), overwriting the bars. Use the intended panel (axes[1] or a third).
State-machine mixing: plt.show() after building with fig, axes is fine, but any further plt.hist-style calls would target the current figure implicitly. Stay in one interface.

title: 0.4 Visualisation & Exploratory Analysis
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. A colleague says: “the histogram is bimodal, so there are two subpopulations.” Give three alternative explanations and describe the EDA you would run to distinguish them.


Hint

Think: sampling noise (Exercise 2), mixtures of process regimes (batch), and transform artifacts.



Solution


Sampling noise: with small n, bin counts fluctuate into a fake second mode — re-draw with different bin widths/seeds (Exercise 2 logic) and bootstrap the histogram. (b) Batch/technical structure: data collected in two runs, sites, or instruments — color the histogram by batch; check within-batch shape; a two-sample test across the suspected split (1.4 Statistical inference) should vanish within batch. (c) Transform artifact: e.g. log of a mixture of a point-mass at zero plus positives, or periodic rounding (integer counts). Plot untransformed, check value granularity. Also consider a genuine mixture — but the burden of proof is after (a)–(c) are excluded: overlay a fitted two-component normal mixture and check the gap depth.


Q2. Explain why ax.set_yscale("log") often “fixes” a scatter where the vertical spread grows with x, and what that visual pattern implies for modeling choices later (name the variance structure).


Solution

Funnel-shaped residuals — spread proportional to the mean level — indicate multiplicative noise: y = f(x)·ε rather than y = f(x) + ε. Multiplicative error becomes additive and roughly homoscedastic after a log transform, which is why log axes tidy such plots. Modeling consequence: fit the model to log(y) (or use a GLM with a log link and variance proportional to mean², gamma/Poisson-style), rather than vanilla least squares which weights the large-y points overwhelmingly. The EDA observation is literally a specification diagnostic for Part 2 regression.

title: 0.4 Visualisation & Exploratory Analysis
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (EDA × 0.3 pandas). Using groupby + the plotting drills, construct the “small multiples” figure: one histogram per group on a shared x-range. Which two pandas/matplotlib mechanics make shared scales essential for honest comparison, and what does each group’s count tell you about how much to trust each panel?
C2 (EDA × 1.1 Descriptive statistics). Generate lognormal data, then plot mean and median of increasing samples (n = 5, 10, 50, 200, 1000, each resampled many times) as dot strips. Which estimator’s strip narrows faster, and how does the histogram shape you saw in Section 1 predict that result? Connect: skew → sampling distribution of the mean vs median → why “median for skewed data” is a precision claim, not just an aesthetic one.

title: 0.4 Visualisation & Exploratory Analysis
text:
7. Summary

EDA protocol: head/dtypes → describe/isna → distributions → relationships → by-group comparisons.
Use the OO interface (fig, ax = plt.subplots()); label everything; end cells with plt.show().
Alpha and jitter reveal density; truncated bar axes and dual y-axes manufacture stories.
Transform skewed data (log) before comparing and plotting — mean ≫ median is the flag.
Bin width is an assumption; look at several before claiming structure.
Boxplots compare distributions; scatter matrices compare everything pairwise.
Pictures suggest; only inference decides — next page sets up the train/test discipline that makes model evaluation honest: 0.5 Data splitting.

title: 0.2 NumPy
text: NumPy is the foundation of the entire Python scientific stack: pandas, scikit-learn, statsmodels, and PyTorch all speak NumPy arrays. The core skill is not memorizing functions — it is learning to think in whole-array operations instead of element-by-element loops.

title: 0.2 NumPy
text:
1. Basic Concept
A NumPy ndarray is an N-dimensional grid of values that are all the same type (dtype), stored in one contiguous block of memory. Because the data is homogeneous and contiguous, operations can be dispatched as compiled loops over memory — this is vectorization, and it is typically 10–100× faster than a Python loop.
Three attributes define an array’s shape story:






Vectorization replaces loops. Here is the same computation both ways:






Broadcasting is how NumPy applies operations between arrays of different but compatible shapes. Rule: compare shapes from the right; each dimension pair must be equal or one of them must be 1; missing (left) dimensions are treated as 1.






This is how you normalize a matrix by column means without writing a loop:

title: 0.2 NumPy
text:
2. Concept Questions

What are the three attributes that describe an array’s structure?
Why is np.array([1, 2, 3]) * np.array([10, 20, 30]) not the dot product, and what is it?
Which shapes can broadcast together: (4, 3) with (3,)? (4, 3) with (4,)?
What does axis=0 mean when calling .sum() on a 2-D array?
a = np.arange(5); b = a[::2]; b[0] = 99 — did a change? Why?



Answers


shape (size per axis), dtype (element type), ndim (number of axes).
* on arrays is elementwise multiplication → [10, 40, 90]. The dot product is a @ b → 140.
(4, 3) with (3,): yes — (3,) is treated as (1, 3) and broadcasts across rows. (4, 3) with (4,): no — right-aligned, 3 vs 4 conflict → ValueError. Fix by making it a column: x[:, None] or x.reshape(-1, 1).
Collapse axis 0, i.e. reduce across rows, producing one value per column.
