Yes. Basic slicing returns a view sharing memory with a, so writing to b writes to a. Use b = a[::2].copy() when you need independence.

title: 0.2 NumPy
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict each output before running.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Given the expression matrix below (4 genes × 6 samples), z-score each gene (each row) using vectorized code — no loops.


Solution







The keepdims=True keeps shape (4,1) so broadcasting subtracts the right mean from the right cells. Without it, (4,) broadcasts across the wrong axis and NumPy raises an error — or worse, silently “works” on a square matrix.

Exercise 2. Simulate 1,000 experiments of 100 fair coin flips each. Estimate the probability that an experiment yields more than 60 heads. Do it with one function call, no loops.


Solution







Sanity check against theory: P(X > 60), X~Binomial(100, 0.5) ≈ 0.0176 — (flips > 60).mean() estimates it via Monte Carlo. The trick (condition).mean() — counting by averaging booleans — is used constantly in simulation work.

Exercise 3. Compute all pairwise Euclidean distances between the rows of a (5, 2) coordinate array using broadcasting only.


Solution







The (i, 1, k) - (1, j, k) pattern broadcasts every row against every row simultaneously. This exact pattern reappears inside KNN, K-means, and kernel methods later in the course.

Exercise 4. One-hot encode the integer labels [2, 0, 3, 1] into a 4-column binary matrix without loops.


Solution







np.eye(4) is the 4×4 identity; fancy-indexing its rows by labels selects row 2, row 0, etc. Same output as sklearn.preprocessing.OneHotEncoder, in one line.

title: 0.2 NumPy
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Views vs copies. Slicing returns a view (memory shared, mutating it mutates the parent); fancy indexing and boolean masking return copies. Silent aliasing bugs look like “my data changed itself.”
Integer overflow is silent. np.array([127], dtype=np.int8) + np.int8(1) wraps to -128 with no warning. NumPy does not upcast like Python ints.
NaN poisons aggregates. np.mean of an array with one NaN is NaN. Use the nan* family (np.nanmean, np.nansum) — but think about why values are missing before averaging around them (see 9.3 Missing values later in the course).
rng.integers(low, high) is high-exclusive; rng.random() spans [0, 1). Off-by-one here produces subtly wrong simulations.
Broadcasting errors vs broadcasting bugs. Shape mismatches raise loud errors, but compatible misaligned shapes (e.g. (4,1) vs (4,)) broadcast “successfully” into something semantically wrong. Print .shape when results look insane.
np.round uses round-half-to-even, unlike naive expectations (np.round(2.5) → 2.0). Same rule as Python’s built-in round.
Floating-point comparison: (a - b) == 0 fails for computed floats; use np.isclose / np.allclose for arrays.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated “normalizer” has three bugs. Run it, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fixed version


Wrong axis / loop mindset: it claims to normalize rows but computes statistics over X[:, j] — columns. For this square matrix the result is column z-scores, exposed by the two checks: row means are not 0, column SDs are 1. (On a non-square matrix the claim and code would diverge even more visibly.) The double loop is also exactly what NumPy exists to avoid.
No invariant check in the original: whoever ran this trusted it because column-SD printed 1s — a check that passes while testing the wrong axis. Always assert the invariant that matches the claim (row means ≈ 0 for row normalization).
int8 overflow: values are within int8 range at construction, but adding 10 in int8 arithmetic wraps past 127 into negatives, silently. Cast to a wider dtype first.







And the honest one-liner replacing the whole loop: (X - X.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True)) / X.std(axis=1, keepdims=True).

title: 0.2 NumPy
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Why is x[:, None] the standard fix when (n,) fails to broadcast against (n, m)? Explain using the right-to-left alignment rule, and give the two operations for which this asymmetry matters most (column-scaling and row-scaling).


Hint

Draw (n,) as (1, n) after alignment and ask which axis it then stretches along.



Solution

Right-aligned, (n,) behaves like (1, n): it varies along columns, so M + v adds v[j] to every row’s j-th entry (row-constant). To scale/shift per row (statistics across columns), you need a (n, 1) array: x[:, None] inserts an axis so the vector varies down rows and broadcasts across columns. It matters most in (1) M - M.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True)-style centering and (2) distance computations A[:, None, :] - B[None, :, :]. The general discipline: every broadcast bug is a shape bug — print shapes, don’t guess.

Q2. np.arange(0, 1, 0.1) and np.linspace(0, 1, 10) look like they should produce the same thing. Explain the actual difference and why linspace is preferred for evenly spaced sampling in continuous ranges.


Hint

How does each decide the step size, and which endpoint is excluded?



Solution

arange(start, stop, step) computes values as start + k*step and excludes stop, accumulating floating-point step error along the way — so np.arange(0, 1, 0.1) yields 10 points ending at ≈0.9 (and can even produce a surprising extra point when the step doesn’t divide the range cleanly). linspace(start, stop, num) takes the count of points and includes both endpoints by default, placing them by index division so spacing is as even as binary floats allow. Rule of thumb: arange for integer steps (e.g. np.arange(10)), linspace for float sampling of an interval.

title: 0.2 NumPy
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (NumPy × 0.5 Data splitting). Using only rng.permutation and slicing, implement train_test_split(X, y, frac=0.8, seed=0) yourself. Then verify it agrees with sklearn.model_selection.train_test_split in spirit (same sizes, same seed → same partition) — where do the implementations necessarily differ? What does this exercise teach you about what random_state actually guarantees?
C2 (NumPy × 9.2 PCA preview). Center a random (100, 3) matrix column-wise, compute its covariance with np.cov(Z, rowvar=False), and take np.linalg.eigh of it. What is the sum of eigenvalues, and how does it relate to np.trace of the covariance and to the total variance Z.var(axis=0, ddof=1).sum()? This identity (total variance = trace = sum of eigenvalues) is the backbone of PCA’s “explained variance ratio.”

title: 0.2 NumPy
text:
7. Summary

An ndarray is a homogeneous, contiguous grid: shape, dtype, ndim describe everything.
Vectorization pushes loops into compiled code — think in whole-array expressions.
Broadcasting aligns shapes from the right; 1s stretch; make column vectors with x[:, None].
Slices are views, masks/fancy indices are copies; keepdims=True keeps broadcasting honest.
Booleans sum as 1/0: (cond).mean() is an estimator, not a trick.
Watch int8 overflow, NaN-poisoned aggregates, exclusive high in integers, and banker’s rounding.
Arrays hold the numbers; labeled data with mixed types needs pandas — next page.

Next: 0.3 pandas puts names, labels, and mixed types on top of this machinery — and introduces its own selection and grouping semantics that you must drill separately.

title: 0.1 Python for Numerical Work
text: Python is the substrate everything else in this course is written in. Before touching NumPy, pandas, or scikit-learn, your reflexes in core Python — types, functions, comprehensions, error messages — need to be automatic. This page drills exactly those reflexes, with a bias toward the numerical/data style of Python rather than web or scripting styles.

title: 0.1 Python for Numerical Work
text:
1. Basic Concept
Python is a dynamically typed language: names are labels attached to objects, not boxes with fixed types. For numerical work you mostly live with four scalar types (int, float, bool, str) and four container types (list, tuple, dict, set).
One fact causes more numerical bugs than anything else: Python float is IEEE-754 binary floating point, so most decimal fractions cannot be stored exactly.






The second fact to internalize: / is always true division; // is floor division; % is the remainder.






A function is defined with def, returns with return (no return means it returns None), and can take default arguments:






Comprehensions are the idiomatic way to transform collections. If you are writing a for loop whose only job is to build a list, you should usually write a comprehension instead:






f-strings format values into text — you will use them constantly to report results:

title: 0.1 Python for Numerical Work
text:
2. Concept Questions
Answer from memory first, then open each answer to check.

What does 10 / 4 evaluate to, and what type is the result?
Why is 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 False? Name the underlying cause.
What is the difference between a list and a tuple? Give one practical consequence.
What does a function return if you never write return?
In f"{x:.2f}", what does the .2f part do?



Answers


2.5, a float. In Python 3, / always produces a float, even for whole-number results (8 / 2 is 4.0).
0.1 and 0.2 have no exact representation in binary floating point (IEEE-754). Their nearest representable values don’t sum to the nearest representable 0.3. Compare with a tolerance (math.isclose) instead.
Lists are mutable, tuples are immutable. Consequence: tuples can be dictionary keys and elements of sets; lists cannot. Also, accidentally mutating a tuple raises an error, which can protect data.
None.
Format x as a fixed-point number with exactly 2 digits after the decimal point (rounding half-to-even on the decimal representation).

title: 0.1 Python for Numerical Work
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict each line’s output before running. These rebuild reflexes — do them until automatic.




















Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Write a function celsius_to_fahrenheit(c) that converts a temperature and returns the result rounded to 1 decimal place. Then use it in a comprehension to convert [0, 37, 100].


Solution








Exercise 2. Given the DNA string below, compute (a) its length, (b) GC content as a percentage with 1 decimal, (c) its reverse complement. Use one comprehension and one dictionary somewhere.


Solution







Note: reversed(seq) + join is O(n); building a string with += in a loop is O(n²) — a classic performance trap.

Exercise 3. FizzBuzz, data edition: for integers 1–20, print Bio if divisible by 3, Stats if divisible by 5, BioStats if divisible by both, otherwise the number — as a single list of strings.


Solution







Order matters: check the compound condition (% 15 == 0) first, otherwise the simple cases win. Same idea as writing mutually exclusive if/elif branches.

Exercise 4. Parse this mini-FASTA (a real task shape in bioinformatics) and report each sequence’s length and GC%:
>gene1
ATGGCC
>gene2
GCGCGCGCGT


Solution







sum(b in "GC" for b in seq) works because True/False sum as 1/0 — an idiom worth owning.

title: 0.1 Python for Numerical Work
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls
Pitfalls that bite numerical/data Python specifically:

Mutable default arguments are created once, at function definition — not at each call. def f(x, acc=[]) shares the same list across all calls. This is the single most common “haunted function” bug.
is compares identity, == compares value. Never write x is 5 — it happens to work for small ints in CPython and breaks everywhere else.
Floats in loops accumulate error. Summing 10 million floats with + loses precision; use math.fsum or better, NumPy (np.sum uses pairwise summation).
Chained comparison is a feature: 0 < x < 1 means (0 < x) and (x < 1). Nice, but it changes short-circuit semantics.
Names resolve at call time, not definition time (closures see the current value of outer variables, a classic loop-closure bug).
Everything is an object: 1 and True compare equal (1 == True), and bool is a subclass of int. So [1, 2].count(True) counts True, not 1… except it counts both, because True == 1. Watch out in data cleaning.


Read & Refactor AI Code
The following AI-generated snippet looks reasonable but contains three bugs. Run it, observe the wrong behavior, find the bugs, and fix them in the editor.








What’s wrong, and the fixed version


Mutable default argument. The default list is created once, so the second call appends to the first call’s list. Fix: default to None and create the list inside.
is with floats. Identity comparison, not equality; 30.0 is not the same object as the literal in the function. Fix: ==, or better math.isclose for computed floats.
// instead of /. Floor division silently truncates the mean. Fix: /.

title: 0.1 Python for Numerical Work
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Explain precisely why 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3 in terms of binary representation. Why is 0.5 stored exactly but 0.1 not?


Hint

Write 0.1, 0.2, 0.5 as sums of powers of 1/2. Which terminate?



Solution

IEEE-754 doubles store numbers as ±m × 2^e with a 53-bit significand. A decimal fraction is exactly representable only if it is a dyadic rational — a fraction whose denominator is a power of 2. 0.5 = 1/2 is dyadic: exact. 0.1 = 1/10 needs denominator 2 × 5; the factor 5 is impossible in binary, so 0.1 rounds to the nearest 53-bit binary fraction: 0.1000000000000000055511151231257827.... Adding the two rounded values 0.1 + 0.2 gives a value whose rounded nearest double is 0.30000000000000004, one ulp above 0.3’s nearest double. Consequence for practice: never test float equality; test abs(a-b) < tol or math.isclose(a, b, rel_tol=1e-9, abs_tol=0.0). For exact decimal money/counting semantics use decimal.Decimal or integers.

Q2. What does this print, and why?








Hint

Closures capture variables, not values. When do the lambdas look up f?



Solution

[9, 9, 9]. Each lambda closes over the variable f; by the time they are called, the loop finished and f holds 3, so every call computes 3*3. Fix by binding at definition time: lambda f=f: f*f (default argument evaluated immediately), or use a factory function def make(f): return lambda: f*f. The same late-binding logic explains why a list of functions that reference a module-level config variable all change behavior when you reassign that variable.

title: 0.1 Python for Numerical Work
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (functions × strings × loops → bioinformatics). Write translate(seq) that translates a DNA string to an amino-acid one-letter string using the standard genetic code, handling (a) lowercase input, (b) a trailing partial codon, (c) stop codons marked *. Test on ATGGCCATTGTAATGGGCCGCTGAAAGGGTGCCCGATAG (you can hardcode just the codons you need, or a 64-entry dict). When you reach 0.2 NumPy, consider which parts of this problem could be vectorized — and which fundamentally cannot (hint: the lookup table is not arithmetic).
C2 (this page × 1.1 Descriptive statistics). Write a pure-Python function summary(xs) returning a dict with n, mean, median, min, max, computed without importing anything. Then check: what happens with an empty list, a list of one element, and a list containing None? Design your function’s error behavior deliberately (raise ValueError? skip None?) — this is exactly the design decision pandas makes for you with skipna=True.

title: 0.1 Python for Numerical Work
text:
7. Summary

Python names point to objects; types live on the objects, not the names.
/ is true division, // floors, % gives the remainder; floats are IEEE-754 binary — compare with math.isclose, never ==.
Comprehensions > loops for building collections; f-strings > string concatenation for output.
Functions returning None by default and mutable default arguments are top sources of silent bugs.
is checks identity; == checks equality; empty containers are falsy.
Closures look up variables at call time — late binding breaks loop-generated functions.
Pure-Python numeric loops are slow: the moment you have arrays of numbers, you want 0.2 NumPy, which pushes loops into compiled code and changes how you express numerical ideas entirely.

title: 0.3 pandas
text: NumPy arrays are fast but anonymous — columns have no names, rows have no identity, and mixed types are impossible. pandas adds labels. It is the Python twin of R’s data frame (the tidyverse’s tibble), and it will be your main tool for loading, cleaning, and summarizing data before any model sees it.

title: 0.3 pandas
text:
1. Basic Concept
A DataFrame is a rectangular table: each column is a Series (a labeled 1-D array with one dtype), and rows share an index. Think: dict of columns + shared row labels.






Two selectors, two jobs. loc selects by label, iloc by integer position, and both use [rows, columns]:






groupby is the split–apply–combine engine and probably the single most used pandas verb:






merging joins two tables on a key — the same mental model as SQL joins:

title: 0.3 pandas
text:
2. Concept Questions

What is the difference between df["expr"] and df[["expr"]]?
When do loc and iloc give different answers for the same-looking call?
Why does df[df["expr"] > 10]["expr"] = 0 silently fail to change df?
What does how="left" in merge guarantee, and what can it create?
What does df.groupby("tissue")["expr"].transform("mean") return, and how is it different from .mean()?



Answers


df["expr"] returns a Series; df[["expr"]] returns a one-column DataFrame. Many methods (.T, joining, multiple columns) behave differently on the two.
When the index labels are not 0..n-1 (e.g. after filtering, or a named index). loc["S2", ...] finds the row named S2; iloc[1, ...] finds the second row whatever it’s called.
Chained indexing: the first bracket may return a temporary copy, so the assignment can land on a copy that’s then discarded (the classic SettingWithCopyWarning). The correct form assigns through one loc call: df.loc[df["expr"] > 10, "expr"] = 0.
Left merge keeps every row of the left table; rows with no match on the right get NaN in the right columns (a merge “fan-out” can also multiply rows if the key is duplicated on the right).
transform("mean") returns a Series the same length/index as df — the group mean broadcast back to each row — so you can subtract it to center within groups. .mean() returns one row per group.

title: 0.3 pandas
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
We’ll build one small cohort table and predict outputs before running each cell.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. From the cohort df above: build a summary table with one row per group showing mean age, mean marker, and patient count, then add a column is_old (age > 50) and recompute the table splitting on both group and is_old.


Solution







The agg(col=("source", "func")) named aggregation syntax produces clean column names in one pass — no renaming afterwards.

Exercise 2. Merge a measurements table with a demographic table (left join), count missing matches, and fill missing site values with "unknown".


Solution







P03 exists in measurements but not demographics → left join keeps it, site becomes NaN. This exact pattern (merge → count NaN → decide policy) is 90% of real data integration.

Exercise 3. Given the wide expression table below (rows = genes, columns = samples), compute each gene’s mean and variance, keep genes with variance above 2.0, and melt the survivors into long format (gene, sample, value).


Solution







Wide ↔︎ long reshaping (melt / pivot) is the pandas equivalent of tidyverse’s pivot_longer / pivot_wider. Most plotting and modeling tools want long format.

title: 0.3 pandas
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Chained assignment is the #1 pandas bug. df[df.a > 0]["b"] = 1 may write to a temporary copy. Always: single loc call → df.loc[mask, "b"] = 1. (pandas 3.0’s copy-on-write makes chained assignment fail loudly; the pyodide pandas here is 2.x, where it can still silently no-op.)
inplace=True is deprecated style. It mutates the object you may not own and prevents method chaining. Prefer df = df.dropna() or df.dropna(subset=["marker"], inplace=False).
Index is not “row number”. After filtering, .iloc[0] and .index[0] diverge. Reset with reset_index(drop=True) when position and label must agree again.
merge can silently multiply rows if the key is duplicated on either side — always check len(result) vs len(left) and result["key"].value_counts().
== on a column with NaN gives False, never NaN: df[df["x"] == np.nan] matches nothing. Use df["x"].isna().
Object dtype columns are slow (Python objects, not arrays). Convert strings to category when few distinct values; parse dates with pd.to_datetime immediately.
groupby drops groups containing NaN keys by default (dropna=True) — a silent row-loss channel in reports.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated analysis has three bugs. Run it, observe, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fixed version


Chained assignment: high may be a copy, so the mark never lands in df (see the printed 0). Fix with df.loc[df["value"] > 10, "site"] = "HIGH".
NaN never equals NaN: count is 0 despite two NaNs. Fix: df["value"].isna().sum().
Loop + manual dict is slower, noisier, and easier to get wrong than groupby; also the loop’s .mean() results are fine here but the pattern invites index bugs. Fix: df.groupby("site")["value"].mean().

title: 0.3 pandas
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. A colleague merges a 20,000-row measurements table with a 200-row annotation table and the result has 23,117 rows. Diagnose the likely causes and give a defensive merge recipe.


Hint

What does validate= in merge do? What does a duplicated key do to row counts?



Solution

The key is duplicated: an m-to-many join multiplies rows (each left row matches every right row with the same key). Diagnosis: anno["gene"].value_counts().head(), compare len(left), len(right), len(merged); check merged["gene"].is_unique. Defensive recipe: merged = meas.merge(anno, on="gene", how="left", validate="m:1") — raises instead of fanning out; or deduplicate anno.drop_duplicates("gene") first; assert len(merged) == len(meas) afterwards. Choosing validate is documentation and a runtime guard.

Q2. Explain the difference between apply, transform, and agg on a groupby object, and why apply is the dangerous one. Give a task where apply is genuinely required.


Solution

agg collapses each group to one value (len = n groups). transform returns one value per input row (len = n rows, group statistic broadcast back). apply returns whatever your function returns — a scalar, a Series, or a DataFrame — so pandas has to guess how to assemble results, which is slower and produces surprising shapes/indexes. Use agg/transform whenever possible; reach for apply when you need genuinely per-group multi-row computation, e.g. fitting a per-group linear model and returning its coefficients as a Series: df.groupby("site").apply(lambda g: pd.Series(np.polyfit(g["x"], g["y"], 1), index=["slope", "intercept"])). In modern pandas, prefer groupby(...).filter(...) for row selection and named agg for summaries to keep types predictable.

title: 0.3 pandas
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (pandas × 0.4 Visualisation). Take the cohort df and produce, in long format, everything needed to plot marker distributions per group: which table shape does matplotlib’s ax.boxplot want (list of arrays) and which does a pandas .boxplot(by=...) want? Convert between wide and long to produce the same figure both ways — internalize why “tidy/long” is the interchange format and “wide” is a display choice.
C2 (pandas × 1.2 Relationships). For the cohort data, compute the correlation matrix of the numeric columns (df.corr(numeric_only=True)), then compute it within groups (df.groupby("group").corr(numeric_only=True)). Under what real-world condition can the pooled correlation have the opposite sign from every within-group correlation (Simpson’s paradox)? Construct a 3-line synthetic example demonstrating it.

title: 0.3 pandas
text:
7. Summary

A DataFrame is labeled columns of Series sharing an index; dtypes tells you what you actually have.
loc = labels, iloc = positions; filtering is df.loc[mask, cols] — one call, no chaining.
groupby + agg/transform covers split–apply–combine; transform broadcasts back to row shape.
merge(how="left", validate="m:1") with NaN-counting afterwards is the safe join recipe.
NaN: use .isna(), skipna defaults, and decide drop-vs-fill deliberately.
Wide is for humans, long is for machines; melt/pivot convert between them.
Numbers on a page lie less than pictures — next page turns these tables into plots that reveal structure before you model it: 0.4 Visualisation & EDA.

title: 0.5 Data Splitting
text: Every model in this course will be judged by one rule: performance on data it did not see during training. The mechanics of splitting data seem trivial — and that’s exactly why leakage bugs are so common. This page drills the mechanics so they’re automatic before Part 2 builds models on top of them.

title: 0.5 Data Splitting
text:
1. Basic Concept
The test set estimates how a model performs on new data. The core failure mode is leakage: any information from the test set (or from future data) influencing the training process inflates that estimate.
The basic protocol with sklearn.model_selection.train_test_split:






random_state seeds the shuffling: same seed → identical split → reproducible results. It does not make the split “better.”
For classification with imbalanced classes, use stratify=y so each split preserves class proportions:






One split gives one noisy number. K-fold cross-validation averages over K splits — every sample is in a validation fold exactly once:

title: 0.5 Data Splitting
text:
2. Concept Questions

Why must the test set be used once, at the end — what exactly is lost if you peek repeatedly?
What does stratify=y protect you from, and when is it useless?
Why does random_state matter in research code even when results “should” be stable?
In 5-fold CV, how many times is each sample used for validation, and how many times for training?
Your test R² is better than your training R². Give one benign explanation and one suspicious one.



Answers


Repeatedly peeking at test performance and making choices (features, hyperparameters, stopping) based on it trains on the test set through you: the estimate stops being out-of-sample and becomes optimistically biased. The test set’s value is spent by adaptation.
It preserves class proportions across splits — essential for rare classes (a 2% class can be absent from a small test split). Useless/unnecessary for regression (continuous y), and it can’t fix too small data: if a class has fewer members than folds, even stratified splitting fails.
Same seed → same split → run-to-run reproducibility, which is what makes bug fixes, reviewer requests, and controlled comparisons possible. Unseeded splits confound “different partition” with “different method.”
Exactly once for validation; K−1 = 4 times for training (in different combinations).
Benign: the test split happens to be easy, or training metrics are computed on a regularized objective (e.g. penalized loss) while test R² is unpenalized. Suspicious: leakage — test information reached training (scaled together, duplicated rows, feature derived from the outcome). Investigate, don’t celebrate.

title: 0.5 Data Splitting
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Simulate a small classification dataset (500 samples, 2% positives), split it badly (no stratify, seed chosen “unluckily”) and well (stratify). Report positives in each test set. Then quantify: repeat the unstratified split 500 times and report the range of positive counts in the test set.


Solution







A test set with zero positives makes recall, AUC, and AUPRC literally undefined. Stratification is not cosmetic.

Exercise 2. Write a 5-fold CV loop by hand (KFold + explicit fit/predict on a LinearRegression) for the synthetic regression data from Section 1, collecting validation R² per fold. Report the mean and the standard deviation across folds — then explain why that SD, not just the mean, matters.


Solution







The mean estimates expected performance; the SD across folds estimates how stable that number is. Mean ± SD ≈ 0.85 ± 0.06 and mean ± SD ≈ 0.85 ± 0.30 are very different claims about your model — an unstable CV is a red flag for high variance (see 4.4 Bias–variance trade-off).

Exercise 3 — the leakage lab. Build a dataset where one feature is derived from the outcome (leaky = y + noise). Compare (a) a model trained with the leaky feature vs (b) without, using a proper split. Then do it “wrong”: scale X on the full dataset before splitting. Which comparisons change? Quantify each difference.


Solution







Read the results: the leaky feature produces near-perfect accuracy by construction — the single most common way “too good to be true” results reach publication. Pre-split scaling is the same crime at lower dose: test-row means/variances shaped the training inputs.

title: 0.5 Data Splitting
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Leakage taxonomy: (1) feature leakage — a column derived from y (outcomes aggregated into features, “post-treatment” variables); (2) preprocessing leakage — scaling/imputation/feature selection fitted before the split; (3) duplication leakage — the same patient/sample appearing in train and test; (4) temporal leakage — shuffling time series so the model trains on the future.
The fix for (2) is always the same shape: fit the transformer inside the training fold only — StandardScaler().fit(X_tr), then .transform(X_te). In pipelines: make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), Ridge()) + cross_val_score does this mechanically and correctly.
Duplicate rows before splitting: drop_duplicates / group-aware splitting by patient ID (GroupKFold) — not by row.
test_size semantics: float = proportion, int = absolute count. Tiny test sets (n < ~30 per class) make every performance estimate mostly noise (4.1 The generalization problem).
shuffle=False is the correct default for time-ordered data — train_test_split shuffles by default, which is wrong for temporal splits.
Reproducibility chain: seed the split and any stochastic model; a notebook is only reproducible if every source of randomness is pinned.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated evaluation pipeline contains three bugs, two of them leakage. Run it, then fix.








What’s wrong, and the fixed version


Pre-split scaling — test statistics leaked into training inputs. Fit the scaler on X_tr only.
No stratification — with ~48% positives here it’s tolerable, but the code must not depend on luck; make stratify=y unconditional.
Evaluating on training data — score(X_tr, y_tr) measures memorization, not generalization. Score on X_te, y_te.







Test ≤ train, and both are believable — that’s what an honest pipeline looks like.

title: 0.5 Data Splitting
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. A reviewer asks why your cross-validation used shuffle=True, random_state=42. Justify both choices, and explain when shuffle=True would be wrong.


Hint

What order were the rows in? What does an unshuffled KFold fold look like if the table is sorted by group or by time?



Solution

shuffle=True protects against order artifacts: real data frames are often sorted (by site, date, or outcome), and unshuffled KFold then makes folds that are systematically different from each other — e.g. sorted-by-class data can place an entire class in one fold, making it a training-only class for other folds. random_state makes the shuffling deterministic so the estimate is reproducible and comparable across code changes. shuffle=True is wrong when row order carries information: time series (train must precede test — use TimeSeriesSplit), spliced biological batches where you want to generalize to a new batch (use GroupKFold/leave-one-batch-out instead), and grouped data where rows share a subject (shuffle splits subject’s rows across train/test — leakage). The seed is part of the protocol, like the test set itself.

Q2. Your test set has 200 samples and true accuracy 80%. What is the standard error of the measured accuracy, and what does that imply about differences of 1–2 points between two models’ test scores?


Hint

Binomial SE = √(p(1−p)/n). Compute it for p = 0.8, n = 200.



Solution

SE = √(0.8·0.2/200) = √0.0008 ≈ 0.028 (2.8 percentage points). Two models measured 81% vs 83% on this test set differ by ~0.7 SE — indistinguishable from partition noise. Implications: (1) report uncertainty with test metrics, not just points; (2) prefer cross-validation for comparisons (averages over splits); (3) reserve the biggest test set you can afford; (4) resist leaderboard-grade conclusions from small test sets. This is the bridge to 4.1 The generalization problem and 4.3 Cross-validation.

title: 0.5 Data Splitting
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (splitting × 0.4 EDA). Construct a dataset where the test set’s marginal distribution differs visibly from training’s (e.g. sample y-dependent data, then split unstratified). Plot both test histograms. Then explain, quantitatively, how a covariate-shifted test set changes the meaning of every metric you compute on it — and why stratify/shuffling fixes the estimation but not a genuinely shifted deployment population.
C2 (splitting × 1.5 Resampling). Repeated train/test splitting (50 random 80/20 splits) gives a distribution of test R². Compare its spread to the K-fold spread from Exercise 2. Which estimator has lower variance here, and what does each split in the repeated scheme share with the others that K-fold handles differently? (This previews why repeated CV and bootstrap (4.5 Bootstrap) exist.)

title: 0.5 Data Splitting
text:
7. Summary

Test data answers one question — “how does this do on new data?” — and must be spent once.
train_test_split(test_size, random_state, stratify=y): stratify classes, seed everything.
K-fold: every sample validated once; report mean and across-fold SD.
Leakage has four faces: y-derived features, pre-fit preprocessing, duplicate subjects, shuffled time.
The universal fix: fit preprocessing inside training folds — or just use a Pipeline.
Small/imbalanced test sets produce undefined metrics and noisy numbers; SE of accuracy ≈ √(p(1−p)/n).
Part 0’s toolkit is complete. Next, Part 1 builds the statistical language — centers, spread, probability, and inference — that turns those splits and plots into claims: 1.1 Descriptive statistics.

title: 1.2 Relationships Between Variables
text: How do two variables move together? Covariance and correlation quantify co-movement; regression (Part 2) will model it. The skill here is knowing what r measures, what it ignores, and the four ways it lies.

title: 1.2 Relationships Between Variables
text:
1. Basic Concept
Covariance averages the products of paired deviations:
\[\text{cov}(x, y) = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum_i (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})\]
Positive when variables move together, negative when opposed — but its magnitude depends on the units (expression levels in raw counts vs log-CPM give different covariances for the same relationship). The Pearson correlation fixes units by dividing both SDs:
\[r = \frac{\text{cov}(x,y)}{s_x s_y} \in [-1, 1]\]






Key reading: r measures linear association strength, not slope (slope lives in regression) and not agreement (r = 1 for y = x + 100, which disagrees by 100 everywhere).
Spearman correlation = Pearson correlation applied to ranks. It detects any monotone relationship and shrugs at outliers:






And the classical caution — curvature: quadratic data can have r ≈ 0 over a symmetric range even though the variables are perfectly dependent:

title: 1.2 Relationships Between Variables
text:
2. Concept Questions

Why is covariance useless for comparing relationships measured in different units, and what exactly does dividing by \(s_x s_y\) fix?
What is the relationship between r and the R² of simple linear regression?
Give two datasets where Spearman = 1 but Pearson < 1.
Does r = 0 mean “no relationship”? Does r = 0.9 mean “x causes y”?
One outlier flips your r from +0.6 to −0.6. Which coefficient is more trustworthy here, and why?



Answers


Covariance’s magnitude scales with the units of both variables (cov(x, y) = 5 for x in minutes is 300 for x in seconds). Pearson divides by the product of SDs — a pure number in [−1, 1] — so relationships are comparable across studies, units, and scalings.
For simple linear regression, \(R^2 = r^2\) — the fraction of y’s variance explained by the best straight line. r = 0.7 → the line explains 49%.
Any perfectly monotone but nonlinear pair: (x, eˣ), (x, x³) over positive x, (age, income) rising with diminishing returns. Ranks are identical; straightness is not.
No and no. r = 0 only rules out linear association (quadratics, U-shapes, interactions can be strong). r measures association; causation requires design (randomization, natural experiments) or much stronger modeling assumptions.
Spearman. A single point moved Pearson’s estimate violently because r is built from raw deviations — the outlier dominates both \(s_x\), \(s_y\) and the cross-products. Spearman caps any point’s influence at “one rank step.”

title: 1.2 Relationships Between Variables
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1 — Anscombe’s quartet, cell 1. This classic dataset has 4 pairs with (nearly) identical mean, SD, r ≈ 0.816, and regression line — utterly different shapes. Build pair I and pair III, compute their summary statistics, and plot both.


Solution







Identical r, identical fitted line — because r and OLS are single-number summaries that different data structures can satisfy. Summary statistics compress away exactly the things you care about; plotting is not optional.

Exercise 2. Construct data where adding ONE observation flips the sign of Pearson r (from negative to positive), while Spearman barely moves. Report all three r values before/after.


Solution







The added point sits at the extreme corner, contributing huge cross-deviations \((x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y)\) — enough to outvote 40 points. Spearman only sees “new highest x, new highest y” — one rank step on each side. Any reported Pearson on real data should come with a scatterplot or a rank-correlation cross-check.

Exercise 3. For a bivariate normal sample (n = 30, true ρ = 0), empirically show the sampling distribution of r under the null, and verify that |r| > \(2/\sqrt{n-1}\) (rough 5% rule) happens about 5% of the time.


Solution







≈ 0.05: with n = 30, “noise correlations” of ±0.37 are routine. Two implications: small-n correlation claims need formal tests (1.4), and large correlation matrices (0.3 pandas drills) will always show impressive-looking r values somewhere — that’s multiplication of opportunities, not biology.

title: 1.2 Relationships Between Variables
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Correlation ≠ causation — and neither correlation nor its absence is about linear vs nonlinear: r ≈ 0 coexists with perfect functional dependence (the x² plot).
Range restriction and range enhancement: selecting only high-GPA applicants lowers r; mixing two clusters inflates it (Simpson’s paradox lives here — see Complex Questions).
Pearson needs rough linearity and tolerates outliers badly; Spearman needs only monotonicity but discards magnitude information (two datasets with identical ranks can have very different practical effect sizes).
Correlation matrices in high dimensions (10,000 genes → 50M pairs): extreme r values appear by chance alone (Exercise 3 logic × opportunities). Multiple-testing discipline (Part 12) applies to “top correlated pairs” lists.
Averaging correlations across groups is invalid (r is not on an additive scale — use Fisher z, or analyze per group).
Bootstrap or Fisher-z CI for r, never “r ± 0.05” from folklore. Formal test: stats.pearsonr returns the p-value alongside.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated “correlation report” has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fixed version


r ≠ slope and ≠ causation. The slope estimate is np.polyfit’s job, and “causes” needs design evidence, not correlation.
Averaging r across groups is invalid and hides sign flips; the two subgroups here correlate +0.91 and −0.91, so the “average” is 0.00 while both groups are near-perfectly associated — in opposite directions. Report per-group r (or a Fisher-z average with justification).
r ≈ 0 ≠ no relationship. The U-shaped dependence is perfect; Pearson only tests the linear projection.

title: 1.2 Relationships Between Variables
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Show that for simple linear regression the fitted slope is \(b = r \cdot (s_y / s_x)\), and explain the two failure modes of “reading” r as if it were an effect size.


Hint

Write the OLS slope for standardized variables; then unstandardize.



Solution

Standardize both variables: \(\tilde x = (x-\bar x)/s_x\), \(\tilde y = (y-\bar y)/s_y\). For standardized data the OLS slope is \(\sum \tilde x_i \tilde y_i / \sum \tilde x_i^2 = (n-1)\,\text{cov}/(n-1)\,\text{var} = r\). Rescaling back multiplies by \(s_y/s_x\), giving \(b = r s_y/s_x\). Failure modes: (1) slope from r — r = 0.5 means nothing about units; a weak correlation with huge \(s_y/s_x\) can be a big effect. (2) r as slope — the same physical relationship yields different r if you restrict the x-range (range restriction lowers both spread and r) while the slope \(r s_y/s_x\) is more stable. Report both: r (strength of linear association), slope (effect per unit x), CI each.

Q2. The t-statistic for testing ρ = 0 is \(t = r\sqrt{(n-2)/(1-r^2)}\). Verify numerically that stats.pearsonr’s p-value matches the two-sided t-test with df = n−2, then explain what happens to that p-value’s meaning when you compute it for the largest of 10,000 gene-pair correlations.


Solution







The p-value is calibrated for one pre-specified pair. For the maximum over 10,000 pairs, the test is applied to the extreme order statistic of ~10,000 correlated tests: even under global null, the smallest p-value is routinely ≪ 0.05 (probability of at least one “significant” pair ≈ 1 − 0.95¹⁰⁰⁰⁰ ≈ 1). The honest procedure re-tests the selected pair in fresh data or applies family-wise/FDR correction — the entire subject of Part 12.

title: 1.2 Relationships Between Variables
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (relationships × 0.3 pandas — Simpson’s paradox). Build 3 groups where within every group r(y, x) is positive, but pooled over all groups r is strongly negative. (Give group intercepts very different levels and equal within-group slopes.) Then answer: which correlation should a model use — and how does adding group dummies (2.6 Categorical predictors) resolve the conflict?
C2 (relationships × 9.2 PCA preview). Generate 3 correlated variables, compute the correlation matrix, and its eigenvalues. What does the dominant eigenvalue/eigenvector tell you about how many “real directions” the data has? Relate this to why the scatter-matrix drill of 0.4 becomes unreadable at 50 variables and PCA becomes necessary.

title: 1.2 Relationships Between Variables
text:
7. Summary

Covariance is direction × scale; Pearson r standardizes it to [−1, 1]; Spearman replaces values with ranks.
r describes linear association only: U-shapes hide at r ≈ 0; monotone curves lose r < 1.
r² is explained-variance for a straight line; slope is r·(sy/sx) — never confuse strength with effect size.
One outlier can flip Pearson; Spearman caps that influence — report both when data is dirty.
Sampling noise gives |r| ≈ 0.3 routinely at n = 30; scanning many pairs manufactures “discoveries.”
Per-group correlation, plots, and range questions come before any causal sentence.
Association is a description; deciding whether a pattern would reappear in new samples requires probability and inference — 1.3 Probability essentials.

title: 1.4 Statistical Inference
text: Inference answers the question every experiment asks: is this pattern real, or would chance produce it? Confidence intervals quantify uncertainty about a population quantity; hypothesis tests quantify how surprising the data would be under a “nothing is happening” model. Both are built on one idea — the sampling distribution of a statistic.

title: 1.4 Statistical Inference
text:
1. Basic Concept
The standard error. A sample mean varies from sample to sample with SD ≈ \(s/\sqrt{n}\) — the standard error (SE). Small n means the SE is big means the sample mean is a shaky estimate of the population mean.
Confidence interval. A 95% CI for a mean is approximately
\[\bar{x} \pm t_{0.975,\,n-1} \cdot \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\]
where the t-quantile widens the interval for small samples. Interpretation (get this exactly right): if the sampling procedure were repeated many times, 95% of the resulting intervals would contain the true mean — it is a property of the procedure, not a 95% probability statement about this particular interval.






Hypothesis test logic. State \(H_0\) (no effect) → compute a statistic measuring departure from \(H_0\) → the p-value is P(data at least this extreme | \(H_0\)). Small p = the null struggles to explain the data. It is not P(\(H_0\) | data).






Errors and power. Two ways to be wrong: Type I — declare an effect under a true null (rate = α); Type II — miss a real effect (rate = β); power = 1 − β, driven by effect size, n, α, and noise.

title: 1.4 Statistical Inference
text:
2. Concept Questions

A 95% CI is (2.1, 3.9). Is “P(true mean is in (2.1, 3.9)) = 0.95” a correct reading?
Why does a p-value not tell you the probability the null hypothesis is true?
What does the t in “t-test” buy you over a z-test, and when does the distinction vanish?
Your test on n = 5 has p = 0.20. Which conclusions are valid: (a) “no effect exists”, (b) “effect not demonstrated”, (c) “need more data or a better design”?
Why is equal_var=False (Welch) the sensible default for two-sample t-tests?



Answers


No. The interval is now fixed — it either contains the mean or not. The 95% describes the procedure’s long-run success rate across hypothetical repetitions. (Frequentist probability attaches to procedures, not fixed quantities.)
The p-value is computed assuming the null is true; it can’t then assign that null a probability. It is P(data at least this extreme | H₀) — evidence about the data under H₀, not about H₀ given the data. That reversal is exactly Bayes’ rule, and frequentist testing deliberately doesn’t do it (a prior on hypotheses would be required).
t replaces the known population σ with the estimated s, adding uncertainty that widens critical values (t₀.₉₇₅,₄ = 2.78 vs z = 1.96). As df → ∞, t → z; by n ≈ 30–50 the difference is negligible.

and (c) only. Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence; a high p-value at tiny n is uninformative, not exculpatory. Never conclude “no effect” without a power/equivalence argument.

Real biological groups rarely have equal variances, and Student’s pooled t can inflate false positives under inequality; Welch’s correction keeps Type I error near nominal with negligible power loss — so it’s the robust default.

title: 1.4 Statistical Inference
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. For the two-sample experiment below, compute (a) Welch t-test, (b) the 95% CI of each group mean, (c) the 95% CI for the difference in means (bootstrap is fine). State the decision and the estimate-with-uncertainty sentence you would put in a report.


Solution







Report sentence: “Treatment was estimated to raise the marker by 0.35 units, but the data are too small to distinguish that from no effect (bootstrap 95% CI −0.73 to 1.43; Welch p = 0.56).” Note what the sentence does not say — it does not claim the treatment “had no effect”, only that this experiment could not detect one. The CI is the quantitative claim; the p-value only grades the surprise under “no difference.” The two agree: the CI includes 0 exactly when the two-sided p exceeds 0.05 (consistency check — verify it by raising the treatment mean to 13.0 and watching both flip together).

Exercise 2. Multiple testing preview, empirically: simulate 100 independent two-group experiments under the global null (α = 0.05 each). (a) Expected number of “significant” results? (b) Empirical probability that at least one is significant? (c) Repeat at α = 0.001. What family-wise lesson emerges?


Solution







At α = 0.05, ~5 false positives per 100-null family and ≈ 99.4% chance of at least one. The family-wise error explodes with the number of tests — the problem Bonferroni and FDR (12.3, 12.4) solve.

Exercise 3. Demonstrate the effect of skew on the t-test/CI: sample n = 10 from a lognormal; bootstrap the sampling distribution of the mean; compare the bootstrap CI to the t-formula CI. Which is trustworthy here, and what sample size restores the t-approximation (test empirically)?


Solution







At n = 10 the mean’s true sampling distribution is strongly right-skewed — the symmetric t-CI is a poor description (and its 95% coverage is off). The bootstrap CI inherits the skew. At n = 100 the CLT has done its work and the two CIs nearly agree. Lesson: t-methods assume approximate normality of the sampling distribution, which skewed small samples violate; alternatives are log-transform, nonparametric tests, or larger n.

title: 1.4 Statistical Inference
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

p-value misreadings (all wrong, all common): P(H₀ true) = p; p = 0.03 means “3% chance the result is chance”; p > 0.05 means “no effect”; p = 0.049 vs 0.051 is a meaningful difference. The p-value is one number about one conditional probability — treat it as such.
The t-test compares means; it does not “prove normality” — with n = 5 you cannot even check the assumption well. Prefer Welch + report effect size + CI.
Paired vs unpaired is a design property: repeated measures on the same unit demand paired analysis (ttest_rel); pairing halves the noise only if the pairing is real.
Effect size ≠ significance: at n = 100,000, a 0.1% difference gets p ≈ 0; at n = 5, a huge effect gets p ≈ 0.3. Report effect + CI, let n decide detectability, not importance.
One-sided tests halve the p-value but require pre-registered direction — switching sides after looking at data is p-hacking.
Stopping rules break calibration: “collect until p < 0.05” inflates Type I error far above 5% (the simulation drill adapts to demonstrate this).


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated analysis has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fixed version


Design mismatch: after is generated from before — paired structure. The unpaired test throws away the pairing and most of the power. Use ttest_rel (or test the differences).
Both printed conclusions are wrong: small p is not “96% chance the treatment works” (it’s P(data|H₀), not P(H₀|data) or power), and large p never “proves useless”. Correct sentence: “data would be surprising under no-effect (p = …)”.
Sequential peeking: continuing until significance guarantees eventual “significance” even under a true null — Type I error ≈ 100%. Fix: pre-set n, or use a formal sequential design (alpha-spending); simplest demonstration — fix n and rerun.

title: 1.4 Statistical Inference
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Derive why the SE of a mean is \(s/\sqrt{n}\) using the variance-addition rule from 1.3, and explain the practical arms race it implies: to halve the SE of the mean, how much more data do you need? To halve the noise of each measurement?


Hint

Write Var(x̄) = Var(Σxᵢ/n²) with independence, then take square roots twice.



Solution

With independent \(x_i\) of variance \(\sigma^2\): \(\text{Var}(\bar x) = \text{Var}\!\big(\tfrac{1}{n}\sum x_i\big) = \tfrac{1}{n^2}\,n\sigma^2 = \sigma^2/n\), so \(\text{SE} = \sigma/\sqrt n\) — square-root law. Halving the SE of the mean requires 4× the data; the SE of the mean is about precision of knowledge, and knowledge is expensive. Halving the noise of each measurement (σ) is an instrument/protocol question, not a statistics question — and it pays off in every subsequent analysis. First optimize measurement noise, then buy n.

Q2. Construct and demonstrate the “optional stopping” inflation: under a true null, run the peeking loop (test after every new pair, stop at p < 0.05 or n = 200). Estimate the realized Type I error. Compare to a fixed-n = 200 test. What does this say about A/B test dashboards that highlight “significance” daily?


Solution







Peeking inflates the false-positive rate from 5% to roughly 30–50% — the more checkpoints, the worse. Daily-looked-at dashboards with “significance” badges are exactly this experiment; the fixes are fixed horizons, sequential designs (alpha spending), or Bayesian monitoring with pre-agreed decision rules.

title: 1.4 Statistical Inference
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (inference × 0.5 Data splitting). Two models score 0.81 and 0.84 accuracy on the same 250-sample test set. Use the binomial SE machinery to judge whether they differ; then design the evaluation protocol (repeated splits or K-fold, paired comparison per fold) that would let you test the difference honestly. What makes the paired fold-wise comparison better than comparing two independent error bars?
C2 (inference × 2.4 Accuracy of the full model preview). Fit a simple linear regression to 30 noisy points; use the standard errors of slope and intercept (available from scipy.stats.linregress or a small manual computation) to build 95% CIs. Now re-fit on 300 points of the same process. How do the SEs scale, and why does “collect 10× more data” not always shrink practical uncertainty (name the two components: sampling error vs measurement/bias)?

title: 1.4 Statistical Inference
text:
7. Summary

Inference = sampling distributions: SE = s/√n; means shrink noise by √n — 4× data per 2× precision.
CI: range of parameter values the data can’t refute (at the chosen level); it’s the procedure that has 95% coverage, not your interval.
p-value = P(data this extreme | H₀); never P(H₀), never “chance of being right.”
Welch two-sample t is the default; paired designs need paired tests; ranks for non-normal data.
Power depends on effect, n, α, noise — underpowered studies “fail” without evidence of absence.
Multiple tests and optional stopping break the 5% guarantee; corrections and fixed protocols restore it.
When assumptions are shaky, resample the data itself: bootstraps and permutation tests — 1.5 Resampling intuition.

title: 2.1 The Regression Problem
text: Regression is the archetypal supervised-learning problem: given inputs \(X\), predict a quantitative response \(Y\) by estimating the underlying function \(f\) with a model \(\hat{f}\) trained on data. Every idea in this course — loss, generalization, bias–variance, tuning — can be seen first through this lens.

title: 2.1 The Regression Problem
text:
1. Basic Concept
We assume data is generated as
\[Y = f(X) + \varepsilon, \qquad \mathbb{E}[\varepsilon \mid X] = 0\]
where \(f\) is the systematic part (what we want to learn) and \(\varepsilon\) is irreducible error (measurement noise, unmeasured variables). We estimate \(\hat{f}\) from training data and measure quality by a loss; for regression, the standard is squared error, whose average on new data is the mean squared error:
\[\text{MSE} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i \big(y_i - \hat{f}(x_i)\big)^2\]
Two distinct goals (ISL’s famous dichotomy — know which one you are doing):

Prediction: \(\hat{Y} = \hat{f}(X)\) for new \(X\) — interpretability optional, accuracy paramount.
Inference: which predictors matter, how, and with what uncertainty — a mis-specified-but-interpretable \(\hat f\) can be worse than useless even if it predicts well.







The regression task: from the dots alone, recover an approximation of the curve.
Reducible vs irreducible error. Even a perfect \(\hat f = f\) leaves MSE \(= \text{Var}(\varepsilon)\). Model improvements can only shrink the reducible part. This decomposes (proved via a completing-the-square argument in 4.4 Bias–variance):
\[\mathbb{E}\big[(Y - \hat{f}(X))^2\big] = \underbrace{\big(f(X) - \mathbb{E}\hat{f}(X)\big)^2}_{\text{bias}^2} + \underbrace{\text{Var}\big(\hat{f}(X)\big)}_{\text{variance}} + \underbrace{\text{Var}(\varepsilon)}_{\text{irreducible}}\]

title: 2.1 The Regression Problem
text:
2. Concept Questions

Your model’s test MSE is 2.31 and you estimate \(\text{Var}(\varepsilon) = 2.25\). How much room is left for model improvement?
Give one scenario where a highly interpretable but slightly-less-accurate model is the right choice, and one where it is not.
Is \(f\) observable? Is \(\hat f\)? What dataset do you need to evaluate \(\hat f\)?
Why is squared error the conventional loss? Name one situation where it is a poor match.
In \(Y = f(X) + \varepsilon\), what role does \(\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon \mid X] = 0\) play?



Answers


\(\text{MSE} \ge \text{Var}(\varepsilon)\) always, so the reducible gap is \(2.31 - 2.25 = 0.06\) — the model is within 6% of the noise floor. Chasing further gains with the same features is wasted effort; collect better features or accept the limit.
Yes: clinical dosing or credit decisions, where the model must be audited and each coefficient argued. Not: real-time image tagging, where nobody reads the model and only accuracy matters.
\(f\) is never observed; \(\hat f\) is computed from training data. To evaluate it honestly you need data not used in fitting (0.5 Data splitting) — evaluating on training data measures memorization.
Squared error is smooth, differentiable, corresponds to Gaussian-noise MLE (A.2 in the appendix), and treats errors symmetrically — but a single outlier contributes quadratically, so for heavy-tailed or gross-error settings, absolute loss or Huber loss fits better (and then “best” means a different model: median regression).
It makes \(\varepsilon\) noise, not bias: the mean of the error is zero at every \(X\), so all systematic structure lives in \(f\). If violated (e.g. calibration drift), the whole decomposition and OLS theory sit on sand.

title: 2.1 The Regression Problem
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.




















Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Generate \(n = 100\) points from \(y = 1 + 2x + \varepsilon\), \(\varepsilon \sim N(0, 4)\). Fit a line with np.polyfit, then report (a) training MSE, (b) fresh test MSE on 10,000 new points, (c) the theoretical noise floor \(\sigma^2\). Which of the two MSEs is closer to the floor, and why — what is the name of that gap?


Solution







Test MSE is closer to the floor but sits above it: training MSE is optimistically biased (the fit adapted to training noise — in-sample optimism), while test MSE = bias² + variance + σ² with small bias² and variance for a well-specified linear model. The excess over 4.0 is reducible error (here: estimation variance, shrinking with n).

Exercise 2. Prediction vs inference framing: you have hours_studied and exam_score data (generated below with a ceiling at 100). Fit a line, predict for hours = 5 and hours = 30, and explain which prediction is trustworthy, which is nonsense, and which word describes the failure (2.2 formalizes it).


Solution







hours = 5 is interpolation — inside the training range (0–12), trustworthy within uncertainty. hours = 30 is extrapolation — 2.5× beyond the observed range; the model silently reports ~175, physically impossible (score caps at 100). The word: extrapolation. Linear models extend the fitted pattern blindly; domain limits must be imposed by the analyst.

Exercise 3. Implement a regress_compare(y_true, y_pred_a, y_pred_b) helper returning MSE, RMSE, and MAE for two competing predictors, and use it to compare the mean-predictor vs the median-predictor on lognormal data. Which loss does each predictor win, and what does that tell you about the mean–median–loss triangle from 1.1?


Solution







The mean-predictor minimizes MSE and the median-predictor minimizes MAE — each wins its own column (check: mean-pred beats median-pred on MSE, median-pred beats mean-pred on MAE). “Which predictor is better” is ill-posed until you name the loss; this is the predictive face of the robustness trade-off from 1.1.

title: 2.1 The Regression Problem
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

In-sample (training) MSE is always optimistic — the model was chosen to make it small. The gap between training and test error is optimism, and estimating it is half of Part 4.
Extrapolation is silent: linear models return values outside any observed region with total confidence. Always compare prediction ranges against training ranges.
The noise floor is a feature of the data, not the model — before tuning hyperparameters for hours, estimate \(\sigma^2\) (replicates, domain knowledge, or residual variance from a saturated fit) and ask what’s left to gain (Concept Question 1).
MSE vs RMSE: RMSE is in y-units (reportable), MSE is differentiable-friendly and decomposable (math-friendly). Don’t average RMSEs across folds — average MSEs, then take the root.
y_true - y_pred sign conventions flip between residual-as-truth-minus-fit and fit-minus-truth; squared losses don’t care, but printed residual diagnostics do — know your library’s convention.
Prediction vs inference changes pre-processing rules: dropping a confounded-but-predictive variable is fine for pure prediction and fatal for inference (2.5).


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated evaluation has three bugs. Run it, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fixed version


Training MSE labeled “test”: polyfit minimized exactly this quantity — it is the in-sample error and cannot evidence generalization. Fix: split first, evaluate on untouched data.
Averaging RMSEs across folds is not the RMSE of anything (root is nonlinear). Fix: collect fold MSEs, average, then take the square root.
Silent extrapolation to x = 50 when training spanned 0–10. Fix: assert/flag predictions outside the training range, or constrain the domain.

title: 2.1 The Regression Problem
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Show that the function \(c \mapsto \frac{1}{n}\sum (y_i - c)^2\) is minimized at \(c = \bar{y}\), and use this to explain why the mean-model’s training MSE equals the sample variance (drill above). What is the analogous statement for the median and MAE?


Hint

Differentiate in \(c\); you already proved the median version in 1.1 Q1.



Solution

\(\frac{d}{dc}\sum(y_i-c)^2 = -2\sum(y_i - c) = 0 \Rightarrow c = \bar y\); substituting back gives \(\frac{1}{n}\sum(y_i - \bar y)^2\), the (population-formula) sample variance. So the intercept-only least-squares model is the sample mean, and its in-sample MSE is the variance — which is exactly why \(R^2 = 1 - \text{RSS}/\text{TSS}\) compares every model against this null (2.4). The MAE analog: constant predictors are minimized by the median, with in-sample MAE = mean absolute deviation.

Q2. A colleague reports: “train MSE 0.9, test MSE 4.1, estimated σ² = 4.0 — my model is optimal, no more work needed.” Evaluate all three numbers as evidence. What additional split or sample-size information would sharpen the claim?


Solution

Test MSE 4.1 ≈ σ² = 4.0 suggests the reducible part is tiny — if the estimate is trustworthy. But (1) a single test split’s MSE has sampling noise (its own SE ≈ σ²·√(2/n_test) under normality — a 100-point test set gives ±0.56 at 1 SE, so 4.1 vs 4.0 is inconclusive); (2) train MSE 0.9 ≪ 4.0 shows substantial in-sample optimism, meaning the model has meaningful variance (complexity) — the test error could still be lowered by regularization or a simpler model family even if it’s near the floor on average; (3) σ² estimated how? If from training residuals of the same model, it inherits the model’s bias (under-specified models inflate apparent σ²). Sharpening: K-fold CV for a stable test estimate, a proper noise estimate (replicates), and n_train/n_test sizes to judge estimation variance.

title: 2.1 The Regression Problem
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (setup × 1.3 Probability). Simulate 500 repetitions of: draw n = 25 training points from the Exercise 1 process, fit the line, record test MSE. Plot the histogram of the 500 test MSEs. Relate its center and spread to (a) the noise floor, (b) the sampling variability of \(\hat\beta\) you will quantify in 2.3 — and predict qualitatively how the histogram changes at n = 200.
C2 (setup × 0.4 EDA). Generate data where \(f(x)\) is multiplicative (\(y = 3x\cdot e^{\varepsilon}\), constant relative noise). Show that regressing \(y\) on \(x\) produces the funnel-shaped residuals of 0.4 Q2, then regress \(\log y\) on \(\log x\) and verify the noise is additive there. State the modeling rule this suggests before any model is fit.

title: 2.1 The Regression Problem
text:
7. Summary

Regression = estimating \(f\) in \(Y = f(X) + \varepsilon\) from data; quality = MSE on data not used for fitting.
\(\text{Var}(\varepsilon)\) is the floor: model work shrinks only bias and variance, never the floor.
Prediction and inference are different games; they impose different rules on feature choice and reporting.
Training MSE is optimism in numbers; test MSE is the only honest currency (Part 4 prices it).
The mean-model is least squares’ null hypothesis; \(R^2\) is measured against it.
Extrapolation is silent failure — police the input range.
With the target defined, 2.2 Simple linear regression builds the first — and still most interpretable — estimator of \(f\).

title: 2.2 Simple Linear Regression
text: Simple linear regression fits a straight line \(\hat{y} = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 x\) by least squares. It is the reference point for every model in this course: transparent, closed-form, and already rich enough to demonstrate estimation, uncertainty, and mis-use.

title: 2.2 Simple Linear Regression
text:
1. Basic Concept
Least squares chooses coefficients minimizing the residual sum of squares \(\text{RSS} = \sum_i (y_i - \hat\beta_0 - \hat\beta_1 x_i)^2\). Minimizing in each parameter (set derivatives to zero) gives the closed forms:
\[\hat{\beta}_1 = \frac{\sum_i (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})}{\sum_i (x_i - \bar{x})^2} = r\,\frac{s_y}{s_x}, \qquad \hat{\beta}_0 = \bar{y} - \hat{\beta}_1 \bar{x}\]
The slope is the correlation rescaled into y-units per x-unit (1.2); the line always passes through \((\bar x, \bar y)\).












Reading the coefficients. \(\hat\beta_1\): predicted change in \(y\) per one-unit increase in \(x\). \(\hat\beta_0\): prediction at \(x = 0\) — meaningful only if 0 is in (or near) the data’s range; otherwise it is an extrapolated anchor, not a “baseline effect.”

title: 2.2 Simple Linear Regression
text:
2. Concept Questions

Why does the least-squares line always pass through \((\bar{x}, \bar{y})\)?
Data in x = Fahrenheit, y = Celsius is fit with slope \(\hat\beta_1\). Refit in x = Kelvin. What happens to the slope and intercept?
Your slope is 4.2 with r = 0.3. What is \(s_y / s_x\) telling you here, and would you call this a “strong” effect?
Two students fit the same data; one forgets the intercept term (forces \(\hat\beta_0 = 0\)). Whose slope changes, and in which direction is it biased if \(\bar y\) and \(\bar x\) are both positive?
What is the RSS of the perfect-intercept model (\(\hat\beta_1 = 0\))? (Connects to 2.1 Q1.)



Answers


\(\hat\beta_0 = \bar y - \hat\beta_1 \bar x\) rearranges to \(\bar y = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 \bar x\) — a direct consequence of the first-order condition in \(\beta_0\) (residuals sum to zero).
Kelvin = Fahrenheit-scaled shift: \(x_K = (x_F + 459.67) \times \frac{5}{9}\). Slope rescales by the x-unit factor: \(\hat\beta_1^{(K)} = \hat\beta_1^{(F)} \cdot \frac{9}{5}\); intercept absorbs the shift via the point \((\bar x, \bar y)\). Slope is unit-sensitive; correlation r is not.
\(s_y/s_x = 4.2/0.3 = 14\) — the slope is large only because y varies 14× more than x. “Strong” is about r (or standardized slope), not \(\hat\beta_1\) alone: r = 0.3 is a weak linear signal with a steep unit conversion. Always report effect in context: 4.2 y-units per x-unit with uncertainty.
Without an intercept, \(\hat\beta_1\) must do double duty (slope + level), and the first-order condition \(\sum r_i = 0\) is lost. With positive \(\bar x, \bar y\), the no-intercept slope is biased upward — it’s pulled toward \(y/x\) ratios rather than the local slope. Force an intercept unless a theory demands the line pass through the origin (and then still check).
\(\text{RSS} = \sum(y_i - \bar y)^2 = \text{TSS}\) — the mean-model. Every slope model is judged by how much it shrinks this number; that comparison becomes \(R^2\) in 2.4.

title: 2.2 Simple Linear Regression
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Compute the least-squares slope and intercept from scratch (sums only, no polyfit/sklearn) for the dataset below, then verify against np.polyfit. Report RSS and compare it to the TSS of the intercept-only model.


Solution







RSS ≪ TSS here: the line explains most of the variation. That ratio — computed again with proper degrees of freedom — becomes \(R^2\) and \(R^2_{\text{adj}}\) in 2.4.

Exercise 2. Regression to the mean, experienced: simulate 200 parents’ heights and children’s heights as child = 0.7*parent + 68 + noise (units: inches). Fit child ~ parent. Report the slope and predicted child height for a parent at 62 in and at 76 in. Explain — in one sentence each — why the predictions sit closer to the population mean than the inputs, and why this is a statistical fact and not a biological force.


Solution







Predictions are pulled toward \(\bar y\) because slope < 1: a parent 4 in below the mean is predicted only ~2.8 in below-average child. The mechanism is pure statistics — the parent’s deviation partially reflects parent-side luck (noise), which doesn’t repeat in the child. Any noisy pair with \(|\rho| < 1\) regresses to the mean; misreading it as causal “correction” is the classic historical error (Galton’s own).

Exercise 3. Prediction interval preview by simulation: fit the line on n = 40 points (\(\sigma = 2\) known truth), then simulate the empirical distribution of predictions at x = 5 over 2,000 re-generated training sets. Report the SD of predictions and compare it to (a) the SD of a single new observation at x = 5 (≈ σ) and (b) the SE of the mean response. Which interval is wider — confidence or prediction — and why?


Solution







The fitted mean response at x = 5 is much more stable than any individual point: individual outcomes add irreducible σ on top of the mean’s uncertainty. Hence the prediction interval (for a new y) is always wider than the confidence interval (for the mean) — quantified properly in 2.3–2.4.

title: 2.2 Simple Linear Regression
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

np.polyfit returns highest-degree first ([slope, intercept] for deg 1) — reversing them is a top silent bug. np.polyval([b1, b0], x_new) matches.
sklearn wants 2-D X: model.fit(x, y) with 1-D x raises — x.reshape(-1, 1) or x[:, None] (0.2 broadcasting).
Extrapolation — the line continues with full confidence beyond the data; the only protection is range-checking (2.1).
Outliers have leverage proportional to \((x - \bar x)^2\) — far-in-x points can rotate the whole line (Anscombe III in 1.2); check the fit with and without suspects.
Slope ≠ effect without design: in observational data \(\hat\beta_1\) is an association per unit x; confounding can give any sign (2.5, 2.6).
Correlation of residuals is the real assumption — independence, not normality, is what makes the classic SEs valid; time-order or cluster structure breaks it quietly (2.10).


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated fit-and-report has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fixed version


polyfit order reversed: it returns [highest-degree, ..., constant], so b0 here is the slope and b1 the intercept — every printed label lies. Fix: b1, b0 = np.polyfit(...) or unpack with names.
Reversed-coefficient prediction then residuals: garbage in, garbage out; also the residual-mean check only works when the intercept is present (it should be ≈ 0 numerically). Fix names, then check.
Self-congratulatory metric: corr(fitted, x) is always ≈ ±1 by construction — it measures the line’s steepness, not fit quality. Fix: compare against y (residual-based: RSS vs TSS, or corr(ŷ, y)).

title: 2.2 Simple Linear Regression
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Prove that regressing standardized $y^* $ on standardized \(x^*\) yields slope = r and intercept = 0, and derive from it the identity \(\hat\beta_1 = r\, s_y / s_x\). Why does this make the slope unit-sensitive while r is not?


Hint

Standardized variables have mean 0, variance 1; apply the closed-form slope.



Solution

With \(x^* = (x-\bar x)/s_x\), \(y^* = (y - \bar y)/s_y\): slope \(= \frac{\sum x_i^* y_i^*}{\sum x_i^{*2}} = \frac{(n-1)\,\text{cov}(x^*,y^*)}{(n-1)\,\text{var}(x^*)} = r\) (both variances are 1); intercept \(= \bar y^* - r\bar x^* = 0\). Rescaling \(y^* \to y\) multiplies the slope by \(s_y\); rescaling \(x^* \to x\) divides it by \(s_x\) — giving \(\hat\beta_1 = r s_y/s_x\). So \(\hat\beta_1\) mixes a dimensionless association strength (r) with a unit conversion (\(s_y/s_x\)): change x to centimeters and the slope divides by 2.54 with no change in reality. This is why cross-study comparisons report standardized coefficients or r, and why “bigger slope = stronger effect” is meaningless across unit systems.

Q2. Under what exact conditions does the least-squares slope equal the causal effect of x on y? Use a simulation where x is correlated with an unobserved driver of y to show \(\hat\beta_1\) ≠ true effect, and connect the size of the gap to the confounder’s correlation with x and y.


Solution

Causal equality requires no confounding: \(\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon \mid x] = 0\) — the error (which contains all other causes) uncorrelated with x; in a randomized experiment this holds by design, in observational data it’s an assumption. Simulation:






The naive slope overshoots: part of z’s influence on y rides in through corr(x, z). First-order intuition: \(\hat\beta_1 \approx \text{true} + \beta_z \cdot \delta\) where δ is the x–confounder association. The general cure is adjusting for measured confounders (2.5, 2.6); unmeasured ones limit every observational claim.

title: 2.2 Simple Linear Regression
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (SLR × 1.5 Resampling). Bootstrap the slope of the Exercise 1 dataset (5,000 resamples) and compare the bootstrap SD of \(\hat\beta_1\) to the formula-based SE from 2.3. Now inject one high-leverage outlier (x = 40, y = 10) and redo both. Which SE detects the fragility first, and what does this say about formula-SE trust on real data?
C2 (SLR × 0.3 pandas). Load the cohort-style frame: 4 groups with different slopes on a shared x. Fit (a) one pooled line, (b) separate lines per group via groupby. Under what parameter constellation does the pooled slope equal a (weighted) average of group slopes, and when can its sign contradict all of them? (This is Simpson’s paradox armed with slopes — resolved with dummies in 2.6.)

title: 2.2 Simple Linear Regression
text:
7. Summary

Least squares has closed forms; the line passes through \((\bar x, \bar y)\); slope = \(r\,s_y/s_x\).
np.polyfit orders coefficients highest-power-first; sklearn wants 2-D X — mechanical details that produce silent bugs.
Intercept = prediction at x = 0: interpret only when 0 is in-range.
Slope is unit-sensitive, r is not; neither is causal without design or adjustment.
Regression to the mean follows from any \(|r| < 1\) — statistical, not substantive.
Confidence interval (mean response) is always narrower than prediction interval (new point): irreducible σ sits on top.
A line is a claim; next page asks how precisely the data pins that claim down: 2.3 Accuracy of the coefficients.

title: 2.4 Accuracy of the Full Model
text: Beyond individual coefficients, we judge the whole fit: how close are predictions to reality (RSE), and what fraction of the response’s variation does the model explain (\(R^2\))? Both have in-sample and out-of-sample versions — and the gap between them is the heart of model evaluation.

title: 2.4 Accuracy of the Full Model
text:
1. Basic Concept
Two classic in-sample summaries of a fit with \(p\) predictors and \(n\) observations:
\[\text{RSE} = \sqrt{\frac{\text{RSS}}{n - p - 1}} \quad\text{(typical prediction miss, in y-units)} \qquad R^2 = 1 - \frac{\text{RSS}}{\text{TSS}} \quad\text{(fraction of variance explained)}\]
where \(\text{RSS} = \sum (y_i - \hat y_i)^2\) and \(\text{TSS} = \sum (y_i - \bar y)^2\). RSE is absolute (compare to σ), \(R^2\) is relative (compare to the mean-model’s floor of 0 and the perfect fit’s ceiling of 1).






The variance-explained identity. With an intercept, total variation splits exactly:
\[\underbrace{\sum (y_i - \bar y)^2}_{\text{TSS}} = \underbrace{\sum (\hat y_i - \bar y)^2}_{\text{ESS, explained}} + \underbrace{\sum (y_i - \hat y_i)^2}_{\text{RSS, unexplained}}\]






In-sample vs out-of-sample \(R^2\) — the same formula on test data, where it can go negative:

title: 2.4 Accuracy of the Full Model
text:
2. Concept Questions

Your model’s RSE is 3.2 and y ranges from 40 to 60. Is this a good model? What extra number do you need?
Why is in-sample \(R^2\) never decreased by adding a predictor — even a column of pure noise?
What does out-of-sample \(R^2 < 0\) mean, and which two models does it compare?
RSE divides by \(n - p - 1\) while RMSE divides by \(n\). Which is the honest estimate of σ, and when do they converge?
Your in-sample \(R^2 = 0.9\), test \(R^2 = 0.55\). Name the phenomenon and two standard remedies.



Answers


Depends on σ, not the range alone: RSE ≈ σ means you’re at the noise floor (2.1); RSE ≫ σ means real structure is unexplained. Range (40–60 → SD maybe ~4) gives context: missing 3.2 when the total SD is ~4 is barely better than predicting the mean. You need an estimate of σ (replicates, domain knowledge).
Least squares minimizes RSS, so RSS weakly decreases with any added column — noise columns get tiny fitted coefficients that shave a little RSS. \(R^2\)’s denominator doesn’t move. This monotone creep is why adjusted \(R^2\) (or CV) exists; more in 2.5/Part 5.
The test-set version compares your model against the test set’s own mean: \(R^2_{\text{test}} = 1 - \sum (y_{te} - \hat y_{te})^2 / \sum (y_{te} - \bar y_{te})^2\). Negative = your model predicts worse than just predicting the test mean — the model (fit elsewhere) has negative transfer to this distribution or is simply terrible.
RSE (df-corrected) estimates σ̂ unbiasedly; RMSE(n) is the descriptive in-sample miss. They converge as \(n \gg p\). Report RSE (or test RMSE), not in-sample RMSE, when the audience cares about truth.
Overfitting (in-sample optimism). Remedies: more data, regularization/simpler model (Part 5), and honest evaluation via CV (4.3).

title: 2.4 Accuracy of the Full Model
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. For the cohort-style data below, fit y ~ x and compute in a single pass: RSS, TSS, ESS, in-sample R², RSE, and the df-corrected vs naive RMSE. Verify TSS = ESS + RSS to 8 decimals.


Solution
