RSE slightly exceeds naive RMSE because the df correction charges the model for the parameters it fitted. With n = 60, p = 1 the difference is tiny; with n = 8, p = 4 it is violent — one more reason small-n fits deserve RSE, not RMSE.

Exercise 2. Demonstrate the noise-collector theorem: for the data above, append (a) a genuine second predictor correlated with the signal, (b) a pure-noise column, and (c) five pure-noise columns. Track in-sample R² and 5-fold out-of-sample R² across the four models. Which number climbs monotonically, and which tells the truth?


Solution







In-sample R² only ever rises — five noise columns “explain” variance that pure chance aligned with y. CV R² is flat or falling: out-of-sample, the noise coefficients are random directions that add variance, not signal. This single experiment is the entire business case for honest validation (Part 4) and for adjusted metrics/penalties (Part 5).

Exercise 3. Build regression_report(y_true, y_pred, k_params) returning a dict with MSE, RMSE, RSE (df-corrected), MAE, and out-of-sample R² computed against the given y’s mean. Test it in three regimes — good model, underfit model, extrapolated predictions — and write one sentence naming each regime from the numbers alone.


Solution







Reading: “good” has RSE ≈ 1 ≈ σ and healthy positive R²; “underfit” has R² ≈ 0 (no better than the mean); “extrapolated” has negative R² and an RMSE far above σ — the fit is fine but the domain is wrong. Numbers diagnose regimes only when you know what σ and R² = 0 mean.

title: 2.4 Accuracy of the Full Model
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

\(R^2\) has no universal “good” — it compares against your response’s variance. In noisy biology, \(R^2 = 0.2\) can be a triumph; in controlled physics, 0.95 can be embarrassing. Context or σ, always.
Out-of-sample \(R^2\) is computed against the test mean — a different denominator than training. Two reported R²s with different test sets are not directly comparable; prefer test RMSE/MSE for comparisons.
Adjusted \(R^2\) charges each predictor with a df penalty: \(1 - (1 - R^2)\frac{n-1}{n-p-1}\); it can decrease when noise columns join. It’s a better in-sample guide, but CV is the real referee.
Comparing \(R^2\) across transformed responses (\(y\) vs \(\log y\)) is invalid — different denominators, different games. Compare test RMSE on the same scale (back-transform with care: exponentiating log-predictions biases; use smearing or accept the median-level prediction).
RSE estimates σ only under correct specification — a quadratic truth fit with a line inflates σ̂ (2.10); your “noise floor” estimate absorbs your model’s bias.
\(R^2\) says nothing about calibration in y: predictions can be well-correlated with y yet systematically offset; plot ŷ vs y (0.4).


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated model report has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fixed version


Training R² as performance: always the best-case number; report CV or holdout.
R² across different response scales: R²(y) and R²(log y) have different denominators (variance of y vs of log y) — the comparison is meaningless. Compare RMSE on one common scale (here: predict log, exponentiate, RMSE in y-space).
Averaging RMSEs across folds: average fold MSEs, take the root (2.1).

title: 2.4 Accuracy of the Full Model
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Prove TSS = ESS + RSS for least squares with an intercept, starting from \(y_i - \bar y = (\hat y_i - \bar y) + (y_i - \hat y_i)\) and showing the cross-term vanishes. Which first-order condition kills the cross-term, and why does the identity fail without an intercept (or with ridge, Part 5)?


Hint

Expand the sum of squares; the cross-term is \(\sum (\hat y_i - \bar y)(y_i - \hat y_i)\).



Solution

Expand: \(\sum(y_i-\bar y)^2 = \sum(\hat y_i - \bar y)^2 + \sum(y_i - \hat y_i)^2 + 2\sum(\hat y_i - \bar y)(y_i - \hat y_i)\). The cross-term equals \(2\,\hat{y}^\top (I - H) y\)-type expressions; concretely, OLS with intercept implies residuals are orthogonal to the fitted values: \(\sum \hat r_i \hat y_i = 0\) (follows from \(\sum \hat r_i = 0\) and \(\sum \hat r_i x_i = 0\), the two first-order conditions). Hence ESS \(= \sum \hat y_i^2 - n\bar y^2\) and TSS = ESS + RSS. Without an intercept the condition \(\sum \hat r_i = 0\) is lost, so fitted values need not be orthogonal to residuals — and \(R^2\) computed as 1 − RSS/TSS can even go negative in-sample. Regularized fits (ridge) similarly aren’t orthogonal projections, so the decomposition and the tidy R² story are OLS-with-intercept privileges.

Q2. Two models on the same n = 40 dataset: A has in-sample R² = 0.70 with 1 predictor; B has in-sample R² = 0.74 with 8 predictors. (a) Compute adjusted R² for both. (b) Then decide the winner by CV, implementing it. (c) At what sample size would B’s raw R² edge become credible? Answer with code and one paragraph.


Solution








Adjusted R² flips the ranking: B’s 8 parameters must earn their keep and don’t. (b) CV agrees — B adds nothing out-of-sample. (c) The noise columns’ spurious gains shrink like 7/n: only at n in the hundreds does B’s raw-R² edge fall below noise level. Lesson: raw in-sample R² gains of ≈ (extra predictors)/n are the signature of pure chance, not signal.

title: 2.4 Accuracy of the Full Model
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (full-model accuracy × 1.5 Resampling). Bootstrap the in-sample R² of the Exercise 2 “x1 + noise5” model (resample rows, refit, recompute R²). Compare its bootstrap distribution to the CV R² distribution. One is centered high and narrow, the other low and honest — explain why resampling rows cannot cure in-sample optimism (the same rows that fit are the rows evaluated), and what this implies for what bootstrap CIs of performance statistics mean.
C2 (full-model accuracy × 2.3 Coefficient accuracy). Generate 200 datasets: n = 30, true slope 0.5, σ = 1. For each, record (a) p-value of the slope, (b) in-sample R², (c) test R² on a fresh 10,000-point set. Estimate: among datasets with p < 0.05, the median test R²; among p ≥ 0.05 likewise. What does this “significance ⇒ magnitude?” experiment teach about the relationship between the two accuracy lenses ([2.3] vs this page)?

title: 2.4 Accuracy of the Full Model
text:
7. Summary

RSE = absolute miss (in σ units); R² = relative variance explained; both in-sample summaries.
TSS = ESS + RSS exactly (with intercept OLS) — R² is the explained share.
In-sample R² rises with any added column; adjusted R² charges for parameters; CV tells the truth.
Out-of-sample R² uses the test mean as its yardstick and can be negative — worse than the mean.
Never compare R² across different response scales; compare same-scale RMSE.
RSE ≈ σ means you’ve hit the noise floor — stop tuning, get better data.
The fit’s average accuracy is settled; next page scales the model to many predictors — with collinearity and confounding in tow: 2.5 Multiple linear regression.

title: 2.6 Categorical Predictors
text: Real predictors are often labels: tissue type, treatment arm, batch, site. Regression is numeric machinery, so categories must become numbers first — dummy (indicator) variables. Get the encoding right and everything from 2.5 applies unchanged; get it wrong and you build the classic dummy-variable trap.

title: 2.6 Categorical Predictors
text:
1. Basic Concept
A categorical predictor with \(k\) levels enters the model as \(k - 1\) dummy columns: each is a 0/1 flag for one level, with one level left out as the baseline (reference). The coefficients are offsets from the baseline:
\[y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 D_{\text{B}} + \beta_2 D_{\text{C}} + \varepsilon\]
means: group A (baseline) has mean \(\beta_0\); groups B and C are shifted by \(\beta_1, \beta_2\) from A. Why \(k-1\), not \(k\)? With all \(k\) dummies plus an intercept, the columns sum to the intercept column — perfect collinearity (2.5) — the dummy variable trap.






Reading: intercept = normal (baseline) mean; each tumor coefficient = offset from normal. Verify against group means — they must match exactly (this model is just three group means):






The same encoding, done manually — so the machinery has no mystery:

title: 2.6 Categorical Predictors
text:
2. Concept Questions

A variable season has 4 levels. How many dummy columns in a model with intercept? Without intercept?
You change the baseline from “control” to “drugB”. Which numbers in the output change, which stay identical, and which scientific conclusions may change?
A colleague encodes low/medium/high severity as 0/1/2 and enters it linearly. What exactly does that assume, and when is it acceptable?
Why is the p-value of the baseline level never in the coefficient table, and how do you test whether the categorical variable matters as a whole?
pd.get_dummies without drop_first=True inside a model with intercept — what happens, and why did statsmodels’ C() not trap you?



Answers


3 with intercept (one baseline absorbed), 4 without (each level gets its own mean, no baseline needed — the “cell-means” parameterization).
Coefficients (now offsets from drugB) and the intercept change; fitted values, R², F-test, residuals are identical — same model space. Conclusions change only if you were interpreting the baseline-specific contrasts: pairwise comparisons are recomputed, the model’s fit is untouched.
It assumes equal spacing of effects per step and a monotone linear trend: high−medium = medium−low. Acceptable when the ordinal scale is genuinely near-evenly spaced in effect (or you only need a trend test); otherwise lose nothing by dummies (k−1 columns) and gain freedom.
The baseline has no coefficient — it is the intercept (its p-value tests whether the baseline mean is 0, almost never the question). To test the variable overall: the F-test dropping all its dummies (anova_lm(reduced, full) from 2.5), or a likelihood-ratio test.
With all k dummies + intercept, columns are collinear (sum of dummies = 1 = intercept) — the trap; OLS is non-identified and software either errors or silently arbitrary-solves. C() automatically leaves out the (alphabetically) first level. If you build dummies manually, drop_first=True (or drop one yourself) is the discipline.

title: 2.6 Categorical Predictors
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. For the three-tissue dataset, run the analysis three ways: (a) C(tissue) with default baseline, (b) explicit Treatment(reference=...) choosing “tumorB”, (c) no-intercept cell-means (expr ~ C(tissue) - 1). Show that all three produce identical fitted values and R², and write out the pairwise mean differences implied by (b)’s coefficients to verify they agree with (a) after arithmetic.


Solution







One model space, three parameterizations. (c) is the most readable (coefficients are group means) but loses the baseline-contrast SEs; (a)/(b) make specific contrasts cheap. Choose the parameterization whose default outputs are the contrasts you care about.

Exercise 2 — ANOVA connection. One-way ANOVA is exactly the categorical-predictor regression above. Verify it: run smf.ols("expr ~ C(tissue)"), then compute the F-statistic for “tissue matters” three ways — (a) the model’s overall F when tissue is the only predictor, (b) anova_lm comparing with/without the factor, (c) a one-way ANOVA (statsmodels.stats.oneway.anova_oneway or scipy f_oneway). All three must agree.


Solution







Regression is the general machine; ANOVA is the special case where every predictor is categorical. Learning them as one object (rather than two rituals) pays off the moment you mix numeric + categorical predictors — which plain ANOVA cannot do.

Exercise 3. Mix numeric and categorical: fit expr ~ age + C(tissue) on the extended cohort below. Interpret each coefficient in one subject-matter sentence, then produce predicted means for each tissue at age = 50 by hand from the coefficients and verify against get_prediction. Finally, explain what this model assumes about the age effect across tissues — and name the page where that assumption gets relaxed.


Solution







The model assumes the same age slope in every tissue — parallel age-lines, offset by tissue. Whether that holds is exactly the interaction question: 2.7 Interaction terms.

title: 2.6 Categorical Predictors
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Baseline choice is a reporting decision: choose the level your audience contrasts against (control/healthy), not whatever comes first alphabetically. Software defaults will happily make “drug” the baseline and “placebo” the contrast.
The dummy-variable trap is the most common hand-built-design bug: all k dummies + intercept. With get_dummies, pass drop_first=True for modeling (keep the full version for display).
Unseen levels at predict time: a category in test data that never appeared in training has no coefficient — sklearn OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown=“infrequent_if_exist”) vs silent NaN in statsmodels. Plan for level drift in productionized models.
High-cardinality categories (patient ID, gene symbol with 20k levels) explode the design matrix — target encoding or hierarchical/mixed models are the remedies, not 20k dummies.
Ordinal ≠ nominal: if order is meaningful and roughly evenly spaced in effect, a single 0/1/2 column can be more parsimonious; but always compare against the k−1 dummy version — the data, not the codebook, decides.
Interactions with dummies are the natural next step: they let each group have its own slope — precisely 2.7.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated model has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fixed version


Numeric codes impose fake arithmetic: the model fits a line through codes 0,1,2 — assuming C = 2×B’s effect and ordering the labels. With nominal categories this is meaningless structure. Fix: dummies via C(site) (or justify numeric coding only for genuinely ordinal, evenly spaced scales).
All three dummies + intercept = singular design (rank deficiency; the trap). statsmodels’ pinv silently absorbs one level — non-reproducible parameterization. Fix: drop_first=True or formula C(site).
“Baseline has no effect” misreads the parameterization: A’s level is in the intercept; the tested contrasts are B−A and C−A. To ask “does site matter at all”, F-test the dummies jointly.

title: 2.6 Categorical Predictors
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Prove that encoding k categories with k−1 dummies + intercept spans exactly the same space of fitted values as k separate group means, and that the OLS fit in both parameterizations assigns each group its own sample mean. What does this imply about residuals, R², and the model’s assumptions?


Hint

Write the design matrix; show each row picks out one group’s parameter; the least-squares problem decomposes per group.



Solution

Every observation’s prediction is “its group’s parameter” in both parameterizations, so the column space is the set of piecewise-constant-on-groups vectors — dimension k in both (k−1 dummies + intercept ≡ k cell means). RSS minimization decouples by group: within group g, minimize \(\sum_{i \in g}(y_i - c_g)^2\), solved by \(\bar y_g\). Hence identical fitted values, residuals, RSS, R², and zero within-group structure assumed — this model makes no assumptions beyond “each group has a mean”; it cannot express group-specific slopes (no numeric predictors interacting) or shared trends. That’s why adding a numeric predictor to dummies (Exercise 3) is a genuine modeling step, and letting the numeric slope vary by group is 2.7.

Q2. A collaborator fits y ~ C(biobank_site) on 40 sites and finds two sites with p < 0.05 offset coefficients, then reports “site effects identified.” Critique using 1.4 and 2.5: what family-wise issue arises, what does the joint F-test say and why does it differ, and design the defensible analysis (which test, which correction, which plot).


Solution


Selection + multiplicity: picking the 2 of 40 site coefficients with p < 0.05 is examining 40 contrasts; even under all-null, expect ~2 “hits” — exactly what was found. The per-coefficient p-values are unconditional; post-hoc selected ones need correction (Tukey/Bonferroni across site contrasts, or FDR). (b) The joint F-test (drop all 39 dummies) tests “any site differences” with one honest alpha; if it’s non-significant, the two “hits” are almost surely noise — the joint test pools all the site information and is the primary test. (c) Defensible: report the joint F (and effect-size spread of site offsets, e.g. SD of BLUPs), then if interest persists in specific sites, test those pre-specified contrasts with multiplicity correction; plot site offsets with their CIs (forest/ caterpillar plot) rather than asterisk-hunting a coefficient table. Mechanistically note also that with many small sites, individual SEs are large — significance at tiny sites is fragile by construction.

title: 2.6 Categorical Predictors
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (categorical × 2.5 confounding). Simulate a study where treatment assignment depends on site (site 1 gives drug 80% of the time, site 3 gives 20%) and the drug effect is homogeneous. Show that (a) the naive drug coefficient is confounded, (b) adding site dummies removes most of the bias, (c) residual bias persists through chance imbalance in small sites. Then quantify: run 500 simulations and histogram the adjusted-coefficient estimates — this is “regression adjustment as a bias-reducer, not a bias-eraser.”
C2 (categorical × 0.3 pandas). Take the wide expression table from 0.3 Exercise 3, melt it long, add a fake batch label, and test batch effect per gene: fit value ~ batch for each of the 5 genes with a loop of formulas. Which genes show batch effects at the joint-F level? Then write the two-sentence methods paragraph you’d put in a paper — this pattern (long-format + per-gene regression + joint F) is the skeleton of differential-expression pipelines like the T2 workflow in Part 12.

title: 2.6 Categorical Predictors
text:
7. Summary

Categories enter regression as k−1 dummies against a chosen baseline; coefficients are offsets from it.
All dummies + intercept = the trap (singular design); C() and drop_first=True are the habits.
Baseline choice changes the printed contrasts, never the fit; pick the baseline your audience reasons in.
Numeric coding of nominal labels fabricates order and spacing — a model, not a convenience.
One-way ANOVA is this page’s regression with a single categorical predictor; the machinery mixes freely with numeric predictors.
Numeric + categorical with a shared slope assumes parallel effects — the assumption 2.7 Interaction terms exists to interrogate.

title: 2.8 Nonlinear Feature Transformations
text: Linear models fit straight lines in their parameters — but the features can be any transform of x you like: polynomials, logs, splines, binned indicators. This buys curvature inside the same least-squares machinery, at the price of the same old dangers (overfitting, extrapolation) in sharper form.

title: 2.8 Nonlinear Feature Transformations
text:
1. Basic Concept
“Linear” in \(X\beta\) refers to the coefficients. Replace \(x\) by any derived columns and the model stays linear-in-parameters:
\[y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \beta_2 x^2 + \varepsilon \qquad \text{or} \qquad \log y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \log x + \varepsilon\]
Polynomial regression of degree d is just OLS on the design matrix \([1, x, x^2, \ldots, x^d]\):






Degree 2 wins here because the truth is quadratic. Degree 9 chases noise — same lesson the U-curve will make quantitative in 4.1.
Log transforms linearize power laws and stabilize multiplicative noise (0.4):






Binning (step features) is the crudest nonlinearity — cut x into ranges, dummy them (2.6):

title: 2.8 Nonlinear Feature Transformations
text:
2. Concept Questions

Why is polynomial regression still a “linear model”? What precisely is linear?
Degree 12 polynomial through 60 points: fitted values look perfect, predictions on new data are wild. Name the two quantities whose divergence you are witnessing.
Your y spans decades of magnitude with constant relative error. Which transform, and what does the slope mean if you regress \(\log_{10} y\) on \(\log_{10} x\)?
Extrapolation danger: compare a linear fit and a degree-9 polynomial fit extended 20% beyond the data. Which fails more catastrophically, and why — what does the polynomial do outside the data’s support?
log(y) model gives RMSE(log-scale) = 0.2. A colleague multiplies by exp to report “RMSE = 1.22” on the raw scale. What did they actually compute, and what is the right comparison?



Answers


Linear in the coefficients \(\beta\): the model is \(\beta^\top \phi(x)\) for basis functions \(\phi\) (powers, logs of x — transforms of features, not of parameters). Estimation is still OLS on a design matrix.
In-sample error (falls as degree rises — more flexibility always fits training better) vs out-of-sample error (rises once curvature fits noise). The gap is overfitting; Part 4 measures it, Part 5 penalizes it.
log–log (power-law) transform; slope = the power exponent (y ∝ x^slope), intercept gives the multiplicative prefactor. Only after confirming constant relative scatter — the log makes multiplicative errors additive (0.4 Q2).
The polynomial. A line continues its slope; a degree-9 fit’s leading coefficient (estimated from noise) dominates outside the data, swinging to ±astronomical values. Polynomials are global basis functions — a wiggle fitted inside must resolve into a violent curve outside. Local bases (splines, Part 6) behave far better.
exp(0.2) = 1.22 is a median-level multiplicative miss (the error of a typical log-residual), not an RMSE in y-units — RMSE is not transform-invertible (Jensen: E[y − ŷ] ≠ exp(E[log-residual])). The honest comparison back-transforms predictions (accepting median-level bias, or smearing-correcting) and computes RMSE on the raw scale.

title: 2.8 Nonlinear Feature Transformations
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. For the quadratic-truth data below, fit degrees 1–7 and collect training MSE and test MSE (fresh points from the same process). Plot both against degree. Mark the argmin of test MSE, then repeat the whole experiment with n = 300 — how does the curve’s shape change and what does that tell you about “more data vs simpler model”?


Solution







At n = 30 the test curve is jagged — degree choice is nearly a coin flip among low degrees. At n = 300 the minimum sharpens around the true degree 2 and high degrees hurt less (more data tames the variance term). Data volume substitutes for model restraint — the trade 4.4 will formalize.

Exercise 2. Linearize a real-ish process: enzyme velocity follows \(v = \frac{V_{max} s}{K_m + s}\) (Michaelis–Menten) with \(V_{max} = 2\), \(K_m = 0.4\). Fit (a) a direct polynomial of degree 2 on (s, v), and (b) the classic Lineweaver–Burk linearization (\(1/v\) vs \(1/s\), whose slope = \(K_m/V_{max}\), intercept = \(1/V_{max}\)) using OLS. Recover \(V_{max}\) and \(K_m\) from each. Which recovers the truth better under noise, and what famous statistical vice does Lineweaver–Burk have?


Solution







The reciprocal transform converts multiplicative-ish errors into heteroscedastic ones and hands all the leverage to the smallest s — the few noisiest points steer the line. The polynomial dodges that trap but estimates \(V_{max}\) as a plateau asymptote. Modern practice: fit the nonlinear model directly with least squares (Part 6 territory) — linearizations are history’s workaround, not a virtue.

Exercise 3. Build poly_cv(x, y, max_degree, k=5) returning mean CV MSE per degree using a Pipeline(StandardScaler-with-PolynomialFeatures, LinearRegression) — scaling before polynomial expansion to keep raw powers numerically sane. Run it on data with a cubic truth; report the chosen degree and the CV curve. Then explain why the pipeline (transform inside each fold) matters — connect to the leakage rule of 0.5.


Solution







If you scaled/expanded before splitting, each fold’s training statistics (means, SDs) leak test-fold information into training — mild here, systematic everywhere. The pipeline runs the transform per-fold inside cross_val_score, guaranteeing the validation fold is touched only by the fitted-for-that-fold transform. The 0.5 rule — “fit preprocessing inside the training fold” — generalizes to every transformer you will ever use.

title: 2.8 Nonlinear Feature Transformations
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Global vs local bases: polynomial features are global — every observation informs every coefficient, so one leverage point reshapes the whole curve. Splines/step functions are local (Part 6 covers them properly; the binned drill is a preview).
Numerical conditioning: raw powers of x (say x ∈ [0, 1000], degree 6) make columns nearly collinear and ill-conditioned — coefficients become garbage even when predictions look fine. Standardize x first, or use orthogonal polynomials (np.polynomial.legendre.legvander, or sklearn’s scaled pipeline).
The polynomial tail kills: never report extrapolated polynomial predictions; if you must extrapolate, extrapolate the physics (a fitted asymptote, a log-linearized regime), not the polynomial.
Transforming y changes the error model: log y regression minimizes log-scale squared error — predictions are medians on the raw scale and need smearing if means are wanted; RMSE comparisons across scales are meaningless (2.4).
Binning throws away information and induces boundary artifacts; it’s a quick diagnostic (is there structure?) rather than an endpoint. Smooth bases or splines dominate it for inference and prediction alike.
Degree choice is a hyperparameter — choosing it by looking at the same data you report performance on is the classic optimism; route the choice through CV now, formally in 4.6.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated curve-fit has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fixed version


Raw powers of x up to 100⁸ — the design matrix has condition number ~10¹⁶; coefficients are numerically meaningless (look at their wild magnitudes). Fix: standardize x before expanding (or orthogonal polynomials).
Extrapolating a degree-8 fit to x = 500 (5× beyond data): the leading noise-driven coefficient explodes — “predictions” of ±billions. Fix: police the range; extrapolate with theory-bounded models only.
RMSEs on different scales (y vs log y) — not comparable (2.4). Fix: back-transform log predictions and compare on one scale.

title: 2.8 Nonlinear Feature Transformations
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Show that adding any column \(g(x)\) to a linear model’s design matrix can only decrease training RSS, and quantify the minimum decrease in terms of the residual regression: if \(g\)’s component orthogonal to the current columns explains RSS reduction \(\Delta\), write the updated fit. Use this to explain why degree-9 training RSS < degree-2 training RSS even when truth is quadratic, and what determines whether the test RSS follows.


Hint

Projection geometry from 2.4 Q1: OLS projects y onto the column space; a bigger space projects further.



Solution

OLS fit = orthogonal projection of y onto span(columns). Adding a column enlarges the span, and projections onto supersets are never worse: new RSS = old RSS − ‖proj of y onto g⊥(old columns)‖² = old RSS − Δ, with Δ ≥ 0. For the noise-only extra powers, Δ = the squared length of the chance alignment of the noise with those directions — positive in every sample, growing with the number of added columns. Test RSS follows only if the true f has a component in the new directions that outweighs the variance those directions import (each extra coefficient costs ~σ²·(df) of variance in predictions — the arithmetic 4.4 makes explicit). In-sample improvement is therefore guaranteed, meaningful only if structural.

Q2. You must model \(y = f(x)\) where f is believed smooth and you have n = 40 points. Compare, in one experiment, (a) global polynomial degree chosen by CV, (b) 10-bin step function, (c) the “transformed linear” model \(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \beta_2 \sin(x)\) when the truth is \(3\sin(x)\). Report test MSEs and state the general lesson about basis choice informed by mechanism vs generic flexible bases.


Solution







The mechanistic two-column model usually wins outright (right basis, 3 parameters); CV-polynomials get close with 5–8 parameters; steps are worst (boundary steps, step noise). Lesson: a small basis derived from how the system works beats generic flexibility at small n — save the flexible machinery for when mechanism is unknown and n is large.

title: 2.8 Nonlinear Feature Transformations
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (transforms × 2.10 Assumptions preview). Generate multiplicative-noise data (\(y = 2x\,e^{\varepsilon}\)). Fit (a) y ~ x, (b) log y ~ log x, and diagnose each with residuals-vs-fitted and QQ plots. State which assumption each fit violates and how the diagnostic revealed it — then connect the funnel and the skewed residuals to 0.4 Q2’s log-scale advice.
C2 (transforms × 4.1 Generalization preview). Using the degree-sweep experiment from Exercise 1, decompose test MSE at each degree into bias² and variance by simulating 300 training sets (evaluate each degree’s fitted curve on a fixed grid, average across training sets). Plot the three curves (bias², variance, total) against degree. You have built the bias–variance picture before the theory page — bring the plot to 4.4 and check it against the decomposition there.

title: 2.8 Nonlinear Feature Transformations
text:
7. Summary

“Linear” means linear in coefficients; polynomials, logs, bins, sin — any derived columns — stay in OLS-land.
Higher degree always improves training fit and eventually wrecks test fit; degree is a hyperparameter, chosen by CV.
Log transforms linearize power laws (slope = exponent) and convert multiplicative noise to additive; back-transform carefully (medians, not means).
Polynomials are global bases: numerically fragile raw, catastrophic in extrapolation; standardize before expanding.
Transforming y changes the error model and the meaning of every metric; compare models on one scale.
Mechanism-informed small bases beat generic flexible bases at small n.
The residual from a transformed fit must still be inspected — the full diagnostic toolkit is next: 2.10 Regression assumptions, after a nonparametric detour in 2.9 KNN regression.

title: 3.1.5 AUPRC for Skewed Datasets
text: When positives are rare (1% disease, 0.1% hits in a screen), ROC-AUC keeps flattering weak classifiers — the huge negative pool absorbs false alarms invisibly. The precision–recall curve and its area (AUPRC / average precision) put the cost of false alarms in a sparse world back in the picture.

title: 3.1.5 AUPRC for Skewed Datasets
text:
1. Basic Concept
Sweeping the threshold from strict to loose traces a curve in precision (PPV = TP/(TP+FP)) vs recall (TPR) space. The area under it — computed as sklearn’s average precision,
\[\text{AP} = \sum_n (R_n - R_{n-1})\, P_n\]
i.e., each precision value weighted by the increase in recall it purchased — is the standard scalar (AUPRC).
Two facts make AUPRC the right lens under skew:

The baseline is the prevalence, not 0.5: a random classifier’s PR curve hovers at precision = prevalence. AUPRC = 0.55 at 1% prevalence is massive; AUC = 0.55 would be negligible.
False positives are priced in the metric: at low prevalence, each FP slashes precision immediately (denominator TP+FP), while in ROC-land an FP just nudges FPR by 1/(huge N).

The flattering-ROC demonstration — 2% prevalence, a barely-informative score:

title: 3.1.5 AUPRC for Skewed Datasets
text:
2. Concept Questions

Why is a random classifier’s PR baseline the prevalence while its ROC baseline is the diagonal?
Two datasets have identical classifier quality; one has 1% prevalence, one 30%. Which metric is comparable across them — AUC, AP, or neither?
AP = 0.35 at 5% prevalence: translate that into “how much better than random” in one sentence.
Your model’s PR curve is strictly below the prevalence line everywhere. What does that tell you, and what single transformation rescues the model?
Why does AP have no nice probabilistic interpretation like AUC’s concordance probability?



Answers


Random scoring means precision ≈ prevalence at every recall level (each retrieved batch is prevalence-random), so the PR “curve” is the horizontal line y = prevalence. In ROC space, random scoring moves TPR and FPR together — the diagonal.
AUC (it’s a within-pair probability, prevalence-independent in expectation). AP is prevalence-dependent by design — its baseline moves with prevalence — so absolute AP values don’t transfer across datasets with different class balance. Neither is a substitute for reporting the dataset’s prevalence alongside.
Random retrieval gets precision 0.05; this model’s precision-recall trade is worth AP = 0.35, i.e. its average precision across recall levels is 7× the random baseline — strong for a 1-in-20 problem.
Precision below prevalence at all recalls means the score is anti-ranked: top-scored items are less likely to be positive than random. Negate the scores (or flip the sign of the decision function) and the same information becomes a good model — always check this before discarding a model.
AUC counts a specific, symmetric random experiment (draw one of each, who wins?). AP is a weighted sum of precisions with data-dependent weights (recall increments) — a different, asymmetric summary with no single natural random-pair story; its “meaning” is operational: expected precision averaged over recall levels you choose to chase.

title: 3.1.5 AUPRC for Skewed Datasets
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. By hand, build the full precision–recall table for the ranked list below (compute P@k, R@k for every k), compute AP from the table, and verify against average_precision_score. Then state the single threshold (top-k) you would choose if the budget allows exactly 3 follow-ups, and its precision.


Solution







The budget answer is a decision the curve exists to inform: with 3 slots you catch 2 of 5 positives (precision 0.67); the curve lets management see exactly what the 4th and 5th slot would buy.

Exercise 2. Prevalence surgery: fix one classifier and one score distribution; vary prevalence from 0.5% to 40% by subsampling negatives, and plot AUC and AP against prevalence. Which curve moves, which holds steady, and what does this experiment say about comparing your AP to a published AP from a different cohort?


Solution







AUC is flat (prevalence-free by construction); AP falls as prevalence falls — the baseline sinks with it. Consequence: AP values are cohort-specific; compare APs only within the same prevalence regime, or convert to “multiple of prevalence baseline” (AP / prevalence) for a rough cross-cohort normalized statement.

Exercise 3. Metric face-off on a realistic screen: build a 1%-positive dataset with a mildly informative score; compute (a) accuracy at 0.5, (b) balanced accuracy, (c) AUC, (d) AP, (e) precision at recall = 0.5. Rank the metrics by how usefully each describes the model for a screening manager who can only follow up 50 samples. Justify the ranking in two sentences per metric.


Solution







Usefulness ranking for the manager: (e) precision@recall-0.5 — an operating point, exactly what “we follow up 50” means; (d) AP — the full-curve summary, prevalence-anchored; (c) AUC — ranks well but abstracts away the FP flood; (b) balanced accuracy — treats classes symmetrically when the budget doesn’t; (a) accuracy — tells the manager nothing (it’s the prevalence in disguise). The general law: the closer a metric sits to the actual decision (budget, costs, threshold), the more decisions it can improve.

title: 3.1.5 AUPRC for Skewed Datasets
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Three names, one thing (mostly): AUPRC (area under PR curve), AP (sklearn’s interpolated area), mean average precision (mAP — averaged over queries, the retrieval convention). sklearn’s average_precision_score uses the recall-increment weighting — not the trapezoidal rule — so hand-trapezoiding your PR points gives slightly different numbers (the worked table uses the sklearn definition; the trapezoid variant appears in Appendix A.7’s worked example).
AP is not comparable across cohorts with different prevalence (Exercise 2) — report prevalence next to every AP, always.
The last point of the PR curve: precision_recall_curve appends the anchor (recall 0, precision 1); the thresholds array is one shorter — off-by-one errors when zip()-ing live here.
Interpolated “best PR” curves (as in some leaderboards) paint an upper envelope that no actual threshold achieves; be explicit which convention you report.
AUPRC noise: with few positives the curve is jagged and AP’s sampling variance is large — bootstrap it (1.5) before declaring one model better than another.
PR wins under skew; ROC still wins for: cost-symmetric ranking questions, prevalence-robust reporting, and comparing against chance (0.5) — the metrics answer different questions; report both under skew.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated “screen performance” report has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Accuracy at 1% prevalence is uninformative, but not automatically 0.99. A classifier that predicts everything negative scores 0.99 trivially; this one thresholds weak scores at 0.5, flags 744 of 1500 as positive, and lands at 0.5073 — barely above chance. The number certifies nothing either way, which is exactly why it should not be the headline. Use AP / precision@budget and always print the prevalence.
PR machinery on 0/1 predictions: only two distinct thresholds exist, so the “curve” is three points, and the area comes out negative (−0.342) because precision_recall_curve returns precision in decreasing-threshold order while the integral expects increasing x. A negative AP is not a small AP — it is a meaningless one. Feed continuous scores to average_precision_score.
Cross-cohort AP comparison without prevalences: their cohort may be 30% positive (AP baseline 0.30) while yours is 1% (baseline 0.01) — 0.07 may be the stronger result. Normalize (AP/prevalence) or recompute both on a common prevalence.

title: 3.1.5 AUPRC for Skewed Datasets
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Prove the AP formula \(\text{AP} = \sum_n (R_n - R_{n-1})P_n\) equals the precision averaged over the recall axis for the step-function PR curve, and show that for a single threshold operating point (R₀, P₀) the formula contributes \(R_0 P_0 = TP_0 / N_+\) — connecting AP to the raw hit count. What does this imply about AP’s sensitivity to the last positives retrieved (high recall, low precision region)?


Hint

Write each recall increment as ΔTP/N₊ and multiply by precision = TP/(TP+FP) at that step.



Solution

\(R_n - R_{n-1} = \Delta TP_n / N_+\) and \(P_n = TP_n/(TP_n + FP_n)\), so each term counts positives gained weighted by their purity; summed, AP = (1/N₊) Σ ΔTP·P = mean precision per positive retrieved. For a model that puts all TPs first at one shot: one increment with \(R_0 = TP_0/N_+\), \(P_0 = 1\), contributing \(TP_0/N_+\) = fraction of positives found perfectly. Consequence: the tail matters — retrieving the final positives at precision ~prevalence adds \((R=1 - R_{prev}) \times \text{prevalence}\)-ish mass; with 5 positives, each late hit adds ~0.2 × 0.1 = 0.02. AP rewards getting most positives cleanly; it is forgiving of the last scrappy recoveries exactly in proportion to how few positives remain — a feature under skew, and the reason AP > AUC Rankings shuffles rarely change AP’s tail.

Q2. Your team must choose between Model A (AP = 0.21, AUC = 0.85) and Model B (AP = 0.24, AUC = 0.80) at 2% prevalence, with a fixed budget of 100 follow-ups per 10,000 screened. Design the decision experiment: what single metric or plot settles it, how do you quantify uncertainty (bootstrap), and how should the budget constraint enter the comparison? Implement it.


Solution







The budget turns the comparison into precision@k (top-100 hits) — AUC and AP both summarize the whole curve, but only k = 100 will be operated. The bootstrap CI on the hit difference says whether B’s sharper head is real or noise (here B wins at the operating point despite losing on AUC — a decisive, budget-aware answer). Generalize the pattern: choose the metric that mirrors the deployment constraint, then attach uncertainty to that metric, not to a curve-wide scalar that no one will ever operate.

title: 3.1.5 AUPRC for Skewed Datasets
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (AUPRC × 3.1 metrics × 1.4 inference). Generate 200 resampled test sets (bootstrap the same test data) and compute AP and AUC distributions for one fixed model. Which metric’s CI is wider at 1% prevalence, and does the ordering of two competing models (by either metric) survive the uncertainty? Write the reporting rule that follows: when do you need the bootstrap before comparing two classifiers, and what sample size of positives makes single-number AP comparisons defensible?
C2 (AUPRC × 12.x multiple testing preview). A biomarker screen tests 20,000 candidates and reports “14 significant hits.” Reinterpret the screen as a classifier: define scores, prevalence, and AP for the hit list, then compute the precision you’d need for the list to beat random selection by a factor of 10. Connect to the FDR viewpoint: precision of a hit list at fixed size is 1 − FDR of that list — the two vocabularies are the same object seen from the ranking and the testing side.

title: 3.1.5 AUPRC for Skewed Datasets
text:
7. Summary

Under class skew, PR curves price false alarms honestly; ROC’s huge negative pool hides them.
AP = Σ Δrecall × precision: mean precision weighted by positives gained; baseline = prevalence.
AUC stays comparable across prevalences; AP does not — report prevalence beside every AP.
Below-baseline PR curve = anti-ranked scores: flip before you discard.
The metric that mirrors the deployment constraint (precision@budget) beats any curve-wide scalar for decisions.
With few positives, bootstrap AP differences before believing them.
With both metric families in hand, ask the orthogonal question — why not just use linear regression on 0/1 labels? — 3.2 Why not linear regression for categories?

title: 3.2 Why Not Linear Regression for Categories?
text: The laziest classifier is tempting: encode the classes as numbers (0/1) and run the Part 2 machinery. This page shows precisely what breaks — and the surprisingly defensible uses of the resulting “linear probability model” — so that logistic regression’s logit link (3.3) earns its complexity honestly.
crumbs: 3.2 Why Not Linear Regression for Categories?

title: 3.2 Why Not Linear Regression for Categories?
text:
1. Basic Concept
Fit \(p(x) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x\) by OLS on 0/1 outcomes. Three structural problems, none fixable by more data:

Out-of-range predictions: a line is unbounded; probabilities must live in [0, 1]. Near the data’s edges (where decisions matter!) the line exits the unit interval.
Heteroscedasticity by construction: with y ∈ {0,1} and mean p(x), \(\text{Var}(\varepsilon \mid x) = p(x)(1 - p(x))\) — variance maximal at p = 0.5, vanishing at the extremes (2.10 Q1). Every classical SE is wrong, automatically.
Wrong error family: Gaussian errors on 0/1 outcomes is a category error; the Bernoulli likelihood is the honest one.







The heteroscedasticity signature, live:
crumbs: 3.2 Why Not Linear Regression for Categories?

title: 3.2 Why Not Linear Regression for Categories?
text:
2. Concept Questions

Why is a predicted probability of −0.2 or 1.3 not merely “slightly wrong” but unusable for decisions built on probabilities?
The heteroscedasticity of the linear probability model is structural. Why can’t a variance-stabilizing transform of y fix it?
For multi-class data encoded 0, 1, 2, what extra assumption does OLS smuggle in beyond the binary case’s problems?
Despite everything, econometricians use linear probability models. Name two properties that make them tolerable in their niche.
Your LPM gives slope 0.06 for a binary predictor. Translate that into the sentence a stakeholder understands.



Answers


Decisions multiply probabilities: expected cost = p × cost; posterior updating; risk thresholds (“treat if p > 0.2”). Negative probability or probability > 1 breaks the arithmetic that decisions are made of — it’s not a small inaccuracy, it’s a type error.
y is 0 or 1; there is nothing to transform (log of 0, arcsine of a constant…). The variance is a function of the mean’s position — only a model whose variance follows the mean (Bernoulli GLM) or robust SEs can cope; no y-transform exists.
Ordinal spacing: coding {control=0, drugA=1, drugB=2} forces the mean response to be linear in the codes — asserting drugB’s effect is exactly double drugA’s and that the categories are ordered at all. Nominal labels have no arithmetic; OLS invents one.

The coefficient is directly interpretable as a percentage-point change in probability per unit x — no odds-ratio translation needed. (b) With mid-range probabilities (0.2–0.8) and modest extrapolation, the line is a decent local approximation, and OLS’s robustness/diagnostics ecosystem applies. (Plus: interaction effects and panel-data fixed-effects machinery are simple in LPM.)

“Moving from the predictor’s 0 to 1 raises the probability of the outcome by 6 percentage points, on average.” (For small probabilities, odds ratios would say something different — this honesty about which summary you’re quoting is the whole game.)
crumbs: 3.2 Why Not Linear Regression for Categories?

title: 3.2 Why Not Linear Regression for Categories?
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.




















Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Quantify the damage: for the simulation below (steep truth), compute (a) the fraction of the x-range where the LPM predicts outside [0, 1]; (b) the classification error rate of thresholding the LPM at 0 vs 0.5 vs 1 (treating clipped values); (c) the same for clipping predictions into [0,1]. Where does clipping help, where does it silently distort?


Solution







Clipping rescues hard decisions but keeps lying about probabilities — any downstream cost arithmetic (Exercise 2 of 3.1) still consumes nonsense. Classification hides LPM’s sin; probability uses expose it.

Exercise 2. The LPM’s one honest superpower — marginal effects: simulate a logistic truth with modest slope, fit (a) logistic regression and (b) LPM. Compute the logistic model’s average marginal effect (mean over data of dp/dx = p(1−p)·β), and compare it with the LPM slope. Write the sentence explaining why practitioners sometimes prefer the LPM coefficient for reporting.


Solution







For gentle slopes, p(1−p)·β is nearly constant, so “the logistic model’s average effect” ≈ “the LPM slope” — but the LPM gets there with no iteration and reads directly off the coefficient table. That convenience is worth having when the probability range is mid-span; it evaporates near 0 or 1, where the LPM’s line can’t follow the logistic curve.

Exercise 3. Multi-class misuse: simulate three groups with distinct means on x and class labels (control/drugA/drugB) where drugB’s shift is not double drugA’s. Fit OLS on 0/1/2 codes and on one-hot dummies (2.6); show the coded model’s predictions are constrained to a line in code-space while the dummy model’s are not, and quantify the prediction error of each against group means.


Solution







The coded fit is dragged by its fake arithmetic: it must place drugB at exactly twice drugA’s offset. With nominal categories the one-hot model is correct by construction (it’s just group means). Coded-label regression is not a shortcut; it’s a different (wrong) model.
crumbs: 3.2 Why Not Linear Regression for Categories?

title: 3.2 Why Not Linear Regression for Categories?
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

The LPM’s coefficient is on the probability scale; logistic’s is on the log-odds scale. Cross-model coefficient comparisons without conversion (e^β, or AMEs) are meaningless — a perennial review-report error.
LPM + HC3 robust SEs fix inference but not the range violations or efficiency losses; it remains an approximation whose quality is a function of how far p sits from 0/1.
Don’t diagnose-and-patch an LPM into a GLM manually — weighting by 1/(p̂(1−p̂)) (“iterated WLS”) is the historical pre-GLM trick; modern practice fits the Bernoulli likelihood directly.
Zero-one-inflated outcomes (p pinned near 0 for most x) make LPM slopes collapse toward 0 and R² meaningless (never above ~prevalence·(1−prevalence)); the rare-event regime is logistic’s home turf.
Thresholding an LPM at 0.5 implicitly equates FP and FN costs — classification thresholds are decision theory (3.1 Exercise 2), not model byproducts.
Why not least squares on probabilities “estimated” from bins? That’s just the binned drill from 2.8 — it works descriptively but has no likelihood, no efficient SEs, and bin boundaries are arbitrary.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated model has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Out-of-range probabilities as deliverables: reporting “P = 1.18” — a number that cannot exist — to stakeholders. Use logistic regression for probability outputs, or at minimum clip-and-disclose (and never feed unclipped values into cost arithmetic).
Classical SEs under structural heteroscedasticity: wrong by construction (2.10 Q1); minimum fix cov_type="HC3", real fix Bernoulli likelihood.
Nominal codes as intensity: “drugB = 2× drugA” was inserted by the encoding, not learned from data (see Exercise 3). Dummies or multinomial logistic, never ordinal codes on nominal labels.
crumbs: 3.2 Why Not Linear Regression for Categories?

title: 3.2 Why Not Linear Regression for Categories?
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Prove \(\text{Var}(\varepsilon \mid x) = p(x)(1 - p(x))\) for a 0/1 response, and use it to show that OLS’s Gauss–Markov efficiency claim fails for binary data: construct (in simulation) an estimator with lower variance than OLS — e.g., the MLE from logistic regression — and quantify the variance ratio as a function of the probability range in the data.


Hint

Gauss–Markov requires homoscedastic errors; binary data violate it structurally. The Bernoulli MLE is (asymptotically) efficient for its model.



Solution

ε = y − p(x) takes values 1−p (prob 1−p… wait: y=1 w.p. p ⇒ ε = 1−p) and −p (prob 1−p): Var = p(1−p)² + (1−p)p² = p(1−p). Since this varies with x, homoscedasticity fails and OLS is not BLUE for binary data. Simulation:






Wider x-ranges (probabilities pushed toward 0/1, variance collapsing at the extremes) increase the LPM’s relative inefficiency — the Bernoulli MLE exploits the variance function OLS ignores.

Q2. The thresholded-LPM classifier is not insane: threshold the linear fit at 0.5 and it often classifies nearly as well as logistic regression. Construct the regime where they differ maximally (steep sigmoid, wide x-range), show the classification agreement rate, and explain why classification metrics hide what probability metrics expose — connecting to the calibration discussion your 3.1 answer promised.


Solution







Both models place the 0.5-crossing near the same x (monotone scores, same ranking locally), so hard labels agree almost everywhere and accuracy/ROC-type views see little difference. But probability-valued outputs — costs, PPV statements, risk tiers — diverge wildly at the extremes (−0.4 vs 0.03!). Classification metrics are invariant to monotone score warping; probability correctness is not. That’s the calibration axis from 3.1 Q5, and it’s why “same AUC” never means “same model.”
crumbs: 3.2 Why Not Linear Regression for Categories?

title: 3.2 Why Not Linear Regression for Categories?
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (LPM × 2.7 Interaction). In an LPM, interaction coefficients are differences of probability effects — directly interpretable as percentage-point moderation. Fit LPM and logistic (with AME-style interpretation) to the same data with a true interaction; show where the two reports agree (mid-range) and disagree (tail). Which would you present to a clinical audience and why — and what does the “one number per moderation” convenience cost in fidelity at the tails?
C2 (LPM × 3.6 GLMs preview). Write the Bernoulli log-likelihood for data (xᵢ, yᵢ) under (a) the linear-probability model p = β₀+β₁x (where you must clamp/penalize parameter values that push p outside [0, 1]) and (b) the logistic model p = σ(β₀+β₁x). Fit both by direct optimization (scipy.optimize.minimize) and compare each MLE against the plain OLS solution. The punchline to verify: OLS is not even the right fitting criterion for the LPM’s own probabilistic story — report how far apart they land and why.
crumbs: 3.2 Why Not Linear Regression for Categories?

title: 3.2 Why Not Linear Regression for Categories?
text:
7. Summary

OLS on 0/1 labels: unbounded predictions, variance = p(1−p) (heteroscedastic by design), wrong likelihood.
Classification metrics can hide all of this; probability uses and costs expose it.
The LPM survives as a local approximation with direct percentage-point readings — defensible mid-range, dangerous at the tails.
Nominal multi-class labels must never be numerically coded: codes fabricate order and spacing (2.6).
Robust SEs patch inference, not probabilities; clipping patches decisions, not probabilities.
The honest machine for binary responses puts the Bernoulli likelihood and a bounded mean function together — logistic regression: 3.3 Logistic regression.

title: 3.4 Generative Classifiers: LDA, QDA, Naive Bayes
text: Instead of modeling P(y|x) directly (discriminative — logistic), generative classifiers model how each class generates data — P(x|y) and P(y) — then flip the conditioning with Bayes’ rule. Three classical instances span the assumption spectrum: LDA (Gaussian, shared covariance), QDA (Gaussian, per-class covariance), Naive Bayes (conditionally independent features).
crumbs: 3.4 Generative Classifiers: LDA, QDA, Naive Bayes

title: 3.4 Generative Classifiers: LDA, QDA, Naive Bayes
text:
1. Basic Concept
Bayes’ rule chooses the class maximizing the posterior:
\[P(y = k \mid x) = \frac{P(x \mid y = k)\, P(y = k)}{\sum_j P(x \mid y = j)\, P(y = j)}\]
LDA assumes each class is Gaussian with its own mean μₖ but one shared covariance Σ. Plugging in and simplifying, the log-posterior becomes linear in x — hence linear discriminant. QDA gives each class its own Σₖ; quadratic terms survive — quadratic boundaries. Gaussian Naive Bayes assumes independence within each class (diagonal covariance): one variance per feature per class, no correlations — crude but fast and parameter-poor.






When the classes’ covariances genuinely differ, QDA earns its extra parameters:






Naive Bayes by hand — the whole method in ten lines, then verified against sklearn:
crumbs: 3.4 Generative Classifiers: LDA, QDA, Naive Bayes

title: 3.4 Generative Classifiers: LDA, QDA, Naive Bayes
text:
2. Concept Questions

What does the “naive” in Naive Bayes assume, and why is it catastrophic for correlated features even when each feature is individually informative?
LDA vs QDA: state the parameter-count trade (in d dimensions, per class) and the sample-size rule of thumb that follows.
Why do generative models need fewer training samples to reach a given accuracy when their assumptions hold — and what happens when the assumptions don’t hold?
LDA’s boundary is linear. Which two simplifications of the Bayes-optimal rule produce that linearity?
Your features are 5,000 gene counts with strong correlations. Which of the three would you reach for first, and what would you need to check before trusting QDA?



Answers


Features are conditionally independent given the class (diagonal class covariance). With correlated informative features, NB double-counts the same evidence: two correlated genes each “voting” for the class push the posterior toward certainty twice — overconfident probabilities, badly calibrated posteriors (accuracy can survive; the probability values don’t).
LDA: one shared Σ = O(d²) parameters total + d means per class; QDA: full Σₖ per class = O(k·d²). With d = 50, LDA’s Σ has 1,275 entries shared; QDA’s two have 2,550 estimated separately. Rule of thumb (ISL): small n or a shared-covariance belief → LDA; large n or visibly different covariances → QDA. (Between them sits “regularized QDA”/shrinkage covariance.)
Modeling the joint densities adds structure the data needn’t discover: with correct assumptions, the estimate converges at parametric rates and out-of-sample accuracy rises quickly with n (fewer effective parameters than a discriminative search over boundaries). When wrong, the bias is baked in — and generative models typically converge to the wrong boundary no matter how much data arrives, while flexible discriminative methods would eventually find the truth.

Gaussian class densities; (b) equal covariance matrices — the quadratic terms x^TΣₖ⁻¹x then coincide across classes and cancel in the log-ratio, leaving a linear score.

Gaussian NB with correlation-aware caution… honestly: none of the three directly. NB’s independence assumption is badly violated (double counting). QDA in d = 5,000 estimates 12.5M covariance entries per class — singular without regularization; you’d need heavy shrinkage (reg_param) or feature reduction first (or logistic regression with penalties — Part 5). The check before QDA: n ≫ d and covariance stability, neither plausible here.
crumbs: 3.4 Generative Classifiers: LDA, QDA, Naive Bayes

title: 3.4 Generative Classifiers: LDA, QDA, Naive Bayes
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Implement LDA’s classification rule from scratch for two classes: estimate μ̂₀, μ̂₁, pooled covariance Σ̂, priors; classify by sign of the linear score \(x^\top \Sigma^{-1}(\mu_1 - \mu_0) - \tfrac12(\mu_1^\top\Sigma^{-1}\mu_1 - \mu_0^\top\Sigma^{-1}\mu_0) + \log(\pi_1/\pi_0)\). Verify 100% agreement with sklearn on training data, then perturb one class’s covariance and show where LDA and QDA begin to disagree.


Solution







The hand version IS sklearn’s rule (up to internal scaling). Once covariances differ, the shared-Σ score is no longer Bayes-optimal and QDA’s quadratic terms capture the elliptical structure — visible as disagreement concentrated far from the boundary.

Exercise 2. The NB double-counting experiment, quantified: build truth where P(y=1|x) depends on a single latent z, and expose it through k increasingly correlated copies (ρ = 0, 0.5, 0.9, 1.0 between copies). For each ρ, fit GaussianNB and logistic regression; report (a) accuracy, (b) the mean predicted probability for true positives (overconfidence meter). Which model’s accuracy degrades with ρ? Which model’s probabilities degrade?


Solution







Accuracy stays similar across ρ for both (the information content doesn’t change much), but NB’s predicted probabilities inflate toward 1 as correlation grows — the same evidence counted twice. Logistic regression, discriminative, never assumed independence and stays calibrated. Lesson: choose the model by what you consume — rankings (NB fine) or probabilities (NB dangerous under correlation).

Exercise 3. Generative vs discriminative sample-efficiency sweep: fixed true model = two Gaussians with equal covariance (LDA’s world, so its assumptions hold). For n per class in {5, 15, 50, 200}, fit LDA and unpenalized logistic on 100 independent training sets, evaluate each on a fixed test set, and plot mean test accuracy vs n. Which converges faster? Then repeat with unequal covariances and re-read the curves.


Solution







Equal covariance (LDA’s assumptions true): LDA leads at every n — the generative parametric payoff. Unequal: LDA’s advantage evaporates/reverses as its bias caps its ceiling while logistic keeps climbing. The generative-vs-discriminative trade, drawn to scale.
crumbs: 3.4 Generative Classifiers: LDA, QDA, Naive Bayes

title: 3.4 Generative Classifiers: LDA, QDA, Naive Bayes
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

LDA’s shared covariance is a modeling claim — check it (visual covariance ellipses, Box’s M in spirit) before trusting its SEs/probabilities; QDA when ellipses differ, and reg_param when n is small.
QDA in high dimensions is numerically fragile: per-class covariance matrices go singular (d > n per class); sklearn’s reg_param adds ridge-like stabilization — tune it, don’t disable it.
NB posteriors are overconfident under any correlation — never quote its probabilities without calibration checks (3.7); its rankings survive much better than its values.
Class priors matter: LDA/NB use empirical priors; in case–control samples the priors are sampling artifacts — correct with priors= (sklearn) or logit-offset (3.3 C2).
LDA is also a projector: its scalings give the k−1 discriminant axes — a supervised alternative to PCA for visualization (9.2 contrast: PCA is unsupervised, ignores y).
Multiclass comes free: all three handle k > 2 natively (no one-vs-rest machinery) — a quiet advantage over the logistic formulations of 3.3.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated classifier has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


NB probabilities quoted as risks: three near-copies of one signal triple-count the evidence; predicted risks inflate toward 1. Report rankings, or recalibrate (3.7), or drop duplicate features / use logistic.
Case–control priors as prevalence: class_prior_ here reflects the sampling design (here 50/50), not biology. Set GaussianNB(priors=...) to real prevalence or correct downstream.
QDA on 6 samples: covariance estimates are garbage (reg_param=0 doesn’t even stabilize); the 1.00 “score” is training-set self-evaluation. Fix: more data, reg_param tuned by CV, or LDA.
crumbs: 3.4 Generative Classifiers: LDA, QDA, Naive Bayes

title: 3.4 Generative Classifiers: LDA, QDA, Naive Bayes
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Derive LDA’s linear score from the Gaussian log-densities: write \(\log P(x|k) + \log \pi_k\) for class k, subtract the two classes’ expressions, and show every quadratic term cancels under Σ₀ = Σ₁. Then state precisely which direction the discriminant points (Σ⁻¹(μ₁−μ₀)) and why it is the Fisher optimal projection (maximizing between-class over within-class variance).


Hint

Expand −½(x−μₖ)ᵀΣ⁻¹(x−μₖ); the xᵀΣ⁻¹x piece is class-independent.



Solution

log P(x|k) = −½(x−μₖ)ᵀΣ⁻¹(x−μₖ) + constₖ. The difference log P(x|1) − log P(x|0) = xᵀΣ⁻¹(μ₁−μ₀) − ½(μ₁ᵀΣ⁻¹μ₁ − μ₀ᵀΣ⁻¹μ₀) — the xᵀΣ⁻¹x terms cancel because Σ is shared. The decision score is linear with direction w = Σ⁻¹(μ₁−μ₀): the class separation, whitened by within-class covariance — which is exactly Fisher’s criterion argmax wᵀ(μ₁−μ₀)/√(wᵀΣw). Two views, one vector: the generative derivation and the optimal-projection problem have the same solution, which is why LDA doubles as both a classifier and a supervised projector.

Q2. You have d = 2,000 features, n = 200 samples, two classes with correlated features. Design the analysis pipeline: which of LDA/QDA/NB/logistic is even feasible as-is, what preprocessing must precede it, how you’d validate the choice (0.5 + 4.6 discipline), and what failure mode each option guards against. Demonstrate with a simulation: compare the candidates’ CV accuracies and calibration under p ≫ n.


Solution

Feasibility triage: QDA — infeasible (4M covariance parameters/class, singular). LDA — pooled Σ is 2000×2000 from 200 samples: singular; needs shrinkage or feature reduction. GaussianNB — feasible (2 diag variances per class) but assumes away the correlations and p ≫ n overconfidence. Logistic with L2 penalty — feasible and standard. Pipeline: standardize → (optionally) reduce dimension (feature screening inside CV only, or PCA) → fit penalized logistic / shrunk-LDA / NB inside a Pipeline → nested CV for model choice, calibration curve at the end.






Typical outcome: penalized logistic ≈ shrunk LDA > NB on accuracy, and only logistic/LDA give trustworthy probability directions; NB’s accuracy is respectable while its probabilities are inflated. The p ≫ n moral: the choice is not “which classifier” but “which regularization + which validation” — the subject of Part 5 and Part 4 respectively.
crumbs: 3.4 Generative Classifiers: LDA, QDA, Naive Bayes

title: 3.4 Generative Classifiers: LDA, QDA, Naive Bayes
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (generative × 2.6 categorical). Extend the Bayes classifier to mixed feature types: one Gaussian feature and one binary feature per class (model the binary one with class-specific Bernoulli probabilities — the “independence” NB way). Implement the joint log-posterior by hand, verify on simulated data against GaussianNB-on-dummified input where possible, and explain where a fully-Naive treatment misprices the joint evidence of (Gaussian, binary) pairs that are correlated within class.
C2 (generative × 4.4 bias–variance preview). Organize the three classifiers on a flexibility axis: NB (diagonal, k·d params) → LDA (shared full Σ) → QDA (per-class Σ). Simulate data under each of the three data-generatings in turn; for each, sweep the three models across n ∈ {20, 100, 500} and record test accuracy. You should reproduce the classic picture: the correctly-specified model dominates at small n; all converge at large n unless misspecified. Bring the resulting 3×3×3 table to 4.4 and map each cell onto bias/variance language.
crumbs: 3.4 Generative Classifiers: LDA, QDA, Naive Bayes

title: 3.4 Generative Classifiers: LDA, QDA, Naive Bayes
text:
7. Summary

Generative = model P(x|y)P(y), classify by posterior; fewer effective parameters, stronger assumptions.
LDA: shared Gaussian covariance → linear boundary + Fisher projection; QDA: per-class covariance → quadratic; NB: conditional independence → diagonal, fast, fragile probabilities.
LDA/QDA need n ≫ d and covariance stability (shrinkage/reg_param); NB needs feature independence to be honest.
Priors are parameters: sampling designs (case–control) must be corrected before quoting posteriors.
Correlated features double-count in NB — rankings survive, probabilities don’t.
Generative wins small-n under true assumptions; discriminative catches up and overtakes when assumptions fail.
The remaining classical classifier is assumption-free neighborhood voting: 3.5 KNN classification.
