title: 3.6 Generalized Linear Models
text: Logistic regression was not a one-off trick — it is one instance of a general recipe: pick a response distribution, a link between its mean and the linear predictor, fit by maximum likelihood. That recipe — the GLM — handles counts, rates, proportions, and skewed positives with the same coefficient-interpretation and inference machinery as Part 2.

title: 3.6 Generalized Linear Models
text:
1. Basic Concept
A GLM has three ingredients:

Random component — the response’s distribution family: Gaussian (linear regression), Binomial (logistic), Poisson (counts), Gamma (positive skewed), etc.
Systematic component — the linear predictor \(\eta = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \cdots\)
Link function — \(g(\mu) = \eta\), connecting the mean μ to the predictor. Identity for Gaussian; logit for Binomial; log for Poisson.

The log link makes coefficients multiplicative: \(e^{\beta}\) is a rate ratio per unit of x. Fitting maximizes the family’s likelihood (IRLS again — same engine as 3.3).






Why not just OLS on counts? Three failures, demonstrated live:






Offsets — exposures enter as a fixed coefficient: counts per differing library sizes model as \(\log \lambda = \eta + \log(\text{depth})\), i.e., modeling the rate not the raw count:

title: 3.6 Generalized Linear Models
text:
2. Concept Questions

Name the three ingredients of a GLM, and identify all three for (a) linear regression, (b) logistic regression, (c) Poisson regression.
β = 0.25 with a log link. State the effect in rate-ratio language, and in plain words if the baseline rate is 2.0.
Why does the Poisson assumption Var = mean matter inferentially — and what is the standard diagnostic when counts are more spread than that?
What does an offset do, when is it required, and why is log(depth) the offset rather than depth itself?
Your response is a proportion of successes out of varying n per row. Which GLM family and what structural detail of the fit?



Answers



Gaussian; η = β₀+β₁x; identity. (b) Bernoulli/Binomial; η; logit. (c) Poisson; η; log. Every classical regression is this triple — memorize the table, and new response types stop being new methods.

Each +1 in x multiplies the mean rate by e^0.25 ≈ 1.284 (+28.4%). At baseline 2.0: new rate ≈ 2.57 — the absolute jump grows with the baseline, which is exactly what multiplicative language encodes.
Poisson’s Var = mean enters the likelihood AND the SEs: if real counts are overdispersed (Var ≫ mean, near-universal in biology), GLM SEs are too small and p-values overconfident — by the same mechanism as 2.10’s equal-variance violation. Diagnostic: Pearson χ²/df ≫ 1; remedies: quasi-Poisson (robust SEs) or negative binomial — the default in differential-expression pipelines (Part 12’s T2 workflow).
An offset is a predictor with its coefficient fixed at 1: log λ = η + log(depth) ⇒ λ = depth × e^η — modeling rate per unit exposure. Required whenever observation effort/size varies (depths, person-years, areas). The log appears because the model is multiplicative: rate × exposure = count on the log scale becomes addition.
Binomial with a logit link, as a 2-column response (successes, failures) — sm.GLM(y, X, family=sm.families.Binomial()) with y = [successes, failures] per row — so each row’s variance follows its own n. A plain 0/1 logistic (3.3) is the n = 1 special case.

title: 3.6 Generalized Linear Models
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Recover a rate model end-to-end: simulate hospital readmissions where each patient has an exposure (days, 1–30) and a covariate x (age, 30–80) with log-rate = −4 + 0.03·age. Fit the Poisson GLM with offset, interpret both parameters in plain words, predict the expected readmission count for a 65-year-old admitted for 10 days, and verify against the true rate.


Solution







Reading: baseline rate ≈ e^−4 ≈ 0.018/day at age 30 (intercept’s reference); each decade multiplies the daily rate by ≈ 1.35. The offset does the bookkeeping for follow-up time — the model speaks in rates, the data arrive as counts.

Exercise 2. Overdispersion forensics: generate counts with Var = 4× mean (negative binomial), fit (a) Poisson GLM, (b) quasi-Poisson (sm.families.Poisson() + scale='X2' — Pearson-scaled SEs), (c) negative binomial GLM. Compare the slope estimates (all ≈ unbiased) and the three SEs, and report each model’s p-value for the slope. Which models “know” the truth about uncertainty?


Solution







All three slopes agree (the mean model is fine); the Poisson SE is the liar — small p-value manufactured by pretending Var = mean. Quasi-Poisson (scaled SEs) and negative binomial (explicit variance function) restore honest uncertainty. In biology, always run the dispersion diagnostic before trusting a Poisson p-value.

Exercise 3. GLM diagnostics, Poisson edition: for the Exercise 1 setup, build the randomized-quantile or deviance-residual diagnostics: plot deviance residuals vs fitted and vs age; QQ-plot them; verify approximate normality of deviance residuals under correct specification. Then inject a mis-fit (drop the offset) and show which diagnostic screams first.


Solution







With the offset, deviance residuals look like N(0,1) noise (dispersion ≈ 1); without it, dispersion explodes (counts without their exposure correction look wildly inconsistent) and the residual-vs-fitted panel develops structure. The first diagnostic to scream: the dispersion ratio — it is the Poisson world’s heteroscedasticity check (2.10 analog).

title: 3.6 Generalized Linear Models
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Log-link counts and zero observations: log(0) never appears in the model (the link acts on the mean, not on y) — but a manual log(y+1) OLS “fix” changes the estimand and breaks at different y’s. Model the counts with the right likelihood instead.
Overdispersion is the default state of biological counts — quasi-Poisson or negative binomial before any p-value is read (Exercise 2); the Poisson is a special-case claim, not a default.
Rate ratios vs risk ratios: with log links, e^β multiplies rates; converting to risk differences/ratios needs the baseline and horizon — the same translation discipline as 3.3’s odds ratios.
Offsets vs exposure covariates: an offset has coefficient fixed at 1; leaving exposure out entirely (or as a free coefficient) answers a different question — model the design, don’t average over it.
Complete separation’s cousin — zero cells: grouped binomial tables with all-success/all-failure strata destabilize fits; the same regularization/futility logic as 3.3 Exercise 2.
GLM SEs are inverse-Hessian (asymptotic): valid for n reasonably large; small-sample counts (few events) need exact/penalized methods — the rare-event caveat again.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated count analysis has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


log(y+1) OLS: changes the estimand (now modeling log-counts, with the +1 bias), mishandles the count nature, and mixes depth in as a free coefficient on the wrong scale. Model rates with log link + offset.
Depth ignored: dose effect is confounded with sequencing effort — samples with higher depth have more counts regardless of dose. Fix: offset=np.log(depth) (or include log-depth as a covariate with free coefficient if effort itself needs modeling).
Dispersion unchecked: with Poisson SEs, significance claims are premature. Run Pearson chi²/df, scale or go negative binomial if ≫ 1.

title: 3.6 Generalized Linear Models
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Derive the Poisson GLM’s IRLS update and show its working response is \(z = \eta + (y - \mu)/\mu\) and its weight is \(w = \mu\). Use this to explain (a) why zero-count observations get high weight in the fit relative to OLS’s treatment of residuals, and (b) why the variance structure (w = μ) automatically produces the funnel-shaped raw residuals of Exercise-drill 2 — and why that funnel is correct behavior, not a violation.


Hint

For Poisson, Var(y) = μ; the IRLS weight is Var⁻¹ evaluated at the current μ; the working response is the linearization of the link.



Solution

With g = log, g′(μ) = 1/μ: working response z = g(μ) + (y − μ)g′(μ) = η + (y−μ)/μ; IRLS weight w = 1/(g′(μ)²Var) = μ. (a) A zero count at μ = 4 gives working residual (0−4)/4 = −1 — the same pull as a count of 8 (+1): the link scales residuals by 1/μ, so relative misses weigh equally; OLS would treat the count-0 miss (−4) as four times the count-8 miss — inverting the information content for heteroscedastic counts. (b) Raw residuals y−μ have SD √μ by construction: the funnel in raw residuals is the model passing its own variance assumption; only deviance/Pearson residuals (normalized) should look homoscedastic. Diagnosing raw GLM residuals with OLS eyes inverts the verdict.

Q2. A colleague fits a Poisson GLM to single-cell UMI counts (dropped-out, overdispersed, zero-inflated) and reports significant genes via Poisson p-values. Design the critique experiment: simulate zero-inflated negative-binomial counts with (a) no real genes and (b) 100 truly differential genes; run the Poisson pipeline; report false-positive rate and sensitivity. Then state which layer of the pipeline each problem (overdispersion, zero-inflation) belongs to, and what the standard production answer is (negative binomial with empirical dispersion — the DESeq2/edgeR view, previewing Part 12’s T2 workflow).


Solution







The Poisson pipeline flags null genes far above 5% (overdispersion + zero-inflation inflate the statistic) while missing many true effects. Layering: overdispersion is a variance-function misspecification (fix: NB/quasi-likelihood); zero-inflation is a mean-process mixture (fix: ZINB hurdle models, or aggregates/normalization strategies). Production pipelines (DESeq2/edgeR) use empirical-Bayes negative binomial dispersions across genes — the principle: share variance information across the feature family rather than trusting per-gene Poisson. Full treatment in 12.6 (T2).

title: 3.6 Generalized Linear Models
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (GLM × 3.3 logistic × 2.7 interaction). Poisson model a count response with treatment × sex interaction on the log-rate scale. Show numerically that the interaction coefficient is a ratio of rate ratios — and that a significant multiplicative interaction can correspond to nearly identical absolute rate differences at low baselines. Produce the two-panel plot (rate ratio and rate difference by baseline) that would let a reviewer see both languages at once.
C2 (GLM × 2.4 model accuracy × 4.3 CV preview). Define and compute an out-of-sample deviance (or Poisson log-loss) for the readmission model of Exercise 1 across 5 folds, and compare in-sample vs CV deviance. What plays the role of R² here (hint: compare against the intercept-only GLM’s deviance)? This “explained deviance” is how GLM model accuracy is reported — practice computing it honestly.

title: 3.6 Generalized Linear Models
text:
7. Summary

GLM = family × linear predictor × link; logistic and linear regression are members; Poisson (counts, log link) is the workhorse you didn’t know you needed.
e^β = rate ratio; offsets convert counts to rates when exposure varies.
OLS on counts predicts negatives, misweights residuals, and misstates variance — the likelihood is the fix, not a transform.
Overdispersion (Pearson χ²/df ≫ 1) is biology’s default; quasi-Poisson/negative binomial before believing p-values.
Diagnostics: deviance residuals (not raw), dispersion ratio as the first alarm.
p ≫ n and rare events strain GLM SEs — regularization and exact methods await in Part 5.
Every model so far needs the same referee: how well does it predict new data, really? Part 4 begins: 4.1 The generalization problem.

title: 4.1 The Generalization Problem
text: Training error is a promise the model makes to itself; test error is the promise it keeps to you. The gap between them — optimism — grows with model flexibility and shrinks with data. This page makes the gap visible, measurable, and predictable: the organizing problem of statistical learning.

title: 4.1 The Generalization Problem
text:
1. Basic Concept
Three error quantities, precisely:

Training (in-sample) error: average loss on the data the model was fitted to. Always optimistic — the fit adapted to this data’s noise.
Test (out-of-sample) error: average loss on fresh data from the same process. The honest quantity — what deployment will see.
Generalization gap (optimism): test − training. Grows with flexibility (more parameters, smaller k, deeper trees…), shrinks with n.

The signature experiment — one figure that contains the entire course:






The same story with a continuous flexibility dial (KNN’s k) — train error rises monotonically with k while test is U-shaped:

title: 4.1 The Generalization Problem
text:
2. Concept Questions

Why is training error guaranteed non-increasing in polynomial degree, while test error is not?
State the direction of each effect on optimism: doubling the number of fitted parameters; doubling n; increasing noise σ.
Your colleague reports train MSE 0.02, test MSE 0.21, σ² ≈ 0.09. Diagnose the model in one sentence and name the two standard remedies.
KNN’s k and polynomial degree are both flexibility dials — which direction is “more flexible” in each, and why are their U-curves mirror images?
A model with training error above the noise floor tells you what, immediately?



Answers


Least squares projects y onto a growing column space: each added polynomial term can only reduce RSS (2.8 Q1). Test error pays for each parameter twice — once through variance in estimating it — so beyond the true structure it climbs.
More parameters → more optimism; more n → less (each parameter is better pinned, and the fit has less room to chase noise); larger σ → more optimism in absolute terms (more noise available to chase) while the noise floor itself also rises.
Overfitting: the gap (0.19) is ≫ the distance to the floor (0.12) — the model has high variance. Remedies: reduce flexibility (lower degree, larger k, regularization) or gather more data; verify by CV either way.
Polynomials: flexibility ↑ with degree (more terms). KNN: flexibility ↑ as k ↓ (locality). So the KNN U-curve is traversed right-to-left relative to the polynomial’s — mirror images of the same phenomenon.
Underfitting (bias-dominated): the model can’t even reach the noise floor, so no amount of validation care will help — increase flexibility before optimizing anything else. It’s the cheap, immediate diagnostic people forget.

title: 4.1 The Generalization Problem
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. The optimism experiment, quantified: for degrees 1–10, repeat 200 times (fresh n = 30 training sets, fixed large test set), and record the mean training MSE, mean test MSE, and the mean gap. Plot all three vs degree. Verify the two qualitative laws: training error falls in degree, and the gap grows in degree; then check quantitatively how much of the test curve’s left side is bias (mean prediction ≠ truth) vs variance (prediction wiggles across training sets).


Solution







Degree 1: bias² dominates (a line can’t trace a sine). Degree 9: variance dominates (curves swing wildly between training sets). The decomposition is 4.4 previewed with your own data.

Exercise 2. Data-volume rescue: fix the degree-9 overfitting disaster by scaling n (30, 100, 300, 1000, 3000). Report test MSE at each n. Then replot the degree-1-vs-9 test comparison across n. Write the two-sentence law: when does flexibility stop hurting, and what never stops hurting?


Solution







Degree 9’s test error falls toward the degree-1 level (and past it, eventually) as n grows — variance is curable with data, since each coefficient gets pinned by more points. Degree 1’s error never improves past its bias floor — no amount of data fixes a wrong model shape. Flexibility’s danger is finite; underfitting’s is permanent.

Exercise 3. p ≫ n theater: n = 25 samples, 200 pure-noise features, pure-noise labels. Fit (a) plain OLS, (b) ridge with α = 10 (Part 5 preview — Ridge(alpha=10)), (c) KNN with k = 10. Report train and test R²/MSE for each. Which method’s training behavior is the most honest? Connect each to a bias/variance profile.


Solution







Read the middle rows carefully — this is where the intuition usually breaks. OLS interpolates (train 0.000, test 1.168), KNN can’t (train 0.648, test 1.106), and it is tempting to conclude that ridge is “honest by constraint.” It is not. Ridge(1) and Ridge(10) are just as optimistic as OLS on the training number (0.000 and 0.002) because at p = 200 ≫ n = 25 the penalty is far too weak: Ridge(10) still has an effective df of 22.7 out of 25, so it nearly interpolates. Only Ridge(100) (train 0.089, test 1.105) actually collapses toward the null model, and it needed an α tuned to the problem. Shrinkage is not a guarantee of honesty — it is a dial, and an untuned dial can sit anywhere (5.2). The training number only fools those who assume a regularized model must be a modest one.

title: 4.1 The Generalization Problem
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Optimism is predictable in size: for linear models, in-sample optimism ≈ (2σ²/n)·(number of parameters) — the engine behind Cp/AIC/BIC and adjusted R². It’s why 2.4’s noise columns added ≈ (k/n) worth of fake R².
The test set is a budget: every look spends it (0.5); adaptive “tune on test, report test” can make a noise-only pipeline score near-perfectly (try it once, to be cured forever — 4.2).
Selection inflates: choosing the best of M models by its CV score reports an extreme order statistic — the winner’s CV score is biased up by roughly (SD of the noise) × E[max of M standard normals]. More candidates = more inflation (4.6).
Modern caveat — double descent: beyond the interpolation threshold (p ≳ n), test error can fall again for some overparameterized models (the deep-learning regime). The classical U-curve is the right mental model for classical models; hold it loosely at the extremes.
Data leakage resurrects optimism invisibly: preprocessing fit before splitting, duplicates across splits, features derived from the outcome — every one shrinks the apparent gap while worsening the real one. The gap being small is good news only if the pipeline earned it.
In-sample diagnostics ≠ out-of-sample validity: residual plots (2.10) certify the fit’s assumptions; only held-out data certifies predictions.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated “experiment” has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Three models, one test set, argmax on test: the winner’s score is an order statistic — biased up even though each individual estimate was unbiased. Select on training-side CV.
Selected-on-test then reported-on-test: the number is now a selection number, not an estimate. Report on data untouched by selection.
Split-shopping: with enough tries, some split flatters any model; keeping the flattering one is p-hacking with a random seed (1.4’s peeking loop in evaluation clothing).

title: 4.1 The Generalization Problem
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. For a linear model with n training points and p parameters, the expected optimism of the training MSE is approximately \(\frac{2\sigma^2}{n} p\). Verify this by simulation (σ = 1, p ∈ {1, 5, 20}, n = 100, truth = zero signal or mild signal), then use it to explain (a) why Cp/AIC-style criteria subtract \(2p\hat\sigma^2/n\) from training error, and (b) why the approximation degrades when p approaches n.


Hint

Optimism = E[test error] − E[train error] for the fitted rule; for linear smoothers with hat matrix H, trace-based arguments give the 2σ²p/n form (Mallows’ Cp derivation).



Solution







Agreement is close while p ≪ n. As p → n, the fit interpolates: training MSE → 0, the hat matrix saturates (H → I, df → n), and the linear approximation’s assumptions (moderate leverage) break — optimism explodes non-linearly rather than tracking 2pσ²/n. The formula is a small-p law; the U-curve is the whole truth.

Q2. A pipeline reports “CV error 0.31” as the performance of the selected model, where selection was: 12 candidate models evaluated by the same 5-fold CV, winner = smallest. Design and run the experiment measuring the selection inflation: simulate null data (no signal) where every model’s true error equals σ², run the selection, record the winner’s CV score; compare its average to σ² and to the average of a fixed model’s CV score. Then derive the practical rule (report the winner’s score from a fresh outer CV, or correct by the expected order statistic).


Solution







Even with zero signal, the winner of 12 candidates reports ≈ 0.8–0.9 — selection alone manufactures a fake improvement over the fixed model’s ≈ 1.0. This gap is pure selection inflation and it grows with the candidate count and CV noise. Rules: (1) estimate the selected pipeline’s performance by wrapping selection itself inside an outer CV (nested — 4.6); (2) or subtract the expected order-statistic bonus (knowable by simulation under the null — exactly what you just built).

title: 4.1 The Generalization Problem
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (generalization × 2.9/3.5 KNN). Build the full 2-D map: for n ∈ {25, 100, 400} and k ∈ {1, 3, 10, 30, 100}, record train and test MSE (regression) or error (classification) on a fixed truth. Produce a heatmap of test error over (n, k) and draw the ridge of optimal k. How does optimal k scale with n, and what does the map predict about KNN’s viability when you can only collect 25 more samples?
C2 (generalization × 3.7 comparison). Six classifiers, one dataset, twenty replications: record each model’s CV accuracy per replication, then compute (a) each model’s mean, (b) the winner-per-replication’s average score, (c) the fixed pre-registered model’s average. Quantify (b) − (c) as measured selection inflation in a non-null setting, and check whether it’s larger or smaller than your null-data estimate from Q2 — then explain the direction.

title: 4.1 The Generalization Problem
text:
7. Summary

Training error is an optimistic estimator; the optimism grows with flexibility and shrinks with n.
The U-curve (test error vs flexibility) is the field’s central picture: underfit left, overfit right, noise floor below.
Flexibility dials point opposite ways (degree ↑, k ↓) but the physics is one: bias² + variance + σ².
Selection among many models inflates the winner’s score — order statistics, not skill.
Test sets are budgets; CV is the renewable subscription (next pages); leakage is counterfeit currency.
Underfitting (train error above σ²) is permanent without more flexibility; overfitting is curable with data or constraints.
The first remedy for optimism is the simplest split of all: 4.2 The validation set approach.

title: 4.3 Cross-Validation
text: Cross-validation (CV) keeps the validation idea but recycles the data: split into K folds, hold each out in turn, average. Every row is validated exactly once and trains K−1 times — more precise estimates from the same data, at K times the compute. It is the default referee of applied machine learning.

title: 4.3 Cross-Validation
text:
1. Basic Concept
K-fold protocol: partition rows into K disjoint folds (shuffled, ideally stratified). For k = 1..K: fit on all folds except k, predict fold k, record the metric. Report the mean (and spread) of the K values.






The full loop, explicitly, then the one-liner that does the same:






Classification needs stratified folds (class proportions preserved per fold — 0.5):






LOOCV — the K = n extreme: every point validated once, training on n−1. Nearly no bias from undertraining, but expensive and with correlated folds:

title: 4.3 Cross-Validation
text:
2. Concept Questions

What exactly does “5-fold CV estimate = 0.31 ± 0.04” estimate, and which model (trained on what fraction of data) does the ± describe?
Why is K-fold CV not K times more precise than a single validation split, despite using K folds?
LOOCV is nearly unbiased for the error of models trained on n−1 points. Name its two practical costs.
You’re comparing two models with fold-wise CV errors. Why must the fold splits be identical across models, and what test formalizes the comparison?
Repeated CV (e.g., 10× 5-fold) — what does repetition add, and what doesn’t it fix?



Answers


It estimates the expected test error of the procedure “fit this model type to 4/5 of data” — i.e., of models trained on 80% of the data. The final deployed model (trained on 100%) will typically be slightly better; the estimate carries that small pessimism (4.2).
The K fold errors share training data (any two training sets overlap in K−2 folds) and evaluate on the same finite dataset — the fold errors are strongly positively correlated, so their mean’s variance doesn’t shrink like independent estimates would (no 1/K). Repetition with fresh shuffles reduces, but never eliminates, this.
Compute (n fits, each on n−1 rows — infeasible for expensive models) and high fold-correlation: the LOOCV mean has low bias but its variance isn’t correspondingly tiny, so per-fold SEs are misleading. Also no stratification granularity at K = n for classification (some folds have 1 positive).
Fold difficulty (which easy/hard rows land together) shifts all models’ scores on a given split — pairing cancels it. With identical folds, compare fold-wise differences with a paired t-test (3.7); with different random splits, you’re comparing two noisy marginals.
Repetition with different shuffles averages out partition luck, tightening the estimate (the SD across repeats estimates the partition-noise). It does NOT fix: selection inflation (picking the winner among many models by CV), leakage, or distribution shift — those are pipeline diseases, not partition noise.

title: 4.3 Cross-Validation
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Variance anatomy: estimate the true test error of a degree-3 model (fit on 80% of n = 120) via (a) one 5-fold CV, (b) 20 repeats of 5-fold CV, (c) 200 independent 80/20 splits. For each, report the estimate and an empirical SD across 300 repetitions of the whole scheme. Which scheme’s repetition-SD is smallest, and what does the comparison say about what CV does and doesn’t recycle?


Solution







All three estimate nearly the same thing and their means agree; the SD ranking (single split worst, one 5-fold in the middle, 20× repeats best) quantifies the partition-noise that CV partially — but not fully — recycles. Diminishing returns set in: 20 repeats ≈ 100 fits for a modest tightening, because folds within a repeat are correlated.
One implementation note that this exercise is really about: the repetition loop must vary the seed. If scheme() ignores the repetition index, all 300 calls compute the identical number and the across-repetition SD is exactly 0.00000 — a silently dead experiment that still prints a confident table. Whenever you report an SD over repetitions, check that it is not suspiciously zero.

Exercise 2. Model selection by CV, done right and wrong: among degrees 1–12 on sinusoidal data (n = 100), (a) select the degree minimizing 5-fold CV MSE; (b) report that minimum as the performance; (c) also compute the true error of the CV-selected degree (big fresh test). Repeat over 200 datasets: compare the distribution of (b) against (c), and against the true error of the fixed degree-3 model. Quantify the optimism of (b) and the quality of CV as a selector.


Solution







The reported minimum sits below the selected model’s true error — that gap is selection optimism, paid for searching 12 candidates. Meanwhile CV-as-selector works well: the selected degrees’ true errors beat (or nearly match) fixed degree-3, because CV’s noise per candidate is small enough that the true winner usually scores near the top. Two hats, one tool: a good selector, an optimistic reporter — never let it wear both hats at once (4.6 formalizes the fix).

Exercise 3. Grouped biological data done properly: 40 patients × 5 visits (200 rows); the signal is at the patient level. Compare three evaluation schemes for a logistic model: (a) row-level StratifiedKFold(5) — patients split across folds; (b) GroupKFold(5) by patient; (c) GroupKFold with LOO-patients (40 folds). Report each scheme’s mean CV AUC and across-fold SD, then evaluate the winning-by-(a) model’s performance on truly unseen patients. Which scheme’s number would you put in a paper claiming “generalizes to new patients”?


Solution







Scheme (a) lets each patient’s rows appear in both train and validation — the model memorizes patient-level drift and reports inflated AUC (“generalizes” only to new visits of known patients). Schemes (b)/(c) answer the new-patient question and their numbers are visibly lower and more honest. The evaluation unit must match the deployment claim: row-level questions (rare in medicine) vs patient-level questions (the usual).

title: 4.3 Cross-Validation
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

K choice folklore: K = 5 or 10 balance bias (training fraction 1−1/K) against compute and fold-correlation. K = 2 gives the most independent folds; LOOCV the least (and is noisier per-unit-cost for unstable learners).
Preprocessing belongs inside the folds — Pipeline + cross_val_score is the mechanical guarantee (0.5); a scaler fit before cross_val_score silently invalidates the whole table.
Fold-level SEs understate uncertainty (correlated folds); for error bars on the CV mean, use repeated CV across random partitions or bootstrap over rows — not sd(fold scores)/√K alone.
CV estimates procedures, not fitted models — after CV, refit on all data for deployment; the CV number is the performance claim, the full-data fit is the artifact (4.2 post-selection note).
Group/cluster leakage is the silent killer of biomarker papers: same patient, same batch, same unit across folds (0.5 bug #3, Exercise 3).
Time series: shuffle-free TimeSeriesSplit or rolling-origin schemes; random K-fold CV on temporal data answers a question nobody deploys against.
Feature selection inside CV only: screening features on the full dataset before CV is leakage — the fold must not know which features exist until it trains (2.8 Exercise 3).


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated evaluation has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Pre-CV scaling: every fold’s training statistics include validation rows. Pipeline inside CV.
Unshuffled folds on sorted data: some folds see one class only; several folds can’t even fit. Shuffle (or stratify).
Feature selection outside CV: the folds’ validation rows voted on which features matter — leakage. Selection must live inside the fold pipeline.

title: 4.3 Cross-Validation
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Estimate the fold-correlation of 5-fold CV errors empirically: generate 400 datasets; for each, compute the 5 fold MSEs of a fixed model; extract the average pairwise correlation of fold errors. Use the observed ρ to explain why the SE of the CV mean is \(\text{SD}(\text{fold})\sqrt{\frac{1+(K-1)\rho}{K}}\) rather than \(\text{SD}(\text{fold})/\sqrt{K}\), and compute the inflation factor at your measured ρ.


Hint

For the mean of K equicorrelated estimates, Var(mean) = (σ²/K)(1 + (K−1)ρ).



Solution

Measure the correlation across datasets: standardize each dataset’s fold errors, pool, and correlate fold positions.






Typical ρ lands well above 0 — folds share rows and the same underlying fit. The naive \(\text{SD}/\sqrt{K}\) understates the CV mean’s uncertainty by the inflation factor \(\sqrt{(1+4\rho)/5}\) (the code prints the ratio to the naive quantity, which is the same thing scaled by \(\sqrt{5}\)); repeated-CV or bootstrap-over-rows error bars are the honest alternative (Q2 of 4.2 for the single-split analogue).

Q2. You have n = 80 rows, an unstable learner (KNN k = 1), and must choose between LOOCV and 5-fold repeated 10 times as your error estimator. Simulate the truth (fresh test sets) and compare both estimators’ bias and variance across 200 datasets. Confirm or refute the folklore “LOOCV has low bias but high variance for unstable learners” and state which you’d use for (a) unstable learners, (b) stable learners (linear regression).


Solution







For the unstable k = 1 learner, LOOCV trains on n−1 ≈ n (low bias) but its per-fold predictions are maximally jumpy and folds nearly identical — high variance across datasets. Repeated 5-fold trades a hair of bias (training on 80%) for substantially lower variance — better for unstable learners, matching the folklore. For stable learners (linear regression), the variance difference largely evaporates and LOOCV’s minimal bias is attractive (compute permitting). The estimator must be matched to the learner’s stability — one more decision CV forces you to own.

title: 4.3 Cross-Validation
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (CV × 3.7 comparison × 12.x multiplicity preview). Ten models, five-fold CV, pairwise McNemar on pooled out-of-fold predictions = 45 comparisons. Simulate null data (no signal) and count how many pairs come out “significant” at p < 0.05. Apply Bonferroni (α/45) and re-count. Connect the result to why model-comparison tables in the wild overclaim — and write the protocol sentence your future papers will include.
C2 (CV × 2.4 R²). Out-of-sample R² from K-fold CV: implement fold-wise \(R^2 = 1 - \text{MSE}_{fold}/\text{Var}_{fold}(y)\) vs pooled \(1 - \sum \text{resid}^2 / \sum (y - \bar{y}_{pooled})^2\) on the same CV predictions. Show the two can differ noticeably on small folds, decide which is the defensible summary for (a) balanced folds, (b) drifting fold composition, and produce the exact sklearn-equivalent computation (cross_val_predict + r2_score) to check your arithmetic.

title: 4.3 Cross-Validation
text:
7. Summary

K-fold CV: every row validated once; report mean fold error ± honest uncertainty (fold correlation!, repeats).
Stratify classification folds; group by patient/batch when deployment means new groups; never shuffle time.
Preprocessing, feature selection, everything data-dependent lives inside the fold pipeline.
CV is a fine selector and an optimistic reporter of its own minimum — separation of hats is [4.6]’s law.
LOOCV: low bias, high compute, high estimator variance for unstable learners; 5/10-fold is the working default.
Fold-level SEs understate; repeat partitions or bootstrap rows for error bars.
The U-curve of 4.1 has a decomposition — bias² + variance + σ² — that explains why the minimum sits where it does: 4.4 The bias–variance trade-off.

title: 4.5 The Bootstrap
text: The bootstrap replaces distributional theory with computation: resample your data, refit, and read uncertainty off the spread. Beyond CIs for statistics (1.5), it prices models: coefficient stability, prediction intervals, and the famous .632 correction for optimistic resubstitution error.

title: 4.5 The Bootstrap
text:
1. Basic Concept
Mechanics for model assessment: draw B bootstrap samples (n rows, sampled with replacement) from the training data; fit the model on each; the collection of B fitted models approximates the sampling variability of the fitting procedure.






The same machinery gives prediction uncertainty — both of the fitted mean and of a new observation:






The .632 estimator — fixing the optimistic resubstitution error. A bootstrap sample omits ≈ 36.8% of rows (since \((1-1/n)^n \to e^{-1}\)); those out-of-bag rows are honest test cases for the bootstrap-fit model:
\[\text{Err}^{(.632)} = 0.368 \cdot \text{Err}_{\text{train}} + 0.632 \cdot \text{Err}_{\text{OOB}}\]

title: 4.5 The Bootstrap
text:
2. Concept Questions

Why must resampling be with replacement — and what fraction of rows does a bootstrap sample typically miss, to first order?
The .632 blend uses the resubstitution error (optimistic!) with weight 0.368. What is the logic of including it at all?
Bootstrap CIs for a model’s coefficients vs the formula SEs of 2.3: when do they agree, and what does it mean when they don’t?
Is the bootstrap valid for time-ordered rows? Name the assumption it needs and the standard fix when it fails.
A model’s OOB error ≈ its 10-fold CV error. Which property of the procedure makes those two estimates target (nearly) the same quantity?



Answers


Replacement generates variability between replicates (each row appears Poisson(1) times; some twice, some never). Missed fraction → \(e^{-1} ≈ 0.368\) — the “out-of-bag” set, which is what makes OOB evaluation possible.
The resubstitution error is the lower anchor (the fit’s error on data it memorized); OOB is closer to honest. Their weighted mix interpolates toward the true error — for stable learners with mild optimism the blend lands closer to truth than OOB alone, whose training sets are smaller (n distinct ≈ 0.632n, inflating OOB error). Advanced Q1 covers the .632+ refinement.
Under the model’s own assumptions (linear, homoscedastic, independent), bootstrap SEs converge to the formula SEs — agreement validates both. Divergence means the assumptions are wrong (heteroscedasticity, outliers, small-n skew) — the bootstrap is measuring the world as it is; the formula measures the world as assumed (2.3 Q2).
It needs exchangeability — rows i.i.d. from one distribution. Time series violate it (resampling destroys temporal dependence → SEs too small). Fixes: block bootstrap (resample contiguous blocks), or model-based resampling of residuals.
Both estimate the expected error of models trained on ≈ 63–80% of the data (bootstrap: ≈ 0.632n distinct rows; 10-fold CV: 90%) evaluated on unseen rows — the training-set-size mismatch is the main difference, and both are slightly pessimistic for the final refit-on-all-data model (4.2).

title: 4.5 The Bootstrap
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Bootstrap vs formula SE shootout under violations: generate data with heteroscedastic noise (\(\sigma \propto x\)) and heavy-tailed noise (t₂), n = 40. For each, compute the OLS formula SE of the slope and the bootstrap SE (B = 3000). Report the ratio. Which violation breaks the formula SE more, and what does the bootstrap’s larger value correspond to in reality?


Solution







The bootstrap SE exceeds the formula SE in both regimes — it prices the real error structure (heteroscedastic variance, outliers that sometimes land in a resample and swing the fit). The formula assumes one σ and thin tails; its number is a statement about the assumed world. When they diverge, trust the bootstrap and reach for robust SEs or a different likelihood.

Exercise 2. Implement the full .632 vs cross-validation comparison: for the k-NN regression setup above (and also k = 1 and k = 25), compute (a) resubstitution error, (b) .632 estimate, (c) 5-fold CV, and (d) the true test error on 20,000 fresh points. Tabulate all four per k. For which k does .632 come closest to truth, and what does the resubstitution column look like at k = 1 (why does that row explain the entire motivation of the estimator)?


Solution







At k = 1, resubstitution is exactly 0 — the estimate that motivated .632. The .632 blend lands near truth for moderate-k stable learners; note its known weakness: for severely overfitting learners the resubstitution anchor (0 at k = 1) drags the blend down (optimistic) — the .632+ correction reweights by relative overfitting rate. CV remains the workhorse; .632 matters when CV is too expensive or training sets are tiny.

Exercise 3. Prediction intervals by bootstrap: for the linear fit, build three bands at x = 0.5: (a) bootstrap CI of the mean response (vary coefficients), (b) bootstrap prediction interval (add simulated residual noise to each bootstrap prediction), (c) the classical t-based prediction interval from statsmodels (get_prediction). Compare widths and centering. Which band is honest for “where will the next point land”?


Solution







Band (a) is narrow (coefficient uncertainty only); bands (b)/(c) are wider by roughly 2σ·1.96 — the irreducible noise of a new point (2.2 Exercise 3). Bootstrap (b) matches classical (c) closely under correct specification and inherits the empirical residual distribution when it isn’t (skew, outliers) — its advantage in exactly the settings where the classical t-interval is fiction.

title: 4.5 The Bootstrap
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

The bootstrap resamples rows — paired/multilevel data must resample the unit (patient), not the visit; otherwise the resamples invent independence that isn’t there (the 2.10 Q2 lesson in resampling clothing).
Order statistics and extremes break it (the max degeneracy drill) — any statistic living at the sample boundary needs parametric or smoothed variants.
B matters, but differently per use: SEs stabilize by B ≈ 500–1000; 95% percentile CIs need B ≈ 2000+ (the 2.5% tail quantile is noisy); never report more digits than B supports.
The bootstrap estimates variability of the procedure, not the specific fit — that’s a feature (matches deployment, where a new sample gets a new fit) and a warning (it cannot tell you about the one fit you shipped beyond its procedure-level behavior).
Bootstrap model selection is optimistic — choosing hyperparameters by OOB score then reporting that OOB score overfits the resamples exactly like CV-selection does (4.6).
.632+ exists because .632 is optimistic for overfitting-heavy learners (Exercise 2’s k = 1 row); it reweights the blend by an estimated relative-overfitting rate — implement only if you must explain it; CV is usually simpler.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated “bootstrap CI” has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Without replacement, every “replicate” is the original data permuted — the slope SD is ~0 and the CI is fake-narrow. Replacement is the entire engine.
x resampled, y left whole: pairs are broken — slopes computed against unrelated responses; garbage variability. Resample row indices, jointly.
B = 50 for a 95% percentile CI: the 2.5%/97.5% quantiles rest on ~1 order statistic each; the third decimal is noise. B ≥ 2000, and report digits B supports.

title: 4.5 The Bootstrap
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Derive the OOB fraction: the probability row i is absent from a bootstrap sample is \((1 - 1/n)^n \to e^{-1} ≈ 0.368\). Then explain the training-size mismatch this creates for OOB error (models trained on ≈ 0.632n distinct rows), and quantify the mismatch’s effect by simulation: compare OOB error of a 5-NN model against its test error when trained on all n, for n ∈ {30, 100, 400}. Which n makes the mismatch negligible?


Hint

OOB evaluates models trained on ~63% of the data; 4.1 Exercise 2’s learning-curve logic prices that.



Solution







OOB is nominally pessimistic, because each bagged model saw only ≈ 63% of the rows — but the measured gap is not reliably signed. Here it is −7% at n = 30, then +17% and +23% at n = 100 and 400. At small n the two effects cancel: the smaller training set should inflate the error, but the OOB rows are the few points each bag happened to miss, and with k = 5 neighbours a bagged fit is noisy enough that the bias in the estimate offsets the variance it was meant to price. The honest summary is that OOB carries an error of roughly ±20% at these sample sizes, not a known upward bias that shrinks away. Treat it as a cheap, slightly-noisy stand-in for the learning curve — not as a number to quote to three decimals. The .632 blend exists to price the training-set shortfall, not to buy precision.

Q2. Bootstrap a model comparison: two models’ test errors on the same 200-row test set are 0.41 and 0.44. Design and implement the paired bootstrap CI for the difference (resample test rows, recompute both errors on the same resample, difference them), and explain (a) why resampling rows jointly is essential (what breaks if the two models’ errors are bootstrapped independently), (b) what assumption about the test set the resulting CI carries, and (c) when the CI overstates confidence (connect to 3.7’s pairing discipline).


Solution








Joint row resampling preserves the per-row pairing of the two models’ errors; independent bootstraps would destroy the negative covariance between their errors and overstate the difference’s variance (the paired-t logic of 1.4, resampled). (b) The CI treats the 200 rows as i.i.d. draws from the deployment population — cluster/row-duplicates or distribution shift break that. (c) It says nothing about selection (these two models were chosen after looking at related data) or about training-set variability — both models were fit once; the CI prices evaluation noise only, not the 4.3-level “refit on a new training set” noise.

title: 4.5 The Bootstrap
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (bootstrap × 4.3 CV). For the KNN k-selection problem, compare three uncertainty procedures for the selected model’s error: (a) .632, (b) 5-fold CV, (c) bootstrap-over-rows of the whole pipeline (resample rows, rerun the entire k-selection inside, evaluate OOB). Which procedure captures the selection step’s variability? Implement (c) — the “bootstrap the pipeline” pattern is the general answer to “my pipeline has many steps; how uncertain is the end number?”
C2 (bootstrap × 2.3 coefficient inference × 4.4 decomposition). For a heteroscedastic dataset, compute slope CIs four ways: formula, HC3 robust, pairs-bootstrap, and residual-bootstrap (resample residuals, refit — check why it’s invalid here: it assumes homoscedastic errors by construction). Report all four intervals and order them by width. Then state which pair of intervals a reviewer should trust and why the residual bootstrap’s failure is instructive about what each resampling scheme assumes.

title: 4.5 The Bootstrap
text:
7. Summary

Bootstrap = resample rows with replacement, refit, read spread; ≈ 36.8% of rows are out-of-bag per sample.
It validates assumptions rather than needing them: agreement with formula SEs is a green light, divergence a diagnosis.
.632 blends the optimistic resubstitution anchor with honest OOB error; .632+ exists for heavy overfitters; CV remains the default.
Resample the unit, keep pairs together, mind order statistics and B-dependent precision.
Paired bootstrap over rows is the universal CI for model differences; pipeline-bootstrap for whole procedures.
Bootstrap prices evaluation and coefficient uncertainty; it does not excuse selection on the same resamples.
Every method here evaluates models honestly; choosing hyperparameters is next: 4.6 Hyperparameter tuning.

title: 5.1 Feature Selection
text: When predictors outnumber good ideas, you must choose a subset — for prediction parsimony, for interpretability, or for cheaper deployment. Feature selection is where statistics meets 4.6 Tuning: a feature set is a hyperparameter, and selecting it on the data you report on is the oldest self-deception in the field.

title: 5.1 Feature Selection
text:
1. Basic Concept
Three families of selection:

Subset selection — search discrete subsets (best-subset by enumeration, forward/backward stepwise), score each by Cp/AIC/BIC or CV.
Filter methods — rank features by a univariate statistic (correlation, F-score), keep the top k.
Embedded methods — selection as a by-product of fitting (lasso’s zeros, 5.3; trees’ split choices, Part 7).

Mallows’ \(C_p\) scores a model with \(d\) fitted parameters by trading fit against size:
\[C_p = \frac{1}{n}\big(\text{RSS} + 2\,d\,\hat\sigma^2\big)\]
— training error plus a \(2\sigma^2/n\)-per-parameter optimism charge (the quantity derived in 4.1 Q1).
Best subset by brute force, scored by \(C_p\), on a small truth:






Filters and CV-tuned selection — the honest one-line production version (selection inside the folds, per 4.3):

title: 5.1 Feature Selection
text:
2. Concept Questions

Why does adding \(2d\hat\sigma^2\) to RSS (per 2.4) make \(C_p\) a fairer comparator than raw RSS?
Forward vs backward stepwise: name one setting where each fails to find the best subset.
Why can’t you compute p-values from the final selected model in the usual way, after the selection used those same p-values?
What is selection instability, and what does it predict about two labs running identical stepwise on their own data?
Your filter keeps the 5 features with the strongest marginal correlation with y. Name two kinds of variables this rule can miss.



Answers


Raw RSS only falls as features join (2.4’s noise-collector theorem). \(C_p\) adds the expected optimism, ≈ 2σ²d/n, so models are compared on their estimated test error — noise columns now lose.
Forward fails when a variable is useless alone but essential in pairs (its first step never picks it; the famous XOR-style trap). Backward fails when p ≥ n — the full model can’t even be fitted (singular design).
The selection step picked the covariates because they looked good in this sample; the post-selection p-values then test “is this good-looking feature good?” on the same data that chose it — double use of the evidence. Valid post-selection inference needs special machinery (or sample splitting: select on half, infer on the rest).
The set of selected features varies wildly across resamples of the same population when features are correlated. Prediction: each lab reports a different “top biomarkers” list with similar performance — a reproducibility red flag that screams correlated features + overfit selection.

Suppressor/joint variables — useless marginally, essential jointly (their combination carries the signal). (b) Low-marginal-but-nonlinear contributors, or features whose signal cancels a confounder’s — anything where the marginal projection hides the conditional effect (2.5 Q2’s suppressor story).

title: 5.1 Feature Selection
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Implement forward stepwise from scratch: start empty; at each step add the feature whose inclusion most reduces RSS; stop when no addition improves \(C_p\). Run it on the Section 1 dataset. Report the selected set and each step’s Cp. Which step would BIC (heavier penalty, \(\log n\) per parameter) have stopped at?


Solution







Forward picked the true pair, then stopped when Cp plateaued. Under BIC’s \(\log n\)-per-parameter penalty the second variable sometimes fails to clear the bar at small n — penalty choice is a statement about how much you fear false positives vs missed variables.

Exercise 2. Selection-on-training vs leakage: build a 20-feature, 5-signal dataset (n = 150). Evaluate two pipelines by nested CV: (a) SelectKBest(k=5) fitted on all data first, then CV the logistic model on the pre-filtered matrix; (b) the identical selection inside the pipeline via GridSearchCV. Report both accuracies and the gap — this is feature-selection leakage priced in dollars.


Solution







The leaky number is a mirage: the CV folds’ validation rows voted on which features matter. With weaker signal or fewer samples the gap widens; with abundant signal it vanishes — which is exactly why the bug survives in careless labs (4.3’s rule 6).

Exercise 3. The filter-vs-joint failure, constructed: build data where x₁ and x₂ are independent noise marginally uncorrelated with y, but y depends on their product (interaction: \(y = 2\,x_1 x_2\,u\), u noise). Run SelectKBest(f_regression, k=2) — check whether either is chosen; then fit a model with the engineered feature \(x_1 x_2\) included and compare test MSE against the filter+OLS pipeline. State the design lesson in one sentence.


Solution







Marginal filters are projections onto single axes (2.5): interaction signal lives in the product direction, invisible to any per-feature score. Lesson: filters are cheap shortlists for enormous p, never the final selection procedure — and interaction-aware search or embedded methods (lasso on an engineered basis, trees) must take over where marginal views end.

title: 5.1 Feature Selection
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Selection is part of the model. Anything chosen from the data — features, transformations (2.8), bin edges — must be re-derivable inside each CV fold, or your performance number describes a model that never existed.
Stepwise p-value thresholds (“add if p < 0.05”) are not tests and don’t control any error rate; they’re heuristics with unknown operating characteristics. Prefer explicit penalties (Cp/AIC/BIC) or CV — quantities with definitions.
Post-selection inference is a real research area (selective inference, data carving) because naive SEs after stepwise/lasso are wrong in ways that matter. The pragmatic default: split-sample — select on half, fit and infer on the other half, at the cost of power.
Selection frequency is the report: with correlated features, print selection frequencies across bootstraps/subsamples (drill 4) instead of one cherry-picked set; a feature selected 55% of the time is a different claim from 99%.
Filters buy speed at truth’s expense: at p = 500,000 univariate screens are the only affordable first pass — but always validate the shortlist jointly, and expect to miss interaction/suppressor structure (Exercise 3).
Unstable selection often means collinearity (2.5): when two features share signal, subset selection coin-flips between them; ridge-style shrinkage or elastic net’s grouping (5.4) is the structural fix.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated pipeline has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Selection before CV — the folds’ validation labels picked the features. Selection belongs inside the pipeline.
Downstream CV of a pre-filtered matrix inherits bug 1; the number is inflated by the selection’s peek at every row.
Univariate p < 0.05 over 15 features is ~0–1 expected false positives with NO FDR guarantee — that’s raw multiplicity (12.4 preview); FDR requires explicit q-value/BH procedure over the full tested set.

title: 5.1 Feature Selection
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Show that selecting the single feature with the largest |t-statistic| from M pure-noise features yields a feature whose in-sample |correlation| has expected value ≈ √(2 log M / n), and verify by simulation for n = 50, M = 1000. What does this tell you about “the top feature explains R² of the selected model” claims?


Hint

The max of M i.i.d. half-normals scales like √(2 log M) — the same order statistic that drove 4.6 Q1’s selection bonus.



Solution

Under the null each sample correlation is ≈ N(0, 1/n); the largest |r| among M is the max of M half-normal draws, whose expectation ≈ √(2 log M / n). Simulation:






≈ 0.38 correlation with pure noise — an in-sample R² near 0.14 for a feature that has nothing. Any “top feature” narrative built on in-sample fit of selected candidates inherits this order-statistic fiction; out-of-sample evaluation is the only corrective.

Q2. Design the stability-selection procedure: given a selection algorithm, sample B subsamples (half the rows), record each feature’s selection frequency, and keep features selected in ≥ π (say 0.6) of subsamples. Implement it for forward selection on the Section 1 data (with correlated features added), report the frequency table, and explain (a) why high threshold controls false selections, (b) why correlated true features can also fail the threshold — and what that asymmetry means for your final claim.


Solution








A noise feature must beat the field in 60% of half-samples — vanishingly unlikely under the null (each has ~50% coin-flip chances, compounded downward). (b) x1 and x3 are both true (x3 inherits signal through correlation) yet each is selected only when the subsample’s noise favors it over its twin — both can hover near 50% and miss a 0.6 threshold. The asymmetry: the procedure certifies unique contributors and abstains on interchangeable ones — which is honest reporting (say “x1 or its proxy x3”), not a flaw.

title: 5.1 Feature Selection
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (selection × 4.6 tuning × 12.x stub). Unify the three selection paradigms on one dataset: k chosen by CV (filter), λ chosen by CV (lasso, 5.3 — implement with LassoCV), and Cp-based best subset — all nested inside a common outer 5-fold loop measuring the whole procedure’s test MSE. Which procedure’s outer error is lowest, and how does the ranking change if you compare their inner best scores instead? This experiment is the practical proof of “selection procedures must be evaluated as procedures.”
C2 (selection × 1.5 resampling). Bootstrap the entire selected-model pipeline (resample rows → re-run forward selection → predict at a fixed x₀) and produce a predictive distribution rather than a feature list. Then compare its 95% interval to the naive interval from the one selected model (formula SEs, ignoring selection). Quantify the undercoverage of the naive interval empirically over 200 true-data draws — this is post-selection uncertainty made visible.

title: 5.1 Feature Selection
text:
7. Summary

Selection has three families — subset, filter, embedded — and one law: selection is data-dependent, so it lives inside validation loops.
Cp/AIC/BIC convert fit into estimated test error; CV does it without σ̂² or parametric assumptions.
Forward fails on joint variables; backward fails when p ≥ n; filters fail on suppressors and interactions.
Post-selection p-values are fiction; use split-sample selection or specialized selective inference.
Selection instability across resamples is diagnostic (collinearity) and reportable (selection frequencies).
The max-of-M order statistic manufactures in-sample stars from pure noise — 4.1 everywhere.
Continuous selection — penalties instead of subsets — is smoother and scales to p ≫ n: 5.2 Ridge regression.

title: 5.3 Lasso Regression
text: The lasso (least absolute shrinkage and selection operator) penalizes the sum of absolute coefficients. The kink at zero that ‖β‖₁ introduces does something ridge never does: it sets coefficients exactly to zero — shrinkage and variable selection in one convex problem, and the workhorse of p ≫ n data.

title: 5.3 Lasso Regression
text:
1. Basic Concept
\[\hat{\beta}^{\text{lasso}} = \arg\min_\beta \Big\{ \sum_i (y_i - \beta_0 - x_i^\top\beta)^2 + \lambda \sum_j |\beta_j| \Big\}\]
No closed form in general (the absolute values aren’t differentiable at zero) — solved by coordinate descent: iterate coefficients one at a time, each update a soft-threshold of the OLS-style partial fit. For orthonormal X the solution is explicit and illuminating:
\[\hat\beta_j = S_\lambda(b_j) = \text{sign}(b_j)\,\max(|b_j| - \lambda,\ 0)\]
— shrink small things to zero, shrink large things by λ:






Against sklearn’s lasso (standardized data, orthonormal-ish case), the same logic appears as zeros you can count:






The lasso path — coefficients entering and leaving the model as λ decreases:






Watch x₀ and x₁ (the near-duplicates): the lasso typically admits one of them and ignores the other — feature selection among twins by coin flip.

title: 5.3 Lasso Regression
text:
2. Concept Questions

Why does the L1 penalty produce exact zeros while L2 never does? (Use the soft-threshold formula’s kink.)
sklearn’s LassoCV selects alpha by CV. What does that alpha optimize, and what does it not optimize?
Two features are near-perfect duplicates and both truly matter. What does lasso do, and is the resulting model wrong?
Your lasso selects 4 features; you then report those 4 features’ p-values from a fresh OLS on just them. What’s still wrong?
As n grows with fixed true sparsity, what happens to lasso’s selection consistency — and which condition on the design can break it (the “irrepresentable” idea, in one sentence)?



Answers


For βⱼ near 0, the L2 penalty’s gradient 2βⱼ → 0 — nothing forces an exact zero (flat, smooth approach). The L1 gradient near zero is sign(βⱼ)·λ — a constant push through zero; the optimum sits at 0 unless the data strongly objects. Zero is a corner, and optima sit at corners.
It optimizes prediction error (default MSE) estimated by CV over the alpha grid. It does not optimize the selected set’s correctness, coefficient unbiasedness, or any inferential property — a good predictive alpha can over- or under-select features relative to the truth.
It picks (essentially) one of the duplicates and zeros the other. The model is not wrong predictively — the kept twin carries the shared signal. It’s wrong interpretively if you conclude “feature A matters, feature B doesn’t”: B is shadowed, not exonerated (2.5’s collinearity in L1 clothing).
The selection step used y (through the lasso), so the refit p-values still condition on a data-chosen set — naive OLS inference after selection is invalid (5.1’s post-selection problem; lasso doesn’t escape it, it’s just smoother). Options: split-sample selection/inference, or selective-inference machinery.
With n → ∞, lasso can consistently recover the true support if the design satisfies the irrepresentable condition — loosely, no feature outside the support may be too correlated with the selected set (the signal must be unambiguous). With strongly correlated “shadowed” features, lasso selection stays inconsistent even as n grows.

title: 5.3 Lasso Regression
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Derive the soft-threshold update: for a single coefficient βⱼ with residual partial correlation fixed (others held), write the objective as a quadratic in βⱼ plus λ|βⱼ|, minimize over βⱼ > 0 and βⱼ < 0 separately, and show the solution is \(S_\lambda(z_j)\) where \(z_j = x_j^\top r_{-j} / (x_j^\top x_j)\) (r₋ⱼ = partial residuals). Then implement one full coordinate-descent pass on a small dataset and verify the objective decreases at every step.


Solution

Holding other coefficients fixed, the objective in βⱼ is \(\frac{1}{2}x_j^\top x_j\,\beta_j^2 - z_j'\beta_j + \lambda|\beta_j| + \text{const}\) (where z′ absorbs the current partial residual). For βⱼ > 0 the minimizer is (z′ − λ)/(xⱼᵀxⱼ); for βⱼ < 0 it’s (z′ + λ)/(xⱼᵀxⱼ); if the unconstrained optimum lies within ±λ, the corner βⱼ = 0 wins — assembling to the soft-threshold.






Each coordinate’s update is the exact minimizer along that coordinate, so convexity guarantees the objective never rises — the guarantee coordinate descent rides on. (The threshold is λ/(xⱼᵀxⱼ) in coefficient units: bigger columns pay proportionally less — one reason practitioners standardize.)

Exercise 2. Lasso vs ridge on sparse truth with junk: n = 80, p = 40, truth uses 3 features. Fit ridge (α tuned by CV) and lasso (LassoCV); compare test MSE on fresh data AND the number of nonzero coefficients. Then flip the truth to dense (all 40 features with small effects) and re-run. Which method wins under which truth, and what does the loser’s nonzero count say about it?


Solution







Sparse truth: lasso’s MSE is competitive-or-better and its nonzero count ≈ the truth — the interpretability win is free. Dense truth: ridge typically edges out lasso on MSE, and lasso’s nonzero count shows it dropped many small-but-real effects (bias on dense signals). The methods embody priors about the world; pick by which prior matches, verified by CV — never by leaderboard reflex.

Exercise 3. The relaxed lasso (post-lasso refit): run LassoCV to select a support; then refit plain OLS on the selected features only. Compare on fresh test data: lasso’s predictions, the relaxed fit’s predictions, and (a) MSE, (b) the relaxed coefficients vs the truth (when you know it). Why does the refit usually reduce shrinkage bias without reintroducing much variance — and when could it blow up?


Solution







Once the support is (mostly) right, refitting OLS on p_support ≪ n parameters removes the lasso’s deliberate shrinkage bias at little variance cost — that’s the relaxed lasso idea. It blows up when the support is wrong or barely stable: the selected set’s near-duplicates recreate collinearity, and selection noise propagates into the refit (which is why the relaxed variant should itself be CV’d against plain lasso, and why 5.1’s selection-uncertainty warnings still apply).

title: 5.3 Lasso Regression
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Standardize before lasso, always — the penalty counts coefficient magnitudes; unstandardized lasso selects by units, not information.
sklearn’s Lasso may not converge silently on correlated data at small alphas — watch ConvergenceWarning, raise max_iter, and prefer LassoCV (which handles warm starts and selection).
Alpha’s scale is objective-dependent (sklearn uses 1/(2n)·RSS + α‖β‖₁): alphas are not portable across n, feature scaling, or libraries — retune everywhere.
Selection ≠ inference: lasso p-values require selective-inference methods or sample splitting (5.1); a selected feature’s “significance” from a naive refit is doubly data-used.
Under correlation, lasso’s choice among twins is unstable — selection frequencies across bootstraps (5.1 drill) are the honest report; elastic net (5.4) is the structural fix.
The oracle doesn’t always appear: lasso consistency needs the irrepresentable condition; under violation it selects extras or misses features even at huge n. Don’t promise “lasso finds the true variables” in any write-up.
Orthonormal-case intuition is honest intuition: soft-thresholding explains every qualitative behavior (zeros, uniform shrinkage, twin coin-flips via correlated columns breaking orthonormality).


Read & Refactor AI Code

What’s wrong, and the fix


Unscaled lasso: feature 5’s tiny coefficient (units!) escapes the penalty while genuinely informative standardized features get taxed — selection by measurement unit. Standardize.
Inherited alpha: α is n-, scale-, and objective-dependent (Advanced pitfalls); it must be re-tuned (LassoCV) per dataset.
Naive refit p-values: the support was chosen with y’s help; these p-values double-dip the data. Use split-sample selection→inference or selective inference; at minimum, disclose that inference is post-selection.

title: 5.3 Lasso Regression
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Prove the orthonormal-case soft thresholding: for X with orthonormal columns, the lasso objective separates across coordinates into \(\frac{1}{2}(b_j - \beta_j)^2 + \lambda|\beta_j| + \text{const}\) where \(b_j = x_j^\top y\). Solve each 1-D problem by cases and assemble \(S_\lambda(b)\). Then state precisely what breaks when columns are merely correlated: which step of the separability argument dies, and what replaces it (coordinate descent on coupled problems).


Hint

Orthonormality makes Xᵀy the OLS estimate coordinatewise and decouples βⱼ’s; correlated columns couple the coordinates through off-diagonal XᵀX entries.



Solution

With \(X^\top X = I\): completing the square gives \(\frac{1}{2}\|\beta - b\|^2 + \lambda\|\beta\|_1 + \text{const}\), which is a sum of independent 1-D problems \(\frac{1}{2}(\beta_j - b_j)^2 + \lambda|\beta_j|\). Case |b_j| ≤ λ: minimum at βⱼ = 0 (the V’s corner). Case b_j > λ: optimal βⱼ = b_j − λ; symmetric below. Assemble: \(\hat\beta = S_\lambda(b)\) — shrink everything by λ, drop anything smaller. With correlated columns, XᵀX has off-diagonal mass: βⱼ’s objective depends on the other β’s through them, separability dies, and the solution is characterized by KKT conditions (subgradient of ‖·‖₁ balanced with gradient of RSS) — solved iteratively by coordinate descent, each step a soft threshold of a partial residual estimate. The twins coin-flip lives exactly here: two near-identical columns share one z, and ties break to whichever coordinate descends first.

Q2. Lasso’s degrees of freedom equal the number of selected features (for the Lasso at a given λ). Verify by simulation: compute the covariance-based degrees-of-freedom estimate, \(\text{df} = \frac{1}{\sigma^2}\text{Cov}(\hat\mu_i, y_i)\) over many training draws (use σ known), for a small problem at several λ, and compare to the nonzero count. What does df = |support| buy you conceptually (Cp-style penalties on the lasso path), and why is it surprising (a discontinuous model can have a smooth, integer-valued complexity)?


Hint

Zou/Tibshirani/Efron: for the lasso, E[df] = E[#nonzeros] under regularity — testable with the covariance formula.



Solution







Two things to take away, and the first is a trap. The naive covariance formula is not a degrees-of-freedom estimator for the lasso. It returns 92.7 against a true complexity of ≈ 2.1, because \(\widehat{\text{cov}}(\hat\mu_i, y_i)\) is dominated by the signal the fit correctly tracks — it measures how much of \(y\)’s variance the fit reproduces, not how many free parameters it spent. Any df-by-covariance argument silently assumes a linear model, where \(\text{df} = \text{tr}(H)\) exactly; the lasso has no such \(H\) to trace. The estimator that survives is the support size itself. \(E[|S|]\) falls smoothly and monotonically with \(\lambda\) — 4.96 → 3.19 → 2.17 → 1.64 → 0.31 — which is exactly the “expected complexity moves smoothly while the fit jumps discontinuously” magic. Note also the across-fit SD: at \(\lambda = 0.1\) the support size itself is a random variable (SD 1.24), so \(|S|\) is a noisy stand-in for a smooth df, and pricing a lasso model as \(\text{RSS} + 2\hat\sigma^2|S|\) is a rule of thumb rather than an identity. Conceptual payoff: this is the bridge between 5.1’s subset penalties and penalized fitting — and a reminder that “trace of the hat matrix” is a linear-model fact, not a universal one.

title: 5.3 Lasso Regression
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (lasso × 5.1 selection instability). Quantify the twin coin-flip at scale: p = 30 features where x₂ = x₁ + small noise and both are truly active with equal coefficients. Run LassoCV selection on 200 bootstrap resamples; report the joint selection frequency of {x₁, x₂} and each individually. Then rerun with elastic net (α_mix = 0.5, 5.4) and compare — the resulting table is the empirical case for the elastic net’s existence.
C2 (lasso × 4.4 bias–variance × 4.1 optimism). Measure lasso’s bias–variance profile across λ with the multi-training-set protocol from 4.4 (300 training sets, n = 60, sparse truth, fixed evaluation grid). Overlay: bias², variance, and the number of selected features per λ. Interpret the three panels jointly — where in λ does variance collapse (sparsity kicks in) relative to where bias starts climbing, and how does that gap explain LassoCV’s typical conservative choice?

title: 5.3 Lasso Regression
text:
7. Summary

L1 penalty → exact zeros: shrinkage and selection in one convex fit, solved by coordinate soft-thresholding.
Standardize; tune α by CV (LassoCV); α is not portable across n/scales/libraries.
Lasso selects twins by coin flip — great for prediction, hazardous for narratives; report selection frequencies.
Post-lasso refit (relaxed lasso) trades a little variance for the shrinkage bias back — when the support is stable.
At most n features survive in p ≫ n; df of the lasso = its support size.
Selection still invalidates naive p-values — the post-selection problem wears a smoother costume.
Ridge groups, lasso splits — the compromise that groups and sparsifies: 5.4 Elastic net.

title: 5.5 PCR and PLS
text: Instead of shrinking coefficients, shrink the feature space: summarize correlated predictors by a few derived directions, then regress on those. PCR builds directions from the predictors alone (PCA); PLS builds them using y. Both trade interpretability of individual coefficients for stability under extreme collinearity — and their contrast is a masterclass in supervised vs unsupervised thinking.

title: 5.5 PCR and PLS
text:
1. Basic Concept
PCR recipe: standardize X → PCA on X → keep the first M principal components → regress y on those M scores. The only new hyperparameter is M. PLS recipe: same pipeline, but directions are chosen to maximize covariance with y, not variance within X.






PLS, same data — and a first contrast:






The pathological case — signal hidden in a low-variance direction, where the two methods diverge:

title: 5.5 PCR and PLS
text:
2. Concept Questions

PCR with M = p (all components, after standardizing) reproduces which estimator exactly? What does that make M, in bias–variance language?
Why must PCA inside PCR be fit on training folds only? Which page’s law is this?
PLS’s first direction maximizes Cov(Xw, y). In one sentence, why can that find the tiny-variance signal that PCR’s first component cannot?
You interpret “component 1 loading +0.5 on gene A” — what stops you from reading it as “gene A’s effect is +0.5”?
Ridge also damps low-variance directions (5.2 SVD view). What is PCR’s version of the same move, and what’s the essential difference?



Answers


OLS on standardized features: keeping all p orthogonal components loses no information, and the regression on full PCA scores equals OLS. M is a pure flexibility dial — M = 0 is the mean-model, M = p is OLS (4.4’s dial again).
PCA is fitted from X — including validation rows’ means/structure; fitting it on all data leaks fold information into training (0.5, 4.3). The Pipeline mechanic enforces it.
PCR ranks directions by X’s internal variance; PLS’s criterion explicitly includes y, so a direction with little X-variance but strong y-relationship wins PLS’s first slot while it lands at the bottom of PCR’s list.
Components are rotations: loadings mix all features with sign/convention freedom, and the component’s coefficient (not the loading) carries the y-relationship, itself shrunken by the regression on scores. Individual-feature effects are unrecoverable without rotating back — interpret the component as a measurement direction, not a mechanism.
PCR truncates small-variance directions (keeps M, drops the rest); ridge damps them smoothly (factor s²/(s²+λ)). Same SVD backdrop (5.2 Q1), hard vs soft; both are blind to y when choosing what to suppress — PLS is the supervised cousin.

title: 5.5 PCR and PLS
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. PCR vs OLS under extreme collinearity: n = 50, p = 15, built from 5 noisy copies of each of 2 latent factors plus 5 pure-noise columns (so the effective rank is ≈ 2–4). Compare: OLS, PCR with M chosen by CV, and ridge with α chosen by CV. Report nested test MSEs via the outer-loop discipline of 4.6. Rank them and explain the ordering in terms of what each does to the noisy small directions.


Solution







Ridge wins (0.902), OLS is essentially tied with it (0.953), and PCR is far and away the worst (2.604) — the opposite of the textbook intuition that PCR “truncates away the noise directions.” The diagnosis is in the last line: inner CV selects M = 6, not the effective rank of 2. The five pure-noise columns were drawn from N(0, 1), the same marginal variance as the latent columns, so they sit high in the variance ordering indistinguishable from signal. PCR’s cutoff is a hard decision made on variance alone, and variance order is not relevance order — it spends its budget on noise columns it cannot tell apart from signal. Ridge never has to make that call: it damps every direction smoothly, so the noise columns are shrunk without ever being adjudicated. This is the first hint of the theme that dominates the rest of the page — when variance ≠ relevance, unsupervised truncation is the wrong tool and a supervised direction method (PLS, next exercise) is the right one.

Exercise 2. The supervised-vs-unsupervised contrast, swept: construct the Section 1 pathological geometry at three signal-to-noise ratios (tiny-direction coefficient c ∈ {5, 20, 60} with direction SD 0.1). For each, compute CV-MSE of PCR(M=1), PCR(M chosen by CV), PLS(M=1). At which c does PCR’s CV finally pick M = 2 — and what does that tell you about using X-internal criteria to hunt y-relevant structure?


Solution







Only when the tiny direction’s signal grows loud enough does CV promote M = 2 (and PCR’s error collapses to PLS-like levels) — the X-internal criterion needed rescue from the y to notice relevance. PLS(1) is insensitive to c’s scale (it locks onto the covariance immediately). Moral: unsupervised compression is a bet that variance = relevance; PLS/weak supervision is the hedge.

Exercise 3. Interpretation audit: fit PCR (M = 2) on a dataset with known truth (y = 3x₁ − x₄ + noise, all features independent so loadings are readable). Report (a) the component loadings, (b) the regression coefficients on components, (c) the reconstructed per-feature coefficients β̂ = V·γ (rotate back), compared to OLS’s coefficients. Then explain to a collaborator why (c) is legitimate for describing the fitted model while per-feature p-values remain unavailable.


Solution







Rotation back through V is exact algebra for the fitted model — the two parameterizations predict identically, so (c) is the honest per-feature description of what PCR actually fit (and with independent features it lands close to OLS, modulo the dropped components’ shrinkage). What’s not available: standard errors/p-values per feature — the components were data-chosen, and the truncation shares information across features (5.1’s post-selection caution, rotated).

title: 5.5 PCR and PLS
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

The Pipeline discipline is existential here: PCA is fitted from X, so fitting it before splitting leaks validation structure into training — the most common PCR bug in the wild (0.5).
Standardize before PCA unless features share natural units and scale: PCA’s variance-ranking is unit-dependent (5.2’s standardization law, inherited).
M is chosen by CV, not by scree plots: “keep components covering 90% variance” optimizes X-description, not y-prediction — the whole lesson of Exercise 2.
PLS with M = p ≈ OLS but is numerically optimized sequentially; don’t treat its M = p endpoint as an identity to 12 decimals.
PLS’s coefficients and loadings are even harder to read than PCR’s (directions tilted toward y, deflation between steps); report predictions and component meanings, not per-feature stories.
y-scaling does not move PLS’s path — a counterintuitive one: PLS component directions are invariant to multiplying y by a constant (x_weights_ on y and on 1000·y agree to 2.6e−16), because every criterion in the NIPALS iteration is a ratio that cancels the scale. Only the final coefficients scale (exactly 1000×). So rescaling y changes the units of the coefficients, never the subspace you are looking at — contrast with PCR, where the y-scale never enters at all. What does matter is scale=True on the X side, since that decides the variance ordering PLS inherits.
Both are linear-in-components: nonlinear structure needs basis expansion first (2.8) or the tree/kernel machinery of later parts.

What’s wrong, and the fix


PCA fit on all rows: test-set means/variances/components shaped the training inputs — leakage (4.3). PCA goes inside the pipeline.
Scree-chosen M: variance covered in X ≠ prediction of y; M is a hyperparameter for CV (Concept Question 3, Exercise 2).
No standardization: columns with big units dominate components; PCA on raw features ranks measurement choices, not structure. StandardScaler first.

title: 5.5 PCR and PLS
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Prove PCR’s M = p equivalence with OLS (after standardization): the PCA scores are X·V where V is the orthogonal loading matrix, and regressing y on X·V with all p components yields coefficients γ = Vᵀβ̂_OLS, so predictions V·γ = β̂_OLS·X exactly.
