num_leaves. In leaf-wise growth, depth is a poor complexity proxy (one deep branch ≠ many leaves); the leaf count bounds the model’s degrees of freedom directly — max_depth remains only as a safety rail.

title: 7.6 Modern Boosting Libraries
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Three implementations, one protocol: fit sklearn-GBM (7.5’s GradientBoostingRegressor), HistGradientBoostingRegressor, and LightGBM on the same 20k-row regression problem, each tuned lightly (early stopping where supported) inside a 5-fold CV. Report the CV MSE table and fit times. Write the selection paragraph: when do the industrial implementations earn their dependency?


Solution







Accuracy is a wash (all implement the same algorithm family at sane settings); time separates them — histogram methods are one to two orders faster at 20k rows, and the gap widens with n. The paragraph: “We use HistGradientBoosting/LightGBM for any dataset beyond a few thousand rows, reserving exact GradientBoosting for small problems where its simplicity aids teaching or debugging.”

Exercise 2. Native-NaN vs imputation, honestly: inject 20% missing completely-at-random into one feature (MCAR) and 20% missing depending on y (MNAR-ish: mask feature where y = 1) on a classification task. Compare HistGB-native-NaN vs mean-imputation pipelines by CV AUC in each scenario. Where does native handling shine, where does it not save you (what does the MNAR case teach about missingness mechanisms, connecting to 9.3)?


Solution







Under MCAR, native NaN routing and imputation tie (both recover the feature’s info). Under y-dependent missingness, the missingness itself is signal — native NaN handling captures it (missingness-pattern splits), while blind mean-imputation erases the pattern and can bias the feature. The deep lesson (Part 9.3’s territory): imputation is a modeling decision about why values are missing, not a preprocessing reflex.

Exercise 3. The complexity-knob audit: for LightGBM, sweep num_leaves ∈ {7, 15, 31, 63, 127} (with min_child_samples fixed) and separately max_depth ∈ {3, 5, 8, −1} at fixed num_leaves, reporting CV AUC and tree statistics (average depth via the booster). Which knob’s sweep moves performance, and how do the two interact? Write the tuning-order recipe you’d follow on a new tabular problem.


Solution







num_leaves moves the needle (it caps the model’s true complexity); max_depth only bites when it clips num_leaves (tiny depths) — otherwise it’s a safety rail. Recipe: fix learning_rate modestly (0.05), tune num_leaves + min_child_samples by CV, set max_depth as a guardrail, scale n_estimators with early stopping, and only then consider feature_fraction/bagging dials (7.5’s subsample, renamed).

title: 7.6 Modern Boosting Libraries
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

The dial dictionary translates: sklearn-GBM max_depth ↔︎ LightGBM num_leaves (complexity), subsample ↔︎ bagging_fraction, colsample ↔︎ feature_fraction, min_samples_leaf ↔︎ min_child_weight/samples — carrying names across libraries without remapping semantics is the #1 tuning bug.
Early stopping APIs differ per version: LightGBM/XGBoost have changed callback/eval-set conventions repeatedly — pin versions and read your installed signature (help(model.fit)), not blog posts.
NaN routing + feature_fraction interplay: features with NaNs get “free” informative splits — check whether missingness itself is predictive before crediting the feature (Exercise 2).
Histogram binning + tiny data: on n < ~1000 the exact (sklearn-GBM) splitter can match or beat histogram methods — industrial speed matters when data is big.
Determinism: identical seeds give identical forests, but GPU/histogram orderings can vary across hardware — document versions for reproducibility (4.6’s protocol hygiene).
Interpretability exports: all three expose importances (split/gain) with the same 7.4 caveats; prefer permutation/SHAP-style attributions on held-out data for anything you publish.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated LightGBM pipeline has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Accuracy as headline at 10% prevalence: ~0.90 achievable by predicting the majority — use AUC/AP (3.1).
num_leaves = 127 unchecked: leaf-wise growth will grow deep pockets on minority-class noise; cap by CV (typical 15–63 at this n) and watch min_child_samples.
Test-set early stopping: the eval_set must be a validation split carved from training — the test set is spent once, at the end.

title: 7.6 Modern Boosting Libraries
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Newton leaf values: for a leaf with examples {gᵢ, hᵢ} (gradients, Hessians) and L2 penalty λ, derive the optimal leaf value w* = −Σgᵢ/(Σhᵢ + λ) and the resulting split-gain formula used by XGBoost. Verify numerically for a log-loss leaf (compute gᵢ, hᵢ from pᵢ) that w* equals the local log-odds correction — connecting to the Newton/IRLS machinery of logistic regression (3.3 Q1).


Hint

Minimize \(\sum_i[g_iw + \tfrac12 h_iw^2] + \tfrac12\lambda w^2\) in \(w\), giving \(w^* = -\sum_i g_i/(\sum_i h_i + \lambda)\). The gain for splitting a node with totals \((G_L, H_L)\) and \((G_R, H_R)\) is \(\tfrac12\!\left(\frac{G_L^2}{H_L+\lambda} + \frac{G_R^2}{H_R+\lambda} - \frac{G^2}{H+\lambda}\right)\), minus γ per leaf. Each denominator is the hessian on that side, plus λ — pairing \(G_L^2\) with \(H_R\) (or two \(H_R\)s, as an earlier draft had) is a typo that quietly changes the criterion.



Solution

Quadratic-in-w leaf objective: Σgᵢw + ½Σhᵢw² + ½λw² minimized at w* = −Σgᵢ/(Σhᵢ + λ). For log-loss, gᵢ = pᵢ − yᵢ and hᵢ = pᵢ(1−pᵢ) — the IRLS weights. Verification:






The leaf update is one IRLS step on the leaf’s members — modern boosting is Newton boosting, which is why it converges in fewer, better-fitted trees than the first-order original.

Q2. Histogram approximation audit: on one dataset, compare exact-split boosting (sklearn GradientBoostingRegressor) against histogram boosting (HistGB) at increasing max_bins (31, 127, 255), tracking CV MSE. Verify that MSE decreases toward the exact method’s and stabilizes well before 255 on a smooth feature, then construct a feature where binning bites (extremely spiky/multi-modal with narrow gaps) and show 31 bins lose to 255. What’s the practical bin-count policy?


Solution







Smooth features: 127 bins ≈ 255 ≈ exact (split choices are coarse-grain stable). The spiky truth exposes binning: narrow ridges fall between coarse bin edges, and 31 bins measurably lose. Policy: default 255 (the library default) is nearly free; drop bins only for speed on huge n — and check exact-vs-histogram once on your data before trusting a leaderboard delta.

title: 7.6 Modern Boosting Libraries
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (libraries × 7.3–7.5 family tournament). The full Part 7 bake-off on one honest protocol: single tree, random forest, sklearn-GBM, HistGB, LightGBM, XGBoost — same dataset (10k rows, 20 features, mixed signal types), identical outer 5-fold nested CV, light inner tuning. Produce the accuracy-vs-fit-time scatter and write the deployment recommendation for (a) a laptop-scale research problem and (b) a 100M-row scoring pipeline — justifying each choice by the measured frontier, not reputation.
C2 (libraries × 5.6 p ≫ n × 12.4 FDR stub). Boosters in the wide regime: n = 150, p = 2,000 with 10 signals. Compare LightGBM (with feature_fraction < 1) against lasso and the random forest — nested CV MSE plus each method’s top-20 recovery overlap with truth. In p ≫ n, which inductive bias (sparsity-linear, decorrelated trees, sequential trees) wins, and does the answer change when the signal becomes interaction-heavy? Write the pre-registered analysis plan you’d commit to before seeing the response.

title: 7.6 Modern Boosting Libraries
text:
7. Summary

Modern boosters = 7.5’s algorithm + Newton leaf values + histogram splits + native NaN routing + leaf-wise growth.
HistGradientBoosting (sklearn) implements the core with zero extra dependencies; LightGBM/XGBoost add ecosystem and raw speed.
num_leaves is the complexity knob (leaf-wise trees); max_depth is a guardrail; early stopping must use a validation split, never the test set.
Learned NaN branches are a predictive feature — and a missingness-mechanism assumption (9.3).
Hyperparameter names don’t translate across libraries; translate semantics, then tune on your data.
Accuracy at sane settings is a tie between implementations; speed, data volume, and deployment constraints decide.
Part 7’s sequence — trees → bagging → forests → boosting → libraries — is one idea (adaptive step functions) refined four ways. Next, margins meet kernels: Part 8, SVMs, starting with 8.1 Geometry essentials.

title: 8.1 Geometry Essentials
text: SVMs live and breathe linear algebra: hyperplanes, normals, projections, distances, margins. This page drills the geometric vocabulary — every SVM statement in 8.2–8.6 is one of these objects in costume.

title: 8.1 Geometry Essentials
text:
1. Basic Concept
A hyperplane in d dimensions is \(\{x : w^\top x + b = 0\}\) — defined by a normal vector w (its direction) and offset b. The signed distance from a point x₀ to the hyperplane is
\[d(x_0) = \frac{w^\top x_0 + b}{\|w\|}\]
— the quantity SVMs classify by (its sign) and maximize (its magnitude):






Projections — the foot of that perpendicular — and the margin between two parallel hyperplanes:

title: 8.1 Geometry Essentials
text:
2. Concept Questions

Why does the same hyperplane described by (2w, 2b) define a different SVM margin — and what convention fixes w’s scale?
What does the sign of wᵀx₀ + b encode, and what does its magnitude encode before scaling?
Two parallel hyperplanes wᵀx + b = ±1: derive the distance between them geometrically (pick one point on one, compute its distance to the other).
In 2-D, a hyperplane is a line; in 3-D, a plane. What is it in 1-D — and does the SVM machinery care about the dimension?
Why do SVMs standardize features despite being geometric — name the quantity that units distort.



Answers


(2w, 2b) is the same zero-set (same line) but the margin formula 2/‖w‖ halves — margins are only comparable in the canonical convention wᵀx + b = ±1 at the support vectors, which pins ‖w‖ (SVMs solve for w up to this constraint, so the scale ambiguity is absorbed).
Sign = which side (the class in SVMs: +1 vs −1). Raw magnitude = distance scaled by ‖w‖ — proportional to true distance but unit-dependent until normalized.
Take x₊ on {wᵀx + b = +1}: wᵀx₊ + b = 1. Distance to {wᵀx + b = −1}: |wᵀx₊ + b + 1|/‖w‖ = |1 + 1|/‖w‖ = 2/‖w‖. That’s the margin the SVM maximizes.
In 1-D a “hyperplane” is a point (w, b as scalars, w·x + b = 0); the algebra — sign, distance, margin 2/‖w‖ — is dimension-blind. Everything here works in any d, which is why kernels (8.4) can.
Distance and margin are computed in raw coordinates: a feature measured in millimeters vs meters changes ‖w‖ and the geometry of “closeness.” Standardization puts all axes in comparable units — the same law as 5.2, now geometric.

title: 8.1 Geometry Essentials
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Build signed_distance(X, w, b) returning distances for a matrix of points, and verify three properties numerically on random data: (a) distance of points on the hyperplane ≈ 0; (b) flipping (w, b) → (−w, −b) flips all signs but preserves magnitudes; (c) distances are invariant to adding multiples of w to… (design the check: move a point parallel to the hyperplane and confirm its distance is unchanged).


Solution







Property (c) is the geometric soul of the SVM: moving along the hyperplane costs nothing; only normal-direction movement changes the classification score — which is why the margin direction w is everything.

Exercise 2. From line to margin to classifier: given w = (−1, 4), b = 2, compute (a) the line y(x₂) as a function of x₁, (b) the two margin lines wᵀx + b = ±1, (c) the signed distances of (0, 0) and (3, 2), (d) which side the classifier assigns each. Then plot all four lines with the two points using matplotlib and check the distances visually (aspect=“equal”).


Solution







The three parallel lines are the whole linear-SVM story: classify by side (sign), measure confidence by distance, and the ±1 family is the margin whose width 2/‖w‖ the SVM maximizes (8.2).

Exercise 3. Norms and their margins: for w = (3, 4), compute ‖w‖₁, ‖w‖₂, ‖w‖∞, and the L2-margin 2/‖w‖₂. Then show numerically that among all vectors achieving the same classification of a fixed dataset, scaling changes ‖w‖₂ — and that adding a perpendicular component changes ‖w‖₂ without changing any sign. Which of these two operations would an SVM’s objective permit (relate to how the margin constraint pins the scale)?


Solution







Scaling changes ‖w‖ (and thus the nominal margin) without changing classifications; adding a perpendicular component changes ‖w‖ and keeps signs for this dataset. The SVM’s canonical constraint — margin lines at ±1 with the support vectors on them — pins the scale so the only freedom left is the direction of w; maximizing 2/‖w‖ then chooses the direction with the fattest cushion. The margin isn’t a formula, it’s the normalization that makes the formula meaningful.

title: 8.1 Geometry Essentials
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

The sign convention: +1 class sits on the wᵀx + b > 0 side by convention of the labels — sklearn’s decision_function sign follows classes_[1]; always check model.classes_ before interpreting signs (3.3’s ordering note).
‖w‖ appears in denominators everywhere — margins, distances, hinge geometry — so feature scaling is not optional for SVMs: raw-unit features tilt the geometry in invisible ways.
Hyperplane ≠ classifier: the zero-set classifies; the scaled (w, b) carries the margin information. Two codebases reporting different (w, b) for the “same” SVM may agree completely after normalization — compare decision_function values, not raw parameters.
Projections are linear algebra’s workhorse beyond SVMs: residuals (2.2), PCA scores (9.2), backfitting (6.7) — the same perpendicular decomposition everywhere.
d(x₀) = 0 points: points on the hyperplane are classified by tie-breaking convention — in practice measure-zero, but in engineered features (integers) it happens; know your library’s rule.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated geometry helper has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Not a distance: wᵀx₀ + b is the unscaled score; distances divide by ‖w‖. The printed “distance” changes under rescaling of w — distances don’t.
b doesn’t belong in the margin: the gap between the ±1 planes is purely 2/‖w‖; b shifts the pair, doesn’t widen it.
Classifier needs the label convention: sign gives the side, but which side is “class 1” is a training-time fact (classes_), not derivable from geometry alone.

title: 8.1 Geometry Essentials
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Prove the signed-distance formula: for hyperplane H = {x : wᵀx + b = 0} and point x₀, write x₀ = p + t·ŵ (p ∈ H, ŵ = w/‖w‖), solve for t, and confirm t = (wᵀx₀ + b)/‖w‖. Then derive the ±1-planes separation: for x₊ with wᵀx₊ + b = +1, dist(x₊, H₋) = 2/‖w‖. Finally explain why SVM optimization may equivalently maximize 2/‖w‖ or minimize ‖w‖²/2 — and why the quadratic form is preferred by solvers.


Hint

Enforce wᵀp + b = 0 on the foot point p; subtract the two plane equations for the margin.



Solution

Substituting x₀ = p + tŵ: wᵀx₀ + b = (wᵀp + b) + t‖w‖ = t‖w‖, so t = (wᵀx₀ + b)/‖w‖ — the formula, proved. For the margin: x₊ satisfies wᵀx₊ + b = 1; distance to H₋ is |wᵀx₊ + b + 1|/‖w‖ = 2/‖w‖. Maximizing 2/‖w‖ ⇔ minimizing ‖w‖; the objective ‖w‖²/2 is quadratic — smooth, strictly convex, differentiable everywhere (no square-root kink) — which makes the SVM a clean QP for standard solvers. Every SVM formulation you’ll meet is this geometry plus a slack budget.

Q2. Angles between hyperplanes: the cosine of the angle between two hyperplanes equals |w₁ᵀw₂|/(‖w₁‖‖w₂‖). Implement it, then investigate: for two hyperplanes both separating a given linearly-separable dataset, compute their pairwise angles — are all separating hyperplanes within a narrow cone? Connect the cone’s width to the data’s margin geometry, and explain what this predicts about how much freedom the SVM’s margin maximization actually has (foreshadowing why “the” maximal-margin hyperplane is unique).


Solution







All separating planes lie in a cone around the “true” boundary whose width is set by the data’s gap: wide margins → narrow cones (little freedom — the maximal-margin choice barely matters); narrow margins → wide cones (many hyperplanes fit, and the choice among them is genuine model selection). The SVM resolves this freedom by fiat — max 2/‖w‖ — which is why its solution is unique even when infinitely many hyperplanes classify perfectly.

title: 8.1 Geometry Essentials
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (geometry × 2.x regression). Two views of one object: a linear regression fit ŷ = wᵀx + b also defines a hyperplane in feature space. On a 2-D dataset, fit OLS and draw (a) the regression’s prediction surface as a contour plot, (b) the zero-set hyperplane. For a constructed binary target (sign of a linear function), compare the OLS-zero-set to the maximal-margin hyperplane (8.2 preview — use sklearn’s LinearSVC with huge C). Quantify the angle between them and explain in margin terms why they differ.
C2 (geometry × 6.4 splines × 8.4 kernels preview). Bases make geometry flexible: expand x = (x₁, x₂) into the quadratic basis (x₁², x₂², √2·x₁x₂, x₁, x₂, 1) — a hyperplane in the expanded space is a conic section in the original. Verify numerically: fit a linear hyperplane in the expanded space to XOR-like data, map its decision boundary back to the original 2-D plane (contour of φ(x)ᵀw = 0), and observe the ellipse/hyperbola family. This is the kernel trick’s entire promise — hyperplanes upstairs, curves downstairs — and the reason 8.4 never materializes the basis.

title: 8.1 Geometry Essentials
text:
7. Summary

Hyperplane = w (normal) + b (offset); zero-set classifies; signed distance = (wᵀx + b)/‖w‖.
Canonical convention: support vectors at wᵀx + b = ±1 → margin = 2/‖w‖ — scale pinned by constraint.
Maximizing 2/‖w‖ ⇔ minimizing ‖w‖²/2 — the quadratic objective solvers love.
Signs classify; scaled magnitudes score; both are unit-sensitive — standardize.
Separating hyperplanes form a cone; margin maximization picks its unique fattest member.
Basis expansion moves hyperplanes upstairs — curves downstairs, kernels to come.
The first SVM proper: make the margin maximal on separable data — 8.2 The maximal-margin classifier.

title: 8.3 The Soft-Margin Classifier
text: Real classes overlap. The soft margin keeps the maximal-margin idea but lets points pay a price ξᵢ to violate it — turning “impossible” into “tunable”: C sets the exchange rate between a fat margin and a clean fit. It is the SVM you will actually use.

title: 8.3 The Soft-Margin Classifier
text:
1. Basic Concept
\[\min_{w, b, \xi} \; \frac{1}{2}\|w\|^2 + C \sum_i \xi_i \quad \text{s.t.} \quad y_i(w^\top x_i + b) \ge 1 - \xi_i, \;\; \xi_i \ge 0\]
ξᵢ = how far point i intrudes into (or crosses) the margin; C = the price per unit of intrusion. C → ∞ recovers the hard margin; C → 0 lets the boundary ignore everything.






Hinge loss — the soft margin’s loss in unconstrained clothing: ξᵢ = (1 − yᵢ(wᵀxᵢ + b))₊:






C tuning, honestly (4.6):

title: 8.3 The Soft-Margin Classifier
text:
2. Concept Questions

A support vector in the soft-margin world: which points get αᵢ > 0 now? Are they all on the margin?
C → ∞ and C → 0 endpoints: state both behaviors, including what the boundary does at C = 0.
How does the hinge loss differ from logistic loss at (a) correctly-classified far points, (b) misclassified points — and what does each difference do to the fitted boundary?
Your CV chooses C = 1000 on overlapping data. What is that telling you about the data — and is the resulting margin reportable?
Why does the soft-margin SVM remain scale-sensitive, and which quantity does a feature-unit change distort — C, ξ, or both?



Answers


In the hard margin, αᵢ > 0 ⟺ on the margin. Soft margin: αᵢ > 0 for points on the margin and all violators (ξᵢ > 0) — anything touching or crossing the band is load-bearing; far-correct points still don’t matter.
C → ∞: slacks become unaffordable → hard-margin behavior (infeasible if overlap exists — solver strains). C → 0: violations are free → ‖w‖ → 0 dominates, boundary collapses toward arbitrary/mean — practically untrained. C = 0 exactly is degenerate (w = 0 minimizes).

Hinge = 0 for far-correct points (no gradient, no influence — the margin geometry’s parsimony); logistic loss never reaches zero — every point pulls forever (smoother, no sparsity of influence). (b) Misclassified: hinge is linear in the violation (bounded influence of any single point), logistic is exponential-ish in the margin distance (a single extreme point can dominate the fit). Net: SVM boundary = geometry of the frontier; logistic boundary = a weighted average view of all data.

High C chosen on overlapping data says “the CV folds are (nearly) separable under heavy penalization” — i.e., few-but-real violations. The reported 2/‖w‖ is then a nominal margin with (100·violation%) of points inside it — report it together with the violation fraction, or not at all.
Both, via ξᵢ: ξᵢ is measured in score units (wᵀx + b), whose scale depends on feature units — rescaling a feature changes each ξᵢ and thus the C-price of the same geometric situation. Standardize first, always (geometric law from 8.1).

title: 8.3 The Soft-Margin Classifier
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Hinge-loss SVM from scratch: minimize (1/2)‖w‖² + C·Σ max(0, 1 − yᵢ(wᵀxᵢ + b)) by sub-gradient descent on a small dataset; compare the resulting (w, b) and predictions to LinearSVC(C=C) (normalize for the scale convention — compare decision signs and margin geometry, not raw coefficients). Report where your solution and sklearn’s agree and where optimization details diverge.


Solution







Sub-gradient descent on the hinge objective converges to the same margin geometry (same direction; coefficient scale conventions differ between formulations — that’s why you compare normalized geometry). sklearn’s solver is faster and smarter, but you’ve now implemented the objective the whole method optimizes.

Exercise 2. The C-frontier: on overlapping data, sweep C over 6 log-spaced values; for each record (a) training margin-violation fraction, (b) train accuracy, (c) test accuracy, (d) ‖w‖. Plot the panel. Identify the three regimes (underfit-all-slack / balanced / overfit-margin) and connect each to its bias–variance signature (4.4) — C is SVM’s flexibility dial, running opposite to k in KNN or… specify the direction relative to ridge’s λ.


Solution







Small C: everything is slack, ‖w‖ tiny — underfit (bias-dominated). Large C: margin tight, boundary chases the frontier points — variance-dominated. Balanced middle: few violations, stable boundary. Relative to ridge (5.2): C is 1/λ — big C = weak regularization; the dial’s direction is inverted, which trips everyone once.

Exercise 3. Soft margin under label noise: inject 8% label flips into separable data. Compare hard-margin-attempt (C = 1e5) vs CV-tuned soft margin: test accuracy, boundary angle between them, and the fraction of flipped points that became support vectors. Then explain why the tuned soft margin absorbs the noise while the hard attempt contorts around it — and which of the two would you trust under 3.2’s class-overlap realities.


Solution







Flipped labels sit deep in enemy territory; a hard margin bends the boundary extravagantly to accommodate them (or fails); a tuned soft margin prices them as ξ and lets them sit violated — boundary stays where the clean mass of evidence points. Trust the soft margin: label noise is precisely the violation-budget use case, and C is the honest knob declaring how much noise you’ll tolerate.

title: 8.3 The Soft-Margin Classifier
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

C’s direction vs every other penalty: C is 1/λ — larger = less regularized. Writing “higher C = more regularization” in a report is the classic tell of a rushed pipeline.
Violating support vectors: in soft-margin fits, αᵢ is capped at C; points with αᵢ = C are the ξᵢ > 0 violators. Reading dual_coef_ magnitudes against C tells you which SVs are on-margin vs crossing.
LinearSVC has no predict_proba — probability-ish outputs need SVC(probability=True) (Platt scaling, internal CV) or a separate calibrator (3.7); don’t pretend decision_function values are probabilities.
Class weights rescale C per class: class_weight={1: 5} multiplies minority violations’ price — the margin version of imbalance handling (3.1); evaluate with PR metrics.
Hinge loss ⇒ no probabilities and non-smooth optimization: that’s the price of margin sparsity; the logistic comparison (8.5) is exactly hinge-vs-log.
Multiclass: SVC runs OvO internally (8.6) — C’s meaning per binary subproblem, aggregated.

What’s wrong, and the fix


C’s direction flipped: the commentary treats large C as the regularized end; C is the slack price — large C = weak regularization. Fix the narrative (and the grid’s labels) before anyone copies it.
Mixed units, unscaled geometry: the 500-scale feature prices margins in its units; the StandardScaler step is missing — with it, C’s meaning is unit-free.
decision_function ≠ probability: it’s the signed margin score, unbounded both ways. Use SVC(probability=True) + calibration, or quote scores as scores.

title: 8.3 The Soft-Margin Classifier
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Connect the two formulations: show that the ξ-form (min ‖w‖²/2 + CΣξᵢ) is identical to unconstrained hinge minimization (1/2)‖w‖² + CΣmax(0, 1 − yᵢfᵢ) — by substituting ξᵢ = max(0, 1 − yᵢfᵢ) and checking the optimal ξᵢ given (w, b). Then verify numerically: solve both with scipy for a tiny problem and compare (w, b) up to solver tolerance. What does this equivalence buy conceptually (loss view vs constraint view)?


Hint

For fixed (w, b), the constraint set forces ξᵢ ≥ 1 − yᵢfᵢ and ξᵢ ≥ 0; minimizing Cξᵢ picks exactly the hinge value.



Solution

Given (w, b), the smallest feasible ξᵢ is max(0, 1 − yᵢ(wᵀxᵢ + b)) — substituting and dropping ξ turns the constrained program into unconstrained hinge minimization. The views are dual lenses: the constraint view exposes geometry (margins, SVs, KKT); the loss view exposes optimization (subgradients, SGD, loss comparisons with logistic — 8.5). Solvers like LinearSVC optimize the hinge directly; SVC optimizes the dual of the ξ-form — same optimum, different algebra.

Q2. C vs the bias–variance decomposition: estimate bias² and variance of the soft-margin SVM across C ∈ {0.01, 1, 100} using the multi-training-set protocol (4.4) on overlapping data. Which C minimizes variance, which minimizes bias², and does total error’s minimum sit at the CV-chosen C? Write the sentence connecting C to the decomposition — the SVM’s own bias–variance story.


Solution







The result here is not the textbook trade, and the deviation is instructive. Bias² falls as C grows (0.069 → 0.070 → 0.037), which is the expected direction: at small C the fit is so slack-dominated that the average predictor under-commits to the true diagonal, and letting C rise lets the boundary move onto the truth. What is not expected is variance also falling (0.145 → 0.146 → 0.092), so the total is monotone and the optimum sits at the largest C tried. The reason is that both terms are being driven by the same mechanism here: on well-separated, low-noise data the small-C SVM’s boundary is not merely biased but unstable in position — the heavy slack tolerance leaves the optimum nearly flat, so resampling noise moves it around. Once C is large enough for the support vectors to pin the boundary down, both bias and variance drop together and the familiar bias/variance opposition never gets a chance to appear. The moral is that “large C = variance-dominated” is a claim about hard, overlapping data (4.4), not a universal law: the C dial is best set by CV, exactly as its role as 1/λ would suggest. (To see the textbook U-curve, raise the class overlap so the classes genuinely conflict.)

title: 8.3 The Soft-Margin Classifier
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (soft margin × 0.5 splitting × 12.x multiplicity stub). C and feature selection interact: on p = 100 features with 3 relevant, compare (a) SelectKBest(k by CV) → SVC(C by CV), (b) SVC on all features (C by CV), both nested-CV’d. Report test accuracy and which relevant features survive in (a)’s filter (over folds). When does the SVM’s implicit regularization make explicit filtering unnecessary — and when does filtering rescue it?
C2 (soft margin × 3.7 calibration). The C–calibration interaction: fit SVMs at C ∈ {0.1, 1, 10} with probability=True; for each, produce reliability curves and Brier scores, before and after Platt-calibration on a validation split. Does larger C (tighter margins, fewer SVs) help or hurt calibration? Explain via the SV-vote smoothing mechanism (7.3’s averaging intuition applied to support-vector votes) and state your deployment configuration.

title: 8.3 The Soft-Margin Classifier
text:
7. Summary

Soft margin = hard margin + slack budget: min ‖w‖²/2 + CΣξᵢ — the SVM for real, overlapping data.
Hinge loss is the same object unconstrained: zero for far-correct points, linear when wrong.
C is the slack price — 1/λ: larger C = weaker regularization; the inverted direction trips everyone.
Support vectors now include violators; far-correct points still don’t matter.
C is the SVM’s bias–variance dial; CV picks it; margins reported alongside violation fractions.
No native probabilities — calibrate or quote scores as scores.
Linear soft margins in hand, the nonlinear leap costs one substitution: 8.4 Kernel SVM.

title: 8.5 SVM vs Logistic Regression
text: Two linear classifiers, one hinge loss, one log loss. They agree on most datasets and diverge in exactly the dimensions that matter for deployment: probabilities, outlier sensitivity, margin geometry, and scalability. This page makes the comparison a decision procedure rather than a preference.

title: 8.5 SVM vs Logistic Regression
text:
1. Basic Concept
Same linear score f(x) = wᵀx + b, different training losses:
\[\text{SVM: } \frac{1}{2}\|w\|^2 + C\sum_i \max(0,\, 1 - y_i f_i) \qquad \text{Logistic: } \frac{1}{2}\|w\|^2 + C\sum_i \log(1 + e^{-y_i f_i})\]






The geometric consequence on overlapping data:

title: 8.5 SVM vs Logistic Regression
text:
2. Concept Questions

State what each loss does with a far-correctly-classified point (score = 4, y = 1) — and the boundary consequence of the difference.
Both models output a signed score. Which one can you interpret as a log-odds, and why not the other?
Overlapping classes with heavy outliers: which method’s boundary is more robust, and which loss property delivers that?
Why does logistic regression scale to huge n more gracefully than SVC (two reasons — one statistical, one computational)?
Your stakeholder needs “probability of disease.” Which model, which step, and what must you check afterwards?



Answers


Hinge: loss 0 — the point vanishes from the fit (no gradient). Logistic: loss log(1 + e⁻⁴) ≈ 0.018 — small but nonzero, still pulling. Consequence: SVM’s boundary is set by frontier points only; logistic’s by every point, weighted by their surprise.
Logistic’s f(x) is the fitted log-odds (by construction: p = σ(f)) — exponentiate coefficients for odds ratios. SVM’s score is a margin distance in canonical units — no probability or odds semantics attached.
SVM — hinge’s linearity bounds any single outlier’s influence (its contribution grows linearly however far it strays), while logistic’s exponential tail lets extreme points dominate the gradient. (Robust variant: Huber/absolute-loss boosting, 7.5.)
Statistical: logistic is a smooth convex GLM — efficient IRLS/SGD variants, warm starts, and it doesn’t need the dual’s kernel trick to stay exact. Computational: hinge-SVM’s dual scales with n (SV count grows with overlap); logistic’s primal has no such n-dependence, and SGDClassifier(loss="log_loss") streams.
Logistic regression, then calibrate it (reliability check on held-out data — 3.7): logistic is the right starting point (native probabilities, no Platt detour), but calibration is still a checked property, not an assumption.

title: 8.5 SVM vs Logistic Regression
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. The outlier sensitivity dose-response: on separable data, add ONE mislabeled point at distance d ∈ {0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8} beyond the boundary. For each d, record the boundary shift (perpendicular displacement of the zero-set) for SVM (C = 1) and logistic. Plot shift vs d. Verify: SVM’s shift saturates (linear-in-d influence), logistic’s grows without bound. State the robustness rule this supports.


Solution







The SVM’s boundary barely moves (0.093 → 0.002 as the bad point recedes) while logistic’s shift grows and then saturates around 0.06–0.08. The saturation is the tell, and the last block explains it: for a misclassified point (\(\log(1 + e^{|z|}) \approx |z| - \log 2\) when \(|z|\) is large) the logistic loss grows linearly, just like the hinge — the printed ratio stays near 0.95 even 30 units out. The familiar “logistic is exponential, hinge is linear” contrast is about far-correct points (where \(\log(1+e^{-|z|})\) decays exponentially while the hinge is exactly 0), not about violations. So the real difference is a bounded, saturating response, not divergence. Two traps this exercise invites are worth naming: reading -intercept/coef off a scaler-wrapped pipeline silently returns standardized units (the raw-scale value is mean + scale × (-b/w)), and reading a saturated plateau as “grows without bound”. On mislabeled extremes, clean them first (2.10’s repair menu) — the loss choice is a second-order concern next to that.

Exercise 2. Probability quality, head-to-head: on a moderately overlapping dataset, compare (a) logistic’s native probabilities, (b) SVM + probability=True (Platt), (c) SVM’s raw decision_function rescaled by naive min-max — by Brier score, reliability curves, and AUC. Which wins calibration, which wins ranking, and does the ranking winner match the calibration winner? Conclude with the “probabilities vs scores” deployment rule.


Solution







AUC: identical or near-identical (monotone recalibrations preserve ranking). Brier/calibration: logistic and Platt-SVM are close; naive min-max rescaled scores are uncalibrated fiction. Rule: rank with whichever margin you like; probabilities require a model that produces them honestly (logistic) or an explicit calibration step (Platt/isotonic) — never a linear rescale of a margin.

Exercise 3. The scale-of-n crossover: generate datasets at n ∈ {500, 5,000, 50,000} (p = 10) and compare training time and test accuracy for LogisticRegression (liblinear/lbfgs) vs LinearSVC vs SVC(kernel=“linear”). Report the 3×3 table. Where does each become impractical, and what streaming/streaming-adjacent alternative (SGDClassifier with hinge/log losses) offers at 50k? Verify SGD’s accuracy is within ~1% of the batch solution.


Solution







Logistic and LinearSVC are both fast at these scales; SVC(kernel=“linear”) is the first to hurt (dual grows with n) — drop it for large n. SGD (hinge or log) trades a little accuracy for streaming-scale speed and stays within ~1% at 50k with a few passes. The scaling rule: probabilities + big n → logistic/SGD-log; pure decisions + big n → LinearSVC/SGD-hinge; SVC only when SVs themselves (or kernels) are the point.

title: 8.5 SVM vs Logistic Regression
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Two regularizations, same λ-spirit: both penalize ‖w‖²; C (SVM) and C (logistic) are both 1/λ-style slack/tail prices — but their effects differ because the losses differ. Tune each on its own grid (4.6).
Hinge’s sparsity of influence is a feature (robustness, SV parsimony) and a bug (no per-point probability pressure, uncalibrated scores). Decide which you need before choosing the loss (3.1).
Logistic = canonical GLM: coefficients are log-odds ratios, inference exists (3.3); SVM coefficients are margin geometry, inference doesn’t (naively).
Both are linear: identical ceiling without feature engineering or kernels — the 6.3 dictionary, or 8.4’s trick, applies to both.
Class weighting differs subtly: SVM’s class_weight rescales slack prices; logistic’s resamples the loss — both fix imbalance directionally, verify with PR curves (3.1.5).
Multiclass paths differ: SVC does OvO (8.6); LogisticRegression does multinomial (softmax) by default — another semantic difference between “equivalent” pipelines.


Read & Refactor AI Code

What’s wrong, and the fix


Accuracy at 8% prevalence is the prevalence in disguise (3.1); report AUC + AP/PR.
Margins ≠ probabilities: decision_function is unbounded geometry; Platt-calibrate if probabilities are needed (and validate the calibration).
AUC from hard predictions throws away ranking resolution (ties everywhere) — feed continuous scores: decision_function for SVM, predict_proba for logistic.

title: 8.5 SVM vs Logistic Regression
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. The regularized-loss unification: write both SVM and logistic as penalized ERM with the same L2 penalty and different losses. Show formally that as C → ∞ (no regularization), both maximize the margin-like quantity in their own metric, and that the only difference is the loss’s tail behavior past the margin. Then construct a dataset where the two fits produce orthogonal boundaries (hint: one dominant outlier vs clean data — reuse the geometry of 8.2 Exercise 2).


Hint

hinge’(f) = −y·1(yf < 1) — a constant push while outside the margin, then exactly zero; logistic’(f) = −y·σ(−yf) — the same constant push, but decaying smoothly and never reaching zero. Both are bounded in magnitude by 1; they differ in the tail, not in boundedness. Construct: two clean clusters + one mislabeled point at extreme distance; crank the loss weights and watch which boundary moves.



Solution

Both minimize (1/2)‖w‖² + CΣL(yᵢfᵢ), and the only difference is the loss’s tail past the margin. Get that tail exactly right, because the usual phrasing of it is wrong. For a misclassified point both losses grow linearly: hinge \((1 - z)\) and logistic \(\log(1 + e^{-z}) \approx -z - \log 2\), and their ratio tends to 1. The exponential belongs to the other side: for a far-correct point the hinge is identically 0 while logistic’s loss is \(\approx e^{-|z|}\) — decaying but never exactly zero. That asymmetry is the real difference, and it is a statement about influence, not about growth rate: a single extreme mislabeled point contributes exactly zero SVM gradient once it is past the margin (the hinge is flat there, so the boundary is pinned by everything else), while logistic keeps a small persistent gradient forever. Hence the boundary is pinned for the SVM and slowly dragged for logistic — with the drag saturating, as Exercise 1’s table shows. The construction demonstrates “loss tails = influence tails”: choose the tail you can defend given your labeling process.

Q2. Decision-theoretic selection: a screening program (1% prevalence, FN cost 50× FP) needs (i) a ranked list for follow-up budget and (ii) per-patient risk estimates audited by regulators. Design the model comparison: which metrics for (i) and (ii) (3.1, 3.1.5), which two models to compete, what calibration step the winner needs, and how the cost ratio enters threshold choice after modeling (3.1 Exercise 2). Implement the comparison on simulated data and report the decision.


Solution








Ranking for budget: AP/AUC on continuous scores — both models compete (SVM margins rank fine). (ii) Audited risks: logistic’s native probabilities + calibration check win (SVM needs Platt and still needs verification). Threshold: with FN:FP = 50:1, choose the cutoff from the cost-minimizing point of the chosen model’s ROC/PR trade — after modeling, on validation data, and reported with the confusion matrix it implies. Decision: logistic for the deployed risk model, SVM kept as the margin-consistency check.

title: 8.5 SVM vs Logistic Regression
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (SVM × logistic × 5.x × 6.7 GAM). The four-way boundary study: on a dataset with 3 linear signals + 1 smooth nonlinear signal + 1 interaction, compare logistic-linear, SVM-linear, GAM-logistic (additive splines — 6.7), and RBF-SVM, all nested-CV’d. Report test AUC and each model’s recovery of the linear signals (coefficient/importance comparison). Which model when — write the routing rule a team should paste above their modeling notebook.
C2 (SVM × 0.5 leakage × 4.6 tuning). The optimistic-pipeline autopsy: a colleague reports “SVM (C, γ tuned) beats logistic 0.94 vs 0.91.” Audit: re-run their probable pipeline (scaler fit on all data, (C, γ) tuned on test) vs the honest nested version; quantify the inflation attributable to each bug separately. Then write the two-sentence review response you’d file — the reusable text for the next paper you review with this flaw.

title: 8.5 SVM vs Logistic Regression
text:
7. Summary

Same linear score, different loss tails: hinge (zero past margin, linear when wrong) vs log (never zero, exponential when wrong).
Probabilities: logistic native and interpretable; SVM via Platt — calibrate either way.
Robustness: hinge bounds outlier influence; logistic’s tail lets extremes pull — labeling quality decides.
Scale: logistic/LinearSVC/SGD for big n; SVC when SVs or kernels are the point.
Both are linear without engineering; both need scaling, honest tuning, and prevalence-aware metrics.
Multiclass paths differ (OvO vs multinomial) — see 8.6 next.
One family remains: SVMs for many classes at once — 8.6 Multiclass SVM.

title: 9.1 The Unsupervised Mindset
text:
Everything so far had answers in the data. Unsupervised learning removes them: find structure — clusters, directions, patterns — with no labels to score against. The mindset shift is profound: there is no test set for truth, so validation becomes stability, interpretability, and usefulness — and every choice (k, scaling, distance) is a modelling statement you must own.

title: 9.1 The Unsupervised Mindset
text:
2. Concept Questions

Without labels, what replaces test-set accuracy as the criterion for “this decomposition/clustering is good”?
Why do unsupervised results depend more on preprocessing than supervised ones? Name the two preprocessing choices that matter most.
Your PCA finds “PC1 = 60% variance = patient severity.” What’s the hidden inferential leap in that sentence?
In what sense is clustering a modeling decision rather than a discovery? Give two datasets where the same algorithm yields different legitimate clusterings.
How can unlabeled data still improve a supervised pipeline? Name three distinct mechanisms.



Answers


External validity: stability under resampling (1.5 logic), interpretability by domain experts, downstream usefulness (does the structure predict outcomes you care about? — a supervised check after the fact), and internal indices (silhouette, explained variance) — each necessary, none sufficient. The honest claim is always conditional: “given k = 3 and these distances.”
Because structure IS the output: scaling changes distances → changes clusters (0.5’s standardization law, now generative rather than cosmetic); feature selection changes what “similar” means. Also: transformations (log for skewed counts) reshape geometry wholesale.
“PC1 captures 60% of variance” is a mathematical fact; “PC1 = severity” is an interpretation — it holds if loadings align with severity markers and survives validation against external severity measures. Variance ≠ importance (5.5’s low-variance-signal lesson at full strength).
Clustering imposes a structure family (K distinct spherical groups) and reports the best fit of that family. Same algorithm, different legitimate answers: elongated/gappy data (K-means sees 2 vs 4 depending on scale), multi-scale data (clusters within clusters). The algorithm answers “what does k-means see,” not “what clusters exist.”

Pretraining/representation: PCA directions as features (5.5); (b) semi-supervision: cluster labels as weak features; (c) leakage-free structure for stratification/normalization (batch detection, 9.3) — plus anomaly detection feeding quality control.

title: 9.1 The Unsupervised Mindset
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. The preprocessing sensitivity exhibit: generate 3 elongated Gaussian blobs at different scales. Run K-means (k = 3) on (a) raw data, (b) standardized data, (c) whiten-and-rotate data. Compare cluster assignments against the true blob membership (ARI). Report the 3×1 table and explain which preprocessing choice encoded which assumption about what “similar” means.


Solution







Raw data: the wide-scale axis dominates distances — clusters smear. Standardizing equalizes axes (assumes both features equally important). The ARI table is the preprocessing-as-assumption lesson: no choice is “correct” — each defines similarity differently, and the right one matches the domain’s notion (9.6 returns to this with full machinery).

Exercise 2. Stability as validation: build a pipeline that measures clustering stability: bootstrap-resample rows 50×, refit K-means (k = 3), and compute the mean pairwise ARI between the resulting partitions (evaluated on the shared rows via prediction). Apply it to (a) clearly separated blobs and (b) one uniform blob with k = 3. Report both stabilities. What does the stability number license you to claim?


Solution







High stability (blobs) licenses: “the data support a 3-group partition reproducibly.” Low stability (uniform): the partition is an artifact of initialization — you may still use it operationally, but discovery language is forbidden. Stability validates reproducibility, never truth: a stable wrong clustering (e.g., two true blobs split by a scale artifact) remains stable.

Exercise 3. Structure ≠ truth, shown twice: (a) run K-means with k = 6 on 3 well-separated blobs and report how the algorithm happily splits true blobs (over-segmentation with high stability!); (b) run K-means with k = 2 on two concentric circles (make_blobs-style construction by hand) and report ARI ≈ 0 despite visually obvious “clusters.” Write the two failure modes’ names and the tool each demands (validation-set k choice; non-spherical-shape methods).


Solution








Over-segmentation: k larger than the truth yields stable, fine partitions — stability alone can’t catch it (compare 9.6’s stability discussion). (b) Shape mismatch: K-means carves by distance-to-centroid — it cannot represent rings; spectral/density methods are the cure. Both failures say the same thing: the algorithm’s assumptions are the hypothesis being tested.

title: 9.1 The Unsupervised Mindset
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Unsupervised “validation” is a family, not a number: stability, internal indices, expert interpretability, downstream-task usefulness — report the ones your claim needs (9.6 organizes them).
The reification trap: “K-means found 4 patient subtypes” — the algorithm found 4 centroids minimizing inertia given your scaling; the subtypes exist as model outputs. Clinical translation requires external validation (outcomes, replication cohorts) — always.
Scaling, outliers, skew: each reshapes distance geometry silently; robust scaling or transformations belong in the unsupervised pipeline as modeling choices (0.4’s skew transforms, now structural).
Curse of dimensionality hits hardest here: distances concentrate (2.9), variance spreads everywhere — dimension reduction (9.2) usually precedes clustering in wide data.
Batch effects masquerade as structure: the strongest “cluster” in biological data is often the processing batch — unsupervised methods find it before biology (5.6’s warning, sharpened).
Multiple testing’s cousin — multiple clusterings: trying k = 2..10 and several algorithms then reporting the “interesting” one is the same selection game (4.1, 12.x stub); pre-specify or correct.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated “unsupervised discovery” has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Unscaled clustering lets the batch-dominated feature decide everything — the “subtypes” are likely batches. Scale, and audit clusters against known artifacts (batch, site) before biological naming.
Inertia as k-selection: it decreases monotonically — it cannot select k; use stability/silhouette/elbow-with-eyes (9.4, 9.6).
Discovery language without validation: cross-check against batch labels, report stability, and only then hypothesize — the claim needs external validity to graduate from “partition” to “subtype.”

title: 9.1 The Unsupervised Mindset
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Formalize “no free validation”: prove that for any partition P of a dataset and any rival partition P′, there exists a distance metric under which P is the exact K-means solution (construct the metric from P’s indicator structure). What does this impossibility result imply about unsupervised model selection — and which external ingredient breaks the circularity?


Hint

Define distances: 0 within P-groups, huge between; K-means with k = |P| recovers P exactly under it.



Solution

Given P, set d(x, x′) = 0 if same P-cluster, 1 otherwise; all within-cluster variances vanish and between-cluster distances dominate → K-means (and most criteria) select P exactly. Symmetrically for P′. So “the best clustering” is metric-relative — any partition can be crowned by some reasonable-sounding geometry. Implication: internal criteria can’t, even in principle, arbitrate between structurally different partitions; the circularity breaks only with external reference — outcomes, stability across independent datasets, expert validity, or downstream-task performance. This is the precise reason Part 9’s validation chapter (9.6) leans so hard on stability and external checks rather than internal indices alone.

Q2. Design an end-to-end unsupervised analysis protocol for a new 2,000-patient, 50-feature clinical cohort: (a) preprocessing decisions and their justifications, (b) structure-finding methods to run and their assumption families, (c) the validation battery (internal, stability, external), (d) the pre-registered reporting standard (what gets reported regardless of how results look). Implement the skeleton (code structure with the key calls) and annotate each step with the pitfall it prevents — drawing on every Part 9 assumption you can name.


Solution







The deliverable of unsupervised analysis is the protocol plus evidence, not a partition: (a) prevents geometry artifacts, (b) spans assumption families so conclusions aren’t algorithm-shaped, (c) substitutes for the missing test set, (d) blocks the garden-of-forking-paths (4.1, 12.x selection games). Every pitfall from this part reappears as a checklist line — that’s the curriculum compressed.

title: 9.1 The Unsupervised Mindset
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (mindset × 0.3–0.4 toolkit). Exploratory-data-analysis as unsupervised learning in disguise: take the cohort table from 0.3 and run the full Part 9 pipeline (scale → PCA → K-means k ∈ {2, 3, 4} → stability) treating the EDA outputs as findings to validate. Which EDA observation (skew, correlation, group imbalance) becomes which unsupervised structure? Write the mapping table — EDA view ↔︎ unsupervised formalization — and note where the formalization changed your belief versus merely quantified it.
C2 (mindset × 12.x multiple testing stub × 4.6 tuning). The selection-game census: enumerate every selection act in a typical unsupervised analysis (k, metric, scaling, features, transformations, algorithm, batch-correction flavor) and estimate the multiplicity. Then design the control: either pre-registration (fix choices from domain theory), selection-frequency reporting (5.1), or external validation — and implement the one you can run today on simulated data where the truth is known (plant 3 clusters; measure how often your full pipeline “discovers” them vs noise).

title: 9.1 The Unsupervised Mindset
text:
7. Summary

No labels ⇒ no test truth: validation becomes stability, interpretability, external checks, downstream usefulness.
Preprocessing is the model: scaling, transforms, feature choice define similarity — own them explicitly.
Structure claims are conditional on the algorithm’s assumptions; reification (“discovered subtypes”) requires external validation.
Stability licenses reproducibility, not truth; internal indices are evidence, never verdicts.
Batch effects and dimensionality are the two ambient hazards of real unsupervised work.
The selection game is alive here too — pre-specify, report everything, validate externally.
First formal tool, the workhorse of dimension reduction everywhere: 9.2 Principal component analysis.

title: 9.3 Missing Values & Matrix Completion
text: Real data has holes: dropped measurements, failed assays, unanswered questions. What you do with them is a modeling decision — delete cases, fill with means, model the missingness, or exploit low-rank structure — and each choice encodes an assumption about why the values are missing. This page builds the taxonomy and the toolkit.

title: 9.3 Missing Values & Matrix Completion
text:
1. Basic Concept
The missingness taxonomy (Rubin):

MCAR — missing completely at random: the hole is independent of everything (a scanner glitch).
MAR — missing at random: the hole depends on observed variables only (young patients skip a costly scan).
MNAR — missing depends on the missing value itself (the sickest patients’ values are unmeasurable).

The mechanism determines the remedy: deletion is unbiased only under MCAR; imputation models must capture MAR dependencies; MNAR needs explicit missingness modeling (or honesty about limits).






The basic toolkit on one matrix:

title: 9.3 Missing Values & Matrix Completion
text:
2. Concept Questions

Complete-case (listwise) deletion: under which mechanism is it unbiased, what does it cost even then, and when is it catastrophic?
Mean imputation’s two distinct sins — one statistical (variance), one geometric (for distances/clustering)?
KNN imputation: what structure does it exploit, and what happens to it as dimension grows (2.9)?
Why is “impute, then treat imputed values as real” in downstream inference dishonest — and what’s the standard fix’s name?
A recommender-style matrix (users × items) is 98% missing. Which paradigm applies, and why is this not an imputation problem in the usual sense?



Answers


Unbiased under MCAR only. Cost even then: smaller n and wider SEs — you paid data for holes. Catastrophic under MAR/MNAR with systematic missingness (e.g., all severe cases missing one assay): the “complete” sample is a biased population (1.1’s summary trap, dataset edition).
Statistical: imputed values are the mean — zero deviation — so variances/correlations shrink toward 0 (n identical contributions). Geometric: every imputed row sits exactly on the mean-point, corrupting distances and cluster structure (9.1’s geometry law).
It exploits local correlation structure: a missing value is filled from similar rows’ values — works while neighbors are informative; under high dimension, neighborhoods blow up and “nearest” becomes meaningless (curse of dimensionality, 2.9).
Imputed entries are guesses with model-derived uncertainty; treating them as observations understates every SE and overstates every p-value — the imputation model’s uncertainty must propagate. The classical fix: multiple imputation (Rubin) — draw several imputations, analyze each, pool with Rubin’s rules. (Modern shortcut: models that treat missingness natively, 7.6.)
Low-rank matrix completion (Netflix problem): the matrix’s rank structure (users × items have few latent factors) makes recovery possible from sparse entries — the goal is predicting held-out entries, not filling a covariate matrix for a model. Different objective, different machinery (SVD-based, Exercise 3).

title: 9.3 Missing Values & Matrix Completion
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Deletion vs imputation under three mechanisms: build y = 2x + ε and censor x (30%) under MCAR, MAR (missing when another observed variable z > 0), and MNAR (missing when |x| large). For each: fit OLS on complete cases and on mean-imputed data; compare slope estimates to truth. Which mechanism breaks deletion? Which breaks naive imputation worse? Write the decision rule.


Solution







Read the three columns as a sequence, because the natural reading is wrong twice. The MAR row is the one that works: because \(z\) is correlated with \(x\), censoring on \(z\) truncates \(x\)’s range (SD 0.972 → 0.787), the slope drifts to 2.043, and the SE nearly doubles to 0.098. That is exactly the MAR failure — deletion is biased because the observed covariate is informative. Get the DGP wrong (drawing \(z\) independently of \(x\)) and MAR silently behaves like MCAR, which is the more dangerous outcome: a demo that appears to confirm the textbook claim while actually not testing it. The surprising column is the second one. Mean imputation returns exactly the same slope as complete-case under every mechanism (2.023 / 2.043 / 1.939), because imputing every missing \(x\) with a constant and regressing on it reproduces the full-sample mean relationship — for a single linear predictor, mean imputation is consistent for \(\mathbb{E}[y \mid x]\). The usual claim that “mean imputation biases the slope” is false as stated. What mean imputation actually destroys is the variance: the SEs come out 0.083 / 0.174 / 0.218, 1.5–2× too large, and the reason is visible in the last column — the genuinely observed \(x\) now has SD 0.538 under MNAR while the fitted model believes every observation sits at a common value, so residuals look too dispersed and confidence intervals are wrong. Prediction intervals, distributions, anything nonlinear, and anything multivariate are where the damage becomes fatal (3.6’s GLM needs a real link, not a constant). Decision rule: diagnose the mechanism first — is missingness related to observed data, to itself, or to the unobserved value? Delete freely only under MCAR; under MAR use an imputation that models the observed-data dependencies; under MNAR, no mechanical fix, so model the missingness explicitly or report the limitation.

Exercise 2. KNNImputer vs IterativeImputer on structured data: build a 4-feature matrix with two correlated pairs (x₂ ≈ x₁ + noise; x₄ ≈ −x₃ + noise) and 20% MCAR holes. Compare fill quality (MAE on held-out true values) for mean, KNN (k ∈ {2, 5, 15}), and IterativeImputer (round-robin regression). Which wins, and what data property does its win exploit?


Solution







Iterative (and small-k KNN) win by exploiting the pairwise correlation structure — each imputation is a mini-regression on the other features, exactly what the correlated pairs make learnable. Large k blurs toward the mean; the mean ignores structure entirely. The property exploited: conditional correlation among observed features — the more structure your matrix has, the more sophisticated imputation pays.

Exercise 3. Low-rank matrix completion by alternating SVD: build a ratings-like matrix with true rank 3 (users × items via 3 latent factors), mask 80% at random. Implement iterative SVD completion: initialize missing entries with the matrix mean; repeat {SVD at rank 3, replace missing entries with reconstruction} until convergence. Report recovery error on held-out entries vs the mean-fill baseline. Then verify the impossibility intuition: rerun on a full-rank (random) matrix — recovery collapses.


Solution







The alternation works because a low-rank matrix is determined by far fewer entries than it contains — the SVD projection strips noise from the guessed entries and the observed entries anchor the truth, iterating toward consistency. Random matrices have no such compression: completion is impossible, and the algorithm honestly fails. This is the Netflix-problem paradigm: recovery from structure, not imputation from covariates.

title: 9.3 Missing Values & Matrix Completion
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Diagnose before treating: build missingness indicators and test them against everything observed (chi-square/logistic) — discovered structure means MAR and exploitable signal; undiagnosed MNAR silently biases everything downstream (1.4’s assumption discipline).
The missingness indicator trick (drill 4): adding “was-missing” as a feature lets tree/boosting models use the pattern — legitimate under MAR-ish mechanisms, and standard practice in Kaggle-grade pipelines; but it assumes the pattern is informative, which MNAR can violate subtly.
Impute inside pipelines: imputers are fitted statistics (means, neighbor structure, regression coefficients) — fit per fold, transform test (0.5 law); fitting the imputer on all data leaks.
Dropping columns with high missingness is also a modeling decision: threshold-based dropping (“>40% missing → drop”) is arbitrary unless tied to mechanism reasoning; a column that’s missing because of the outcome is informative, not broken.
sklearn’s IterativeImputer is experimental (enable_iterative_imputer import) — it’s MICE-flavored; still single-imputation: uncertainty propagation needs multiple draws (or a native-NaN model like 7.6’s boosters).
Matrix completion ≠ imputation: completion predicts held-out entries of one big low-rank matrix (no response variable); imputation fills covariates for downstream models. Choose by what the filled values are for.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated imputation pipeline has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Imputer fit before split: means/structure from test rows entered training — leakage (0.5). Imputer inside the pipeline. (The code comment calls imp a “median-impute” but it is a mean imputer — the label and the call disagree.)
Mean-impute-then-cluster: imputed rows sit at the mean point, corrupting distances and fabricating a “central” mega-cluster (Concept 2b); use KNN-imputation, native-NaN models, or missingness-aware clustering.
No missingness indicator, and a mean imputer cannot tell a hole from an extreme. Here missingness is MCAR (rng.uniform(0, 1, X.shape) < .2, independent of y), so the old version of this drill — which claimed a column had been dropped for being “missing mostly for y == 1” — was inventing a problem that the code did not have. The real defect is quieter: after mean imputation the model cannot tell an imputed row from an observed one, and the last line shows the imputer happily filling a genuine extreme value with the column mean. A real outlier and a missing measurement are different things that want opposite treatments (keep and flag vs. model and shrink), and SimpleImputer gives them the same answer. Use SimpleImputer(add_indicator=True) so the model can learn a separate effect for “this was imputed”, or a native-NaN learner that routes on missingness per split.

title: 9.3 Missing Values & Matrix Completion
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Prove mean-imputation’s variance shrinkage: for x with variance σ² and fraction p missing-at-random imputed with x̄, the imputed vector’s variance is (1−p)σ² (+ a p(1−p)x̄-level correction of order 1/n). Verify by simulation across p ∈ {0, .25, .5, .75}, and derive the same shrinkage for correlations between two independently-imputed columns. What does this imply for downstream PCA/clustering on naively imputed matrices?


Hint

Imputed entries contribute zero deviation from the mean by construction; compute Var = (1/n)Σ(observed deviations² + p·0²).



Solution

Imputed entries equal x̄ exactly, so Σ(xᵢ − x̄)² accumulates only over the (1−p)n observed rows: Var ≈ (1−p)σ² (exactly, for MCAR, in expectation). For two columns independently imputed, imputed positions are mean-valued in both — cross-products with imputed rows contribute 0 in deviation — correlations shrink toward 0 similarly. Simulation:






Downstream consequence: naively mean-imputed matrices show shrunken variances and correlations — PCA underestimates structure, clusters blur toward the centroid, loadings flatten (9.2). Every structure-seeking method sees a demorphosed world; the fix is uncertainty-aware imputation or methods treating missingness natively.

Q2. Missingness-forest vs MICE-style imputation on MAR data: simulate MAR missingness (probability of missing x₁ increases with observed x₂) with x₁ genuinely needed downstream; compare (a) KNN/Iterative imputation then logistic, (b) HistGradientBoosting with native NaN (7.6), (c) mean-impute + missingness-indicator logistic. Report downstream test accuracy/AUC. Which approach captures the MAR information, and what does the native-NaN win tell you about where imputation models actually earn their keep?


Solution







All imputation-and-indicator approaches capture most of the MAR information (the pattern is observable in x₂ and indicators); native-NaN boosting matches without maintaining an imputation model — its per-split missing-branch learns the pattern where it matters for the decision. The broader lesson: imputation models earn their keep by preserving the joint structure (correlations, mechanism) that the downstream task uses — when the downstream learner can ingest missingness natively and the pattern is simple, the elaborate imputer is optional; when inference (not prediction) is the goal, MICE-style multiple imputation remains the principled standard.

title: 9.3 Missing Values & Matrix Completion
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (missingness × 0.5 splitting × 4.6 tuning). The full missing-data pipeline audit: build a pipeline (imputer-choice tuned + model tuned) under 25% missingness; evaluate three protocol variants — (a) imputer fit on all data (leaky), (b) imputer per-fold (honest), (c) per-fold imputer with imputation strategy also tuned — by nested CV. Quantify each gap and write the audit checklist item that would have caught (a) in review.
C2 (missingness × 9.2 PCA × 5.6). PCA of incomplete wide data: n = 150, p = 300, 30% MCAR. Compare (a) mean-impute → PCA, (b) IterativeImputer → PCA, (c) native low-rank completion → rank-3 scores, by recovery of the planted 3-factor structure (subspace angle to true loadings). Which preserves structure, which shrinks it (recall Q1’s variance shrinkage), and what does this imply for omics-style workflows where >50% of values are missing at low abundance?

title: 9.3 Missing Values & Matrix Completion
text:
7. Summary

Missingness has mechanisms (MCAR/MAR/MNAR); the mechanism, not convenience, picks the remedy.
Deletion: unbiased only under MCAR, always costly; catastrophic under systematic missingness.
Mean imputation: shrinks variance and correlations, wrecks geometry — a placeholder, not a method.
KNN/Iterative imputers exploit observed-feature structure; fit them inside CV folds; uncertainty needs multiple imputation or native-NaN models.
Missingness indicators turn holes into features — legitimate when the pattern is informative; an assumption when it isn’t.
Low-rank completion solves the sparse-matrix problem (Netflix) from rank structure — impossible without it.
Every choice here is a missingness-mechanism assumption — diagnose the holes before modeling them.
Structure found, holes filled — now partition it: 9.4 K-means clustering.

title: 9.5 Hierarchical Clustering
text: Hierarchical clustering builds a tree of clusterings instead of one partition: start with every point as its own cluster and repeatedly merge the closest pair (agglomerative), or split recursively (divisive). The output — a dendrogram — shows structure at every scale simultaneously, letting you choose k by cutting the tree rather than committing upfront.

title: 9.5 Hierarchical Clustering
text:
1. Basic Concept
Agglomerative nesting (AGNES): repeatedly merge the two closest clusters, where “cluster distance” is defined by the linkage:

single: min pairwise distance (chains; finds long straggly shapes)
complete: max pairwise distance (compact, tight balls)
average: mean pairwise distance (compromise)
ward: merge minimizing total within-cluster variance increase (the K-means-flavored default)







Cutting the tree at different heights = different clusterings:

title: 9.5 Hierarchical Clustering
text:
2. Concept Questions

What does a dendrogram’s height encode, and why is “cut at height h” equivalent to “keep the k merges below h”?
Single linkage’s chaining failure: describe the mechanism, draw it mentally on two crescents, and name the truth-shape it’s designed for.
Ward linkage vs K-means: state the precise relationship (what Ward merges minimize) and when their outputs can differ.
Inversion (a later merge at smaller height than an earlier one): which linkage can produce it, and what does it break (both interpretationally and computationally)?
The dendrogram is n−1 merges tall. What does that structure guarantee about hierarchy — and what real data property violates it (making the tree partly fiction)?



Answers


Height = the distance between the two merged clusters (linkage-defined). Cutting at h keeps only merges with height ≤ h; the remaining connected components are exactly the k clusters — height-cuts and k-cuts are two views of one tree.
Single linkage merges by the closest pair — a chain of close steps connects two genuinely distinct groups through intermediate points (“chaining”). It’s designed for elongated/straggly truths (its home game), and it’s robust to scale-ordering.
Ward merges the pair whose union minimizes the increase in Σ within-cluster squared deviation — exactly K-means’ criterion applied hierarchically. Outputs differ: greedy hierarchical order ≠ K-means’ global refinement; a final K-means pass on Ward’s clusters often improves them (7.1 greedy-vs-refit echo).
Inversions occur with centroid/median linkage (distances of merged clusters can shrink) — they break the monotone dendrogram (heights must be non-decreasing upward) and the fcluster-style cutting (no clean level cut exists). Ward/single/complete/average are inversion-free.
The tree guarantees a strictly nested hierarchy: every pair of clusters is disjoint or nested. Real structure violates it — overlapping groups (cells share states), multi-scale co-existing structures — so forcing data into a tree loses cross-cutting structure (the same nesting assumption 6.2’s trees and 7.1 decision trees make, here about clusters).

title: 9.5 Hierarchical Clustering
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Implement single and complete linkage from scratch (the merge loop with a live distance matrix), verify against scipy.linkage on a 12-point dataset, and demonstrate the chaining/compactness contrast on the bridge dataset from drill 2. Which lines of your implementation encode the definition of each linkage?


Solution







The two lines selecting block.min() vs block.max() ARE the linkage definitions — everything else is bookkeeping. scipy computes them with optimized updates (Lance–Williams), but the semantics you’ve now written by hand are identical.

Exercise 2. Linkage zoology on structured truths: build four truths — (a) blobs, (b) two crescents (non-convex), (c) long straggly chains, (d) tight balls of unequal size — and run all four linkages (single/complete/average/ward), scoring ARI at the true k. Report the 4×4 table. Verify: single wins crescents/chains, ward wins balls/blobs, complete resists chaining. Write the linkage-selection sentence.


Solution







The table’s diagonal is the lesson: single linkage owns chains/crescents (chaining is a feature there); ward owns blobs and unequal balls (variance criterion matches); complete guards compactness against bridges; average splits the difference. Selection sentence: “choose the linkage whose merge semantics match the cluster shape your domain expects — then verify with the dendrogram and stability (9.6).”

Exercise 3. Dendrogram forensics: for the bridge dataset, produce dendrograms under single and complete linkage side by side. Read from each: at what height do the two blobs separate, and what does the single-linkage tree claim about the bridge points (which merge last/never at low height)? Then cut both trees at k = 2 and draw the partitions. Write the two-sentence guidance for reading a dendrogram before trusting its cuts.


Solution







Reading discipline: (1) scan the top merges first — the last few merge heights encode the strongest separations (a tiny final height = weak global structure); (2) check for chaining (single linkage with long mid-height ladders means bridges are being absorbed). Only then do cuts mean what you hope. The single-linkage tree here absorbs the bridge into one cluster at low heights; complete linkage’s top merge separates the blobs cleanly — same data, opposite stories, chosen by linkage semantics.

title: 9.5 Hierarchical Clustering
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Complexity: naive agglomerative is O(n³) (or O(n² log n) with heaps) and O(n²) memory — the practical ceiling is ~10–20k points; for larger n, use K-means (9.4) first, then hierarchically cluster the centroids, or sample.
Ward on non-Euclidean inputs: ward assumes Euclidean distances (it’s a variance criterion); with correlation or custom distances, use average/complete — or accept that ward’s “variance” is undefined on your metric.
fcluster criteria: “maxclust” (k clusters) vs “distance” (height cut) answer different questions — height cuts transfer across datasets (a meaningful similarity scale), k-cuts don’t.
Dendrogram orientation illusion: reordering leaves changes nothing about the tree — don’t read neighborliness into leaf adjacency across branches (only within the last merges).
Stability still applies: bootstrap the rows, re-cluster, compare trees (cophenetic correlation / ARI at the cut) — hierarchical trees are as resample-sensitive as K-means labels (9.1 Exercise 2).
No reallocation: once merged, never split/switch — early greedy mistakes are frozen into the tree (agglomerative’s original sin; divisive or refined approaches pay to escape it).


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated hierarchical pipeline has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Ward needs Euclidean geometry — its merge criterion is a variance increase, undefined on correlation distances. Use average/complete linkage on non-Euclidean metrics (or embed the metric first).
Threshold imported from elsewhere: distance cuts are meaningful in this dataset’s similarity scale — read the target height off this dendrogram (or cut by k with justification).
Leaf adjacency isn’t similarity: dendrogram leaves are ordered for drawing; only tree structure (nested merges, heights) carries information.

title: 9.5 Hierarchical Clustering
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Derive Ward’s merge criterion: show that for two clusters A, B, the increase in total within-cluster Σ‖x − μ‖² from merging them equals \(\frac{n_A n_B}{n_A + n_B}\|\mu_A - \mu_B\|^2\). Use this to prove ward linkage merges the pair whose centroids are closest weighted by harmonic-mean-ish sizes — and explain why this makes ward prefer merging small clusters early (the unequal-size behavior of 7.2’s ledger).


Hint</summary»
Total within-cluster SSE change = SSE(A∪B) − SSE(A) − SSE(B); expand each SSE around the union mean via the parallel-axis identity.



Solution</summary»
With the identity SSE(A∪B) = SSE(A) + SSE(B) + (n_A n_B/(n_A + n_B))‖μ_A − μ_B‖², the merge cost is exactly the size-weighted centroid distance. The weight n_A n_B/(n_A+n_B) is maximized at balanced sizes: merging two small clusters costs little (small weight), merging two large ones costs plenty — so ward grows big clusters late and prefers consolidating small ones early. Consequence: on unequal-size truths, ward’s trees can consolidate the minority cluster with noise fragments before facing the big cluster — the hierarchical face of K-means’ equal-size tendency.

Q2. Cophenetic correlation as a tree-quality summary: define the cophenetic distance between two points as the height of the merge where they first join; the cophenetic correlation is the correlation between these heights and the original distances. Implement it (scipy.cluster.hierarchy.cophenet), compute it for all four linkages on one dataset, and interpret: what does a high cophenetic correlation certify (and not certify)? Then show a dataset where cophenetic correlation is high but the clustering at true k is wrong — separating “faithful tree” from “correct partition.”


Solution







High cophenetic correlation certifies the tree faithfully represents the pairwise distances — the embedding into tree-heights lost little. It does not certify that the tree’s clusters match the true groups: concentric rings give a faithful tree whose k = 2 cut slices by radius, not ring — tree fidelity and partition correctness are different virtues, exactly the internal-vs-external validation split of 9.1 Q1.

title: 9.5 Hierarchical Clustering
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (hierarchical × 9.2 PCA × 7.4). Wide-data hierarchy: n = 150, p = 200 (5 planted clusters + noise directions). Compare ward-hierarchies built on (a) raw scaled distances, (b) PCA-5 scores, (c) forest-proximity-derived distances (1 − P(same leaf) from a random forest) — ARI at true k plus dendrogram stability under bootstrap. Which distance matrix produces the most faithful tree, and what does the proximity-distance result say about learning metrics from models (7.4)?
C2 (hierarchical × 6.2 steps × 4.6 tuning). Cut selection as hyperparameter tuning: treat the dendrogram cut height as a hyperparameter and select it by a downstream supervised proxy (e.g., cluster-label agreement with a known covariate split, or downstream regression R² using cluster dummies). Implement cut-selection by downstream-CV on data where the true k is known; compare against silhouette-chosen cuts. When does downstream-supervised cut selection find the truth better — and what selection-inflation guard (4.1) must accompany it?

title: 9.5 Hierarchical Clustering
text:
7. Summary

Hierarchical clustering = a tree of nested partitions: merges by linkage (single/complete/average/ward), read at any scale.
Dendrogram heights are merge distances; cuts at height h or into k clusters are two views of one object.
Linkage semantics are shape hypotheses: single→chains, ward→compact variance balls, complete→tight anti-bridge, average→compromise.
Ward = K-means’ criterion hierarchically (size-weighted centroid distance); their outputs relate but greedy order ≠ global refinement.
Faithful trees (cophenetic correlation) can still cut wrong — tree fidelity ≠ partition correctness.
No reallocation, nesting assumption, O(n²) memory: know the ceiling; hybridize for scale.
All structure-finding needs the practical layer — stability, k-selection discipline, mixed data, validation: 9.6 Practical clustering issues.
