title: 9.7 Manifolds, t-SNE, UMAP & Autoencoders
text: 9.2 found linear directions of maximum variance. That is the right tool when the data really is a linear shadow of a lower-dimensional truth — and the wrong tool the moment it is not. PCA cannot find the Swiss roll’s axis no matter how many components you give it, because the roll’s geometry is curved: no straight line in R³ unrolls it. Everything on this page replaces “maximize variance along a straight line” with “preserve the neighbourhood structure,” and every method pays for it differently. The honest summary at the end is that none of these embeddings are maps of your data — they are claims about it.

title: 9.7 Manifolds, t-SNE, UMAP & Autoencoders
text:
1. Basic Concept
The manifold premise. Data that lives in R^p but concentrates near a lower-dimensional surface of intrinsic dimension d ≪ p. The surface is curved, so no linear projection can find it — but distances along the surface still mean something. Isomap approximates that with geodesic (shortest-path-along-the-surface) distances and then finds the flat layout that reproduces them, which is classical MDS (9.3’s matrix-completion machinery in disguise).
Worked example — a Swiss roll, where PCA provably fails and Isomap does not:






Isomap’s embedding-neighbours share 0.737 of the roll coordinate on average; PCA’s share 1.643 — 2.2× worse, even though PCA is optimizing a criterion (maximum variance) that is genuinely achieved. The failure is not optimization, it is specification: variance is the wrong objective for a curved surface.
t-SNE takes a different route entirely. It does not preserve distances at all. It matches, for each point, the distribution of distances to its neighbours (a “similarity” \(P_{j|i}\), softened by a bandwidth) against a target low-dimensional distribution \(Q\) that is a Student-t — chosen precisely so the objective is cheap. The loss is a KL divergence, and the whole game is the perplexity parameter, which fixes that bandwidth as \(\exp(\text{perplexity})\) effective neighbours.

Unlike Isomap/MDS, t-SNE optimizes a global KL and lets local neighbourhoods dominate. Good at revealing fine structure; bad at telling you how big anything is.
UMAP is a close cousin with a different objective — it optimizes cross-entropy against a fuzzy set union rather than KL against a Student-t, which makes it faster and gives more globally-coherent layouts. It needs umap-learn, which Pyodide does not bundle → the Colab lab.
An autoencoder attacks the problem with a network instead of a distance: encode \(x \to h\) through a bottleneck, decode \(\hat x\) from \(h\), and train to minimize reconstruction error. The bottleneck is what forces a low-dimensional representation. With a linear map, a linear activation, and squared error, the optimal solution is exactly PCA — provable, and demonstrable live:







The principal cosines are 0.997 and 0.990 — the network found PCA’s 2-D subspace, found it without being told what PCA was, purely from a reconstruction objective. (The MSE has not fully converged, 0.1012 vs 0.0925: gradient descent on this ill-conditioned problem is slow, and the subspace is already correct. That gap is a budget statement, not a disagreement.) This is the key bridge to 10.3: make the map non-linear, add a non-linear activation, and the autoencoder stops being PCA and starts being something PCA cannot do. The Colab lab runs that version in PyTorch.

title: 9.7 Manifolds, t-SNE, UMAP & Autoencoders
text:
2. Concept Questions

PCA optimizes total variance; t-SNE optimizes a KL divergence between neighbour-similarity distributions. On a linear Gaussian dataset, which should you use, and why does the “better” objective lose?
Perplexity in t-SNE is a bandwidth. A colleague shows two t-SNE plots of the same data, one with visibly separated clusters and one with everything touching, and asks which is “really” true. What is the correct answer, and what would you write in the paper?
Trustworthiness is 0.999 for a t-SNE embedding, yet almost no pairwise distance is preserved. Is that a contradiction? State precisely what each number certifies — and then say what a trustworthiness of 0.94 on pure noise implies about using this metric as evidence of structure.
Why is a t-SNE embedding of a test set impossible with a fitted t-SNE object, and what does that imply about using these coordinates as features for a downstream classifier?
The linear autoencoder provably converges to PCA. If a non-linear autoencoder with the same bottleneck is strictly more expressive, why is it not automatically the better representation?



Answers


PCA wins, and the reason is that t-SNE’s objective is not an approximation of PCA’s on linear data. On a linear Gaussian, PCA is a sufficient statistic: the top-d subspace captures all the recoverable structure, and t-SNE has to spend its optimization finding that same subspace through a non-convex objective with a free bandwidth. Isomap recovers it too (it equals PCA’s subspace up to rotation on linear data), which is why neighbour_spread is the right way to compare. A method that is “more expressive” can still lose when the extra flexibility buys nothing.
Neither is “really” true — separation in a t-SNE plot is a dial, not a finding. The perplexity parameter sets the bandwidth, and the cell below shows apparent cluster separation moving by 9× while the clustering itself is unchanged. What t-SNE legitimately reports is which points are neighbours of which, and that must be the claim. If you want a defensible global geometry, use MDS/Isomap and report distances with uncertainties; if you want a picture of local structure, use t-SNE/UMAP and say the axes are meaningless.
No — they certify different things, which is exactly the trap. Trustworthiness asks whether each point’s embedding-neighbours were already neighbours in the original space: t-SNE scores 0.999, essentially perfect. The distance check asks whether the numerical distances survive, and they do not (0.2% do). t-SNE’s loss contains a term for the first and no constraint at all on the second. High trustworthiness plus destroyed distances is the normal output of t-SNE, not a defect. The follow-up is the important one: run trustworthiness on structureless Gaussian data and you still get 0.94, because in 5-D a random 2-D projection preserves “neighbourhoods” almost perfectly (in moderate dimensions all pairwise distances concentrate, so any point’s 10 nearest neighbours are roughly equidistant — the effect 9.2 flags as distance concentration). So a trustworthiness near 1 is a weak signal: only a large gap between your data’s value and the null value is evidence of anything.
Because t-SNE has no out-of-sample transform. Its optimization is over the whole dataset jointly — the positions of every point depend on every other point, so there is no function \(f\) mapping a new \(x\) to coordinates. The same is true of most t-SNE pipelines in practice. So t-SNE coordinates cannot be features for a downstream model: the classifier would be trained on coordinates that will not exist at prediction time. (UMAP and most manifold methods do have a transform, which is the practical reason people prefer them for pipelines; the coordinates are still not distances.)
Because a strictly larger function class is not a strictly better one. A non-linear autoencoder can represent the linear PCA solution exactly (initialize near zero, the non-linearities pass identity), so the minimum reconstruction error is ≤ PCA’s — but it is not attained at the PCA solution, because the network will happily use its extra capacity to fit the noise in directions that do not generalize. You are buying expressiveness with variance: the representation must be selected by held-out reconstruction, early stopping, or a bottleneck small enough to bite (10.5’s identical problem one layer up). The extra flexibility only pays when there is real non-linear structure to capture — the Swiss roll, and nothing else.

title: 9.7 Manifolds, t-SNE, UMAP & Autoencoders
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.






The two lines are the whole lesson in one cell. t-SNE keeps essentially all of the neighbourhood structure and 0.2% of the distance magnitudes; PCA keeps 100% of the distance magnitudes and (here) none of the visual clustering. Neither is broken — they answer different questions, and reading t-SNE output as a map is the mistake. Hold on to the caveat printed under the first line, though: this trustworthiness is not impressive evidence of anything until you compare it against the null value, because structureless data scores 0.94 too.






Apparent separation between clusters moves from 66.4 down to 7.1 — a 9× swing — while ARI stays pinned at 1.000 for every setting. The clustering is completely stable; only the picture changed. Perplexity is a resolution dial, and the spacing you see is a free parameter you chose.








Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. The picture is a dial, quantified. On the four-blob data, sweep perplexity ∈ {5, 10, 20, 40, 80, 160} and for each report (a) the mean inter-cluster centroid gap, (b) the ARI of K-means on the embedding against the true labels, and (c) trustworthiness(k=10). Report the ratio of largest to smallest gap across the sweep, and the same ratio for ARI and trustworthiness. Then: a colleague ships a figure with a chosen perplexity. Write the two sentences that must appear in the caption, and state the one quantity from your table that is perplexity-invariant and therefore safe to report.


Solution







The gap varies by about 20× across the sweep (perplexity 5 gives visibly huge separations; 160 collapses them) while ARI moves by a factor of 1.000 and trustworthiness by 1.006 — both flat. So the picture is a free parameter and the clustering is not. But note the trap in the last ratio: flat does not mean informative. The negative control in Exercise 2 shows trustworthiness is already 0.94 on pure noise, so a flat-0.99 trustworthiness is not by itself evidence of anything. The only quantity in this table that is genuinely safe to report is ARI against external labels — because it is the one that requires the ground truth you are actually trying to say something about. The caption sentences: (i) the axis scale and inter-cluster distances in this figure are not meaningful and must not be interpreted; (ii) the embedding is shown at perplexity = p and the recovered neighbourhood structure was stable across p ∈ [5, 160] — which is the honest form of a robustness claim, because the picture itself is not robust.

Exercise 2. Choosing the tool — and the negative control. Four datasets: (a) structureless 5-D Gaussian, (b) a 2-D plane embedded in 20 noisy dimensions, (c) a Swiss roll, (d) two concentric rings in 2-D. Each of (b)–(d) has a known generative coordinate (the first latent, the roll parameter \(t\), the radius). For every dataset × method in {PCA-2, Isomap-2, t-SNE} report coherence: the spread of that coordinate among each point’s 10 embedding-neighbours, in units of the coordinate’s own SD (lower = the embedding recovered the structure). Then run trustworthiness on the null dataset as a control, and write the routing rule — including the case where the intuitively-right method is the worst one.


Solution







Three results, and the third is the reason to run the control.
Linear truth (plane+noise): 0.613 / 0.651 / 0.624 — all within noise of each other, with PCA marginally ahead. No curved structure exists to be found, so the extra machinery of Isomap and t-SNE buys nothing and costs optimization. This is 9.2’s sufficiency result showing up as a measurement.
Curved truth (swiss roll): PCA 1.108 vs Isomap 0.770 and t-SNE 0.820. PCA is clearly worst, by 30–44%, and this is the case the page exists for. Isomap edges out t-SNE here, but read the next row before concluding which is better.
The surprise (concentric rings): PCA 0.796 beats both manifold methods — Isomap is the worst of the three at 1.002. Intuition says “rings are curved, so use the curved-structure method,” and that is exactly backwards. Rings already live in 2-D, so a linear projection keeps them intact and coherent; Isomap then does something actively unhelpful: it replaces the true distances with shortest-path distances on a k-NN graph, and a closed circular curve unrolls into a line, which re-scales the radius information the metric was supposed to preserve. The failure is in the one non-exact step of the algorithm, and it is invisible unless you check.
The control decides what any of this means. Trustworthiness on structureless Gaussian data is 0.776 (PCA), 0.755 (Isomap) and 0.936 (t-SNE) — all “high” — because in 5 dimensions all pairwise distances concentrate, so nearly any 2-D projection has plausible-looking local neighbourhoods. A trustworthiness near 1 is therefore weak evidence, and a t-SNE plot of pure noise will still look tidy. Routing rule, in order: run the negative control first and keep only statistics that separate the real data from it; if a linear projection already recovers the generative structure, stop there (PCA); reach for Isomap/MDS when the structure is genuinely curved and the data is higher-dimensional than its intrinsic dimension; use t-SNE/UMAP when what you need is a picture of local neighbourhoods and you will report it as such. And note the general lesson: no method dominates, and the two that are “supposed” to handle curvature are the ones that fail on a closed curve. Choose per data, verify per data.
Exercise 3. The autoencoder/PCA bridge, closed. (a) Prove that a tied, linear autoencoder minimizing \(\|Z - ZWW^\top\|_F^2\) has stationary points satisfying \(Z^\top Z W = W\Lambda\) for symmetric \(\Lambda\), and identify the solutions. (b) Verify numerically by gradient descent (as in Section 1) that the recovered subspace matches PCA’s. (c) Explain in one sentence why breaking the tie (a non-tied autoencoder, the usual architecture) does not change the linear result but does change the non-linear one. Then state what the Colab lab has to add to make the non-linear case strictly better than PCA.


Solution

Differentiating \(L = \|Z - ZWW^\top\|_F^2\) gives \(\partial L/\partial W = 2Z^\top(ZWW^\top - Z)W\), which vanishes when \(Z^\top Z W = W W^\top W W^\top = W(W^\top W)\), i.e. \(Z^\top Z W = W\Lambda\) with \(\Lambda = W^\top W\) symmetric — the eigenvector equation for \(Z^\top Z\). Its solutions are \(W\)’s columns equal to the top eigenvectors, and by Eckart–Young (9.2) that is precisely the optimal low-rank reconstruction. (b) the Section-1 cell measures principal cosines of 0.997 and 0.990 between the two subspaces. (c) Untying removes the \(W^\top W\) symmetry so the stationary equations become \(Z^\top(Z - \hat Z)W = 0\) and \(\hat Z^\top(\hat Z - Z)W^\top = 0\) — for linear maps the decoupled solution is still the PCA subspace (the decoder is simply \(W^\top\) with a rescaling, which is absorbed by the scale degeneracy of a bilinear model), but with a non-linear encoder the invariance is gone and the encoder directions are no longer pinned to an eigendecomposition of \(Z^\top Z\). So the Colab lab must add exactly three things: a non-linear activation, a bottleneck small enough that the extra capacity cannot absorb the noise (else it overfits rather than compresses — 10.5), and held-out reconstruction or early stopping to pick the stopping point. The measurable claim to test there is the one from Section 1: does the non-linear encoder beat PCA on the Swiss roll, and by how much — while matching it on the Gaussian.

title: 9.7 Manifolds, t-SNE, UMAP & Autoencoders
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

t-SNE has no out-of-sample transform. Positions are fitted jointly, so you cannot embed new points. This is a hard architectural limit, not a missing feature, and it rules out using t-SNE coordinates as model features.
Perplexity is a resolution control, not a tuning target — the sweep above moves apparent cluster separation 9× at fixed clustering. Tune it against a question (“how large a neighbourhood do I claim?”) and report the neighbourhood claim, never the gap.
Axes, distances and areas in a t-SNE plot are meaningless. Only the neighbour graph is meaningful. (If you need a map, use MDS/Isomap, whose axes are the reconstructed coordinates.)
Cluster sizes in t-SNE plots are not comparable across clusters or across runs. Density in the embedding is shaped by the density in the data plus the bandwidth, so a dense region gets spread out and a sparse one contracts.
UMAP vs t-SNE: same motivation, different objective (fuzzy-set cross-entropy vs KL against a Student-t). UMAP is usually faster and its layouts tend to be more globally coherent, and — unlike t-SNE — UMAP objects have .transform(). Neither is a distance-preserving map.
Isomap/MDS need the full pairwise distance matrix — O(n²) memory. On high-dimensional data, k-NN-graph approximations (LLE, UMAP) or metric="precomputed" chunking are the practical route.
Non-linear ≠ better. Every method here spends expressiveness; on linear data PCA wins and t-SNE is strictly worse. Establish linear structure first (9.2’s scree/elbow) before reaching for these.
A manifold is an assumption, not a finding. That the data concentrates near a low-dimensional surface is a claim with evidence (9.1’s standard: stability, interpretability, usefulness). Do not fit a manifold to noise and read structure into the output.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated “clustering on t-SNE features” has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Apparent separation is a knob, not a measurement. This number is a deterministic function of perplexity, which the next line then optimizes — so the pipeline is explicitly selecting the parameter that makes its own reported statistic largest. The cell in Section 3 shows this quantity moving 9× while the actual clustering (ARI vs true labels) never changes. The fix: if you want a separation statistic, compute it in a geometry that has one (MDS/Isomap distances, or a silhouette in the original space), and never let a reporting metric choose a hyperparameter.
Choosing perplexity by eye is choosing a picture. “Cleanest-looking” is a criterion on the rendering, and it is the criterion most vulnerable to the failure mode this page is about. Tune perplexity against a substantive target instead (a held-out neighbourhood consistency, or a downstream 9.6-style stability criterion), and report a sweep.
t-SNE coordinates as a feature matrix is not a pipeline. A KMeans fit on Z cannot score a new sample: t-SNE has no .transform, so at prediction time there is no way to place new data in the same coordinates — the model is unreproducible outside the training set. Worse, the distances in Z are not meaningful (0.2% of pairwise distances survive), so even in-sample the clustering is built on a distorted geometry. This is why pipelines use UMAP (which does have .transform) or the raw features, and why 9.6 insists on a pre-registered policy evaluated by resampling stability rather than by how the picture reads.

title: 9.7 Manifolds, t-SNE, UMAP & Autoencoders
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Why does t-SNE’s objective make the embedding’s scale undetermined, and what is the practical consequence for reading two t-SNE plots side by side? Work from the form of the KL objective and show the scale symmetry explicitly. Then explain why adding a repulsive term (as UMAP does) partially fixes this and why the fix is only partial.
Q2. Derive the geodesic-distance construction behind Isomap and show that on a linear dataset it reduces (up to rotation) to PCA. Then construct a dataset where Isomap and PCA agree and one where Isomap fails, and explain the failure in terms of the k-NN graph step (the only non-exact part of the algorithm).


Hints

Q1: the Student-t target \(Q_{ij} \propto (1 + \|y_i - y_j\|^2)^{-1}\) plus the \(\sum_j Q_{ij} = 1\) constraint; try scaling all \(y\) by a constant and see what KL does. Q2: Isomap = shortest paths on a k-NN graph, then classical MDS on that distance matrix. Ask when the graph is disconnected, and what MDS does with an indefinite distance matrix.

title: 9.7 Manifolds, t-SNE, UMAP & Autoencoders
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (embeddings × 4.1 generalization × 9.6 practical). Embeddings are fitted on data, so their “error” is a resampling question like any other estimator. Design a protocol that measures the stability of a t-SNE/UMAP embedding under bootstrap resampling (e.g. overlap of the k-NN graph across resamples, Procrustes-aligned), apply it to real structure vs null Gaussian data, and report the statistic that separates the two. Then state the pre-registered rule: below what stability should you refuse to report the embedding at all?
C2 (embeddings × 10.3 multilayer networks × 5.6 high-dimensional). The autoencoder as a supervised-target alternative: fit a non-linear autoencoder with a 2-unit bottleneck on high-dimensional data (p ≫ n), then use the learned 2-D code as features for a classifier, and compare against (a) PCA-2 features, (b) a supervised 2-component model (5.5’s PLS), and (c) raw features. Report held-out performance for each. When does the unsupervised bottleneck win, and what is the diagnostic that predicts it in advance? Connect to the 9.2 lesson that variance order ≠ relevance order.

title: 9.7 Manifolds, t-SNE, UMAP & Autoencoders
text:
7. Summary

PCA finds the best linear shadow; on curved data no number of components will unroll a Swiss roll. Isomap/MDS buy a defensible geometry by preserving (geodesic) distances.
t-SNE optimizes a KL divergence over neighbour similarities, not distances. On the 4-blob data it keeps 100% of neighbourhoods and 0.2% of distance magnitudes — high trustworthiness and destroyed distances are its normal output, not a defect.
Perplexity is a picture dial: apparent cluster separation moves 9× across a sweep while ARI stays at 1.000. Never report the gap, never tune perplexity by eye, and never read t-SNE axes, distances or areas.
t-SNE has no out-of-sample transform, so its coordinates cannot be model features or scored on new data. UMAP is the pipeline-friendly cousin (has .transform), and is Colab-only here.
A tied, linear autoencoder provably is PCA (stationary points satisfy \(Z^\top Z W = W\Lambda\)); verified at principal cosines 0.997/0.990. Non-linearity only pays when there is real non-linear structure — and costs variance, so the bottleneck needs held-out selection.
Every method on this page spends expressiveness, and on linear data PCA beats all of them. Establish linear structure first, then reach for curvature.
Embeddings are fitted quantities: their stability under resampling is evidence, and their pictures are claims. A manifold is an assumption; run the negative control (9.6’s refusal rule) before believing one.
Next: Part 11 turns to censored time-to-event data — where the response is a distribution with censoring, the same reason embeddings must report neighbourhoods rather than point estimates.

title: 10.10 When Deep Learning Is Appropriate
text: You now own the deepest toolbox in the course — which makes the most valuable skill knowing when not to use it. Deep learning wins when structure (images, sequences, language) meets data volume and transferable representations. On modest tabular data, gradient-boosted trees (7.5) remain the strongest default in applied work. This page turns that folklore into measurements you can reproduce live, and ends with a decision rule you can defend.

title: 10.10 When Deep Learning Is Appropriate
text:
1. Basic Concept
The decision axes, in the order they usually matter:

Data structure — is there perceptual/spatial/sequential/language structure for representation learning to exploit, or is it a table of heterogeneous features? Deep nets earn their keep on the former; on the latter their flexibility is variance (4.4).
n, honestly counted — end-to-end representation learning wants 10⁴–10⁶+ examples per concept; below that, either engineered features or transfer (pretrained representations) must supply the structure.
Label cost — DL amortizes best when labels are cheap and abundant; 300 expensive clinical labels argue for a regularized classical model + honest CV (4.3).
Interpretability/regulatory needs — a Cox model’s hazard ratio (11.5) or a tree path explains itself; a 12-layer net gets post-hoc (weak) explanations.
Compute/latency budget — training on Colab is free-ish; serving a transformer per API call is not always.
Transfer availability — the modern unlock: when a pretrained backbone exists for your data type, the bar for DL drops enormously (fine-tune > train from scratch, always).

Worked example — the tabular bake-off, live: same data, three model classes:






The MLP closes the gap as n grows but never clearly leads on this generic tabular problem — while costing hyperparameter care the trees didn’t ask for. This is the empirical content of “boosted trees first, DL when structure or scale demands it.”

title: 10.10 When Deep Learning Is Appropriate
text:
2. Concept Questions

Your dataset: 800 rows, 40 mixed-type clinical columns, goal = risk prediction for a regulatory submission. Rank the axes above by how decisively each argues, and name the model you defend.
“Deep learning needs big data” is half-true since transfer learning. Restate the constraint precisely: what must be big — and give an example where 100 labeled images suffice.
Why does a 1-parameter-per-feature logistic model underfit the bake-off data while the MLP only matches the trees — where is the MLP’s capacity going that the trees’ isn’t?
You must choose the horizon: deep net trained today vs gradient boosting updated monthly with new data. Which infrastructure costs differ, and which one is more likely to silently rot?
Name a data type where “classical first” is the wrong default, and the classical method people still mistakenly reach for.



Answers


Structure: none perceptual (argues against DL). n: small (against). Labels: expensive (against). Interpretability: required (decisively against). Compute: irrelevant at this size. Transfer: none for heterogeneous clinical tables (against). Defensible choice: regularized logistic/Cox with honest CV; gradient boosting as the accuracy-seeking challenger; the deep net is indefensible here.
The pretraining corpus must be big and structurally aligned; your labeled set can be tiny because representation learning already happened. Example: fine-tuning an ImageNet-pretrained backbone on 100 labeled histology patches, or a pretrained sentence embedder + logistic head on 200 labeled notes.
The MLP spends capacity learning smooth axis-aligned-to-rotated feature geometry that the axis-aligned tree splits get for free on this generative process; the linear model underfits because some informative structure is genuinely nonlinear (interactions). The MLP’s extra capacity is spent re-deriving what trees hard-code — on generic tabular data, that re-derivation is overhead, not insight.
The DL route: fixed architecture, retrain pipeline, GPU access, drift in representation (silent). The trees: cheap retrains, but tree models also rot silently (feature drift → stale splits). The difference is monitoring surface area: classical pipelines are simpler to re-validate; deep pipelines have more places (preprocessing, tokenizer, init) for undetected drift.
Perceptual data with tiny classical feature sets — e.g., raw-audio keyword spotting or pathology images: “logistic regression on 50 engineered features” is the wrong default when pretrained representations exist. People still reach for hand-crafted features + shallow models because the classical toolkit feels safer — the mismatch costs accuracy, not correctness.

title: 10.10 When Deep Learning Is Appropriate
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. The bake-off, three generative processes: build three datasets — (a) near-linear signal, (b) pure axis-aligned interactions (target = XOR of thresholded features), (c) smooth nonlinear boundary — at n = 500. Fit logistic, HistGradientBoosting, and MLPClassifier on each; tabulate 5-fold CV accuracy. Verify the folklore ranking per column and explain why each winner wins in one sentence apiece.


Solution







Expected pattern: (a) logistic wins or ties — the truth is in its model class, extra capacity only adds variance; (b) trees dominate — XOR is axis-aligned boxes, exactly what splits express natively while linear/MLP models must compose many units to carve diagonal-oblique boundaries; (c) MLP catches the trees — a smooth ring is not axis-aligned, so the tree must staircase toward it while the net’s smooth activations match the geometry. The decision rule is generative, not tribal: match the model class to the boundary’s geometry and your n.

Exercise 2. Sample-size curves for a structured problem: on the digits dataset, plot test accuracy vs training-set size n ∈ {50, 100, 250, 500, 1000} for logistic regression and an MLP (one hidden layer). Where do the curves cross, what is the asymptotic gap, and how does this justify “DL when structure + data” even for a problem as small as 8×8 images? State what a CNN would add (and why we defer it to Colab).


Solution







Both climb; the MLP starts below (capacity without data = variance) and crosses above as n feeds it, ending 2–5 points ahead — pixels have spatial structure the hidden units partially exploit. The CNN would add weight sharing over that spatial structure (the 10.6 argument) and push another few points — the Colab lab shows it. The full pattern — classical competitive when n is small, representation learning pulling ahead as n grows — is the entire “data + structure” quadrant in one plot.

Exercise 3. The leakage trap, DL edition: feature selection is preprocessing that silently reads \(y\). Compare two protocols on 300 noisy tabular samples with 200 features (p/n > 0.5): (a) SelectKBest(k=10) fitted on the full dataset, then CV of an MLP on the selected features; (b) the selector embedded inside the CV pipeline (re-selected per fold). Quantify the optimism of (a). Then state the general rule this exercise installs — which preprocessing steps must live inside the fold, and where does the early-stopping variant of this trap hide?


Solution







Selecting the 10 most promising columns using all labels hands the validator features pre-screened by the answers — each fold’s test rows influenced their own selection. The inflation grows with p/n and noise (here +0.01; in noisier, wider regimes it reaches several points) — and it is pure profit for doing nothing, which is what makes it dangerous. The rule: any step whose output depends on \(y\) — selection, imputation values, scaling, PCA rotation, tokenizer vocab — lives inside the fold; a Pipeline object is the enforcement mechanism, not bureaucracy (4.3). Early stopping hides the same trap one level deeper: a validation set used for stopping is in the model-selection loop, so the final test estimate must come from data that touched neither training nor stopping.

title: 10.10 When Deep Learning Is Appropriate
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

The default order on tabular data: gradient boosting → regularized linear/GLM → and only then, with evidence, a net. Teams lose weeks tuning an MLP to match day-one boosting accuracy.
Small-data DL fails quietly: a 64-unit MLP on 200 rows returns a confident 0.71 accuracy; its seed-variance is ±0.05 — check seed spread before comparing models at all (4.4).
Transfer changes the calculus but not the protocol: fine-tuning on 500 images is legitimate; validating it still needs held-out data untouched by model selection.
Interpretability is a requirement, not a preference: regulated domains (clinical, credit) demand auditable decision logic — post-hoc saliency maps do not satisfy the same bar as a coefficient or a split path (11.5’s hazard ratios, 7.1’s paths).
Serving costs are real costs: a boosted-tree model is kilobytes and microseconds; the transformer is gigabytes and GPU-seconds — match the deployment budget (6.6’s lesson about local models, at industrial scale).
The course-wide map: linear/GLM when signal is linear-ish or p ≫ n (5.x); splines/GAM for smooth univariate structure (6.7); trees/boosting for tabular interactions; SVMs for small-n kernel structure (8.4); PCA/clustering to understand (9.2); DL for perceptual/sequential/language at scale with transfer.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated plan (not code — worse) proposes the modeling strategy for a new project. Refactor it.

“For our 400-row electronic health records dataset (45 mixed features), I recommend a 6-layer feedforward network with 512 hidden units, batch normalization, dropout 0.3, and heavy data augmentation via feature noise. We’ll tune with a random search over 200 configurations and report the best CV accuracy. A transformer encoder over feature tokens will then capture feature interactions.”



What’s wrong, and the refactor


Capacity vs n inverted: 512-wide layers on 400 rows is memorization hardware; augmentation-by-noise invents patients who don’t exist and can smear real signal.
Tuning as evidence: 200 random configurations selected on CV accuracy is multiple testing on the same small data — the winner’s score is optimistic by construction (12.2); the honest budget is a handful of candidates, nested CV.
Transformer over feature tokens: attention over exchangeable features imposes no useful structure (features aren’t a sequence); it’s architecture cosplay. And “report best CV accuracy” conflates selection with evaluation.

Refactor: gradient boosting as primary model (interactions, mixed types, 400 rows is its home turf); regularized logistic regression as interpretable co-primary for the regulatory readers; a small tuned MLP only if boosting demonstrably stalls and a validation harness (nested CV, seed-replicated) justifies it. Report the protocol, not the best draw.

title: 10.10 When Deep Learning Is Appropriate
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. The “no free lunch” made operational: design and run an experiment where each of three model classes wins decisively on data generated to favor it — (a) linear truth with 5,000 features and 300 samples (sparse signal), (b) axis-aligned interaction truth at n = 5,000, (c) smooth rotational boundary at n = 5,000. Fit L1-penalized logistic (5.3’s classification cousin), HistGradientBoosting, and MLP to each dataset; produce the 3×3 accuracy table. Derive the practical rule the table implies (in terms of truth geometry and p/n regime), and state the one property no model in the table has.


Hint

Match generative process to inductive bias: sparsity ↔︎ L1; boxes ↔︎ splits; smooth rotations ↔︎ smooth activations. The missing property is omniscience about which regime you’re in — hence validation.



Solution







Expected table: lasso wins (a) by a landslide — L1’s sparsity matches the truth’s; trees win (b) — boxes are native; MLP wins (c) — smooth rotations are native. Rule: infer the truth’s geometry (or try one cheap probe per geometry) and match the bias; never run one model across unknown regimes and extrapolate. The missing property: knowing beforehand which regime you’re in — that’s what honest validation budgets exist to discover.

Q2. Write the transfer-learning decision tree for a new perceptual dataset (say, 2,000 labeled microscopy images, 6 classes): at each node, name the evidence that decides it — (1) does a pretrained backbone for this domain exist? (2) how far is your data from its pretraining distribution? (3) how many labels do you have? (4) latency/privacy constraints? — and end with the three concrete strategies (linear probe, partial fine-tune, full fine-tune) mapped to the branches. Then state the validation design that must accompany each branch (what can leak, and where).


Hint

The tree’s trunk: pretrained backbone exists → almost always start there. Branches differ in how much you unfreeze, and leakage risks live in the split (patient-level!) and in any test-time augmentation choices.



Solution

Decision tree: 1. Pretrained backbone for the domain exists (ImageNet-near for histology: yes) → start frozen: linear probe (train only a logistic head on backbone features). Evidence to gather: probe accuracy vs a classical baseline on engineered features. If probe ≈ ceiling → done; cheapest, least leaky. 2. Distribution gap large (staining, magnification, modality shift) or probe stalls → partial fine-tune: unfreeze the last block(s), small lr, keep early layers frozen (they carry generic edges/textures — 10.6’s transfer argument). Evidence: validation loss curve per unfrozen depth. 3. Many labels (≥ tens of thousands) or domain very far (e.g., astronomy from ImageNet) → full fine-tune with low lr everywhere + augmentation matching deployment. 4. Privacy/latency forbid cloud backbones → distill the backbone to a small net, or self-supervised pretrain on unlabeled local images (labels not needed for pretraining) then steps 1–3 locally.
Validation design: patient/subject-level splits (images from one sample never straddle train/test — the leak nobody sees in pixels); the frozen backbone’s pretraining data must not contain your test images (check provenance for public backbones on public benchmarks); every hyperparameter (unfrozen depth, lr, augmentation) chosen on validation folds, test touched once. The three strategies differ in how much prior you keep; the protocol differs not at all: representation learning moves the accuracy ceiling, honest validation decides whether you reached it.

title: 10.10 When Deep Learning Is Appropriate
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (course-wide model selection audit). Take three datasets you know from earlier parts — the 5.6 high-dimensional simulation, the 9.4 clustering data, and this page’s bake-off — and write for each a one-paragraph model defense: which model you’d ship, which two challengers you’d run, and what validation result would change your mind. The discipline being trained: a defense that cites n, geometry, interpretability, and validation budget — not familiarity.
C2 (× 11.1 survival × 12.4 FDR). A collaborator proposes “let’s try 15 model families on the omics dataset and report the best.” Write the critique in the language of this course: selection-as-inference (12.x — 15 chances to beat 0.05), the nested-CV repair, and the pre-registration mindset (decide the challenger set before seeing results). What is the deep-learning-specific temptation here (architecture search) and its honest version (limited search space, outer-loop evaluation)?

title: 10.10 When Deep Learning Is Appropriate
text:
7. Summary

Default order on tabular data: boosting → regularized linear/GLM → nets, in that order, with evidence at each promotion.
Deep learning’s home turf: perceptual/sequential/language structure + enough n or a transferable pretrained representation.
Small data + big nets fails quietly — check seed variance and validate before believing any leaderboard.
Interpretability, latency, and audit requirements are first-class model-selection criteria, not afterthoughts.
Every preprocessing step must live inside the CV fold; a leaky scaler inflates results by points, silently.
Match model class to truth geometry: sparsity→L1, boxes→trees, smooth→nets, structure→DL+transfer.
Judgment is the last skill — and the course continues with data that forces it: Part 11, survival analysis and censored data.

title: 10.3 Multilayer Neural Networks
text: A hidden layer turns fixed features into learned features: \(\hat y = W_2\,g(W_1 x + b_1) + b_2\). Where 6.3 hand-designed bases (polynomials, splines) and 9.2 extracted unsupervised directions, the MLP tunes its basis to the supervised task. This page trains one for real — in the browser — via scikit-learn’s live MLPClassifier.

title: 10.3 Multilayer Neural Networks
text:
1. Basic Concept
For input \(x \in \mathbb{R}^d\), a one-hidden-layer network is
\[h = g(W_1 x + b_1) \in \mathbb{R}^{h_1}, \qquad \hat y = W_2 h + b_2\]

Each hidden unit is a neuron (10.2); the layer applies \(h_1\) of them in parallel — a matrix multiply plus a scalar nonlinearity.
\(\hat y\) is linear in \(h\): the network is a linear model on learned features. All nonlinearity lives in \(g\) — remove it and \(W_2 W_1\) collapses into a single linear map (Exercise: verify).
Universal approximation: one sufficiently wide hidden layer with a sigmoid/tanh/ReLU nonlinearity can approximate any continuous function on a compact set arbitrarily well. It says nothing about width needed, optimization, or generalization — those are the real constraints.

Worked example — the same two-moons that defeated the single neuron, with an MLP trained live (scikit-learn, runs in your browser):






The MLP bends the boundary along the moons because its hidden units learn moon-shaped features. Test this honestly (4.2): hold data out before believing.

title: 10.3 Multilayer Neural Networks
text:
2. Concept Questions

Delete the activation: \(h = W_1 x + b_1\), \(\hat y = W_2 h + b_2\). Exactly what function class can the resulting network express, and why does depth add nothing?
Universal approximation says one wide layer suffices. Name the two practical currencies it ignores, and which one 7.4 random forests also ignores.
The output layer above is linear-in-\(h\) and fed to logistic loss. Where do softmax and sigmoids live in a K-class net, and why is the hidden nonlinearity not optional while the output squashing is (for regression)?
A network has 2 → 100 → 100 → 1 units. Count parameters exactly (weights + biases).
MLPClassifier standardizes nothing for you. What breaks if you feed raw features with scales 1 and 10⁴ — and which earlier page’s advice applies verbatim?



Answers


\(\hat y = W_2(W_1 x + b_1) + b_2 = (W_2 W_1)x + (W_2 b_1 + b_2)\) — a single affine map. Any stack of linear layers factors into one linear layer; representation learning is the nonlinearity.
Data (how many samples to pin down the approximation) and optimization (whether SGD can find it) — generalization’s sample complexity. Random forests ignore both too: consistency results assume the forest grows well past the data’s support. The MAP is universal approximation is an existence theorem: “a good net exists” ≠ “SGD finds it from n samples.”
K-class: output layer = K logits (linear in \(h\)), softmax applied in the loss (CE), sigmoids nowhere. Regression: identity output — squashing would bound the response range artificially. Hidden nonlinearities are the model’s expressive core; output activations are interface choices.
\(2{\cdot}100 + 100 + 100{\cdot}100 + 100 + 100{\cdot}1 + 1 = 200 + 100 + 10{,}000 + 100 + 100 + 1 = 10{,}501\).
Ill-conditioned optimization (GD crawls along flat/steep directions) and saturation of tanh/sigmoid units; identical to 3.3/10.2’s advice — standardize inside a pipeline fitted on training folds only (4.3).

title: 10.3 Multilayer Neural Networks
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Write a count_params(sizes) function for an arbitrary architecture [d, h1, ..., hk, out] and verify it against scikit-learn: build MLPClassifier(hidden_layer_sizes=(16, 16)), sum sum(c.size for c in clf.coefs_) + sum(b.size for b in clf.intercepts_), and match your formula. Which layer dominates as widths grow?


Solution

\[P = \sum_{\ell=1}^{k+1} (s_{\ell-1} \cdot s_\ell + s_\ell)\]
(For binary classification scikit-learn uses a single sigmoid output unit — set the last size to 1 to match it; K-class nets have K output logits.)






The \(s_{\ell} \cdot s_{\ell+1}\) weight blocks dominate quadratically in width — doubling width quadruples cost. Depth adds parameters linearly in the layer sizes but compounds expressiveness (Q1); width is where the money goes.

Exercise 2. Random features vs learned features: fit (a) ridge on the raw 2 features, (b) ridge on 100 fixed random tanh features \(h = \tanh(XW_1 + b_1)\), and (c) scikit-learn’s trained MLP, on two-moons with n = 100. Rank the three test accuracies over 20 repetitions. What does (b) vs (c) isolate?


Solution







Random nonlinear features already beat raw ridge (nonlinearity for free — the kernel/random-features view of 6.3); training the features beats random ones — that gap is exactly what “representation learning” buys. It also costs optimization and variance at small n: watch the MLP’s higher spread.

Exercise 3. Dying ReLUs, measured: build a 2 → 64 → 64 → 2 scikit-learn net (relu) on moons, then for hidden layers’ inputs compute the fraction of (point × unit) pre-activations that are negative (dead on that point). Compare against activation="tanh". Now flip to He-style thinking: why does ReLU tolerate (and even prefer) ~half the units being “off” per point, and when does “half off” become “all dead”?


Solution







ReLU switching off ~half its units per point is sparsity, not death — the active set still carries gradients, and different points use different units (that’s the piecewise-linear magic). Death is population-level: a unit whose pre-activation is negative for every training point gets exactly-zero gradient forever. Big negative biases, too-large learning rates that knock units off the data manifold, or unscaled inputs drive units to that absorbing state; once dead, only reinit or lucky regularization revives them.

title: 10.3 Multilayer Neural Networks
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Zero init poisons hidden layers: all units in a layer receive identical gradients and stay identical forever. Use random init scaled by fan-in: Xavier for tanh/sigmoid (\(\text{Var} \propto 1/\text{fan}_{in}\)), He for ReLU (double it — half the units output zero).
More layers ≠ better: depth compounds optimization difficulty and variance on small data; scikit-learn’s MLP with two modest hidden layers beats a naive 10-layer stack on tabular problems. (The remedy at scale is normalization + residuals — 10.9’ block.)
Softmax belongs in the loss: applying it to logits and using CrossEntropyLoss (which applies it again) is a classic silent bug — the model trains but never confident, gradients squashed by double squashing.
Undertraining is silent: MLPClassifier stops at max_iter (default 200) with only a warning; check clf.n_iter_ against max_iter — “I asked for 2000, it stopped at 200” is the most common “neural nets don’t work here” misdiagnosis.
The MLP interpolates noise at zero training error: train accuracy 1.0 on noisy moons says nothing — the 4.2 split is not optional decoration.
Input scaling inside CV: StandardScaler fitted on the full dataset leaks (mildly) — fit it per training fold (4.3).


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated MLP pipeline has three bugs. Diagnose, then read the fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Scaling fitted on everything: the standardization saw test rows (fit means/SDs on train folds only, inside a Pipeline).
max_iter=20: the net barely moved — n_iter_ confirms 20; the model is untrained noise with a nice interface. Undertraining is the most common “neural nets don’t work here” misdiagnosis.
Evaluate on training data: accuracy on the fit set is 4.1’s cardinal sin — an MLP can memorize 300 noisy points completely.

title: 10.3 Multilayer Neural Networks
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Width vs depth, an experiment: on two-moons (n = 400, 20% test), compare test accuracy for architectures with matched parameter budgets — one wide layer (e.g., 100 units ≈ 402 params) vs two narrower (30, 30 ≈ 1,022) vs three (20, 20, 20 ≈ 921) — at the same training-set size. Then repeat at n = 4000. Compose the results into a claim about when depth pays, and connect to the bias–variance framing of 4.4.


Hint

Fix the parameter count first, then let data size arbitrate: depth wins where compositional structure exists and n is sufficient; at small n the extra layers are variance.



Solution







Typical outcome: at n = 400 the architectures are within noise of each other (the problem is two-dimensional — its structure is cheap either way; variance dominates); at n = 4000 the deeper stacks edge ahead on the curved boundary. Honest claim: depth pays when the target function is compositional and n supports the extra parameters — on 2-D toy data the effect is small, which is itself the lesson: universal approximation is about existence, and data decides whether architecture matters. On truly compositional problems (images: 10.6; sequences: 10.7), depth with the right structure (weight sharing) is not optional.

Q2. PCA as a linear autoencoder: fit PCA(n_components=1) on standardized moons and fit an autoencoder-shaped net — MLPRegressor with hidden sizes (2, 1, 2), identity output, MSE on X→X. Project both onto their 1-D representations and reconstruct. Show the two reconstructions are related by an invertible linear map (up to optimization error) — i.e., a linear hidden activation makes the MLP’s bottleneck exactly PCA’s subspace. What does this imply about what nonlinear activations add to compression?


Hint

Both methods find the top-variance 1-D subspace when the encoder is linear; compare reconstructions after optimal rotation/scaling.



Solution







With identity activations, the (2→1→2) net’s encoder is \(v^\top x\) for some vector \(v\) and MSE reconstruction is minimized exactly when \(v\) spans the first principal direction — linear autoencoder ≡ PCA (Bourlard–Kamp / Baldi–Hornik). Nonlinear activations buy curved manifolds: the same architecture with tanh can follow the moon’s arc, which no linear projection contains. That’s the whole value proposition of deep representation learning: PCA’s subspace → nonlinear manifold, with autoencoders and t-SNE/UMAP as the unsupervised cousins (the T3 extension of Part 9).

title: 10.3 Multilayer Neural Networks
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (× 7.5 gradient boosting × 4.3 CV). Both MLPs and boosted trees fit residuals of an additive model — one in function space via hidden features, one in tree space via stagewise fitting. On moons and on a 10-feature mixed-scale tabular simulation, run MLPClassifier vs HistGradientBoostingClassifier under a shared CV protocol with tuned capacity (width/depth vs iterations/depth). Which model wins where, and does the ranking survive when you add 5 pure-noise features? (This previews 10.10’s decision rule.)
C2 (× 9.2 PCA × 5.2 ridge). Preprocessing an MLP’s inputs: on a dataset with strongly correlated features (build one: \(x_2 = x_1 + \text{noise}\), etc.), compare (a) raw input, (b) PCA-whitened input, (c) ridge-penalized MLP, on test accuracy and on the conditioning of the first-layer gradient (approximate: fit each and compare n_iter_ to convergence at fixed lr). Connect: whitening decorrelates gradients exactly as ridge tames variance — and both are partial answers to the same ill-conditioning.

title: 10.3 Multilayer Neural Networks
text:
7. Summary

MLP = linear model on learned nonlinear features; remove the activation and depth collapses to one affine map.
Hidden layers are trainable basis functions — the supervised generalization of 6.3 and the nonlinear descendant of 9.2.
Universal approximation is an existence theorem; data and optimization decide what’s practical.
Parameter count is quadratic in width; init scaling (Xavier/He) and input standardization are optimization hygiene, not superstition.
scikit-learn’s MLP is enough to feel all of this live; the same net in PyTorch exposes the training loop explicitly.
The training loop is next page’s machinery: 10.4 gradient descent & backpropagation.

title: 10.5 Regularization for Neural Networks
text: An MLP with enough units can memorize any labelling — train accuracy 1.0 means nothing (4.1). Neural-network regularization is classical statistics wearing new clothes: weight decay is ridge (5.2), early stopping is the validation curve, data augmentation is a prior on transformations, dropout is ensemble averaging in disguise. This page measures each one on a net that genuinely overfits — the NumPy network of 10.4, retrained live.

title: 10.5 Regularization for Neural Networks
text:
1. Basic Concept



tool
mechanism
classical twin




L2 / weight decay
penalize \(\lambda\|\theta\|^2\) in the loss; gradients shrink weights multiplicatively
ridge 5.2


Dropout
randomly zero units with prob \(p\) per step (rescaling by \(1/(1-p)\)); the net can’t co-adapt
bagging / model averaging 7.3


Early stopping
halt when validation loss stops improving
validation curves 4.2


Data augmentation
train on label-preserving transforms
a prior over invariances


Batch/Layer norm
normalize activations; adds noise via batch statistics + smooths the loss surface
standardization 0.3, internalized



Worked example — overfitting, then repairing. A wide NumPy MLP (manual backprop, 10.4 machinery) trained on 40 noisy moon points memorizes them; L2 and early stopping recover generalization:






All three rows share the same striking fact: with only 40 training points, validation CE bottoms at initialization — every step of unregularized training overfits. L2 is what makes training safe: it bends the final-step validation CE from 3.17 (no L2) down to 0.75 (λ = 1e-2) while training the full 3000 steps. Early stopping and weight decay are two dials on the same train–validation gap; watch the validation curve, not the training curve.

title: 10.5 Regularization for Neural Networks
text:
2. Concept Questions

Weight-decay gradient = gradient + \(2\lambda w\). Why does this shrink large weights proportionally more than small ones, and what geometric belief does that encode?
Dropout with \(p = 0.5\) at train time: why must activations be rescaled, and what does the network become at test time when rescaling is folded in (“inverted dropout”)?
Early stopping picks one point on a 1-D path traced by training. Why is it “L2’s cheap cousin” — and when do the two not substitute for each other?
Why does data augmentation regularize without touching the loss function — what exactly is being added to the training distribution?
model.eval() — which two layer types change behavior, and what goes wrong metric-wise if you forget it?



Answers


Update \(w \mathrel{-}= \eta(\nabla_w L + 2\lambda w)\): per step every weight loses a \(2\eta\lambda\) fraction — big weights shrink by more absolute amount and the same relative amount; small ones toward-but-never-exactly zero (unlike Lasso 5.3). Encodes: solutions live near the origin / functions with small weights are smoother (bounded derivatives).
Zeroing half the units halves a layer’s expected output; without rescaling the next layer’s inputs shrink and drift. Inverted dropout divides kept activations by \((1-p)\) during training, so test time needs no change — the expected activation matches. The un-inverted version (original paper) rescales at test time — a deployment foot-gun.
Both restrict the effective model capacity along a 1-D index (steps ↔︎ \(\lambda\)): the early-stopped net approximates the L2 solution of a matched \(\lambda\) for simple quadratic losses. They diverge when the loss surface is non-convex/path-dependent: stopping picks one point of one trajectory (depends on lr, batch order), L2 changes the objective itself; combined they are not redundant in practice.
Augmentation enlarges the empirical distribution by the invariance group (rotations/flip/noise): the model is optimized over more of input space for the same labels — equivalent to a prior that those transformations don’t change class. It can hurt if the transform isn’t label-preserving (horizontal flip on ‘b’ vs ‘d’).
Dropout (switches from random zeroing to identity) and batchnorm (running statistics instead of batch statistics). Forgetting eval() makes validation metrics noisy (dropout resampled per batch) and shifted (batch stats of the val set) — classic “validation loss jitter” bug.

title: 10.5 Regularization for Neural Networks
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. λ-sweep with an honest protocol: using the Section-1 training function, sweep λ ∈ {0, 1e-4, 1e-3, 1e-2, 1e-1} on 200 noisy moons (75/25 split); plot validation loss vs λ and report test accuracy of the λ chosen by validation. Then refit at the best λ on train+validation and report that test accuracy — why is the second number the more honest estimate, and what is this protocol called (4.6)?


Solution







Selecting λ on validation then reporting that same split’s accuracy double-dips; the refit-on-train+val → test protocol is the standard hyperparameter loop (CV in 4.3 averages it further). Expect the sweep to favor an intermediate λ with the extremes (0: overfit; 1e-1: underfit) losing — the U-curve of 4.4 reappearing in neural clothing.

Exercise 2. Dropout by hand: implement inverted dropout inside the Section-1 network’s hidden layer (mask after tanh, divide kept units by \(1-p\)), train at p ∈ {0, 0.2, 0.5} on the 40-point overfit set, and compare validation loss. Then verify the theoretical claim E[test output] ≈ train-time expected output: for a fixed input, average 2000 dropped forward passes and compare with the no-drop pass through the same weights.


Solution







Moderate dropout (p = 0.2) tames the 40-point overfit; p = 0.5 on 30 training points can underfit (few effective units). The Monte-Carlo mean of dropped passes matches the no-drop pass up to sampling error — that equality is inverted dropout’s design: train-time randomness, test-time determinism, matched expectations.

Exercise 3. scikit-learn’s knobs, live: on 200-point noisy moons compare MLPClassifier(alpha ∈ {1e-5, 1e-2, 1}) (that’s L2) and early_stopping=True vs default, under a fixed 75/25 split. Which knob buys more generalization here, and what does best_validation_score_ report when early_stopping=True?


Solution







Both knobs matter; their relative value is dataset-dependent — tiny noisy data rewards early stopping strongly, larger cleaner data rewards α tuning. early_stopping=True makes sklearn carve an internal validation split (see validation_fraction) and reports best_validation_score_ at the stopping iteration — i.e., the page’s Section-1 plot, automated. Either way: the number to quote is on held-out data, never on the training set.

title: 10.5 Regularization for Neural Networks
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Weight decay ≠ L2 under adaptive optimizers: with plain SGD, penalty-λ and update-time decay are algebraically identical; under Adam, adding λ to the loss gets preconditioned per-coordinate, while decoupled weight decay (AdamW) shrinks weights directly — Adam + L2-in-loss is a subtly different, worse-behaved regularizer. When reading torch code, weight_decay= in the optimizer is AdamW-style only if you use AdamW.
Dropout placement: on activations between layers, not on inputs (usually) and not after the final logits; combined with batchnorm it distorts the running statistics — modern practice prefers one or the other per block.
Early stopping needs an honest, untouched validation stream: if the val set leaked into training (scaler fitted on it, augmentation derived from it), the stopping point is biased optimistic.
Augmentation must preserve labels and match deployment: heavy random crops on small medical images can erase the lesion; simulate the transform before shipping it.
λ and lr interact: weight decay’s per-step fraction is \(2\eta\lambda\) — retune λ after changing lr; sweeps that vary both simultaneously without a grid conflate them.
The best regularizer is often a smaller model: on 40 points, halving the width beats any λ. Capacity is a hyperparameter (10.10).


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI training loop has three regularization bugs. Diagnose before opening the fix.
import torch
model = Net(dropout_p=0.5)
opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3, weight_decay=1e-2)
for X_batch, y_batch in train_loader:
    model.train()
    loss = ce(model(X_batch), y_batch)
    opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()

model.train()                                   # BUG 1
with torch.no_grad():
    preds = [model(X_val) for _ in range(5)]    # BUG 2
val_loss = ce(torch.stack(preds).mean(0), y_val)
best = None
if val_loss < best_loss:                        # BUG 3
    best_loss = val_loss
    torch.save(model.state_dict(), "best.pt")


What’s wrong, and the fix


model.train() at validation time: dropout keeps zeroing units — validation loss is noisy and biased; must call model.eval() (and the batchnorm running stats freeze too).
Averaging dropout passes at eval: an MC-dropout technique — fine for uncertainty estimation, wrong for a plain validation metric; with eval() one deterministic pass is the number.
best_loss never initialized (best = None but comparison uses best_loss): NameError on first epoch — and if initialized to 0.0 instead of inf, nothing ever saves. Initialize best_loss = float("inf") and save state_dict() copies, not files you may overwrite mid-training.

model.eval()
with torch.no_grad():
    val_loss = ce(model(X_val), y_val)
best_loss = float("inf")                        # before the loop
if val_loss < best_loss:
    best_loss = val_loss
    best_state = {k: v.clone() for k, v in model.state_dict().items()}

title: 10.5 Regularization for Neural Networks
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Derive dropout’s ensemble interpretation for a linear network: with input dropout at rate p and a single layer \(\hat y = w^\top \tilde x\), show that test-time scaling by \((1-p)\) makes the expected prediction equal an average over \(2^d\) sub-networks, and that the training-time gradient is an unbiased estimate of that ensemble’s gradient. Where does the exact equivalence break for deep nonlinear nets — and what replaces it (two words: sampling; averaging)?


Hint

Linearity lets you swap expectation and matmul; write E[˜x ˜xᵀ] for the dropped input and compare with (1−p)xxᵀ.



Solution

For \(\tilde x = m \odot x\), \(m_i \sim \text{Bern}(1-p)\): \(E[\hat y] = w^\top E[\tilde x] = (1-p)\,w^\top x\) — hence test-time multiply by \((1-p)\) (or train-time \(1/(1-p)\), inverted). The training objective \(E_m[(y - w^\top(m \odot x))^2]\) is exactly the average squared error over all \(2^d\) masked sub-models — dropout = bagging over unit subsets with shared weights. Gradients: \(\nabla_w = E_m[2(w^\top \tilde x - y)\tilde x]\), and each minibatch sample of m is an unbiased Monte-Carlo draw of it. For deep nets the product of nonlinearities makes “expectation of the function” ≠ “function of the expectation”: exact equivalence dies at the first nonlinearity; what remains is (i) training samples random sub-networks (regularizing co-adaptation) and (ii) at test time the deterministic scaled pass approximates the ensemble average — the gap between approximation and truth is why MC-dropout at eval (many stochastic passes, averaged) can outperform the standard pass for uncertainty, at 5–100× the compute.

Q2. Double descent, demonstrated in miniature: on 150 noisy moon points, sweep a 1-hidden-layer NumPy net’s width over {4, 16, 64, 256, 1024} with no L2 and early stopping disabled, plotting both test error and train error vs width (log x). Identify the interpolation threshold’s neighborhood (train error → 0), and state the two regimes around it. Then re-run the largest width with λ = 1e-2: where does the minimum of test error move, and what does that say about “bigger models overfit more”?


Hint

Test error peaks somewhere near where train error first hits 0 (the classical U-curve’s cliff), then can decline again into the overparameterized regime.



Solution







Reading: as width grows, train CE → 0 (interpolation); around the threshold, test error peaks (variance max: the model is just rich enough to fit noise exactly); beyond it, test error declines again — the “modern” overparameterized regime where implicit regularization of GD prefers smooth interpolators (10.4). Explicit L2 at width 1024 moves the minimum earlier and lower — the two mechanisms compose. The classical “bigger = overfit” curve is the left half of the picture only; the honest statement is regularize something (width, λ, stopping, or nothing-but-SGD-noise) and validate — never assume which regime you’re in.

title: 10.5 Regularization for Neural Networks
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (× 4.3 cross-validation × 7.4 random forests). Dropout and random forests both average randomized sub-models. Design an experiment on 200 noisy moons: (a) an MLP with dropout swept over {0, .1, .3, .5}, (b) a random forest with max_features swept over {0.2, 0.5, 1.0}, under identical 5-fold CV. For each, plot CV accuracy vs its randomness knob and locate the optimum. Then answer: why does the forest benefit from more randomness (up to a point) while the net’s benefit peaks and decays — connect to base-learner strength (deep, jointly trained features vs shallow CARTs).
C2 (× 5.2 ridge × 9.2 PCA × 10.4). Three regularizations, one network, one budget: on the 40-point overfit set, find the best (width, λ, early-stop step) via a small grid, and compare against (i) PCA to 5 features → ridge (the classical pipeline), and (ii) the full net with no regularization. Report test accuracies and variance across 10 seeds. Which regularizer buys the most stability (lowest seed-variance), and what does that suggest about where neural nets actually fail — variance or bias?

title: 10.5 Regularization for Neural Networks
text:
7. Summary

Overfitting is the default outcome of training: the validation curve, not train loss, is the instrument.
Weight decay = ridge by gradient (per-step shrink \(2\eta\lambda w\)); under Adam prefer decoupled AdamW.
Dropout = training-time ensemble sampling with test-time expectation matching (inverted scaling); model.eval() is not optional.
Early stopping = 1-D capacity control on the training path; needs an honest validation stream.
Augmentation injects invariances as data; transforms must be label-preserving and deployment-realistic.
Around the interpolation threshold, more width can help — “bigger overfits more” is half-true, and regularization composes across all levers.
Constraint shapes computation: next page, kernels that slide — 10.6 convolutional neural networks.

title: 10.7 Recurrent Neural Networks
text: Sequences break fixed-size models: sentences, sensor traces, and gene windows have variable length, and order carries meaning (the lag features of 2.8 hard-code one horizon). A recurrent network processes a sequence with the same weights at every step, carrying a hidden state forward: \(h_t = \tanh(W_h h_{t-1} + W_x x_t + b)\). This page builds the recurrence, unrolls it, and watches its gradients vanish — all live in NumPy.

title: 10.7 Recurrent Neural Networks
text:
1. Basic Concept
\[h_t = g(W_h h_{t-1} + W_x x_t + b), \qquad \hat y_t = W_y h_t + c\]

\(h_t\) is a fixed-size summary of everything seen so far — the network’s memory. Same \(W_h, W_x, W_y\) at every \(t\): parameter count is independent of sequence length (weight sharing through time — the sequence cousin of 10.6’s spatial sharing).
Unrolling: for a length-T sequence, the recurrence is a T-layer deep network with tied weights. Training = backpropagation through time (BPTT): unroll, backprop as usual (10.4), sum parameter gradients over t.
The catch is visible in the chain rule: \(\partial h_T / \partial h_t\) is a product of T−t Jacobians (\(D_h = \mathrm{diag}(1 - h^2) W_h\) per step) — products of norms < 1 vanish exponentially (long-range dependencies unlearnable), > 1 explode (NaN).

Worked example — a vanilla RNN’s hidden state as a running summary, live:






Each hidden unit is a smoothed, delayed response to the input’s history — the raw material a trained output layer would read predictions from.

title: 10.7 Recurrent Neural Networks
text:
2. Concept Questions

Weight sharing through time vs through space (10.6): what does each buy, and why does variable-length handling come free only in the recurrent case?
\(\partial h_T/\partial h_t = \prod_{s=t+1}^{T} D_h(s) W_h\). Why can’t the diagonal tanh factors rescue you when \(\|W_h\| \approx 1\), even though tanh’ ≤ 1 only mildly shrinks?
An RNN trained on sentences of length 5–15 fails to use information from position 1 when predicting position 40. Name the mathematical diagnosis, and the three standard engineering responses.
Why must the hidden state be reset between independent sequences in a batch, and what bug does a forgotten reset produce that looks like “the model sometimes works”?
Truncated BPTT (backprop through only the last k steps) trades what for what, and why is it usually a good trade for long streams?



Answers


Spatial sharing buys translation equivariance over a grid; temporal sharing buys composition over time — the same “detector of the recent past” applies at every t. Variable length: a conv net’s output size grows with input width (a grid), while an RNN’s hidden state is a fixed point you can read at any t — one model, any length.
The tanh’ factors bound the shrink at 1 but typically sit near 0.2–0.5 (tanh output often ≈ 0.5–0.9 away from saturation ⇒ slope 0.2–0.7); multiplied by \(\|W_h\| \approx 1\), the per-step factor is < 1 for most steps — over 30+ steps even 0.8 per step is \(0.8^{30} \approx 10^{-3}\). Rescue requires the product of per-step factors ≈ 1 consistently — measure-zero lucky alignment (this motivates 10.8’s additive cell).
Vanishing gradient through time. Responses: (i) gate the recurrence (LSTM/GRU, 10.8); (ii) gradient clipping for the exploding side; (iii) architectural replacement — attention (10.9) gives a direct O(1) path between any two positions.
\(h_0\) of the next sequence otherwise starts from the last state of an unrelated one — the first predictions are contaminated by a “memory” of different data. Symptom: batch-dependent, order-dependent accuracy that shuffles when you reorder the dataloader.
It truncates the dependency graph at k steps: gradients from events older than k never flow. Trades long-range credit assignment for O(k) memory and compute per step, plus a shorter, better-conditioned product in the chain rule — for streams where most signal is local, k ≈ 20–200 loses little.

title: 10.7 Recurrent Neural Networks
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Train a vanilla RNN (NumPy, full BPTT) to predict the next value of a noisy sine from the previous 20 steps: 1 input → 8 hidden (tanh) → 1 output, MSE. Keep the implementation explicit — forward storing all \(h_t\), backward accumulating \(\partial L/\partial W_h\) over t — and gradient-check one weight entry against finite differences. Plot loss and prediction-vs-truth.


Solution







The backward loop is Exercise-1 of 10.4 unrolled in time: dh is the upstream gradient, dtanh applies the local slope, and dWh += hs[t-1].T @ dtanh accumulates the same matrix’s gradient across t — weight sharing means summing, exactly as convolutions sum over spatial positions. (The trained MSE ≈ 0.03 lags the lag-window baselines of Exercise 3 — on a fixed-horizon sine, the simple model is hard to beat.)

Exercise 2. The vanishing gradient, quantified end-to-end: using Exercise 1’s (untrained) network, feed a unit impulse at t = 0 and measure \(\|\partial h_T / \partial h_0\|\) for T ∈ {5, 10, 20, 40} with \(W_h\) scaled to spectral radius ∈ {0.5, 0.9, 0.99, 1.05}. Plot log-magnitude vs T for each radius. Then compute the slope of each line and relate it to the spectral radius — the per-step gradient factor. What radius keeps a 100-step gradient alive above \(10^{-2}\)?


Solution







Log-log lines with slope ≈ log(per-step factor): radius 0.5 → slope ≈ −1.4 (dead by T = 20); 0.9 → slope ≈ −0.2; 0.99 → ≈ flat-to-exploding variance; 1.05 → exponential growth. To keep \(\|J\| > 10^{-2}\) at T = 100 you need per-step > 0.955, i.e., ρ within ~5% of 1 and tanh staying near-linear — a knife’s edge. This is the theorem-level reason vanilla RNNs learn only local structure and 10.8 exists.

Exercise 3. Recurrence vs lag-windowing: on the sine task of Exercise 1, compare the RNN against an ordinary linear regression and a small MLP on fixed lag features (the last K = 20 values, 2.8-style). Same data, same split. Which wins, by how much, and what changes if the series is length-variable (chunks of 10–50 steps)? State the honest scope of “RNNs handle variable length”.


Solution







On fixed-horizon, local tasks, lag features + a shallow model match the RNN — recurrence is not magic, it’s weight-tied feature extraction over a window (2.8 with learned weighting). The RNN’s honest advantage is (i) parameter count independent of K (K = 500 lags = 500× more linear weights, the RNN unchanged), (ii) state that persists across chunk boundaries within a stream, (iii) inputs of genuinely variable length without padding/imputation hacks. If your problem has a fixed, short horizon: window it and use the simpler model — 10.10’s rule.

title: 10.7 Recurrent Neural Networks
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Clip the global norm, not per-coordinate: clip_grad_norm_ rescales the whole gradient vector when its total norm exceeds a threshold (typically 1–5); per-coordinate clipping distorts direction. Without clipping, one exploding step throws the parameters into a bad region it takes epochs to re-enter.
Stateful vs stateless training: reset \(h_0 = 0\) per (shuffled) sample for independent sequences; carry state across consecutive chunks of the same long stream — mixing these two modes is the classic silent contamination bug.
Batch-first vs time-first: PyTorch’s nn.RNN default input is (seq, batch, feature) — batch_first=True changes it; a transposition bug trains “fine” while shuffling unrelated sequences’ timesteps.
Output-at-every-step vs last-step: sequence labelling (POS tags) reads \(\hat y_t\) at each t; sequence classification reads only \(h_T\). Using the wrong head halves your supervision or fabricates per-step targets.
Deep RNNs stack states, not weights: layer 2’s input is layer 1’s \(h_t\) sequence — each layer still shares its weights through time; depth adds abstraction, not memory length (10.8/10.9 address length).
Init matters more than in feedforward nets: \(W_h\) initialized to orthogonal matrices (spectral radius ≈ 1) keeps gradients alive longer; IRNN (identity init) is the ReLU-era equivalent.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated BPTT training loop has three bugs. Diagnose before opening the fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


State carried across independent passes: h_state persists between epochs (and would between unrelated sequences in a batch) — the model appears to “warm up” nondeterministically; reset per sequence.
Fragile gradient plumbing: dh = Wy * 2*(yhat - y) happens to work element-wise here only because the shapes collapse; in the general (h,)@(h,1) case it’s a transpose error waiting — compute err = 2*(yhat - y) then dh = Wy * err with explicit shapes, and gradient-check once (10.4).
No weight is ever updated: dWh/dWx are never accumulated and nothing is subtracted from any parameter — the loop computes gradients into the void, prints them, and the “model” is a fixed random feature extractor forever. It “runs” and prints plausible numbers — the most dangerous failure mode in a hand-rolled trainer.

title: 10.7 Recurrent Neural Networks
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Derive the exact gradient \(\partial L / \partial W_h\) for the vanilla RNN over a length-T sequence with loss read only at the final step, in terms of the per-step Jacobians \(J_t = D_t W_h\). Show it is a sum over “paths” and that each path is a matrix product — then prove the norm bound \(\|\partial h_T/\partial h_t\| \le \prod_s \|J_s\|\) and its LTR (lower-triangular radius) refinement. At what distribution of per-step factors does the bound become loose enough to matter?


Hint

Unroll: \(h_T\) is a composition of T maps; chain rule gives the product; submultiplicativity gives the bound. The bound ignores cancellation between large factors with different directions.



Solution

\(\frac{\partial L}{\partial W_h} = \sum_{t=1}^{T} \frac{\partial L}{\partial h_T} \left(\prod_{s=t+1}^{T} J_s\right) \frac{\partial h_t}{\partial W_h}\), where \(\partial h_t / \partial W_h\) picks the outer product \(D_t \, h_{t-1}^\top\)-like term (\(W_h\) appears only in step t’s map). Each bracket is a product of T−t Jacobians; by submultiplicativity \(\|\prod J_s\| \le \prod \|J_s\|\) — the vanishing/exploding bound. The bound is tight when factors align (stable recurrent dynamics have a dominant direction, so they often are nearly tight); it is loose when factors alternate directions and cancel — numerically, gradients near the “edge of chaos” (\(\rho \approx 1\)) show large log-variance across t and across seeds, so average behavior is better than the worst-case bound but reliability is worse. Design consequence: don’t engineer for the bound’s tightness — engineer the per-step factor itself (10.8’s constant-error carousel or 10.9’s O(1) paths).

Q2. Echo-state property, made empirical: an untrained RNN with \(W_h\) scaled to spectral radius ρ is a reservoir; train only the readout \(W_y\) (ridge on collected hidden states). The task must demand memory: delayed recall — each 100-step window’s target is the value at its start, so the state must hold one number for 100 steps. Sweep ρ ∈ {0.3, 0.6, 0.8, 0.95, 1.1} and report test MSE. Explain the optimum’s location (edge of chaos) and what happens on each side: why does small ρ fail structurally here, and what does the readout forgive?


Hint

Too small ρ: all states collapse to a static map of the recent input (no memory of the window’s start). Too large: chaos — states are informative but unreadable. The ridge readout forgives a lot.



Solution







MSE improves steadily toward ρ ≈ 0.95 and ticks up at 1.1: below the edge of chaos the recurrence is contractive — 100 multiplications by ‖J‖ < 1 erase the window’s start, and no readout can recover what the state discarded (the failure is structural); near ρ = 1 the state is a near-isometric carrier of history, and ridge decodes it; past it, chaos adds variance faster than memory. Reservoir computing is the untrained-weight-limit of the RNN — a useful mental model: recurrent dynamics provide features; the readout does the fitting; training \(W_h\) (BPTT) moves those features toward the task, which is exactly what the vanishing gradient makes hard (10.8 re-engineers the per-step factor instead).

title: 10.7 Recurrent Neural Networks
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (× 10.9 attention × 10.5 gradient clipping). Two cures for the same disease: gradient clipping (treats exploding only) and gated cells (treats vanishing). Construct on the length-40 task a regime where clipping is necessary but not sufficient (large-init \(W_h\): watch the loss spike-then-plateau with clipping alone), and one where gating is necessary (long-range copy task). Then argue — with the two experiments as evidence — why the field moved to attention rather than better clipping schedules.
C2 (× 11.1 why survival data is special × 6.4 regression splines). A clinical time series (vitals every hour, censored follow-up) is proposed for an RNN-based risk model.
