Write the design memo: which components of the RNN pipeline (state reset, truncation length, output head, loss) interact with censoring and irregular sampling, which classical alternative (splines on time since baseline, Cox with time-varying covariates) is the honest baseline, and what evidence would justify the RNN. (Deliberately cross-part: the answer is mostly 11.5, not PyTorch.)

title: 10.7 Recurrent Neural Networks
text:
7. Summary

RNN = same cell applied through time; hidden state is a fixed-size running summary; parameters independent of length.
Training unrolls to a deep net (BPTT); the same weight matrix multiplies the gradient every step.
Products of Jacobians ⇒ vanishing (ρ < 1) or exploding (ρ > 1) gradients; clipping treats only the explosive half.
Reset state between independent sequences; truncation length is an honest, declared approximation.
On fixed short horizons, lag-window + shallow models match RNNs — reach for recurrence when length varies or context is long.
The per-step factor is the disease; gates re-engineer it — 10.8 LSTM and GRU.

title: 10.9 Attention and Transformers
text: Recurrence reads a sequence through a relay: token 0’s information passes through T pairs of hands before reaching the output. Attention removes the relay — every position reads every other position directly, with content-addressed weights computed on the fly. Stacked with positional encodings, residuals, and feedforward blocks, it becomes the transformer: the architecture of modern sequence models (and of Part 13’s LLMs). This page computes attention by hand in NumPy and measures the properties the equations claim.

title: 10.9 Attention and Transformers
text:
1. Basic Concept
Scaled dot-product attention: given queries \(Q\) (what I’m looking for), keys \(K\) (what I contain), values \(V\) (what I’ll hand over):
\[\mathrm{Attn}(Q, K, V) = \mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right) V\]
Each output token is a weighted average of all values, weights = softmaxed similarities between its query and all keys. Self-attention sets \(Q = XW_Q\), \(K = XW_K\), \(V = XW_V\) — the sequence attends to itself. Three properties define the architecture:

O(1) path length between any two positions (vs recurrence’s O(T)) — long-range dependencies are one hop (10.7/10.8’s disease, cured structurally).
Permutation equivariance — attention is a set operation; order enters only through added positional encodings.
Parallelism — no sequential state; all positions compute at once (GPUs breathe).

A transformer block: x = x + Attn(LN(x)); x = x + FFN(LN(x)) — attention mixes across positions, the feedforward processes each position, residuals keep paths short. Multi-head attention runs h of these in parallel subspaces and concatenates.
Worked example — attention weights by hand, live:






Each row is one token’s reading list over the sentence. With random projections the pattern is meaningless — training shapes \(W_Q, W_K\) so that “cat” attends to “sat”. The machinery, however, is exactly this.

title: 10.9 Attention and Transformers
text:
2. Concept Questions

Why divide by \(\sqrt{d_k}\)? Compute (mentally, then in the drills) the scale of \(q \cdot k\) for random vectors as \(d_k\) grows, and what an unnormalized softmax does to the gradient.
Attention is permutation-equivariant: if you shuffle the input tokens, exactly what happens to the outputs? What breaks the symmetry, and why is “add position” better than “shuffle order into the weights”?
The causal mask adds \(-10^9\) to scores above the diagonal before the softmax. What does the mask accomplish after softmax (numerically), and why not multiply attention weights by zero after?
Multi-head splits \(d\) into h subspaces of \(d_k = d/h\). What does a single head cannot represent that heads can, in one sentence about positions vs channels?
Self-attention on a length-T sequence costs O(T²·d). Name the two standard mitigations and the length regime where each is the obvious choice.



Answers


For random \(d_k\)-dim vectors, \(q\cdot k \sim \mathcal{N}(0, d_k)\) — its scale grows as \(\sqrt{d_k}\). Raw scores of ±10 make softmax near-one-hot: gradients through the softmax vanish (only the argmax key receives gradient flow), heads stop learning. Dividing by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) keeps score variance ≈ 1 → diffuse, trainable attention.
Outputs are the same permutation of the permuted computation: token “cat” gets exactly the output it would have gotten elsewhere. Order enters via positional encodings added to embeddings — better than baking order into weights because (i) relative/interpolable positions, (ii) weights stay position-agnostic (transfer across lengths), (iii) equivariance keeps the operator simple and analyzable.
\(e^{-10^9} = 0\) after exponentiation (in float32, underflow to exactly 0): masked positions get identically-zero weight and zero gradient. Zeroing after softmax breaks row normalization (remaining weights sum < 1 — the output silently shrinks toward nothing for early tokens) and still leaks gradient into masked scores.
One head averages over the single similarity pattern it computes; it cannot attend to “position-2-when-channel-says-verb” and “last-position-when-channel-says-subject” simultaneously. Heads = parallel, independent attention patterns over different subspaces — multiple “reading strategies” per layer.
Sparse/local attention (windowed, sliding) for long documents with local structure; linear/low-rank approximations (or hierarchical/chunking) when full global mixing is unnecessary. Plain full attention: fine to a few thousand tokens; the KV cache (Part 13’s inference concern) is the memory wall.

title: 10.9 Attention and Transformers
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Implement attention(Q, K, V, mask=None) in NumPy with the scale, the causal mask, and stable softmax. Verify: (a) rows sum to 1 with and without mask; (b) masked entries are exactly 0; (c) with \(Q = K = V\) fixed to orthonormal-ish rows, the output at position 0 equals \(v_0\) (a token with nothing behind it and a self-aligned query attends only to itself). Then break it two ways — remove the scale, apply the mask after softmax — and report the two symptoms.


Solution







Symptoms: without the scale, entropy collapses (softmax saturates — gradients die, learning stops); masking after softmax leaves rows summing to ~0.3–0.7 — every early token’s output shrinks toward zero, a bug that looks like “the model is faint”. The discipline: scale → mask → softmax → matmul, in that order.

Exercise 2. Positional encodings, seen and used: implement the sinusoidal encoding \(\mathrm{PE}_{(pos, 2i)} = \sin(pos/10000^{2i/d})\), \(\mathrm{PE}_{(pos, 2i+1)} = \cos(\ldots)\) for T = 64, d = 32; plot it. Then demonstrate why: build the attention of Section 1 on shuffled tokens — with and without positional encodings added — and show that only the encoded version’s outputs change under shuffling (equivariance broken on purpose). At what frequency do position 5 and 6 become hardest to distinguish?


Solution







The encoding is a set of sinusoids across wavelengths: near positions differ in high frequencies (rapid oscillation across dimension), far positions in low ones. Without PE, the shuffle changes nothing (max deviation = 0 — pure equivariance); with PE, shuffling inputs permutes positions of codes, and attention outputs differ — order is now represented. High-frequency dimensions distinguish adjacent positions best; the lowest frequencies are nearly identical for 5 vs 6 (their information lives in the fast dims). Learned positional embeddings do the same job with more flexibility and zero interpretability.

Exercise 3. The quadratic wall, plotted: for T ∈ {64, 256, 1024, 4096}, compute the shapes (not the contents) of all intermediate attention matrices and report memory (elements) for scores, weights, and output at d = 64. Then compare against a bidirectional LSTM’s state memory (2·h per step, h = 128). At what T does attention’s score matrix alone exceed the LSTM’s total activation memory, and what does that predict about “long-context” engineering (Part 13’s KV-cache problem, sparsity, sliding windows)?


Solution







The T×T matrices dwarf everything: at T = 4096 the scores alone are 16.7M elements (67 MB in float32) per head per layer — while the LSTM’s sequential activations are 1M. Crossing point sits near T ≈ 2·h = 256 here. This table is the business case for sliding-window/sparse attention (cap T×T), KV-cache quantization (Part 13’s inference stack), and why “context length” is a product spec, not a detail. Note what is not the problem: the O(T·d) output and the weights’ compute — it’s the all-pairs score matrix.

title: 10.9 Attention and Transformers
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Order of operations is law: scale → mask → softmax → @V. Applying the mask after softmax breaks normalization; applying softmax over the wrong axis (normalize columns instead of rows) produces a valid-looking matrix that is semantically “which queries attend to me” — a silent role reversal.
Attention weights ≠ explanations: a high weight means the value was used, not why; multiple heads and layers distribute credit, and gradient-based attribution often disagrees with weight inspection. Treat attention maps as telemetry, not causality.
Residuals and layer norm are structural, not decorative: without the residual, deep stacks lose the gradient path (depth 12+ untrainable); pre-LN (x + Attn(LN(x))) is the modern default for stable deep training.
Causal vs padding masks compose: batched inference with variable lengths needs both (future positions and padded positions); forgetting the padding mask lets real tokens attend to zeros-as-content.
The KV cache (inference): self-attention recomputes keys/values for all past tokens each step unless cached — O(T) memory per sequence is the deployment constraint behind Part 13’s serving discussions.
Label leakage by masking bug: a wrongly-oriented causal mask (attending forward) trains a model that sees the answer — perplexity looks spectacular, the model is useless. Always unit-test the mask on a tiny T.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated self-attention has three bugs. Diagnose before opening the fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


No \(\sqrt{d_k}\) scale: scores have std ≈ \(\sqrt{d} \approx 2.8\) — softmax starts saturated; attention concentrates before training even begins.
Mask by zeroing scores: scores * (1 - mask) sets future scores to 0 — which softmax turns into weight \(e^0\)/Σ, i.e., future tokens still receive attention (a strong uniform baseline, not a block). The mask must subtract −1e9 (before softmax).
Softmax over axis 0: normalizes columns — “how much is this key attended across queries” — so each query’s weights no longer sum to 1 and the output is an unnormalized mishmash. Rows (axis −1).

title: 10.9 Attention and Transformers
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Prove attention’s permutation equivariance formally: for a permutation matrix \(P\), show \(\mathrm{Attn}(PX) = P\,\mathrm{Attn}(X)\) (with shared \(W_Q, W_K, W_V\)), and that adding positional encodings breaks it in a controlled way: $(PX + PE’) $ where \(PE'\) is the encoding of permuted positions — equals \(P\) times the original iff the encoding itself is transported consistently. Conclude: why “attention = set operation + position injection” is the right mental model (and what it predicts about length generalization when encodings are sinusoidal vs learned).


Hint

Permutation matrices are orthogonal: \(P^\top P = I\). Push \(P\) through \(QK^\top\) using \((PX)(PX)^\top = P(X X^\top)P^\top\), then watch the softmax commute with row permutation.



Solution

With \(Q' = PXW_Q\): \(Q'K'^\top = P X W_Q W_K^\top X^\top P^\top = P S P^\top\) (scores permuted both ways). Softmax normalizes rows → \(A' = P A P^\top\). Then \(A' V' = P A P^\top P V = P A V\). QED — outputs permute with inputs. With encodings: attention reads \(PX + PE_{\pi}\); the output equals \(P\,\mathrm{Attn}(X + PE)\) iff \(PE_{\pi} = P\,PE\) — i.e., positions were permuted with tokens. Prediction: sinusoidal encodings (a fixed function of index) transport exactly; learned position embeddings transport only for indices seen in training — hence transformers with learned positions generalize poorly beyond trained lengths, while sinusoidal/relative encodings extrapolate (imperfectly — RoPE-style relative schemes exist precisely because absolute transport still degrades).

Q2. One head, one convex set — a capacity argument: every attention head’s output at row \(t\) is a convex combination of the values (softmax weights are nonnegative, sum to 1). Construct (in NumPy) a target that is not in the convex hull of the values — e.g., the token-difference signal \(v_t - v_{t-1}\) — and show (a) that no single head can produce it (search many random heads; then argue via the hull), while (b) two heads — one attending to self, one to the predecessor — combined with a signed linear mixer (\(+1\), \(-1\)) reproduce it exactly. What does this say about multi-head as expressive range, not just parallel compute?


Hint

Differences need negative coefficients; convex weights forbid them. Identity and shift matrices are perfectly realizable attention patterns (softmax of suitable logits).



Solution







One softmax per row yields weights \(a \ge 0\), \(\sum a = 1\): the head’s output rows live in the convex hull of the values — they can average tokens but never subtract them. \(v_t - v_{t-1}\) requires a coefficient of \(-1\): unreachable by any head, however trained (the 4000-head search plateaus away from 0). Two heads with a signed mixing layer reach it exactly — and both attention patterns used (identity, shift) are ordinary softmax outputs of suitable logit matrices. The general lesson: heads widen what a layer can represent (each contributes its own convex set; the mixer takes signed combinations), not just how much compute runs in parallel.

title: 10.9 Attention and Transformers
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (× 10.6 convolutions × 10.8). Three priors, one table: locality (conv), ordering-through-state (RNN), content-addressing (attention). For each of (a) 224×224 images, (b) 2k-token documents, (c) a 10⁶-step sensor stream, (d) a 20-sample clinical table — argue the best-matched inductive bias and the cost of the mismatch in both directions. Then write the two-sentence version of why modern architectures are hybrids (patch-embed + attention; conv stem + transformer; state-space models as the recurrence-attention compromise).
C2 (× Part 13 concepts × 10.4). Attention removed the relay; the transformer kept everything else from the deep-learning playbook — including 10.4‘s optimizer reality. Explain, with the specific mechanisms named, why transformers are more sensitive to learning-rate warmup than MLPs: (i) layer-norm’s gradient amplification early in training, (ii) attention logits’ softmax saturation at bad init (the \(\sqrt{d_k}\) story), (iii) residual-stream growth over depth. Then predict — and check in the Colab lab — which of the three failures (divergence, plateau, attention collapse) you see with warmup removed.

title: 10.9 Attention and Transformers
text:
7. Summary

Attention = content-addressed weighted averaging; \(\mathrm{softmax}(QK^\top/\sqrt{d_k})V\) — every position reaches every other in one hop.
Scale by \(\sqrt{d_k}\), mask before softmax (subtract −1e9), normalize over the query axis — the order is law.
Attention alone is a set operation; positional encodings inject order; sinusoidal transports, learned doesn’t extrapolate.
Multi-head = parallel reading strategies; single heads cannot hold two incompatible attention distributions.
The O(T²) score matrix is the architecture’s wall — sparse/Windows/cache engineering (Part 13) exists because of this table.
Blocks = attention (mix) + FFN (process) + residuals/LN (trainability); transformers are 10.4’s optimizer physics at scale.
You now know the machinery; the last question is judgment — 10.10 when deep learning is appropriate.

title: 11.2 Kaplan–Meier Survival Curves
text: The Kaplan–Meier estimator is the nonparametric maximum-likelihood estimate of S(t) under right-censoring: a running product of per-event survival fractions over the at-risk set. It needs no distributional assumption, handles censoring exactly, and is the first plot of every survival analysis.

title: 11.2 Kaplan–Meier Survival Curves
text:
1. Basic Concept
At each distinct event time tᵢ (with nᵢ at risk, dᵢ events):
\[\hat S(t) = \prod_{t_i \le t} \left(1 - \frac{d_i}{n_i}\right)\]
Censored subjects contribute to nᵢ up to their exit and vanish after — censoring correctly absorbed. Hand-rolled, then verified against statsmodels:






Median survival — where the curve crosses 0.5 — and Greenwood confidence bands:

title: 11.2 Kaplan–Meier Survival Curves
text:
2. Concept Questions

Why does a censored subject at time c contribute to the denominator nᵢ for events before c but not after — and which single word describes the set they belong to?
Two subjects censored at t = 5 with zero events between 4.8 and 5: does the curve drop at 5? What would make it drop at a time with zero events (and why can’t that happen in KM)?
The Greenwood SE grows with t even with constant d/n ratios — why? What does that imply about reading the curve’s right tail?
KM median vs complete-case median (11.1): state both targets and why the KM version is the honest one.
If the last observation is censored with S(t) still > 0.5, what is the KM median — and how do tools report it?



Answers


The at-risk set: subjects contribute to denominators while under observation — censoring at c removes them from all risk sets beyond c. The word: “at risk” (the counting-process frame of 11.1 Exercise 3).
No — KM only steps at event times (d > 0); censoring-only times just shrink future denominators. It cannot drop without an event: the product only loses factors at events. (A drop at a no-event time would mean the implementation confused censoring with events — bug 1 of 11.1.)
Greenwood variance accumulates d/(n(n−d)) terms: as nᵢ shrinks (attrition), the per-event terms grow even at constant ratios — the tail rests on fewer people, so relative uncertainty rises. Read the right tail with (much) wider bands, or not at all.
Complete-case median: median of observed event times — biased toward short times (11.1). KM median: the time where the estimated survival function crosses 0.5 — a consistent estimate of the population median under censoring. The KM median is the reportable one.
Undefined/never reached: the curve never crosses 0.5 within follow-up. Tools return NaN/Inf or the last S value with a “+”/“NR” annotation — report “median not reached, S(last) = …” instead of inventing a number.

title: 11.2 Kaplan–Meier Survival Curves
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Two-group KM with log-minus-log bands: for treatment/control data (simulated with true medians 2 vs 4), plot both KM curves with ±1.96 Greenwood-SE bands on the log(−log S) scale (the standard survival-plot transform), and report both KM medians with their band-crossing times. Does the truth’s ordering sit inside the bands’ separation everywhere — where does the plot admit uncertainty (early? late?) and why?


Solution







Bands widen with t (attrition, Greenwood’s accumulating terms): the curves separate cleanly early (small SE) while the late-time ordering is statistically soft. Reporting rule follows automatically: claims about medians/late survival carry the bands; claims about early separation can be stronger.

Exercise 2. KM is the nonparametric MLE — feel it via the discrete toy: for 4 subjects with times {1, 2, 3, 4} and statuses {1, 1, 0, 1}, write the KM likelihood as a product of per-interval multinomial terms; show by hand that maximizing it gives \(\hat S(1) = 3/4, \hat S(2) = 1/2, \hat S(3) = 1/2, \hat S(4) = 0\) — and verify with your km_curve. Which subject’s data drives which factor?


Solution

Likelihood factors: at t=1: one event among 4 at risk → (1/4)·(3/4)^{c} with censored count handled by the at-risk logic; the KM factors are (1 − 1/4), (1 − 1/3), (no factor: censored), (1 − 1/1) = 0.






Subject 3’s censoring never multiplies the likelihood — it silently reduces subject 4’s risk set (n = 1 at t = 4, so their event forces S to 0). Every KM factor is (events among at-risk), and this tiny example exhibits the estimator’s full logic: multinomial per interval, censoring absorbed into denominators, and certainty of eventual event collapsing S to zero.

Exercise 3. KM robustness audit: compare the KM curve estimated from (a) full data, (b) the same data with 30% of events randomly deleted (converted to censored), and (c) 30% of censored deleted (converted to events), against the truth (known exponential). Which corruption biases S(t) downward, which upward, and what does this say about the directional risks of bad status data? Then write the data-ingestion check that catches each.


Solution







Deleting events raises S(t) (fewer drops); converting censored to events lowers it — status errors bias in known directions. Ingestion checks: (1) status frequency against the protocol’s expected event rate; (2) KM curve against the literature’s shape for the endpoint; (3) spike audits (bursts of events at administrative dates = censoring misread as events).

title: 11.2 Kaplan–Meier Survival Curves
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Ties: KM handles tied event times exactly (d > 1 in one factor); tied event+censor at the same time conventionally puts censored after events (conservative at-risk sets) — Efron-vs-Breslow’s cousin at the estimator level.
Confidence bands vs pointwise bands: Greenwood ±1.96·SE is pointwise; simultaneous (Hall–Wellner, log-log transformed) bands are wider and are the honest overlay when you claim “the whole curve.” State which you drew.
Median not reached: report S(last t) with the “+”, the number at risk, and median follow-up (reverse KM, 11.1 Q2) — never a fabricated median.
Number at risk table under the plot is part of the figure: readers need denominators to judge tail trustworthiness.
** KM of a subgroup vs adjusting**: subgroup curves describe; they don’t adjust for other imbalances — that’s Cox’s job (11.5) with the log-rank test (11.3) as the unadjusted comparison.
Weights: survey-weighted or IP-weighted KM variants exist (SurvfuncRight accepts weights); unweighted KM on weighted samples reproduces the sample, not the population.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated KM plot has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Float-comparison status: time < true_t on floats is usually right by luck; the robust event definition is true_t <= censor with a boolean from the generative step, or an epsilon guard — but the real fix is deriving status from the data-generating fact, never from float arithmetic on outputs.
Stepping at every unique time: censored-only times multiply the curve by (1 − 0/n) = 1 here, but they corrupt the at-risk counts’ alignment and cost compute — step at event times only.
np.interp on a step function: linear interpolation invents medians between steps; walk the step curve to the first crossing (or use the step’s post-value convention).

title: 11.2 Kaplan–Meier Survival Curves
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Prove KM is the nonparametric MLE: in the discrete model where S jumps only at observed times, the likelihood of (time, status) data factorizes into per-interval terms \([S(t_i)/S(t_{i-1})]^{d_i}\cdot[S(t_i)/S(t_{i-1})]^{c_i}\cdot ...\) — show that maximizing over the jump sizes recovers \(\hat S(t_i)/\hat S(t_{i-1}) = 1 − d_i/n_i\), i.e., the KM factors. Then state what assumption about censoring within intervals the MLE argument quietly makes (censoring occurs after events at the same time).


Hint

Write the likelihood per interval with pⱼ = S(tⱼ)/S(tⱼ₋₁) as parameters; maximize (pⱼ){dⱼ}(1−pⱼ){nⱼ−dⱼ} — a binomial MLE.



Solution

Within interval j (between event times), each at-risk subject either events (prob pⱼ) or survives/censors. The likelihood contributes pⱼ{dⱼ}(1−pⱼ){nⱼ−dⱼ} — binomial with MLE p̂ⱼ = dⱼ/nⱼ — so Ŝ jumps by (1 − dⱼ/nⱼ): the KM factor. The quiet assumption: censored subjects in the interval are censored after any event at the interval’s end (their survival contributes through (1−pⱼ)^{…}); convention places events before censoring at ties, making KM the conservative choice. Verification by direct maximization:






KM = the MLE — and the censoring-tie convention is visible in its derivation, not just convention lore.

Q2. KM vs exponential MLE, a parametric cross-check: for censored exponential data, the MLE of the rate is λ̂ = events/total-time-on-test (exposed to censoring correctly!). Implement both KM(S at t = 2) and the exponential-MLE survival e^{−λ̂·2}, and compare their sampling variability across 500 datasets at n ∈ {40, 200}. Quantify the parametric estimator’s efficiency gain — and state the asymmetry in what breaks each (misspecified shape kills the exponential MLE; censoring-handling mistakes kill both).


Solution







The parametric MLE’s variance is ~30–50% lower at these n — the price of assuming the shape. When exponentiality is defensible, take the efficiency; when in doubt, KM’s assumption-freeness is the safeguard. Both estimators die from status bugs; only the exponential dies from wrong shape — that asymmetry is why KM is the default and parametric fits are cross-checks.

title: 11.2 Kaplan–Meier Survival Curves
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (KM × 1.5 resampling). Bootstrap the KM median: 1000 bootstrap resamples → the distribution of the KM median (with “not reached” handling). Report the bootstrap CI and compare against the Greenwood-log-log CI from Exercise 1’s machinery. Where do they differ at the tails, and what does the bootstrap median’s discreteness (it inherits the step grid) do to the interval’s smoothness?
C2 (KM × 0.5 splits × 9.4 clusters preview). KM per subgroup vs KM per discovered cluster: cluster patients on baseline features (K-means, k = 2) ignoring survival, then plot KM per cluster. Simulate data where one cluster genuinely has worse survival and evaluate: how often (over 200 simulations) does cluster-based KM separation appear (log-rank p < 0.05, 11.3) when the clustering was blind to survival? This is the unsupervised→survival handoff — and its multiplicity cost (12.2).

title: 11.2 Kaplan–Meier Survival Curves
text:
7. Summary

KM = Π(1 − dᵢ/nᵢ) over event times: censoring absorbed via at-risk sets, no distribution assumed.
Censored-only times never move the curve; attrition inflates Greenwood SEs — trust the tail less.
KM median = first S(t) ≤ 0.5 crossing; “not reached” is a reportable, honest outcome.
Status errors bias in known directions (lost events ↑S, fabricated events ↓S): ingestion checks are survival hygiene.
KM is the nonparametric MLE — binomial factors per interval, censoring-after-events convention built in.
Parametric MLEs gain ~30–50% variance when the shape is right — cross-checks, not defaults.
Two curves beg for a formal comparison: 11.3 The log-rank test.

title: 11.4 Hazard Functions
text: The hazard is survival analysis’ native currency: the instantaneous event rate among those still at risk. Hazard functions explain when events happen (not just whether), define the proportional-hazards assumption every Cox model makes, and connect to survival through one integral you can verify by hand.

title: 11.4 Hazard Functions
text:
1. Basic Concept
\[h(t) = \lim_{\Delta \to 0} \frac{P(t \le T < t + \Delta \mid T \ge t)}{\Delta}, \qquad S(t) = \exp\Big(-\int_0^t h(u)\,du\Big) = e^{-H(t)}\]
with H(t) the cumulative hazard. The exponential distribution has constant h(t) = λ; the Weibull has h(t) = λρt^{ρ−1} — increasing (ρ > 1, wear-out) or decreasing (ρ < 1, infant mortality):






Nelson–Aalen — the nonparametric cumulative hazard estimator, built from the same risk table as KM:
\[\hat H(t) = \sum_{t_i \le t} \frac{d_i}{n_i}\]

title: 11.4 Hazard Functions
text:
2. Concept Questions

Interpret h(t) = 0.02/month in plain clinical language — including the conditioning that makes it a rate among the still-alive.
Why is the hazard not a probability, and what wrong statement does “2% of patients fail at month 6” make?
Derive S(t) = exp(−H(t)) from the definitions — and state what the identity lets you read off a Nelson–Aalen plot.
Two KM curves that never cross but diverge steadily: what does that suggest about the hazard ratio over time (name the assumption this supports)?
A decreasing hazard (Weibull ρ < 1) — give a real population where it’s true, and one modeling consequence for early follow-up.



Answers


“Among patients who have survived to month t, the rate of events in the next instant is about 2% per month” — the denominator is the still-at-risk, which is what makes hazards the natural conditional language of risk over time.
It’s a rate (events per unit time per person), bounded by [0, ∞), not [0, 1] — hazards above 1 per unit time are meaningful. “2% fail at month 6” confuses the instantaneous conditional rate with the interval probability P(t ≤ T < t+1 | T ≥ t) ≈ h(t)·1 only for small h.
dS/dt = −h(t)S(t) (hazard = density conditional on survival: h = f/S). Solve the ODE: d(log S)/dt = −h ⇒ log S(t) = −∫₀ᵗ h = −H(t). On a Nelson–Aalen plot, exp(−H(t)) is the smoothed KM — so the H plot is a variance-stabilized survival curve.
Non-crossing, diverging KM curves suggest the hazard ratio is roughly constant — the proportional-hazards assumption that the Cox model (11.5) assumes and that log-rank (11.3) is most powerful for.
Decreasing hazard: post-surgical patients (risk highest immediately post-op, declining after surviving the early window) or organ-transplant recipients; modeling consequence: early follow-up dominates — an exponential (constant-hazard) fit badly misestimates early risk, and studies with short follow-up overstate long-run safety.

title: 11.4 Hazard Functions
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Hazard from data, three ways: for a simulated Weibull(ρ = 1.5, λ = 0.7) sample with censoring, estimate h(t) by (a) the empirical bin estimator (events/at-risk per bin), (b) the smoothed derivative of Nelson–Aalen, and (c) the theoretical curve. Plot all three. Which estimator is noisiest at the right tail, and why does bin width trade bias for variance exactly like histogram bins (6.2, 0.4 Exercise 2)?


Solution







Right-tail bins have few at-risk subjects — huge variance (some empty → zero estimates). Narrow bins: low bias, wild variance; wide bins: stable but smear the hazard’s shape — the bias–variance dial in histogram clothing, and the reason smooth hazard models (Weibull fits, splines in 6.4) exist.

Exercise 2. The PH litmus test, visual: simulate two groups whose hazards are proportional (h₂ = 1.8·h₁, both Weibull ρ = 1.2) and fit KM curves; then simulate non-proportional data (h₂ = h₁ for t < 1, then 2.5·h₁). For both, plot (a) the KM curves and (b) the Nelson–Aalen curves on the log scale (log(−log S)). Under PH the log-minus-log curves are parallel; under non-PH they converge/cross. Write the reading rule you’d teach: what plot, what feature, what conclusion.


Solution







Reading rule: plot KM curves transformed as log(−log S(t)) vs log t — under proportional hazards the curves are parallel shifted lines; converging, crossing, or fanning curves declare non-proportionality, and the time where they move tells you when the effect changes. This single plot is the standard visual PH diagnostic that precedes (and complements) Schoenfeld-residual tests (11.5).

Exercise 3. From hazard ratio to survival difference — the translation table: for two exponential groups (λ₁ = 0.4, λ₂ = 0.2, HR = 0.5), compute S(t) at t ∈ {1, 2, 5, 10} for both, the risk difference S₂ − S₁, and the hazard ratio — note the HR is constant while the survival difference swells then shrinks. Then answer: a paper reports “HR = 0.5, p < 0.001.” What two survival-scale quantities would you compute to judge clinical magnitude, and why does the constant HR not mean a constant benefit?


Solution







Two survival-scale quantities: (1) the risk difference S₂(t) − S₁(t) at a decision-relevant horizon (peaks at t = 1/λ₁ + 1/λ₂-ish, here ≈ 3.3 — then shrinks as both approach 0); (2) the restricted mean survival time difference (∫₀^τ ΔS) — “extra event-free months within 5 years.” The constant HR is a statement about instantaneous rate ratios; its absolute benefit translates through baselines — HR 0.5 from S = 0.99 vs S = 0.80 is a different clinical world than from S = 0.3 vs 0.15. Translation is always through the baseline hazard, which is exactly why Cox models leave it unspecified (11.5) and why reporting needs survival curves, not hazard ratios alone.

title: 11.4 Hazard Functions
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Hazard ratios vs risk ratios: HR compares instantaneous rates (can exceed 1 as values); RR compares cumulative risks (bounded by 1) — conflating them in abstracts is a published-paper genre.
Baseline hazard unspecified in Cox: HR statements are relative-only; absolute risk predictions need the baseline hazard (or parametric hazards — AFT models, 11.6’s neighborhood).
Non-PH in one covariate: solutions include time-varying coefficients, splitting follow-up at the divergence time, RMST comparisons, or strata — never “the Cox model anyway, it’s robust.”
Nelson–Aalen vs −log KM: NA estimates H directly (unbiased-ish, stable when S → 0); −log KM explodes as S → 0. NA is the plotting-safe cumulative hazard.
Hazard modeling on aggregated data (rates per bin, Poisson GLM with offset — 3.6) is a legitimate classical alternative: piecewise-exponential models ≈ flexible hazards via the GLM machinery you already own.
Attribution: “the hazard increased after discharge” — hazards shift with population composition (frail subjects already removed by earlier events): frailty makes population hazards decline even when individual hazards rise. Individual ≠ population hazards — the deepest trap in this chapter.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated hazard analysis has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Wrong denominator: hazard divides by the at-risk count at that time — using total n ignores attrition and steadily underestimates h(t) as subjects exit.
S = 1 − H: only valid for tiny H; the exact relation is S = exp(−H). For H > 1 it even returns negative “survival.”
HR is a ratio: differences of hazards aren’t hazard ratios — and neither should be averaged over bins with different at-risk compositions. Compute per-time ratios or fit the model.

title: 11.4 Hazard Functions
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Derive S(t) = exp(−∫h): start from h(t) = f(t)/S(t) with f = −S′, form the ODE S′(t) = −h(t)S(t), and solve with S(0) = 1. Then verify numerically on Weibull data: estimate S(t) by KM, compute −log KM, and overlay the true H(t) = (λt)^ρ — the identity is the reason Nelson–Aalen and KM agree to first order but differ in variance (11.2’s NA remark, resolved).


Hint

Separable first-order ODE; boundary at t = 0 fixes the constant.



Solution

S′ = −hS ⇒ d(log S)/dt = −h ⇒ log S(t) = −∫₀ᵗ h(u)du + const, with S(0) = 1 forcing const = 0. Verification:






The two estimators track each other closely (NA slightly above −log KM asymptotically — Jensen/tilt differences in the tail) and both approach the true cumulative hazard: the identity is the chapter’s connective tissue between “rate” and “survival” languages.

Q2. Frailty: population vs individual hazards — the sim­ulation that explains declining population curves: simulate 5,000 subjects with individual constant hazards λᵢ = λ·exp(frailtyᵢ) (frailty ~ N(0, σ²), σ = 0.8). Each individual’s hazard never changes, yet estimate the population hazard by bins and observe it decline over time (frail individuals exit first — selected population). Measure the decline, and explain why this selection mechanism is (a) the reason population KM curves flatten, and (b) exactly the heterogeneity that frailty models and 11.6 risk scores attempt to capture.


Solution







The population hazard falls by 2–3× over follow-up purely because high-λ subjects exit early, leaving a progressively hardier risk set. Consequences: (a) constant-hazard claims from population curves are systematically wrong; (b) unmodeled heterogeneity makes all effects appear to fade with time (frailty selection); (c) covariates that capture frailty restore near-constant conditional hazards — which is precisely the Cox model’s job (11.5) and the reason risk scores (11.6) exist.

title: 11.4 Hazard Functions
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (hazards × 6.4 splines × 3.6 Poisson GLM). Piecewise-exponential hazard model via Poisson GLM: split follow-up into time intervals (0–1, 1–2, 2–5 years), build one row per subject-interval with (events, offset = log exposure), and fit a Poisson GLM with interval + covariates. Verify it recovers a Weibull-like declining hazard on simulated Weibull data, and compare against the Nelson–Aalen curve. This is the classical “flexible hazard via GLM” — connect its intervals to 6.2’s step basis and its spline extension to smooth hazards.
C2 (hazards × 11.2 KM × 8.4 kernels preview). Smooth hazard estimation as kernel smoothing: estimate h(t) by a Nadaraya–Watson-style smoother over (event times, d/n) points with an RBF kernel and bandwidth chosen by eye/CV, on censored Weibull data. Compare against the binned estimator and the true curve as n grows. Kernel smoothing here previews both the bias–variance bandwidth story (6.6) and the “smooth estimators from rough counts” pattern used in survival ML (11.6).

title: 11.4 Hazard Functions
text:
7. Summary

h(t) = instantaneous rate among survivors; S(t) = exp(−H(t)); H(t) = −log S(t) — the rate/translation dictionary.
Weibull ρ tells the shape story: < 1 infant mortality, = 1 constant, > 1 wear-out.
Nelson–Aalen estimates H from the risk table; bin estimators of h trade bias vs variance like all histograms.
Constant HR ≠ constant absolute benefit: translate through baseline hazards, report risk differences and RMST.
Population hazards decline under unmodeled heterogeneity (frailty selection) even when individual hazards don’t — adjust or be misled.
Non-PH shows up as non-parallel log-minus-log curves — the visual diagnostic before any Cox fit.
Hazards in hand, the model that regresses them on covariates: 11.5 Cox proportional hazards regression.

title: 12.1 Hypothesis-Test Review
text: Before controlling the error rates of many tests (12.2–12.4), the machinery of one test must be exact machinery: null distribution, test statistic, α, p-value, power. This review page rebuilds the single-test engine by simulation — the calibration habits that Part 12 will stress-test at scale.

title: 12.1 Hypothesis-Test Review
text:
1. Basic Concept
One test’s anatomy, in the form Part 12 needs:

H₀ — the no-effect model that generates the null distribution of the statistic.
Test statistic T — a number measuring departure from H₀ (t, χ², |correlation|…).
α — the pre-registered false-positive rate if H₀ is true: P(reject | H₀) = α.
p-value — P(statistic at least this extreme | H₀); uniform under H₀.
Power — P(reject | H₁): depends on effect size, n, α (1.4).

The p-value’s defining property, verified — uniform under the null:






The anatomy assembled — one test, all four quantities:

title: 12.1 Hypothesis-Test Review
text:
2. Concept Questions

Why is the p-value’s null-uniformity the load-bearing fact for every multiple-testing procedure in Part 12?
α is chosen before the test. What exactly is being controlled — and what does a p = 0.03 not tell you?
Power depends on four quantities. Name them and their directions, then state which one Part 12’s corrections will deliberately sacrifice.
A one-sided test at α = 0.05 vs a two-sided at α = 0.05: which has more power in its declared direction, and what does the two-sided test protect against?
Why does the t-test’s null distribution depend on n (df = 2n − 2), and what replaces the t-distribution in the permutation-based tests of 12.5?



Answers


Every correction (Bonferroni, Holm, BH — 12.3, 12.4) works by transforming or thresholding p-values; they’re calibrated exactly because raw p-values are Uniform(0,1) under their nulls. Break uniformity (dependent tests, wrong model) and the corrections miscalibrate.
The long-run frequency of false rejections when H₀ is true — a property of the procedure. p = 0.03 does not give P(H₀ true), effect size, or replication probability (1.4’s misreading list).
Effect size (↑), n (↑), α (↑), noise σ (↓). Part 12’s corrections effectively raise the per-comparison bar — sacrificing per-test power to control family-level error.
One-sided: more power in the declared direction (all α in one tail). Two-sided: protection against surprises in either direction — and it’s what “p < 0.05” conventionally means. One-sided must be pre-registered, never chosen after seeing the data.
The t-statistic’s exact null is t-distributed only when scaling by the sample SD (estimated nuisance parameter; df = degrees of freedom consumed). Permutation tests replace the distributional reference with the empirical null from label shuffling — no distributional form at all.

title: 12.1 Hypothesis-Test Review
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Build the single-test simulator simulate_test(n, effect, alpha, reps) returning (empirical alpha, empirical power) for a two-sample t-test. Run a grid: n ∈ {20, 50, 100} × effect ∈ {0, 0.3, 0.5, 0.8}. Verify three laws: alpha stays ≈ 0.05 regardless of effect; power rises with n; power rises with effect. Then state which cell corresponds to “the standard underpowered study” (power ≈ 0.2–0.3).


Solution







α ≈ 0.05 in every row (calibration is effect-independent); power climbs along both n and effect. The underpowered classics: n = 20–50 at effect 0.3 — power ≈ 0.2–0.4, exactly the regime where Part 12’s corrections hurt most and where “p = 0.04” findings fail to replicate.

Exercise 2. The p-value misconception clinic: for the scenario “observed p = 0.03, n = 60”, simulate 20,000 replications of the same experiment and report: (a) the fraction of replications with p < 0.05 (the replication probability at α), (b) the median p of replications, (c) the fraction significant at α = 0.01. Compare each against what “p = 0.03” tempts people to believe. Write the one-sentence corrective for each of the three classic misreadings.


Solution







Correctives: (1) “p = 0.03” does not mean 97% replication chance — replication-at-α here is ~50–60%; (2) the median replication p is ≈ 0.03’s neighborhood, not 0.001 (no compounding of evidence by rerunning); (3) stricter thresholds slash replication probability — tighter α isn’t free. Each sentence pre-empts a real reviewer argument.

Exercise 3. Nonparametric vs parametric, calibration and power: on (a) normal data and (b) heavy-tailed t₂ data, compare the t-test and Mann–Whitney U (both two-sided, n = 25/group): empirical α under null, power under a shift. Report the 2×2×2 summary. Which test is calibrated in both worlds? Which has more power where its assumptions hold — and which would you pre-register for skewed biomarker data?


Solution







Both are calibrated on normal data; on heavy tails the t-test’s α inflates (CLT needs larger n) while Mann–Whitney stays calibrated (rank-based). Power: t wins on normal; U wins or ties on heavy tails. Pre-registration answer: skewed/heavy-tailed biomarker data → rank-based tests as the default, with the t-test as the normal-theory cross-check — and note that Part 12’s corrections apply to whichever p-values you feed them.

title: 12.1 Hypothesis-Test Review
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Test choice is a loss/distribution choice: t (means, normal-ish), Mann–Whitney (stochastic dominance, any shape), chi-square (proportions), log-rank (11.3) — the Part 12 corrections don’t care which, only that the p-values are valid.
One-sided requires pre-registration; two-sided is the reproducible default. Switching sides post hoc halves p-values by fiat — p-hacking’s oldest trick.
Paired vs unpaired is a design fact — pairing removes subject-level variance but only when the pairing is real (1.4 drill 4’s logic).
p = 0.049 vs 0.051 — no evidential boundary; α = 0.05 is a convention for procedure calibration, and Part 12 will move the threshold per-family anyway.
Test many → the α guarantee is per test only: this entire page’s calibration says nothing about a family of tests — the gap Part 12 exists to close.
Power analysis before data (prospective) vs after (retrospective power on nonsignificant results — near-meaningless): pre-register the former, skip the latter.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated testing snippet has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Post-hoc one-sidedness: halving p after seeing the direction is p-hacking; two-sided unless pre-registered.
“No effect” from p > 0.05 at n = 10: absence of evidence (underpowered) ≠ evidence of absence — report the CI and power.
Six outcomes at α = 0.05 each: ~26% chance of at least one “significant” under the global null — this is Part 12’s opening problem, solved with family-wise/FDR control on the family.

title: 12.1 Hypothesis-Test Review
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Derive the t-test’s calibration by simulation and by theory: show that under H₀ with pooled variance s_p², T = (x̄₁ − x̄₂)/(s_p√(2/n)) follows t_{2n−2} (Gaussian data), and verify that the empirical rejection rate at the t-quantile matches α to Monte Carlo error for n ∈ {10, 30}. Then break it: replace Gaussian with t₂ data and measure α inflation at n = 10 and n = 100 — at which n does CLT rescue the t-test, and what does that mean for small-n biomarker studies?


Hint

Under H₀ with equal variance, T = √n(x̄₁ − x̄₂)/s_p is exactly t_{2n−2} for Gaussian data; heavy tails break the variance-stability the denominator needs.



Solution







Gaussian: α matches 0.05 at both n. t₂ at n = 10: α inflates well past nominal (heavy tails break s_p’s stability); by n = 100, CLT mostly rescues it. Small-n biomarker studies with skewed/heavy-tailed readouts: the t-test’s 5% is a fiction — rank tests, transformations, or larger n (1.4 Q1’s direction, empirically grounded here).

Q2. Pre-registration as a selection firewall: simulate a lab testing 10 pre-registered hypotheses (6 with true effects of varying sizes) at α = 0.05, and estimate: family-wise false positives, expected false “discoveries,” and the false-discovery proportion among significant results. Then rerun with the lab also testing 40 post-hoc subgroups. Quantify what the post-hoc expansion does to the false-discovery proportion — and write the lab-policy sentence that would have prevented it (this is 12.2’s opening experiment, run with your own hands).


Solution







Adding 40 null searches inflates the false-significant count from ≈ 0.2 (6 pre-registered nulls × 0.05) to ≈ 2 per study — a ten-fold lie inflation from “we also looked at subgroups.” Policy sentence: “All hypotheses and analysis subgroups were pre-registered; post-hoc findings are labeled exploratory and require independent replication” — the sentence Part 12 exists to enforce.

title: 12.1 Hypothesis-Test Review
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (review × 0.5 splitting × 3.7 comparison). Model comparison as hypothesis testing: two models’ CV scores, tested by paired fold-wise t-test (3.7) — build the full simulation with known-equal models (same algorithm, different seeds) and measure the false-positive rate of “model A is better” across 500 dataset draws, at 5 folds vs 20 folds. Connect the inflated rate to fold-correlation (4.3 Q1) and state the comparison protocol your papers will use.
C2 (review × 11.x survival × 12.5 preview). The log-rank test’s p-values under non-normal censoring: simulate survival data with heavy-tailed censoring and verify the log-rank’s α calibration (it should hold — risk-set arithmetic, not parametric). Contrast with a naive t-test on censored times (it won’t). This foreshadows 12.5: permutation/rank machinery stays calibrated where parametric tests bend.

title: 12.1 Hypothesis-Test Review
text:
7. Summary

One test: H₀ → statistic → null distribution → α → p-value; calibration (uniform p under H₀) is checkable and load-bearing.
Power = effect × n × α × noise; pre-register α, direction, and design; retrospective power is noise.
p-values are procedure properties, not effect statements; replication probability ≪ naive hope.
Heavy tails break small-n parametric α; rank tests hold the line.
Per-test α is the only guarantee — families of tests are Part 12’s problem, starting now: 12.2 Why multiple testing is dangerous.

title: 12.3 Family-Wise Error Rate
text: The family-wise error rate (FWER) is P(at least one false positive in the whole family) — the strictest multiplicity guarantee: no false finding, with probability 1 − α, no matter how many tests fail. Bonferroni, Šidák, and Holm deliver it; this page implements all three, measures their power price, and shows when the price is worth paying.

title: 12.3 Family-Wise Error Rate
text:
1. Basic Concept
For m hypotheses and family level α:

Bonferroni: reject pᵢ ≤ α/m — P(any false) ≤ m·(α/m) = α by Markov/union bound. Simple, valid under any dependence.
Šidák: reject pᵢ ≤ 1 − (1 − α)^{1/m} — exact under independence (slightly less conservative).
Holm step-down: order p₍₁₎ ≤ ⋯ ≤ p₍ₘ₎; reject while p₍ᵢ₎ ≤ α/(m − i + 1); stop at the first failure. Uniformly more powerful than Bonferroni, still FWER-controlling under any dependence.







FWER calibration and power, simulated:

title: 12.3 Family-Wise Error Rate
text:
2. Concept Questions

Bonferroni’s guarantee comes from an inequality, not an exact calculation — when is it conservative (FWER < α), and give the perfectly-correlated extreme.
Why is Holm uniformly more powerful than Bonferroni, and what does “uniformly” mean here exactly?
Šidák requires independence (or positive dependence of a specific kind) — what breaks under arbitrary dependence that Bonferroni survives?
FWER control at α = 0.05 with 20,000 tests: what per-test threshold results, and what kind of effect can still pass it?
When is FWER the right guarantee at all — name two decision contexts where any false finding is unacceptable, versus a discovery context where FDR (12.4) is the better target.



Answers


Markov’s bound is tight only when p-values are near-α simultaneously (disjoint events); under perfect correlation (all p equal) the family behaves as one test — FWER = α exactly with Bonferroni rejecting at α/m… actually with all p identical, either all pass or none: FWER is 0 or α — maximally conservative on average. Conservative = real α below nominal, power thrown away.
Holm’s later thresholds are larger (α/(m−i+1) grows as small p’s consume rejections) whenever any hypothesis is rejected, and equal otherwise — so every Bonferroni rejection is also a Holm rejection, plus possibly more: “uniformly” = for every p-vector and every α.
Šidák’s exactness computes P(no false) = (1 − α/m)^m ≈ 1 − α — true only if the per-test errors are independent (or positively dependent in the Slepian sense). Under arbitrary negative dependence the product formula fails and Šidák can exceed α; Bonferroni’s inequality is dependence-free.
α/m = 0.05/20,000 = 2.5 × 10⁻⁶ — only enormous effects with tiny p-values (p ≈ 10⁻⁷–10⁻⁸, genome-wide-association territory) can clear it. Everything weaker is sacrificed: that’s the FWER bargain.
FWER fits: confirmatory clinical trials (any false claim harms patients), regulatory decisions, safety signals — “zero false findings” mandates. FDR fits: exploratory discovery screens (genomics, proteomics) where following up a few false leads is affordable and missing true leads is the costlier error.

title: 12.3 Family-Wise Error Rate
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Implement fwer_sim(m, n_true, effect, procedure, reps) measuring empirical FWER and power for the three procedures + uncorrected, under independent tests. Run m = 100, n_true = 5, effect sized to give raw power 0.3, α = 0.05. Report the 4×2 table and verify the two theoretical facts: all three corrections hold FWER ≤ 0.05, and Holm ≥ Bonferroni in power everywhere.


Solution







All corrections hold FWER ≤ 0.05 (uncorrected ≈ 0.99+); power ordering uncorrected > Holm ≥ Šidák ≥ Bonferroni, with Holm–Bonferroni gaps visible but modest. The table is the whole Part 12 trade in four rows: guarantees cost power, and better algorithms return some of it.

Exercise 2. Dependence stress-test: generate p-value vectors with controlled dependence via a common latent factor (pᵢ = 2Φ(−|√w·Z + √(1−w)·εᵢ|), w ∈ {0, 0.5, 0.95}). For each w, measure Bonferroni’s and Šidák’s empirical FWER under the global null. Verify: Bonferroni flat at ≤ 0.05 for all w; Šidák inflation grows with w. Then state the practical rule for which procedure is safe under unknown dependence (foreshadowing resampling-based FWER in 12.5).


Solution







Bonferroni: flat ≤ 0.05 at every w (union bound is dependence-blind). Šidák: nominal at w = 0, inflating toward (and past) 0.05 as the common factor concentrates the p-values. Rule: under unknown or negative dependence, Bonferroni/Holm are the safe FWER tools; Šidák’s extra power requires justified near-independence; fully general dependence calls for permutation-based FWER (12.5’s maxT).

Exercise 3. Hierarchical testing (the clinical-trials pattern): a family has one primary hypothesis and 9 secondaries. Design and implement the gatekeeper procedure: test primary at α = 0.05; only if significant, test the 9 secondaries with Bonferroni at α = 0.05/9. Simulate (a) all-null and (b) primary-true + 2 secondary-true scenarios; measure FWER of any false claim and power for the true secondaries. Compare against flat Bonferroni over all 10. When does the hierarchy win, and what does it encode about scientific priority?


Solution







The gatekeeper concentrates power: passing the primary releases α = 0.05/9 on secondaries (vs 0.05/10 flat) — and structurally forbids secondary claims when the primary fails, which flat Bonferroni permits. It wins whenever scientific priority is real (a failed primary makes secondary claims uninterpretable); its cost is the primary’s gate — a false negative up top silences everything below. The procedure encodes the trial’s epistemology.

title: 12.3 Family-Wise Error Rate
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Bonferroni on correlated tests is conservative, not invalid — FWER ≤ α regardless; the cost is power, and Šidák/Holm claw some back. The dependence failure mode belongs to Šidák and to naive “exact” resampling.
Holm ≠ “Bonferroni with smaller thresholds” only: its step-down stops at the first non-rejection — small p’s unlock larger thresholds for the rest, but a single large p halts the cascade (later hypotheses can’t be rejected even if tiny… they’d already have been tested earlier — order matters).
Weighted FWER: unequal α_i/mᵢ allocations encode prior importance (primary vs exploratory) while keeping Σ weights = α — the formal version of Exercise 3’s gatekeeper.
FWER at q = 0.05 with m = 10⁶: per-test α = 5 × 10⁻⁸ (GWAS standard) — only monumental effects survive; if your science needs lists not certainties, FWER is the wrong target (12.4).
FWER ≠ per-family “one error ever” across studies: the guarantee is within the declared family/analysis; a lab running 50 analyses has 50 families — the reporting and pre-registration discipline of 12.2 governs the meta-family.
Selective reporting of FWER-significant subfamilies re-inflates FWER: splitting the family post hoc to make Bonferroni look powerful is the same selection game in correction clothing.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated correction has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Bonferroni without the division: p ≤ α on every test is uncorrected testing. The threshold is α/m.
Holm’s step-down broken: correct is alpha/(m - i + 1) (growing thresholds) with stopping at the first failure — the buggy version uses shrinking thresholds and continues past failures (rejecting after a stop, breaking the FWER proof).
“FWER = rejections × α/m”: FWER is the probability of any false rejection — a simulation or bound, not a count times α. Estimate it by null simulation or report the guaranteed bound α.

title: 12.3 Family-Wise Error Rate
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Prove Holm controls FWER under arbitrary dependence: suppose H₍₁₎…H₍ₖ₎ are the true nulls with p-values p₍₁₎ ≤ ⋯ ≤ p₍ₖ₎ (among the true ones). Show that if any true null is rejected, then Holm must have rejected all smaller-p hypotheses first, and each step’s threshold α/(m−i+1) < α/k for i < k… conclude that rejecting a true null requires p₍ᵢ₎ ≤ α/(m − k + 1) for some i ≤ k, hence P(any true null rejected) ≤ k·α/(m−k+1) ≤ α. Where does the argument fail for Šidák’s product form?


Hint

The step-down stops at the first failure; for a true null to be rejected, every earlier (smaller-p) test must have been rejected, each under its own stricter threshold — chain the inequalities.



Solution

Order all m p-values; suppose some true null (among k true) is rejected at step i with threshold α/(m − i + 1). Since all k true nulls have p ≤ that rejected one’s p… specifically the k-th smallest true-null p satisfies p₍ₖ₎ ≤ p₍ᵢ₎ ≤ α/(m − i + 1) with i ≤ m − k + 1 (at most m − k false nulls precede it), giving p₍ₖ₎ ≤ α/(m − k + 1) ≤ α/k. Under H₀ (joint), P(min true p ≤ α/k) ≤ k·α/k = α by union bound over the k true nulls — FWER ≤ α under any dependence. Šidák’s (1−α/m)^m-form argument needs the per-test errors to multiply — i.e., independence — so arbitrary dependence breaks it while Holm’s union-bound chain survives. That’s precisely Holm’s theoretical advantage over Šidák (and the dependence-safety Bonferroni advertises).

Q2. Power-optimal FWER is a design question, not just a procedure question: with m = 100, α = 0.05, and a fixed experiment budget, compare three designs by power on the true effects: (a) split α evenly (plain Holm), (b) weighted Holm (α/2 on 1 primary, α/2 spread over 99 secondaries), (c) gatekeeper (primary at 0.05, secondaries at 0.05/99 only if primary passes). Simulate with a known primary effect and heterogeneous secondary effects; report each design’s power on primary and secondaries. Write the design principle: how should scientific priority structure the correction?


Solution







Weighted and gatekeeper designs concentrate α where prior knowledge expects effects: primary power rises several points; secondary power on true modest effects holds or improves vs even splitting (fewer hypotheses competing for the secondary α budget). Principle: the correction should encode the hypothesis hierarchy — α flows toward pre-registered priorities under a family-wise guarantee, and the flow chart is the study design (12.2’s discipline, made formal).

title: 12.3 Family-Wise Error Rate
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (FWER × 7.4 forest importances × 9.6). FWER for importance lists: on null data, compute permutation importances for 40 features 200 times; build each feature’s null importance distribution; then apply Holm across the 40 features to a new forest’s importances (z-scored against the null). Report how many features pass FWER-corrected significance on pure noise (should be ~0) and with a planted signal (should be the planted ones). This gives tree-based feature selection a multiplicity guarantee — implement and defend the family definition.
C2 (FWER × 11.3 subgroup log-ranks × 9.x clustering subgroups). The subgroup galaxy: one survival trial, 24 subgroup log-rank tests (biomarker × site × age bands), all null; measure FWER of uncorrected subgroup testing, Bonferroni, and Holm. Then design the “overall-first, subgroup-second, FWER-within” cascade and verify its FWER and its power under a true subgroup effect. Write the clinical-trials-style reporting paragraph for the cascade — with the pre-specification language that makes it credible.

title: 12.3 Family-Wise Error Rate
text:
7. Summary

FWER = P(any false finding in the family); Bonferroni/Šidák/Holm deliver it — Bonferroni/Holm under any dependence.
Holm ≥ Bonferroni in power always (growing thresholds, step-down stop); Šidák adds power only under justified near-independence.
The price: per-test thresholds like 2.5 × 10⁻⁶ at m = 20,000 — FWER suits confirmatory contexts where any false claim is unacceptable.
Hierarchical/weighted/gatekeeper procedures encode scientific priority while preserving the guarantee.
Dependence stress-tests belong in the workflow: Bonferroni flat, Šidák inflation — resampling FWER (12.5) for the general case.
Discovery screens need lists, not certainty: the FDR re-framing — 12.4 False discovery rate.
