The biological thread, made explicit. The course’s running theme — biological data — has a natural LLM layer: protein language models (ESM-2) treat amino-acid sequences as a language, pretrained on ~65M sequences, and learn the same way 13.3 describes — next-token (next-residue) prediction. The applications mirror the text ones: variant effect prediction (does this mutation break the protein? — a classification head on the LM’s embeddings, 3.4’s generative story), protein design (sampling from the LM), and function annotation (zero-shot classification from sequence alone). The statistics you now own — multiple testing for genomics (12.x), survival for censored outcomes (11.x), honest evaluation (13.7) — is exactly what those applications need to be believed.
The decision procedure (the course in one flow):

Is the structure in the data or in the language? Tables → 7.x trees/boosting; images/sequences → 10.x deep nets; text → LLMs.
Is the knowledge in the model or in your documents? In the model → prompt it. In your documents → RAG. In your data’s style → LoRA.
What does failure cost? Low → use it directly. High → ground it (RAG), verify it (tools), route it (confidence), monitor it (13.7).
What would change your mind? Pre-register the eval before looking (12.3, 13.7).

Worked example — the cost of a real workflow, computed: a literature-triage pipeline over 10,000 papers.






The speedup is real and large; the catch is the 13.7 lesson — the auto-dropped 80% are dropped on the model’s judgment, and the errors are concentrated in the tail (the papers that look irrelevant but aren’t). The honest deployment: sample the dropped papers for audit, and measure the triage’s recall on a labeled subset before trusting it.

title: 13.8 Applications and Next Steps
text:
2. Concept Questions

The decision procedure’s first question is “structure in the data or in the language?” For a clinical-notes dataset (free text + structured fields), which parts go to which tool, and what is the interface between them?
Protein LMs and text LMs share the 13.3 recipe. What is the “vocabulary” of a protein LM, why is it so much smaller than a text tokenizer’s, and what does that imply for the model’s context length in residues?
The triage example’s 20% review rate is a design choice. What does the optimal rate depend on, and how would you find it? (Frame it as the 4.6 tuning problem it is.)
“The model is a junior colleague, not an oracle.” Map each half of that metaphor to a specific practice from the course (two for “junior colleague,” two for “not an oracle”).
What is the single most important habit from the first twelve parts that an LLM user must keep, and why is it most at risk exactly when the model is most fluent?



Answers


The structured fields (labs, diagnoses, dates) go to the classical stack — a database, then 7.x models or 11.x survival models for prediction; the free text goes to the LLM for extraction (text → structured fields) and grounded Q&A (RAG over the corpus). The interface is the schema: the LLM’s structured output becomes the database’s input, and the classical models consume the database. Neither tool does the other’s job well — the art is the seam.
The vocabulary is the 20 amino acids (+ a few special tokens) — ~22 tokens vs a text tokenizer’s 32k–128k. Sequences are short (hundreds to ~2000 residues), so the context window is a non-issue — a protein LM can see an entire protein in one pass. The small vocabulary also means the model spends its capacity on structure (which residues co-occur, which are conserved) rather than on a large lexical inventory — the same objective, a very different language.
The optimal rate is a cost–risk trade-off: review more when the cost of a missed relevant paper is high (a systematic review for guidelines) and the review is cheap; review less when the volume is overwhelming and the cost of a miss is low (a first-pass scan). Find it like any 4.6 hyperparameter: sweep the rate on a labeled dev set, plot the recall–cost curve, pick the knee for your risk tolerance. The metric is recall on the relevant class — the 3.1.5 lesson: for a rare-but-important class, accuracy is the wrong objective.
Junior colleague: it can draft, summarize, and code — but you review its work (human-in-the-loop); it has broad but shallow knowledge — you supply the domain context (RAG, your data). Not an oracle: it hallucinates fluently (13.7) — you verify its claims against sources; it has no persistent memory or accountability — you own the decision and the audit trail.
Verify against held-out data. The model’s fluency is the most dangerous property in the course: it makes unverified output feel correct, and the feeling scales with the model’s quality. Every statistical habit — split before you look, stratify the eval, pre-register the primary metric, distrust the winner — exists because humans are bad at self-auditing, and the LLM is a fluent generator of things to self-audit. The habit is most at risk exactly when the model is most fluent, because fluency is the strongest possible “looks right” signal.

title: 13.8 Applications and Next Steps
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Build the triage eval: simulate 10,000 papers with 500 relevant, an LLM ranker with a known recall–rank curve, and compute (a) the recall at each review rate, (b) the precision of the review queue (what fraction of flagged papers are relevant — the number that determines whether reviewers trust the tool), (c) the 3.1.5 AUPRC of the ranker. State which of the three numbers you’d report to a hospital’s review board and why.


Solution








Recall rises with the review rate — more review, more catches. (b) Queue precision falls — the first 5% of the queue is nearly pure relevant papers; by 50% it’s diluted. The precision is the number that determines whether reviewers trust the tool: a queue that’s 90% relevant feels useful; one that’s 30% feels like noise. (c) AUPRC summarizes the whole curve (0.5 = random here). Report to the review board: recall at the chosen operating rate (did we catch the relevant papers?) and queue precision (is the review queue worth a human’s time?) — the two numbers that together determine the workflow’s value, with AUPRC as the single summary for comparing rankers. The 3.1.5 lesson: for a rare class, the precision–recall view is the honest one.


Exercise 2. The protein-LM connection: ESM-2’s vocabulary is 22 tokens; a sequence of length \(L\) is \(L\) tokens. Compute: (a) the embedding matrix size for a 650M-param protein LM (most of the parameters are the FFN, 13.4) — how does the tiny vocabulary change the parameter distribution vs a text LM? (b) The context window in residues: a 1024-token window covers how many average proteins (≈350 residues)? (c) Why does the small vocabulary mean the model’s capacity goes to structure rather than lexicon?


Solution








The embedding matrix is 22 × 1280 ≈ 28k parameters — 0.004% of the model. In a text LM the embeddings are a real fraction (13.4 drill 4); here they’re nothing, so essentially all the capacity is in the transformer layers. (b) A 1024-token window covers ~3 average proteins — the whole-structure-in-one-pass property. (c) The model can’t spend parameters on a lexicon (there are only 22 words), so every parameter learns structure: which residues co-occur, which positions are conserved, which folds are possible. The 13.3 compression argument applied to proteins: to predict the next residue well, the model must internalize the statistical structure of protein sequence space — which is why a protein LM’s embeddings are good features for variant-effect prediction (the 3.4 generative-classifier story: the LM is a model of the protein distribution).


Exercise 3. The course in one experiment: you have a clinical dataset — 2,000 patient notes (free text) + structured labs + a censored survival outcome. Design the full pipeline using at least four parts of the course, naming the specific technique from each part and the seam between them. Then state the single most likely failure point and the check that would catch it.


Solution

Pipeline: (1) LLM extraction (13.6): the notes → structured fields (diagnoses, medications) via a schema-constrained prompt — the text/database seam from drill 3. (2) Classical prediction (11.5): the structured fields + labs → a Cox model for the censored outcome (or 7.5 gradient boosting if the interactions matter more than the hazard ratios). (3) Honest evaluation (4.3, 13.7): patient-level splits (never note-level — the same patient’s notes must not straddle train/test), time-based validation (train on earlier patients, test on later — deployment is always in the future), and a pre-registered primary metric. (4) Multiple-testing discipline (12.4): if the pipeline screens many biomarkers from the extracted fields, the FDR correction applies to the screening. The most likely failure point: the extraction step’s errors propagate silently — a mis-extracted medication becomes a wrong feature, and the downstream model is confidently wrong on exactly the patients whose notes were ambiguous. The check: audit a random sample of extractions against the source notes (the 13.7 habit — measure the system’s error, not the model’s), and report the end-to-end outcome conditioned on extraction quality. The general principle: a pipeline is only as good as its noisiest stage, and the noisiest stage is usually the one that “looks like” language.

title: 13.8 Applications and Next Steps
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

The hype cycle is a selection effect. The applications you hear about are the ones that worked and got written up — the 12.2 winner’s curse at the level of the field’s anecdotes. For every demo, ask: what’s the eval, what’s the tail, what’s the cost of a miss?
Automation bias is the human failure mode: people over-trust fluent system output and under-trust their own correct instincts. The mitigation is structural (verification steps, audit sampling, keeping a human in the loop for high-stakes decisions), not willpower.
The model is a component, not a product. Every successful application is a system: model + data + verification + monitoring + human oversight. The model is the most visible and least sufficient part.
Costs are lumpy and non-obvious: API costs scale with tokens (the triage example), local costs scale with hardware and electricity (13.5), and the human cost of reviewing output is often the largest line item — and the one nobody budgets.
The field moves; the principles don’t. The specific models, benchmarks, and leaderboards of 2026 will be obsolete; the decision procedure (structure → tool, knowledge → RAG/LoRA, failure cost → verification, pre-registration → honesty) is the durable part. Learn the principles deeply and the tools shallowly — the tools you can look up.
Your data is the moat. A model is a commodity (the field’s models converge, 13.4); your documents, your schemas, your domain knowledge, and your eval are the defensible assets. Invest accordingly.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated project plan has three flaws. Diagnose before running the fixed version.

“We’ll fine-tune GPT-4 on our 500 clinical notes to predict 30-day readmission, evaluate on a random 80/20 split, and deploy if accuracy is above 85%. The model’s fluency will also let it summarize the notes for the doctors.”



What’s wrong, and the fix


Random split on patient data: notes from the same patient (or the same time period) straddle train/test — the 4.3 leakage that inflates every metric. Split by patient, and by time (train on the past, test on the future).
Accuracy on an imbalanced outcome: 30-day readmission is ~10–15% — an 85% accuracy bar is met by predicting “no readmission” for everyone. The metric must be recall/AUPRC on the positive class (3.1.5) with a clinically meaningful operating threshold.
“Fluency” as a requirement for the summary task: the summary is a clinical artifact — a fluent hallucination is worse than a terse correct one. The summary task needs its own eval (factuality against the source note) and is a separate workstream from the prediction task; bundling them means neither gets the verification it needs.

Refactor: patient-level and time-based splits; AUPRC + recall at a pre-registered threshold as the primary metric; a baseline (logistic regression on the structured fields — 3.3) that the LLM pipeline must beat to justify its cost; the summary task scoped separately with a factuality audit. The discipline: every claim in the plan gets an eval, a baseline, and a leakage check before a single GPU-hour is spent.

title: 13.8 Applications and Next Steps
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. The endgame of the decision procedure: as models get cheaper and more capable, the optimal boundary between “classical model” and “LLM” shifts. Model it: let the classical model’s cost be \(C_c\) (fixed, cheap) with accuracy \(A_c\), and the LLM’s cost be \(C_l\) (per-query, falling over time) with accuracy \(A_l > A_c\). The LLM’s accuracy advantage is task-dependent — it’s large for language-shaped tasks and ~zero for tabular ones. Compute the break-even query volume where the LLM’s total cost (including the 13.7 verification overhead) beats the classical model’s, and state how the boundary moves as \(C_l\) falls.


Hint

The break-even is where (cost per query) × (queries) + (verification cost) equal — with the accuracy advantage as the benefit side.



Solution







The break-even is per-query, not a volume threshold: if the LLM’s net value per query (accuracy advantage × value − cost − verification) is positive, it wins at any volume; if negative, at none. As \(C_l\) falls (models get cheaper), the per-query advantage rises and the boundary moves toward the LLM — but the verification term is the floor: it’s the 13.7 cost of the model’s structural hallucination, and it doesn’t fall with the model’s price. The durable boundary: tasks where the accuracy advantage is real (language-shaped) and the verification is cheap (low-stakes, high-volume) move to the LLM; tasks where the advantage is ~zero (tabular) or the verification is expensive (high-stakes) stay classical — regardless of how cheap the LLM gets.

Q2. The course’s final synthesis: take the four most important ideas from the course — one from statistics, one from classical ML, one from deep learning, one from LLMs — and state how each one changes what you do on Monday morning in a data-driven biology lab. Then state the one idea that, if you remember nothing else, prevents the most errors.


Hint

The ideas should be practices, not facts: things you do, not things you know.



Solution


Statistics (12.3): pre-register the primary analysis and correct for the number of tests you run — the habit that separates a finding from a fishing expedition. On Monday: when the screen comes back with 20,000 p-values, the FDR correction is the difference between a paper and a retraction.
Classical ML (4.3): every preprocessing step lives inside the CV fold, and the split respects the data’s structure (patient, not sample; past, not future). On Monday: the pipeline is a Pipeline object, and the split is by patient — the two lines of code that prevent the most common irreproducible result.
Deep learning (10.4): you can derive and verify any gradient by hand and finite differences — no black boxes, no “the library said so.” On Monday: when the model misbehaves, you check the gradient before you check the hyperparameters.
LLMs (13.7): evaluate on your data, stratify the tail, and verify the output — the model is a fluent probability machine, not an oracle. On Monday: the LLM’s answer is the input to your verification, never the conclusion.

The one idea that prevents the most errors: verify against held-out data you didn’t touch. It is the common root of every statistical habit in the course — the split, the fold, the pre-registration, the contamination check, the audit sample. Every way this course has found to be wrong (leakage, selection, contamination, the winner’s curse, hallucination) is a version of the same failure: letting the answer influence the evaluation. The habit is one sentence — decide how you’ll judge before you see the result — and it is the whole course.

title: 13.8 Applications and Next Steps
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (applications × 12.6 differential expression × 13.6). A genomics core facility wants to add an LLM to its analysis pipeline: researchers will ask it to interpret DESeq2 results (“what do these 200 significant genes mean?”). Design the system: the LLM gets the results table + RAG over pathway databases + a schema for structured output. State the three places the pipeline can silently produce a wrong biological conclusion, and the check at each. This is the course’s bioinformatics thread and its LLM thread, joined.
C2 (applications × 11.5 Cox × 13.7 × 13.8). The final exam, in one question: a hospital’s LLM-based triage tool has been running for a year. Its monthly eval (200 fresh questions) shows 94% accuracy, stable. Using 11.5’s framing, define the “failure event” and the covariates that predict it; using 13.7, state why the stable 94% might be hiding a rising hazard; using this page’s decision procedure, state the monitoring and update policy. The answer is a design, not a number.

title: 13.8 Applications and Next Steps
text:
7. Summary

Choose the tool by where the structure lives: tables → classical, perception → deep nets, language → LLMs; the seam is the schema.
Knowledge in the model → prompt; in your documents → RAG; in your data’s style → LoRA; failure cost high → ground, verify, route, monitor.
Protein LMs are the course’s bioinformatics thread made explicit: next-residue prediction, tiny vocabulary, capacity spent on structure — and the same statistics applies.
The triage workflow: speedup is real, the tail is the risk — audit the auto-dropped, measure recall on a labeled subset.
The course in four habits: pre-register (statistics), split by structure (ML), verify gradients (DL), evaluate on your data (LLMs).
The one idea: decide how you’ll judge before you see the result — every failure in this course is a version of its opposite.
The course is the toolbox; the decision procedure is the craft. Go build something — and evaluate it like you mean it.

title: A.3 Logistic Regression: Deriving the Gradient
text: A.1 and A.2 had a closed form because the mean is linear in the parameters. Logistic regression — the workhorse of 3.3 — is the first model in this course where the MLE has no closed form, and the reason is one derivative away. This page derives the gradient and Hessian symbolically, verifies them numerically, and shows why the resulting optimization is as well-behaved as A.2’s.
crumbs: A.3 Logistic Regression: Deriving the Gradient

title: A.3 Logistic Regression: Deriving the Gradient
text:
1. Basic Concept
The model. For binary \(y_i \in \{0, 1\}\), model the probability as a sigmoid of a linear predictor:
\[p_i = P(y_i = 1 \mid x_i) = \sigma(x_i^\top \beta) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-x_i^\top \beta}}\]
The log-likelihood (Bernoulli, one observation at a time):
\[\ell(\beta) = \sum_i \big[ y_i \log p_i + (1 - y_i) \log(1 - p_i) \big]\]
The gradient, derived:






The chain rule does all the work: \(\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial \beta} = \frac{y - p}{p(1-p)} \cdot \frac{\partial p}{\partial \beta}\), and the sigmoid’s magic identity \(\sigma' = \sigma(1-\sigma)\) cancels the \(p(1-p)\) in the denominator — leaving the famously simple gradient = (target − prediction) × features. The same form as A.1’s OLS gradient (up to the link), and for the same reason: the canonical link makes the derivative telescoping.
The Hessian and convexity:






The second derivative is \(-p(1-p)x^2 \le 0\) — the log-likelihood is concave in \(\beta\), so any stationary point is the global maximum, and gradient-based methods can’t get stuck in local optima. This is the logistic regression counterpart of A.1’s convex RSS.
The numerical check — gradient and Hessian against finite differences:
crumbs: A.3 Logistic Regression: Deriving the Gradient

title: A.3 Logistic Regression: Deriving the Gradient
text:
2. Concept Questions

The gradient is \(X^\top(y - p)\). Why does this have no closed-form solution (unlike A.1’s \(X^\top X \beta = X^\top y\))? What is the structural difference?
The sigmoid identity \(\sigma' = \sigma(1-\sigma)\) is what makes the gradient simple. What would the gradient be for a probit model (normal CDF instead of sigmoid) — and why is logistic regression still the default?
The Hessian is \(-X^\top W X\) with \(W = \text{diag}(p_i(1-p_i))\). Why is this negative semidefinite, and what does the weight matrix \(W\) tell you about which observations contribute most to the curvature?
Perfect separation: the data is linearly separable, so the MLE wants \(p_i \to 1\) for the positives — which needs \(\|\beta\| \to \infty\). What happens to the gradient, the Hessian, and the optimization in this case?
The gradient’s form (target − prediction) × features appears in OLS, logistic regression, and every GLM with a canonical link. Why is this form universal, and what breaks it for non-canonical links?



Answers


The normal equations are linear in \(\beta\) because the mean \(X\beta\) is linear. Here the mean is \(\sigma(X\beta)\) — a nonlinear function of \(\beta\) — so the score equation \(X^\top(y - \sigma(X\beta)) = 0\) is a system of nonlinear equations: \(\beta\) appears inside the sigmoid, and no algebraic manipulation isolates it. The structural difference: linearity of the mean ⇔ closed form; nonlinearity ⇔ iterative solution (Newton’s method / gradient descent).
The probit gradient is \(X^\top \big(y - \Phi(X\beta)\big) \cdot \frac{\phi(X\beta)}{\Phi(X\beta)(1-\Phi(X\beta))}\) — the extra factor (the inverse Mills ratio) doesn’t cancel, so the gradient is messier and the Hessian isn’t as clean. Logistic regression keeps the simple gradient, the concave likelihood, and an interpretable link (log-odds); probit and logit give nearly identical predictions in practice, so the simpler one wins on convenience.
\(X^\top W X\) is a weighted sum of outer products \(x_i x_i^\top\) with weights \(p_i(1-p_i) \ge 0\) — a sum of positive semidefinite matrices, so it’s PSD, and its negative (the Hessian) is NSD: concavity. The weights \(p_i(1-p_i)\) are largest for observations with \(p_i \approx 0.5\) — the uncertain ones, near the decision boundary. Observations the model is already sure of (\(p_i \approx 0\) or \(1\)) contribute almost nothing to the curvature — they’re “already classified” and the optimization effectively ignores them.
As the data separates, the likelihood’s supremum is approached as \(\|\beta\| \to \infty\): the gradient never quite reaches zero (it decays exponentially), the Hessian becomes nearly singular (the weights \(p_i(1-p_i) \to 0\) for all points), and the optimization diverges — coefficients blow up, standard errors explode. This is complete separation, and it’s why 3.3 recommends regularization (ridge on \(\beta\)) as the default: the penalty keeps the coefficients finite and the Hessian well-conditioned.
The form is universal for canonical links because the score of any exponential-family GLM is \(\sum (y_i - \mu_i) x_i\) — the derivative of the log-likelihood w.r.t. the natural parameter is always (target − mean), and the chain rule through the canonical link makes the parameter-derivative exactly that. For a non-canonical link (e.g., log-link on a binomial), the chain rule leaves a residual factor — the gradient is still (target − mean) × features, but with an extra weight that depends on the link’s derivative. The canonical link is the choice that makes the algebra disappear.

title: A.3 Logistic Regression: Deriving the Gradient
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Derive the gradient for multiple features and multiple observations: with \(p_i = \sigma(x_i^\top \beta)\), show \(\nabla_\beta \ell = X^\top(y - p)\) and \(\nabla^2_\beta \ell = -X^\top W X\) with \(W = \text{diag}(p_i(1-p_i))\), using sympy on a 2-observation, 2-feature system. Then verify the Newton step \(\beta \leftarrow \beta - H^{-1} g\) converges to the MLE in a handful of iterations.


Solution







Each component is \(\sum_i (y_i - p_i) x_{ij}\) — the \(j\)-th feature’s column dotted with the residual \((y - p)\), i.e. \(\nabla_\beta \ell = X^\top(y - p)\). The Hessian follows by differentiating again: \(\frac{\partial^2 \ell}{\partial \beta_j \partial \beta_k} = -\sum_i p_i(1-p_i) x_{ij} x_{ik}\), i.e. \(-X^\top W X\). Newton’s method: \(\beta^{(t+1)} = \beta^{(t)} + (X^\top W X)^{-1} X^\top(y - p)\) — the IRLS update (iteratively reweighted least squares), which is A.1’s normal equations applied to a weighted, re-linearized problem at each step. It converges quadratically: from a reasonable start, 5–10 iterations reach machine precision.

Exercise 2. The probit contrast: derive the gradient of the probit log-likelihood \(\ell = \sum [y_i \log \Phi(x_i^\top\beta) + (1-y_i)\log(1 - \Phi(x_i^\top\beta))]\) and show it does not simplify — the extra factor is the inverse Mills ratio. Then verify numerically that logistic and probit fits on the same data give nearly identical predicted probabilities (the two links are practically interchangeable).


Solution







The probit gradient is \((y - \Phi(x\beta)) \cdot \frac{\phi(x\beta)}{\Phi(x\beta)(1-\Phi(x\beta))} \cdot x\) — the inverse Mills ratio \(\frac{\phi}{\Phi(1-\Phi)}\) stays in the gradient (it has no closed form), so every iteration needs numerical evaluation of \(\Phi\) and \(\phi\), and the Hessian is messier. The practical equivalence: fitting both on the same data and comparing predicted probabilities — the logit and probit links differ only in the tails (logit has heavier tails), so on the same data the predicted probabilities agree to within ~0.01–0.02 almost everywhere. The choice is convention and interpretability (log-odds), not accuracy.

Exercise 3. Regularized logistic regression: add the ridge penalty \(\frac{\lambda}{2}\|\beta\|^2\) to the negative log-likelihood, derive the gradient and Hessian, and show the penalty fixes the separation problem of drill 4 — the penalized MLE always exists and is finite. Then verify: fit the drill-4 separated data with increasing \(\lambda\) and watch the coefficients stabilize.


Solution







The penalized gradient is \(X^\top(y-p) - \lambda\beta\) and the penalized Hessian is \(-(X^\top W X + \lambda I)\) — the \(\lambda I\) makes it strictly negative definite, so the penalized likelihood is strictly concave with a unique finite maximum, even under separation. As \(\lambda\) grows, the coefficients shrink toward zero (the prior’s pull) — the separation blow-up is cured by the same penalty that A.4 derives for OLS. The two regularizations are one idea: the penalty is the price of a well-posed problem.

title: A.3 Logistic Regression: Deriving the Gradient
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

No closed form ≠ no theory. The concavity of the logistic log-likelihood means the optimization is globally well-behaved — the absence of a closed form is a computational inconvenience, not a statistical one. Every GLM with a canonical link shares this.
Complete separation is a data property, not a bug: it means the features perfectly predict the outcome — the MLE is at infinity, standard errors explode, and the honest report is “the data separates; the effect is at least this large” (or regularize). Firth’s penalization is the classical fix; ridge is the practical one.
The Hessian’s weights \(p_i(1-p_i)\) mean the effective sample size is smaller than \(n\): observations near 0 or 1 contribute almost nothing to the curvature — a dataset of 10,000 easy points can have the information content of a few hundred uncertain ones. This is why 3.3’s standard errors can look optimistic on easy data.
Newton = IRLS: the Newton step for logistic regression is iteratively reweighted least squares — at each iteration you solve a weighted least-squares problem (A.1) with weights \(p_i(1-p_i)\) and a working response \(x_i^\top\beta + (y_i - p_i)/(p_i(1-p_i))\). The whole of A.1 is the engine inside logistic regression’s solver.
Numerical care in the sigmoid: for very negative \(z\), \(\exp(-z)\) overflows; use the stable form \(\sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1+e^{-z}}\) for \(z \ge 0\) and \(\frac{e^z}{1+e^z}\) for \(z < 0\) (or scipy.special.expit). The same overflow kills naive log-likelihood evaluations — use logaddexp.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated logistic regression gradient has three bugs. Diagnose before running the fixed version.
# AI-generated: one gradient-ascent step for logistic regression (will not run here)
def sigmoid(z):
    return 1 / (1 + np.exp(z))                        # BUG 1

def gradient(X, y, beta):
    p = sigmoid(X @ beta)
    return X.T @ (p - y)                              # BUG 2

def fit(X, y, lr=0.1, iters=1000):
    beta = np.zeros(X.shape[1])
    for _ in range(iters):
        beta += lr * gradient(X, y, beta) / len(y)
    return beta, sigmoid(X @ beta)                    # BUG 3


What’s wrong, and the fix


Sign error in the sigmoid: np.exp(z) should be np.exp(-z) — as written, the “sigmoid” is \(\sigma(-z)\), which flips every prediction (the model learns the opposite of the data).
Gradient sign flipped: the gradient of the log-likelihood is \(X^\top(y - p)\); the code has \(X^\top(p - y)\) — the descent direction. With beta += lr * gradient, the code descends the likelihood (maximizes the loss). Either flip the sign or use -=.
The fit returns probabilities computed with the broken sigmoid — even if bugs 1–2 were fixed, the returned probabilities would be wrong. (The deeper issue: the function never checks convergence — no gradient-norm stopping criterion, so it always runs all 1000 iterations.)

# fixed
def sigmoid(z):
    return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))

def gradient(X, y, beta):
    p = sigmoid(X @ beta)
    return X.T @ (y - p)                    # ascent direction

def fit(X, y, lr=0.1, iters=1000, tol=1e-8):
    beta = np.zeros(X.shape[1])
    for _ in range(iters):
        g = gradient(X, y, beta)
        if np.linalg.norm(g) < tol:
            break
        beta += lr * g / len(y)
    return beta, sigmoid(X @ beta)

title: A.3 Logistic Regression: Deriving the Gradient
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. IRLS as Newton’s method, formally: show that the Newton update for the logistic log-likelihood, \(\beta^{(t+1)} = \beta^{(t)} - H^{-1} g\), equals the IRLS update — solve the weighted least-squares problem \(\min_\beta \sum_i w_i (z_i - x_i^\top\beta)^2\) with \(w_i = p_i(1-p_i)\) and working response \(z_i = x_i^\top\beta^{(t)} + (y_i - p_i)/(p_i(1-p_i))\). Then state why IRLS converges quadratically and what can still go wrong (two things).


Hint

Substitute the Newton update into the WLS normal equations — the weights and working response are the Hessian and gradient in disguise.



Solution

The Newton update is \(\beta^{(t+1)} = \beta^{(t)} + (X^\top W X)^{-1} X^\top(y - p)\). The WLS problem with weights \(W = \text{diag}(p_i(1-p_i))\) and working response \(z_i = x_i^\top\beta^{(t)} + (y_i - p_i)/(p_i(1-p_i))\) has normal equations \(X^\top W X \beta = X^\top W z\); expanding \(X^\top W z = X^\top W X \beta^{(t)} + X^\top(y - p)\), so the WLS solution is exactly \(\beta^{(t+1)}\) — Newton = IRLS. Quadratic convergence: Newton’s method on a concave function with a Lipschitz Hessian converges quadratically near the optimum (the error squares each step). What can still go wrong: (i) separation — the Hessian is nearly singular, the Newton step overshoots, and the iteration diverges (the penalty of A.4 fixes this); (ii) bad starting points far from the optimum — Newton is only locally convergent, so a step-size damping (line search) is standard in practice. The deep point: the normal equations of A.1 are not just the OLS solution — they are the inner loop of every GLM solver.

Q2. The gradient’s geometry: the score \(X^\top(y - p) = 0\) says the residuals are orthogonal to the features — the same “no exploitable signal” condition as A.1’s normal equations. Show the parallel precisely: OLS’s condition is \(X^\top(y - X\beta) = 0\) (residuals orthogonal to features), logistic’s is \(X^\top(y - \sigma(X\beta)) = 0\) (the same, with the predicted probability in place of the linear fit). Then state what this means for the calibration of a logistic model: at the MLE, the average predicted probability equals the empirical event rate.


Hint

The intercept’s column of 1s is one of the features — its score equation is \(\sum (y_i - p_i) = 0\).



Solution

The intercept’s score equation is \(\sum_i (y_i - p_i) = 0\) — the residuals sum to zero, so \(\bar p = \bar y\): at the MLE, the model’s average predicted probability equals the observed event rate. This is the logistic model’s calibration guarantee (and it holds for any GLM with an intercept and canonical link): the fit is calibrated on the training data by construction. The parallel with OLS is exact: OLS’s intercept equation is \(\sum (y_i - \hat y_i) = 0\) (mean residual zero), logistic’s is \(\sum (y_i - p_i) = 0\) (mean probability equals event rate). Both are the “intercept absorbs the mean” property, and both are why the intercept is never penalized (A.4’s caveat) — penalizing it would break the calibration guarantee. The caveat: calibration on the training data is automatic; calibration on new data is the generalization question of 4.1.

C1 (logistic gradient × A.5 lasso × 5.3). The lasso logistic regression gradient is \(X^\top(y - p) - \lambda \cdot \text{sign}(\beta)\) — the smooth part from this page plus the subgradient from A.5. A one-layer neural network with a sigmoid output and binary cross-entropy loss is logistic regression — show that the backprop gradient \(\frac{\partial L}{\partial W} = (p - y) x^\top\) is this page’s gradient transposed, and that the “neural” and “statistical” views are the same computation. Then state what the deep-learning view adds (the layer stack, the feature learning) and what the statistical view adds (the likelihood, the standard errors, the calibration guarantee) — and why both are needed.

title: A.3 Logistic Regression: Deriving the Gradient
text:
7. Summary

Logistic regression: \(p = \sigma(x^\top\beta)\); the gradient is \(X^\top(y - p)\) — the sigmoid identity \(\sigma' = \sigma(1-\sigma)\) makes the chain rule cancel.
No closed form (the mean is nonlinear in \(\beta\)), but the Hessian \(-X^\top W X\) is negative semidefinite — concave, unique maximum, no local optima.
The Hessian’s weights \(p_i(1-p_i)\) mean uncertain points (near the boundary) carry the curvature.
Complete separation sends \(\|\beta\| \to \infty\) — the ridge penalty \(\lambda I\) restores a well-posed problem (the same fix as A.4).
Newton’s method = IRLS = weighted least squares at each iteration — A.1 is the inner loop.
At the MLE, the average predicted probability equals the event rate — calibration by construction (on the training data).
Next: A.4 Ridge regression: deriving the closed form — the penalty that makes the normal equations always solvable.

title: A.1 Normal Equations for Linear Regression
text: Every model page in this course uses \(\hat\beta = (X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top y\) — this appendix page derives it from first principles, so the formula is a conclusion rather than an incantation. The derivation is three lines of calculus; the interesting parts are the assumptions underneath and the numerical warnings on top.
crumbs: A.1 Normal Equations for Linear Regression

title: A.1 Normal Equations for Linear Regression
text:
1. Basic Concept
The least-squares problem: given \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times p}\) (design matrix, one row per observation, one column per feature, plus an intercept column of 1s) and \(y \in \mathbb{R}^n\), find \(\beta\) minimizing the residual sum of squares:
\[\text{RSS}(\beta) = (y - X\beta)^\top (y - X\beta) = \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - x_i^\top \beta)^2\]
The derivation, symbolically:






The gradient of RSS is \(-2X^\top(X\beta - y)\); setting it to zero gives the normal equations \(X^\top X \beta = X^\top y\), and when \(X^\top X\) is invertible:
\[\hat\beta = (X^\top X)^{-1} X^\top y\]
The geometric reading (the one to keep): \(\hat y = X\hat\beta\) is the orthogonal projection of \(y\) onto the column space of \(X\) — the residual \(y - \hat y\) is perpendicular to every column of \(X\), which is exactly what \(X^\top(y - X\hat\beta) = 0\) says. Least squares = closest point in the feature subspace.
The numerical check:
crumbs: A.1 Normal Equations for Linear Regression

title: A.1 Normal Equations for Linear Regression
text:
2. Concept Questions

The normal equations are \(X^\top X \beta = X^\top y\). What is the \(i\)-th row of this system, in words — what does each equation say about the residuals?
Why is \(X^\top X\) invertible if and only if \(X\) has full column rank? What does rank deficiency mean for the data (two ways it happens)?
The geometric reading says \(\hat y\) is the projection of \(y\) onto \(\text{col}(X)\). What is the projection matrix \(H = X(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top\) called, and what are its two key algebraic properties?
Why does the course recommend solve(X.T @ X, X.T @ y) over inv(X.T @ X) @ X.T @ y — what is the numerical difference?
The derivation never mentioned probability. What assumption about the data-generating process would make \(\hat\beta\) the maximum-likelihood estimate? (Forward reference: A.2.)



Answers


The \(i\)-th row says \(\sum_j (X^\top X)_{ij} \beta_j = (X^\top y)_i\) — but the meaning is in the residual form: \(X^\top(y - X\hat\beta) = 0\) says the residual vector is orthogonal to every feature column, i.e., no feature has any linear association with the residuals left. If a feature did correlate with the residual, you could reduce RSS by moving \(\beta\) along it — so the equations are the “no exploitable linear signal left” condition.
\(X^\top X\) is invertible iff its columns are linearly independent iff \(X\) has full column rank (\(p\) independent columns). Rank deficiency happens when: (i) two features are collinear (one is a linear combination of others — e.g., including both “cm” and “inches” of the same measurement), or (ii) \(n < p\) (more features than observations — the 5.6 regime, where infinitely many \(\beta\) fit perfectly).
The hat matrix (it “puts the hat on \(y\)”). Properties: idempotent (\(H^2 = H\) — projecting twice is the same as projecting once) and symmetric (\(H = H^\top\) — the projection is orthogonal). Its trace is \(p\): the “degrees of freedom” of the fit.
inv explicitly forms \((X^\top X)^{-1}\) — an \(O(p^3)\) operation that squares the condition number (the inverse of a nearly-singular matrix is numerically unstable). solve factors \(X^\top X\) (Cholesky) and solves the system directly — same answer, half the condition-number exposure. At \(p\) = 10,000 features the difference is the difference between an answer and NaN.
Gaussian noise: if \(y = X\beta + \varepsilon\) with \(\varepsilon \sim N(0, \sigma^2 I)\), the likelihood is maximized exactly when RSS is minimized — least squares is maximum likelihood under Gaussian errors. That is A.2, the next page.
crumbs: A.1 Normal Equations for Linear Regression

title: A.1 Normal Equations for Linear Regression
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Derive the normal equations for simple linear regression without matrices: minimize \(\sum (y_i - a - b x_i)^2\) over \((a, b)\) by setting both partial derivatives to zero, and show the solution is the familiar \(\hat b = \text{Cov}(x,y)/\text{Var}(x)\), \(\hat a = \bar y - \hat b \bar x\). Then verify the matrix and scalar forms agree on a random dataset.


Solution







The two equations are \(n a + b\sum x_i = \sum y_i\) and \(a\sum x_i + b\sum x_i^2 = \sum x_i y_i\). Solving: subtract \(\bar x\)×(first) from the second to get \(b = \frac{\sum(x_i - \bar x)(y_i - \bar y)}{\sum(x_i - \bar x)^2} = \text{Cov}(x,y)/\text{Var}(x)\), and \(a = \bar y - b\bar x\) — the covariance-over-variance form you know from 2.2, now derived. The matrix form with the intercept column of 1s produces exactly these two equations — the scalar and matrix derivations are the same calculus in different notation.







Exercise 2. The projection view, verified: for a random \(X\) and \(y\), compute \(\hat y = X\hat\beta\), the residual \(r = y - \hat y\), and verify (a) \(X^\top r = 0\) (orthogonality), (b) \(\hat y\) is in the column space of \(X\) (it is \(X\hat\beta\) by construction — verify it’s unchanged by re-projecting: \(H\hat y = \hat y\)), (c) the Pythagorean decomposition \(\|y\|^2 = \|\hat y\|^2 + \|r\|^2\). State why (c) is the geometric content of \(R^2\).


Solution








is the geometric \(R^2\): the total sum of squares splits into the explained (projected) and residual (orthogonal) parts — because the projection is orthogonal, the Pythagorean theorem applies, and \(R^2\) is the fraction of \(\|y\|^2\) lying in the feature subspace. This is why \(R^2\) is a geometric quantity, not just a formula: it’s the squared cosine of the angle between \(y\) and its projection.


Exercise 3. The singular case and its fix: construct \(X\) with \(n < p\) (more features than observations), show that \(X^\top X\) is singular and infinitely many solutions achieve RSS = 0, then show that adding \(\lambda I\) (ridge, A.4) makes the system solvable for any \(\lambda > 0\). State the statistical moral.


Solution







With \(n < p\) the system is underdetermined: a \(p\)-dimensional coefficient space, only \(n\) equations — a \((p-n)\)-dimensional affine space of exact solutions (all achieving RSS = 0, all overfit). Ridge’s \(\lambda I\) adds \(p\) independent equations’ worth of curvature, making \(X^\top X + \lambda I\) positive definite and the solution unique — at the cost of a nonzero RSS. The statistical moral: when the data can’t identify the model, you must supply the missing information — ridge supplies it as a prior belief (“coefficients are small”), which is A.4’s Bayesian reading. The normal equations are a identification result first and a fitting result second.
crumbs: A.1 Normal Equations for Linear Regression

title: A.1 Normal Equations for Linear Regression
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

\(X^\top X\) squares the condition number. If \(X\) has condition number \(\kappa\), \(X^\top X\) has \(\kappa^2\) — near-collinear features (the drill-4 example) make the normal equations numerically treacherous. The stable path is QR or SVD factorization of \(X\) itself (never forming \(X^\top X\)); np.linalg.lstsq does this, which is why it’s the default recommendation.
The intercept is a column of 1s — including it makes the first normal equation \(\sum r_i = 0\) (the residuals sum to zero). Forgetting the intercept forces the regression line through the origin and biases every slope.
Centering changes the conditioning, not the fit: with an intercept, the slopes are identical whether or not you center \(X\) — but the numerical problem is better conditioned when features are centered (the intercept column is orthogonal to the centered features). Same math, kinder floating point.
The normal equations are not the definition of least squares — they’re the first-order condition. RSS is convex (its Hessian \(2X^\top X\) is positive semidefinite), so the stationary point is the global minimum — but only when \(X^\top X\) is invertible is it unique. Convexity is why the derivation “just works”; invertibility is why it sometimes doesn’t.
Weighted least squares (heteroscedastic errors, 2.10): replace \(X^\top X\) with \(X^\top W X\) and \(X^\top y\) with \(X^\top W y\) for a diagonal weight matrix \(W\) — the same derivation, reweighted. The normal equations are a template, not a one-off.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated regression solver has three bugs. Diagnose before running the fixed version.
# AI-generated: least squares via the normal equations (will not run here — spot the bugs)
def fit(X, y):
    beta = np.linalg.inv(X.T @ X) @ X.T @ y     # BUG 1
    return beta

def predict(X, beta):
    return X @ beta + np.mean(y)                # BUG 2

X = np.array([[1, 1], [1, 2], [1, 3]])          # BUG 3
y = np.array([2, 3, 4])
print(fit(X, y))


What’s wrong, and the fix


Explicit inverse: inv(X.T @ X) forms the inverse — squares the condition number and is slower than solving. Use np.linalg.solve(X.T @ X, X.T @ y) (or lstsq for the rank-deficient case).
Prediction adds the mean of the training y: the model’s prediction is X @ beta — the intercept is already in \(\beta\) (via the column of 1s). Adding np.mean(y) double-counts the intercept and shifts every prediction.
The design matrix is integer-typed: np.array([[1, 1], ...]) creates an int64 array — X.T @ X is integer arithmetic, and the solve can silently truncate. Cast to float: X = np.array(..., dtype=float).

# fixed
def fit(X, y):
    X = np.asarray(X, dtype=float)
    return np.linalg.solve(X.T @ X, X.T @ y)

def predict(X, beta):
    return np.asarray(X, dtype=float) @ beta
crumbs: A.1 Normal Equations for Linear Regression

title: A.1 Normal Equations for Linear Regression
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. The normal equations as a template: derive the weighted least squares solution for heteroscedastic errors \(\text{Var}(\varepsilon_i) = \sigma^2/w_i\), showing the solution is \(\hat\beta = (X^\top W X)^{-1} X^\top W y\) with \(W = \text{diag}(w_i)\). Then show the transformation trick: WLS is OLS on the transformed data \(\tilde X = W^{1/2}X\), \(\tilde y = W^{1/2}y\) — and state why this means every OLS diagnostic (residuals, hat matrix, \(R^2\)) has a weighted version.


Hint

Multiply both sides of each equation by \(\sqrt{w_i}\) — the weights become a change of units.



Solution

With \(\text{Var}(\varepsilon) = \sigma^2 W^{-1}\), the MLE minimizes the weighted RSS \(\sum w_i (y_i - x_i^\top\beta)^2 = (y - X\beta)^\top W (y - X\beta)\). The gradient is \(-2X^\top W(X\beta - y)\); setting it to zero gives \(\hat\beta = (X^\top W X)^{-1} X^\top W y\). The transformation: let \(\tilde X = W^{1/2}X\), \(\tilde y = W^{1/2}y\) — then the weighted RSS is exactly \((\tilde y - \tilde X\beta)^\top(\tilde y - \tilde X\beta)\), the unweighted RSS of the transformed data, so the WLS solution is the OLS solution on \((\tilde X, \tilde y)\). Consequence: every OLS result transfers — the hat matrix becomes \(\tilde X(\tilde X^\top \tilde X)^{-1}\tilde X^\top\), residuals and \(R^2\) are computed on the transformed scale, and the geometry (projection, orthogonality) is unchanged because \(W^{1/2}\) is just a change of inner product. The deep point: weights are a geometry, not a correction — WLS is OLS in a space where the axes are scaled by the precision.

Q2. The normal equations in the \(n \to \infty\) limit: show that \(X^\top X / n\) converges to the feature second-moment matrix \(\Sigma = \mathbb{E}[x x^\top]\) and \(X^\top y / n\) to \(\mathbb{E}[x y]\), so the population normal equations are \(\Sigma \beta = \mathbb{E}[xy]\). Then state what this says about what least squares estimates (the best linear predictor, not the true causal effect) and connect to 2.10’s assumptions.


Hint

The law of large numbers turns sums into expectations — the normal equations become a statement about the population, not the sample.



Solution

Dividing the normal equations by \(n\): \(\frac{1}{n}X^\top X \beta = \frac{1}{n}X^\top y\). As \(n \to \infty\), \(\frac{1}{n}X^\top X \to \mathbb{E}[x x^\top] = \Sigma\) and \(\frac{1}{n}X^\top y \to \mathbb{E}[x y]\) (law of large numbers, assuming i.i.d. draws), so the population solution solves \(\Sigma \beta^* = \mathbb{E}[xy]\) — the best linear predictor of \(y\) from \(x\) in the population, minimizing \(\mathbb{E}[(y - x^\top\beta)^2]\). The crucial distinction: \(\beta^*\) is the best linear prediction rule, which equals the true causal effect only under 2.10’s assumptions (exogeneity: \(\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon | x] = 0\)). With omitted variables or reverse causality, \(\Sigma\) and \(\mathbb{E}[xy]\) are still well-defined, the normal equations still have a solution — but it estimates the projection of \(y\) onto \(x\), not the effect of \(x\) on \(y\). The normal equations are a prediction device; causality is a modeling assumption you add on top. This is the gap between 2.5’s “the coefficients” and what they mean.

title: A.1 Normal Equations for Linear Regression
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (normal equations × A.4 ridge × 5.2). The ridge solution \((X^\top X + \lambda I)^{-1}X^\top y\) is the normal equations of a modified problem — derive what problem (add \(\lambda\|\beta\|^2\) to RSS), then show the two solutions coincide in the limit \(\lambda \to 0\) (when \(X^\top X\) is invertible) and that ridge is the unique solution when \(X^\top X\) is singular. The normal equations are the fixed point of this whole family: OLS, ridge, WLS, and (via the KKT conditions) lasso (A.5) are all “solve a linear system” at heart.
C2 (normal equations × 9.2 PCA × A.6). PCA’s first component is the unit vector maximizing \(w^\top X^\top X w\) — the same matrix as the normal equations’ \(X^\top X\), but maximizing a quadratic form instead of solving a linear system. Show that the PCA solution is the top eigenvector of \(X^\top X\) while the OLS solution is \((X^\top X)^{-1}\) applied to \(X^\top y\) — then state the unifying view: both are spectral statements about the same matrix, one about its largest eigenvalue, the other about its inverse. This is the bridge from regression to dimensionality reduction.

title: A.1 Normal Equations for Linear Regression
text:
7. Summary

Least squares = minimize RSS; the gradient is \(-2X^\top(X\beta - y)\); the normal equations \(X^\top X\beta = X^\top y\) are the “no linear signal left in the residuals” condition.
\(\hat\beta = (X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top y\) when \(X\) has full column rank; the solution is the orthogonal projection of \(y\) onto the column space (the hat matrix, idempotent and symmetric).
Rank deficiency (collinearity or \(n < p\)) breaks invertibility — ridge’s \(\lambda I\) is the fix (A.4).
Use solve/lstsq, never inv — \(X^\top X\) squares the condition number.
The population limit is the best linear predictor \(\Sigma\beta = \mathbb{E}[xy]\) — prediction, not causation (2.10).

title: A.5 Why Lasso Has No Closed Form
text: A.4’s L2 penalty gave a closed form because the squared norm is smooth. The lasso’s L1 penalty — \(\lambda\|\beta\|_1 = \lambda\sum_j|\beta_j|\) — is not differentiable at zero, and that single kink is the whole story: it destroys the closed form and creates sparsity. This page derives the subgradient condition, solves the orthogonal case exactly (soft-thresholding), and shows why the kink is a feature, not a bug.
crumbs: A.5 Why Lasso Has No Closed Form

title: A.5 Why Lasso Has No Closed Form
text:
1. Basic Concept
The objective. The lasso minimizes RSS plus the sum of absolute coefficient values:
\[\hat\beta_\lambda = \arg\min_\beta \; (y - X\beta)^\top(y - X\beta) + \lambda \sum_{j=1}^p |\beta_j|\]
Why A.4’s derivation breaks: the gradient of \(|\beta_j|\) doesn’t exist at \(\beta_j = 0\). The tool is the subgradient — the set of all slopes that lie below the function:
\[\partial|\beta_j| = \begin{cases} +1 & \beta_j > 0 \\ -1 & \beta_j < 0 \\ [-1, +1] & \beta_j = 0 \end{cases}\]






The solution — soft-thresholding. Combining the three cases (the “if positive / if negative / zero” logic collapses into one formula):
\[\hat\beta_j = \text{sign}(\hat\beta_j^{\text{OLS}}) \cdot \max(|\hat\beta_j^{\text{OLS}}| - \tfrac{\lambda}{2}, \; 0)\]






Every OLS coefficient is shrunk toward zero by \(\lambda/2\) — and any coefficient whose OLS magnitude is below \(\lambda/2\) is set to exactly zero. That is the sparsity mechanism: the kink at zero creates a dead zone where small signals are annihilated rather than shrunk.
crumbs: A.5 Why Lasso Has No Closed Form

title: A.5 Why Lasso Has No Closed Form
text:
2. Concept Questions

The subgradient of \(|\beta_j|\) at zero is the interval \([-1, +1]\), not a number. Why does this interval — rather than a single slope — make the lasso solution possible at all, and what does the condition “\(0 \in \partial\)” mean geometrically?
Soft-thresholding sets small coefficients to exactly zero. What is the bias introduced (vs ridge’s smooth shrinkage), and what is the variance benefit — why does zeroing a coefficient reduce variance more than shrinking it?
The lasso’s solution path is piecewise linear in \(\lambda\) (the LARS property). Why does the kink make the path piecewise linear, and what does that enable computationally?
Why does the lasso require even more careful standardization than ridge? (Hint: the L1 penalty’s scale-dependence is worse — the dead zone is in units of the coefficients.)
The lasso can select at most \(n\) features when \(p > n\) (the 5.6 regime). Why — what is the geometric reason?



Answers


At the kink, no single line supports the function — but every slope in \([-1,1]\) does. The stationarity condition “\(0 \in \partial f(\hat\beta)\)” means: there exists a supporting line through the solution with slope zero — the function is “flat enough” at the kink to balance the data’s pull. Geometrically: the data’s gradient (\(-2x(y-x\beta)\), pulling away from zero) is exactly cancelled by some subgradient in \([-1,1]\) — the kink is wide enough to catch it. This is why the solution can sit at zero: the penalty’s flat spot is a trap for small signals.
Bias: a zeroed coefficient is biased by its full OLS value (ridge biases by a fraction). Variance: a zeroed coefficient has zero variance — it’s not estimated at all, so its sampling variability is removed entirely. The trade: lasso accepts more bias (full shrinkage to zero) for more variance reduction (elimination, not just damping) — the 4.4 trade-off at its most aggressive. When the zeroed coefficient was noise, this is pure win; when it was signal, it’s the lasso’s characteristic error.
Because the solution is piecewise linear: as \(\lambda\) decreases, each coefficient moves linearly from zero until it hits a kink (another coefficient’s entry/exit), then the path bends. The kinks are the only places the path can change direction — between kinks, the active set is fixed and the solution is the OLS solution on that set (a linear function of \(\lambda\)). LARS exploits this: it walks the path from kink to kink in \(O(p^3)\) — the whole regularization path for the cost of a few OLS fits.
The dead zone is \(|\hat\beta}^{\text{OLS}}| \le \lambda/2\) — in units of the coefficients. A feature in millimeters has coefficients 1000× smaller than in meters, so the same \(\lambda\) annihilates the millimeter feature and barely touches the meter one. Standardization puts all features in the same units so the dead zone is fair — and the L1 penalty’s scale-dependence is more dangerous than ridge’s because the consequence is annihilation (a hard zero), not just shrinkage.
With \(p > n\), the lasso’s solution is the OLS solution on the active set — and the active set has at most \(n\) members, because the fit \(\hat y = X_A\beta_A\) lives in the column space of \(X_A\), which has dimension at most \(n\) (the residual is orthogonal to \(\le n\) directions). More selected features than observations would mean a rank-deficient active set with no unique solution — the lasso’s geometry (the diamond’s corners) can’t reach those. This is why the lasso is a selector in the \(p \gg n\) regime: it picks at most \(n\), and the choice of which \(n\) is the model.

title: A.5 Why Lasso Has No Closed Form
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Derive the general (non-orthogonal) stationarity condition: for each \(j\), the lasso solution satisfies \(-2x_j^\top(y - X\beta) + \lambda s_j = 0\) where \(s_j \in \partial|\beta_j|\) — i.e. \(s_j = \text{sign}(\beta_j)\) if \(\beta_j \ne 0\), and \(|2x_j^\top(y - X\beta)| \le \lambda\) if \(\beta_j = 0\). Verify this KKT condition against coordinate descent on a random design, and state what the second case means (the “why is this coefficient zero” certificate).


Solution







The second case is the zero-certificate: a coefficient is zero exactly when the absolute correlation between its feature and the current residual is below \(\lambda/2\) — the feature isn’t correlated enough with what’s left to explain to overcome the penalty. This is the lasso’s variable-selection logic made checkable: every zero comes with a proof (the gradient is inside the dead zone), and every nonzero comes with a proof (the gradient exactly balances the penalty). The KKT conditions turn “the lasso zeroed this” from a mystery into an auditable fact.

Exercise 2. The geometry of sparsity: plot the constraint regions — the L2 ball \(\{\beta: \|\beta\|_2 \le t\}\) (a circle) and the L1 ball \(\{\beta: \|\beta\|_1 \le t\}\) (a diamond) — with a contour of RSS, and show that the constrained minimum lands on an axis for the diamond (sparsity) but on the round boundary for the circle (no sparsity). Then state the general principle: the solution is where the RSS contour first touches the constraint, and the constraint’s corners are where zeros come from.


Solution







The picture: the RSS contours are ellipses centered at the OLS solution (off-axis, since the true coefficients are nonzero). The constrained solution is the first contact point. For the round L2 ball, the contact is on the smooth boundary — both coordinates nonzero (ridge shrinks, never zeroes). For the diamond, the contact is at a corner — one coordinate exactly zero (lasso selects). The general principle: zeros come from corners — any constraint with axis-aligned corners (L1, and the L1’s generalizations) produces sparsity; any smooth constraint (L2) produces shrinkage. The geometry of the penalty is the geometry of the solution — the same lesson as A.4’s spectral view, in the coefficient space instead of the singular-value space.

Exercise 3. The lasso’s bias, measured: on a dataset with 5 true signals and 95 noise features, compare OLS, ridge, and lasso at their cross-validated \(\lambda\) — measure (a) the MSE of the coefficient estimates, (b) the selection accuracy (which features are nonzero), (c) the prediction MSE on held-out data. State the regime where lasso wins and where it loses.


Solution







Lasso wins in the sparse regime: it recovers the 5 true signals, zeroes the 95 noise features, and has the best held-out prediction MSE — the variance reduction from elimination beats the bias from zeroing. It loses when the truth is dense (many small true effects): zeroing them all introduces more bias than the variance is worth, and ridge’s smooth shrinkage is better. The rule: lasso when you believe the signal is sparse (few true features), ridge when it’s dense (many small effects) — the 5.1 selection-vs-shrinkage distinction, with the bias–variance trade-off (4.4) as the reason. Elastic net (5.4) hedges when you don’t know.

title: A.5 Why Lasso Has No Closed Form
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

The kink is the feature. Every property that makes lasso annoying (no closed form, non-unique solutions under heavy collinearity) is the same property that makes it useful (sparsity, selection). You cannot have one without the other — the non-differentiability is the selection mechanism.
Non-uniqueness under collinearity: with two identical features, any split of the coefficient between them has the same L1 norm — the lasso picks one (arbitrarily, by the solver’s path). Ridge splits evenly. If interpretability matters, this is a real caveat: “the lasso selected feature A” can mean “A and B are identical and the solver happened to pick A.”
Standardization is non-negotiable — the dead zone is in coefficient units, so unscaled features get unfairly annihilated or unfairly spared. Center and scale, always.
\(\lambda\) selection is by cross-validation (4.6) — the path (Exercise in Section 3) makes it cheap: fit the whole path, pick the \(\lambda\) with the lowest CV error. The “1-SE rule” (largest \(\lambda\) within one standard error of the minimum) gives a sparser, more stable model at nearly the same accuracy.
The lasso’s \(\lambda\) has a null-distribution interpretation: \(\lambda_{\max} = \max_j |2x_j^\top y|\) is the smallest \(\lambda\) that zeroes everything — the path always starts there. This is the lasso’s “screening” rule: features enter the path in order of their correlation with \(y\).


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated lasso solver has three bugs. Diagnose before running the fixed version.
# AI-generated: one coordinate-descent sweep for the lasso (will not run here)
def lasso_cd(X, y, lam, iters=100):
    beta = np.zeros(X.shape[1])
    for _ in range(iters):
        for j in range(X.shape[1]):
            r = y - X @ beta                    # BUG 1
            rho = X[:, j] @ r
            beta[j] = np.sign(rho) * max(abs(rho) - lam, 0) / (X[:, j] @ X[:, j])
    return beta

def standardize_lasso(X):
    return X / X.std(axis=0)                    # BUG 2

X = np.array([[1, 2], [1, 4], [1, 6]])          # BUG 3


What’s wrong, and the fix


The residual doesn’t add back the current coordinate: r = y - X @ beta excludes \(\beta_j\)’s own contribution — the coordinate update needs the partial residual \(r = y - X\beta + x_j\beta_j\) (the residual as if \(\beta_j\) were zero). As written, the update double-subtracts \(\beta_j\) and the iteration diverges.
Standardization without centering (same bug as A.4’s refactor): X / X.std() scales but doesn’t center — the dead zone is then in the wrong units and the intercept handling breaks. Center and scale.
Integer-typed design matrix (same bug as A.1 and A.4): np.array([[1, 2], ...]) is int64 — the @ products and the division silently truncate. Cast to float.

# fixed
def standardize_lasso(X):
    X = np.asarray(X, dtype=float)
    return (X - X.mean(axis=0)) / X.std(axis=0)

def lasso_cd(X, y, lam, iters=1000):
    beta = np.zeros(X.shape[1])
    for _ in range(iters):
        for j in range(X.shape[1]):
            r = y - X @ beta + X[:, j] * beta[j]      # partial residual
            rho = X[:, j] @ r
            beta[j] = np.sign(rho) * max(abs(rho) - lam, 0) / (X[:, j] @ X[:, j])
    return beta

title: A.5 Why Lasso Has No Closed Form
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. The KKT conditions as a complete characterization: prove that for the lasso, the KKT conditions (Exercise 1) are not just necessary but sufficient — any \(\beta\) satisfying them is the global solution. Then state the consequence: the lasso solution is unique when \(X\) has full column rank (and may be non-unique when it doesn’t — the collinearity caveat), and the active set’s coefficients are the OLS solution on the active set with a sign constraint.


Hint

The lasso objective is convex (RSS convex + \(\lambda\|\beta\|_1\) convex) — for convex problems, KKT is sufficient. The sign constraint comes from the subgradient’s sign matching \(\beta_j\)’s sign.



Solution

Convexity: RSS is convex in \(\beta\) (its Hessian \(2X^\top X\) is PSD) and \(\lambda\|\beta\|_1\) is convex (a norm), so the objective is convex — and for convex objectives, the KKT conditions are sufficient: any \(\beta\) with \(0 \in \partial(\text{objective})\) is a global minimizer. The sign constraint: for \(\beta_j \ne 0\), the stationarity condition forces \(s_j = \text{sign}(\beta_j)\) — the subgradient must match the coefficient’s sign, so the active coefficients are the OLS solution on the active set projected onto the correct orthant. Uniqueness: when \(X\) has full column rank, the active set’s OLS solution is unique and the orthant constraint doesn’t create alternatives — the lasso solution is unique. Under collinearity (rank-deficient active set), multiple coefficient vectors give the same fit and the same L1 norm — non-unique, and the solver picks one by its path. The practical consequence: the KKT conditions give you a verification algorithm — any claimed lasso solution can be checked in \(O(np)\) — and the non-uniqueness is exactly the “identical features” caveat of Section 4.

Q2. The lasso as a Bayesian estimator — the Laplace prior: A.4 showed ridge is the posterior mode under a Gaussian prior. Show the lasso is the posterior mode under a Laplace prior \(p(\beta_j) = \frac{1}{2b}e^{-|\beta_j|/b}\) — the log-prior is \(-\|\beta\|_1/b\), so the posterior mode minimizes \(\text{RSS} + \frac{2\sigma^2}{b}\|\beta\|_1\). Then state the deep connection: the prior’s shape determines the penalty’s shape (Gaussian → L2, Laplace → L1), and the Laplace’s sharp peak at zero is exactly what produces sparsity.


Hint

The log of the Laplace density is \(-|\beta_j|/b + \text{const}\) — the L1 penalty is the Laplace log-prior, read backwards.



Solution

With \(\beta_j \sim \text{Laplace}(0, b)\) i.i.d., the log-prior is \(-\sum_j |\beta_j|/b + \text{const}\), so the posterior mode minimizes \(\text{RSS}/(2\sigma^2) + \|\beta\|_1/b\) — the lasso objective with \(\lambda = 2\sigma^2/b\). The connection: the penalty is the negative log-prior — ridge’s L2 is the Gaussian’s log-density, lasso’s L1 is the Laplace’s. The Laplace’s sharp peak at zero (vs the Gaussian’s smooth dome) puts prior mass at zero — the prior believes coefficients are exactly zero with high probability, and the posterior mode inherits that belief as exact zeros. This is the same “loss = noise model” dictionary as A.2, now for priors: Gaussian prior → ridge, Laplace prior → lasso, and (completing the pattern) the “spike-and-slab” prior (a point mass at zero plus a diffuse component) → best-subset selection. The Bayesian view doesn’t just re-derive the penalties — it tells you which prior you’re committing to when you pick one, and the Laplace’s sharp peak is a strong belief (“most coefficients are exactly zero”) that should be a deliberate choice, not a default.

title: A.5 Why Lasso Has No Closed Form
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (lasso × A.3 logistic × 5.3). The lasso logistic regression gradient is \(X^\top(y - p) - \lambda s\) with \(s \in \partial\|\beta\|_1\) — this page’s smooth gradient plus A.5’s subgradient. Derive the coordinate-descent update for one coefficient (soft-threshold the quadratic approximation of the log-likelihood), and state why the same kink that makes lasso sparse makes its solver a coordinate-wise soft-threshold. The two derivations compose into the modern sparse-GLM solver — the workhorse of genomics (5.6’s \(p \gg n\) regime).
C2 (lasso × A.6 PCA × 9.2). The lasso’s selection and PCA’s truncation are both answers to “too many features” — but they fail differently. The lasso selects a subset (losing the others’ information); PCA keeps all features but compresses them (losing the identity of any single one). Construct a dataset where each fails and the other succeeds: (a) two correlated features where only one matters — lasso picks one (loses the shared signal), PCA keeps both directions (dilutes the signal); (b) many weak features that jointly matter — lasso zeroes most (loses the joint signal), PCA’s top components capture it. State the general principle: selection vs compression is a bet on the signal’s sparsity — and the bet is checkable with the bias–variance trade-off (4.4).

title: A.5 Why Lasso Has No Closed Form
text:
7. Summary

The L1 penalty’s kink at zero has no derivative — the subgradient \([-1, +1]\) replaces it, and the stationarity condition “\(0 \in \partial\)” is the lasso’s normal equations.
Soft-thresholding: \(\hat\beta_j = \text{sign}(\hat\beta^{\text{OLS}}_j)\max(|\hat\beta^{\text{OLS}}_j| - \lambda/2, 0)\) — shrink by \(\lambda/2\), annihilate below it. The dead zone is the sparsity mechanism.
The KKT conditions give every zero a certificate (\(|2x_j^\top r| \le \lambda\)) and every nonzero a balance — selection is auditable.
Zeros come from corners: the L1 diamond’s axis-aligned corners are where the RSS contour first touches; the L2 ball’s smooth boundary never gives exact zeros.
Lasso wins when the signal is sparse, ridge when it’s dense — the bet is checkable with held-out MSE.
The lasso is the posterior mode under a Laplace prior — the penalty is the negative log-prior, and the prior’s sharp peak at zero is the sparsity belief.
